title: Mr. VVilliam Shakespeares comedies, histories, & tragedies Published according to the true originall copies.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.

plays.play_title: THE TEMPEST.

speeches.speaker: Master.
prose: BOte-swaine.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: Heere Master: What cheere?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
prose: Good: Speake to th' Mariners: fall too't, yarely, or we run our selues a ground, bestirre, bestirre.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: Heigh my hearts, cheerely, cheerely my harts: yare, yare: Take in the toppe-sale: Tend to th' Masters whistle: Blow till thou burst thy winde, if roome enough.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
prose: Good Boteswain^ haue care: where's the Master? Play the men.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: I pray now keepe below.

speeches.speaker: Auth.
prose: Where is the Master, Boson?

speeches.speaker: Botes.
verse: Do you not heare him? you marre our labour,
Keepe your Cabines: you do assist the storme.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
prose: Nay, good be patient.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: When the Sea is: hence, what cares these roarers for the name of King? to Cabine; silence: trouble vs not.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Good, yet remember whom thou hast aboord.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: None that I more loue then my selfe. You are a Counsellor, if you can command these Elements to silence, and worke the peace of the present, wee will not hand a rope more, vse your authoritie: If you cannot, giue thankes you haue liu'd so long, and make your selfe readie in your Cabine for the mischance of the houre, if it so hap. Cheerely good hearts: out of our way I say.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: I haue great comfort from this fellow: methinks he hath no drowning marke vpon him, his complexion is perfect Gallowes: stand fast good Fate to his hanging, make the rope of his destiny our cable, for our owne doth little aduantage: If he be not borne to bee hang'd, our case is miserable.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose:
Downe with the top-Mast: yare, lower, lower, bring her to Try with Maine-course. A plague —

vpon this howling: they are lowder then the weather, or our office: yet againe? What do you heere? Shal we giue ore and drowne, haue you a minde to sinke?

speeches.speaker: Sebas.
prose: A poxe o' your throat, you bawling, blasphemous incharitable Dog.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: Worke you then.

speeches.speaker: Anth.
prose: Hang cur, hang, you whoreson insolent Noysemaker, we are lesse afraid to be drownde, then thou art.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
prose: I'le warrant him for drowning, though the Ship were no stronger then a Nutt-shell, and as leaky as an vnstanched wench.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: Lay her a hold, a hold, set her two courses off to Sea againe, lay her off.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
prose: All lost, to prayers, to prayers, all lost.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: What must our mouths be cold?

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
prose: The King, and Prince, at prayers, let's assist them, for our case is as theirs.

speeches.speaker: Sebas.
prose: I' am out of patience.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: We are meerly cheated of our liues by drunkards,
This wide-chopt-rascall, would thou mightst lye drowning the washing of ten Tides.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Hee'l be hang'd yet,
Though euery drop of water sweare against it.
And gape at widst to glut him.
Mercy on vs.
We split, we split, Farewell my wife, and children.
Farewell brother: we split, we split, we split.

speeches.speaker: Anth.
prose: Let's all sinke with' King

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Let's take leaue of him.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
prose: Now would I giue a thousand furlongs of Sea, for an Acre of barren ground: Long heath, Browne firrs, any thing; the wills aboue be done, but I would faine dye a dry death.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: If by your Art (my deerest father) you haue
Put the wild waters in this Ro^e; alay them:
The skye it seemes would powre down stinking pitch,
But that the Sea, mounting to th' welkins cheeke,
Dashes the fire out. Oh! I haue suffered
With those that I saw suffer: A braue vessell
(Who had no doubt some noble creature in her)
Dash'd all to peeces: O the cry did knocke
Against my very heart: poore soules, they perish'd.
Had I byn any God of power, I would
Haue suncke the Sea within the Earth, or ere
It should the good Ship so haue swallow'd, and
The fraughting Soules within her.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Be collected,
No more amazement: Tell your pitteous heart there's no harme done.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: O woe, the day.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: No harme:
I haue done nothing, but in care of thee
(Of thee my deere one; thee my daughter) who
Art ignorant of what thou art. naught knowing
Of whence I am: nor that I am more better
Then Prospero, Master of a full poore cell,
And thy no greater Father.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: More to know
Did neuer medle with my thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: 'Tis time
I should informe thee farther: Lend thy hand
And plucke my Magick garment from me: So,
Lye there my Art: wipe thou thine eyes, haue comfort,
The direfull spectacle of the wracke which touch'd
The very vertue of compassion in thee:
I haue with such prouision in mine Art
So safely ordered, that there is no soule
No not so much perdition as an hayre
Betid to any creature in the vessell
Which thou heardst cry, which thou saw'st sinke: Sit downe,
For thou must now know farther.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: You haue often
Begun to tell me what I am, but stopt
And left me to a bootelesse Inquisition,
Concluding, stay: not yet.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: The howr's now come
The very minute byds thee ope thine care,
Obey, and be attentiue. Canst thou remember
A time before we came vnto this Cell?
I doe not thinke thou canst, for then thou was't not
Out three yeeres old.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: Certainely Sir, I can.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: By what? by any other house, or person?
Of any thing the Image, tell me, that
Hath kept with thy remembrance.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: 'Tis farre off:
And rather like a dreame, then an assurance
That my remembrance warrants: Had I not
Fowre, or fiue women once, that tended me?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Thou hadst; and more Miranda: But how is it
That this liues in thy minde? What seest thou els
In the dark-backward and Abisme of Time?
Yf thou remembrest ought ere thou cam'st here,
How thou cam'st here thou maist.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: But that I doe not.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Twelue yere since (Miranda) twelue yere since,
Thy father was the Duke of Millaine and
A Prince of power:

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: Sir, are not you my Father?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Thy Mother was a peece of vertue, and
She said thou wast my daughter; and thy father
Was Duke of Millaine, and his onely heire,
And Princesse; no worse Issued.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: O the heauens,
What fowle play had we, that we came from thence?
Or blessed was't we did?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Both, both my Girle.
By fowle-play (as thou saist) were we heau'd thence,
But blessedly holpe hither.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: O my heart bleedes
To thinke oth' teene that I haue turn'd you to,
Which is from my remembrance, please you, farther;

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: My brother and thy vncle, call'd Anthonio:
I pray thee marke me, that a brother should
Be so perfidious: he, whom next thy selfe
Of all the world I lou'd, and to him put
The mannage of my state, as at that time
Through all the signories it was the first,
And Prospero, the prime Duke, being so reputed
In dignity; and for the liberall Artes,
Without a paralell; those being all my studie,
The Gouernment I cast vpon my brother,
And to my State grew stranger, being transported
And rapt in secret studies, thy false vncle
(Do'st thou attend me?)

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: Sir, most heedefully.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Being once perfected how to graunt suites, how to deny them: who t' aduance, and who
To trash for ouer-topping; new created
The creatures that were mine, I say, or chang'd 'em,
Or els new form'd 'em; hauing both the key,
Of Officer, and office, set all hearts i' th state
To what tune pleas'd his eare, that now he was
The Iuy which had hid my princely Trunck,
And suckt my verdure out on't: Thou attend'st not?

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: O good Sir, I doe.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: I pray thee marke me:
I thus neglecting worldly ends, all dedicated
To closenes, and the bettering of my mind with that, which but by being so retir'd
Ore-priz'd all popular rate: in my false brother
Awak'd an euill nature, and my trust
Like a good parent, did beget of him
A falsehood in it's contrarie, as great
As my trust was, which had indeede no limit,
A confidence sans bound. He being thus Lorded,
Not onely with what my reuenew yeelded,
But what my power might els exact. Like one
Who hauing into truth, by telling of it,
Made such a synner of his memorie
To credite his owne lie, he did beleeue
He was indeed the Duke, out o' th' Substitution
And executing th' outward face of Roialtie
With all prerogatiue: hence his Ambition growing:
Do'st thou heare?

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: Your tale, Sir, would cure deafenesse.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: To haue no Schreene between this part he plaid,
And him he plaid it for, he needes will be
Absolute Millaine, Me (poore man) my Librarie
Was Dukedome large enough: of temporall roalties
He thinks me now incapable. Confederates
(so drie he was for Sway) with King of Naples
To giue him Annuall tribute, doe him homage
Subiect his Coronet, to his Crowne and bend
The Dukedom yet vnbow'd (alas poore Millaine)
To most ignoble stooping.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: Oh the heauens:

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Marke his condition, and th' euent, then tell me
If this might be a brother.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: I should sinne
To thinke but Noblie of my Grand-mother,
Good wombes haue borne bad sonnes.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Now the Condition.
This King of Naples being an Enemy
To me inueterate, hearkens my Brothers suit,
Which was, That he in lieu o' th' premises,
Of homage, and I know not how much Tribute,
Should presently extirpate me and mine
Out of the Dukedome, and confer faire Millaine
With all the Honors, on my brother: Whereon
A treacherous Armie leuied, one mid-night
Fated to th' purpose, did Anthonio open
The gates of Millaine, and ith' dead of darkenesse
The ministers for th' purpose hurried thence
Me, and thy crying selfe.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Alack, for pitty:
I not remembring how I cride out then
Will cry it ore againe: it is a hint
That wrings mine eyes too't.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Heare a little further,
And then I'le bring thee to the present businesse
Which now's vpon's: without the which, this Story
Were most impertinent.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Wherefore did they not
That howre destroy vs?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Well demanded, wench:
My Tale prouokes that question: Deare, they durst not,
So deare the loue my people bore me: nor set
A marke so bloudy on the businesse; but
With colours fairer, painted their foule ends.
In few, they hurried vs a-boord a Barke,
Bore vs some Leagues to Sea, where they prepared
A rotten carkasse of a Butt, not rigg'd,
Nor tackle, sayle, nor mast, the very rats
Instinctiuely haue quit it: There they hoyst vs
To cry to th' Sea, that roard to vs; to sigh
To th' windes, whose pitty sighing backe againe
Did vs but louing wrong.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Alack, what trouble
Was I then to you?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: O, a Cherubin
Thou was't that did preserue me; Thou didst smile,
Infused with a fortitude from heauen,
When I haue deck'd the sea with drops full salt,
Vnder my burthen groan'd, which rais'd in me
An vndergoing stomacke, to beare vp
Against what should ensue.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: How came we a shore?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: By prouidence diuine,
Some food, we had, and some fresh water, that
A noble Neopolitan Gonzalo
Out of his Charity, (who being then appointed
Master of this designe) did giue vs, with
Rich garments, linnens, stuffs, and necessaries
Which since haue steeded much, so of his gentlenesse
Knowing I lou'd my bookes, he furnishd me
From mine owne Library, with volumes, that
I prize aboue my Dukedome.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Would I might
But euer see that man.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Now I arise,
Sit still, and heare the last of our sea-sorrow:
Heere in this Iland we arriu'd, and heere
Haue I, thy Schoolemaster, made thee more profit
Then other Princesse can, that haue more time
For vainer howres; and Tutors, not so carefull.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Heuens thank you for't. And now I pray you Sir,
For still 'tis beating in my minde; your reason
For raysing this Sea-storme?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Know thus far forth,
By accident most strange, bountifull Fortune
(Now my deere Lady) hath mine enemies
Brought to this shore: And by my prescience
I finde my Zenith doth depend vpon
A most auspitious starre, whose influence
If now I court not, but omit; my fortunes
Will euer after droope: Heare cease more questions,
Thou art inclinde to sleepe: 'tis a good dulnesse,
And giue it way: I know thou canst not chuse:
Come away, Seruant, come; I am ready now,
Approach my Ariel. Come.

speeches.speaker: Ari.
verse: All haile, great Master, graue Sir, haile: I come
To answer thy best pleasure; be't to fly,
To swim, to diue into the fire: to-ride
On the curld clowds: to thy strong bidding, taske
Ariel, and all his Qualitie.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Hast thou, Spirit,
Performd to point, the Tempest that I bad thee.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: To euery Article.
I boorded the Kings ship: now on the Beake,
Now in the Waste, the Decke, in euery Cabyn,
I flam'd amazement, sometime I'ld diuide
And burne in many places; on the Top-mast,
The Yards and Bore-spritt, would I flame distinctly,
Then meete, and ioyne. Ioues Lightning, the precursers
O' th dreadfull Thunder-claps more momentarie
And fight out-running were not; the fire, and cracks
Of sulphurous roaring, the most mighty Neptune
Seeme to besiege, and make his bold waues tremble,
Yea, his dread Trident shake.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: My braue Spirit,
Who was so firme, so constant, that this coyle
Would not infect his reason?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Not a soule
But felt a Feauer of the madde, and plaid
Some tricks of desperation; all but Mariners
Plung'd in the foaming bryne, and quit the vessell;
Then all a fire with me the Kings sonne Ferdinand
With haire vp-staring (then like reeds, not haire)
Was the first man that leapt; cride hell is empty,
And all the Diuels are heere.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Why that's my spirit:
But was not this nye shore?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Close by, my Master.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But are they (Ariell) safe?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Not a haire perishd:
On their sustaining garments not a blemish,
But fresher then before: and as thou badst me,
In troops I haue dispersd them 'bout the Isle:
The Kings sonne haue I landed by himselfe,
Whom I left cooling of the Ayre with sighes,
In an odde Angle of the Isle, and sitting
His armes in this sad knot.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Of the Kings ship,
The Marriners, say how thou hast disposd,
And all the rest o' th' Fleete?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Safely in harbour
Is the Kings shippe, in the deepe Nooke, where once
Thou calldst me vp at midnight to fetch dewe
From the still-vext Bermoothes, there she's hid;
The Marriners all vnder hatches stowed,
Who, with a Charme ioynd to their suffred labour
I haue left asleep: and for the rest o' th' Fleet
(Which I dispers'd) they all haue met againe,
And are vpon the Mediterranian Flote
Bound sadly home for Naples,
Supposing that they saw the Kings ship wrackt,
And his great person perish.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Ariel, thy charge
Exactly is perform'd; but there's more worke:
What is the time o' th' day?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Past the mid season.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: At least two Glasses: the time 'twixt six & now
Must by vs both be spent most preciously.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Is there more toyle? Since yu dost giue me pains,
Let me remember thee what thou hast promis'd,
Which is not yet perform'd me.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: How now? moodie?
What is't thou canst demand?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: My Libertie.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Before the time be out? no more:

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I prethee,
Remember I haue done thee worthy seruice,
Told thee no lyes, made thee no mistakings, serv'd
Without or grudge, or grumblings; thou did promise
To bate me a full yeere.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Do'st thou forget
From what a torment I did free thee?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Thou do'st: & thinkst it much to tread ye Ooze
Of the salt deepe;
To run vpon the sharpe winde of the North,
To doe me businesse in the veines o' th' earth
When it is bak'd with frost.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: I doe not Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Thou liest, malignant Thing: hast thou forgot
The fowle Witch Sycorax, who with Age and Enuy
Was growne into a hoope? hast thou forgot her?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Thou hast: where was she born? speak: tell me:

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Sir, in Argier.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Oh, was she so: I must
Once in a moneth recount what thou hast bin,
Which thou forgetst. This damn'd Witch Sycorax
For mischiefes manifold, and forceries terrible
To enter humane hearing, from Argier
Thou know'st was banish'd: for one thing she did
They wold not take her life: Is not this true?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: I, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: This blew ey'd hag, was hither brought with child,
And here was left by th' Saylors; thou my slaue,
As thou reportst thy selfe, was then her seruant,
And for thou wast a Spirit too-delicate
To act her earthy, and abhord commands,
Refusing her grand hefts, she did confine thee
By helpe of her more potent Ministers,
And in her most vnmittigable rage,
Into a clouen Pyne, within which rift
Imprison'd, thou didst painefully remaine
A dozen yeeres: within which space she di'd,
And left thee there: where thou didst vent thy groanes
As fast as Mill-wheeles strike: Then was this Island
(Saue for the Son, that he did littour heere,
A frekelld whelpe, hag-borne) not honour'd with
A humane shape.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Yes: Caliban her sonne.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Dull thing, I say so: he, that Caliban
Whom now I keepe in seruice, thou best know'st
What torment I did finde thee in; thy grones
Did make wolues howle, and penetrate the breasts
Of euer-angry Beares; it was a torment
To lay vpon the damn'd, which Sycorax
Could not againe vndoe: it was mine Art,
When I arriu'd, and heard thee, that made gape
The Pyne, and let thee out.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: I thanke thee Master.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: If thou more murmur'st, I will rend an Oake
And peg-thee in his knotty entrailes, till
Thou hast howl'd away twelue winters.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Pardon, Master,
I will be correspondent to command
And doe my spryting, gently.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Doe so: and after two daies
I will discharge thee.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: That's my noble Master:
What shall I doe? say what? what shall I doe?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Goe make thy selfe like a Nymph o' th' Sea,
Be subiect to no sight but thine, and mine: inuisible
To euery eye-ball else: goe take this shape
And hither come in't: goe: hence
With diligence.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Awake, deere hart awake, thou hast slept well,
Awake.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: The strangenes of your story, put
Heauinesse in me.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Shake it off: Come on,
Wee'll visit Caliban, my slaue, who neuer
Yeelds vs kinde answere.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: 'Tis a villaine Sir, I doe not loue to looke on.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: But as 'tis
We cannot misse him: he do's make our fire,
Fetch in our wood, and serues in Offices
That profit vs: What hoa: slaue: Caliban:
Thou Earth, thou: speake.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: within. There's wood enough within.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Come forth I say, there's other busines for thee:
Come thou Tortoys, when?
Fine apparision: my queint Ariel,
Hearke in thine eare.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: My Lord, it shall be done.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Thou poysonous slaue, got by ye diuell himselfe
Vpon thy wicked Dam; come forth.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: As wicked dewe, as ere my mother brush'd
With Rauens feather from vnwholesome Fen
Drop on you both: A Southwest blow on yee,
And blister you all ore.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: For this be sure, to night thou shalt haue cramps,
Side-stitches, that shall pen thy breath vp, Vrchins
Shall for that vast of night, that they may worke
All exercise on thee: thou shalt be pinch'd
As thicke as hony-combe, each pinch more stinging
Then Bees that made 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I must eat my dinner:
This Island's mine by Sycorax my mother,
Which thou tak'st from me: when thou cam'st first
Thou stroakst me, & made much of me: wouldst giue me
Water with berries in't: and teach me how
To name the bigger Light, and how the lesse
That burne by day, and night: and then I lou'd thee
And shew'd thee all the qualities o' th' Isle,
The fresh Springs, Brine-pits; barren place and fertill,
Curs'd be I that did so: All the Charmes
Of Sycorax: Toades, Beetles, Batts light on you:
For I am all the Subiects that you haue,
Which first was min owne King: and here you sty-me
In this hard Rocke, whiles you doe keepe from me
The rest o' th' Island.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Thou most lying slaue,
Whom stripes may moue, not kindnes: I haue vs'd thee
(Filth as thou art) with humane care, and lodg'd thee
In mine owne Cell, till thou didst seeke to violate
The honor of my childe.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Oh ho, oh ho, would't had bene done:
Thou didst preuent me, I had peopel'd else
This Isle with Calibans.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: Abhorred Slaue,
Which any print of goodnesse wilt not take,
Being capable of all ill: I pittied thee,
Took pains to make thee speak, taught thee each houre
One thing or other: when thou didst not (Sauage)
Know thine owne meaning; but wouldst gabble, like
A thing most brutish. I endow'd thy purposes
With words that made them knowne: But thy vild race
(Tho thou didst learn) had that in't, which good natures
Could not abide to be with; therefore wast thou
Deseruedly confin'd into this Rocke, who hadst
Deseru'd more then a prison.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: You taught me Language, and my profit on't
Is, I know how to curse: the red-plague rid you
For learning me your language.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Hag-seed, hence:
Fetch vs in Fewell, and be quicke thou'rt best
To answer other businesse: shrug'st thou (Malice)
If thou neglectst, or dost vnwillingly
What I command, Ile racke thee with old Crampes,
Fill all thy bones with Aches, make thee rore,
That beasts shall tremble at thy dyn.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: No, 'pray thee.
I must obey, his Art is of such pow'r,
It would controll my Dams god Setebos,
And make a vassaile of him.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: So slaue, hence.

speeches.speaker: Ariel
verse: Come vnto these yellow sands, and then take hands:
Curt sied when you haue, and kist the wilde waues whist:
Foote it featly heere, and there, and sweete Sprights beare the burthen.
Harke, harke, bowgh wawgh: the watch-Dogges barke, bowgh-wawgh.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Hark, hark, I heare, the straine of strutting Chanticlere cry cockadidle-dowe.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Where shold this Musick be? I' th aire, or th' earth?
It sounds no more: and sure it waytes vpon
Some God' oth' Iland, sitting on a banke,
Weeping againe the King my Fathers wracke.
This Musicke crept by me vpon the waters,
Allaying both their fury, and my passion
With it's sweet ayre; thence I haue follow'd it
(Or it hath drawne me rather) but 'tis gone.
No, it begins againe.

speeches.speaker: Ariell
verse: Full fadom fiue thy Father lies.
Of his bones are Corrall made:
Those are pearles that were his eies,
Nothing of him that doth fade,
But doth suffer a Sea-change
Into something rich, & strange:
Sea-Nimphs hourly ring his knell.
Harke now I heare them, ding-dong bell.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: The Ditty do's remember my drown'd father,
This is no mortall busines, nor no found
That the earth owes: I heare it now aboue me.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: The fringed Curtaines of thine eye aduance,
And say what thou see'st yond.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: What is't a Spirit?
Lord, how it lookes about: Beleeue me sir,
It carries a braue forme. But 'tis a spirit.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: No wench, it eats, and sleeps, & hath such senses
As we haue: such. This Gallant which thou seest
Was in the wracke: and but hee's something stain'd
With greefe (that's beauties canker) yu might'st call him
A goodly person: he hath lost his fellowes,
And strayes about to finde 'em.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I might call him
A thing diuine, for nothing naturall
I euer saw so Noble.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: It goes on I see
As my soule prompts it: Spirit, fine spirit, Ile free thee
Within two dayes for this.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Most sure the Goddesse
On whom these ayres attend: Vouchsafe my pray'r
May know if you remaine vpon this Island,
And that you will some good instruction giue
How I may beare me heere: my prime request
(Which I do last pronounce) is (O you wonder)
If you be Mayd, or no?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No wonder Sir,
But certainly a Mayd.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: My Language? Heauens:
I am the best of them that speake this speech,
Were I but where 'tis spoken.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: How? the best?
What wer't thou if the King of Naples heard thee?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: A single thing, as I am now, that wonders
To heare thee speake of Naples: he do's heare me,
And that he do's, I weepe: my selfe am Naples,
Who, with mine eyes (neuer since at ebbe) beheld
The King my Father wrack't.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Alacke, for mercy.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Yes faith, & all his Lords, the Duke of Millaine
And his braue sonne, being twaine.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: The Duke of Millaine
And his more brauer daughter, could controll thee
If now 'twere sit to do't: At the first sight
They haue chang'd eyes: Delicate Ariel,
Ile set thee free for this. A word good Sir,
I feare you haue done your selfe some wrong: A word.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why speakes my father so vngently? This
Is the third man that ere I saw: the first
That ere I sigh'd for: pitty moue my father
To be enclin'd my way.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: O, if a Virgin,
And your affection not gone forth, Ile make you
The Queene of Naples.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Soft sir, one word more.
They are both in eythers pow'rs: But this swift busines
I must vneasie make, least too light winning
Make the prize light. One word more: I charge thee
That thou attend me: Thou do'st heere vsurpe
The name thou ow'st not, and hast put thy selfe
Vpon this Island, as a spy, to win it
From me, the Lord on't.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: No, as I am a man.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Ther's nothing ill, can dwell in such a Temple,
If the ill-spirit haue so fayre a house.
Good things will striue to dwell with't.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Follow me.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Speake not you for him: hee's a Traitor: come,
Ile manacle thy necke and feete together:
Sea water shalt thou drinke: thy food shall be
The fresh-brooke Mussels, wither'd roots, and huskes
Wherein the Acorne cradled. Follow.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: No,
I will resist such entertainment, till
Mine enemy ha's more pow'r.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: O deere Father,
Make not too rash a triall of him, for
Hee's gentle, and not fearfull.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: What I say,
My foote my Tutor? Put thy sword vp Traitor,
Who mak'st a shew, but dar'st not strike: thy conscience
Is so possest with guilt: Come, from thy ward,
For I can heere disarme thee with this sticke,
And make thy weapon drop.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
prose: Beseech you Father.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
prose: Hence: hang not on my garments.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: Sir haue pity,
Ile be his surety.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Silence: One word more
Shall make me chide thee, if not hate thee: What,
An aduocate for an Impostor? Hush:
Thou think'st there is no more such shapes as he,
(Hauing seene but him and Caliban:) Foolish wench,
To th' most of men, this is a Caliban,
And they to him are Angels.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: My affections
Are then most humble: I haue no ambition
To see a goodlier man.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Come on, obey:
Thy Nerues are in their infancy againe.
And haue no vigour in them.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: So they are:
My spirits, as in a dreame, are all bound vp:
My Fathers losse, the weaknesse which I feele,
The wracke of all my friends, nor this mans threats,
To whom I am subdude, are but light to me,
Might I but through my prison once a day
Behold this Mayd: all corners else o' th' Earth
Let liberty make vse of: space enough
Haue I in such a prison.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: It workes: Come on.
Thou hast done well, fine Ariell: follow me,
Harke what thou else shalt do mee.

speeches.speaker: Mira.
verse: Be of comfort,
My Fathers of a better nature (Sir)
Then he appeares by speech: this is vnwonted
Which now came from him.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Thou shalt be as free
As mountaine windes; but then exactly do
All points of my command.

speeches.speaker: Ariell.
prose: To th' syllable.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
prose: Come follow: speake not for him.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Beseech you Sir, be merry; you haue cause,
(So haue we all) of ioy; for our escape
Is much beyond our losse; our hint of woe
Is common, euery day, some Saylors wife,
The Masters of some Merchant, and the Merchant
Haue iust our Theame of woe: But for the miracle,
(I meane our preseruation) few in millions
Can speake like vs: then wisely (good Sir) weigh
Our sorrow, with our comfort.

speeches.speaker: Alons.
prose: Prethee peace.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: He receiues comfort like cold porredge.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The Visitor will not giue him ore so.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Looke, hee's winding vp the watch of his wit, By and by it will strike.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: One: Tell.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: When euery greefe is entertaind,
That's offer'd comes to th' entertainer.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: A dollor.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Dolour comes to him indeed, you haue spoken truer then you purpos'd.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: You haue taken it wiselier then I meant you should.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Therefore my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Fie, what a spend-thrift is he of his tongue.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
prose: I pre-thee spare.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Well, I haue done: But yet

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: He will be talking.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Which, of he, or Adrian, for a good wager,
First begins to crow?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: The old Cocke.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The Cockrell.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Done: The wager?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: A Laughter.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: A match.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Though this Island seeme to be desert.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: So: you'r paid.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Vninhabitable, and almost inaccessible.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Yet

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Yet

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: He could not misse't.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: It must needs be of subtle, tender, and delicate temperance.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Temperance was a delicate wench.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: I, and a subtle, as he most learnedly deliuer'd.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: The ayre breathes vpon vs here most sweetly.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: As if it had Lungs, and rotten ones.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Or, as 'twere perfum'd by a Fen.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Heere is euery thing aduantageous to life.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: True, saue meanes to liue.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Of that there's none, or little.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: How lush and lusty the grasse lookes?
How greene?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The ground indeed is tawny.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: With an eye of greene in't.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: He misses not much.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: No: he doth but mistake the truth totally.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: But the rariety of it is, which is indeed almost beyond credit.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: As many voucht rarieties are.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: That our Garments being (as they were) drencht in the Sea, hold notwithstanding their freshnesse and glosses, being rather new dy'de then stain'd with salte water.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: If but one of his pockets could speake, would it not say he lyes?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: I, or very falsely pocket vp his report.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Me thinkes our garments are now as fresh as when we put them on first in Affricke, at the marriage of the kings faire daughter Claribel to the king of Tunis.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: 'Twas a sweet marriage, and we prosper well in our returne.

speeches.speaker: Adri.
prose: Tunis was neuer grac'd before with such a Paragon to their Queene.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Not since widdow Dido's time.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Widow? A pox o' that: how came that Widdow in? Widdow Dido!

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: What if he had said Widdower Aeneas too?
Good Lord, how you take it?

speeches.speaker: Adri.
prose: Widdow Dido said you? You make me study of that: She was of Carthage, not of Tunis.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: This Tunis Sir was Carthage.

speeches.speaker: Adri.
prose: Carthage?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: I assure you Carthage.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: His word is more then the miraculous Harpe.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: He hath rais'd the wall, and houses too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: What impossible matter wil he make easy next?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: I thinke hee will carry this Island home in his pocket, and giue it his sonne for an Apple.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: And sowing the kernels of it in the Sea, bring forth more Islands.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why in good time.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Sir, we were talking, that our garments seeme now as fresh as when we were at Tunis at the marriage of your daughter, who is now Queene.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: And the rarest that ere came there.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Bate (I beseech you) widdow Dido.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: O Widdow Dido? I, Widdow Dido.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Is not Sir my doublet as fresh as the first day I wore it? I meane in a sort.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: That sort was well fish'd for.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: When I wore it at your daughters marriage.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: You cram these words into mine eares, against the stomacke of my sense: would I had neuer
Married my daughter there: For comming thence
My sonne is lost, and (in my rate) she too,
Who is so farre from Italy remoued,
I ne're againe shall see her: O thou mine heire
Of Naples and of Millaine, what strange fish
Hath made his meale on thee?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Sir he may liue,
I saw him beate the surges vnder him,
And ride vpon their backes; he trod the water
Whose enmity he flung aside: and brested
The surge most swolne that met him: his bold head
'Boue the contentious waues he kept. and oared
Himselfe with his good armes in lusty stroke
To th' shore; that ore his waue-worne basis bowed
As stooping to releeue him: I not doubt
He came aliue to Land.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
prose: No, no, hee's gone.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Sir you may thank your selfe for this great losse,
That would not blesse our Europe with your daughter,
But rather loose her to an Affrican,
Where she at least, is banish'd from your eye,
Who hath cause to wet the greefe on't.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
prose: Pre-thee peace.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: You were kneel'd too, & importun'd otherwise
By all of vs: and the faire soule her selfe
Waigh'd betweene loathnesse, and obedience, at
Which end o' th' beame should bow: we haue lost your son,
I feare for euer: Millaine and Naples haue
Mo widdowes in them of this businesse making,
Then we bring men to comfort them:
The faults your owne.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
prose: So is the doer'st oth' losse.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: My Lord Sebastian,
The truth you speake doth lacke some gentlenesse,
And time to speake it in: you rub the sore,
When you should bring the plaister.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Very well.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: And most Chirurgeonly.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: It is foule weather in vs all, good Sir,
When you are cloudy.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Fowle weather?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Very foule.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Had I plantation of this Isle my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Hee'd sow't vvith Nettle-seed.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Or dockes, or Mallowes.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: And were the King on't, what vvould I do?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Scape being drunke, for want of Wine.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: I' th' Commonwealth I vvould (by contraries)
Execute all things: For no kinde of Trafficke
Would I admit: No name of Magistrate:
Letters should not be knowne: Riches, pouerty,
And vse of seruice, none: Contract, Succession,
Borne, bound of Land, Tilth, Vineyard none:
No vse of Mettall, Corne, or Wine, or Oyle:
No occupation, all men idle, all:
And Women too, but innocent and pure:
No Soueraignty.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Yet he vvould be King on't.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The latter end of his Common-wealth forgets the beginning.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: All things in common Nature should produce
Without sweat or endeuour: Treason, fellony,
Sword, Pike, Knife, Gun, or neede of any Engine
Would I not haue: but Nature should bring forth
Of it owne kinde, all foyzon, all abundance
To feed my innocent people.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: No marrying 'mong his subiects?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: None (man) all idle; Whores and knaues,

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: I vvould vvith such perfection gouerne Sir:
T' Excell the Golden Age.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: 'Saue his Maiesty.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Long liue Gonzalo.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: And do you marke me, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Alon.
prose: Pre-thee no more: thou dost talke nothing to me.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: I do vvell beleeue your Highnesse, and did it to minister occasion to these Gentlemen, who are of such sensible and nimble Lungs, that they alwayes vse to laugh at nothing.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: 'Twas you vve laugh'd at.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Who, in this kind of merry fooling am nothing to you: so you may continue, and laugh at nothing still.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: What a blow vvas there giuen?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: And it had not falne flat-long.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: You are Gentlemen of braue mettal: you would lift the Moone out of her spheare, if she would continue in it fiue weekes vvithout changing.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: We vvould so, and then go a Bat-fowling.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Nay good my Lord, be not angry.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: No I warrant you, I vvill not aduenture my discretion so weakly: Will you laugh me asleepe, for I am very heauy.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Go sleepe, and heare vs.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: What, all so soone asleepe? I wish mine eyes
Would (with themselues) shut vp my thoughts,
I finde they are inclin'd to do so.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Please you Sir,
Do not omit the heauy offer of it:
It sildome visits sorrow, when it doth, it is a Comforter.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: We two my Lord, will guard your person,
While you take your rest, and watch your safety.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
prose: Thanke you: Wondrous heauy.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: What a strange drowsines possesses them?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: It is the quality o' th' Clymate.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Why
Doth it not then our eye-lids sinke? I finde
Not my selfe dispos'd to sleep.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nor I, my spirits are nimble:
They fell together all, as by consent
They dropt, as by a Thunder-stroke: what might
Worthy Sebastian? O, what might? no more:
And yet, me thinkes I see it in thy face,
What thou should'st be: th' occasion speaks thee, and
My strong imagination see's a Crowne
Dropping vpon thy head.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: What? art thou waking?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Do you not heare me speake?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I do, and surely
It is a sleepy Language; and thou speak'st
Out of thy sleepe: What is it thou didst say?
This is a strange repose, to be asleepe
With eyes wide open: standing, speaking, mouing:
And yet so fast asleepe.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Noble Sebastian,
Thou let'st thy fortune sleepe: die rather: wink'st
Whiles thou art waking.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Thou do'st snore distinctly,
There's meaning in thy snores.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I am more serious then my custome: you
Must be so too, if heed me: which to do,
Trebbles thee o're.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Well: I am standing water.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Ile teach you how to flow.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Do so: to ebbe
Hereditary Sloth instructs me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: O!
If you but knew how you the purpose cherish
Whiles thus you mocke it: how in stripping it
You more inuest it: ebbing men, indeed
(Most often) do so neere the bottome run
By their owne feare, or sloth.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: 'Pre-thee say on,
The setting of thine eye, and cheeke proclaime
A matter from thee; and a birth, indeed,
Which throwes thee much to yeeld.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Thus Sir:
Although this Lord of weake remembrance; this
Who shall be of as little memory
When he is earth'd, hath here almost perswaded
(For hee's a Spirit of perswasion, onely
Professes to perswade) the King his sonne's aliue,
'Tis as impossible that hee's vndrown'd,
As he that sleepes heere, swims.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I haue no hope
That hee's vndrown'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: O, out of that no hope,
What great hope haue you? No hope that way, Is
Another way so high a hope, that euen
Ambition cannot pierce a winke beyond
But doubt discouery there. Will you grant with me
That Ferdinand is drown'd.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: He's gone.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Then tell me, who's the next heire of Naples?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Claribell.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: She that is Queene of Tunis she that dwels
Ten leagues beyond mans life: she that from Naples
Can haue no note, vnlesse the Sun were post:
The Man i' th Moone's too slow, till new-borne chinnes
Be rough, and Razor-able: She that from whom
We all were sea-swallow'd, though some cast againe,
(And by that destiny) to performe an act
Whereof, what's past is Prologue; what to come
In yours, and my discharge.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: What stuffe is this? How say you?
'Tis true my brothers daughter's Queene of Tunis,
So is she heyre of Naples, 'twixt which Regions
There is some space.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: A space, whose eu'ry cubit
Seemes to cry out, how shall that Claribell
Measure vs backe to Naples? keepe in Tunis,
And let Sebastian wake. Say, this were death
That now hath seiz'd them, why they were no worse
Then now they are: There be that can rule Naples
As well as he that sleepes: Lords, that can prate
As amply, and vnnecessarily
As this Gonzallo: I my selfe could make
A Chough of as deepe chat: O, that you bore
The minde that I do; what a sleepe were this
For your aduancement? Do you vnderstand me?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Me thinkes I do.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And how do's your content
Tender your owne good fortune?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I remember
You did supplant your Brothet Prospero.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: True:
And looke how well my Garments sit vpon me,
Much feater then before: My Brothers seruants
Were then my fellowes, now they are my men.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: But for your conscience.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I Sir: where lies that? If 'twere a kybe
'Twould put me to my slipper: But I feele not
This Deity in my bosome: 'Twentie consciences
That stand 'twixt me, and Millaine, candied be they,
And melt ere they mollest: Heere lies your Brother,
No better then the earth he lies vpon,
If he were that which now hee's like (that's dead)
Whom I with this obedient steele (three inches of it)
Can lay to bed for euer: whiles you doing thus,
To the perpetuall winke for aye might put
This ancient morsell: this Sir Prudence, who
Should not vpbraid our course: for all the rest
They'l take suggestion, as a Cat laps milke,
They'l tell the clocke, to any businesse that
We say befits the houre.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Thy case, deere Friend
Shall be my president: As thou got'st Millaine,
I'le come by Naples: Draw thy sword, one stroke
Shall free thee from the tribute which thou paiest,
And I the King shall loue thee.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Draw together:
And when I reare my hand, do you the like
To fall it on Gonzalo.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: O, but one word.

speeches.speaker: Ariel.
verse: My Master through his Art foresees the danger
That you (his friend) are in, and sends me forth
(For else his proiect dies) to keepe them liuing.
While you here do snoaring lie,
Open-ey'd Conspiracie
His time doth take:
If of Life you keepe a care,
Shake off slumber and beware.
Awake, awake.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Then let vs both be sodaine.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Now, good Angels preserue the King.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: Why how now hoa; awake? why are you drawn?
Wherefore this ghastly looking?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Whiles we stood here securing your repose,
(Euen now) we heard a hollow burst of bellowing
Like Buls, or rather Lyons, did't not wake you?
It strooke mine eare most terribly.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: I heard nothing.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: O, 'twas a din to fright a Monsters eare;
To make an earthquake: sure it was the roare
Of a whole heard of Lyons.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: Heard you this Gonzalo?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Vpon mine honour, Sir, I heard a humming,
(And that a strange one too) which did awake me:
I shak'd you Sir, and cride: as mine eyes opend,
I saw their weapons drawne: there was a noyse,
That's verily: 'tis best we stand vpon our guard;
Or that we quit this place: let's draw our weapons.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: Lead off this ground & let's make further search
For my poore sonne.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Heauens keepe him from these Beasts:
For he is sure i' th Island.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: Lead away.

speeches.speaker: Ariell.
verse: Prospero my Lord, shall know what I haue done.
So (King) goe safely on to seeke thy Son.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: All the infections that the Sunne suckes vp
From Bogs, Fens, Flats, on Prosper fall, and make him
By ynch-meale a disease: his Spirits heare me,
And yet I needes must curse. But they'll nor pinch,
Fright me with Vrchyn-shewes, pitch me i' th mire,
Nor lead me like a fire-brand, in the darke
Out of my way, vnlesse he bid 'em; but
For euery trifle, are they set vpon me,
Sometime like Apes, that moe and chatter at me,
And after bite me: then like Hedg-hogs, which
Lye tumbling in my bare-foote way, and mount
Their pricks at my foot-fall: sometime am I
All wound with Adders, who with clouen tongues
Doe hisse me into madnesse: Lo, now Lo,
Here comes a Spirit of his, and to torment me
For bringing wood in slowly: I'le fall flat,
Perchance he will not minde me.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Here's neither bush, nor shrub to beare off any weather at all: and another Storme brewing, I heare it sing i th' winde: yond same blacke cloud, yond huge one, lookes like a foule bumbard that would shed his licquor: if it should thunder, as it did before, I know not where to hide my head: yond same cloud cannot choose but fall by paile-fuls. What haue we here, a man, or a fish? dead or aliue? a fish, hee smels like a fish: a very ancient and fish-like smell: a kinde of, not of the newest poore-Iohn: a strange fish: were I in England now (as once I was) and had but this fish painted; not a holiday-foole there but would giue a peece of siluer: there, would this Monster, make a man: any strange beast there, makes a man: when they will not giue a do it to relieue a lame Begger, they will lay out ten to see a dead Indian: Leg'd like a man; and his Finnes like Armes: warme o' my troth: I doe now let loose my opinion; hold it no longer; this is no fish, but an Islander, that hath lately suffered by a Thunderbolt: Alas, the storme is come againe: my best way is to creepe vnder his Gaberdine: there is no other shelter hereabout: Misery acquaints a man with strange bedfellowes: I will here shrowd till the dregges of the storme be past.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: I shall no more to sea, to sea, here shall I dye ashore.
This is a very scuruy tune to sing at a mans
Funerall: well, here's my comfort.
The Master, the Swabber, the Boate-swaine & I;
The Gunner, and his Mate
Lou'd Mall, Meg, and Marrian, and Margerie,
But none of vs car'd for Kate.
For she had a tongue with a tang,
Would cry to a Sailor goe hang:
She lou'd not the sauour of Tar nor of Pitch,
Yet a Tailor might scratch her where ere she did itch.
Then to Sea Boyes, and let her goe hang.
This is a scuruy tune too:
But here's my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Doe not torment me: oh.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: What's the matter?
Haue we diuels here?

Doe you put trickes vpon's with Saluages, and Men of Inde? ha? I haue not scap'd drowning, to be afeard now of your foure legges: for it hath bin said; as proper a man as euer went on foure legs, cannot make him giue ground: and it shall be said so againe, while Stephano breathes at' nostrils.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: The Spirit torments me: oh.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: This is some Monster of the Isle, with foure legs; who hath got (as I take it) an Ague: where the diuell should he learne our language? I will giue him some reliefe if it be but for that: if I can recouer him, and keepe him tame, and get to Naples with him, he's a Present for any Emperour that euer trod on Neates-leather.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Doe not torment me 'prethee: I'le bring my wood home faster.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: He's in his fit now; and doe's not talke after the wisest; hee shall taste of my Bottle: if hee haue neuer drunke wine afore, it will goe neere to remoue his Fit: if I can recouer him, and keepe him tame, I will not take too much for him; hee shall pay for him that hath him, and that soundly.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Thou do'st me yet but little hurt; thou wilt anon, I know it by thy trembling: Now Prosper workes vpon thee.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Come on your wayes: open your mouth: here is that which will giue language to you Cat; open your mouth; this will shake your shaking, I can tell you, and that soundly: you cannot tell who's your friend; open your chaps againe.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: I should know that voyce:
It should be,
But hee is dround; and these are diuels; O defend me.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Foure legges and two voyces; a most delicate Monster his forward voyce now is to speake well of his friend; his backward voice, is to vtter soule speeches, and to detract: if all the wine in my bottle will recouer him, I will helpe his Ague: Come: Amen, I will poure some in thy other mouth.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Stephano.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Doth thy other mouth call me? Mercy, mercy: This is a diuell, and no Monster: I will leaue him, I haue no long Spoone.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Stephano: if thou beest Stephano, touch me, and speake to me: for I am Trinculo; be not afeard, thy good friend Trinculo.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: If thou bee'st Trinculo: come foorth: I'le pull thee by the lesser legges: if any be Trinculo's legges, these are they: Thou art very Trinculo indeede: how cam'st thou to be the siege of this Moone-calfe? Can he vent Trinculo's?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: I tooke him to be kil'd with a thunder-strok; but art thou not dround Stephano: I hope now thou art not dround: Is the Storme ouer-blowne? I hid mee vnder the dead Moone-Calfes Gaberdine, for feare of the Storme: And art thou liuing Stephano? O Stephano, two Neapolitanes scap'd?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: 'Prethee doe not turne me about, my stomacke is not constant.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: These be fine things, and if they be not spright's: that's a braue God, and beares Celestiall liquor: I will kneele to him.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: How did'st thou scape?
How cam'st thou hither?

Sweare by this Bottle how thou cam'st hither: I escap'd vpon a But of Sacke, which the Saylors heaued o' reboord, by this Bottle which I made of the barke of a Tree, with mine owne hands, since I was cast a'shore.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: I'le sweare vpon that Bottle, to be thy true subiect, for the liquor is not earthly.

speeches.speaker: St.
prose: Heere: sweare then how thou escap'dst.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Swom ashore (man) like a Ducke: I can swim like a Ducke i'le be sworne.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Here, kisse the Booke.
Though thou canst swim like a Ducke, thou art made like a Goose.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: O Stephano, ha'st any more of this?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: The whole But (man) my Cellar is in a rocke by th' sea-side, where my Wine is hid:
How now Moone-Calfe, how do's thine Ague?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Ha'st thou not dropt from heauen?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Out o' th Moone I doe assure thee. I was the Man ith' Moone, when time was.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I haue seene thee in her: and I doe adore thee:
My Mistris shew'd me thee, and thy Dog, and thy Bush.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Come, sweare to that: kisse the Booke: I will furnish it anon with new Contents: Sweare.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: By this good light, this is a very shallow Monster: I afeard of him? a very weake Monster:
The Man ith' Moone?
A most poore creadulous Monster:
Well drawne Monster, in good sooth.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Ile shew thee euery fertill ynch 'oth Island: and I will kisse thy foote: I prethee be my god.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: By this light, a most perfidious, and drunken Monster, when's god's a sleepe he'll rob his Bottle.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Ile kisse thy foot. Ile sweare my selfe thy Subiect.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Come on then: downe and sweare.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: I shall laugh my selfe to death at this puppi-headed Monster: a most scuruie Monster: I could finde in my heart to beate him.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Come, kisse.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: But that the poore Monster's in drinke:
An abhominable Monster.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I'le shew thee the best Springs: I'le plucke thee
Berries: I'le fish for thee; and get thee wood enough.
A plague vpon the Tyrant that I serue;
I'le beare him no more Stickes, but follow thee, thou wondrous man.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: A most rediculous Monster, to make a wonder of a poore drunkard.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: I' prethee let me bring thee where Crabs grow; and I with my long nayles will digge thee pig-nuts; show thee a Iayes nest, and instruct thee how to snare the nimble Marmazet: I'le bring thee to clustring Philbirts, and sometimes I'le get thee young Scamels from the Rocke: Wilt thou goe with me?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: I pre'thee now lead the way without any more talking. Trinculo, the King, and all our company else being dround, wee will inherit here: Here; beare my Bottle: Fellow Trinculo; we'll fill him by and by againe.
Farewell Master; farewell, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: A howling Monster: a drunken Monster.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: No more dams I'le make for fish,
Nor fetch in firing, at requiring,
Nor scrape trenchering, nor wash dish,
Ban' ban' Cacalyban
Has a new Master, get a new Man.
Freedome, high-day, high-day freedome, freedome high-day, freedome.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: O braue Monster; lead the way.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: There be some Sports are painfull; & their labor
Delight in them set off: Some kindes of basenesse
Are nobly vndergon; and most poore matters
Point to rich ends: this my meane Taske
Would be as heauy to me, as odious, but
The Mistris which I serue, quickens what's dead,
And makes my labours, pleasures: O She is
Ten times more gentle, then her Father's crabbed;
And he's compos'd of harshnesse. I must remoue
Some thousands of these Logs, and pile them vp,
Vpon a sore iniunction; my sweet Mistris
Weepes when she sees me worke, & saies, such basenes
Had neuer like Executor: I forget:
But these sweet thoughts, doe euen refresh my labours,
Most busie lest, when I doe it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Alas, now pray you
Worke not so hard: I would the lightning had
Burnt vp those Logs that you are enioynd to pile:
Pray set it downe, and rest you: when this burnes
'Twill weepe for hauing wearied you: my Father
Is hard at study; pray now rest your selfe,
Hee's safe for these three houres.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: O most deere Mistris.
The Sun will set before I shall discharge
What I must striue to do.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: If you'l sit downe
Ile beare your Logges the while: pray giue me that,
Ile carry it to the pile.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: No precious Creature,
I had rather cracke my sinewes, breake my backe,
Then you should such dishonor vndergoe,
While I sit lazy by.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: It would become me
As well as it do's you; and I should do it
With much more ease: for my good will is to it,
And yours it is against.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Poore worme thou art infected,
This visitation shewes it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: You looke wearily.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: No, noble Mistris, 'tis fresh morning with me
When you are by at night: I do beseech you
Cheefely, that I might set it in my prayers,
What is your name?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Miranda, O my Father,
I haue broke your hest to say so.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Admit'd Miranda,
Indeede the top of Admiration, worth
What's deerest to the world: full many a Lady
I haue ey'd with best regard, and many a time
Th' harmony of their tongues, hath into bondage
Brought my too diligent eare: for seuerall vertues
Haue I lik'd seuerall women, neuer any
VVith so full soule, but some defect in her
Did quarrell with the noblest grace she ow'd,
And put it to the foile. But you, O you,
So perfect, and so peetlesse, are created
Of euerie Creatures best.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I do not know
One of my sexe; no womans face remember,
Saue from my glasse, mine owne: Nor haue I seene
More that I may call men, then you good friend,
And my deere Father: how features are abroad
I am skillesse of; but by my modestie
(The iewell in my dower) I would not wish
Any Companion in the world but you:
Nor can imagination forme a shape
Besides your selfe, to like of: but I prattle
Something too wildely, and my Fathers precepts
I therein do forget.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I am, in my condition
A Prince (Miranda) I do thinke a King
(I would not so) and would no more endure
This wodden slauerie, then to suffer
The flesh-flie blow my mouth: heare my soule speake.
The verie instant that I saw you, did
My heart flie to your seruice, there resides
To make me slaue to it, and for your sake
Am I this patient Logge-man.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Do you loue me?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: O heauen; O earth, beare witnes to this sound,
And crowne what I professe with kinde euent
If I speake true: if hollowly, inuert
VVhat best is boaded me, to mischiefe: I,
Beyond all limit of what else i' th world
Do loue, prize, honor you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I am a foole
To weepe at what I am glad of.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Faire encounter
Of two most rare affections: heauens raine grace
On that which breeds betweene 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: VVherefore weepe you?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: At mine vnworthinesse, that dare not offer
VVhat I desire to giue; and much lesse take
VVhat I shall die to want: But this is trifling,
And all the more it seekes to hide it selfe,
The bigger bulke it shewes. Hence bashfull cunning,
And prompt me plaine and holy innocence.
I am your wife, if you will marrie me;
If not, Ile die your maid: to be your fellow
You may denie me, but Ile be your seruant
VVhether you will or no.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: My Mistris (deerest)
And I thus humble euer.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: My husband then?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I, with a heart as willing
As bondage ere of freedome: heere's my hand.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And mine, with my heart in't; and now farewel
Till halfe an houre hence.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: A thousand, thousand.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: So glad of this as they I cannot be,
VVho are surpriz'd with all; but my reioycing
At nothing can be more: Ile to my booke,
For yet ere supper time, must I performe
Much businesse appertaining.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Tell not me, when the But is out we will drinke water, not a drop before; therefore beare vp, & boord em' Seruant Monster, drinke to me.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Seruant Monster? the folly of this Iland, they say there's but fiue vpon this Isle; we are three of them, if th' other two be brain'd like vs, the State totters.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Drinke seruant Monster when I bid thee, thy eies are almost set in thy head.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: VVhere should they bee set else? hee were a braue Monster indeede if they were set in his taile.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: My man-Monster hath drown'd his tongue in sacke: for my part the Sea cannot drowne mee, I swam ere I could recouer the shore, fiue and thirtie Leagues off and on, by this light thou shalt bee my Lieutenant Monster, or my Standard.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Your Lieutenant if you lift, hee's no standard.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: VVeel not run Monsieur Monster.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Nor go neither: but you'l lie like dogs, and yet say nothing neither.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Moone-calfe, speak once in thy life, if thou beest a good Moone-calfe.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: How does thy honour? Let me licke thy shooe:
Ile not serue him, he is not valiant.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Thou liest most ignorant Monster, I am in case to iustle a Constable: why, thou debosh'd Fish thou, was there euer man a Coward, that hath drunk so much Sacke as I to day? wilt thou tell a monstrous lie, being but halfe a Fish, and halfe a Monster?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Loe, how he mockes me, wilt thou let him my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Lord, quoth he? that a Monster should be such a Naturall?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Loe, loe againe: bite him to death I prethee.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Trinculo, keepe a good tongue in your head: If you proue a mutineere, the next Tree: the poore Monster's my subiect, and he shall not suffer indignity.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: I thanke my noble Lord. Wilt thou be pleas'd to hearken once againe to the suite I made to thee?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Marry will I: kneele, and repeate it,
I will stand, and so shall Trinculo.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: As I told thee before, I am subiect to a Tirant,
A Sorcerer, that by his cunning hath cheated me
Of the Island.

speeches.speaker: Ariell.
prose: Thou lyest.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Thou lyest, thou iesting Monkey thou:
I would my valiant Master would destroy thee.
I do not lye.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Trinculo, if you trouble him any more in's tale,
By this hand, I will supplant some of your teeth.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Why, I said nothing.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Mum then, and no more: proceed.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I say by Sorcery he got this Isle
From me, he got it. If thy Greatnesse will
Reuenge it on him, (for I know thou dar'st)
But this Thing dare not.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: That's most certaine.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Thou shalt be Lord of it, and Ile serue thee.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: How now shall this be compast?
Canst thou bring me to the party?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Yea, yea my Lord, Ile yeeld him thee asleepe,
Where thou maist knocke a naile into his head.

speeches.speaker: Ariell.
prose: Thou liest, thou canst not.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: What a py'de Ninnie's this? Thou scuruy patch:
I do beseech thy Greatnesse giue him blowes,
And take his bottle from him: When that's gone,
He shall drinke nought but brine, for Ile not shew him
Where the quicke Freshes are.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Trinculo, run into no further danger:
Interrupt the Monster one word further, and by this hand, Ile turne my mercie out o' doores, and make a Stockfish of thee.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
verse: Why, what did I? I did nothing:
Ile go farther off,

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Didst thou not say he lyed?

speeches.speaker: Ariell.
prose: Thou liest.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Do I so? Take thou that,
As you like this, giue me the lye another time.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
verse: I did not giue the lie: Out o' your wittes, and hearing too?
A pox o' your bottle, this can Sacke and drinking doo:
A murren on your Monster, and the diuell take your fingers.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Now forward with your Tale: prethee stand further off.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Beate him enough: after a little time
Ile beate him too.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Stand farther: Come proceede.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why, as I told thee, 'tis a custome with him
I' th afternoone to sleepe: there thou maist braine him,
Hauing first seiz'd his bookes: Or with a logge
Batter his skull, or paunch him with a stake,
Or cut his wezand with thy knife. Remember
First to possesse his Bookes; for without them
Hee's but a Sot, as I am; nor hath not
One Spirit to command: they all do hate him
As rootedly as I. Burne but his Bookes,
He ha's braue Vtensils (for so he calles them)
Which when he ha's a house, hee'l decke withall.
And that most deeply to consider, is
The beautie of his daughter: he himselfe
Cals her a non-pareill: I neuer saw a woman
But onely Sycorax my Dam, and she;
But she as farre surpasseth Sycorax,
As great'st do's least.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Is it so braue a Lasse?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I Lord, she will become thy bed, I warrant,
And bring thee forth braue brood.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Monster, I will kill this man: his daughter and I will be King and Queene, saue our Graces: and Trinculo, and thy selfe shall be Vice-royes:
Dost thou like the plot Trinculo?

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Excellent.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Giue me thy hand, I am sorry I beate thee:
But while thou liu'st keepe a good tongue in thy hea^

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Within this halfe houre will he be asleepe,
Wilt thou destroy him then?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: I on mine honour.

speeches.speaker: Ariell.
prose: This will I tell my Master.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Thou mak'st me merry: I am full of pleasure,
Let vs be iocond. Will you troule the Catch
You taught me but whileare?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: At thy request Monster, I will do reason,
Any reason: Come on Trinculo, let vs sing.
Flout 'em, and cout 'em: and skowt 'em, and flout 'em,
Thought is free.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: That's not the tune.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: What is this same?

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: This is the tune of our Catch, plaid by the picture of No-body.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: If thou beest a man, shew thy selfe in thy likenes:
If thou beest a diuell, take't as thou list.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: O forgiue me my sinnes.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: He that dies payes all debts: I defie thee;
Mercy vpon vs.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Art thou affeard?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: No Monster, not I.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Be not affeard, the Isle is full of noyses,
Sounds, and sweet aires, that giue delight and hurt not:
Sometimes a thousand twangling Instruments
Will hum about mine eares; and sometime voices,
That if I then had wak'd after long sleepe,
Will make me sleepe againe, and then in dreaming,
The clouds me thought would open, and shew riches
Ready to drop vpon me, that when I wak'd
I cri'de to dreame againe.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: This will proue a braue kingdome to me,
Where I shall haue my Musicke for nothing.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: When Prospero is destroy'd.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: That shall be by and by:
I remember the storie.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
verse: The sound is going away.
Lets follow it, and after do our worke.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Leade Monster,
Wee'l follow: I would I could see this Taborer,
He layes it on.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
verse: Wilt come?
Ile follow Stephano.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: By'r lakin, I can goe no further, Sir,
My old bones akes: here's a maze trod indeede
Through fourth rights, & Meanders: by your patience,
I needes must rest me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Old Lord, I cannot blame thee,
Who, am my selfe attach'd with wearinesse
To th' dulling of my spirits: Sit downe, and rest:
Euen here I will put off my hope, and keepe it
No longer for my Flatterer: he is droun'd
Whom thus we stray to finde, and the Sea mocks
Our frustrate search on land: well, let him goe.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I am right glad, that he's so out of hope:
Doe not for one repulse forgoe the purpose
That you resolu'd t' effect.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: The next aduantage will we take throughly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let it be to night,
For now they are oppress'd with trauaile, they
Will not, nor cannot vse such vigilance
As when they are fresh.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: I say to night: no more.

speeches.speaker: Al.
prose: What harmony is this? my good friends, harke.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
prose: Maruellous sweet Musicke.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: Giue vs kind keepers, heaue~s: what were these?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: A liuing Drolerie: now I will beleeue
That there are Vnicornes: that in Arabia
There is one Tree, the Phoenix throne, one Phoenix
At this houre reigning there.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ile beleeue both:
And what do's else want credit, come to me
And Ile besworne 'tis true: Trauellers nere did lye,
Though fooles at home condemne 'em.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: If in Naples
I should report this now, would they beleeue me?
If I should say I saw such Islands;
(For certes, these are people of the Island)
Who though they are of monstrous shape, yet note
Their manners are more gentle, kinde, then of
Our humaine generation you shall finde
Many, nay almost any.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Honest Lord,
Thou hast said well: for some of you there present;
Are worse then diuels.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I cannot too much muse
Such shapes, such gesture, and such sound expressing
(Although they want the vse of tongue) a kinde
Of excellent dumbe discourse.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Praise in departing.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: They vanish'd strangely.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: No matter, since
They haue left their Viands behinde; for wee haue stomacks.
Wilt please you taste of what is here.

speeches.speaker: Ale.
prose: Not I.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Faith Sir, you neede not feare when wee were Boyes
Who would beleeue that there were Mountayneeres,
Dew-lapt, like Buls whose throats had hanging at 'em
Wallets of flesh? or that there were such men
Whose heads stood in their brests? which now we finde
Each putter out of fiue for one, will bring vs
Good warrant of.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I will stand to, and feede,
Although my last, no matter, since I feele
The best is past: brother: my Lord, the Duke,
Stand too, and doe as we.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You are three men of sinne, whom destiny
That hath to instrument this lower world,
And what is in't: the neuer surfeited Sea,
Hath caus'd to belch vp you; and on this Island,
Where man doth not inhabit, you 'mongst men,
Being most vnfit to liue: I haue made you mad;
And euen with such like valour, men hang, and drowne
Their proper selues: you fooles, I and my fellowes
Are ministers of Fate, the Elements
Of whom your swords are temper'd, may as well
Wound the loud windes, or with bemockt-at-Stabs
Kill the still closing waters, as diminish
One dowle that's in my plumbe: My fellow ministers
Are like-invulnerable: if you could hurt,
Your swords are now too massie for your strengths,
And will not be vplifted: But remember
(For that's my businesse to you) that you three
From Millaine did supplant good Prospero,
Expos'd vnto the Sea (which hath requit it)
Him, and his innocent childe: for which foule deed,
The Powres, delaying (not forgetting) haue
Incens'd the Seas, and Shores; yea, all the Creatures
Against your peace: Thee of thy Sonne, Alonso
They haue bereft; and doe pronounce by me
Lingring perdition (worse then any death
Can be at once) shall step, by step attend
You, and your wayes, whose wraths to guard you from,
Which here, in this most desolate Isle, else fals
Vpon your heads, is nothing but hearts-sorrow,
And a cleere life ensuing.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Brauely the figure of this Harpie, hast thou
Perform'd (my Ariell) a grace it had deuouring:
Of my Instruction, hast thou nothing bated
In what thou had'st to say: so with good life,
And obseruation strange, my meaner ministers
Their seuerall kindes haue done: my high charmes work,
And these (mine enemies) are all knit vp
In their distractions: they now are in my powre;
And in these fits, I leaue them, while I visit
Yong Ferdinand (whom they suppose is droun'd)
And his, and mine lou'd darling.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: I' th name of something holy, Sir, why stand you
In this strange stare?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: O, it is monstrous: monstrous:
Me thought the billowes spoke, and told me of it,
The windes did sing it to me: and the Thunder
(That deepe and dreadfull Organ-Pipe) pronounc'd
The name of Prosper: it did base my Trespasse,
Therefore my Sonne i' th' Ooze is bedded; and
I'le seeke him deeper then ere plummet sounded,
And with him there lye mudded.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: But one feend at a time,
Ile fight their Legions ore.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Ile be thy Second.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: All three of them are desperate: their great guilt
(Like poyson giuen to worke a great time after)
Now gins to bite the spirits: I doe beseech you
(That are of suppler ioynts) follow them swiftly,
And hinder them from what this extasie
May now prouoke them to.

speeches.speaker: Ad.
prose: Follow, I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: There be some Sports are painfull; & their labor
Delight in them set off: Some kindes of basenesse
Are nobly vndergon; and most poore matters
Point to rich ends: this my meane Taske
Would be as heauy to me, as odious, but
The Mistris which I serue, quickens what's dead,
And makes my labours, pleasures: O She is
Ten times more gentle, then her Father's crabbed;
And he's compos'd of harshnesse. I must remoue
Some thousands of these Logs, and pile them vp,
Vpon a sore iniunction; my sweet Mistris
Weepes when she sees me worke, & saies, such basenes
Had neuer like Executor: I forget:
But these sweet thoughts, doe euen refresh my labours,
Most busie lest, when I doe it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Alas, now pray you
Worke not so hard: I would the lightning had
Burnt vp those Logs that you are enioynd to pile:
Pray set it downe, and rest you: when this burnes
'Twill weepe for hauing wearied you: my Father
Is hard at study; pray now rest your selfe,
Hee's safe for these three houres.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: O most deere Mistris.
The Sun will set before I shall discharge
What I must striue to do.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: If you'l sit downe
Ile beare your Logges the while: pray giue me that,
Ile carry it to the pile.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: No precious Creature,
I had rather cracke my sinewes, breake my backe,
Then you should such dishonor vndergoe,
While I sit lazy by.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: It would become me
As well as it do's you; and I should do it
With much more ease: for my good will is to it,
And yours it is against.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Poore worme thou art infected,
This visitation shewes it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: You looke wearily.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: No, noble Mistris, 'tis fresh morning with me
When you are by at night: I do beseech you
Cheefely, that I might set it in my prayers,
What is your name?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Miranda, O my Father,
I haue broke your hest to say so.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Admit'd Miranda,
Indeede the top of Admiration, worth
What's deerest to the world: full many a Lady
I haue ey'd with best regard, and many a time
Th' harmony of their tongues, hath into bondage
Brought my too diligent eare: for seuerall vertues
Haue I lik'd seuerall women, neuer any
VVith so full soule, but some defect in her
Did quarrell with the noblest grace she ow'd,
And put it to the foile. But you, O you,
So perfect, and so peetlesse, are created
Of euerie Creatures best.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I do not know
One of my sexe; no womans face remember,
Saue from my glasse, mine owne: Nor haue I seene
More that I may call men, then you good friend,
And my deere Father: how features are abroad
I am skillesse of; but by my modestie
(The iewell in my dower) I would not wish
Any Companion in the world but you:
Nor can imagination forme a shape
Besides your selfe, to like of: but I prattle
Something too wildely, and my Fathers precepts
I therein do forget.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I am, in my condition
A Prince (Miranda) I do thinke a King
(I would not so) and would no more endure
This wodden slauerie, then to suffer
The flesh-flie blow my mouth: heare my soule speake.
The verie instant that I saw you, did
