My heart flie to your seruice, there resides
To make me slaue to it, and for your sake
Am I this patient Logge-man.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Do you loue me?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: O heauen; O earth, beare witnes to this sound,
And crowne what I professe with kinde euent
If I speake true: if hollowly, inuert
VVhat best is boaded me, to mischiefe: I,
Beyond all limit of what else i' th world
Do loue, prize, honor you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I am a foole
To weepe at what I am glad of.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Faire encounter
Of two most rare affections: heauens raine grace
On that which breeds betweene 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: VVherefore weepe you?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: At mine vnworthinesse, that dare not offer
VVhat I desire to giue; and much lesse take
VVhat I shall die to want: But this is trifling,
And all the more it seekes to hide it selfe,
The bigger bulke it shewes. Hence bashfull cunning,
And prompt me plaine and holy innocence.
I am your wife, if you will marrie me;
If not, Ile die your maid: to be your fellow
You may denie me, but Ile be your seruant
VVhether you will or no.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: My Mistris (deerest)
And I thus humble euer.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: My husband then?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I, with a heart as willing
As bondage ere of freedome: heere's my hand.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And mine, with my heart in't; and now farewel
Till halfe an houre hence.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: A thousand, thousand.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: So glad of this as they I cannot be,
VVho are surpriz'd with all; but my reioycing
At nothing can be more: Ile to my booke,
For yet ere supper time, must I performe
Much businesse appertaining.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: If I haue too austerely punish'd you,
Your compensation makes amends, for I
Haue giuen you here, a third of mine owne life,
Or that for which I liue: who, once againe
I tender to thy hand: All thy vexations
Were but my trials of thy loue, and thou
Hast strangely stood the test: here, afore heauen
I ratifie this my rich guift: O Ferdinand,
Doe not smile at me, that I boast her of,
For thou shalt finde she will out-strip all praise
And make it halt, behinde her.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I doe beleeue it
Against an Oracle.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Then, as my guest, and thine owne acquisition
Worthily purchas'd, take my daughter: But
If thou do'st breake her Virgin-knot, before
All sanctimonious ceremonies may
With full and holy right, be ministred,
No sweet aspersion shall the heauens let fall
To make this contract grow; but barraine hate,
Sower-ey'd disdaine, and discord shall bestrew
The vnion of your bed, with weedes so loathly
That you shall hate it both: Therefore take heede,
As Hymens Lamps shall light you.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: As I hope
For quiet dayes, faire Issue, and long life,
With such loue, as 'tis now the murkiest den,
The most opportune place, the strongst suggestion,
Our worser Genius can, shall neuer melt
Mine honor into lust, to take away
The edge of that dayes celebration,
When I shall thinke, or Phoebus Steeds are founderd,
Or Night kept chain'd below.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Fairely spoke;
Sit then, and talke with her, she is thine owne;
What Ariell; my industrious serua~t Ariell.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: What would my potent master? here I am.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Thou, and thy meaner fellowes, your last seruice
Did worthily performe: and I must vse you
In such another tricke: goe bring the rabble
(Ore whom I giue thee powre) here, to this place:
Incite them to quicke motion, for I must
Bestow vpon the eyes of this yong couple
Some vanity of mine Art: it is my promise,
And they expect it from me.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Presently?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I: with a twincke.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Before you can say come, and goe,
And breathe twice; and cry, so, so:
Each one tripping on his Toe,
Will be here with mop, and mowe.
Doe you loue me Master? no?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Dearely, my delicate Ariell: doe not approach
Till thou do'st heare me call.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Well: I conceiue.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Looke thou be true: doe not giue dalliance
Too much the raigne: the strongest oathes, are straw
To th' fire ith' blood: be more abstenious,
Or else good night your vow.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I warrant you, Sir,
The white cold virgin Snow, vpon my heart
Abates the ardour of my Liuer.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Well.
Now come my Ariell, bring a Corolary,
Rather then want a Spirit; appear, & pertly.
No tongue: all eyes: be silent.

speeches.speaker: Ir.
verse: Ceres, most bounteous Lady, thy rich Leas
Of Wheate, Rye, Barley, Fetches, Oates and Pease;
Thy Turphie-Mountaines, where liue nibling Sheepe,
And flat Medes thetchd with Stouer, them to keepe:
Thy bankes with pioned, and twilled brims
Which spungie Aprill, at thy hest betrims;
To make cold Nymphes chast crownes; & thy broome-groues;
Whose shadow the dismissed Batchelor loues,
Being lasse-lorne: thy pole-clipt vineyard,
And thy Sea-marge stirrile, and rockey-hard,
Where thou thy selfe do'st ayre, the Queene o' th Skie,
Whose watry Arch, and messenger, am I.
Bids thee leaue these, & with her soueraigne grace,
Here on this grasse-plot, in this very place
To come, and sport: here Peacocks flye amaine:
Approach, rich Ceres, her to entertaine.

speeches.speaker: Cer.
verse: Haile, many-coloured Messenger, that nere
Do'st disobey the wife of Iupiter:
Who, with thy saffron wings, vpon my flowres
Diffusest hony drops, refreshing showres,
And with each end of thy blew bowe do'st crowne
My boskie acres, and my vnshrubd downe,
Rich scarph to my proud earth: why hath thy Queene
Summond me hither, to this short gras'd Greene?

speeches.speaker: Ir.
verse: A contract of true Loue, to celebrate,
And some donation freely to estate
On the bles'd Louers.

speeches.speaker: Cer.
verse: Tell me heauenly Bowe,
If Venus or her Sonne, as thou do'st know,
Doe now attend the Queene? since they did plot
The meanes, that duskie Dis, my daughter got,
Her, and her blind-Boyes scandald company,
I haue forsworne.

speeches.speaker: Ir.
verse: Of her societie
Be not afraid: I met her deitie
Cutting the clouds towards Paphos: and her Son
Doue-drawn with her: here thought they to haue done
Some wanton charme, vpon this Man and Maide,
Whose vowes are, that no bed-right shall be paid
Till Hymens Torch be lighted: but in vaine,
Marses hot Minion is returnd againe,
Her waspish headed sonne, has broke his arrowes,
Swears he will shoote no more, but play with Sparrows,
And be a Boy right out.

speeches.speaker: Cer.
verse: Highest Queene of State,
Great Iuno comes, I know her by her gate.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: How do's my bounteous sister? goe with me
To blesse this twaine, that they may prosperous be,
And honourd in their Issue.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: Honor, riches, marriage, blessing,
Long continuance, and encreasing,
Hourely ioyes, be still vpon you,
Iuno sings her blessings on you.
Earths increase, foyzon plentie,
Barnes, and Garners, neuer empty.
Vines, with clustring bunches growing,
Plants, wtth goodly burthen bowing:
Spring come to you at the farthest,
In the very end of Haruest.
Scarcity and want shall shun you,
Ceres blessing so is on you.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: This is a most maiesticke vision, and
Harmonious charmingly: may I be bold
To thinke these spirits?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Spirits, which by mine Art
I haue from their confines call'd to enact
My present fancies.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Let me liue here euer,
So rare a wondred Father, and a wise
Makes this place Paradise.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Sweet now, silence:
Iuno and Ceres whisper seriously,
There's something else to doe: hush, and be mute
Or else our spell is mar'd.

speeches.speaker: Iris.
verse: You Nimphs cald Nayades of ye windring brooks,
With your sedg'd crownes, and euer-harmelesse lookes,
Leaue your crispe channels, and on this greene-Land

Answere your summons.
Iuno do's command.
Come temperate Nimphes, and helpe to celebrate
A Contract of true Loue: be not too late.
You Sun-burn'd Sicklemen of August weary,
Come hether from the furrow, and be merry,
Make holly day: your Rye-straw hats put on,
And these fresh Nimphes encounter euery one
In Country footing.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I had forgot that foule conspiracy
Of the beast Calliban, and his confederates
Against my life: the minute of their plot
Is almost come: Well done, auoid: no more.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: This is strange: your fathers in some passion
That workes him strongly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Neuer till this day
Saw I him touch'd with anger, so distemper'd.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: You doe looke (my son) in a mou'd sort,
As if you were dismaid: be cheerefull Sir,
Our Reuels now are ended: These our actors,
(As I foretold you) were all Spirits, and
Are melted into Ayre, into thin Ayre,
And like the baselesse fabricke of this vision
The Clowd-capt Towres, the gorgeous Pallaces,
The solemne Temples, the great Globe it selfe,
Yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolue,
And like this insubstantiall Pageant faded
Leaue not a racke behinde: we are such stuffe
As dreames are made on; and our little life
Is rounded with a sleepe: Sir, I am vext,
Beare with my weakenesse, my old braine is troubled:
Be not disturb'd with my infirmitie,
If you be pleas'd, retire into my Cell,
And there repose, a turne or two, Ile walke
To still my beating minde.

speeches.speaker: Fer. Mir.
verse: We wish your peace.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Come with a thought; I thank thee Ariell: come.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Thy thoughts I cleaue to, what's thy pleasure?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Spirit: We must prepare to meet with Caliban.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I my Commander, when I presented Ceres
I thought to haue told thee of it, but I fear'd
Least I might anger thee.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Say again, where didst thou leaue these varlots?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I told you Sir, they were red-hot with drinking,
So full of valour, that they smote the ayre
For breathing in their faces: beate the ground
For kissing of their feete; yet alwaies bending
Towards their proiect: then I beate my Tabor,
At which like vnback't colts they prickt their eares,
Aduanc'd their eye-lids, lifted vp their noses
As they smelt musicke, so I charm'd their eares
That Calfe-like, they my lowing follow'd, through
Tooth'd briars, sharpe firzes, pricking gosse, & thorns,
Which entred their fraile shins: at last I left them
I' th' filthy mantled poole beyond your Cell,
There dancing vp to th' chins, that the fowle Lake
Ore-stunck their feet.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: This was well done (my bird)
Thy shape inuisible retaine thou still:
The trumpery in my house, goe bring it hither
For stale to catch these theeues.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: I go, I goe.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: A Deuill, a borne-Deuill, on whose nature
Nurture can neuer sticke: on whom my paines
Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost,
And, as with age, his body ouglier growes,
So his minde cankers: I will plague them all,
Euen to roaring: Come, hang on them this line.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Pray you tread softly, that the blinde Mole may not heare a foot fall: we now are neere his Cell.

speeches.speaker: St.
verse: Monster, your Fairy, wc you say is a harmles Fairy,
Has done little better then plaid the lacke with vs.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
verse: Monster, I do smell all horse-pisse, at which
My nose is in great indignation.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: So is mine. Do you heare Monster: If I should
Take a displeasure against you: Looke you.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Thou wert but a lost Monster.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Good my Lord, giue me thy fauour stil,
Be patient, for the prize Ile bring thee too
Shall hud winke this mischance: therefore speake softly,
All's husht as midnight yet.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: I, but to loose our bottles in the Poole.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: There is not onely disgrace and dishonor in that Monster, but an infinite losse.

speeches.speaker: Tr.
verse: That's more to me then my wetting:
Yet this is your harmlesse Fairy, Monster.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: I will fetch off my bottle,
Though I be o're eares for my labour.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Pre-thee (my King) be quiet. Seest thou heere
This is the mouth o' th Cell: no noise, and enter:
Do that good mischeefe, which may make this Island
Thine owne for euer, and I thy Caliban
For aye thy foot-licker.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Giue me thy hand,
I do begin to haue bloody thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
verse: O King Stephano, O Peere: O worthy Stephano,
Looke what a wardrobe heere is for thee.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Let it alone thou foole, it is but trash.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Oh, ho, Monster: wee know what belongs to a frippery, O King Stephano.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Put off that gowne (Trinculo) by this hand Ile haue that gowne.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Thy grace shall haue it.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: The dropsie drowne this foole, what doe you meane
To doate thus on such luggage? let's alone
And doe the murther first: if he awake,
From toe to crowne hee'l fill our skins with pinches,
Make vs strange stuffe.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Be you quiet (Monster) Mistris line, is not this my Ierkin? now is the Ierkin vnder the line: now Ierkin you are like to lose your haire, & proue a bald Ierkin.

speeches.speaker: Trin.
prose: Doe, doe; we steale by lyne and leuell, and't like your grace.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: I thank thee for that iest; heer's a garment for't: Wit shall not goe vn-rewarded while I am King of this Country: Steale by line and leuell, is an excellent passe of pate: there's another garment for't.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Monster, come put some Lime vpon your fingers, and away with the rest.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I will haue none on't: we shall loose our time,
And all be turn'd to Barnacles, or to Apes
With foreheads villanous low.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Monster, lay to your fingers: helpe to beare this away, where my hogshead of wine is, or Ile turne you out of my kingdome: goe to, carry this.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: And this.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: I, and this.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Hey Mountaine, hey.

speeches.speaker: Ari.
prose: Siluer: there it goes, Siluer.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Fury, Fury: there Tyrant, there: harke, harke.
Goe, charge my Goblins that they grinde their ioynts
With dry Convultions, shorten vp their sinewes
With aged Cramps, & more pinch-spotted make them,
Then Pard, or Cat o' Mountaine.

speeches.speaker: Ari.
prose: Harke, they rore.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Let them be hunted soundly: At this houre
Lies at my mercy all mine enemies:
Shortly shall all my labours end, and thou
Shalt haue the ayre at freedome: for a little
Follow, and doe me seruice.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Now do's my Proiect gather to a head:
My charmes cracke not: my Spirits obey, and Time
Goes vpright with his carriage: how's the day?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: On the sixt hower, at which time, my Lord
You said our worke should cease.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I did say so,
When first I rais'd the Tempest: say my Spirit,
How fares the King, and's followers?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Confin'd together
In the same fashion, as you gaue in charge,
Iust as you left them; all prisoners Sir
In the Line-groue which weather-fends your Cell,
They cannot boudge till your release: The King,
His Brother, and yours, abide all three distracted,
And the remainder mourning ouer them,
Brim full of sorrow, and dismay: but chiefly
Him that you term'd Sir, the good old Lord Gonzallo,
His teares runs downe his beard like winters drops
From eaues of reeds: your charm so strongly works 'em
That if you now beheld them, your affections
Would become tender.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Dost thou thinke so, Spirit?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Mine would, Sir, were I humane.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: And mine shall.
Hast thou (which art but aire) a touch, a feeling
Of their afflictions, and shall not my selfe,
One of their kinde, that rellish all as sharpely,
Passion as they, be kindlier mou'd then thou art?
Thogh with their high wrongs I am strook to th' quick,
Yet, with my nobler reason, gainst my furie
Doe I take part: the rarer Action is
In vertue, then in vengeance: they, being penitent,
The sole drift of my purpose doth extend
Not a frowne further: Goe, release them Ariell,
My Charmes Ile breake, their sences Ile restore,
And they shall be themselues.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Ile fetch them, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Ye Elues of hils, brooks, sta~ding lakes & groues,
And ye, that on the sands with printlesse foote
Doe chase the ebbing-Neptune, and doe flie him
When he comes backe: you demy-Puppets, that
By Moone-shine doe the greene sowre Ringlets make,
Whereof the Ewe not bites: and you, whose pastime
Is to make midnight-Mushrumps, that reioyce
To heare the solemne Curfewe, by whose ayde
(Weake Masters though ye be) I haue bedymn'd
The Noone-tide Sun, call'd forth the mutenous windes,
And twixt the greene Sea, and the azur'd vault
Set roaring warre: To the dread ratling Thunder
Haue I giuen fire, and rifted Ioues stowt Oke
With his owne Bolt: The strong bass'd promontorie
Haue I made shake, and by the spurs pluckt vp
The Pyne, and Cedar. Graues at my command
Haue wak'd their sleepers, op'd, and let 'em forth
By my so potent Art. But this rough Magicke
I heere abiure: and when I haue requir'd
Some heauenly Musicke (which euen now I do)
To worke mine end vpon their Sences, that
This Ayrie-charme is for, I'le breake my staffe,
Bury it certaine fadomes in the earth,
And deeper then did euer Plummet sound
Ile drowne my booke.
A solemne Ayre, and the best comforter,
To an vnsetled fancie, Cure thy braines
(Now vselesse) boile within thy skull: there stand
For you are Spell-stopt.
Holy Gonzallo, Honourable man,
Mine eyes ev'n sociable to the shew of thine
Fall fellowly drops: The charme dissolues apace,
And as the morning steales vpon the night
(Melting the darkenesse) so their rising sences
Begin to chace the ignorant fumes that mantle
Their cleerer reason. O good Gonzallo
My true preseruer, and a loyall Sir,
To him thou follow'st; I will pay thy graces
Home both in word, and deede: Most cruelly
Did thou Alonso, vse me, and my daughter:
Thy brother was a furtherer in the Act,
Thou art pinch'd for't now Sebastian. Flesh, and bloud,
You, brother mine, that entertaine ambition,
Expelld remorse, and nature, whom, with Sebastian
(Whose inward pinches therefore are most strong)
Would heere haue kill'd your King: I do forgiue thee,
Vnnaturall though thou art: Their vnderstanding
Begins to swell, and the approching tide
Will shortly fill the reasonable shore
That now ly foule, and muddy: not one of them
That yet lookes on me, or would know me: Ariell,
Fetch me the Hat, and Rapier in my Cell,
I will discase me, and my selfe present
As I was sometime Millaine: quickly Spirit,
Thou shalt ere long be free.
Where the Bee sucks, there suck I,
In a Cowslips bell, I lie,
There I cowch when Owles doe crie,
On the Batts backe I doe flie after Sommer merrily.
Merrily, merrily, shall I liue now,
Vnder the blossom that hangs on the Bow.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Why that's my dainty Ariell: I shall misse
Thee, but yet thou shalt haue freedome: so, so, so.
To the Kings ship, inuisible as thou art,
There shalt thou finde the Marriners asleepe
Vnder the Hatches: the Master and the Boat-swaine
Being awake, enforce them to this place;
And presently, I pre'thee.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I drinke the aire before me, and returne
Or ere your pulse twice beate.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: All torment, trouble, wonder, and amazement
Inhabits heere: some heauenly power guide vs
Out of this fearefull Country.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Behold Sir King
The wronged Duke of Millaine, Prospero:
For more assurance that a liuing Prince
Do's now speake to thee, I embrace thy body,
And to thee, and thy Company, I bid
A hearty welcome.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: Where thou bee'st he or no,
Or some inchanted triflle to abuse me,
(As late I haue beene) I not know: thy Pulse
Beats as of flesh, and blood: and since I saw thee,
Th' affliction of my minde amends, with which
I feare a madnesse held me. this must craue
(And if this be at all) a most strange story.
Thy Dukedome I resigne, and doe entreat
Thou pardon me my wrongs: But how shold Prospero
Be liuing and be heere?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: First, noble Frend,
Let me embrace thine age, whose honor cannot
Be measur'd, or confin'd.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Whether this be,
Or be not, I'le not sweare.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: You doe yet taste
Some subtleties o' th' Isle, that will not let you
Beleeue things certaine: Wellcome, my friends all,
But you, my brace of Lords, were I so minded
I heere could plucke his Highnesse frowne vpon you
And iustifie you Traitors: at this time
I will tell no tales.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: The Diuell speakes in him:

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: No:
For you (most wicked Sir) whom to call brother
Would euen infect my mouth, I do forgiue
Thy rankest fault; all of them: and require
My Dukedome of thee, which, perforce I know
Thou must restore.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: If thou beest Prospero
Giue vs particulars of thy preferuation,
How thou hast met vs heere, whom three howres since
Were wrackt vpon this shore? where I haue lost
(How sharp the point of this remembrance is)
My deere sonne Ferdinand.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I am woe for't, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: Irreparable is the losse, and patience
Saies, it is past her cure.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I rather thinke
You haue not sought her helpe, of whose soft grace
For the like losse, I haue her soueraigne aid,
And rest my selfe content.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: You the like losse?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: As great to me, as late, and supportable
To make the deere losse, haue I meanes much weaker
Then you may call to comfort you; for I
Haue lost my daughter.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: A daughter?
Oh heauens, that they were liuing both in Nalpes
The King and Queene there, that they were, I wish
My selfe were mudded in that oo-zie bed
Where my sonne lies: when did you lose your daughter?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: In this last Tempest. I perceiue these Lords
At this encounter doe so much admire,
That they deuoure their reason, and scarce thinke
Their eies doe offices of Truth: Their words
Are naturall breath: but howsoeu'r you haue
Beene iustled from your sences, know for certain
That I am Prospero, and that very Duke
Which was thrust forth of Millaine, who most strangely
Vpon this shore (where you were wrackt) was landed
To be the Lord on't: No more yet of this,
For 'tis a Chronicle of day by day,
Not a relation for a break-fast, nor
Befitting this first meeting: Welcome, Sir;
This Cell's my Court: heere haue I few attendants,
And Subiects none abroad: pray you looke in:
My Dukedome since you haue giuen me againe,
I will requite you with as good a thing,
At least bring forth a wonder, to content ye
As much, as me my Dukedome.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Sweet Lord, you play me false.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: No my dearest loue,
I would not for the world.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, for a score of Kingdomes, you should wrangle,
And I would call it faire play.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: If this proue
A vision of the Island, one deere Sonne
Shall I twice loose.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: A most high miracle.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Though the Seas threaten they are mercifull,
I haue curs'd them without cause.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: Now all the blessings
Of a glad father, compasse thee about:
Arise, and say how thou cam'st heere.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: O wonder!
How many goodly creatures are there heere?
How beauteous mankinde is? O braue new world
That has such people in't.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: 'Tis new to thee.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: What is this Maid, with whom thou was't at play?
Your eld'st acquaintance cannot be three houres:
Is she the goddesse that hath seuer'd vs,
And brought vs thus together?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Sir, she is mortall;
But by immortall prouidence, she's mine;
I chose her when I could not aske my Father
For his aduise: nor thought I had one: She
Is daughter to this famous Duke of Millaine,
Of whom, so often I haue heard renowne,
But neuer saw before: of whom I haue
Receiu'd a second life; and second Father
This Lady makes him to me.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: I am hers.
But O, how odly will it sound, that I
Must aske my childe forgiuenesse?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: There Sir stop,
Let vs not burthen our remembrances, with
A heauinesse that's gon.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: I haue inly wept,
Or should haue spoke ere this: looke downe you gods
And on this couple drop a blessed crowne;
For it is you, that haue chalk'd forth the way
Which brought vs hither.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: I say Amen, Gonzallo.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Was Millaine thrust from Millaine, that his Issue
Should become Kings of Naples? O reioyce
Beyond a common ioy, and set it downe
With gold on lasting Pillers: In one voyage
Did Claribell her husband finde at Tunis,
And Ferdinand her brother, found a wife,
Where he himselfe was lost: Prospero, his Dukedome
In a poore Isle: and all of vs, our selues,
When no man was his owne.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: Giue me your hands:
Let griefe and sorrow still embrace his heart,
That doth not wish you ioy.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Be it so, Amen.
O looke Sir, looke Sir, here is more of vs:
I prophesi'd, if a Gallowes were on Land
This fellow could not drowne: Now blasphemy,
That swear'st Grace ore-boord, not an oath on shore,
Hast thou no mouth by land?
What is the newes?

speeches.speaker: Bot.
verse: The best newes is, that we haue safely found
Our King, and company: The next: our Ship,
Which but three glasses since, we gaue out split,
Is tyte, and yare, and brauely rig'd, as when
We first put out to Sea.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Sir, all this seruice
Haue I done since I went.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: My tricksey Spirit.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: These are not naturall euens, they strengthen
From strange, to stranger: say, how came you hither?

speeches.speaker: Bot.
verse: If I did thinke, Sir, I were well awake,
I'ld striue to tell you: we were dead of sleepe,
And (how we know not) all clapt vnder hatches,
Where, but euen now, with strange, and seuerall noyses
Of roring, shreeking, howling, gingling chaines,
And mo diuersitie of sounds, all horrible.
We were awak'd: straight way, at liberty;
Where we, in all our trim, freshly beheld
Our royall, good, and gallant Ship: our Master
Capring to eye her: on a trice, so please you,
Euen in a dreame, were we diuided from them,
And were brought moaping hither.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Was't well done?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Brauely (my diligence) thou shalt be free.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: This is as strange a Maze, as ere men trod,
And there is in this businesse, more then nature
Was euer conduct of: some Oracle
Must rectifie our knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Sir, my Leige,
Doe not infest your minde, with beating on
The strangenesse of this businesse, at pickt leisure
(Which shall be shortly single) I'le resolue you,
(Which to you shall seeme probable) of euery
These happend accidents: till when, be cheerefull
And thinke of each thing well: Come hither Spirit,
Set Caliban, and his companions free:
Vntye the Spell: How fares my gracious Sir?
There are yet missing of your Companie
Some few odde Lads, that you remember not.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Euery man shift for all the rest, and let
No man take care for himselfe; for all is
But fortune: Coragio Bully-Monster Corasio.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: If these be true spies which I weare in my head, here's a goodly sight.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: O Setebos, these be braue Spirits indeede:
How fine my Master is? I am afraid
He will chastise me.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Ha, ha:
What things are these, my Lord Anthonio?
Will money buy em?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Very like: one of them
Is a plaine Fish, and no doubt marketable.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Marke but the badges of these men, my Lords,
Then say if they be true: This mishapen knaue;
His Mother was a Witch, and one so strong
That could controle the Moone; make flowes, and eb^,
And deale in her command, without her power:
These three haue robd me, and this demy-diuell;
(For he's a bastard one) had plotted with them
To take my life: two of these Fellowes, you
Must know, and owne, this Thing of darkenesse, I
Acknowledge mine.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: I shall be pincht to death.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: Is not this Stephano, my drunken Butler?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: He is drunke now;
Where had he wine?

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: And Trinculo is reeling ripe: where should they
Finde this grand Liquor that hath gilded 'em?
How cam'st thou in this pickle?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: I haue bin in such a pickle since I saw you last,
That I feare me will neuer out of my bones:
I shall not feare fly-blowing.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Who how now Stephano?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: O touch me not, I am not Stephano, but a Cramp.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: You'ld be King o' the Isle, Sirha?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: I should haue bin a sore one then.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: This is a strange thing as ere I look'd on.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: He is as disproportion'd in his Manners
As in his shape: Goe Sirha, to my Cell,
Take with you your Companions: as you looke
To haue my pardon, trim it handsomely.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I that I will: and Ile be wise hereafter,
And seeke for grace: what a thrice double Asse
Was I to take this drunkard for a god?
And worship this dull foole?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Goe to, away.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
prose: Hence, and bestow your luggage where you found it.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Or stole it rather.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Sir, I inuite your Highnesse, and your traine
To my poore Cell: where you shall take your rest
For this one night, which part of it, Ile waste
With such discourse, as I not doubt, shall make it
Goe quicke away. The story of my life,
And the particular accidents, gon by
Since I came to this Isle: And in the morne
I'le bring you to your ship, and so to Naples,
Where I haue hope to see the nuptiall
Of these our deere-belou'd, solemnized,
And thence retire me to my Millaine, where
Euery third thought shall be my graue.

speeches.speaker: Alo.
verse: I long
To heare the story of your life; which must
Take the eare starngely.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I'le deliuer all,
And promise you calme Seas, auspicious gales,
And saile, so expeditious, that shall catch
Your Royall fleete farre off: My Ariel; chicke
That is thy charge: Then to the Elements
Be free, and fare thou well: please you draw neere.

plays.play_title: THE Two Gentlemen of Verona.

speeches.speaker: Valentine.
verse: CEase to perswade. my louing Protheus;
Home-keeping youth; haue euer homely wits,
Wer't not affection chaines thy tender dayes
To the sweet glaunces of thy honour'd Loue,
I rather would entreat thy company,
To see the wonders of the world abroad,
Then (liuing dully sluggardiz'd at home)
Weare out thy youth with shapelesse idlenesse.
But since thou lou'st; loue still, and thriue therein,
Euen as I would, when I to loue begin.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Wilt thou be gone? Sweet Valentine ad ew,
Thinke on thy Protheus, when thou (hap'ly) seest
Some rare note-worthy obiect in thy trauaile.
With me partaker in thy happinesse,
When thou do'st meet good hap; and in thy danger,
(If euer danger doe enuiron thee)
Commend thy grieuance to my holy prayers,
For I will be thy beades-man, Valentine.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: And on a loue-booke pray for my successe?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Vpon some booke I loue, I'le pray for thee.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: That's on some shallow Storie of deepe loue,
How yong Leander crost the Hellespont.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: That's a deepe Storie, of a deeper loue,
For he was more then ouer-shooes in loue.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: 'Tis true; for you are ouer-bootes in loue,
And yet you neuer swom the Hellespont.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Ouer the Bootes? nay giue me not the Boots.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No, I will not; for it boots thee not.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: To be in loue; where scorne is bought with grones:
Coy looks, with hart-sore sighes: one fading moments mirth,
With twenty watchfull, weary, tedious nights;
If hap'ly won, perhaps a haplesse gaine;
If lost, why then a grieuous labour won;
How euer: but a folly bought with wit,
Or else a wit, by folly vanquished.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: So, by your circumstance, you call me foole.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: So, by your circumstance, I feare you'll proue.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: 'Tis Loue you cauill at, I am not Loue.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Loue is your master, for he masters you;
And he that is so yoked by a foole,
Me thinkes should not be chronicled for wise.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Yet Writers say; as in the sweetest Bud,
The eating Canker dwels; so eating Loue
Inhabits in the finest wits of all.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: And Writers say; as the most forward Bud
Is eaten by the Canker ere it blow,
Euen so by Loue, the yong, and tender wit
Is turn'd to folly, blasting in the Bud,
Loosing his verdure, euen in the prime,
And all the faire effects of future hopes.
But wherefore waste I time to counsaile thee
That art a votary to fond desire?
Once more adieu: my Father at the Road
Expects my comming, there to see me ship'd.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: And thither will I bring thee Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Sweet Protheus, no: Now let vs take our leaue:
To Millaine let me heare from thee by Letters
Of thy successe in loue; and what newes else
Betideth here in absence of thy Friend:
And I likewise will visite thee with mine.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: All happinesse be chance to thee in Millaine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: As much to you at home: and so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: He after Honour hunts, I after Loue;
He leaues his friends, to dignifie them more;
I loue my selfe, my friends, and all for loue:

Thou Iulia.
thou hast metamorphis'd me:
Made me neglect my Studies, loose my time;
Warre with good counsaile; set the world at nought;
Made Wit with musing, weake; hart sick with thought.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Sir Protheus: 'saue you: saw you my Master?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But now he parted hence to embarque for Millain.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: Twenty to one then, he is ship'd already,
And I haue plaid the Sheepe in loosing him.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Indeede a Sheepe doth very often stray,
And if the Shepheard be awhile away.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: You conclude that my Master is a Shepheard then, and I Sheepe?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I doe.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Why then my hornes are his hornes, whether I wake or sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: A silly answere, and fitting well a Sheepe.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: This proues me still a Sheepe.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: True: and thy Master a Shepheard.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Nay, that I can deny by a circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: It shall goe hard but ile proue it by another.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: The Shepheard seekes the Sheepe, and not the Sheepe the Shepheard; but I seeke my Master, and my Master seekes not me: therefore I am no Sheepe.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: The Sheepe for fodder follow the Shepheard, the Shepheard for foode followes not the Sheepe: thou for wages followest thy Master, thy Master for wages followes not thee: therefore thou art a Sheepe.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Such another proofe will make me cry baâ.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But do'st thou heare: gau'st thou my Letter to Iulia?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: I Sir: I (a lost-Mutton) gaue your Letter to her (a lac'd-Mutton) and she (a lac'd-Mutton) gaue mee (a lost-Mutton) nothing for my labour.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Here's too small a Pasture for such store of Muttons.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: If the ground be ouer-charg'd, you were best sticke her.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Nay, in that you are astray: 'twere best pound you.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Nay Sir, lesse then a pound shall serue me for carrying your Letter.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: You mistake; I meane the pound, a Pinfold.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: From a pound to a pin? fold it ouer and ouer,
'Tis threefold too little for carrying a letter to your louer

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But what said she?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Nod-I, why that's noddy.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: You mistooke Sir: I say she did nod;
And you aske me if she did nod, and I say I.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: And that set together is noddy.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Now you haue taken the paines to set it together, take it for your paines.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: No, no, you shall haue it for bearing the letter.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Well, I perceiue I must be faine to beare with you.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Why Sir, how doe you beare with me?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: Marry Sir, the letter very orderly,
Hauing nothing but the word noddy for my paines.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Beshrew me, but you haue a quicke wit.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: And yet it cannot ouer-take your slow purse.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Come, come, open the matter in briefe; what said she.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Open your purse, that the money, and the matter may be both at once deliuered.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Well Sir: here is for your paines: what said she?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Truely Sir, I thinke you'll hardly win her.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Why? could'st thou perceiue so much from her?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: Sir, I could perceiue nothing at all from her;
No, not so much as a ducket for deliuering your letter:
And being so hard to me, that brought your minde;
I feare she'll proue as hard to you in telling your minde.
Giue her no token but stones, for she's as hard as steele.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What said she, nothing?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: No, not so much as take this for thy pains:
To testifie your bounty, I thank you, you haue cestern'd me;
In requital whereof, henceforth, carry your letters your selfe; And so Sir, I'le commend you to my Master.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Go, go, be gone, to saue your Ship from wrack,
Which cannot perish hauing thee aboarde,
Being destin'd to a drier death on shore:
I must goe send some better Messenger,
I feare my Iulia would not daigne my lines,
Receiuing them from such a worthlesse post.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: But say Lucetta (now we are alone)
Would'st thou then counsaile me to fall in loue?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I Madam, so you stumble not on heedfully.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Of all the faire rest^ of Gentlemen,
That euery day with par'd^ encounter me,
In thy opinion which is worthiest loue?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Please you repeat their names, ile shew my minde,
According to my shallow simple skill.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: What thinkst thou of the faire sir Eglamoure?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: As of a Knight, well-spoken, neat, and fine;
But were I you, he neuer should be mine.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: What think'st thou of the rich Mercatio?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Well of his wealth; but of himselfe, so, so.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: What think'st thou of the gentle Protheus?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Lord, Lord: to see what folly raignes in vs.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: How now? what meanes this passion at his name?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Pardon deare Madam, 'tis a passing shame,
That I (vnworthy body as I am)
Should censure thus on louely Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Why not on Protheus, as of all the rest?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Then thus: of many good, I thinke him best.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Your reason?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: I haue no other but a womans reason:
I thinke him so, because I thinke him so.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: And would'st thou haue me cast my loue on him?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: I: if you thought your loue not cast away.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Why he, of all the rest, hath neuer mou'd me.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Yet he, of all the rest, I thinke best loues ye.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: His little speaking, shewes his loue but small.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Fire that's closest kept, burnes most of all.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: They doe not loue, that doe not shew their loue.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Oh, they loue least, that let men know their loue.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I would I knew his minde.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Peruse this paper Madam.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: To Iulia: say, from whom?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: That the Contents will shew.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Say, say: who gaue it thee?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Sir Valentines page: & sent I think from Protheus;
He would haue giuen it you, but I being in the way,
Did in your name receiue it: pardon the fault I pray.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Now (by my modesty) a goodly Broker:
Dare you presume to harbour wanton lines?
To whisper, and conspire against my youth?
Now trust me, 'tis an office of great worth,
And you an officer fit for the place:
There: take the paper: see it be return'd,
Or else returne no more into my sight.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: To plead for loue, deserues more fee, then hate.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Will ye be gon?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: That you may ruminate.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And yet I would I had ore-look'd the Letter;
It were a shame to call her backe againe,
And pray her to a fault, for which I chid her.
What 'foole is she, that knowe^ I am a Maid.
And would not force the letter to my view?
Since Maides, in modesty, say no, to that,
Which they would haue the profferer construe, I.
Fie, fie: how way-ward is this foolish loue;
That (like a testie Babe) will scratch the Nurse,
And presently, all humbled kisse the Rod?
How churlishly, I chid Lucetta hence,
When willingly, I would haue had her here?
How angerly I taught my brow to frowne,
When inward ioy enforc'd my heart to smile?
My pennance is, to call Lucetta backe
And aske remission, for my folly past.
What hoe: Lucetta.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: What would your Ladiship?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Is't neere dinner time?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: I would it were,
That you might kill your stomacke on your meat,
And not vpon your Maid.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: What is't that you
Tooke vp so gingerly?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Nothing.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Why didst thou stoope then?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: To take a paper vp, that I let fall.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: And is that paper nothing?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Nothing concerning me.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Then let it lye, for those that it concernes.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Madam, it will not lye where it concernes,
Vnlesse it haue a false Interpreter.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Some loue of yours, hath writ to you in Rime.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: That I might sing it (Madam) to a tune:
Giue me a Note, your Ladiship can set

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: As little by such toyes, as may be possible:
Best sing it to the tune of Light O, Loue.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: It is too heauy for so light a tune.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Heauy? belike it hath some burden then?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: I: and melodious were it, would you sing it,

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: And why not you?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: I cannot reach so high.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: Let's see your Song:
How now Minion?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Keepe tune there still; so you will sing it out:
And yet me thinkes I do not like this tune.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: You doe not?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: No (Madam) tis too sharpe.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: You (Minion) are too saucie.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Nay, now you are too flat;
And marre the concord, with too harsh a descant:
There wanteth but a Meane to fill your Song.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: The meane is dround with you vnruly base.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Indeede I bid the base for Protheus.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: This babble shall not henceforth trouble me;
Here is a coile with protestation:
Goe, get you gone: and let the papers lye:
You would be fingring them, to anger me.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: She makes it stra~ge, but she would be best pleas'd
To be so angred with another Letter.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: Nay, would I were so angred with the same:
Oh hatefull hands, to teare such louing words;
Iniurious Waspes, to feede on such sweet hony,
And kill the Bees that yeelde it, with your stings;
Ile kisse each seuerall paper, for amends:
Looke, here is writ, kinde Iulia: vnkinde Iulia,
As in reuenge of thy ingratitude,
I throw thy name against the bruzing-stones,
Trampling contemptuously on thy disdaine.
And here is writ, Loue wounded Protheus.
Poore wounded name: my bosome, as a bed,
Shall lodge thee till thy wound be throughly heal'd;
And thus I search it with a soueraigne kisse.
But twice, or thrice, was Protheus written downe:
Be calme (good winde) blow not a word away,
Till I haue found each letter, in the Letter,
Except mine own name: That, some whirle-winde beare
Vnto a ragged, fearefull, hanging Rocke,
And throw it thence into the raging Sea.
Loe, here in one line is his name twice writ:
Poore forlorne Protheus, passionate Protheus:
To the sweet Iulia: that ile teare away:
And yet I will not, sith so prettily
He couples it, to his complaining Names;
Thus will I fold them, one vpon another;
Now kisse, embrace, contend, doe what you will.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Madam: dinner is ready: and your father staies.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Well, let vs goe.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: What, shall these papers lye, like Tel-tales here?

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: If you respect them; best to take them vp.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Nay, I was taken vp, for laying them downe.
Yet here they shall not lye, for catching cold.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: I see you haue a months minde to them.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: I (Madam) you may say what sights you see;
I see things too, although you iudge I winke.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Come, come, wilt please you goe.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Tell me Panthino, what sad talke was that,
Wherewith my brother held you in the Cloyster?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: 'Twas of his Nephew Protheus, your Sonne.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why? what of him?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: He wondred that your Lordship
Would suffer him, to spend his youth at home,
While other men, of slender reputation
Put forth their Sonnes, to seeke preferment out.
Some to the warres, to try their fortune there;
Some, to discouer Islands farre away:
Some, to the studious Vniuersities;
For any, or for all these exercises,
He said, that Protheus, your sonne, was meet;
And did request me, to importune you
To let him spend his time no more at home;
Which would be great impeachment to his age,
In hauing knowne no trauaile in his youth.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nor need'st thou much importune me to that
Whereon, this month I haue bin hamering.
I haue consider'd well, his losse of time,
And how he cannot be a perfect man,
Not being tryed, and tutord in the world:
Experience is by industry atchieu'd,
And perfected by the swift course of time:
Then tell me, whether were I best to send him?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I thinke your Lordship is not ignorant
How his companion, youthfull Valentine,
Attends the Emperour in his royall Court.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I know it well.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: 'Twere good, I thinke, your Lordship sent him thither,
There shall he practise Tilts, and Turnaments;
Heare sweet discourse, conuerse with Noble-men,
And be in eye of euery Exercise
Worthy his youth, and noblenesse of birth.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I like thy counsaile: well hast thou aduis'd:
And that thou maist perceiue how well I like it,
The execution of it shall make knowne;
Euen with the speediest expedition,
I will dispatch him to the Emperors Court.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: To morrow, may it please you, Don Alphonso,
With other Gentlemen of good esteeme
Are iournying, to salute the Emperor,
And to commend their seruice to his will.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Good company: with them shall Protheus go:
And in good time: now will we breake with him.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Sweet Loue, sweet lines, sweet life,
Here is her hand, the agent of her heart;
Here is her oath for loue, her honors paune;
O that our Fathers would applaud our loues
To seale our happinesse with their consents.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Oh heauenly Iulia.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: How now? What Letter are you reading there?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: May't please your Lordship, 'tis a word or two
Of commendations sent from Valentine;
Deliuer'd by a friend, that came from him.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Lend me the Letter: Let me see what newes.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: There is no newes (my Lord) but that he writes
How happily he liues, how well-belou'd,
And daily graced by the Emperor;
Wishing me with him, partner of his fortune.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: And how stand you affected to his wish?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: As one relying on your Lordships will,
And not depending on his friendly wish.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: My will is something sorted with his wish:
Muse not that I thus sodainly proceed;
For what I will, I will, and there an end:
I am resolu'd, that thou shalt spend some time
With Valentinus, in the Emperors Court:
What maintenance he from his friends receiues,
Like exhibition thou shalt haue from me,
To morrow be in readinesse, to goe,
Excuse it not: for I am peremptory.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: My Lord I cannot be so soone prouided,
Please you deliberate a day or two.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Look what thou want'st shalbe sent after thee:
No more of stay: to morrow thou must goe;
Come on Panthino; you shall be imployd,
To hasten on his Expedition.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Thus haue I shund the fire, for feare of burning,
And drench'd me in the sea, where I am drown'd.
I fear'd to shew my Father Iulias Letter,
Least he should take exceptions to my loue,
And with the vantage of mine owne excuse
Hath he excepted most against my loue.
Oh, how this spring of loue resembleth
The vncertaine glory of an Aprill day,
Which now shewes all the beauty of the Sun,
And by and by a clowd takes all away.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Sir Protheus, your Fathers call's for you,
He is in hast, therefore I pray you go.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Why this it is: my heart accords thereto,
And yet a thousand times it answer's no.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Sir, your Gloue.

speeches.speaker: Valen.
prose: Not mine: my Gloues are on.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Why then this may be yours: for this is but one.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Ha? Let me see: I, giue it me, it's mine:
Sweet Ornament, that deckes a thing diuine,
Ah Siluia, Siluia.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Madam Siluia: Madam Siluia.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How now Sirha?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Shee is not within hearing Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why sir, who had you call her?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Your worship s^, or else I mistooke.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Well: you'll still be too forward.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: And yet I was last chidden for being too slow.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Goe to, sir, tell me: do you know Madam Siluia?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Shee that your worship loues?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why, how know you that I am in loue?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Marry by these speciall markes: first, you haue learn'd (like Sir Protheus) to wreath your Armes like a Male-content: to rellish a Loue-song, like a Robin-red-breast: to walke alone like one that had the pestilence: to sigh, like a Schoole-boy that had lost his A. B. C. to weep like a yong wench that had buried her Grandam: to fast, like one that takes diet: to watch, like one that feares robbing: to speake puling, like a beggar at Hallow-Masse: You were wont, when you laughed, to crow like a cocke; when you walk'd, to walke like one of the Lions: when you fasted, it was presently after dinner: when you look'd sadly, it was for want of money: And now you are Metamorphis'd with a Mistris, that when I looke on you, I can hardly thinke you my Master.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Are all these things perceiu'd in me?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: They are all perceiu'd without ye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Without me? they cannot.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Without you? nay, that's certaine: for without you were so simple, none else would: but you are so without these follies, that these follies are within you, and shine through you like the water in an Vrinall: that not an eye that sees you, but is a Physician to comment on your Malady.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: But tell me: do'st thou know my Lady Siluia?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Shee that you gaze on so, as she sits at supper?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Hast thou obseru'd that? euen she I meane.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Why sir, I know her not.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Do'st thou know her by my gazing on her, and yet know'st her not?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Is she not hard-fauour'd, sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not so faire (boy) as well fauour'd.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Sir, I know that well enough.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: What dost thou know?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: That shee is not so faire, as (of you) well-fauourd?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I meane that her beauty is exquisite,
But her fauour infinite.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: That's because the one is painted, and the other out of all count.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How painted? and how out of count?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Marry sir, so painted to make her faire, that no man counts of her beauty.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How esteem'st thou me? I account of her beauty.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: You neuer saw her since she was deform'd.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: How long hath she beene deform'd?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Euer since you lou'd her.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I haue lou'd her euer since I saw her,
And still I see her beautifull.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: If you loue her, you cannot see her.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Because Loue is blinde: O that you had mine eyes, or your owne eyes had the lights they were wont to haue, when you chidde at Sir Protheus, for going vngarter'd.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What should I see then?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Your owne present folly, and her passing deformitie: for hee beeing in loue, could not see to garter his hose; and you, beeing in loue, cannot see to put on your hose.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Belike (boy) then you are in loue, for last morning
You could not see to wipe my shooes.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose:
True sir: I was in loue with my bed, I thanke you, you swing'd me for my loue, which makes mee the

bolder to chide you, for yours.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: In conclusion, I stand affected to her.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: I would you were set, so your affection would cease.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Last night she enioyn'd me,
To write some lines to one she loues.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: And haue you?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: I haue.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Are they not lamely writt?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: No (Boy) but as well as I can do them:
Peace, here she comes.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
verse: Oh excellent motion; oh exceeding Puppet:
Now will he interpret to her.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Madam & Mistres, a thousand good-morrows.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Oh, 'giue ye-good-ev'n: heer's a million of manners.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Sir Valentine, and seruant, to you two thousand.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: He should giue her interest: & she giues it him.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: As you inioynd me; I haue writ your Letter
Vnto the secret, nameles friend of yours:
Which I was much vnwilling to proceed in,
But for my duty to your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: I thanke you (gentle Seruant) 'tis very Clerkly-done.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Now trust me (Madam) it came hardly-off:
For being ignorant to whom it goes,
I writ at randome, very doubtfully.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Perchance you think too much of so much pains?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No (Madam) so it steed you I will write (Please you command) a thousand times as much: And yet —

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: A pretty period: well: I ghesse the sequell;
And yet I will not name it: and yet I care not.
And yet, take this againe: and yet I thanke you:
Meaning henceforth to trouble you no more.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: And yet you will: and yet, another yet.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: What meanes your Ladiship?
Doe you not like it?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Yes, yes: the lines are very queintly writ,
But (since vnwillingly) take them againe.
Nay, take them.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Madam, they are for you.

speeches.speaker: Silu.
verse: I, I: you writ them Sir, at my request,
But I will none of them: they are for you:
I would haue had them writ more mouingly:

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Please you, Ile write your Ladiship another.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: And when it's writ: for my sake read it ouer,
And if it please you, so: if not: why so:

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: If it please me, (Madam?) what then?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Why if it please you, take it for your labour;
And so good-morrow Seruant.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
verse: Oh Iest vnseene: inscrutible: inuisible,
As a nose on a mans face, or a Wethercocke on a steeple:
My Master sues to her: and she hath taught her Sutor,
He being her Pupill, to become her Tutor.
Oh excellent deuise, was there euer heard a better?
That my master being scribe,
To himselfe should write the Letter?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: How now Sir?
What are you reasoning with your selfe?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Nay: I was riming: 'tis you yt haue the reason.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: To doe what?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: To be a Spokes-man from Madam Siluia.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: To whom?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: To your selfe: why, she woes you by a figure.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What figure?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: By a Letter, I should say.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: Why she hath not writ to me?

speeches.speaker: Speed.
verse: What need she,
When shee hath made you write to your selfe?
Why, doe you not perceiue the iest?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No, beleeue me.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
verse: No beleeuing you indeed sir:
But did you perceiue her earnest?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: She gaue me none, except an angry word.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Why she hath giuen you a Letter.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: That's the Letter I writ to her friend.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: And yt letter hath she deliuer'd, & there an end.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I would it were no worse.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
verse: Ile warrant you, 'tis as well:
For often haue you writ to her: and she in modesty,
Or else for want of idle time, could not againe reply,
Or fearing els some messe~ger, yt might her mind discouer
Her self hath taught her Loue himself, to write vnto her louer.
All this I speak in print, for in print I found it.
Why muse you sir, 'tis dinner time.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: I haue dyn'd.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: I, but hearken sir: though the Cameleon Loue can feed on the ayre, I am one that am nourish'd by my victuals; and would faine haue meate: oh bee not like your Mistresse, be moued, be moued.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Haue patience, gentle Iulia:

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I must where is no remedy.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: When possibly I can, I will returne.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: If you turne not: you will return the sooner:
Keepe this remembrance for thy Iulia's sake.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Why then wee'll make exchange;
Here, take you this.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: And seale the bargaine with a holy kisse.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Here is my hand, for my true constancie:
And when that howre ore-slips me in the day,
Wherein I sigh not (Iulia) for thy sake,
The next ensuing howre, some foule mischance
Torment me for my Loues forgetfulnesse:
My father staies my comming: answere not:
The tide is now: nay, not thy tide of teares,
That tide will stay me longer then I should,
Iulia, farewell: what, gon without a word?
I, so true loue should doe: it cannot speake,
For truth hath better deeds, then words to grace it.

speeches.speaker: Panth.
prose: Sir Protheus: you are staid for.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Goe: I come, I come:
Alas, this parting strikes poore Louers dumbe.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose:
Nay, 'twill bee this howre ere I haue done weeping: all the kinde of the Launce^, haue this very fault: I haue receiu'd my proportion, like the prodigious

Sonne, and am going with Sir Protheus to the Imperialls Court: I thinke Crab my dog, be the sowrest natured dogge that liues: My Mother weeping: my Father wayling: my Sister crying: our Maid howling: our Catte wringing her hands, and all our house in a great perplexitie, yet did not this cruell-hearted Curre shedde one teare: he is a stone, a very pibble stone, and has no more pitty in him then a dogge: a Iew would haue wept to haue seene our parting: why my Grandam hauing no eyes, looke you, wept her selfe blinde at my parting: nay, Ile shew you the manner of it. This shooe is my father: no, this left shooe is my father; no, no, this left shooe is my mother: nay, that cannot bee so neyther: yes; it is so, it is so: it hath the worser sole: this shooe with the hole in it, is my mother: and this my father: a veng'ance on't, there 'tis: Now sir, this staffe is my sister: for, looke you, she is as white as a lilly, and as small as a wand: this hat is Nan our maid: I am the dogge: no, the dogge is himselfe, and I am the dogge: oh, the dogge is me, and I am my selfe: I; so, so: now come I to my Father; Father, your blessing: now should not the shooe speake a word for weeping: now should I kisse my Father; well, hee weepes on: Now come I to my Mother: Oh that she could speake now, like a would-woman: well, I kisse her: why there 'tis; heere's my mothers breath vp and downe: Now come I to my sister; marke the moane she makes: now the dogge all this while sheds not a teare: nor speakes a word: but see how I lay the dust with my teares.

speeches.speaker: Panth.
prose: Launce, away, away: a Boord: thy Master is ship'd, and thou art to post after with oares; what's the matter? why weep'st thou man? away asse, you'l loose the Tide, if you tarry any longer.

speeches.speaker: Laun.
prose: It is no matter if the tide were lost, for it is the vnkindest Tide, that euer any man tide.

speeches.speaker: Panth.
prose: What's the vnkindest tide?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Why, he that's tide here, Crab my dog.

speeches.speaker: Pant.
prose: Tut, man: I meane thou'lt loose the flood, and in loosing the flood, loose thy voyage, and in loosing thy voyage, loose thy Master, and in loosing thy Master, loose thy seruice, and in loosing thy seruice: — why dost thou stop my mouth?

speeches.speaker: Laun.
prose: For feare thou shouldst loose thy tongue.

speeches.speaker: Panth.
prose: Where should I loose my tongue?

speeches.speaker: Laun.
prose: In thy Tale.

speeches.speaker: Panth.
prose: In thy Taile.

speeches.speaker: Laun.
prose: Loose the Tide, and the voyage, and the Master, and the Seruice, and the tide: why man, if the Riuer were drie, I am able to fill it with my teares: if the winde were downe, I could driue the boate with my sighes.

speeches.speaker: Panth.
prose: Come: come away man, I was sent to call thee.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Sir: call me what thou dar'st.

speeches.speaker: Pant.
prose: Wilt thou goe?

speeches.speaker: Laun.
prose: Well, I will goe.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Seruant.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: Master, Sir Thurio frownes on you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I Boy, it's for loue.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: Not of you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Of my Mistresse then.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: 'Twere good you knockt him.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Seruant, you are sad.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Indeed, Madam, I seeme so.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Seeme you that you are not?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Hap'ly I doe.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: So doe Counterfeyts.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: So doe you.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: What seeme I that I am not?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Wise.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: What instance of the contrary?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Your folly.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: And how quoat you my folly?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: I quoat it in your Ierkin.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: My Ierkin is a doublet.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Well then, Ile double your folly.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: What, angry, Sir Thurio, do you change colour?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Giue him leaue, Madam, he is a kind of Camelion.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: That hath more minde to feed on your bloud, then liue in your ayre.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: You haue said Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: I Sir, and done too for this time.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I know it wel sir, you alwaies end ere you begin.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: A fine volly of words, gentleme~, & quickly shot off

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'Tis indeed, Madam, we thank the giuer.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Who is that Seruant?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Your selfe (sweet Lady) for you gaue the fire,
Sir Thurio borrows his wit from your Ladiships lookes,
And spends what he borrowes kindly in your company

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Sir, if you spend word for word with me, I shall make your wit bankrupt.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I know it well sir: you haue an Exchequer of words,
And I thinke, no other treasure to giue your followers:
For it appeares by their bare Liueries
That they liue by your bare words.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: No more, gentlemen, no more:
Here comes my father.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Now, daughter Siluia, you are hard beset.
Sir Valentine, your father is in good health,
What say you to a Letter from your friends
Of much good newes?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: My Lord, I will be thankfull,
To any happy messenger from thence.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Know ye Don Antonio, your Countriman?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I, my good Lord, I know the Gentleman
To be of worth, and worthy estimation,
And not without desert so well reputed.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Hath he not a Sonne?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: I, my good Lord, a Son, that well deserues
The honor, and regard of such a father.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: You know him well?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: I knew him as my selfe: for from our Infancie
We haue conuerst, and spent our howres together,
And though my selfe haue beene an idle Trewant,
Omitting the sweet benefit of time
To cloath mine age with Angel-like perfection:
Yet hath Sir Protheus (for that's his name)
Made vse, and faire aduantage of his daies:
His yeares but yong, but his experience old:
His head vn-mellowed, but his Iudgement ripe;
And in a word (for far behinde his worth
Comes all the praises that I now bestow.)
He is compleat in feature, and in minde,
With all good grace, to grace a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Beshrew me sir, but if he make this good
He is as worthy for an Empresse loue,
As meet to be an Emperors Councellor:
Well, Sir: this Gentleman is come to me
With Commendation from great Potentates,
And heere he meanes to spend his time a while,
I thinke 'tis no vn-welcome newes to you.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: Should I haue wish'd a thing, it had beene he.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Welcome him then according to his worth:
Siluia, I speake to you, and you Sir Thurio,

For
~alentine, I need not cite him to it,
I will send him hither to you presently.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: This is the Gentleman I told your Ladiship
Had come along with me, but that his Mistresse
Did hold his eyes, lockt in her Christall lookes.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Be-like that now she hath enfranchis'd them
Vpon some other pawne for fealty.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Nay sure, I thinke she holds them prisoners stil.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Nay then he should be blind, and being blind
How could he see his way to seeke out you?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: Why Lady, Loue hath twenty paire of eyes.

speeches.speaker: Thur.
prose: They say that Loue hath not an eye at all.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: To see such Louers, Thurio, as your selfe,
Vpon a homely obiect, Loue can winke.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Haue done, haue done: here comes ye gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Welcome, deer Protheus: Mistris, I beseech you
Confirme his welcome, with some speciall fauor.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: His worth is warrant for his welcome hether,
If this be he you oft haue wish'd to heare from.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Mistris, it is: sweet Lady, entertaine him
To be my fellow-seruant to your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Too low a Mistres for so high a seruant.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Not so, sweet Lady, but too meane a seruant
To haue a looke of such a worthy a Mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Leaue off discourse of disabilitie:
Sweet Lady, entertaine him for your Seruant.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: My dutie will I boast of, nothing else.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: And dutie neuer yet did want his meed.
Seruant, you are welcome to a worthlesse Mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Ile die on him that saies so but your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: That you are welcome?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: That you are worthlesse.

speeches.speaker: Thur.
prose: Madam, my Lord your father wold speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I wait vpon his pleasure: Come Sir Thurio,
Goe with me: once more, new Seruant welcome;
Ile leaue you to confer of home affaires,
When you haue done, we looke too heare from you.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Wee'll both attend vpon your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Now tell me: how do al from whence you came?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Your frends are wel, & haue the~ much co~mended.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And how doe yours?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I left them all in health.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How does your Lady? & how thriues your loue?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: My tales of Loue were wont to weary you,
I know you ioy not in a Loue-discourse.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I Protheus, but that life is alter'd now,
I haue done pennance for contemning Loue,
Whose high emperious thoughts haue punish'd me
With bitter fasts, with penitentiall grones,
With nightly teares, and daily hart-sore sighes,
For in reuenge of my contempt of loue,
Loue hath chas'd sleepe from my enthralled eyes,
And made them watchers of mine owne hearts sorrow.
O gentle Protheus, Loue's a mighty Lord,
And hath so humbled me, as I confesse
There is no woe to his correction,
Nor to his Seruice, no such ioy on earth:
Now, no discourse, except it be of loue:
Now can I breake my fast, dine, sup, and sleepe,
Vpon the very naked name of Loue.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Enough; I read your fortune in your eye:
Was this the Idoll, that you worship so?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Euen She; and is she not a heauenly Saint?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: No; But she is an earthly Paragon.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Call her diuine.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I will not flatter her.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: O flatter me: for Loue delights in praises.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: When I was sick, you gaue me bitter pils,
And I must minister the like to you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Then speake the truth by her; if not diuine,
Yet let her be a principalitie,
Soueraigne to all the Creatures on the earth,

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Except my Mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Sweet: except not any,
Except thou wilt except against my Loue.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Haue I not reason to prefer mine owne?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: And I will help thee to prefer her to:
Shee shall be dignified with this high honour,
To beare my Ladies traine, left the base earth
Should from her vesture chance to steale a kisse,
And of so great a fauor growing proud,
Disdaine to roote the Sommer-swelling flowre,
And make rough winter euerlastingly.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose:
Why
~alentine, what Bragadisme is this?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Pardon me (Protheus) all I can is nothing,
To her, whose worth, make other worthies nothing;
Shee is alone.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Then let her alone.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Not for the world: why man, she is mine owne,
And I as rich in hauing such a Iewell
As twenty Seas, if all their sand were pearle,
The water, Nectar, and the Rocks pure gold.
Forgiue me that I doe not dreame on thee,
Because thou seest me doate vpon my loue:
My foolish Riuall that her Father likes
(Onely for his possessions are so huge)
Is gone with her along, and I must after,
For Loue (thou know'st is full of iealousie.)

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But she loues you?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I, and we are betroathd: nay more, our mariage howre,
With all the cunning manner of our flight
Determin'd of: how I must climbe her window,
The Ladder made of Cords, and all the means
Plotted, and 'greed on for my happinesse.
Good Protheus goe with me to my chamber,
In these affaires to aid me with thy counsaile.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Goe on before: I shall enquire you forth:
I must vnto the Road, to dis-embarque
Some necessaries, that I needs must vse,
And then Ile presently attend you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Will you make haste?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I will.
Euen as one heate, another heate expels,
Or as one naile, by strength driues out another.
So the remembrance of my former Loue
Is by a newer obiect quite forgotten,
It is mine, or Valentines praise?
Her true perfection, or my false transgression?
That makes me reasonlesse, to reason thus?
Shee is faire: and so is Iulia that I loue,
(That I did loue, for now my loue is thaw'd,
Which like a waxen Image 'gainst a fire
Beares no impression of the thing it was.)
Me thinkes my zeale to Valentine is cold,
And that I loue him not as I was wont:
O, but I loue his Lady too-too much,
And that's the reason I loue him so little.
How shall I doate on her with more aduice,
That thus without aduice begin to loue her?
'Tis but her picture I haue yet beheld,
And that hath dazel'd my reasons light:
But when I looke on her perfections,
There is no reason, but I shall be blinde.
If I can checke my erring loue, I will,
If not, to compasse her Ile vse my skill.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Launce, by mine honesty welcome to Padua.

speeches.speaker: Laun.
prose: Forsweare not thy selfe, sweet youth, for I am not welcome. I reckon this alwaies, that a man is neuer vndon till hee be hang'd, nor neuer welcome to a place, till some certaine shot be paid, and the Hostesse say welcome.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: Come-on you mad-cap: Ile to the Ale-house with you presently; where, for one shot of fiue pence, thou shalt haue fiue thousand welcomes: But sirha, how did thy Master part with Madam Iulia?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Marry after they cloas'd in earnest, they parted very fairely in iest.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: But shall she marry him?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: How then? shall he marry her?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: No, neither.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: What, are they broken?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: No; they are both as whole as a fish.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: Why then, how stands the matter with them?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Marry thus, when it stands well with him, it stands well with her.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: What an asse art thou, I vnderstand thee not.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
verse: What a blocke art thou, that thou canst not?
My staffe vnderstands me?

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: What thou saist?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: I, and what I do too: looke thee, Ile but leane, and my staffe vnderstands me.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: It stands vnder thee indeed.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Why, stand-vnder: and vnder-stand is all one.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: But tell me true, wil't be a match?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Aske my dogge, if he say I, it will: if hee say no, it will: if hee shake his taile, and say nothing, it will.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: The conclusion is then, that it will.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Thou shalt neuer get such a secret from me, but by a parable.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: 'Tis well that I get it so: but Launce, how saist thou that that my master is become a notable Louer?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: I neuer knew him otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: Then how?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: A notable Lubber: as thou reportest him to bee.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: Why, thou whorson Asse, thou mistak'st me,

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Why Foole, I meant not thee, I meant thy Master.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: I tell thee, my Master is become a hot Louer.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
