prose: Why, I tell thee, I care not, though hee burne himselfe in Loue. If thou wilt goe with me to the Ale-house: if not, thou art an Hebrew, a Iew, and not worth the name of a Christian.

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Because thou hast not so much charity in thee as to goe to the Ale with a Christian: Wilt thou goe?

speeches.speaker: Spee.
prose: At thy seruice.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: To leaue my Iulia; shall I be forsworne?
To loue faire Siluia; shall I be forsworne?
To wrong my friend, I shall be much forsworne.
And ev'n that Powre which gaue me first my oath
Prouokes me to this three-fold periurie.
Loue bad mee sweare, and Loue bids me for-sweare;
O sweet-suggesting Loue, if thou hast sin'd,
Teach me (thy tempted subiect) to excuse it.
At first I did adore a twinkling Starre,
But now I worship a celestiall Sunne:
Vn-heedfull vowes may heedfully be broken,
And he wants wit, that wants resolued will,
To learne his wit, t' exchange the bad for better;
Fie, fie, vnreuerend tongue, to call her bad,
Whose soueraignty so oft thou hast preferd,
With twenty thousand soule-confirming oathes.
I cannot leaue to loue; and yet I doe:
But there I leaue to loue, where I should loue.
Iulia I loose, and Valentine I loose,
If I keepe them, I needs must loose my selfe:
If I loose them, thus finde I by their losse,
For Valentine, my selfe: for Iulia, Siluia.
I to my selfe am deerer then a friend,
For Loue is still most precious in it selfe,
And Siluia (witnesse heauen that made her faire)
Shewes Iulia but a swarthy Ethiope.
I will forget that Iulia is aliue,
Remembring that my Loue to her is dead.

And
~alentine Ile hold an Enemie,
Ayming at Siluia as a sweeter friend.
I cannot now proue constant to my selfe,
Without some treachery vs'd to Valentine.
This night he meaneth with a Corded-ladder
To climbe celestiall Siluia's chamber window,
My selfe in counsaile his competitor.
Now presently Ile giue her father notice
Of their disguising and pretended flight:
Who (all inrag'd) will banish Valentine:
For Thurio he intends shall wed his daughter,
But Valentine being gon, Ile quickely crosse
By some slie tricke, blunt Thurio's dull proceeding.
Loue lend me wings, to make my purpose swift
As thou hast lent me wit, to plot this drift.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Counsaile, Lucetta, gentle girle assist me,
And eu'n in kinde loue, I doe coniure thee,
Who art the Table wherein all my thoughts
Are visibly Character'd, and engrau'd,
To lesson me, and tell me some good meane
How with my honour I may vndertake
A iourney to my louing Protheus.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Alas, the way is wearisome and long.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: A true-deuoted Pilgrime is not weary
To measure Kingdomes with his feeble steps,
Much lesse shall she that hath Loues wings to flie,
And when the flight is made to one so deere,
Of such diuine perfection as Sir Protheus.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Better forbeare, till Protheus make returne.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Oh, know'st yu not, his looks are my soules food?
Pitty the dearth that I haue pined in,
By longing for that food so long a time.
Didst thou but know the inly touch of Loue,
Thou wouldst as soone goe kindle fire with snow
As seeke to quench the fire of Loue with words.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I doe not seeke to quench your Loues hot fire,
But qualifie the fires extreame rage,
Lest it should burne aboue the bounds of reason.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: The more thou dam'st it vp, the more it burnes:
The Current that with gentle murmure glides
(Thou know'st) being stop'd, impatiently doth rage:
But when his faire course is not hindered,
He makes sweet musicke with th' enameld stones,
Giuing a gentle kisse to euery sedge
He ouer-taketh in his pilgrimage.
And so by many winding nookes he straies
With willing sport to the wilde Ocean.
Then let me goe, and hinder not my course:
Ile be as patient as a gentle streame,
And make a pastime of each weary step,
Till the last step haue brought me to my Loue,
And there Ile rest, as after much turmoile
A blessed soule doth in Elizium.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: But in what habit will you goe along?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Not like a woman, for I would preuent
The loose encounters of lasciuious men:
Gentle Lucetta, fit me with such weedes
As may beseeme some well reputed Page.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Why then your Ladiship must cut your haire.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: No girle, Ile knit it vp in silken strings,
With twentie od-conceited true-loue knots:
To be fantastique, may become a youth
Of greater time then I shall shew to be.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: What fashion (Madam) shall I make your breeches?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: That fits as well, as tell me (good my Lord)
What compasse will you weare your Farthingale?
Why eu'n what fashion thou best likes (Lucetta.)

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: You must needs haue the~ with a cod-peece (Madam)

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Out, out, (Lucetta) that wilbe illfauourd.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: A round hose (Madam) now's not worth a pin
Vnlesse you haue a cod-peece to stick pins on.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Lucetta, as thou lou'st me let me haue
What thou think'st meet, and is most mannerly.
But tell me (wench) how will the world repute me
For vndertaking so vnstaid a iourney?
I feare me it will make me scandaliz'd.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: If you thinke so, then stay at home, and go not.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Nay, that I will not.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Then neuer dreame on Infamy, but go:
If Protheus like your iourney, when you come,
No matter who's displeas'd, when you are gone:
I feare me he will scarce be pleas'd with all.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: That is the least (Lucetta) of my feare:
A thousand oathes, an Ocean of his teares,
And instances of infinite of Loue,
Warrant me welcome to my Protheus.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: All these are seruants to deceitfull men.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Base men, that vse them to so base effect;
But truer starres did gouerne Protheus birth,
His words are bonds, his oathes are oracles,
His loue sincere, his thoughts immaculate,
His teares, pure messengers, sent from his heart,
His heart, as far from fraud, as heauen from earth.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Pray heau'n he proue so when you come to him.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Now, as thou lou'st me, do him not that wrong,
To beare a hard opinion of his truth:
Onely deserue my loue, by louing him,
And presently goe with me to my chamber
To take a note of what I stand in need of,
To furnish me vpon my longing iourney:
All that is mine I leaue at thy dispose,
My goods, my Lands, my reputation,
Onely, in lieu thereof, dispatch me hence:
Come; answere not: but to it presently,
I am impatient of my tarriance.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Sir Thurio, giue vs leaue (I pray) a while,
We haue some secrets to confer about.
Now tell me Protheus, what's your will with me?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: My gracious Lord, that which I wold discouer,
The Law of friendship bids me to conceale,
But when I call to minde your gracious fauours
Done to me (vndeseruing as I am)
My dutie pricks me on to vtter that
Which else, no worldly good should draw from me:
Know (worthy Prince) Sir Valentine my friend
This night intends to steale away your daughter:
My selfe am one made priuy to the plot.
I know you haue determin'd to bestow her
On Thurio, whom your gentle daughter hates,
And should she thus be stolne away from you,
It would be much vexation to your age.
Thus (for my duties sake) I rather chose
To crosse my friend in his intended drift,
Then (by concealing it) heap on your head
A pack of sorrowes, which would presse you downe
(Being vnpreuented) to your timelesse graue.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Protheus, I thank thee for thine honest care,
Which to requite, command me while I liue.
This loue of theirs, my selfe haue often seene,
Haply when they haue iudg'd me fast asleepe,
And oftentimes haue purpos'd to forbid

Sir
~alentine her companie, and my Court.
But fearing lest my iealous ayme might erre,
And so (vnworthily) disgrace the man
(A rashnesse that I euer yet haue shun'd)
I gaue him gentle lookes, thereby to finde
That which thy selfe hast now disclos'd to me.
And that thou maist perceiue my feare of this,
Knowing that tender youth is soone suggested,
I nightly lodge her in an vpper Towre,
The key whereof, my selfe haue euer kept:
And thence she cannot be conuay'd away.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Know (noble Lord) they haue deuis'd a meane
How he her chamber-window will ascend,
And with a Corded-ladder fetch her downe:
For which, the youthfull Louer now is gone,
And this way comes he with it presently.
Where (if it please you) you may intercept him.
But (good my Lord) doe it so cunningly
That my discouery be not aimed at:
For, loue of you, not hate vnto my friend,
Hath made me publisher of this pretence.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Vpon mine Honor, he shall neuer know
That I had any light from thee of this.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Adiew, my Lord, Sir Valentine is comming.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Sir Valentine, whether away so fast?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Please it your Grace, there is a Messenger
That stayes to beare my Letters to my friends,
And I am going to deliuer them.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Be they of much import?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: The tenure of them doth but signifie
My health, and happy being at your Court.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Nay then no matter: stay with me a while,
I am to breake with thee of some affaires
That touch me neere: wherein thou must be secret.
'Tis not vnknown to thee, that I haue sought
To match my friend Sir Thurio, to my daughter.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I know it well (my Lord) and sure the Match
Were rich and honourable: besides, the gentleman
Is full of Vertue, Bounty, Worth, and Qualities
Beseeming such a Wife, as your faire daughter:
Cannot your Grace win her to fancie him?

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: No, trust me, She is peeuish, sullen, froward,
Prowd, disobedient, stubborne, lacking duty,
Neither regarding that she is my childe,
Nor fearing me, as if I were her father:
And may I say to thee, this pride of hers
(Vpon aduice) hath drawne my loue from her,
And where I thought the remnant of mine age
Should haue beene cherish'd by her child-like dutie,
I now am full resolu'd to take a wife,
And tur^ her out, to who will take her in:
Then let her beauty be her wedding dowre:
For me, and my possessions she esteemes not.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What would your Grace haue me to do in this?

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: There is a Lady in Verona heere
Whom I affect: but she is nice, and coy,
And naught esteemes my aged eloquence.
Now therefore would I haue thee to my Tutor
(For long agone I haue forgot to court,
Besides the fashion of the time is chang'd)
How, and which way I may bestow my selfe
To be regarded in her sun-bright eye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Win her with gifts, if she respect not words,
Dumbe Iewels often in their silent kinde
More then quicke words, doe moue a womans minde.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: But she did scorne a present that I sent her,

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: A woman somtime scorns what best co~tents her.
Send her another: neuer giue her ore,
For scorne at first, makes after-loue the more.
If she doe frowne, 'tis not in hate of you,
But rather to beget more loue in you.
If she doe chide, 'tis not to haue you gone,
For why, the fooles are mad, if left alone.
Take no repulse, what euer she doth say,
For, get you gon, she doth not meane away.
Flatter, and praise, commend, extoll their graces:
Though nere so blacke, say they haue Angells faces,
That man that hath a tongue, I say is no man,
If with his tongue he cannot win a woman.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: But she I meane, is promis'd by her friends
Vnto a youthfull Gentleman of worth,
And kept seuerely from resort of men,
That no man hath accesse by day to her.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why then I would resort to her by night.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I, but the doores be lockt, and keyes kept safe,
That no man hath recourse to her by night.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: What letts but one may enter at her window?

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Her chamber is aloft, far from the ground,
And built so sheluing, that one cannot climbe it
Without apparant hazard of his life.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Why then a Ladder quaintly made of Cords
To cast vp, with a paire of anchoring hookes,
Would serue to scale another Hero's towre,
So bold Leander would aduenture it.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Now as thou art a Gentleman of blood
Aduise me, where I may haue such a Ladder.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: When would you vse it? pray sir, tell me that.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: This very night; for Loue is like a childe
That longs for euery thing that he can come by.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: By seauen a clock, ile get you such a Ladder.

speeches.speaker: Duk
verse: But harke thee: I will goe to her alone,
How shall I best conuey the Ladder thither?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: It will be light (my Lord) that you may beare it
Vnder a cloake, that is of any length.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: A cloake as long as thine will serue the turne?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: I my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Then let me see thy cloake,
Ile get me one of such another length.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why any cloake will serue the turn (my Lord)

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: How shall I fashion me to weare a cloake?
I pray thee let me feele thy cloake vpon me.
What Letter is this same? what's here? to Siluia?
And heere an Engine fit for my proceeding,
Ile be so bold to breake the seale for once.
What's here? Siluia, this night I will enfranchise thee.
'Tis so: and heere's the Ladder for the purpose.
Why Phaeton (for thou art Merops sonne)
Wilt thou aspire to guide the heauenly Car?
And with thy daring folly burne the world?
Wilt thou reach stars, because they shine on thee?
Goe base Intruder, ouer-weening Slaue,
Bestow thy fawning smiles on equall mates,
And thinke my patience, (more then thy desert)
Is priuiledge for thy departure hence.
Thanke me for this, more then for all the fauors
Which (all too much) I haue bestowed on thee.
But if thou linger in my Territories
Longer then swiftest expedition
Will giue thee time to leaue our royall Court,
By heauen, my wrath shall farre exceed the loue
I euer bore my daughter, or thy selfe.
Be gone, I will not heare thy vaine excuse,
But as thou lou'st thy life, make speed from hence.
prose:
My thoughts do harbour with my Siluia nightly,
And slaues they are to me, that send them flying.
Oh, could their Master come, and goe as lightly,
Himselfe would lodge where (senceles) they are lying.
My Herald Thoughts, in thy pure bosome rest-them,
While I (their King) that thither them importune
Doe curse the grace, that with such grace hath blest them,
Because my selfe doe want my seruants fortune.
I curse my selfe, for they are sent by me,
That they should harbour where their Lord should be.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: And why not death, rather then liuing torment?
To die, is to be banisht from my selfe,
And Siluia is my selfe: banish'd from her
Is selfe from selfe. A deadly banishment:
What light, is light, if Siluia be not seene?
What ioy is ioy, if Siluia be not by?
Vnlesse it be to thinke that she is by
And feed vpon the shadow of perfection.
Except I be by Siluia in the night,
There is no musicke in the Nightingale.
Vnlesse I looke on Siluia in the day,
There is no day for me to looke vpon.
Shee is my essence, and I leaue to be;
If I be not by her faire influence
Foster'd, illumin'd, cherish'd, kept aliue.
I flie not death, to flie his deadly doome,
Tarry I heere, I but attend on death,
But flie I hence, I flie away from life.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Run (boy) run, run, and seeke him out.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: So-hough, Soa hough —

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What seest thou?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
verse: Him we goe to finde,
There's not a haire on's head, but t'is a Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Valentine?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Who then? his Spirit?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Neither,

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What then?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: Nothing.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Can nothing speake? Master, shall I strike?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Who wouldst thou strike?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Nothing.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Villaine, forbeare.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Why Sir, Ile strike nothing: I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Sirha, I say forbeare: friend Valentine, a word.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: My eares are stopt, & cannot hear good newes,
So much of bad already hath possest them.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Then in dumbe silence will I bury mine,
For they are harsh, vn-tuneable, and bad.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Is Siluia dead?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: No, Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: No Valentine indeed, for sacred Siluia,
Hath she forsworne me?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose:
No,
~alentine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: No Valentine, if Siluia haue forsworne me.
What is your newes?

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: Sir, there is a proclamation, yt you are vanished.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: That thou art banish'd: oh that's the newes,
From hence, from Siluia, and from me thy friend.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Oh, I haue fed vpon this woe already,
And now excesse of it will make me surfet.
Doth Siluia know that I am banish'd?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I, I: and she hath offered to the doome
(Which vn-reuerst stands in effectuall force)
A Sea of melting pearle, which some call teares;
Those at her fathers churlish feete she tenderd,
With them vpon her knees, her humble selfe,
Wringing her hands, whose whitenes so became them,
As if but now they waxed pale for woe:
But neither bended knees, pure hands held vp,
Sad sighes, deepe grones, nor siluer-shedding teares
Could penetrate her vncompassionate Sire;
But Valentine, if he be tane, must die.
Besides, her intercession chaf'd him so,
When she for thy repeale was suppliant,
That to close prison he commanded her,
With many bitter threats of biding there.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: No more: vnles the next word that thou speak'st
Haue some malignant power vpon my life:
If so: I pray thee breath it in mine eare,
As ending Antheme of my endlesse dolor.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Cease to lament for that thou canst not helpe,
And study helpe for that which thou lament'st,
Time is the Nurse, and breeder of all good;
Here, if thou stay, thou canst not see thy loue:
Besides, thy staying will abridge thy life:
Hope is a louers staffe, walke hence with that
And manage it, against despairing thoughts:
Thy letters may be here, though thou art hence,
Which, being writ to me, shall be deliuer'd
Euen in the milke-white bosome of thy Loue.
The time now serues not to expostulate,
Come, Ile conuey thee through the City-gate.
And ere I part with thee, confer at large
Of all that may concerne thy Loue-affaires:
As thou lou'st Siluia (though not for thy selfe)
Regard thy danger, and along with me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I pray thee Launce, and if thou seest my Boy
Bid him make haste, and meet me at the North-gate.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose:
Goe sirha, finde him out: Come
~alentine.

speeches.speaker: Val
prose: Oh my deere Siluia; haplesse Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: I am but a foole, looke you, and yet I haue the wit to thinke my Master is a kinde of a knaue: but that's all one, if he be but one knaue: He liues not now that knowes me to be in loue, yet I am in loue, but a Teeme of horse shall not plucke that from me: nor who 'tis I loue: and yet 'tis a woman; but what woman, I will not tell my selfe: and yet 'tis a Milke-maid: yet 'tis not a maid: for shee hath had Gossips: yet 'tis a maid, for she is her Masters maid, and serues for wages. Shee hath more qualities then a Water-Spaniell, which is much in a bare Christian: Heere is the Cate-log of her Condition. Inprimis. Shee can fetch and carry: why a horse can doe no more; nay, a horse cannot fetch, but onely carry, therefore is shee better then a Iade. Item. She can milke, looke you, a sweet vertue in a maid with cleane hands.

speeches.speaker: Speed.
prose: How now Signior Launce? what newes with your Mastership?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: With my Mastership? why, it is at Sea:

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Well, your old vice still: mistake the word: what newes then in your paper?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: The black'st newes that euer thou heard'st.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Why man? how blacke?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Why, as blacke as Inke.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Let me read them?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Fie on thee Iolt-head, thou canst not read.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Thou lyest: I can.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I will try thee: tell me this: who begot thee?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Marry, the son of my Grand-father.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Oh illiterate loyterer. it was the sonne of thy Grand-mother: this proues that thou canst not read.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Come foole, come: try me in thy paper.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: There: and S. Nicholas be thy speed.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Inprimis she can milke.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I that she can.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she brewes good Ale.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: And thereof comes the prouerbe: (Blessing of your heart, you brew good Ale.)

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she can sowe.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: That's as much as to say (Can she so?)

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item she can knit.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: What neede a man care for a stock with a wench,
When she can knit him a stocke?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she can wash and scoure.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: A speciall vertue: for then shee neede not be wash'd, and scowr'd.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she can spin.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Then may I set the world on wheeles, when she can spin for her liuing.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she hath many namelesse vertues.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: That's as much as to say Bastard-vertues: that indeede know not their fathers; and therefore haue no names.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Here follow her vices.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Close at the heeles of her vertues.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, shee is not to be fasting in respect of her breath.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Well: that fault may be mended with a breakfast: read on.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she hath a sweet mouth.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: That makes amends for her soure breath.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she doth talke in her sleepe.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: It's no matter for that; so shee sleepe not in her talke.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she is slow in words.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Oh villaine, that set this downe among her vices;
To be slow in words, is a womans onely vertue:
I pray thee out with't, and place it for her chiefe vertue.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she is proud.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Out with that too:
It was Eues legacie, and cannot be t'ane from her.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she hath no teeth.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I care not for that neither: because I loue crusts.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she is curst.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Well: the best is, she hath no teeth to bite.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she will often praise her liquor.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: If her liquor be good, she shall: if she will not,
I will; for good things should be praised.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she is too liberall.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Of her tongue she cannot; for that's writ downe she is slow of: of her purse, shee shall not, for that ile keepe shut: Now, of another thing shee may, and that cannot I helpe. Well, proceede.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, shee hath more haire then wit, and more faults then haires, and more wealth then faults.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Stop there: Ile haue her: she was mine, and not mine, twice or thrice in that last Article: rehearse that once more.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Item, she hath more haire then wit.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: More haire then wit: it may be ile proue it: The couer of the salt, hides the salt, and therefore it is more then the salt; the haire that couers the wit, is more then the wit; for the greater hides the lesse: What's next?

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: And more faults then haires.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: That's monstrous: oh that that were out.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: And more wealth then faults.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Why that word makes the faults gracious:
Well, ile haue her: and if it be a match, as nothing is impossible.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: What then?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Why then, will I tell thee, that thy Master staies for thee at the North gate.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: For me?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: For thee? I, who art thou? he hath staid for a better man then thee.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: And must I goe to him?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Thou must run to him; for thou hast staid so long, that going will scarce serue the turne.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
prose: Why didst not tell me sooner? 'pox of your loue Letters.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Now will he be swing'd for reading my Letter; An vnmannerly slaue, that will thrust himselfe into secrets: Ile after, to reioyce in the boyes correctio~.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Sir Thurio, feare not, but that she will loue you
Now Valentine is banish'd from her sight.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: Since his exile she hath despis'd me most,
Forsworne my company, and rail'd at me,
That I am desperate of obtaining her.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: This weake impresse of Loue, is as a figure
Trenched in ice, which with an houres heare
Dissolues to water, and doth loose his forme.
A little time will melt her frozen thoughts,
And worthlesse Valentine shall be forgot.
How now sir Protheus, is your countriman
(According to our Proclamation) gon?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Gon, my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: My daughter takes his going grieuously?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: A little time (my Lord) will kill that griefe.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: So I beleeue: but Thurio thinkes not so:
Protheus, the good conceit I hold of thee,
(For thou hast showne some signe of good desert)
Makes me the better to confer with thee.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Longer then I proue loyall to your Grace,
Let me not liue, to looke vpon your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thou know'st how willingly, I would effect
The match betweene sir Thurio, and my daughter?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I doe my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And also, I thinke, thou art not ignorant
How she opposes her against my will?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose:
She did my Lord, when
~alentine was here.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I, and peruersly, she perseuers so:
What might we doe to make the girle forget
The loue of Valentine, and loue sir Thurio?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse:
The best way is, to slander
~alentine,
With falsehood, cowardize, and poore discent:
Three things, that women highly hold in hate.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: I, but she'll thinke, that it is spoke in hate.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I, if his enemy deliuer it.
Therefore it must with circumstance be spoken
By one, whom she esteemeth as his friend.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Then you must vndertake to slander him.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: And that (my Lord) I shall be loath to doe:
'Tis an ill office for a Gentleman,
Especially against his very friend.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Where your good word cannot aduantage him,
Your slander neuer can endamage him;
Therefore the office is indifferent,
Being intreated to it by your friend.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: You haue preuail'd (my Lord) if I can doe it
By ought that I can speake in his dispraise,
She shall not long continue loue to him:
But say this weede her loue from Valentine,
It followes not that she will loue sir Thurio.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: Therefore, as you vnwinde her loue from him;
Least it should rauell, and be good to none,
You must prouide to bottome it on me:
Which must be done, by praising me as much

As you, in worth dispraise, sir
~alentine.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And Protheus, we dare trust you in this kinde,
Because we know (on Valentines report)
You are already loues firme votary,
And cannot soone reuolt, and change your minde.
Vpon this warrant, shall you haue accesse,
Where you, with Siluia, may conferre at large.
For she is lumpish, heauy, mellancholly,
And (for your friends sake) will be glad of you;
Where you may temper her, by your perswasion,

To hate yong
~alentine, and loue my friend.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: As much as I can doe, I will effect:
But you sir Thurio, are not sharpe enough:
You must lay Lime, to tangle her desires
By walefull Sonnets, whose composed Rimes
Should be full fraught with seruiceable vowes.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: I, much is the force of heauen-bred Poesie.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Say that vpon the altar of her beauty
You sacrifice your teares, your sighes, your heart:
Write till your inke be dry. and with your teares
Moist it againe: and frame some feeling line,
That may discouer such integrity:
For Orpheus Lute, was strung with Poets sinewes,
Whose golden touch could soften steele and stones;
Make Tygers tame, and huge Leuiathans
Forsake vnsounded deepes, to dance on Sands.
After your dire-lamenting Elegies,
Visit by night your Ladies chamber-window
With some sweet Consort; To their Instruments
Tune a deploring dumpe: the nights dead silence
Will well become such sweet complaining grieuance:
This, or else nothing, will inherit her.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: This discipline, showes thou hast bin in loue.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: And thy aduice, this night, ile put in practise:
Therefore, sweet Protheus, my direction-giuer,
Let vs into the City presently
To sort some Gentlemen, well skil'd in Musicke.
I haue a Sonnet, that will serue the turne
To giue the on-set to thy good aduise.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: About it Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: We'll wait vpon your Grace, till after Supper,
And afterward determine our proceedings.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Euen now about it, I will pardon you.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out-l.
prose: Fellowes, stand fast: I see a passenger.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
prose: If there be ten, shrinke not, but down with 'em.

speeches.speaker: 3. Out.
verse: Stand sir, and throw vs that you haue about 'ye.
If not: we'll make you sit, and rifle you.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: Sir we are vndone; these are the Villaines
That all the Trauailers doe feare so much.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: My friends.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
prose: That's not so, sir: we are your enemies.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
prose: Peace: we'll heare him.

speeches.speaker: 3. Out.
prose: I by my beard will we: for he is a proper man.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Then know that I haue little wealth to loose;
A man I am, cross'd with aduersitie:
My riches, are these poore habiliments,
Of which, if you should here disfurnish me,
You take the sum and substance that I haue.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
prose: Whether trauell you?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: To Verona.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
prose: Whence came you?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: From Millaine.

speeches.speaker: 3. Out.
prose: Haue you long soiourn'd there?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Some sixteene moneths, and longer might haue staid,
If crooked fortune had not thwarted me.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
prose: What, were you banish'd thence?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I was.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
prose: For what offence?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: For that which now torments me to rehearse;
I kil'd a man, whose death I much repent,
But yet I slew him manfully, in fight,
Without false vantage, or base treachery.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
verse: Why nere repent it, if it were done so;
But were you banisht for so small a fault?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I was, and held me glad of such a doome.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
prose: Haue you the Tongues?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: My youthfull trauaile, therein made me happy,
Or else I often had beene often miserable.

speeches.speaker: 3. Out.
verse: By the bare scalpe of Robin Hoods fat Fryer,
This fellow were a King, for our wilde faction.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
prose: We'll haue him: Sirs, a word.

speeches.speaker: Sp.
verse: Master, be one of them:
It's an honourable kinde of theeuery.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Peace villaine.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
prose: Tell vs this: haue you any thing to take to?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Nothing but my fortune.

speeches.speaker: 3. Out.
verse: Know then, that some of vs are Gentlemen,
Such as the fury of vngouern'd youth
Thrust from the company of awfull men.
My selfe was from Verona banished,
For practising to steale away a Lady,
And heire and Neece, alide vnto the Duke.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
verse: And I from Mantua, for a Gentleman,
Who, in my moode, I stab'd vnto the heart.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
verse: And I, for such like petty crimes as these.
But to the purpose: for we cite our faults,
That they may hold excus'd our lawlesse liues;
And partly seeing you are beautifide
With goodly shape; and by your owne report,
A Linguist, and a man of such perfection,
As we doe in our quality much want.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
verse: Indeede because you are a banish'd man,
Therefore, aboue the rest, we parley to you:
Are you content to be our Generall?
To make a vertue of necessity,
And liue as we doe in this wildernesse?

speeches.speaker: 3. Out.
verse: What saist thou? wilt thou be of our consort?
Say I, and be the captaine of vs all:
We'll doe thee homage, and be rul'd by thee,
Loue thee, as our Commander, and our King.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
prose: But if thou scorne our curtesie, thou dyest.

speeches.speaker: 2. Out.
prose: Thou shalt not liue, to brag what we haue offer'd.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I take your offer, and will liue with you,
Prouided that you do no outrages
On silly women, or poore passengers.

speeches.speaker: 3. Out.
verse: No, we detest such vile base practises.
Come, goe with vs, we'll bring thee to our Crewes,
And show thee all the Treasure we haue got;
Which, with our selues, all rest at thy dispose.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Already haue I bin false to Valentine,
And now I must be as vniust to Thurio,
Vnder the colour of commending him,
I haue accesse my owne loue to prefer.
But Siluia is too faire, too true, too holy,
To be corrupted with my worthlesse guifts;
When I protest true loyalty to her,
She twits me with my falsehood to my friend;
When to her beauty I commend my vowes,
She bids me thinke how I haue bin forsworne
In breaking faith with Iulia, whom I lou'd;
And notwithstanding all her sodaine quips,
The least whereof would quell a louers hope:
Yet (Spaniel-like) the more she spurnes my loue,
The more it growes, and fawneth on her still;
But here comes Thurio; now must we to her window,
And giue some euening Musique to her eare.

speeches.speaker: Th.
prose: How now, sir Protheus, are you crept before vs?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I gentle Thurio, for you know that loue
Will creepe in seruice, where it cannot goe.

speeches.speaker: Th.
prose: I, but I hope, Sir, that you loue not here.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Sir, but I doe: or else I would be hence.

speeches.speaker: Th.
prose: Who, Siluia?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I, Siluia, for your sake.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: I thanke you for your owne: Now Gentlemen
Let's tune: and too it lustily a while.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Now, my yong guest; me thinks your' allyeholly;
I pray you why is it?

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Marry (mine Host) because I cannot be merry.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Come, we'll haue you merry: ile bring you where you shall heare Musique, and see the Gentleman that you ask'd for.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: But shall I heare him speake.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I that you shall.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: That will be Musique.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Harke, harke.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Is he among these?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I: but peace, let's heare'm.

verse: Who is Siluia? what is she?
That all our Swaines commend her?
Holy, faire, and wise is she,
The heauen such grace did lend her, that she might admired be.
Is she kinde as she is faire?
For beauty liues with kindnesse:
Loue doth to her eyes repaire,
To helpe him of his blindnesse:
And being help'd, inhabits there.
Then to Siluia, let vs sing,
That Siluia is excelling;
She excels each mortall thing
Vpon the dull earth dwelling.
To her let vs Garlands bring.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: How now? are you sadder then you were before;
How doe you, man? the Musicke likes you not.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: You mistake: the Musitian likes me not.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Why, my pretty youth?

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: He plaies false (father.)

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: How, out of tune on the strings.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: Not so: but yet
So false that he grieues my very heart-strings.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: You haue a quicke eare.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: I, I would I were deafe: it makes me haue a slow heart.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I perceiue you delight not in Musique.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Not a whit, when it iars so.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Harke, what fine change is in the Musique.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: I: that change is the spight.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: You would haue them alwaies play but one thing.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: I would alwaies haue one play but one thing.
But Host, doth this Sir Protheus, that we talke on,
Often resort vnto this Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: I tell you what Launce his man told me,
He lou'd her out of all nicke.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Where is Launce?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Gone to seeke his dog, which to morrow, by his Masters command, hee must carry for a present to his Lady.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: Peace, stand aside, the company parts.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Sir Thurio, feare not you, I will so pleade,
That you shall say, my cunning drift excels.

speeches.speaker: Th.
prose: Where meete we?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: At Saint Gregories well.

speeches.speaker: Th.
prose: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Madam: good eu'n to your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I thanke you for your Musique (Gentlemen)
Who is that that spake?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: One (Lady) if you knew his pure hearts truth,
You would quickly learne to know him by his voice.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Sir Protheus, as I take it.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Sir Protheus (gentle Lady) and your Seruant.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: What's your will?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: That I may compasse yours.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: You haue your wish: my will is euen this,
That presently you hie you home to bed:
Thou subtile, periur'd, false, disloyall man:
Think'st thou I am so shallow, so conceitlesse,
To be seduced by thy flattery,
That has't deceiu'd so many with thy vowes.
Returne, returne and make thy loue amends:
For me (by this pale queene of night I sweare)
I am so farre from granting thy request,
That I despise thee, for thy wrongfull suite;
And by and by intend to chide my selfe,
Euen for this time I spend in talking to thee.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I grant (sweet loue) that I did loue a Lady,
But she is dead.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: 'Twere false, if I should speake it;
For I am sure she is not buried.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Say that she be: yet Valentine thy friend
Suruiues; to whom (thy selfe art witnesse)
I am betroth'd; and art thou not asham'd
To wrong him, with thy importunacy?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I likewise heare that Valentine is dead.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: And so suppose am I; for in her graue
Assure thy selfe, my loue is buried.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Sweet Lady, let me take it from the earth.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Goe to thy Ladies graue and call hers thence,
Or at the least, in hers, sepulcher thine.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: He heard not that.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Madam: if your heart be so obdurate:
Vouchsafe me yet your Picture for my loue,
The Picture that is hanging in your chamber:
To that ile speake, to that ile sigh and weepe:
For since the substance of your perfect selfe
Is else deuoted, I am but a shadow;
And to your shadow, will I make true loue.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: If 'twere a substance you would sure deceiue it,
And make it but a shadow, as I am.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I am very loath to be your Idoll Sir;
But, since your falsehood shall become you well
To worship shadowes, and adore false shapes,
Send to me in the morning, and ile send it:
And so, good rest.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: As wretches haue ore-night
That wait for execution in the morne.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Host, will you goe?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: By my hallidome, I was fast asleepe.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Pray you, where lies Sir Protheus?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Marry, at my house:
Trust me, I thinke 'tis almost day.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Not so: but it hath bin the longest night
That ere I watch'd, and the most heauiest.

speeches.speaker: Eg.
verse: This is the houre that Madam Siluia
Entreated me to call, and know her minde:
Ther's some great matter she'ld employ me in.
Madam, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Who cals?

speeches.speaker: Eg.
verse: Your seruant, and your friend;
One that attends your Ladiships command.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Sir Eglamore, a thousand times good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Eg.
verse: As many (worthy Lady) to your selfe:
According to your Ladiships impose,
I am thus early come, to know what seruice
It is your pleasure to command me in.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Oh Eglamoure, thou art a Gentleman:
Thinke not I flatter (for I sweare I doe not)
Valiant, wise, remorse-full, well accomplish'd.
Thou art not ignorant what deere good will

I beare vnto the banish'd
~alentine:
Nor how my father would enforce me marry
Vaine Thurio (whom my very soule abhor'd.)
Thy selfe hast lou'd, and I haue heard thee say
No griefe did euer come so neere thy heart,
As when thy Lady, and thy true-loue dide,
Vpon whose Graue thou vow'dst pure chastitie:
Sir Eglamoure: I would to Valentine
To Mantua, where I heare, he makes aboad;
And for the waies are dangerous to passe,
I doe desire thy worthy company,
Vpon whose faith and honor, I repose.
Vrge not my fathers anger (Eglamoure)
But thinke vpon my griefe (a Ladies griefe)
And on the iustice of my flying hence,
To keepe me from a most vnholy match,
Which heauen and fortune still rewards with plagues.
I doe desire thee, euen from a heart
As full of sorrowes, as the Sea of sands,
To beare me company, and goe with me:
If not, to hide what I haue said to thee,
That I may venture to depart alone.

speeches.speaker: Egl.
verse: Madam, I pitty much your grieuances,
Which, since I know they vertuously are plac'd,
I giue consent to goe along with you,
Wreaking as little what betideth me,
As much, I wish all good befortune you.
When will you goe?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: This euening comming.

speeches.speaker: Eg.
prose: Where shall I meete you?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: At Frier Patrickes Cell,
Where I intend holy Confession.

speeches.speaker: Eg.
verse: I will not faile your Ladiship:
Good morrow (gentle Lady.)

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Good morrow, kinde Sir Eglamoure.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose:
When a mans seruant shall play the Curre with him (looke you) it goes hard: one that I brought vp of a puppy: one that I sau'd from drowning, when three or foure of his blinde brothers and sisters went to it: I haue taught him (euen as one would say precisely, thus I would teach a dog) I was sent to deliuer him, as a present to Mistris Siluia, from my Master; and I came no sooner into the dyning-chamber, but he steps me to her Trencher, and steales her Capons-leg: O, 'tis a foule thing, when a Cur cannot keepe himselfe in all companies: I would haue (as one should say) one that takes vpon him to be a dog indeede, to be, as it were, a dog at all things. If I had not had more wit then he, to take a fault vpon me that he did, I thinke verily hee had bin hang'd for't: sure as I liue he had suffer'd for't: you shall iudge: Hee thrusts me himselfe into the company of three or foure gentleman-like-dogs, vnder the Dukes table: hee had not bin there (blesse the marke) a pissing while, but all the chamber smelt him: out with the dog (saies one) what cur is that (saies another) whip him out (saies the third) hang him vp (saies the Duke.) I hauing bin acquainted with the smell before, knew it was Crab; and goes me to the fellow that whips the dogges: friend (quoth I) you meane to whip the dog: I marry doe I (quoth he) you doe him the more wrong (quoth I) 'twas I did the thing you wot of: he makes me no more adoe, but whips me out of the chamber: how many Masters would doe this for his Seruant? nay, ile be sworne I haue sat in the stockes, for puddings he hath stolne, otherwise he had bin executed: I haue stood on the Pillorie for Geese he hath kil'd, otherwise he had sufferd for't: thou think'st not of this now: nay, I remember the tricke you seru'd me, when I tooke my leaue of Madam Siluia: did

not I bid thee still marke me, and doe as I doe, when did'st thou see me heaue vp my leg, and make water against a Gentlewomans farthingale? did'st thou euer see me doe such a tricke?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Sebastian is thy name: I like thee well,
And will imploy thee in some seruice presently.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: In what you please, ile doe what I can.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I hope thou wilt.
How now you whor-son pezant,
Where haue you bin these two dayes loytering?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Marry Sir, I carried Mistris Siluia the dogge you bad me.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: And what saies she to my little Iewell?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Marry she saies your dog was a cur, and tels you currish thanks is good enough for such a present.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But she receiu'd my dog?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: No indeede did she not:
Here haue I brought him backe againe.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What, didst thou offer her this from me?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: I Sir, the other Squirrill was stolne from me
By the Hangmans boyes in the market place,
And then I offer'd her mine owne, who is a dog
As big as ten of yours, & therefore the guift the greater.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Goe, get thee hence, and finde my dog againe,
Or nere returne againe into my sight.
Away, I say: stayest thou to vexe me here;
A Slaue, that still an end, turnes me to shame:
Sebastian, I haue entertained thee,
Partly that I haue neede of such a youth,
That can with some discretion doe my businesse:
For 'tis no trusting to yond foolish Lowt;
But chiefely, for thy face, and thy behauiour,
Which (if my Augury deceiue me not)
Witnesse good bringing vp, fortune, and truth:
Therefore know thee, for this I entertaine thee.
Go presently, and take this Ring with thee,
Deliuer it to Madam Siluia;
She lou'd me well, deliuer'd it to me.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: It seemes you lou'd not her, not leaue her token:
She is dead belike?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Not so: I thinke she liues.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Alas.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Why do'st thou cry alas?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I cannot choose but pitty her.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Wherefore should'st thou pitty her?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Because, me thinkes that she lou'd you as well
As you doe loue your Lady Siluia:
She dreames on him, that has forgot her loue,
You doate on her, that cares not for your loue.
'Tis pitty Loue, should be so contrary:
And thinking on it, makes me cry alas.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Well: giue her that Ring, and therewithall
This Letter: that's her chamber: Tell my Lady,
I claime the promise for her heauenly Picture:
Your message done, hye home vnto my chamber,
Where thou shalt finde me sad, and solitarie.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: How many women would doe such a message?
Alas poore Protheus, thou hast entertain'd
A Foxe, to be the Shepheard of thy Lambs;
Alas, poore foole, why doe I pitty him
That with his very heart despiseth me?
Because he loues her, he despiseth me,
Because I loue him, I must pitty him.
This Ring I gaue him, when he parted from me,
To binde him to remember my good will:
And now am I (vnhappy Messenger)
To plead for that, which I would not obtaine;
To carry that, which I would haue refus'd;
To praise his faith, which I would haue disprais'd.
I am my Masters true confirmed Loue,
But cannot be true seruant to my Master,
Vnlesse I proue false traitor to my selfe.
Yet will I woe for him but yet so coldly,
As (heauen it knowes) I would not haue him speed.
Gentlewoman, good day: I pray you be my meane
To bring me where to speake with Madam Siluia.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: What would you with her, if that I be she?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: If you be she, I doe intreat your patience
To heare me speake the message I am sent on.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: From whom?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: From my Master, Sir Protheus, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Oh: he sends you for a Picture?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Vrsula, bring my Picture there,
Goe, giue your Master this: tell him from me,
One Iulia, that his changing thoughts forget
Would better fit his Chamber, then this Shadow.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Madam, please you peruse this Letter;
Pardon me (Madam) I haue vnaduis'd
Deliuer'd you a paper that I should not;
This is the Letter to your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: I pray thee let me looke on that againe.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: It may not be: good Madam pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: There, hold:
I will not looke vpon your Masters lines:
I know they are stuft with protestations,
And full of new-found oathes, which he will breake
As easily as I doe teare his paper.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Madam, he sends your Ladiship this Ring.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: The more shame for him, that he sends it me;
For I haue heard him say a thousand times,
His Iulia gaue it him, at his departure:
Though his false finger haue prophan'd the Ring,
Mine shall not doe his Iulia so much wrong.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: She thankes you.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: What sai'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I thanke you Madam, that you tender her:
Poore Gentlewoman, my Master wrongs her much.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Do'st thou know her?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Almost as well as I doe know my selfe.
To thinke vpon her woes, I doe protest
That I haue wept a hundred seuerall times.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Belike she thinks that Protheus hath forsook her?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I thinke she doth: and that's her cause of sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Is she not passing faire?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: She hath bin fairer (Madam) then she is,
When she did thinke my Master lou'd her well;
She, in my iudgement, was as faire as you.
But since she did neglect her looking-glasse,
And threw her Sun-expelling Masque away,
The ayre hath staru'd the roses in her cheekes,
And pinch'd the lilly-tincture of her face,
That now she is become as blacke as I.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: How tall was she?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: About my stature: for at Pentecost,
When all our Pageants of delight were plaid,
Our youth got me to play the womans part,
And I was trim'd in Madam Iulius gowne,
Which serued me as fit, by all mens iudgements,
As if the garment had bin made for me:
Therefore I know she is about my height,
And at that time I made her weepe a good.
For I did play a lamentable part.
(Madam) 'twas Ariadne, passioning
For Thesus periury, and vniust flight;
Which I so liuely acted with my teares:
That my poore Mistris moued therewithall,
Wept bitterly: and would I might be dead,
If I in thought felt not her very sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: She is beholding to thee (gentle youth)
Alas (poore Lady) desolate, and left;
I weepe my selfe to thinke vpon thy words:
Here youth: there is my purse; I giue thee this
For thy sweet Mistris sake, because thou lou'st her. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And she shall thanke you for't, if ere you know her.
A vertuous gentlewoman, milde, and beautifull.
I hope my Masters suit will be but cold,
Since she respects my Mistris loue so much.
Alas, how loue can trisle with it selfe:
Here is her Picture: let me see, I thinke
If I had such a Tyre, this face of mine
Were full as louely, as is this of hers;
And yet the Painter flatter'd her a little,
Vnlesse I flatter with my selfe too much.
Her haire is Aburne, mine is perfect Yellow;
If that be all the difference in his loue,
Ile get me such a coulour'd Perrywig:
Her eyes are grey as glasse, and so are mine:
I, but her fore-head's low, and mine's as high:
What should it be that he respects in her,
But I can make respectiue in my selfe?
If this fond Loue, were not a blinded god.
Come shadow, come, and take this shadow vp,
For 'tis thy riuall: O thou sencelesse forme.
Thou shalt be worship'd, kiss'd, lou'd, and ador'd;
And were there sence in his Idolatry,
My substance should be statue in thy stead.
Ile vse thee kindly, for thy Mistris sake
That vs'd me so: or else by Ioue, I vow,
I should haue scratch'd out your vnseeing eyes,
To make my Master out of loue with thee.

speeches.speaker: Egl.
verse: The Sun begins to guild the westerne skie,
And now it is about the very houre
That Siluia, at Fryer Patricks Cell should meet me,
She will not faile; for Louers breake not houres,
Vnlesse it be to come before their time,
So much they spur their expedition.
See where she comes: Lady a happy euening.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Amen, Amen: goe on (good Eglamoure)
Out at the Posterne by the Abbey wall;
I feare I am attended by some Spies.

speeches.speaker: Egl.
verse: Feare not: the Forrest is not three leagues off,
If we recouer that, we are sure enough.

speeches.speaker: Th.
prose: Sir Protheus, what saies Siluia to my suit?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Oh Sir, I finde her milder then she was,
And yet she takes exceptions at your person.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: What? that my leg is too long?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: No, that it is too little.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Ile weare a Boote, to make it somewhat rounder.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But loue will not be spurd to what it loath^.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: What saies she to my face?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: She saies it is a faire one.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Nay then the wanton lyes: my face is blacke.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: But Pearles are faire; and the old saying is,
Blacke men are Pearles, in beauteous Ladies eyes.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
verse: 'Tis true, such Pearles as put out Ladies eyes,
For I had rather winke, then looke on them.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: How likes she my discourse?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Ill, when you talke of war.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: But well, when I discourse of loue and peace.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: But better indeede, when you hold you peace.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: What sayes she to my valour?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Oh Sir, she makes no doubt of that.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: She needes not, when she knowes it cowardize.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: What saies she to my birth?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: That you are well deriu'd.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: True: from a Gentleman, to a foole.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Considers she my Possessions?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Oh, I: and pitties them.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Wherefore?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: That such an Asse should owe them.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: That they are out by Lease.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Here comes the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How now sir Protheus; how now Thurio?
Which of you saw Eglamoure of late?

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Not I.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Nor I.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Saw you my daughter?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Neither.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why then
She's fled vnto that pezant, Valentine;
And Eglamoure is in her Company:
'Tis true: for Frier Laurence met them both
As he, in pennance wander'd through the Forrest:
Him he knew well: and guesd that it was she,
But being mask'd, he was not sure of it.
Besides she did intend Confession
At Patricks Cell this euen, and there she was not.
These likelihoods confirme her flight from hence;
Therefore I pray you stand, not to discourse,
But mount you presently, and meete with me
Vpon the rising of the Mountaine foote
That leads toward Mantua, whether they are fled:
Dispatch (sweet Gentlemen) and follow me.

speeches.speaker: Thu.
verse: Why this it is, to be a peeuish Girle,
That flies her fortune when it followes her:
Ile after; more to be reueng'd on Eglamoure,
Then for the loue of reck-lesse Siluia.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: And I will follow, more for Siluas loue
Then hate of Eglamoure that goes with her.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And I will follow, more to crosse that loue
Then hate for Siluia, that is gone for loue.

speeches.speaker: 1. Out.
verse: Come, come be patient:
We must bring you to our Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: A thousand more mischances then this one
Haue learn'd me how to brooke this patiently.

speeches.speaker: 2 Out.
prose: Come, bring her away.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out.
prose: Where is the Gentleman that was with her?

speeches.speaker: 3 Out.
verse: Being nimble footed, he hath out. run vs.
But Moyses and Valerius follow him:
Goe thou with her to the West end of the wood,
There is our Captaine: Wee'll follow him that's fled,
The Thicket is beset, he cannot scape.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out.
verse: Come, I must bring you to our Captains caue.
Feare not: he beares an honourable minde,
And will not vse a woman lawlesly.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: O Valentine: this I endure for thee.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: How vse doth breed a habit in a man?
This shadowy desart, vnfrequented woods
I better brooke then flourishing peopled Townes:
Here can I sit alone, vn-seene of any,
And to the Nightingales complaining Notes
Tune my distrestes, and record my woes.
O thou that dost inhabit in my brest,
Leaue not the Mansion so long Tenant-lesse,
Lest growing ruinous, the building fall,
And leaue no memory of what it was,
Repaire me, with thy presence, Siluia:
Thou gentle Nimph, cherish thy for-lorne swaine.
What hallowing, and what stir is this to day?
These are my mates, that make their wills their Law,
Haue some vnhappy passenger in chace;
They loue me well: yet I haue much to doe
To keepe them from vnciuill outrages.
Withdraw thee Valentine: who's this comes heere?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Madam, this seruice I haue done for you
(Though you respect not aught your seruant doth)
To hazard life, and reskew you from him,
That would haue forc'd your honour, and your loue,
Vouchsafe me for my meed, but one faire looke:
(A smaller boone then this I cannot beg,
And lesse then this, I am sure you cannot giue.)

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: How like a dreame is this? I see, and heare:
Loue, lend me patience to forbeare a while.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: O miserable, vnhappy that I am.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Vnhappy were you (Madam) ere I came:
But by my comming, I haue made you happy.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: By thy approach thou mak'st me most vnhappy.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: And me, when he approcheth to your presence

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Had I beene ceazed by a hungry Lion,
I would haue beene a break-fast to the Beast,
Rather then haue false Protheus reskue me:
Oh heauen be iudge how I loue Valentine,
Whose life's as tender to me as my soule,
And full as much (for more there cannot be)
I doe detest false periur'd Protheus:
Therefore be gone, sollicit me no more.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: What dangerous action, stood it next to death
Would I not vndergoe, for one calme looke:
Oh 'tis the curse in Loue, and still approu'd
When women cannot loue, where they're belou'd.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: When Protheus cannot loue, where he's belou'd:
Read ouer Iulia's heart, (thy first best Loue)
For whose deare sake, thou didst then rend thy faith
Into a thousand oathes; and all those oathes,
Descended into periury, to loue me,
Thou hast no faith left now, vnlesse thou'dst two,
And that's farre worse then none: better haue none
Then plurall faith, which is too much by one:
Thou Counterfeyt, to thy true friend.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: In Loue,
Who respects friend?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: All men but Protheus.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Nay, if the gentle spirit of mouing words
Can no way change you to a milder forme;
Ile wooe you like a Souldier, at armes end,
And loue you 'gainst the nature of Loue: force ye.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Oh heauen.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Ile force thee yeeld to my desire.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Ruffian: let goe that rude vnciuill touch,
Thou friend of an ill fashion.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: ~alentine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Thou co~mon friend, that's without faith or loue,
For such is a friend now: treacherous man,
Thou hast beguil'd my hopes; nought but mine eye
Could haue perswaded me: now I dare not say
I haue one friend aliue; thou wouldst disproue me:
Who should be trusted, when ones right hand
Is periured to the bosome? Protheus
I am sorry I must neuer trust thee more,
But count the world a stranger for thy sake:
The priuate wound is deepest: oh time, most accurst:
'Mongst all foes that a friend should be the worst?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: My shame and guilt confounds me:
Forgiue me Valentine: if hearty sorrow
Be a sufficient Ransome for offence,
I tender't heere: I doe as truely suffer,
As ere I did commit.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Then I am paid:
And once againe, I doe receiue thee honest;
Who by Repentance is not satisfied,
Is nor of heauen, nor earth; for these are pleas'd:
By Penitence th' Eternalls wrath's appeas'd:
And that my loue may appeare plaine and free,
All that was mine, in Siluia, I giue thee.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Oh me vnhappy.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Looke to the Boy.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Why, Boy?
Why wag: how now? what's the matter? look vp: speak.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: O good sir, my master charg'd me to deliuer a ring to Madam Siluia: wc (out of my neglect) was neuer done.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Where is that ring? boy?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Heere 'tis. this is it.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: How? let me see.
Why this is the ring I gaue to Iulia.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Oh, cry you mercy sir, I haue mistooke:
This is the ring you sent to Siluia.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: But how cam'st thou by this ring? at my depart
I gaue this vnto Iulia.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And Iulia her selfe did giue it me,
And Iulia her selfe hath brought it hither.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: How? Iulia?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Behold her, that gaue ayme to all thy oathes,
And entertain'd 'em deepely in her heart.
How oft hast thou with periury cleft the roote?
Oh Protheus, let this habit make thee blush.
Be thou asham'd that I haue tooke vpon me,
Such an immodest rayment; if shame liue
In a disguise of loue?
It is the lesser blot modesty findes,
Women to change their shapes, then men their minds.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Then men their minds? tis true: oh heuen, were man
But Constant, he were perfect; that one error
Fils him with faults: makes him run through all th' sins;
Inconstancy falls-off, ere it begins:
What is in Siluia's face, but I may spie
More fresh in Iulia's, with a constant eye?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Come, come: a hand from either:
Let me be blest to make this happy close:
'Twere pitty two such friends should be long foes.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Beare witnes (heauen) I haue my wish for euer.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: And I mine.

speeches.speaker: Out-l.
prose: A prize: a prize: a prize.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Forbeare, forbeare I say: It is my Lord the Duke.
Your Grace is welcome to a man disgrac'd,
Banished Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Sir Valentine?

speeches.speaker: Thu.
prose: Yonder is Siluia: and Siluia's mine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Thurio giue backe; or else embrace thy death:
Come not within the measure of my wrath:
Doe not name Siluia thine: if once againe,
~erona shall not hold thee: heere she stands,
Take but possession of her, with a Touch:
I dare thee, but to breath vpon my Loue.

speeches.speaker: Thur.
verse: Sir Valentine, I care not for her, I:
I hold him but a foole that will endanger
His Body, for a Girle that loues him not:
I claime her not, and therefore she is thine.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: The more degenerate and base art thou
To make such meanes for her, as thou hast done,
And leaue her on such slight conditions.
Now, by the honor of my Ancestry,
I doe applaud thy spirit, Valentine,
And thinke thee worthy of an Empresse loue:
Know then, I heere forget all former greefes,
Cancell all grudge, repeale thee home againe,
Plead a new state in thy vn-riual'd merit,

To which I thus subscribe: Sir
~alentine,
Thou art a Gentleman, and well deriu'd,
Take thou thy Siluia, for thou hast deseru'd her.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: I thank your Grace, ye gift hath made me happy:
I now beseech you (for your daughters sake)
To grant one Boone that I shall aske of you.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I grant it (for thine owne) what ere it be.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: These banish'd men, that I haue kept withall,
Are men endu'd with worthy qualities:
Forgiue them what they haue committed here,
And let them be recall'd from their Exile:
They are reformed, ciuill, full of good,
And fit for great employment (worthy Lord.)

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Thou hast preuaild, I pardon them and thee:
Dispose of them, as thou knowst their deserts.
Come, let vs goe, we will include all iarres,
With Triumphes, Mirth, and rare solemnity.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: And as we walke along, I dare be bold
With our discourse, to make your Grace to smile.
What thinke you of this Page (my Lord?)

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I think the Boy hath grace in him, he blushes.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I warrant you (my Lord) more grace, then Boy.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: What meane you by that saying?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Please you, Ile tell you, as we passe along,
That you will wonder what hath fortuned:
Come Protheus, 'tis your pennance, but to heare
The story of your Loues discouered.
That done, our day of marriage shall be yours,
One Feast, one house, one mutuall happinesse.

plays.play_title: THE Merry Wiues of Windsor.

speeches.speaker: Shallow.
prose: SIr Hugh, perswade me not: I will make a Star-Chamber matter of it, if hee were twenty Sir Iohn Falstoffs, he shall not abuse Robert Shallow Esquire.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: In the County of Glocester, Iustice of Peace and Coram.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: I (Cosen Slender) and Cust-alorum.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I, and Rato lorum too; and a Gentleman borne (Master Parson) who writes himselfe Armigero, in any Bill, Warrant, Quittance, or Obligation, Armigero.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: I that I doe, and haue done any time these three hundred yeeres.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: All his successors (gone before him) hath don't: and all his Ancestors (that come after him) may: they may giue the dozen white Luces in their Coate.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: It is an olde Coate.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: The dozen white Lowses doe become an old Coat well: it agrees well passant: It is a familiar beast to man, and signifies Loue.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: The Luse is the fresh-fish, the salt-fish, is an old Coate.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I may quarter (Coz).

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: You may, by marrying.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: It is marring indeed, if he quarter it.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Not a whit.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Yes per-lady: if he ha's a quarter of your coat, there is but three Skirts for your selfe, in my simple coniectures; but that is all one: if Sir Iohn Falstaffe haue committed disparagements vnto you, I am of the Church and will be glad to do my beneuolence, to make attonements and compremises betweene you.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: The Councell shall heare it, it is a Riot.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: It is not meet the Councell heare a Riot: there is no feare of Got in a Riot: The Councell (looke you) shall desire to heare the feare of Got, and not to heare a Riot: take your viza-ments in that.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Ha; o' my life, if I were yong againe, the sword should end it.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: It is petter that friends is the sword, and end it: and there is also another deuice in my praine, which peraduenture prings goot discretions with it. There is Anne Page, which is daughter to Master Thomas Page, which is pretty virginity.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Mistris Anne Page? she has browne haire, and speakes small like a woman.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: It is that ferry person for all the orld, as iust as you will desire, and seuen hundred pounds of Moneyes, and Gold, and Siluer, is her Grand-sire vpon his deaths-bed, (Got deliuer to a ioyfull resurrections) giue, when she is able to ouertake seuenteene yeeres old. It were a goot motion, if we leaue our pribbles and prabbles, and desire a marriage betweene Master Abraham, and Mistris Anne Page.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Did her Grand-sire leaue her seauen hundred pound?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: I, and her father is make her a petter penny.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I know the young Gentlewoman, she has good gifts.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Seuen hundred pounds, and possibilities, is goot gifts.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose:
Wel, let vs see honest Mr
Page: is Falstaffe there?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Shall I tell you a lye? I doe despise a lyer, as I doe despise one that is false, or as I despise one that is not true: the Knight Sir Iohn is there, and I beseech you be ruled by your well-willers: I will peat the doore for Mr. Page. What hoa? Got-plesse your house heere.

speeches.speaker: Mr. Page.
prose: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Here is go't's plessing and your friend, and Iustice Shallow, and heere yong Master Slender: that peraduentures shall tell you another tale, if matters grow to your likings.

speeches.speaker: M^. Page.
prose: I am glad to see your Worships well: I thanke you for my Venison Master Shallow.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Master Page, I am glad to see you: much good doe it your good heart: I wish'd your Venison better, it was ill killd: how doth good Mistresse Page? and I thank you alwaies with my heart, la: with my heart.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Sir, I thanke you.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Sir, I thanke you: by yea, and no I doe.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: I am glad to see you, good Master Slender.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: How do's your fallow Greyhound, Sir, I heard say he was out-run on Cotsall.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: It could not be iudg'd, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: You'll not confesse: you'll not confesse.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: That he will not, 'tis your fault, 'tis your fault: 'tis a good dogge.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: A Cur, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Sir: hee's a good dog, and a faire dog, can there be more said? he is good, and faire. Is Sir Iohn Falstaffe heere?

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: Sir, hee is within: and I would I could doe a good office betweene you.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: It is spoke as a Christians ought to speake.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: He hath wrong'd me (Master Page.)

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: Sir, he doth in some sort confesse it.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: If it be confessed, it is not redressed; is not that so (M. Page?) he hath wrong'd me, indeed he hath, at a word he hath: beleeue me, Robert Shallow Esquire, saith he is wronged.

speeches.speaker: Ma. Pa.
prose: Here comes Sir Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Now, Master Shallow, you'll complaine of me to the King?

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Knight, you haue beaten my men, kill'd my deere, and broke open my Lodge.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: But not kiss'd your Keepers daughter?

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Tut, a pin: this shall be answer'd.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: I will answere it strait, I haue done all this:
That is now answer'd.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: The Councell shall know this.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: 'Twere better for you if it were known in councell: you'll be laugh'd at.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Pauca verba; (Sir Iohn) good worts.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Good worts? good Cabidge; Slender, I broke your head: what matter haue you against me?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Marry sir, I haue matter in my head against you, and against your cony-catching Rascalls, Bardolf, Nym, and Pistoll.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: You Banbery Cheese.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I, it is no matter.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: How now, Mephostophilus?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I, it is no matter.

speeches.speaker: Nym.
prose: Slice, I say; pauca. pauca: Slice, that's my humor.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Where's Simple my man? can you tell, Cosen?

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: Peace, I pray you: now let vs vnderstand: there is three Vmpires in this matter, as I vnderstand; that is, Master Page (fidelicet Master Page,) & there is my selfe, (fidelicet my selfe) and the three party is (lastly, and finally) mine Host of the Gater.

speeches.speaker: Ma. Pa.
prose: We three to hear it, & end it between them.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Ferry goo't, I will make a priefe of it in my note-booke, and we wil afterwards orke vpon the cause, with as great discreetly as we can.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Pistoll.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: He heares with eares.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: The Teuill and his Tam: what phrase is this? he heares with eare? why, it is affectations.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Pistoll, did you picke M. Slenders purse?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I, by these gloues did hee, or I would I might neuer come in mine owne great chamber againe else, of seauen groates in mill-sixpences, and two Edward Shouelboords, that cost me two shilling and two pence a peece of Yead Miller: by these gloues.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Is this true, Pistoll?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: No, it is false, if it is a picke-purse.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Ha, thou mountaine Forreyner: Sir Iohn, and Master mine, I combat challenge of this Latine Bilboe: word of deniall in thy labras here; word of denial; froth, and scum thou liest.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: By these gloues, then 'twas he.

speeches.speaker: Nym.
prose: Be auis'd sir, and passe good humours: I will say marry trap with you, if you runne the nut-hooks humor on me, that is the very note of it.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: By this hat, then he in the red face had it: for though I cannot remember what I did when you made me drunke, yet I am not altogether an asse.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: What say you Scarlet, and Iohn?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Why sir, (for my part) I say the Gentleman had drunke himselfe out of his fiue sentences.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: It is his fiue sences: fie, what the ignorance is.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: And being fap, sir, was (as they say) casheerd: and so conclusions past the Car-eires.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I, you spake in Latten then to: but 'tis no matter; Ile nere be drunk whilst I liue againe, but in honest, ciuill, godly company for this tricke: if I be drunke, Ile be drunke with those that haue the feare of God, and not with drunken knaues.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: So got-udge me, that is a vertuons minde.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: You heare all these matters deni'd, Gentlemen; you heare it.

speeches.speaker: Mr. Page.
prose: Nay daughter, carry the wine in, wee'll drinke within.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Oh heauen: This is Mistresse Anne Page.

speeches.speaker: Mr. Page.
prose: How now Mistris Ford?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Mistris Ford, by my troth you are very wel met: by your leaue good Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Mr. Page.
prose: Wife, bid these gentlemen welcome: come, we haue a hot Venison pasty to dinner; Come gentlemen, I hope we shall drinke downe all vnkindnesse.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I had rather then forty shillings I had my booke of Songs and Sonnets heere: How now Simple, where haue you beene? I must wait on my selfe, must I? you haue not the booke of Riddles about you, haue you?

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: Booke of Riddles? why did you not lend it to Alice Short-cake vpon Alhallowmas last, a fortnight afore Michaelmas.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Come Coz, come Coz, we stay for you: a word with you Coz: marry this, Coz: there is as 'twere a tender, a kinde of tender, made a farre-off by Sir Hugh here: doe you vnderstand me?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I Sir, you shall finde me reasonable; if it be so, I shall doe that that is reason.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Nay, but vnderstand me.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: So I doe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Giue eare to his motions; (Mr. Slender) I will description the matter to you, if you be capacity of it.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Nay, I will doe as my Cozen Shallow saies: I pray you pardon me, he's a Iustice of Peace in his Countrie, simple though I stand here.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: But that is not the question: the question is concerning your marriage.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: I, there's the point Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Marry is it: the very point of it, to Mi. An Page.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Why if it be so; I will marry her vpon any reasonable demands.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
