prose: But can you affection the 'o-man, let vs command to know that of your mouth, or of your lips: for diuers Philosophers hold, that the lips is parcell of the mouth: therfore precisely, ca~ you carry your good wil to ye maid?

speeches.speaker: Sh.
prose: Cosen Abraham Slender, can you loue her?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I hope sir, I will do as it shall become one that would doe reason.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Nay, got's Lords, and his Ladies, you must speake possitable, if you can carry-her your desires towards her.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
verse: That you must:
Will you, (vpon good dowry) marry her?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I will doe a greater thing then that, vpon your request (Cosen) in any reason.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Nay conceiue me, conceiue mee, (sweet Coz): what I doe is to pleasure you (Coz:) can you loue the maid?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I will marry her (Sir) at your request; but if there bee no great loue in the beginning, yet Heauen may decrease it vpon better acquaintance, when wee are married, and haue more occasion to know one another: I hope vpon familiarity will grow more content: but if you say mary-her, I will mary-her, that I am freely dissolued, and dissolutely.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: It is a fery discetion-answere; saue the fall is in the'ord, dissolutely: the ort is (according to our meaning) resolutely: his meaning is good.

speeches.speaker: Sh.
prose: I: I thinke my Cosen meant well.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: I, or else I would I might be hang'd (la.)

speeches.speaker: Sh.
prose: Here comes faire Mistris Anne; would I were yong for your sake, Mistris Anne.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: The dinner is on the Table, my Father desires your worships company.

speeches.speaker: Sh.
prose: I will wait on him, (faire Mistris Anne.)

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Od's plessed-wil: I wil not be abse~ce at the grace.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Wil't please your worship to come in, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: No, I thank you forsooth, hartely; I am very well.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: The dinner attends you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: I am not a-hungry, I thanke you, forsooth: goe, Sirha, for all you are my man, goe wait vpon my Cosen Shallow: a Iustice of peace sometime may be beholding to his friend, for a Man; I keepe but three Men, and a Boy yet, till my Mother be dead: but what though, yet I liue like a poore Gentleman borne.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I may not goe in without your worship: they will not sit till you come.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: I' faith, ile eate nothing: I thanke you as much as though I did.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I pray you Sir walke in.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: I had rather walke here (I thanke you) I bruiz'd my shin th' other day, with playing at Sword and Dagger with a Master of Fence (three veneys for a dish of stew'd Prunes) and by my troth, I cannot abide the smell of hot meate since. Why doe your dogs barke so? be there Beares ith' Towne?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I thinke there are, Sir, I heard them talk'd of.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: I loue the sport well, but I shall as soone quarrell at it, as any man in England: you are afraid if you see the Beare loose, are you not?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I indeede Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: That's meate and drinke to me now: I haue seene Sackerson loose, twenty times, and haue taken him by the Chaine: but (I warrant you) the women haue so cride and shrekt at it, that it past: But women indeede, cannot abide'em, they are very ill-fauour'd rough things.

speeches.speaker: Ma. Pa.
prose: Come, gentle M. Slender, come; we stay for you.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: Ile eate nothing, I thanke you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ma. Pa.
prose: By cocke and pie, you shall not choose, Sir: come, come.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: Nay, pray you lead the way.

speeches.speaker: Ma. Pa.
prose: Come on, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: Mistris Anne: your selfe shall goe first.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Not I Sir, pray you keepe on.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: Truely I will not goe first: truely-la: I will not doe you that wrong.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I pray you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sl.
prose: Ile rather be vnmannerly, then troublesome: you doe your selfe wrong indeede-la.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Go your waies, and aske of Doctor Caius house, which is the way; and there dwels one Mistris Quickly; which is in the manner of his Nurse; or his dry-Nurse; or his Cooke; or his Laundry; his Washer, and his Ringer.

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: Well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Nay, it is petter yet: giue her this letter; for it is a'oman that altogeathers acquainta~ce with Mistris Anne Page; and the Letter is to desire, and require her to solicite your Masters desires, to Mistris Anne Page: I pray you be gon: I will make an end of my dinner; ther's Pippins and Cheese to come.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Mine Host of the Garter?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: What saies my Bully Rooke? speake schollerly, and wisely.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Truely mine Host; I must turne away some of my followers.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Discard, (bully Hercules) casheere; let them wag; trot, trot.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I sit at ten pounds a weeke.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Thou'rt an Emperor (Cesar, Keiser and Pheazar) I will entertaine Bardolfe: he shall draw; he shall tap; said I well (bully Hector?)

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Doe so (good mine Host.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I haue spoke: let him follow: let me see thee froth, and liue: I am at a word: follow.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Bardolfe, follow him: a Tapster is a good trade: an old Cloake, makes a new Ierkin: a wither'd Seruing-man, a fresh Tapster: goe, adew.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
prose: It is a life that I haue desir'd: I will thriue.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: O base hungarian wight: wilt yu the spigot wield.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: He was gotten in drink: is not the humor co~ceited?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I am glad I am so acquit of this Tinderbox: his Thefts were too open: his filching was like an vnskilfull Singer, he kept not time.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: The good humor is to steale at a minutes rest.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Conuay: the wise it call: Steale? foh: a fico for the phrase.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Well sirs, I am almost out at heeles.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Why then let Kibes ensue.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: There is no remedy: I must conicatch, I must shift.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Yong Rauens must haue foode.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Which of you know Ford of this Towne?

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: I ken the wight: he is of substance good.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: My honest Lads, I will tell you what I am about.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Two yards, and more.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: No quips now Pistoll: (Indeede I am in the waste two yards about: but I am now about no waste: I am about thrift) briefely: I doe meane to make loue to Fords wife: I spie entertainment in her: shee discourses: shee carues: she giues the leere of inuitation: I can construe the action of her familier stile, & the hardest voice of her behauior (to be english'd rightly) is, I am Sir Iohn Falstafs.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: He hath studied her will; and translated her will: out of honesty, into English.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: The Anchor is deepe: will that humor passe?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Now, the report goes, she has all the rule of her husbands Purse: he hath a legend of Angels.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: As many diuels entertaine: and to her Boy say I.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: The humor rises: it is good: humor me the angels.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I haue writ me here a letter to her: & here another to Pages wife, who euen now gaue mee good eyes too; examind my parts with most iudicious illiads: sometimes the beame of her view, guilded my foote: sometimes my portly belly.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Then did the Sun on dung-hill shine.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: I thanke thee for that humour.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: O she did so course o're my exteriors with such a greedy intention, that the appetite of her eye, did seeme to scorch me vp like a burning-glasse: here's another letter to her: She beares the Purse too: She is a Region in Guiana: all gold, and bountie: I will be Cheaters to them both, and they shall be Exchequers to mee: they shall be my East and West Indies, and I will trade to them both: Goe, beare thou this Letter to Mistris Page; and thou this to Mistris Ford: we will thriue (Lads) we will thriue.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: Shall I Sir Pandarus of Troy become,
And by my side weare Steele? then Lucifer take all.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: I will run no base humor: here take the humor-Letter; I will keepe the hauior of reputation.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: Hold Sirha, beare you these Letters tightly,
Saile like my Pinnasse to these golden shores.
Rogues, hence, auaunt, vanish like haile-stones; goe,
Trudge; plod away ith' hoofe: seeke shelter, packe:
Falstaffe will learne the honor of the age,
French-thrift, you Rogues, my selfe, and skirted Page.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: Let Vultures gripe thy guts: for gourd, and
Fullam holds: & high and low beguiles the rich & poore,
Tester ile haue in pouch when thou shalt lacke,
Base Phrygian Turke.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
verse: I haue opperations,
Which be humors of reuenge.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Wilt thou reuenge?

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: By Welkin, and her Star.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: With wit, or Steele?

speeches.speaker: Ni.
verse: With both the humors, I:
I will discusse the humour of this Loue to Ford.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: And I to Page shall eke vnfold
How Falstaffe (varlet vile)
His Doue will proue; his gold will hold,
And his soft couch defile.

speeches.speaker: Ni.
prose: My humour shall not coole: I will incense Ford to deale with poyson: I will possesse him with yallownesse, for the reuolt of mine is dangerous: that is my true humour.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Thou art the Mars of Malecontents: I second thee: troope on.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: What, Iohn Rugby, I pray thee goe to the Casement, and see if you can see my Master, Master Docter Caius comming: if he doe (I' faith) and finde any body in the house; here will be an old abusing of Gods patience, and the Kings English.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
prose: Ile goe watch.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Goe, and we'll haue a posset for't soone at night, (in faith) at the latter end of a Sea-cole-fire: An honest, willing, kinde fellow, as euer seruant shall come in house withall: and I warrant you, no tel-tale, nor no breedebate: his worst fault is, that he is giuen to prayer; hee is something peeuish that way: but no body but has his fault: but let that passe. Peter Simple, you say your name is?

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: I: for fault of a better.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: And Master Slender's your Master?

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: I forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Do's he not weare a great round Beard, like a Glouers pairing-knife?

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: No forsooth: he hath but a little wee face; with a little yellow Beard: a Caine colourd Beard.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: A softly-sprighted man, is he not?

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: I forsooth: but he is as tall a man of his hands, as any is betweene this and his head: he hath fought with a Warrener.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: How say you: oh, I should remember him: do's he not hold vp his head (as it were?) and strut in his gate?

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: Yes indeede do's he.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Well, heauen send Anne Page, no worse fortune: Tell Master Parson Euans, I will doe what I can for your Master: Anne is a good girle, and I wish —

speeches.speaker: Ru.
prose: Out alas: here comes my Master.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: We shall all be shent: Run in here, good young man: goe into this Closset: he will not stay long: what Iohn Rugby? Iohn: what Iohn I say? goe Iohn, goe enquire for my Master, I doubt he be not well, that hee comes not home: (and downe, downe, adowne'a. &c.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: Vat is you sing? I doe not like des-toyes: pray you goe and vetch me in my Closset, vnboyteene verd; a Box, a greene-a-Box: do intend vat I speake? a greene-a-Box.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: I forsooth ile fetch it you: I am glad hee went not in himselfe: if he had found the yong man he would haue bin horne-mad.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: Fe, fe, fe, fe, maifoy, il fait for ehando, Ie man voi a le Court la grand affaires.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Is it this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ca.
verse: Ony mette le au mon pocket, de-petch quickly:
Vere is dat knaue Rugby?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: What Iohn Rugby, Iohn?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
prose: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
verse: You are Iohn Rugby, aad you are Iacke Rugby:
Come, take-a-your Rapier, and come after my heele to the Court.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
prose: 'Tis ready Sir, here in the Porch.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: By my trot: I tarry too long: od's-me: que ay ie oublie: dere is some Simples in my Closset, dat I vill not for the varld I shall leaue behinde.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Ay-me, he'll finde the yong man there, & be mad.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
verse: O Diable, Diable: vat is in my Closset?
Villanie, La-roone: Rugby, my Rapier.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Good Master be content.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: Wherefore shall I be content-a?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: The yong man is an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: What shall de honest man do in my Closset: dere is no honest man dat shall come in my Closset.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: I beseech you be not so flegmaticke: heare the truth of it. He came of an errand to mee, from Parson Hugh.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: Vell.

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: I forsooth: to desire her to —

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Peace, I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: Peace-a-your tongue: speake-a-your Tale.

speeches.speaker: Si.
prose: To desire this honest Gentlewoman (your Maid) to speake a good word to Mistris Anne Page, for my Master in the way of Marriage.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: This is all indeede-la: but ile nere put my finger in the fire, and neede not.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: Sir Hugh send-a you? Rugby, ballow mee some paper: tarry you a littell-a-while.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: I am glad he is so quiet if he had bin throughly moued, you should haue heard him so loud, and so melancholly: but notwithstanding man, Ile doe yoe your Master what good I can: and the very yea, & the no is, ye French Doctor my Master, (I may call him my Master, looke you, for I keepe his house; and I wash, ^ing, brew, bake, scowre, dresse meat and drinke, make the beds, and doe all my selfe.)

speeches.speaker: Simp.
prose: 'Tis a great charge to come vnder one bodies hand.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Are you a-uis'd o' that? you shall finde it a great charge: and to be vp early, and down later but notwithstanding, (to tell you in your eare, I wold haue no words of it) my Master himselfe is in loue with Mistris Anne Page: but notwithstanding that I know Ans mind, that's neither heere nor there.

speeches.speaker: Caius.
prose: You, lack 'Nape: giue-'a this Letter to Sir Hugh, by gar it is a shallenge: I will cut his troat in de Parke, and I will teach a souruy lack-a-nape Priest to meddle, or make: — you may be gon: it is not good you tarry here: by gar I will cut all his two stones: by gar, he shall not haue a stone to throw at his dogge.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Alas: he speakes but for his friend.

speeches.speaker: Caius.
prose: It is no matter'a ver dat: do not you tell-a-me dat I shall haue Anne Page for my selfe? by gar, I vill kill de Iack-Priest: and I haue appointed mine Host of de Iarteer to measure our weapon: by gar, I wil my selfe haue Anne Page.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Sir, the maid loues you, and all shall bee well:
We must giue folkes leaue to prate: what the good-ier.

speeches.speaker: Caius.
prose: Rugby, come to the Court with me: by gar, if I haue not Anne Page, I shall turne your head out of my dore: follow my heeles, Rugby.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: You shall haue An-fooles head of your owne: No, I know Ans mind for that: neuer a woman in Windsor knowes more of Ans minde then I doe, nor can doe more then I doe with her, I thanke heauen.

speeches.speaker: Fenton.
prose: Who's with in there, hoa?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Who's there, I troa? Come neere the house I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: How now (good woman) how dost thou?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: The better that it pleases your good Worship to aske?

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: What newes? how do's pretty Mistris Anne?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: In truth Sir, and shee is pretty, and honest, and gentle, and one that is your friend, I can tell you that by the way, I praise heauen for it.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: Shall I doe any good thinkst thou? shall I not loose my suit?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Troth Sir, all is in his hands aboue: but notwithstanding (Master Fenton) Ile be sworne on a booke shee loues you: haue not your Worship a wart aboue your eye?

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: Yes marry haue I, what of that?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Wel, thereby hangs a tale: good faith, it is such another Nan; (but (I detest) an honest maid as euer broke bread: wee had an howres talke of that wart; I shall neuer laugh but in that maids company: but (indeed) shee is giuen too much to Allicholy and musing: but for you — well — goe too —

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: Well: I shall see her to day: hold, there's money for thee: Let mee haue thy voice in my behalfe: if thou seest her before me, commend me. —

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Will I? I faith that wee will: And I will tell your Worship more of the Wart, the next time we haue confidence, and of other wooers.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: Well, fare-well, I am in great haste now.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Fare-well to your Worship: truely an honest Gentleman: but Anne loues hiim not: for I know Ans minde as well as another do's: out vpon't: what haue I forgot.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse: What a Herod of Iurie is this? O wicked, wicked world:
One that is well-nye worne to peeces with age
To show himselfe a yong Gallant? What an vnwaied
Behauiour hath this Flemish drunkard pickt (with
The Deuills name) out of my conuersation, that he dares
In this manner assay me? why, hee hath not beene thrice
In my Company: what should I say to him? I was then
Frugall of my mirth: (heauen forgiue mee:) why Ile
prose: What, haue scap'd Loue-letters in the holly-day-time of my beauty, and am I now a subiect for them? let me see?

Aske me no reason why I loue you, for though Loue vse Reason for his precisian, hee admits him not for his Counsailour: you are not yong, no more am I: goe to then, there's simpathie: you are merry, so am I: ha, ha, then there's more simpathie: you loue sacke, and so do I: would you desire better simpathie? Let it suffice thee (Mistris Page) at the least if the Loue of Souldier can suffice, that I loue thee: I will not say pitty mee, 'tis not a Souldier-like phrase; but I say, loue me:


By me, thine owne true Knight, by day or night:
Or any kinde of light, with all his might,
For thee to fight.


Iohn Falstaffe.
Exhibit a Bill in the Parliament for the putting downe of men: how shall I be reueng'd on him? for reueng'd I will be? as sure as his guts are made of puddings.

speeches.speaker: Mis Ford.
prose: Mistris Page, trust me, I was going to your house.

speeches.speaker: Mis Page.
prose: And trust me, I was comming to you: you looke very ill.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: Nay, Ile nere beleeee that; I haue to shew to the contrary.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: 'Faith but you doe in my minde.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: Well: I doe then: yet I say, I could shew you to the contrary: O Mistris Page, giue mee some counsaile.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: What's the matter, woman?

speeches.speaker: Mi. Ford.
prose: O woman: if it were not for one trifling respect, I could come to such honour.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Page.
prose: Hang the trifle (woman) take the honour: what is it? dispence with trifles: what is it?

speeches.speaker: Mi. Ford.
prose: If I would but goe to hell, for an eternall moment, or so: I could be knighted.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Page.
prose: What thou liest? Sir Alice Ford? these Knights will hacke, and so thou shouldst not alter the article of thy Gentry.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Ford.
prose:
Wee burne day-light: heere, read, read: perceiue how I might bee knighted, I shall thinke the worse of fat men, as long as I haue an eye to make difference of mens liking: and yet hee would not sweare:

praise womens modesty: and gaue such orderly and wel-behaued reproofe to al vncomelinesse, that I would haue sworne his disposition would haue gone to the truth of his words: but they doe no more adhere and keep place together, then the hundred Psalms to the tune of Green-sleeues: What tempest (I troa) threw this Whale, (with so many Tuns of oyle in his belly) a'shoare at Windsor? How shall I bee reuenged on him? I thinke the best way were, to entertaine him with hope, till the wicked fire of lust haue melted him in his owne greace: Did you euer heare the like?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Letter for letter; but that the name of Page and Ford differs: to thy great comfort in this mystery of ill opinions, heere's the twyn-brother of thy Letter: but let thine inherit first, for I protest mine neuer shall: I warrant he hath a thousand of these Letters, writ with blancke-space for different names (sure more): and these are of the second edition: hee will print them out of doubt: for he cares not what hee puts into the presse, when he would put vs two: I had rather be a Giantesse, and lye vnder Mount Pelion: Well; I will find you twentie lasciuious Turtles ere one chaste man.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: Why this is the very same: the very hand: the very words: what doth he thinke of vs?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Nay I know not: it makes me almost readie to wrangle with mine owne honesty: Ile entertaine my selfe like one that I am not acquainted withall: for sure vnlesse hee know some straine in mee, that I know not my selfe, hee would neuer haue boorded me in this furie.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Ford.
prose: Boording, call you it? Ile bee sure to keepe him aboue decke.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Page.
prose: So will I: if hee come vnder my hatches, Ile neuer to Sea againe: Let's bee reueng'd on him: let's appoint him a meeting: giue him a show of comfort in his Suit, and lead him on with a fine baited delay, till hee hath pawn'd his horses to mine Host of the Garter.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Ford.
prose: Nay, I wil consent to act any villany against him, that may not sully the charinesse of our honesty: oh that my husband saw this Letter: it would giue eternall food to his iealousie.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Why look where he comes; and my good man too: hee's as farre from iealousie, as I am from giuing him cause, and that (I hope) is an vnmeasurable distance.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: You are the happier woman.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Let's consult together against this greasie Knight: Come hither.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Well: I hope, it be not so.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: Hope is a curtall-dog in some affaires:
Sir Iohn affects thy wife.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Why sir, my wife is not young.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: He wooes both high and low, both rich & poor, both yong and old, one with another (Ford) he loues the Gally-mawfry (Ford) perpend.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Loue my wife?

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: With liuer, burning hot: preuent:
Or goe thou like Sir Acteon he, with
Ring-wood at thy heeles: O, odious is the name.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: What name Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: The horne I say: Farewell:
Take heed, haue open eye, for theeues doe foot by night.
Take heed, ere sommer comes, or Cuckoo-birds do sing.
Away sir Corporall Nim:
Beleeue it (Page) he speakes sence.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I will be patient: I will find out this.

speeches.speaker: Nim.
prose: And this is true: I like not the humor of lying: hee hath wronged mee in some humors: I should haue borne the humour'd Letter to her: but I haue a sword: and it shall bite vpon my necessitie: he loues your wife; There's the short and the long: My name is Corporall Nim: I speak, and I auouch; 'tis true: my name is Nim: and Falstaffe loues your wife: adieu, I loue not the humour of bread and cheese: adieu.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: The humour of it (quoth'a?) heere's a fellow frights English out of his wits.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I will seeke out Falstaffe.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: I neuer heard such a drawling-affecting rogue.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: If I doe finde it: well.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: I will not beleeue such a Cataian, though the Priest o' th' Towne commended him for a true man.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: 'Twas a good sensible fellow: well.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: How now Meg?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Whether goe you (George?) harke you.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: How now (sweet Frank) why art thou melancholy?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: I melancholy? I am not melancholy:
Get you home: goe.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
verse: Faith, thou hast some crochets in thy head,
Now: will you goe, Mistris Page?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Haue with you: you'll come to dinner George? Looke who comes yonder: shee shall bee our Messenger to this paltrie Knight.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: Trust me, I thought on her: shee'll fit it.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: You are come to see my daughter Anne?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: I forsooth: and I pray how do's good Mistresse Anne?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Go in with vs and see: we haue an houres talke with you.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: How now Master Ford?

speeches.speaker: For.
prose: You heard what this knaue told me, did you not?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Yes, and you heard what the other told me?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Doe you thinke there is truth in them?

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: Hang 'em slaues: I doe not thinke the Knight would offer it: But these that accuse him in his intent towards our wiues, are a yoake of his discarded men: very rogues, now they be out of seruice.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Were they his men?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Marry were they.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: I like it neuer the beter for that,
Do's he lye at the Garter?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: I marry do's he: if hee should intend this voyage toward my wife, I would turne her loose to him; and what hee gets more of her, then sharpe words, let it lye on my head.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I doe not misdoubt my wife: but I would bee loath to turne them together: a man may be too confident: I would haue nothing lye on my head: I cannot be thus satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Looke where my ranting-Host of the Garter comes: there is eyther liquor in his pate, or mony in his purse, when hee lookes so merrily: How now mine Host?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: How now Bully-Rooke: thou'rt a Gentleman Caueleiro Iustice, I say.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: I follow, (mine Host) I follow: Good-euen, and twe^ty (good Master Page.) Master Page, wil you go with vs? we haue sport in hand.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Tell him Caueleiro-Iustice: tell him Bully-Rooke.

speeches.speaker: Shall.
prose: Sir, there is a fray to be fought, betweene Sir Hugh the Welch Priest, and Caius the French Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Good mine Host o' th' Garter: a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: What saist thou, my Bully-Rooke?

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Will you goe with vs to behold it? My merry Host hath had the measuring of their weapons; and (I thinke) hath appointed them contrary places: for (beleeue mee) I heare the Parson is no Iester: harke, I will tell you what our sport shall be.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Hast thou no suit against my Knight? my guest-Caualeire?

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: None, I protest: but Ile giue you a pottle of burn'd sacke, to giue me recourse to him, and tell him my name is Broome: onely for a ^est.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: My hand, (Bully:) thou shalt haue egresse and regresse, (said I well?) and thy name shall be Broome. It is a merry Knight: will you goe An-heires?

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Haue with you mine Host.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: I haue heard the French-man hath good skill in his Rapier.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Tut sir: I could haue told you more: In these times you stand on distance: your Passes, Stoccado's, and I know not what: 'tis the heart (Master Page) 'tis heere, 'tis heere: I haue seene the time, with my long-sword, I would haue made you fowre tall fellowes skippe like Rattes.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Heere boyes, heere, heere: shall we wag?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Haue with you: I had rather heare them scold, then fight.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Though Page be a secure foole, and stands so firmely on his wiues frailty; yet, I cannot put-off my opinion so easily: she was in his company at Pages house: and what they made there, I know not. Well, I wil looke further into't, and I haue a disguise, to sound Falstaffe; if I finde her honest, I loose not my labor: if she be otherwise, 'tis labour well bestowed.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I will not lend thee a penny.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Why then the world's mine Oyster, which I, with sword will open.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Not a penny: I haue beene content (Sir,) you should lay my countenance to pawne: I haue grated vpon my good friends for three Repreeues for you, and your Coach-fellow Nim; or else you had look'd through the grate, like a Geminy of Baboones: I am damn'd in hell, for swearing to Gentlemen my friends, you were good Souldiers, and tall-fellowes. And when Mistresse Bright lost the handle of her Fan, I took't vpon mine honour thou hadst it not.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Didst not thou share? hadst thou not fifteene pence?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Reason, you roague, reason: thinkst thou Ile endanger my soule, gratis? at a word, hang no more about mee, I am no gibbet for you: goe, a short knife, and a throng, to your Mannor of Pickt-hatch: goe, you'll not beare a Letter for mee you roague? you stand vpon your honor: why, (thou vnconfinable basenesse) it is as much as I can doe to keepe the termes of my hononor precise: I, I, I my selfe sometimes, leauing the feare of heauen on the left hand, and hiding mine honor in my necessity, am faine to shufflle: to hedge, and to lurch, and yet, you Rogue, will en-sconce your raggs; your Cat-a-Mountaine-lookes, your red-lattice phrases, and your bold-beating-oathes, vnder the shelter of your honor? you will not doe it? you?

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: I doe relent: what would thou more of man?

speeches.speaker: Robin.
prose: Sir, here's a woman would speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Let her approach.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Giue your worship good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Good-morrow, good-wife.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Not so and't please your worship.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Good maid then.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Ile be sworne,
As my mother was the first houre I was borne.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I doe beleeue the swearer; what with me?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Shall I vouch-safe your worship a word, or two?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Two thousand (faire woman) and ile vouchsafe thee the hearing.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: There is one Mistresse Ford, (Sir) I pray come a little neerer this waies: I my selfe dwell with M. Doctor Caius:

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Well, on; Mistresse Ford, you say.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Your worship saies very true: I pray your worship come a little neerer this waies.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I warrant thee, no-bodie heares: mine owne people, mine owne people.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Are they so? heauen-blesse them, and make them his Seruants.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Well; Mistresse Ford, what of her?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Why, Sir; shee's a good-creature; Lord, Lord, your Worship's a wanton: well: heauen forgiue you, and all of vs, I pray—.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Mistresse Ford: come, Mistresse Ford.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Marry this is the short, and the long of it: you haue brought her into such a Canaries, as 'tis wonderfull: the best Courtier of them all (when the Court lay at Windsor) could neuer haue brought her to such a Canarie: yet there has beene Knights, and Lords, and Gentlemen, with their Coaches; I warrant you Coach after Coach, letter after letter, gift after gift, smelling so sweetly; all Muske, and so rushling, I warrant you, in silke and golde, and in such alligant termes, and in such wine and suger of the best, and the fairest, that would haue wonne any womans heart: and I warrant you, they could neuer get an eye-winke of her: I had my selfe twentie Angels giuen me this morning, but I defie all Angels (in any such sort, as they say) but in the way of honesty: and I warrant you, they could neuer get her so much as sippe on a cup with the prowdest of them all, and yet there has beene Earles: nay, (which is more) Pentioners, but I warrant you all is one with her.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: But what saies shee to mee? be briefe my good shee-Mercurie.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Marry, she hath receiu'd your Letter: for the which she thankes you a thousand times; and she giues you to notifie, that her husband will be absence from his house, betweene ten and eleuen.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Ten, and eleuen.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: I, forsooth: and then you may come and see the picture (she sayes) that you wot of: Master Ford her husband will be from home: alas, the sweet woman leades an ill life with him: hee's a very iealousie-man; she leads a very frampold life with him, (good hart.)

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: Ten, and eleuen.
Woman, commend me to her, I will not faile her.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Why, you say well: But I haue another messenger to your worship: Mistresse Page hath her heartie commendations to you to: and let mee tell you in your eare, shee's as fartuous a ciuill modest wife, and one (I tell you) that will not misse you morning nor euening prayer, as any is in Windsor, who ere bee the other: and shee bade me tell your worship, that her husband is seldome from home, but she hopes there will come a time. I neuer knew a woman so doate vpon a man; surely I thinke you haue charmes, la: yes in truth.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Not I, I assure thee; setting the attraction of my good parts aside, I haue no other charmes.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Blessing on your heart for't.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: But I pray thee tell me this: has Fords wife, and Pages wife acquainted each other, how they loue me?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: That were a iest indeed: they haue not so little grace I hope, that were a tricke indeed: But Mistris Page would desire you to send her your little Page of al loues: her husband has a maruellous infectio~ to the little Page: and truely Master Page is an honest man: neuer a wife in Windsor leades a better life then she do's: doe what shee will, say what she will, take all, pay all, goe to bed when she list, rise when she list, all is as she will: and truly she deserues it; for if there be a kinde woman in Windsor, she is one: you must send her your Page, no remedie.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Why, I will.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Nay. but doe so then, and looke you, hee may come and goe betweene you both: and in any case haue a nay-word, that you may know one anothers minde, and the Boy neuer neede to vnderstand any thing; for 'tis not good that children should know any wickednes: olde folkes you know, haue discretion, as they say, and know the world.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Farethee-well, commend mee to them both: there's my purse, I am yet thy debter: Boy, goe along with this woman, this newes distracts me.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: This Puncke is one of Cupids Carriers,
Clap on more sailes, pursue: vp with your fights:
Giue fire: she is my prize, or Ocean whelme them all.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Saist thou so (old Iacke) go thy waies: Ile make more of thy olde body then I haue done: will they yet looke after thee? wilt thou after the expence of so much money, be now a gainer? good Body, I thanke thee: let them say 'tis grossely done, so it bee fairely done, no matter.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Sir Iohn, there's one Master Broome below would faine speake with you, and be acquainted with you; and hath sent your worship a mornings draught of Sacke.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Broome is his name?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: I Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Call him in: such Broomes are welcome to mee, that ore' flowes such liquor: ah ha, Mistresse Ford and Mistresse Page, haue I encompass'd you? goe to, via.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: 'Blesse you sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: And you sir: would you speake with me?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I make bold, to presse, with so little preparation vpon you.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: You'r welcome, what's your will? giue vs leaue Drawer.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Sir, I am a Gentleman that haue spent much, my name is Broome.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Good Master Broome, I desire more acquaintance of you.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Good Sir Iohn, I sue for yours: not to charge you, for I must let you vnderstand, I thinke my selfe in better plight for a Lender, then you are: the which hath something emboldned me to this vnseason'd intrusion: for they say, if money goe before, all waies doe lye open.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Money is a good Souldier (Sir) and will on.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Troth, and I haue a bag of money heere troubles me: if you will helpe to beare it (Sir Iohn) take all, or halfe, for easing me of the carriage.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Sir, I know not how I may deserue to bee your Porter.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I will tell you sir, if you will giue mee the hearing.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Speake (good Master Broome) I shall be glad to be your Seruant.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Sir, I heare you are a Scholler: (I will be briefe with you) and you haue been a man long knowne to me, though I had neuer so good means as desire, to make my selfe acquainted with you. I shall discouer a thing to you, wherein I must very much lay open mine owne imperfection: but (good Sir Iohn) as you haue one eye vpon my follies, as you heare them vnfolded, turne another into the Register of your owne, that I may passe with a reproofe the easier, sith you your selfe know how easie it is to be such an offender.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Very well Sir, proceed.

speeches.speaker: Ford
prose: There is a Gentlewoman in this Towne, her husbands name is Ford.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose:
I haue long lou'd her, and I protest to you, bestowed much on her: followed her with a doating obseruance: Ingross'd opportunities to meete her: fee'd euery slight occasion that could but nigardly giue mee sight of her: not only bought many presents to giue her, but haue giuen largely to many, to know what shee would haue giuen: briefly, I haue pursu'd her, as Loue hath pursued mee, which hath beene on the wing of all occasions: but whatsoeuer I haue merited, either in my minde, or in my meanes, meede I am sure I haue receiued none, vnlesse Experience be a Iewell, that I haue purchased at an infinite rate, and that hath taught mee to say this,

" Loue like a shadow flies, when substance Loue pursues,
" Pursuing that that flies, and flying what pursues.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Haue you receiu'd no promise of satisfaction at her hands?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Neuer.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Haue you importun'd her to such a purpose?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Neuer.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Of what qualitie was your loue then?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Like a fair house, built on another mans ground, so that I haue lost my edifice, by mistaking the place, where I erected it.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: To what purpose haue you vnfolded this to me?

speeches.speaker: For.
prose: When I haue told you that, I haue told you all: Some say, that though she appeare honest to mee, yet in other places shee enlargeth her mirth so farre, that there is shrewd construction made of her. Now (Sir Iohn) here is the heart of my purpose: you are a gentleman of excellent breeding, admirable discourse, of great admittance, authenticke in your place and person, generally allow'd for your many war-like, court-like, and learned preparations.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: O Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose:
Beleeue it, for you know it: there is money, spend it, spend it, spend more; spend all I haue, onely

giue me so much of your time in enchange of it, as to lay an amiable siege to the honesty of this Fords wife: vse your Art of wooing; win her to consent to you: if any man may, you may as soone as any.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Would it apply well to the vehemency of your affection that I should win what you would enioy? Methinkes you prescribe to your selfe very preposterously.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: O, vnderstand my drift: she dwells so securely on the excellency of her honor, that the folly of my soule dares not present it selfe: shee is too bright to be look'd against. Now, could I come to her with any detection in my hand; my desires had instance and argument to commend themselues, I could driue her then from the ward of her purity, her reputation, her marriage-vow, and a thousand other her defences, which now are too-too strongly embattaild against me: what say you too't, Sir Iohn?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Master Broome, I will first make bold with your money: next, giue mee your hand: and last, as I am a gentleman, you shall, if you will, enioy Fords wife.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: O good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I say you shall.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Want no money (Sir Iohn) you shall want none.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Want no Mistresse Ford (Master Broome) you shall want none: I shall be with her (I may tell you) by her owne appointment, euen as you came in to me, her assistant, or goe-betweene, parted from me: I say I shall be with her betweene ten and eleuen: for at that time the iealious-rascally-knaue her husband will be forth: come you to me at night, you shall know how I speed.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I am blest in your acquaintance: do you know Ford Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Hang him (poore Cuckoldly knaue) I know him not: yet I wrong him to call him poore: They say the iealous wittolly-knaue hath masses of money, for the which his wife seemes to me well-fauourd: I will vse her as the key of the Cuckoldly-rogues Coffer, & ther's my haruest-home.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I would you knew Ford, sir, that you might auoid him, if you saw him.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Hang him, mechanicall-salt-butter rogue; I wil stare him out of his wits: I will awe-him with my cudgell: it shall hang like a Meteor ore the Cuckolds horns: Master Broome, thou shalt know, I will predominate ouer the pezant, and thou shalt lye with his wife. Come to me soone at night: Ford's a knaue, and I will aggrauate his stile: thou (Master Broome) shalt know him for knaue, and Cuckold. Come to me soone at night.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: What a damn'd Epicurian-Rascall is this? my heart is ready to cracke with impatience: who saies this is improuident iealousie? my wife hath sent to him, the howre is fixt, the match is made: would any man haue thought this? see the hell of hauing a false woman: my bed shall be abus'd, my Coffers ransack'd, my reputation gnawne at, and I shall not onely receiue this villanous wrong, but stand vnder the adoption of abhominable termes, and by him that does mee this wrong: Termes, names: Amaimon sounds well: Lucifer, well: Barbason, well: yet they are Diuels additions, the names of fiends: But Cuckold, Wittoll, Cuckold? the Diuell himselfe hath not such a name. Page is an Asse, a secure Asse; hee will trust his wife, hee will not be iealous: I will rather trust a Fleming with my butter, Parson Hugh the Welshman with my Cheese, an Irish-man with my Aqua-vitae-bottle, or a Theefe to walke my ambling gelding, then my wife with her selfe. Then she plots, then shee ruminates, then shee deuises: and what they thinke in their hearts they may effect; they will breake their hearts but they will effect. Heauen bee prais'd for my iealousie: eleuen o' clocke the howre, I will preuent this, detect my wife, bee reueng'd on Falstaffe, and laugh at Page. I will about it, better three houres too soone, then a mynute too late: fie, fie, fie: Cuckold, Cuckold, Cuckold.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Caius.
prose: Vat is the clocke, Iack.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
prose: 'Tis past the howre (Sir) that Sir Hugh promis'd to meet.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By gar, he has saue his soule, dat he is no-come: hee has pray his Pible well, dat he is no-come: by gar (Iack Rugby) he is dead already, if he be come.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
prose: Hee is wise Sir: hee knew your worship would kill him if he came.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By gar, de herring is no dead, so as I vill kill him: take your Rapier, (Iacke) I vill tell you how I vill kill him.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
prose: Alas sir, I cannot fence.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Villanie, take your Rapier.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
prose: Forbeare: heer's company.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: 'Blesse thee, bully-Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: 'Saue you Mr. Doctor Caius.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Now, good Mr. Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: 'Giue you good-morrow, sir.

speeches.speaker: Caius.
prose: Vat be all you one, two, tree, fowre, come for?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: To see thee fight, to see thee foigne, to see thee trauerse, to see thee heere, to see thee there, to see thee passe thy puncto, thy flock, thy reuerse, thy distance, thy montant: Is he dead, my Ethiopian? Is he dead, my Francisco? ha Bully? what saies my Esculapius? my Galien? my heart of Elder? ha? is he dead bully-Stale? is he dead?

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By gar, he is de Coward-Iack-Priest of de vorld: he is not show his face.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Thou art a Castalion-king-Vrinall: Hector of Greece (my Boy)

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: I pray you beare witnesse, that me haue stay, sixe or seuen, two tree howres for him, and hee is nocome.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: He is the wiser man (M. Docto) rhe is a curer of soules, and you a curer of bodies: if you should fight, you goe against the haire of your professions: is it not true, Master Page?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Master Shallow; you haue your selfe beene a great fighter, though now a man of peace.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Body-kins M. Page, though I now be old, and of the peace; if I see a sword out, my finger itches to make one: though wee are Iustices, and Doctors, and Church-men (M. Page) wee haue some salt of our youth in vs, we are the sons of women (M. Page.)

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: 'Tis true, Mr. Shallow.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: It wil be found so, (M. Page:) M. Doctor Caius, I am come to fetch you home: I am sworn of the peace: you haue show'd your selfe a wise Physician, and Sir Hugh hath showne himselfe a wise and patient Churchman: you must goe with me, M. Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Host
prose: Pardon, Guest-Iustice; a Mounseur: Mocke-water.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Mock-vater? vat is dat?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Mock-water, in our English tongue, is Valour (Bully.)

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By gar, then I haue as much Mock-vater as de Englishman: scuruy-Iack-dog-Priest: by gar, mee vill cut his eares.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: He will Clapper-claw thee tightly (Bully.)

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Clapper-de-claw? vat is dat?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: That is, he will make thee amends.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By-gar, me doe looke hee shall clapper-de-claw me, for by-gar, me vill haue it.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: And I will prouoke him to't, or let him wag.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Me tanck you for dat.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: And moreouer, (Bully) but first, Mr. Ghuest, and M. Page, & eeke Caualeiro Slender, goe you through the Towne to Frogmore.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Sir Hugh is there, is he?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: He is there, see what humor he is in: and I will bring the Doctor about by the Fields: will it doe well?

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: We will doe it.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Adieu, good M. Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By-gar, me vill kill de Priest, for he speake for a Iack-an-Ape to Anne Page.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Let him die: sheath thy impatience: throw cold water on thy Choller: goe about the fields with mee through Frogmore, I will bring thee where Mistris Anne Page is, at a Farm-house a Feasting: and thou shalt wooe her: Cride-game, said I well?

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By-gar, mee dancke you vor dat: by gar I loue you: and I shall procure 'a you de good Guest: de Earle, de Knight, de Lords, de Gentlemen, my patients.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: For the which, I will be thy aduersary toward Anne Page: said I well?

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By-gar, 'tis good: vell said.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Let vs wag then.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Come at my heeles, Iack Rugby.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: I pray you now, good Master Slenders seruing-man, and friend Simple by your name; which way haue you look'd for Master Caius, that calls himselfe Doctor of Phisicke.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: Marry Sir, the pittie-ward, the Parke-ward: euery way: olde Windsor way, and euery way but the Towne-way.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: I most fehemently desire you, you will also looke that way.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: I will sir.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: 'Plesse my soule: how full of Chollors I am, and trempling of minde: I shall be glad if he haue deceiued me: how melancholies I am? I will knog his Vrinalls about his knaues costard, when I haue good oportunities for the orke: 'Plesse my soule: To shallow Ruiers to whose falls: melodious Birds sings Madrigalls: There will we make our Peds of Roses: and a thousand fragrant posies. To shallow: 'Mercie on mee, I haue a great dispositions to cry. Melodious birds sing Madrigalls: — When as I sat in Pabilon: and a thousand vagram Posies. To shallow, &c.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: Yonder he is comming, this way, Sir Hugh.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
verse: Hee's welcome: To shallow Riuers, to whose fals:
Heauen prosper the right: what weapons is he?

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: No weapons, Sir: there comes my Master, Mr. Shallow, and another Gentleman; from Frogmore, ouer the stile, this way.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Pray you giue mee my gowne, or else keepe it in your armes.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: How now Master Parson? good morrow good Sir Hugh: keepe a Gamester from the dice, and a good Studient from his booke, and it is wonderfull.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Ah sweet Anne Page.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: 'Saue you, good Sir Hugh.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: 'Plesse you from his mercy-sake, all of you.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
verse: What? the Sword, and the Word?
Doe you study them both, Mr. Parson?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: And youthfull still, in your doublet and hose, this raw-rumaticke day?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: There is reasons, and causes for it.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: We are come to you, to doe a good office, Mr. Parson.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Fery-well: what is it?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Yonder is a most reuerend Gentleman; who (be-like) hauing receiued wrong by some person, is at most odds with his owne grauity and patience, that euer you saw.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: I haue liued foure-score yeeres, and vpward: I neuer heard a man of his place, grauity, and learning, so wide of his owne respect.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: What is he?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: I thinke you know him: Mr. Doctor Caius the renowned French Physician.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Got's-will, and his passion of my heart: I had as lief you would tell me of a messe of porredge.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: He has no more knowledge in Hibocrates and Galen, and hee is a knaue besides: a cowardly knaue, as you would desires to be acquainted withall.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: I warrant you, hee's the man should fight with him.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: O sweet Anne Page.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: It appeares so by his weapons: keepe them asunder: here comes Doctor Caius.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Nay good Mr. Parson, keepe in your weapon.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: So doe you, good Mr. Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Disarme them, and let them question: let them keepe their limbs whole, and hack our English.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: I pray you let-a-mee speake a word with your eare; vherefore vill you not meet-a me?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Pray you vse your patience in good time.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By-gar, you are de Coward: de Iack dog: Iohn Ape.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Pray you let vs not be laughing-stocks to other mens humors: I desire you in friendship, and I will one way or other make you amends: I will knog your Vrinal about your knaues Cogs-combe.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Diablo: Iack Rugby: mine Host de Iarteer: haue I not stay for him, to kill him? haue I not at deplace I did appoint?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: As I am a Christians-soule, now looke your: this is the place appointed, Ile bee iudgement by mine Host of the Garter.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Peace, I say, Gallia and Gaule, French & Welch, Soule-Curer, and Body-Curer.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: I, dat is very good, excellant.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Peace, I say: heare mine Host of the Garter, Am I politi^ke? Am I subtle? Am I a Machiuell?

Shall I loose my Doctor? No, hee giues me the Potions and the Motions. Shall I loose my Parson? my Priest? my Sir Hugh? No, he giues me the Prouerbes, and the No-verbes. Giue me thy hand (Celestiall) so: Boyes of Art, I haue deceiu'd you both: I haue directed you to wrong places: your hearts are mighty, your skinnes are whole, and let burn'd Sacke be the issue: Come, lay their swords to pawne: Follow me, Lad of peace, follow, follow, follow.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Trust me, a mad Host: follow Gentlemen, follow.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: O sweet Anne Page.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Ha' do I perceiue dat? Haue you make-a-de-sot of vs, ha, ha?

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: This is well, he has made vs his vlowting-stog: I desire you that we may be friends: and let vs knog our praines together to be reuenge on this same scall scuruy-cogging-companion the Host of the Garter.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: By gar, with all my heart: he promise to bring me where is Anne Page: by gar he deceiue me too.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Well, I will smite his noddles: pray you follow.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Nay keepe your way (little Gallant) you were wont to be a follower, but now you are a Leader: whether had you rather lead mine eyes, or eye your masters heeles?

speeches.speaker: Rob.
prose: I had rather (forsooth) go before you like a man, then follow him like a dwarfe.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: O you are a flattering boy, now I see you'l be a Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Well met mistris Page, whether go you.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: Truly Sir, to see your wife, is she at home?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I, and as idle as she may hang together for want of company: I thinke if your husbands were dead, you two would marry.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: Be sure of that, two other husbands.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Where had you this pretty weather-cocke?

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: I cannot tell what (the dickens) his name is my husband had him of, what do you cal your Knights name sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Rob.
prose: Sir. Iohn Falstaffe.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Sir. Iohn Falstaffe.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: He, he, I can neuer hit on's name; there is such a league betweene my goodman, and he: is your Wife at home indeed?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Indeed she is.

speeches.speaker: M. Pa.
prose: By your leaue sir, I am sicke till I see her.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Has Page any braines? Hath he any eies? Hath he any thinking? Sure they sleepe, he hath no vse of them: why this boy will carrie a letter twentie mile as easie, as a Canon will shoot point-blanke twelue score: hee peeces out his wiues inclination; he giues her folly motion and advantage; and now she's going to my wife, & Falstaffes boy with her: A man may heare this showre sing in the winde; and Falstaffes boy with her: good plots, they are laide, and our reuolted wiues share damnation together. Well, I will take him, then torture my wife, plucke the borrowed vaile of modestie from the so-seeming Mist. Page, divulge Page himselfe for a secure and wilfull Acteon, and to these violent proceedings all my neighbors shall cry aime. The clocke giues me my Qu, and my assurance bids me search, there I shall finde Falstaffe: I shall be rather praisd for this, then mock'd, for it is as possitiue, as the earth is firme, that Falstaffe is there: I will go.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose:
Page, &c. Well met Mr
Ford.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Trust me, a good knotte; I haue good cheere at home, and I pray you all go with me.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose:
I must excuse my selfe Mr
Ford.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
verse: And so must I Sir,
We haue appointed to dine with Mistris Anne,
And I would not breake with her for more mony
Then Ile speake of.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: We haue linger'd about a match betweene An Page, and my cozen Slender, and this day wee shall haue our answer.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I hope I haue your good will Father Page.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse:
You haue Mr
Slender, I stand wholly for you,
But my wife (Mr Doctor) is for you altogether.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: I be-gar, and de Maid is loue-a-me: my nursha-Quickly tell me so mush

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose:
What say you to yong Mr
Fenton? He capers, he dances, he has eies of youth: he writes verses, hee speakes holliday, he smels April and May, he wil carry't, he will carry't, 'tis in his buttons, he will carry't.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Not by my consent I promise you. The Gentleman is of no hauing, hee kept companie with the wilde Prince, and Pointz: he is of too high a Region, he knows too much: no, hee shall not knit a knot in his fortunes, with the finger of my substance: if he take her, let him take her simply: the wealth I haue waits on my consent, and my consent goes not that way.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose:
I beseech you heartily, some of you goe home with me to dinner: besides your cheere you shall haue sport, I will shew you a monster: Mr Doctor, you shal go, so shall you Mr
Page, and you Sir Hugh.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
verse: Well, fare you well:
We shall haue the freer woing at Mr. Pages.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Go home Iohn Rugby, I come anon.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Farewell my hearts, I will to my honest Knight Falstaffe, and drinke Canarie with him.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I thinke I shall drinke in Pipe-wine first with him, Ile make him dance. Will you go, Gentles?

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Haue with you, to see this Monster.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: What Iohn, what Robert.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Quickly, quickly: Is the Buck-basket —

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: I warrant. What Robin I say.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Come, come, come.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Heere, set it downe.

speeches.speaker: M. Pag.
prose: Giue your men the charge, we must be briefe.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Marrie. as I told you before (Iohn & Robert) be ready here hard-by in the Brew-house, & when I sodainly call you, come forth, and (without any pause, or staggering) take this basket on your shoulders: yt done, trudge with it in all hast, and carry it among the Whitsters in Dotchet Mead, and there empty it in the muddie ditch, close by the Thames side.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: You will do it?

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
verse: I ha told them ouer and ouer, they lacke no direction
Be gone, and come when you are call'd.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Here comes little Robin.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: How now my Eyas-Musket, what newes with you?

speeches.speaker: Rob.
prose: My M. Sir Iohn is come in at your backe doore (Mist. Ford, and requests your company.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: You litle Iack-a-lent, haue you bin true to vs

speeches.speaker: Rob.
prose: I, Ile be sworne: my Master knowes not of your being heere: and hath threatned to put me into euerlasting liberty, if I tell you of it: for he sweares he'll turne me away.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Thou'rt a good boy: this secrecy of thine shall be a Tailor to thee, and shal make thee a new doublet and hose. Ile go hide me.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Ford.
prose: Do so: go tell thy Master, I am alone: Mistris Page, remember you your Qu.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: I warrant thee, if I do not act it, hisse me.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Go-too then: we'l vse this vnwholsome humidity, this grosse-watry Pumpion; we'll teach him to know Turtles from Iayes.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Haue I caught thee, my heauenly Iewell? Why now let me die, for I haue liu'd long enough: This is the period of my ambition: O this blessed houre.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: O sweet Sir Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Mistris Ford, I cannot cog, I cannot prate (Mist. Ford) now shall I sin in my wish; I would thy Husband were dead, Ile speake it before the best Lord, I would make thee my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: I your Lady Sir Iohn? Alas, I should bee a pittifull Lady.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Let the Court of France shew me such another: I see how thine eye would emulate the Diamond: Thou hast the right arched-beauty of the brow, that becomes the Ship-tyre, the Tyre-valiant, or any Tire of Venetian admittance.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
verse: A plaine Kerchiefe, Sir Iohn:
My browes become nothing else, nor that well neither.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Thou art a tyrant to say so: thou wouldst make an absolute Courtier, and the firme fixture of thy foote, would giue an excellent motion to thy gate, in a semicircled Farthingale. I see what thou wert if Fortune thy foe, were not Nature thy friend: Come, thou canst not hide it.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Beleeue me, ther's no such thing in me.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: What made me loue thee? Let that perswade thee. Ther's something extraordinary in thee: Come, I cannot cog, and say thou art this and that, like a-manie of these lisping-hauthorne buds, that come like women in mens apparrell, and smell like. Bucklers-berry in simple time: I cannot, but I loue thee, none but thee; and thou deseru'st it.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Do not betray me sir, I fear you loue M. Page.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Thou mightst as well say, I loue to walke by the Counter-gate, which is as hatefull to me, as the reeke of a Lime-kill.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
verse: Well, heauen knowes how I loue you,
And you shall one day finde it.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Keepe in that minde, Ile deserue it.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
verse: Nay, I must tell you, so you doe;
Or else I could not be in that minde.

speeches.speaker: Rob.
prose: Mistris Ford, Mistris Ford: heere's Mistris Page at the doore, sweating, and blowing, and looking wildely, and would needs speake with you presently.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: She shall not see me, I will ensconce mee behinde the Arras.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Pray you do so, she's a very tatling woman. Whats the matter? How now?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse: O mistris Ford what haue you done?
You'r sham'd, y' are ouerthrowne, y' are vndone for euer.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: What's the matter, good mistris Page?

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: O weladay, mist. Ford, hauing an honest man to your husband, to giue him such cause of suspition.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: What cause of suspition?

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
verse: What cause of suspition? Out vpon you:
How am I mistooke in you?

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Why (alas) what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Your husband's comming hether (Woman) with all the Officers in Windsor, to search for a Gentleman, that he sayes is heere now in the house; by your consent to take an ill aduantage of his absence: you are vndone.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: 'Tis not so, I hope.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Pray heauen it be not so, that you haue such a man heere: but 'tis most certaine your husband's comming, with halfe Windsor at his heeles, to serch for such a one, I come before to tell you: If you know your selfe cleere, why I am glad of it: but if you haue a friend here, conuey, conuey him out. Be not amaz'd, call all your senses to you, defend your reputation, or bid farwell to your good life for euer.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: What shall I do? There is a Gentleman my deere friend: and I feare not mine owne shame so much, as his perill. I had rather then a thousand pound he were out of the house.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: For shame, neuer stand (you had rather, and you had rather:) your husband's heere at hand, bethinke you of some conueyance: in the house you cannot hide him. Oh, how haue you deceiu'd me? Looke, heere is a basket, if he be of any reasonable stature, he may creepe in heere, and throw fowle linnen vpon him, as if it were going to bucking: Or it is whiting time, send him by your two men to Datchet-Meade:

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: He's too big to go in there: what shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: Let me see't, let me see't, O let me see't:
Ile in, Ile in: Follow your friends counsell, Ile in.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: What Sir Iohn Faistasse? Are these your Letters, Knight?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I loue thee, helpe mee away: let me creepe in heere: ile neuer—

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Helpe to couer your master (Boy:) Call your men (Mist. Ford.) You dissembling Knight.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: What Iohn, Robert, Iohn; Go, take vp these cloathes heere, quickly: Wher's the Cowle-staffe? Look how you drumble? Carry them to the Landresse in Datchet mead: quickly, come.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: 'Pray you come nere: if I suspect without cause,
Why then make sport at me, then let me be your iest,
I deserue it: How now? Whether beare you this?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: To the Landresse forsooth?

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Why, what haue you to doe whether they beare it? You were best meddle with buck-washing.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: Bucke I would I could wash my selfe of ye Buck:
Bucke, bucke, bucke, I bucke: I warrant you Bucke,
And of the season too; it shall appeare.
prose: Gentlemen, I haue dream'd to night, Ile tell you my dreame: heere, heere, heere bee my keyes, ascend my Chambers, search, seeke, finde out: Ile warrant wee'le vnkennell the Fox. Let me stop this way first: so, now vncape.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Good master Ford, be contented:
You wrong your selfe too much.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: True (master Page) vp Gentlemen,
You shall see sport anon:
Follow me Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: This is fery fantasticall humors and iealousies.

speeches.speaker: Caius.
verse: By gar, 'tis no-the fashion of France:
It is not iealous in France.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Nay follow him (Gentlemen) see the yssue of his search.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page
prose: Is there not a double excellency in this?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
verse: I know not which pleases me better,
That my husband is deceiued, or Sir Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: What a taking was hee in, when your husband askt who was in the basket?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: I am halfe affraid he will haue neede of washing: so throwing him into the water, will doe him a benefit.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Hang him dishonest rascall: I would all of the same straine, were in the same distresse.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: I thinke my husband hath some speciall suspition of Falstaffs being heere: for I neuer saw him so grosse in his iealousie till now.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: I will lay a plot to try that, and wee will yet haue more trickes with Falstaffe: his dissolute disease will scarse obey this medicine.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: Shall we send that foolishion Carion, Mist. Quickly to him, and excuse his throwing into the water, and giue him another hope, to betray him to another punishment?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: We will do it: let him be sent for to morrow eight a clocke to haue amends.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I cannot finde him: may be the knaue bragg'd of that he could not compasse.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Heard you that?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: You vse me well, M. Ford? Do you?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I, I do so.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Heauen make you better then your thoghts

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Page.
prose: You do your selfe mighty wrong (M. Ford)

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I, I: I must beare it.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: If there be any pody in the house, & in the chambers, and in the coffers, and in the presses: heauen forgiue my sins at the day of iudgement.

speeches.speaker: Caius.
prose: Be gar, nor I too: there is no-bodies.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Fy, fy, M. Ford, are you not asham'd? What spirit, what diuell suggests this imagination? I wold not ha your distemper in this kind, for ye welth of Windsor castle.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: 'Tis my fault (M. Page) I suffer for it.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: You suffer for a pad conscience: your wife is as honest a o' mans, as I will desires among fiue thousand, and fiue hundred too.

speeches.speaker: Cai
prose: By gar, I see 'tis an honest woman.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Well, I promisd you a dinner: come, come, walk in the Parke, I pray you pardon me: I wil hereafter make knowne to you why I haue done this. Come wife, come Mi. Page, I pray you pardon me. Pray hartly pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Let's go in Gentlemen, but (trust me) we'l mock him: I doe inuite you to morrow morning to my house to breakfast: after we'll a Birding together, I haue a fine Hawke for the bush. Shall it be so:

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Any thing.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: If there is one, I shall make two in the Companie

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: If there be one, or two, I shall make-a-theturd.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Pray you go, M. Page.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: I pray you now remembrance to morrow on the lowsie knaue, mine Host.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Dat is good by gar, withall my heart.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: A lowsie knaue, to haue his gibes, and his mockeries.

speeches.speaker: Fen:
verse: I see I cannot get thy Fathers loue,
Therefore no more turne me to him (sweet Nan.)

speeches.speaker: Anne.
prose: Alas, how then?

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: Why thou must be thy selfe.
He doth obiect, I am too great of birth,
And that my state being gall'd with my expence,
I seeke to heale it onely by his wealth.
Besides these, other barres he layes before me,
My Riots past, my wilde Societies,
And tels me 'tis a thing impossible
I should loue thee, but as a property.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: May be he tels you true.
No, heauen so speed me in my time to come,
Albeit I will confesse, thy Fathers wealth
Was the first motiue that I woo'd thee (Anne:)
Yet wooing thee, I found thee of more valew
Then stampes in Gold, or summes in sealed bagges:
And 'tis the very riches of thy selfe,
That now I ayme at.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Gentle M. Fenton,
Yet seeke my Fathers loue, still seeke it sir,
If opportunity and humblest suite
Cannot attaine it, why then harke you hither.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
verse: Breake their talke Mistris Quickly,
My Kinsman shall speake for himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Ile make a shaft or a bolt on't, slid, tis but venturing.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Be not dismaid.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
verse: No, she shall not dismay me:
I care not for that, but that I am affeard.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Hark ye, M. Slender would speak a word with you

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: I come to him. This is my Fathers choice:
O what a world of vilde ill-fauour'd faults
Lookes handsome in three hundred pounds a yeere?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: And how do's good Master Fenton?
Pray you a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
verse: Shee's comming; to her Coz:
O boy, thou hadst a father.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I had a father (M. An) my vncle can tel you good iests of him: pray you Vncle tel Mist. Anne the iest how my Father stole two Geese out of a Pen, good Vnckle.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Mistris Anne, my Cozen loues you.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I that I do, as well as I loue any woman in Glocestershire.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: He will maintaine you like a Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I that I will, come cut and long-taile, vnder the degree of a Squire.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: He will make you a hundred and fiftie pounds ioynture.

speeches.speaker: Anne.
prose: Good Maister Shallow let him woo for himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: Marrie I thanke you for it: I thanke you for that good comfort: she cals you (Coz) Ile leaue you.

speeches.speaker: Anne.
prose: Now Master Slender.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Now good Mistris Anne.

speeches.speaker: Anne.
prose: What is your will?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: My will? Odd's-hart-lings, that's a prettie iest indeede: I ne're made my Will yet (I thanke Heauen:) I am not such a sickely creature, I giue Heauen praise.

speeches.speaker: Anne.
prose: I meane (M. Slender) what wold you with me?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Truely, for mine owne part, I would little or nothing with you: your father and my vncle hath made motion,: if it be my lucke, so; if not, happy man bee his dole, they can tell you how things go, better then I can: you may aske your father, heere he comes.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse:
Now Mr
Slender; Loue him daughter Anne.

Why how now? What does Mr
Fenter here?
You wrong me Sir, thus still to haunt my house.
I told you Sir, my daughter is disposd of.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose:
Nay Mr
Page, be not impatient.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose:
Good M. Fenton.
come not to my child.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: She is no match for you.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: Sir, will you heare me?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: No, good M. Fenton.
Come M. Shallow: Come sonne Slender, in;
Knowing my minde, you wrong me (M. Fenton.)

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Speake to Mistris Page.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: Good Mist. Page, for that I loue your daughter
In such a righteous fashion as I do,
Perforce, against all checkes, rebukes, and manners,
I must aduance the colours of my loue,
And not retire. Let me haue your good will.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Good mother, do not marry me to yond foole.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: I meane it not, I seeke you a better husband.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: That's my master, M. Doctor.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Alas I had rather be set quick i' th earth,
And bowl'd to death with Turnips.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse: Come, trouble not your selfe good M.
Fenton, I will not be your friend, nor enemy:
My daughter will I question how she loues you,
And as I finde her, so am I affected:
Till then, farewell Sir, she must needs go in,
Her father will be angry.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
prose: Farewell gentle Mistris: farewell Nan.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: This is my doing now: Nay, saide I, will you cast away your childe on a Foole, and a Physitian: Looke on M. Fenton, this is my doing.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: I thanke thee: and I pray thee once to night,
Giue my sweet Nan this Ring: there's for thy paines.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Now heauen send thee good fortune, a kinde heart he hath: a woman would run through fire & water for such a kinde heart. But yet, I would my Maister had Mistris Anne, or I would M. Slender had her: or (in sooth) I would M. Fenton had her; I will do what I can for them all three, for so I haue promisd, and Ile bee as good as my word, but speciously for M. Fenton. Well, I must of another errand to Sir Iohn Falstaffe from my two Mistresses: what a beast am I to slacke it.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Bardolfe I say.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Heere Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Go, fetch me a quart of Sacke, put a tost in't. Haue I liu'd to be carried in a Basket like a barrow of butchers Offall? and to be throwne in the Thames? Wel, if I be seru'd such another tricke, Ile haue my braines 'tane out and butter'd, and giue them to a dogge for a New-yeares gift. The rogues slighted me into the riuer with as little remorse, as they would haue drown'de a blinde bitches Puppies, fifteene i' th litter: and you may know by my size, that I haue a kinde of alacrity in sinking: if the bottome were as deepe as hell, I shold down. I had beene drown'd, but that the shore was sheluy and shallow: a death that I abhorre: for the water swelles a man; and what a thing should I haue beene, when I had beene swel'd? I should haue beene a Mountaine of Mummie.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Here's M. Quickly Sir to speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
