prose: Come, let me poure in some Sack to the Thames water: for my bellies as cold as if I had swallow'd snowbals, for pilles to coole the reines. Call her in.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Come in woman.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: By your leaue: I cry you mercy?
Giue your worship good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: Take away these Challices:
Go, brew me a pottle of Sacke finely.

speeches.speaker: Bard.
prose: With Egges, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Simple of it selfe: Ile no Pullet-Spersme in my brewage. How now?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Marry Sir, I come to your worship from M. Ford.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Mist. Ford? I haue had Ford enough: I was thrown into the Ford; I haue my belly full of Ford.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Alas the day, (good-heart) that was not her fault: she do's so take on with her men; they mistooke their erection.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: So did I mine, to build vpon a foolish Womans promise.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Well, she laments Sir for it, that it would yern your heart to see it: her husband goes this morning a birding; she desires you once more to come to her, betweene eight and nine: I must carry her word quickely, she'll make you amends I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Well, I will visit her, tell her so: and bidde her thinke what a man is: Let her consider his frailety, and then iudge of my merit.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: I will tell her.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Do so. Betweene nine and ten saist thou?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Eight and nine Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Well, be gone: I will not misse her.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Peace be with you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose:
I meruaile I heare not of Mr
Broome: he sent me word to stay within: I like his money well. Oh, heere be comes.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Blesse you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: Now M. Broome, you come to know
What hath past betweene me, and Fords wife.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: That indeed (Sir Iohn) is my businesse.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: M. Broome I will not lye to you,
I was at her house the houre she appointed me.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: And sped you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: very ill-fauouredly M. Broome.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: How so sir, did she change her determination?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: No (M. Broome) but the peaking Curnuto her husband (M. Broome) dwelling in a continual larum of ielousie, coms me in the instant of our encounter, after we had embrast, kist, protested, & (as it were) spoke the prologue of our Comedy: and at his heeles, a rabble of his companions, thither prouoked and instigated by his distemper, and (forsooth) to serch his house for his wiues Loue.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: What? While you were there?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: While I was there.

speeches.speaker: For.
prose: And did he search for you, & could not find you?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose:
You shall heare. As good lucke would haue it, comes in one Mist. Page.
giues intelligence of Fords approch: and in her inuention, and Fords wiues distraction, they conuey'd me into a bucke-basket.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: A Buck-basket?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Yes: a Buck-basket: ram'd mee in with foule Shirts and Smockes, Socks, foule Stockings, greasie Napkins, that (Master Broome) there was the rankest compound of villanous smell, that euer offended nostrill.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: And how long lay you there?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Nay, you shall heare (Master Broome) what I hau^ sufferd, to bring this woman to euill, for your good: Being thus cram'd in the Basket, a couple of Fords knaues, his Hindes, were cald forth by their Mistris, to carry mee in the name of foule Cloathes to Datchet-lane: they tooke me on their shoulders: met the iealous knaue their Master in the doore; who ask'd them once or twice what they had in their Basket? I quak'd for feare least the Lunatique Knaue would haue search'd it: but Fate (ordaining he should be a Cuckold) held his hand: well, on went hee, for a search, and away went I for foule Cloathes: But marke the sequell (Master Broome) I suffered the pangs of three seuerall deaths: First, an intollerable fright, to be detected with a iealious rotten Bell-weather: Next to be compass'd like a good Bilbo in the circumference of a Pecke, hilt to point, heele to head. And then to be stopt in like a strong distillation with stinking Cloathes, that fretted in their owne grease: thinke of that, a man of my Kidney; thinke of that, that am as subiect to heate as butter; a man of continuall dissolution, and thaw: it was a miracle to scape suffocation. And in the height of this Bath (when I was more then halfe stew'd in grease (like a Dutchdish) to be throwne into the Thames, and coold, glowing-hot, in that serge like a Horseshoo; thinke of that; hissing hot: thinke of that (Master Broome.)

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: In good sadnesse Sir, I am sorry, that for my sake you haue sufferd all this.
My suite then is desperate: You'll vndertake her no more?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Master Broome: I will be throwne into Etna, as I haue beene into Thames, ere I will leaue her thus; her Husband is this morning gone a Birding: I haue receiued from her another ambassie of meeting: 'twixt eight and nine is the houre (Master Broome.)

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: 'Tis past eight already Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Is it? I will then addresse mee to my appointment: Come to mee at your conuenient leisure, and you shall know how I speede: and the conclusion shall be crowned with your enioying her: adiew: you shall haue her (Master Broome) Master Broome, you shall cuckold Ford.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Hum: ha? Is this a vision? Is this a dreame? doe I sleepe? Master Ford awake, awake Master Ford: ther's a hole made in your best coate (Master Ford:) this 'tis to be married; this 'tis to haue Lynnen, and Buck-baskets: Well, I will proclaime my selfe what I am: I will now take the Leacher: hee is at my house: hee cannot scape me: 'tis impossible hee should: hee cannot creepe into a halfe-penny purse, nor into a Pepper-Boxe: But least the Diuell that guides him, should aide him, I will search impossible places: though what I am, I cannot auoide; yet to be what I would not, shall not make me tame: If I haue hornes, to make one mad, let the prouerbe goe with me, Ile be hornemad.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Is he at M. Fords already think'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Sure he is by this; or will be presently; but truely he is very couragious mad, about his throwing into the water. Mistris Ford desires you to come sodainely.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Ile be with her by and by: Ile but bring my yong-man here to Schoole: looke where his Master comes; 'tis a playing day I see: how now Sir Hugh, no Schoole to day?

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: No: Master Slender is let the Boyes leaue to play.

speeches.speaker: Qui
prose: 'Blessing of his heart.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Sir Hugh, my husband saies my sonne profits nothing in the world at his Booke: I pray you aske him some questions in his Accidence.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Come hither William; hold vp your head; come.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Come-on Sirha; hold vp your head; answere your Master, be not afraid.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: William, how many Numbers is in Nownes?

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Two.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: Truely, I thought there had bin one Number more, because they say od's-Nownes.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: Peace, your tatlings. What is (Faire) William?

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Pulcher.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Powlcats? there are fairer things then Powlcats, sure.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: You are a very simplicity o' man: I pray you peace. What is (Lapis) William?

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: A Stone.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: And what is a Stone (William?)

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: A Peeble.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: No; it is Lapis: I pray you remember in your praine.

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Lapis.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: That is a good William: what is he (William) that do's lend Articles.

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Articles are borrowed of the Pronoune; and be thus declined. Singulariter nominatiuo hic haec, hoc.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: Nominatiuo hig, hag, hog: pray you marke: genitiuo huius: Well: what is your Accusatiue-case?

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Accusatiuo hinc.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: I pray you haue your remembrance (childe) Accusatiuo hing, hang, hog.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Hang-hog, is latten for Bacon, I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: Leaue your prables (o' man) What is the Focatiue case (William?)

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: O, Vocatiuo, O.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: Remember William, Focatiue, is caret.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: And that's a good roote.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: O' man, forbeare.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Peace.

speeches.speaker: Eua:
prose: What is your Genitiue case plurall (William?)

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Genitiue case?

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Genitiue horum, harum, horum.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: 'Vengeance of Ginyes case; fie on her; neuer name her (childe) if she be a whore.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: For shame o' man.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: You doe ill to teach the childe such words: hee teaches him to hic, and to hac; which they'll doe fast enough of themselues, and to call horum; fie vpon you.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: O' man, art thou Lunaties? Hast thou no vnderstandings for thy Cases, & the numbers of the Genders? Thou art as foolish Christian creatures, as I would desires.

speeches.speaker: Mi. Page.
prose: Pre'thee hold thy peace.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Shew me now (William) some declensions of your Pronounes.

speeches.speaker: Will.
prose: Forsooth, I haue forgot.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: It is Qui, que, quod; if you forget your Quies, your Ques, and your Quods, you must be preeches: Goe your waies and play, go.

speeches.speaker: M. Pag.
prose: He is a better scholler then I thought he was.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: He is a good sprag-memory: Farewel Mis. Page.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
verse: Adieu good Sir Hugh:
Get you home boy, Come we stay too long.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Mi. Ford, Your sorrow hath eaten vp my sufferance; I see you are obsequious in your loue, and I professe requitall to a haires bredth, not onely Mist. Ford, in the simple office of loue, but in all the accustrement, complement, and ceremony of it: But are you sure of your husband now?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: Hee's a birding (sweet Sir Iohn.)

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: What hoa, gossip Ford: what hoa.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: Step into th' chamber, Sir Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: How now (sweete heart) whose at home besides your selfe?

speeches.speaker: Mis Ford
prose: Why none but mine owne people.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Ford.
prose: No certainly: Speake louder.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Truly, I am so glad you haue no body here.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
prose: Why woman, your husband is in his olde lines againe: he so takes on yonder with my husband, so railes against all married mankinde; so curses all Eues daughters, of what complexion soeuer; and so buffettes himselfe on the for-head: crying peere-out, peere-out, that any madnesse I euer yet beheld, seem'd but tamenesse, ciuility, and patience to this his distemper he is in now: I am glad the fat Knight is not heere.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Why, do's he talke of him?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Of none but him, and sweares he was caried out the last time hee search'd for him, in a Basket: Protests to my husband he is now heere, & hath drawne him and the rest of their company from their sport, to make another experiment of his suspition: But I am glad the Knight is not heere; now he shall see his owne foolerie.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: How neere is he Mistris Page?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pag.
prose: Hard by, at street end; he wil be here anon.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: I am vndone, the Knight is heere.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Why then you are vtterly sham'd, & hee's but a dead man. What a woman are you? Away with him, away with him. Better shame, then murther.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Which way should he go? How should I bestow him? Shall I put him into the basket againe?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: No, Ile come no more i' th Basket:
May I not go out ere he come?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Alas: three of Mr. Fords brothers watch the doore with Pistols, that none shall issue out: otherwise you might slip away ere hee came: But what make you heere?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: What shall I do? Ile creepe vp into the chimney.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: There they alwaies vse to discharge their Birding-peeces: creepe into the Kill-hole.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Where is it?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: He will seeke there on my word: Neyther Presse, Coffer, Chest, Trunke, Well, Vault, but he hath an abstract for the remembrance of such places, and goes to them by his Note: There is no hiding you in the house.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Ile go out then.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: If you goe out in your owne semblance, you die Sir Iohn, vnlesse you go out disguis'd.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: How might we disguise him?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Alas the day I know not, there is no womans gowne bigge enough for him: otherwise he might put on a hat, a muffler, and a kerchiefe, and so escape.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Good hearts, deuise something: any extremitie, rather then a mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: My Maids Aunt the fat woman of Brainford, has a gowne aboue.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: On my word it will serue him: shee's as big as he is: and there's her thrum'd hat, and her muffler too: run vp Sir Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Go, go, sweet Sir Iohn: Mistriis Page and I will looke some linnen for your head.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Quicke, quicke, wee'le come dresse you straight: put on the gowne the while.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: I would my husband would meete him in this shape: he cannot abide the old woman of Brainford; he sweares she's a witch, forbad her my house, and hath threatned to beate her.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Heauen guide him to thy husbands cudgell: and the diuell guide his cudgell afterwards.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: But is my husband comming?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: I in good sadnesse is he, and talkes of the basket too, howsoeuer he hath had intelligence.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Wee'l try that: for Ile appoint my men to carry the basket againe, to meete him at the doore with it, as they did last time.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Nay, but hee'l be heere presently: let's go dresse him like the witch of Brainford.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Ile first direct direct my men, what they shall doe with the basket: Goe vp, Ile bring linnen for him straight.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse: Hang him dishonest Varlet,
We cannot misuse enough:
We'll leaue a proofe by that which we will doo,
Wiues may be merry, and yet honest too:
We do not acte that often, iest, and laugh,
'Tis old, but true, Still Swine eats all the draugh.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Go Sirs, take the basket againe on your shoulders: your Master is hard at doore: if hee bid you set it downe, obey him: quickly, dispatch.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: Come, come, take it vp.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
prose: Pray heauen it be not full of Knight againe.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: I hope not, I had liefe as beare so much lead.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose:
I, but if it proue true (Mr. Page) haue you any way then to vnfoole me againe. Set downe the basket villaine: some body call my wife: Youth in a basket: Oh you Panderly Rascals, there's a knot: a gin, a packe, a conspiracie against me: Now shall the diuel be sham'd. What wife I say: Come, come forth: behold what honest

cloathes you send forth to bleaching.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Why, this passes M. Ford: you are not to goe loose any longer, you must be pinnion'd.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: Why, this is Lunaticks: this is madde, as a mad dogge.

speeches.speaker: Shall.
prose: Indeed M. Ford, thi is not well indeed.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: So say I too Sir, come hither Mistris Ford, Mistris Ford, the honest woman, the modest wife, the vertuous creature, that hath the iealious foole to her husband: I suspect without cause (Mistris) do I?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Heauen be my witnesse you doe, if you suspect me in any dishonesty.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Well said Brazon-face, hold it out: Come forth sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: This passes.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Are you not asham'd, let the cloths alone.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I shall finde you anon.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: 'Tis vnreasonable; will you take vp your wiues cloathes? Come, away.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Empty the basket I say.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Why man, why?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Master Page, as I am a man, there was one conuay'd out of my house yesterday in this basket: why may not he be there againe, in my house I am sure he is: my Intelligence is true, my iealousie is reasonable, pluck me out all the linnen.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: If you find a man there, he shall dye a Fleas death.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Heer's no man.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: By my fidelity this is not well Mr. Ford: This wrongs you.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose:
Mr
Ford, you must pray, and not follow the imaginations of your owne heart: this is iealousies.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Well, hee's not heere I seeke for.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: No, nor no where else but in your braine.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Helpe to search my house this one time: if I find not what I seeke, shew no colour for my extremity: Let me for euer be your Table-sport: Let them say of me, as iealous as Ford, that search'd a hollow Wall-nut for his wiues Lemman. Satisfie me once more, once more serch with me.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: What hoa (Mistris Page,) come you and the old woman downe: my husband will come into the Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Old woman? what old womans that?

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Why it is my maids Aunt of Brainford.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: A witch, a Queane, an olde couzening queane: Haue I not forbid her my house. She comes of errands do's she? We are simple men, wee doe not know what's brought to passe vnder the profession of Fortune-telling. She workes by Charmes, by Spels, by th' Figure, & such dawbry as this is, beyond our Element: wee know nothing. Come downe you Witch, you Hagge you, come downe I say.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Nay, good sweet husband, good Gentlemen, let him strike the old woman.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Come mother Prat, Come giue me your hand.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Ile Prat-her: Out of my doore, you Witch, you Ragge, you Baggage, you Poulcat, you Runnion, out, out: Ile coniure you, Ile fortune-tell you.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Are you not asham'd? I thinke you haue kill'd the poore woman.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Nay he will do it, 'tis a goodly credite for you.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Hang her witch.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: By yea, and no, I thinke the o' man is a witch indeede: I like not when a o' man has a great peard; I spie a great peard vnder his muffler.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Will you follow Gentlemen, I beseech you follow: see but the issue of my iealousie: If I cry out thus vpon no traile, neuer trust me when I open againe.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Let's obey his humour a little further:
Come Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Trust me he beate him most pittifully.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Nay by th' Masse that he did not: he beate him most vnpittifully, me thought.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Ile haue the cudgell hallow'd, and hung ore the Altar, it hath done meritorious seruice.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: What thinke you? May we with the warrant of woman hood, and the witnesse of a good conscience, pursue him with any further reuenge?

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: The spirit of wantonnesse is sure scar'd out of him, if the diuell haue him not in fee-simple, with fine and recouery, he will neuer (I thinke) in the way of waste, attempt vs againe.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Shall we tell our husbands how wee haue seru'd him?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Yes, by all meanes: if it be but to scrape the figures out of your husbands braines: if they can find in their hearts, the poore vnuertuous fat Knight shall be any further afflicted, wee two will still bee the ministers.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Ile warrant, they'l haue him publiquely sham'd, and me thinkes there would be no period to the iest, should he not be publikely sham'd.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse: Come, to the Forge with it, then shape it:
I would not haue things coole.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Sir, the Germane desires to haue three of your horses: the Duke himselfe will be to morrow at Court, and they are going to meet him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: What Duke should that be comes so secretly? I heare not of him in the Court: let mee speake with the Gentlemen, they speake English?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: I Sir? Ile call him to you.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: They shall haue my horses, but Ile make them pay: Ile sauce them, they haue had my houses a week at commaund: I haue turn'd away my other guests, they must come off, Ile sawce them, come.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: 'Tis one of the best discretions of a o' man as euer I did looke vpon.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: And did he send you both these Letters at an instant?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: VVithin a quarter of an houre.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: Pardon me (wife) henceforth do what yu wilt:
I rather will suspect the Sunne with gold,
Then thee with wantonnes: Now doth thy honor stand
(In him that was of late an Heretike)
As firme as faith.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: 'Tis well, 'tis well, no more:
Be not as extreme in submission, as in offence,
But let our plot go forward: Let our wiues
Yet once againe (to make vs publike sport)
Appoint a meeting with this old fat-fellow,
Where we may take him, and disgrace him for it.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: There is no better way then that they spoke of.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: How? to send him word they'll meete him in the Parke at midnight? Fie, fie, he'll neuer come.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: You say he has bin throwne in the Riuers: and has bin greeuously peaten, as an old o' man: me-thinkes there should be terrors in him, that he should not come: Me-thinkes his flesh is punish'd, hee shall haue no desires.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: So thinke I too.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
verse: Deuise but how you'l vse him whe~ he comes,
And let vs two deuise to bring him thether.

speeches.speaker: Mis Page.
verse: There is an old tale goes, that Herne the
Hunter (sometime a keeper heere in Windsor Forrest)
Doth all the winter time, at still midnight
Walke round about an Oake, with great rag'd-hornes,
And there he blasts the tree, and takes the cattle,
And make milch-kine yeeld blood, and shakes a chaine
In a most hideous and dreadfull manner.
You haue heard of such a Spirit, and well you know
The superstitious idle-headed-Eld
Receiu'd, and did deliuer to our age
This tale of Herne the Hunter, for a truth.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Why yet there want not many that do feare
In deepe of night to walke by this Hernes Oake:
But what of this?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
verse: Marry this is our deuise,
That Falstaffe at that Oake shall meete with vs.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Well, let it not be doubted but he'll come,
And in this shape, when you haue brought him thether,
What shall be done with him? What is your plot?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Pa.
verse: That likewise haue we thoght vpon: & thus:
Nan Page (my daughter) and my little sonne,
And three or foure more of their growth, wee'l dresse
Like Vrchins, Ouphes, and Fairies, greene and white,
With rounds of waxen Tapers on their heads,
And rattles in their hands; vpon a sodaine,
As Falstaffe, she, and I, are newly met,
Let them from forth a saw-pit rush at once
With some diffused song: Vpon their sight
We two, in great amazednesse will flye:
Then let them all encircle him about,
And Fairy-like to pinch the vncleane Knight;
And aske him why that houre of Fairy Reuell,
In their so sacred pathes, he dares to tread
In shape prophane.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: And till he tell the truth,
Let the supposed Fairies pinch him, sound,
And burne him with their Tapers.

speeches.speaker: Mist Page.
verse: The truth being knowne,
We'll all present our selues; dis-horne the spirit,
And mocke him home to Windsor.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: The children must
Be practis'd well to this, or they'll neu'r doo't.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: I will teach the children their behauiours: and I will be like a Iacke-an-Apes also, to burne the Knight with my Taber.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: That will be excellent,
Ile go buy them vizards.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: My Nan shall be the Queene of all the Fairies, finely attired in a robe of white.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: That silke will I go buy, and in that time
Shall M. Slender steale my Nan away,
And marry her at Eaton: go, send to Falstaffe straight.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: Nay, Ile to him againe in name of Broome,
Hee'l tell me all his purpose: sure hee'l come.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse: Feare not you that: Go get vs properties
And tricking for our Fayries.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
verse: Let vs about it,
It is admirable pleasures, and ferry honest knaueries.

speeches.speaker: Mis. Page.
verse: Go Mist. Ford,
Send quickly to Sir Iohn, to know his minde:
Ile to the Doctor, he hath my good will,
And none but he to marry with Nan Page:
That Slender (though well landed) is an Ideot:
And he, my husband best of all affects:
The Doctor is well monied, and his friends
Potent at Court: he, none but he shall haue her,
Though twenty thousand worthier come to craue her.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: What wouldst thou haue? (Boore) what? (thick skin) speake, breathe, discusse: breefe, short, quicke, snap.

speeches.speaker: Simp.
prose: Marry Sir, I come to speake with Sir Iohn Falstaffe from M. Slender.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: There's his Chamber, his House, his Castle, his standing-bed and truckle-bed: 'tis painted about with the story of the Prodigall, fresh and new: go, knock and call: hee'l speake like an Anthropophaginian vnto thee: Knocke I say.

speeches.speaker: Simp.
prose: There's an olde woman, a fat woman gone vp into his chamber: Ile be so bold as stay Sir till she come downe: I come to speake with her indeed.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Ha? A fat woman? The Knight may be robb'd: Ile call, Bully-Knight, Bully Sir Iohn: speake from thy Lungs Military: Art thou there? It is thine Host, thine Ephesian cals.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: How now, mine Host?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Here's a Bohemian-Tartar taries the comming downe of thy fat-woman: Let her descend (Bully) let her descend: my Chambers are honourable: Fie, priuacy? Fie.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: There was (mine Host) an old-fat-woman euen now with me, but she's gone.

speeches.speaker: Simp.
prose: Pray you Sir, was't not the Wise-woman of Brainford?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I marry was it (Mussel-shell) what would you with her?

speeches.speaker: Simp.
prose: My Master (Sir) my master Slender, sent to her seeing her go thorough the streets, to know (Sir) whether one Nim (Sir) that beguil'd him of a chaine, had the chaine, or no.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I spake with the old woman about it.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: And what sayes she, I pray Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Marry shee sayes, that the very same man that beguil'd Master Slender of his Chaine, cozon'd him of it.

speeches.speaker: Simp.
prose:
I would I could haue spoken with the Woman

her selfe, I had other things to haue spoken with her too, from him.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: What are they? let vs know.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: I: come: quicke.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I may not conceale them (Sir.)

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Conceale them, or thou di'st.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: Why sir, they were nothing but about Mistris Anne Page, to know if it were my Masters fortune to haue her, or no.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: 'Tis, 'tis his fortune.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: What Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: To haue her, or no: goe; say the woman told me so.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: May I be bold to say so Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I Sir: like who more bold.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: I thanke your worship: I shall make my Master glad with these tydings.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Thou are clearkly: thou art clearkly (Sir Iohn) was there a wise woman with thee?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I that there was (mine Host) one that hath taught me more wit, then euer I learn'd before in my life: and I paid nothing for it neither, but was paid for my learning.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Out alas (Sir) cozonage: meere cozonage.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Where be my horses? speake well of them varletto.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Run away with the cozoners: for so soone as I came beyond Eaton, they threw me off, from behinde one of them, in a slough of myre; and set spurres, and away; like three Germane-diuels; three Doctor Faustaffes.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: They are gone but to meete the Duke (villaine) doe not say they be fled: Germanes are honest men.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Where is mine Host?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: What is the matter Sir?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: Haue a care of your entertainments: there is a friend of mine come to Towne, tels mee there is three Cozen-Iermans, that has cozend all the Hosts of Readins, of Maidenhead; of Cole-brooke, of horses and money: I tell you for good will (looke you) you are wise, and full of gibes, and vlouting-stocks: and 'tis not conuenient you should be cozoned. Fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Ver' is mine Host de Iarteere?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Here (Master Doctor) in perplexitie, and doubtfull delemma.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: I cannot tell vat is dat: but it is tell-a-me, dat you make grand preparation for a Duke de Iamanie: by my trot: der is no Duke that the Court is know, to come: I tell you for good will: adieu.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Huy and cry, (villaine) goe: assist me Knight, I am vndone: fly, run: huy, and cry (villaine) I am vndone.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose:
I would all the world might be cozond, for I haue beene cozond and beaten too: if it should come to the eare of the Court, how I haue beene transformed; and how my transformation hath beene washd, and cudgeld, they would melt mee out of my fat drop by drop, and liquor Fishermens-boots with me: I warrant they would whip me with their fine wits, till I were as crest-falne as a dride-peare: I neuer prosper'd, since I forswore my selfe at Primer^
: well, if my winde were but long enough; I would repent: Now? Whence come you?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: From the two parties forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: The Diuell take one partie, and his Dam the other: and so they shall be both bestowed; I haue suffer'd more for their sakes; more then the villanous inconstancy of mans disposition is able to beare.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
prose: And haue not they suffer'd? Yes, I warrant; speciously one of them; Mistris Ford (good heart) is beaten blacke and blew, that you cannot see a white spot about her.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: What tell'st thou mee of blacke, and blew? I was beaten my selfe into all the colours of the Rainebow: and I was like to be apprehended for the Witch of Braineford, but that my admirable dexteritie of wit, my counterfeiting the action of an old woman deliuer'd me, the knaue Constable had set me ith' Stocks, ith' common Stocks, for a Witch.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Sir: let me speake with you in your Chamber, you shall heare how things goe, and (I warrant) to your content: here is a Letter will say somewhat: (good-hearts) what a-doe here is to bring you together? Sure, one of you do's not serue heauen well, that you are so cross'd.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Come vp into my Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Master Fenton, talke not to mee, my minde is heauy: I will giue ouer all.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: Yet heare me speake: assist me in my purpose,
And (as I am a gentleman) ile giue thee
A hundred pound in gold, more then your losse.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: I will heare you (Master Fenton) and I will (at the least) keepe your counsell.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: From time to time, I haue acquainted you
With the deare loue I beare to faire Anne Page,
Who, mutually, hath answer'd my affection,
(So farre forth, as her selfe might be her chooser)
Euen to my wish; I haue a letter from her
Of such contents, as you will wonder at;
The mirth whereof, so larded with my matter,
That neither (singly) can be manifested
Without the shew of both: fat Falstaffe
Hath a great Scene; the image of the iest
Ile show you here at large (harke good mine Host:)
To night at Hernes-Oke, iust 'twixt twelue and one,
Must my sweet Nan present the Faerie-Queene:
The purpose why, is here: in which disguise
VVhile other Iests are something ranke on foote,
Her father hath commanded her to slip
Away with Slender, and with him, at Eaton
Immediately to Marry: She hath consented: Now Sir,
Her Mother, (euen strong against that match
And firme for Doctor Caius) hath appointed
That he shall likewise shuffle her away,
While other sports are tasking of their mindes,
And at the Deanry, where a Priest attends
Strait marry her: to this her Mothers plot
She seemingly obedient) likewise hath
Made promise to the Doctor: Now, thus it rests,
Her Father meanes she shall be all in white;
And in that habit, when Slender sees his time
To take her by the hand, and bid her goe,
She shall goe with him: her Mother hath intended
(The better to deuote her to the Doctor;
For they must all be mask'd, and vizarded)
That quaint in greene, she shall be loose en-roab'd,
With Ribonds-pendant, flaring 'bout her head;
And when the Doctor spies his vantage ripe,
To pinch her by the hand, and on that token,
The maid hath giuen consent to go with him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Which meanes she to deceiue? Father, or Mother.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: Both (my good Host) to go along with me:
And heere it rests, that you'l procure the Vicar
To stay for me at Church, 'twixt twelue, and one,
And in the lawfull name of marrying,
To giue our hearts vnited ceremony.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Well, husband your deuice; Ile to the Vicar,
Bring you the Maid, you shall not lacke a Priest.

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: So shall I euermore be bound to thee;
Besides, Ile make a present recompence.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Pre'thee no more pratling: go, Ile hold, this is the third time: I hope good lucke lies in odde numbers: Away, go, they say there is Diuinity in odde Numbers, either in natiuity, chance, or death: away.

speeches.speaker: Qai.
prose: Ile prouide you a chaine, and Ile do what I can to get you a paire of hornes.

speeches.speaker: Fall.
prose: Away I say, time weares, hold vp your head & mince. How now M. Broome? Master Broome, the matter will be knowne to night, or neuer. Bee you in the Parke about midnight, at Hernes-Oake, and you shall see wonders.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: Went you not to her yesterday (Sir) as you told me you had appointed?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I went to her (Master Broome) as you see, like a poore-old-man, but I came from her (Master Broome) like a poore-old-woman; that same knaue (Ford hir husband) hath the sinest mad diuell of ^ealousie in him (Master Broome) that euer gouern'd Frensie. I will tell you, he beate me greeuously, in the shape of a woman: (for in the shape of Man (Master Broome) I feare not Goliah with a Weauers beame, because I know also, life is a Shuttle) I am in hast, go along with mee, Ile tell you all (Master Broome:) since I pluckt Geese, plaide Trew^nt, and whipt Top, I knew not what 'twas to be beaten, till lately. Follow mee, Ile tell you strange things of this knaue Ford, on whom to night I will be reuenged, and I will deliuer his wife into your hand. Follow, straunge things in hand (M. Broome) follow.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Come, come: wee'll couch i' th Castle-ditch, till we see the light of our Fairies. Remember son Slender, my

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I forsooth, I haue spoke with her, & we haue a nay-word, how to know one another. I come to her in white, and cry Mum; she cries Budget, and by that we know one another.

speeches.speaker: Shal.
prose: That's good too: But what needes either your Mum, or her Budget? The white will decipher her well enough. It hath strooke ten a'clocke.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: The night is darke, Light and Spirits will become it wel: Heauen prosper our sport. No man means euill but the deuill, and we shal know him by his hornes. Lets away: follow me.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Mr Doctor, my daughter is in green, when you see your time, take her by the hand, away with her to the Deauerie, and dispatch it quickly: go before into the Parke: we two must go together.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: I know vat I haue to do, adieu.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Fare you well (Sir.) my husband will not reioyce so much at the abuse of Falstaffe, as he will chafe at the Doctors marrying my daughter: But 'tis no matter; better a little chiding, then a great deale of heartbreake.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Where is Nan now? and her troop of Fairies? and the Welch-deuill Herne?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: They are all couch'd in a pit hard by Hernes Oake, with obscur'd Lights; which at the very instant of Falstaffes and our meeting, they will at once display to the night.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: That cannot choose but amaze him.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: If he be not amaz'd he will be mock'd: If he be amaz'd, he will euery way be mock'd.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: Wee'll betray him finely.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse: Against such Lewdsters, and their lechery,
Those that betray them, do no treachery.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Ford.
prose: The houre drawes-on: to the Oake, to the Oake.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: Trib, trib Fairies: Come, and remember your parts: be pold (I pray you) follow me into the pit, and when I giue the watch-'ords, do as I pid you: Come, come, trib, trib.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose:
The Windsor-bell hath stroke twelue: the Minute drawes-on: Now the hot-bloodied-Gods assist me: Remember lou^, thou was't a Bull for thy Europa, Loue set on thy hornes. O powerfull Loue, that in some respects makes a Beast a Man: in som other, a Man a beast. You were also (Iupiter) a Swan, for the loue of Leda: O

omnipotent Loue, how nere the God drew to the complexion of a Goose: a fault done first in the forme of a beast, (O Ioue, a beastly fault:) and then another fault, in the semblance of a Fowle, thinke on't (Ioue) a fowle-fault. When Gods haue hot backes, what shall poore men do? For me, I am heere a Windsor Stagge, and the fattest (I thinke) i' th Forrest. Send me a coole rut-time (Ioue) or who can blame me to pisse my Tallow? Who comes heere? my Doe?

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
verse: Sir Iohn? Art thou there (my Deere?)
My male-Deere?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: My Doe, with the blacke Scut? Let the skie raine Potatoes: let it thunder, to the tune of Greenesleeues, haile-kissing Comfits, and snow Eringoes: Let there come a tempest of prouocation, I will shelter mee heere.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Mistris Page is come with me (sweet hart.)

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Diuide me like a brib'd-Bucke, each a Haunch: I will keepe my sides to my selfe, my shoulders for the fellow of this walke; and my hornes I bequeath your husbands. Am I a Woodman, ha? Speake I like Herne the Hunter? Why, now is Cupid a child of conscience, he makes restitution. As I am a true spirit, welcome.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Alas, what noise?

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Heauen forgiue our sinnes.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: What should this be?

speeches.speaker: M. Ford. M. Page.
prose: Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: I thinke the diuell wil not haue me damn'd,
Least the oyle that's in me should set hell on fire;
He would neuer else crosse me thus.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Fairies blacke, gray, greene, and white,
You Moone-shine reuellers, and shades of night.
You Orphan heires of fixed destiny,
Attend your office, and your quality.
Crier Hob-goblyn, make the Fairy Oyes.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
verse: Elues, list your names: Silence you aiery toyes.
Cricket, to Windsor-chimnies shalt thou leape;
Where fires thou find'st vnrak'd, and hearths vnswept,
There pinch the Maids as blew as Bill-berry,
Our radiant Queene, hates Sluts, and Sluttery.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: They are Fairies, he that speaks to them shall die,
Ile winke, and couch: No man their workes must eie.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
verse: Wher's Bede? Go you, and where you find a maid
That ere she sleepe has thrice her prayers said,
Raise vp the Organs of her fantasie,
Sleepe she as sound as carelesse infancie,
But those as sleepe, and thinke not on their sins,
Pinch them armes, legs, backes, shoulders, sides, & shins.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: About, about:
Search Windsor Castle (Elues) within, and out.
Strew good ^k^ (Ouphes) on euery sacred roome,
That it may stand till the perpetuall doome,
In state as wholsome, as in state 'tis sit,
Worthy the Owner, and the Owner it.
The seuerall Chai^ of Order, tooke you s^owre
With iuyce of Balme; and euery precious flowre,
Each faire Instalment, Coate, and seu'rall Crest,
With loyall Blazon, euermore be blest.
And Nightly-meadow-Fairies, looke you sing
Like to the Garters-Compasse, in a ring,
Th' expressure that it beares: Greene let it be,
Mote fertile-fresh then all the Field to see:
And, Hony Soit Qui Mal-y-Pence, write
In Emrold-tuffes, Flowres purple, blew, and white,
Like Saphire-pearle, and rich embroiderie,
Buckled below faire Knight-hoods bending knee;
Fairies vse Flowres for their characterie.
Away, disperse: But till 'tis one a clocke,
Our Dance of Custome, round about the Oke
Of Herne the Hunter, let vs not forget.

speeches.speaker: Euan.
verse: Pray you lock hand in hand: your selues in order set:
And twenty glow-wormes shall our Lanthornes bee
To guide our Measure round about the Tree.
But stay, I smell a man of middle earth.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
verse: Heauens defend me from that Welsh Fairy,
Least he transforme me to a peece of Cheese.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: Vilde worme, thou wast ore-look'd euen in thy birth.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: With Triall-fire touch me his finger end:
If he be chaste, the flame will backe descend
And turne him to no paine: but if he start,
It is the flesh of a corrupted hart.

speeches.speaker: Pist.
prose: A triall, come.

speeches.speaker: Eua.
prose: Come: will this wood take fire?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Oh, oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Corrupt, corrupt, and tainted in desire.
About him (Fairies) sing a scornfull rime,
And as you trip, still pinch him to your time.
Fie on sinnefull phantasie. Fie on Lust, and Luxurie:
Lust is but a bloudy fire, kindled with vnchaste desire,
Fed in heart whose flames aspire,
As thoughts do blow them higher and higher.
Pinch him (Fairies) mutually: Pinch him for his villanie.
Pinch him, and burne him, and turne him about,
Till Candles, & Star-light, & Moone-shine be out.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Nay do not flye, I thinke we haue watcht you now: VVill none but Herne the Hunter serue your turne?

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
verse: I pray you come, hold vp the iest no higher.
Now (good Sir Iohn) how like you Windsor wiues?
See you these husband? Do not these faire yoakes
Become the Forrest better then the Towne?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: Now Sir, whose a Cuckold now?

Mr
Broome, Falstaffes a Knaue, a Cuckoldly knaue,
Heere are his hornes Master Broome:
prose:
And Master Broome, he hath enioyed nothing of Fords, but his Buck-basket, his cudgell, and twenty pounds of money, which must be paid to Mr
Broome, his horses are arrested for it, Mr
Broome.

speeches.speaker: M. Ford.
prose: Sir Iohn, we haue had ill lucke: wee could neuer meete: I will neuer take you for my Loue againe, but I will alwayes count you my Deere.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I do begin to perceiue that I am made an Asse.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I, and an Oxe too: both the proofes are extant.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: And these are not Fairies. I was three or foure times in the thought they were not Fairies, and yet the guiltinesse of my minde, the sodaine surprize of my powers, droue the grossenesse of the foppery into a receiu'd beleefe, in despight of the teeth of all rime and reason, that they were Fairies. See now how wit may be made a Iacke-a-Lent, when 'tis vpon ill imployment.

speeches.speaker: Euant.
prose: Sir Iohn Falstaffe, serue Got, and leaue your desires, and Fairies will not pinse you.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: VVell said Fairy Hugh.

speeches.speaker: Euans.
prose: And leaue you your iealouzies too, I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: I will neuer mistrust my wife againe, till thou art able to woo her in good English.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Haue I laid my braine in the Sun, and dri'de it, that it wants matter to preuent so grosse ore-reaching as this? Am I ridden with a Welch Goate too? Shal I haue a Coxcombe of Frize? Tis time I were choak'd with a peece of toasted Cheese.

speeches.speaker: Eu.
prose: Seese is not good to giue putter; your belly is al putter.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Seese, and Putter? Haue I liu'd to stand at the taunt of one that makes Fritters of English? This is enough to be the decay of lust and late-walking through the Realme.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Why Sir Iohn, do you thinke though wee would haue thrust vertue out of our hearts by the head and shoulders, and haue giuen our selues without scruple to hell, that euer the deuill could haue made you our delight?

speeches.speaker: Ford
prose: What, a hodge-pudding? A bag of flax?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: A puft man?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Old, cold, wither'd, and of intollerable entrailes?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: And one that is as slanderous as Sathan?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: And as poore as Iob?

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: And as wicked as his wife?

speeches.speaker: Euan.
prose: And giuen to Fornications, and to Tauernes, and Sacke, and Wine, and Metheglins, and to drinkings and swearings, and starings? Pribles and prables?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: Well, I am your Theame: you haue the start of me. I am deiected: I am not able to answer the Welch Flannell, Ignorance it selfe is a plummet ore me, vse me as you will.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose:
Marry Sir, wee'l bring you to Windsor to one Mr
Broome, that you haue cozon'd of money, to whom you should haue bin a Pander: ouer and aboue that you haue suffer'd, I thinke, to repay that money will be a biting affliction.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose:
Yet be cheerefull Knight. thou shalt eat a posset to night at my house, wher I will desire thee to laugh at my wife, that now laughes at thee: Tell her Mr
Slender hath married her daughter.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Doctors doubt that;
If Anne Page be my daughter, she is (by this) Doctour Caius wife.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Whoa hoe, hoe, Father Page.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Sonne? How now? How now Sonne,
Haue you dispatch'd?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: Dispatch'd? Ile make the best in Gloftershire know on't: would I were hang'd la, else.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Of what sonne?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I came yonder at Eaton to marry Mistris Anne Page, and she's a great lubberly boy. If it had not bene i' th Church, I would haue swing'd him, or hee should haue swing'd me. If I did not thinke it had beene Anne Page, would I might neuer stirre, and 'tis a Post-masters Boy.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Vpon my life then, you tooke the wrong.

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: What neede you tell me that? I think so, when I tooke a Boy for a Girle: If I had bene married to him, (for all he was in womans apparrell) I would not haue had him.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Why this is your owne folly,
Did not I tell you how you should know my daughter,
By her garments?

speeches.speaker: Slen.
prose: I went to her in greene, and cried Mum, and she cride budget, as Anne and I had appointed, and yet it was not Anne, but a Post-masters boy.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
prose: Good George be not angry, I knew of your purpose: turn'd my daughter into white, and indeede she is now with the Doctor at the Deanrie, and there married.

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: Ver is Mistris Page: by gar I am cozoned, I ha married oon Garsoon, a boy; oon pesant, by gar. A boy, it is not An Page, by gar, I am cozened.

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: VVhy? did you take her in white?

speeches.speaker: Cai.
prose: I bee gar, and 'tis a boy: be gar, Ile raise all Windsor.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
prose: This is strange: Who hath got the right Anne?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse:
My heart misgiues me, here comes Mr
Fenton.

How now Mr
Fenton?

speeches.speaker: Anne.
prose: Pardon good father, good my mother pardon

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Now Mistris:

How chance you went not with Mr
Slender?

speeches.speaker: M. Page.
prose: Why went you not with Mr Doctor, maid?

speeches.speaker: Fen.
verse: You do amaze her: heare the truth of it,
You would haue married her most shamefully,
Where there was no proportion held in loue:
The truth is, she and I (long since contracted)
Are now so sure that nothing can dissolue vs:
Th' offence is holy, that she hath committed,
And this deceit looses the name of craft,
Of disobedience, or vnduteous title,
Since therein she doth euitate and shun
A thousand irreligious cursed houres
Which forced marriage would haue brought vpon her.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: Stand not amaz'd, here is no remedie:
In Loue, the heauens themselues do guide the state,
Money buyes Lands, and wiues are sold by fate.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: I am glad, though you haue tane a special stand to strike at me, that your Arrow hath glanc'd.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Well, what remedy? Fenton, heauen giue thee ioy, what cannot be eschew'd, must be embrac'd.

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose: When night-dogges run, all sorts of Deere are chac'd.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Page.
verse:
Well, I will muse no further: Mr
Fenton,
Heauen giue you many, many merry dayes:
Good husband, let vs euery one go home,
And laugh this sport ore by a Countrie fire,
Sir Iohn and all.

speeches.speaker: Ford.
verse: Let it be so (Sir Iohn:)
To Master Broome, you yet shall hold your word,
For he, to night, shall lye with Mistris Ford.

plays.play_title: MEASVRE, For Measure.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: EScalus.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Of Gouernment, the properties to vnfold,
Would seeme in me t' affect speech & discourse,
Since I am put to know, that your owne Science
Exceedes (in that) the lists of all aduice
My strength can giue you: Then no more remaines
But that, to your sufficiency, as your worth is able,
And let them worke: The nature of our People,
Our Cities Institutions, and the Termes
For Common Iustice, y' are as pregnant in
As Art, and practise, hath inriched any
That we remember: There is our Commission,
From which, we would not haue you warpe; call hither,
I say, bid come before vs Angelo:
What figure of vs thinke you, he will beare.
For you must know, we haue with speciall soule
Elected him our absence to supply;
Lent him our terror, drest him with our loue,
And giuen his Deputation all the Organs
Of our owne powre: What thinke you of it?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
verse: If any in Vienna be of worth
To vndergoe such ample grace, and honour,
It is Lord Angelo.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Looke where he comes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Alwayes obedient to your Graces will.
I come to know your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Angelo:
There is a kinde of Character in thy life,
That to th' obseruer, doth thy history
Fully vnfold: Thy selfe, and thy belongings
Are not thine owne so proper, as to waste
Thy selfe vpon thy vertues; they on thee:
Heauen doth with vs, as we, with Torches doe,
Not light them for themselues: For if our vertues
Did not goe forth of vs, 'twere all alike
As if we had them not: Spirits are not finely touch'd,
But to fine issues: nor nature neuer lends
The smallest scruple of her excellence,
But like a thrifty goddesse, she determines
Her selfe the glory of a creditour,
Both thanks, and vse; but I do bend my speech
To one that can my part in him aduertise;
Hold therefore Angelo:
In our remoue, be thou at full, our selfe:
Mortallitie and Mercie in Vienna
Liue in thy tongue, and heart: Old Escalus
Though first in question, is thy secondary.
Take thy Commission.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Now good my Lord
Let there be some more test, made of my mettle,
Before so noble, and so great a figure
Be stamp't vpon it.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: No more euasion:
We haue with a leauen'd, and prepared choice
Proceeded to you; therefore take your honors:
Our haste from hence is of so quicke condition,
That it prefers it selfe, and leaues vnquestion'd
Matters of needfull value: We shall write to you
As time, and our concernings shall importune,
How it goes with vs, and doe looke to know
What doth befall you here. So fare you well:
To th' hopefull execution doe I leaue you,
Of your Commissions.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Yet giue leaue (my Lord.)
That we may bring you something on the way.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: My haste may not admit it,
Nor neede you (on mine honor) haue to doe
With any scruple: your scope is as mine owne,
So to inforce, or qualifie the Lawes
As to your soule seemes good: Giue me your hand,
Ile priuily away: I loue the people,
But doe not like to stage me to their eyes:
Though it doe well, I doe not rellish well
Their lowd applause, and Aues vehement:
Nor doe I thinke the man of safe discretion
That do's affect it. Once more fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: The heauens giue safety to your purposes.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Lead forth, and bring you backe in happinesse.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I thanke you, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
verse: I shal desire you, Sir, to giue me leaue
To haue free speech with you; and it concernes me
To looke into the bottome of my place:
A powre I haue, but of what strength and nature,
I am not yet instructed.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: 'Tis so with me: Let vs with-draw together,
And we may soone our satisfaction haue
Touching that point.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Ile wait vpon your honor.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: If the Duke, with the other Dukes, come not to composition with the King of Hungary, why then all the Dukes fall vpon the King.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: Heauen grant vs its peace, but not the King of Hungaries.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Thou conclud'st like the Sanctimonious Pirat, that went to sea with the ten Commandements, but scrap'd one out of the Table.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: Thou shalt not Steale?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I, that he raz'd.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: Why? 'twas a commandement, to command the Captaine and all the rest from their functions: they put forth to steale: There's not a Souldier of vs all, that in the thanks-giuing before meate, do rallish the petition well, that praies for peace.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: I neuer heard any Souldier dislike it.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I beleeue thee: for I thinke thou neuer was't where Grace was said.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: No? a dozen times at least.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: What? In meeter?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: In any proportion. or in any language.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: I thinke, or in any Religion.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I, why not? Grace, is Grace, despight of all controuersie: as for example; Thou thy selfe art a wicked villaine, despight of all Grace.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: Well: there went but a paire of sheeres betweene vs.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I grant: as there may betweene the Lists, and the Veluet. Thou art the List.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: And thou the Veluet; thou art good veluet; thou'rt a three pild-peece I warrant thee: I had as liefe be a Lyst of an English Kersey, as be pil'd, as thou art pil'd, for a French Veluet. Do I speake feelingly now?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I thinke thou do'st: and indeed with most painfull feeling of thy speech: I will, out of thine owne confession, learne to begin thy health; but, whilst I liue forget to drinke after thee.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gen.
prose: I think I haue done my selfe wrong, haue I not?

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: Yes, that thou hast; whether thou art tainted, or free.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Behold, behold, where Madam Mitigation comes. I haue purchas'd as many diseases vnder her Roofe, As come to

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: To what, I pray?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Iudge.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: To three thousand Dollours a yeare.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: I, and more.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: A French crowne more.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: Thou art alwayes figuring diseases in me; but thou art full of error, I am sound.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Nay, not (as one would say) healthy: but so sound, as things that are hollow; thy bones are hollow; Impiety has made a feast of thee.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: How now, which of your hips has the most profound Ciatica?

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: Well, well: there's one yonder arrested, and carried to prison, was worth fiue thousand of you all.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: Who's that I pray'thee?

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: Marry Sir, that's Claudio, Signior Claudio.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: Claudio to prison? 'tis not so.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: Nay, but I know 'tis so: I saw him arrested: saw him carried away: and which is more, within these three daies his head to be chop'd off.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: But, after all this fooling, I would not haue it so: Art thou sure of this?

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: I am too sure of it: and it is for getting Madam Iulietta with childe.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Beleeue me this may be: he promis'd to meete me two howres since, and he was euer precise in promise keeping.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
prose: Besides you know, it drawes somthing neere to the speech we had to such a purpose.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
prose: But most of all agreeing with the proclamatio~.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Away: let's goe learne the truth of it.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: Thus, what with the war; what with the sweat, what with the gallowes, and what with pouerty, I am Custom-shrunke. How now? what's the newes with you.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Yonder man is carried to prison.

speeches.speaker: Baw.
prose: Well: what has he done?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: A Woman.

speeches.speaker: Baw.
prose: But what's his offence?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Groping for Trowts, in a peculiar Riuer.

speeches.speaker: Baw.
prose: What? is there a maid with child by him?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No: but there's a woman with maid by him you haue not heard of the proclamation, haue you?

speeches.speaker: Baw.
prose: What proclamation, man?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: All howses in the Suburbs of Vienna must bee pluck'd downe.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: And what shall become of those in the Citie?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: They shall stand for seed: they had gon down to, but that a wise Burger put in for them.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: But shall all our houses of resort in the Suburbs be puld downe?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: To the ground, Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: Why heere's a change indeed in the Commonwealth: what shall become of me?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Come: feare not you: good Counsellors lacke no Clients: though you change your place, you neede not change your Trade: Ile bee your Tapster still; courage, there will bee pitty taken on you; you that haue worne your eyes almost out in the seruice, you will bee considered.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: What's to doe heere, Thomas Tapster? let's withdraw?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Here comes Signior Claudio, led by the Prouost to prison: and there's Madam Iuliet.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Fellow, why do'st thou show me thus to th' world? Beare me to prison, where I am committed.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I do it not in euill disposition, But from Lord Angelo by speciall charge.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Thus can the demy-god (Authority)
Make vs pay downe, for our offence, by waight
The words of heauen. on whom it will, it will,
On whom it will not (soe) yet still 'tis iust.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Why how now Claudio.
whence comes this restraint.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: From too much liberty, (my Lucio) Liberty
As surfet is the father of much fast,
So euery Scope by the immoderate vse
Turnes to restraint: Our Natures doe pursue
Like Rats that rauyn downe their proper Bane,
A thirsty euill, and when we drinke, we die.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: If I could speake so wisely vnder an arrest, I would send for certaine of my Creditors: and yet, to say the truth, I had as lief haue the foppery of freedome, as the mortality of imprisonment: what's thy offence, Claudio?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: What (but to speake of) would offend againe.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: What, is't murder?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Lecherie?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Call it so.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Away, Sir, you must goe.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: One word, good friend:
Lucio, a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: A hundred:
If they'll doe you any good: Is Lechery so look'd after?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Thus stands it with me: vpon a true contract
I got possession of Iulietas bed,
You know the Lady, she is fast my wife,
Saue that we doe the denunciation lacke
Of outward Order. This we came not to,
Onely for propogation of a Dowre
Remaining in the Coffer of her friends,
From whom we thought it meet to hide our Loue
Till Time had made them for vs. But it chances
The stealth of our most mutuall entertainment
With Character too grosse, is writ on Iuliet.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: With childe, perhaps?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Vnhappely, euen so.
And the new Deputie, now for the Duke,
Whether it be the fault and glimpse of newnes,
Or whether that the body publique, be
A horse whereon the Gouernor doth ride,
Who newly in the Seate, that it may know
He can command; lets it strait feele the spur:
Whether the Tirranny be in his place,
Or in his Eminence that fills it vp
I stagger in: But this new Gouernor
Awakes me all the inrolled penalties
Which haue (like vn-scowr'd Armor) hung by th' wall
So long, that ninteene Zodiacks haue gone round,
And none of them beene worne; and for a name
Now puts the drowsie and neglected Act
Freshly on me: 'tis surely for a name.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I warrant it is: And thy head stands so tickle on thy shoulders, that a milke-maid, if she be in loue, may sigh it off: Send after the Duke, and appeale to him.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I haue done so, but hee's not to be found.
I pre'thee (Lucio) doe me this kinde seruice:
This day, my sister should the Cloyster enter,
And there receiue her approbation.
Acquaint her with the danger of my state,
Implore her, in my voice, that she make friends
To the strict deputie: bid her selfe assay him,
I haue great hope in that: for in her youth
There is a prone and speechlesse dialect,
Such as moue men: beside, she hath prosperous Art
When she will play with reason, and discourse,
And well she can perswade.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I pray shee may; aswell for the encouragement of the like, which else would stand vnder greeuous imposition: as for the enioying of thy life, who I would be sorry should bee thus foolishly lost, at a game of ticke-tacke: Ile to her.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: I thanke you good friend Lucio.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Within two houres.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Come Officer, away.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: No: holy Father, throw away that thought,
Beleeue not that the dribling dart of Loue
Can pierce a compleat bosome: why, I desire thee
To giue me secret harbour, hath a purpose
More graue, and wrinkled, then the aimes, and ends
Of burning youth.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: May your Grace speake of it?

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: My holy Sir, none better knowes then you
How I haue euer lou'd the life remoued
And held in idle price, to haunt assemblies
Where youth, and cost, witlesse brauery keepes.
I haue deliuerd to Lord Angelo
(A man of stricture and firme abstinence)

My absolute power, and place here in
~ienna,
And he supposes me trauaild to Poland,
(For so I haue strewd it in the common eare)
And so it is receiu'd: Now (pious Sir)
You will demand of me, why I do this.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: Gladly, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: We haue strict Statutes, and most biting Laws,
(The needfull bits and curbes to headstrong weedes,)
Which for this foureteene yeares, we haue let slip,
Euen like an ore-growne Lyon in a Caue
That goes not out to prey: Now, as fond Fathers,
Hauing bound vp the threatning twigs of birch,
Onely to sticke it in their childrens sight,
For terror, not to vse: in time the rod
More mock'd, then fear'd: so our Decrees,
Dead to infliction, to themselues are dead,
And libertie, plucks Iustice by the nose;
The Baby beates the Nurse, and quite a thwart
Goes all decorum.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: It rested in your Grace
To vnloose this tyde-vp Iustice, when you pleas'd:
And it in you more dreadfull would haue seem'd
Then in Lord Angelo.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I doe feare: too dreadfull:
Sith 'twas my fault, to giue the people scope,
'T would be my tirrany to strike and gall them,
For what I bid them doe: For, we bid this be done
When euill deedes haue their permissiue passe,
And not the punishment: therefore indeede (my father)
I haue on Angelo impos'd the office,
Who may in th' ambush of my name, strike home,
And yet, my nature neuer in the fight
To do in slander: And to behold his sway
I will, as 'twere a brother of your Order,
Visit both Prince, and People: Therefore I pre'thee
Supply me with the habit, and instruct me
How I may formally in person beare
Like a true Frier: Moe reasons for this action
At our more leysure, shall I render you;
Onely, this one: Lord Angelo is precise,
Stands at a guard with Enuie: scarce confesses
That his blood flowes: or that his appetite
Is more to bread then stone: hence shall we see
If power change purpose: what our Seemers be.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: And haue you Nuns no farther priuiledges?

speeches.speaker: Nun.
prose: Are not these large enough?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Yes truely; I speake not as desiring more,
But rather wishing a more strict restraint
Vpon the Sisterstood, the Votarists of Saint Clare.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Hoa? peace be in this place.

speeches.speaker: Isa:
prose: Who's that which cals?

speeches.speaker: Nun.
verse: It is a mans voice: gentle Isabella
Turne you the key, and know his businesse of him;
You may; I may not: you are yet vnsworne:
When you haue vowd, you must not speake with men,
But in the presence of the Prioresse;
Then if you speake, you must not show your face;
Or if you show your face, you must not speake:
He cals againe: I pray you answere him.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Peace and prosperitie: who is't that cals?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Haile Virgin, (if you be) as those cheeke-Roses
Proclaime you are no lesse: can you so steed me,
As bring me to the fight of Isabella,
A Nouice of this place, and the faire Sister
To her vnhappie brother Claudio?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Why her vnhappy Brother? Let me aske,
The rather for I now must make you know
I am that Isabella, and his Sister.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Gentle & faire: your Brother kindly greets you;
Not to be weary with you; he's in prison.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Woe me; for what?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: For that, which if my selfe might be his Iudge,
He should receiue his punishment, in thankes:
He hath got his friend with childe.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Sir, make me not your storie.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: 'Tis true; I would not, though 'tis my familiar sin,
With Maids to seeme the Lap wing, and to iest
Tongue, far from heart: play with all Virgins so:
I hold you as a thing en-skied, and sainted,
By your renouncement, an imortall spirit
And to be talk'd with in sincerity,
As with a Saint.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: You doe blaspheme the good, in mocking me.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Doe not beleeue it: fewnes, and truth; tis thus,
Your brother, and his louer haue embrac'd;
As those that feed, grow full: as blossoming Time
That from the seednes, the bare fallow brings
To teeming foyson: euen so her plenteous wombe
Expresseth his full Tilth, and husbandry.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Some one with childe by him? my cosen Iuliet?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Is she your cosen?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Adoptedly, as schoole-maids change their names By vaine, though apt affection.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: She it is.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Oh, let him marry her.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: This is the point.
The Duke is very strangely gone from hence;
Bore many gentlemen (my selfe being one)
In hand, and hope of action: but we doe learne,
By those that know the very Nerues of State,
His giuing-out, were of an infinite distance
From his true meant designe: vpon his place,
(And with full line of his authority)
Gouernes Lord Angelo; A man, whose blood
Is very snow-broth: one, who neuer feeles
The wanton stings, and motions of the sence;
But doth rebate, and blunt his naturall edge
With profits of the minde: Studie, and fast
He (to giue feare to vse, and libertie,
Which haue, for long, run-by the hideous law,
As Myce, by Lyons) hath pickt out an act,
Vnder whose heauy sence, your brothers life
Fals into forfeit: he arrests him on it,
And followes close the rigor of the Statute
To make him an example: all hope is gone,
Vnlesse you haue the grace, by your faire praier
To soften Angelo: And that's my pith of businesse
'Twixt you, and your poore brother.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Doth he so,
Seeke his life?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Has censur'd him already,
And as I heare, the Prouost hath a warrant
For's execution.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Alas: what poore Abilitie's in me, to doe him good.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Assay the powre you haue.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: My power? alas, I doubt.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Our doubts are traitors
And makes vs loose the good we oft might win,
By fearing to attempt: Goe to Lord Angelo
And let him learne to know, when Maidens sue
Men giue like gods: but when they weepe and kneele,
All their petitions, are as freely theirs
As they themselues would owe them.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Ile see what I can doe.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: But speedily.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: I will about it strait;
No longer staying, but to giue the Mother
Notice of my affaire: I humbly thanke you:
Commend me to my brother: soone at night
Ile send him certaine word of my successe.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I take my leaue of you.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Good sir, adieu.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: We must not make a scar-crow of the Law,
Setting it vp to feare the Birds of prey,
And let it keepe one shape, till custome make it
Their pearch, and not their terror.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
verse: I, but yet
Let vs be keene, and rather cut a little
Then fall, and bruise to death: alas, this gentleman
Whom I would saue, had a most noble father,
Let but your honour know
(Whom I beleeue to be most strait in vertue)
That in the working of your owne affections,
Had time coheard with Place, or place with wishing,
Or that the resolute acting of our blood
Could haue attained th' effect of your owne purpose,
Whether you had not sometime in your life
Er'd in this point, which now you censure him,
And puld the Law vpon you.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: 'Tis one thing to be tempted (Escalus)
Another thing to fall: I not deny
The Iury passing on the Prisoners life
May in the sworne-twelue haue a thiefe, or two
Guiltier then him they try; what's open made to Iustice,
That Iustice ceizes; What knowes the Lawes
That theeues do passe on theeues? 'Tis very pregnant,
The Iewell that we finde, we stoope, and take't,
Because we see it; but what we doe not see,
We tread vpon, and neuer thinke of it.
You may not so extenuate his offence,
For I haue had such faults; but rather tell me
When I, that censure him, do so offend,
Let mine owne Iudgement patterne out my death,
And nothing come in partiall. Sir, he must dye.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Be it as your wisedome will.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Where is the Prouost?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Here if it like your honour.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: See that Claudio
Be executed by nine to morrow morning,
Bring him his Confessor, let him be prepar'd,
For that's the vtmost of his pilgrimage.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
verse: Well: heauen forgiue him; and forgiue vs all:
Some rise by sinne, and some by vertue fall:
Some run from brakes of Ice, and answere none,
And some condemned for a fault alone.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Come, bring them away: if these be good people in a Common-weale, that doe nothing but vse their abuses in common houses, I know no law: bring them away.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: How now Sir, what's your name? And what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: If it please your honour, I am the poore Dukes Constable, and my name is Elbow; I doe leane vpon Iustice Sir, and doe bring in here before your good honor, two notorious Benefactors.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Benefactors? Well: What Benefactors are they? Are they not Malefactors?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: If it please your honour, I know not well what they are: But precise villaines they are, that I am sure of and void of all prophanation in the world, that good Christians ought to haue.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: This comes off well: here's a wise Officer.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Goe to: What quality are they of? Elbow is your name?
Why do'st thou not speake Elbow?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: He cannot Sir: he's out at Elbow.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: What are you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: He Sir: a Tapster Sir: parcell Baud: one that serues a bad woman: whose house Sir was (as they say) pluckt downe in the Suborbs: and now shee professes a hot-house; which, I thinke is a very ill house too.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: How know you that?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: My wife Sir? whom I detest before heauen, and your honour.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: How? thy wife?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: I Sir: whom I thanke heauen is an honest woman.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Do'st thou detest her therefore?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: I say sir, I will detest my selfe also, as well as she, that this house, if it be not a Bauds house, it is pitty of her life, for it is a naughty house.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: How do'st thou know that, Constable?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Marry sir, by my wife, who, if she had bin a woman Cardinally giuen, might haue bin accus'd in fornication, adultery, and all vncleanlinesse there.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: By the womans meanes?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: I sir, by Mistris Ouer-dons meanes: but as she spit in his face, so she defide him.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir, if it please your honor, this is not so.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Proue it before these varlets here, thou honorable man, proue it.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Doe you heare how he misplaces?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir, she came in great with childe: and longing (sauing your honors reuerence) for stewd prewyns; sir, we had but two in the house, which at that very distant time stood, as it were in a fruit dish (a dish of some three pence; your honours haue seene such dishes) they are not China-dishes, but very good dishes.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Go too: go too: no matter for the dish sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No indeede sir not of a pin; you are therein in the right: but, to the point: As I say, this Mistris Elbow, being (as I say) with childe, and being great bellied, and longing (as I said) for prewyns: and hauing but two in the dish (as I said) Master Froth here, this very man, hauing eaten the rest (as I said) & (as I say) paying for them very honestly: for, as you know Master Froth, I could not giue you three pence againe.

speeches.speaker: Fro.
prose: No indeede.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Very well: you being then (if you be remembred) cracking the stones of the foresaid prewyns.

speeches.speaker: Fro.
prose: I, so I did indeede.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why, very well: I telling you then (if you be remembred) that such a one, and such a one, were past cure of the thing you wot of, vnlesse they kept very good diet, as I told you.

speeches.speaker: Fro.
prose: All this is true.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why very well then.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
