prose: Come: you are a tedious foole: to the purpose: what was done to Elbowes wife, that hee hath cause to complaine of? Come me to what was done to her.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir, your honor cannot come to that yet.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: No sir, nor I meane it not.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir, but you shall come to it, by your honours leaue: And I beseech you, looke into Master Froth here sir, a man of foure-score pound a yeare; whose father died at Hallowmas: Was't not at Hallowmas Master Froth?

speeches.speaker: Fro.
prose: Allhallond-Eue.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why very well: I hope here be truthes: he Sir, sitting (as I say) in a lower chaire, Sir, 'twas in the bunch of Grapes, where indeede you haue a delight to sit, haue you not?

speeches.speaker: Fro.
prose: I haue so, because it is an open roome, and good for winter.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why very well then: I hope here be truthes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: This will last out a night in Russia
When nights are longest there: Ile take my leaue,
And leaue you to the hearing of the cause;
Hoping youle finde good cause to whip them all.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: I thinke no lesse: good morrow to your Lordship. Now Sir, come on: What was done to Elbowes wife, once more?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Once Sir? there was nothing done to her once.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: I beseech you Sir, aske him what this man did to my wife.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I beseech your honor, aske me.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Well sir, what did this Gentleman to her?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I beseech you sir, looke in this Gentlemans face: good Master Froth looke vpon his honor; 'tis for a good purpose: doth your honor marke his face?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: I sir, very well.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Nay, I beseech you marke it well.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Well, I doe so.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Doth your honor see any harme in his face?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Why no.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Ile be supposd vpon a booke, his face is the worst thing about him: good then: if his face be the worst thing about him, how could Master Froth doe the Constables wife any harme? I would know that of your honour.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: He's in the right (Constable) what say you to it?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: First, and it like you, the house is a respected house; next, this is a respected fellow; and his Mistris is a respected woman.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: By this hand Sir, his wife is a more respected person then any of vs all.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Varlet, thou lyest; thou lyest wicked varlet: the time is yet to come that shee was euer respected with man, woman, or childe.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir, she was respected with him, before he married with her.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Which is the wiser here; Iustice or Iniquitie? Is this true?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: O thou caytiffe: O thou varlet: O thou wicked Hanniball; I respected with her, before I was married to her? If euer I was respected with her, or she with me, let not your worship thinke mee the poore Dukes Officer: proue this, thou wicked Hanniball, or ile haue mine action of battry on thee.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: If he tooke you a box' oth' eare, you might haue your action of slander too.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Marry I thanke your good worship for it: what is't your Worships pleasure I shall doe with this wicked Caitiffe?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Truly Officer, because he hath some offences in him, that thou wouldst discouer, if thou couldst, let him continue in his courses, till thou knowst what they are.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Marry I thanke your worship for it: Thou seest thou wicked varlet now, what's come vpon thee. Thou art to continue now thou Varlet, thou art to continue.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Where were you borne, friend?

speeches.speaker: Froth.
prose: Here in Vienna, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Are you of fourescore pounds a yeere?

speeches.speaker: Froth.
prose: Yes, and 't please you sir.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: So: what trade are you of, sir?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: A Tapster, a poore widdowes Tapster.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Your Mistris name?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Mistris Ouer-do^.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Hath she had any more then one husband?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Nine, sir: Ouer-don by the last.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Nine? come hether to me, Master Froth; Master Froth, I would not haue you acquainted with Tapsters; they will draw you Master Froth, and you wil hang them: get you gon, and let me heare no more of you.

speeches.speaker: Fro.
prose: I thanke your worship: for mine owne part, I neuer come into any roome in a Tap-house, but I am drawne in.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Well: no more of it Master Froth: farewell: Come you hether to me, Mr. Tapster: what's your name Mr. Tapster?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: What else?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Bum, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Troth, and your bum is the greatest thing about you, so that in the beastliest sence, you are Pompey the great; Pompey, you are partly a bawd, Pompey; howsoeuer you colour it in being a Tapster, are you not? come, tell me true, it shall be the better for you.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Truly sir, I am a poore fellow that would liue.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: How would you liue Pompey? by being a bawd? what doe you thinke of the trade Pompey? is it a lawfull trade?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: If the Law would allow it, sir.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose:
But the Law will not allow it Pompey; nor it shall not be allowed in
~ienna.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Do's your Worship meane to geld and splay all the youth of the City?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: No, Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Truely Sir, in my poore opinion they will too't then: if your worship will take order for the drabs and the knaues, you need not to feare the bawds.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: There is pretty orders beginning I can tell you: It is but heading, and hanging.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: If you head, and hang all that offend that way but for ten yeare together; you'll be glad to giue out a Commission for more heads: if this law hold in Vienna ten yeare, ile rent the fairest house in it after three pence a Bay: if you liue to see this come to passe, say Pompey told you so.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Thanke you good Pompey; and in requitall of your prophesie, harke you: I aduise you let me not finde you before me againe vpon any complaint whatsoeuer; no, not for dwelling where you doe: if I doe Pompey, I shall beat you to your Tent, and proue a shrewd Caesar to you: in plaine dealing Pompey, I shall haue you whipt; so for this time, Pompey, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I thanke your Worship for your good counsell; but I shall follow it as the flesh and fortune shall better determine. Whip me? no, no, let Carman whip his Iade, The valiant heart's not whipt out of his trade.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Come hether to me, Master Elbow: come hither Master Constable: how long haue you bin in this place of Constable?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Seuen yeere, and a halfe sir.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: I thought by the readinesse in the office, you had continued in it some time: you say seauen yeares together.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: And a halfe sir.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Alas, it hath beene great paines to you: they do you wrong to put you so oft vpon't. Are there not men in your Ward sufficient to serue it?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: 'Faith sir, few of any wit in such matters: as they are chosen, they are glad to choose me for them; I do it for some peece of money, and goe through with all.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Looke you bring mee in the names of some sixe or seuen, the most sufficient of your parish.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: To your Worships house sir?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: To my house: fare you well: what's a clocke, thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Eleuen, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: I pray you home to dinner with me.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: I humbly thanke you.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
verse: It grieues me for the death of Claudio
But there's no remedie:

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Lord Angelo is seuere.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
verse: It is but needfull.
Mercy is not it selfe, that oft lookes so,
Pardon is still the nurse of second woe:
But yet, poore Claudio; there is no remedie.
Come Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Hee's hearing of a Cause; he will come straight, I'le tell him of you.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: 'Pray you doe; Ile know
His pleasure, may be he will relent; alas
He hath but as offended in a dreame,
All Sects, all Ages smack of this vice, and he
To die for't?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Now, what's the matter Prouost?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Is it your will Claudio shall die to morrow?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Did not I tell thee yea? hadst thou not order? Why do'st thou aske againe?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Lest I might be too rash:
Vnder your good correction, I haue seene
When after execution, Iudgement hath
Repented ore his doome.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Goe to; let that be mine,
Doe you your office, or giue vp your Place,
And you shall well be spar'd.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I craue your Honours pardon:
What shall be done Sir, with the groaning Iuliet?
Shee's very neere her howre.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Dispose of her
To some more fitter place; and that with speed.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Here is the sister of the man condemn'd,
Desires accesse to you.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Hath he a Sister?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I my good Lord, a very vertuous maid,
And to be shortlie of a Sister-hood,
If not alreadie.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Well: let her be admitted,
See you the Fornicatresse be remou'd,
Let her haue needfull, but not lauish meanes,
There shall be order for't.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: 'Saue your Honour.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Stay a little while: y' are welcome: what's your will?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I am a wofull Sutor to your Honour,
'Please but your Honor heare me.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Well: what's your suite.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: There is a vice that most I doe abhorre,
And most desire should meet the blow of Iustice;
For which I would not plead, but that I must,
For which I must not plead, but that I am
At warre, twixt will, and will not.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Well: the matter?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I haue a brother is condemn'd to die,
I doe beseech you let it be his fault,
And not my brother.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Heauen giue thee mouing graces.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Condemne the fault, and not the actor of it,
Why euery fault's condemnd ere it be done:
Mine were the verie Cipher of a Function
To fine the faults, whose fine stands in record,
And let goe by the Actor:

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Oh iust, but seuere Law:
I had a brother then; heauen keepe your honour.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Giue't not ore so: to him againe, entreat him,
Kneele downe before him, hang vpon his gowne,
You are too cold: if you should need a pin,
You could not with more t^me tongue desire it:
To him, I say.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Must he needs die?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Maiden, no remedie.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Yes: I doe thinke that you might pardon him,
And neither heauen, nor man grieue at the mercy.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I will not doe't.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: But can you if you would?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Looke what I will not, that I cannot doe.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: But might you doe't & do the world no wrong
If so your heart were touch'd with that remorse,
As mine is to him?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Hee's sentenc'd, tis too late.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: You are too cold.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Too late? why no: I that doe speak a word
May call it againe: well, beleeue this
No ceremony that to great ones longs,
Not the Kings Crowne; nor the deputed sword,
The Marshalls Truncheon, nor the Iudges Robe
Become them with one halfe so good a grace
As mercie does: If he had bin as you, and you as he,
You would haue slipt like him, but he like you
Would not haue beene so sterne.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Pray you be gone.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I would to heauen I had your potencie,
And you were Isabell: should it then be thus?
No: I would tell what 'twere to be a Iudge,
And what a prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I, touch him: there's the vaine.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Your Brother is a forfeit of the Law,
And you but waste your words.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Alas, alas:
Why all the soules that were, were forfeit once,
And he that might the vantage best haue tooke,
Found out the remedie: how would you be,
If he, which is the top of Iudgement, should
But iudge you, as you are? Oh, thinke on that,
And mercie then will breathe within your lips
Like man new made.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Be you content, (faire Maid)
It is the Law, not I, condemne your brother,
Were he my kinsman, brother, or my sonne,
It should be thus with him: he must die to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: To morrow? oh, that's sodaine,
Spare him, spare him:
Hee's not prepar'd for death; euen for our kitchins
We kill the fowle of season: shall we serue heauen
With lesse respect then we doe minister
To our grosse-selues? good, good my Lord, bethink you;
Who is it that hath di'd for this offence?
There's many haue committed it.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I, well said.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: The Law hath not bin dead, thogh it hath slept
Those many had not dar'd to doe that euill
If the first, that did th' Edict infringe
Had answer'd for his deed. Now 'tis awake.
Takes note of what is done, and like a Prophet
Lookes in a glasse that shewes what future euils
Either now, or by remissenesse, new conceiu'd,
And so in progresse to be hatc'hd, and borne,
Are now to haue no successiue degrees,
But here they liue to end.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Yet shew some pittie.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I shew it most of all, when I show Iustice;
For then I pittie those I doe not know,
Which a dismis'd offence, would after gaule
And doe him right, that answering one foule wrong
Liues not to act another. Be satisfied;
Your Brother dies to morrow; be content.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: So you must be ye first that giues this sentence,
And hee, that suffers: Oh, it is excellent
To haue a Giants strength: but it is tyrannous
To vse it like a Giant.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: That's well said.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Could great men thunder
As Ioue himselfe do's, Ioue would neuer be quiet,
For euery pelting petty Officer
Would vse his heauen for thunder;
Nothing but thunder: Mercifull heauen,
Thou rather with thy sharpe and sulpherous bol^
Splits the vn-wedgable and gnarled Oke,
Then, the soft Mertill: But man, proud man,
Drest in a little briefe authoritie,
Most ignorant of what he's most assur'd,
(His glassie Essence) like an angry Ape
Plaies such phantastique tricks before high heauen,
As makes the Angels weepe: who with our spleenes,
Would all themselues laugh mortall.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Oh, to him, to him wench: he will relent,
Hee's comming: I perceiue't.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Pray heauen she win him.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: We cannot weigh our brother with our selfe,
Great men may iest with Saints: tis wit in them,
But in the lesse fowle prophanation.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Thou'rt i' th right (Girle) more o' that.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: That in the Captaine's but a chollericke word,
Which in the Souldier is flat blasphemie.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Art auis'd o' that? more on't.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Why doe you put these sayings vpon me?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Because Authoritie, though it erre like others,
Hath yet a kinde of medicine in it selfe
That skins the vice o' th top; goe to your bosome,
Knock there, and aske your heart what it doth know
That's like my brothers fault: if it confesse
A naturall guiltinesse, such as is his,
Let it not sound a thought vpon your tongue
Against my brothers life.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Shee speakes, and 'tis such sence
That my Sence breeds with it; fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Gentle my Lord, turne backe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I will bethinke me: come againe to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Hark, how Ile bribe you: good my Lord turn back.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: How? bribe me?

speeches.speaker: Is.
prose: I, with such gifts that heauen shall share with you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: You had mar'd all else.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Not with fond Sickles of the tested-gold,
Or Stones, whose rate are either rich, or poore
As fancie values them: but with true prayers,
That shall be vp at heauen, and enter there
Ere Sunne rise: prayers from preserued soules,
From fasting Maides, whose mindes are dedicate
To nothing temporall.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Well: come to me to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Goe to: 'tis well; away.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Heauen keepe your honour safe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Amen.
For I am that way going to temptation,
Where prayers crosse.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: At what hower to morrow,
Shall I attend your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: At any time 'fore-noone.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: 'Saue your Honour.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: From thee: euen from thy vertue.
What's this? what's this? is this her fault, or mine?
The Tempter, or the Tempted, who sins most? ha?
Not she: nor doth she tempt: but it is I,
That, lying by the Violet in the Sunne,
Doe as the Carrion do's, not as the flowre,
Corrupt with vertuous season: Can it be,
That Modesty may more betray our Sence
Then womans lightnesse? hauing waste ground enough,
Shall we desire to raze the Sanctuary
And pitch our euils there? oh fie, fie, fie:
What dost thou? or what art thou Angelo?
Dost thou desire her fowly, for those things
That make her good? oh, let her brother liue:
Theeues for their robbery haue authority,
When Iudges steale themselues: what, doe I loue her,
That I desire to heare her speake againe?
And feast vpon her eyes? what is't I dreame on?
Oh cunning enemy, that to catch a Saint,
With Saints dost bait thy hooke: most dangerous
Is that temptation, that doth goad vs on
To sinne, in louing vertue: neuer could the Strumpet
With all her double vigor, Art, and Nature
Once stir my temper: but this vertuous Maid
Subdues me quite: Euer till now
When men were fond, I smild, and wondred how.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Haile to you, Prouost, so I thinke you are.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I am the Prouost: whats your will, good Frier?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Bound by my charity, and my blest order,
I come to visite the afflicted spirits
Here in the prison: doe me the common right
To let me see them: and to make me know
The nature of their crimes, that I may minister
To them accordingly.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I would do more then that, if more were needfull
Looke here comes one: a Gentlewoman of mine,
Who falling in the flawes of her owne youth,
Hath blisterd her report: She is with childe,
And he that got it, sentenc'd: a yong man,
More fit to doe another such offence,
Then dye for this.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: When must he dye?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: As I do thinke to morrow.
I haue prouided for you, stay a while
And you shall be conducted.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Repent you (faire one) of the sin you carry?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I doe; and beare the shame most patiently.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Ile teach you how you shal araign your conscie~ce
And try your penitence, if it be sound,
Or hollowly put on.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Ile gladly learne.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Loue you the man that wrong'd you?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Yes, as I loue the woman that wrong'd him.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: So then it seemes your most offence full act
Was mutually committed.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Mutually.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Then was your sin of heauier kinde then his.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I doe confesse it, and repent it (Father.)

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: 'Tis meet so (daughter) but least you do repent
As that the sin hath brought you to this shame,
Which sorrow is alwaies toward our selues, not heauen,
Showing we would not spare heauen, as we loue it,
But as we stand in feare.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I doe repent me as it is an euill,
And take the shame with ioy.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: There rest:
Your partner (as I heare) must die to morrow,
And I am going with instruction to him:
Grace goe with you, Benedicite.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Must die tomorrow? oh iniurious Loue
That respits me a life, whose very comfort
Is still a dying horror.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: 'Tis pitty of him.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: When I would pray, & think, I thinke, and pray
To seuerall subiects: heauen hath my empty words,
Whilst my Inuention, hearing not my Tongue,
Anchors on Isabell: heauen in my mouth,
As if I did but onely chew his name,
And in my heart the strong and swelling euill
Of my conception: the state whereon I studied
Is like a good thing, being often read
Growne feard, and tedious: yea, my Grauitie
Wherein (let no man heare me) I take pride,
Could I, with boote, change for an idle plume
Which the ayre beats for vaine: oh place, oh forme,
How often dost thou with thy case, thy habit
Wrench awe from fooles, and tye the wiser soules
To thy false seeming? Blood, thou art blood,
Let's write good Angell on the Deuills horne
'Tis not the Deuills Crest: how now? who's there?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: One Isabell, a Sister, desires accesse to you,

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Teach her the way: oh, heauens
Why doe's my bloud thus muster to my heart,
Making both it vnable for it selfe,
And dispossessing all my other parts
Of necessary fitnesse?
So play the foolish throngs with one that swounds,
Come all to help him, and so stop the ayre
By which hee should reuiue: and euen so
The generall subiect to a wel-wisht King
Quit their owne part, and in obsequious fondnesse
Crowd to his presence, where their vn-taught loue
Must needs appear offence: how now faire Maid.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I am come to know your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: That you might know it, wold much better please me,
Then to demand what 'tis: your Brother cannot liue.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Euen so: heauen keepe your Honor.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Yet may he liue a while: and it may be
As long as you, or I: yet he must die.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Vnder your Sentence?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Yea.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: When, I beseech you: that in his Reprieue
(Longer, or shorter) he may be so fitted
That his soule sicken not.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Ha? fie, these filthy vices: It were as good
To pardon him, that hath from nature stolne
A man already made, as to remit
Their sawcie sweetnes, that do coyne heauens Image
In stamps that are forbid: 'tis all as easie,
Falsely to take away a life true made,
As to put mettle in restrained meanes
To make a false one.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: 'Tis set downe so in heauen, but not in earth.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Say you so: then I shall poze you quickly.
Which had you rather, that the most iust Law
Now tooke your brothers life, and to redeeme him
Giue vp your body to such sweet vncleannesse
As she that he hath staind?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Sir, beleeue this.
I had rather giue my body, then my soule.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I talke not of your soule: our compel'd sins
Stand more for number, then for accompt.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: How say you?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Nay Ile not warrant that: for I can speake
Against the thing I say: Answere to this,
I (now the voyce of the recorded Law)
Pronounce a sentence on your Brothers life,
Might there not be a charitie in sinne,
To saue this Brothers life?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Please you to doo't,
Ile take it as a perill to my soule,
It is no sinne at all, but charitie.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Pleas'd you to doo't, at perill of your soule
Were equall poize of sinne, and charitie.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: That I do beg his life, if it be sinne
Heauen let me beare it: you granting of my suit,
If that be sin, Ile make it my Morne-praier,
To haue it added to the faults of mine,
And nothing of your answere.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Nay, but heare me.
Your sence pursues not mine: either you are ignorant,
Or seeme so crafty; and that's not good.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Let be ignorant, and in nothing good,
But graciously to know I am no better.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Thus wisdome wishes to appeare most bright,
When it doth taxe it selfe: As these blacke Masques
Proclaime an en-shield beauty ten times louder
Then beauty could displaied: But marke me,
To be receiued plaine, Ile speake more grosse:
Your Brother is to dye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: So.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: And his offence is so, as it appeares,
Accountant to the Law, vpon that paine.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: True.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Admit no other way to saue his life
(As I subscribe not that, nor any other,
But in the lesse of question) that you, his Sister,
Finding your selfe desir'd of such a person,
Whose creadit with the Iudge, or owne great place,
Could fetch your Brother from the Manacles
Of the all-building-Law: and that there were
No earthly meane to saue him, but that either
You must lay downe the treasures of your body,
To this supposed, or else to let him suffer:
What would you doe?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: As much for my poore Brother, as my selfe;
That is: were I vnder the tearmes of death,
Th' impression of keene whips, I'ld weare as Rubies,
And strip my selfe to death, as to a bed,
That longing haue bin sicke for, ere I'ld yeeld
My body vp to shame.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Then must your brother die.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: And 'twer the cheaper way:
Better it were a brother dide at once,
Then that a sister, by redeeming him
Should die for euer.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Were not you then as cruell as the Sentence,
That you haue slander'd so?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Ignomie in ransome, and free pardon
Are of two houses: lawfull mercie,
Is nothing kin to fowle redemption.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: You seem'd of late to make the Law a tirant,
And rather prou'd the sliding of your brother
A merriment, then a vice.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Oh pardon me my Lord, it oft fals out
To haue, what we would haue,
We speake not what vve meane;
I something do excuse the thing I hate,
For his aduantage that I dearely loue.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: We are all fraile.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Else let my brother die,
If not a fedarie but onely he
Owe, and succeed thy weaknesse.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Nay, women are fraile too.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: I, as the glasses where they view themselues,
Which are as easie broke as they make formes:
Women? Helpe heauen; men their creation marre
In profiting by them: Nay, call vs ten times fraile,
For we are soft, as our complexions are,
And credulous to false prints.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I thinke it well:
And from this testimonie of your owne sex
(Since I suppose we are made to be no stronger
Then faults may shake our frames) let me be bold;
I do arrest your words. Be that you are,
That is a woman; if you be more, you'r none.
If you be one (as you are well exprest
By all externall warrants) shew it now,
By putting on the destin'd Liuerie.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: I haue no tongue but one; gentle my Lord,
Let me entreate you speake the former language.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Plainlie conceiue I loue you.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: My brother did loue Iuliet,
And you tell me that he shall die for't.

speeches.speaker: Ang
prose: He shall not Isabell if you giue me loue.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: I know your vertue hath a licence in't,
Which seemes a little fouler then it is,
To plucke on others.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Beleeue me on mine Honor,
My words expresse my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Ha? Little honor, to be much beleeu'd,
And most pernitious purpose: Seeming, seeming.
I will proclaime thee Angelo, looke for't.
Signe me a present pardon for my brother,
Or with an out-stretcht throate Ile tell the world aloud
What man thou art.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Who will beleeue thee Isabell?
My vnsoild name, th' austeerenesse of my life,
My vouch against you, and my place i' th State,
Will so your accusation ouer-weigh,
That you shall stifle in your owne report,
And smell of calumnie. I haue begun,
And now I giue my sensuall race, the reine,
Fit thy consent to my sharpe appetite,
Lay by all nicetie, and prolixious blushes
That banish what they sue for: Redeeme thy brother,
By yeelding vp thy bodie to my will,
Or else he must not onelie die the death,
But thy vnkindnesse shall his death draw out
To lingring sufferance: Answer me to morrow,
Or by the affection that now guides me most,
Ile proue a Tirant to him. As for you,
Say what you can; my false, ore-weighs your true.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: To whom should I complaine? Did I tell this,
Who would beleeue me? O perilous mouthes
That beare in them, one and the selfesame tongue,
Either of condemnation, or approofe,
Bidding the Law make curtsie to their will,
Hooking both right and wrong to th' appetite,
To follow as it drawes. Ile to my brother,
Though he hath falne by prompture of the blood,
Yet hath he in him such a minde of Honor,
That had he twentie heads to tender downe
On twentie bloodie blockes, hee'ld yeeld them vp,
Before his sister should her bodie stoope,
To such abhord pollution.
Then Isabell liue chaste, and brother die;
"More then our Brother, is our Chastitie.
Ile tell him yet of Angelo's request,
And fit his minde to death, for his soules rest.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: So then you hope of pardon from Lord Angelo?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: The miserable haue no other medicine
But onely hope: I' haue hope to liue, and am prepar'd to die.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Be absolute for death: either death or life
Shall thereby be the sweeter. Reason thus with life:
If I do loose thee, I do loose a thing
That none but fooles would keepe: a breath thou art,
Seruile to all the skyie-influences,
That dost this habitation where thou keepst
Hourely afflict: Meerely, thou art deaths foole,
For him thou labourst by thy flight to shun,
And yet runst toward him still. Thou art not noble,
For all th' accommodations that thou bearst,
Are nurst by basenesse: Thou'rt by no meanes valiant,
For thou dost feare the soft and tender forke
Of a poore worme: thy best of rest is sleepe,
And that thou oft prouoakst, yet grosselie fearst
Thy death, which is no more. Thou art not thy selfe,
For thou exists on manie a thousand graines
That issue out of dust. Happie thou art not,
For what thou hast not, still thou striu'st to get,
And what thou hast forgetst. Thou art not certaine,
For thy complexion shifts to strange effects,
After the Moone: If thou art rich, thou'rt poore,
For like an Asse, whose backe with Ingots bowes;
Thou bearst thy heauie riches but a iournie,
And death vnloads thee; Friend hast thou none.
For thine owne bowels which do call thee, fire
The meere effusion of thy proper loines
Do curse the Gowt, Sapego, and the Rheume
For ending thee no sooner. Thou hast nor youth, nor age
But as it were an after-dinners sleepe
Dreaming on both, for all thy blessed youth
Becomes as aged, and doth begge the almes
Of palsied-Eld: and when thou art old, and rich
Thou hast neither heate, affection, limbe, nor beautie
To make thy riches pleasant: what's yet in this
That beares the name of life? Yet in this life
Lie hid moe thousand deaths; yet death we feare
That makes these oddes, all euen.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I humblie thanke you.
To sue to liue, I finde I seeke to die,
And seeking death, finde life: Let it come on.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What hoa? Peace heere; Grace, and good companie.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Who's there? Come in, the wish deserues a welcome.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Deere sir, ere long Ile visit you againe.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Most bolie Sir; I thanke you.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: My businesse is a word or two with Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: And verie welcom: looke Signior, here's your sister.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Prouost, a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: As manie as you please.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Bring them to heare me speak, where I may be conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Now sister, what's the comfort?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Why,
As all comforts are: most good, most good indeede,
Lord Angelo hauing affaires to heauen
Intends you for his swift Ambassador,
Where you shall be an euerlasting Leiger;
Therefore your best appointment make with speed,
To Morrow you set on.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Is there no remedie?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: None, but such remedie, as to saue a head
To cleaue a heart in twaine:

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: But is there anie?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Yes brother, you may liue;
There is a diuellish mercie in the Iudge,
If you'l implore it, that will free your life,
But fetter you till death.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Perpetuall durance?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: I iust, perpetuall durance, a restraint
Through all the worlds vastiditie you had
To a determin'd scope.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: But in what nature?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: In such a one, as you consenting too't,
Would barke your honor from that trunke you beare,
And leaue you naked.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Let me know the point.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Oh, I do feare thee Claudio, and I quake,
Least thou a feauorous life shouldst entertaine,
And six or seuen winters more respect
Then a perpetuall Honor. Dar'st thou die?
The sence of death is most in apprehension,
And the poore Beetle that we treade vpon
In corporall sufferance, finds a pang as great.
As when a Giant dies.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Why giue you me this shame?
Thinke you I can a resolution fetch
From flowrie tendernesse? If I must die,
I will encounter darknesse as a bride,
And hugge it in mine armes.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: There spake my brother: there my fathers graue
Did vtter forth a voice. Yes, thou must die:
Thou art too noble to conserue a life
In base appliances. This outward sainted Deputie,
Whose setled visagn, and deliberate word
Nips youth i' th head, and follies doth ^new
As Falcon doth the Fowle, is yet a diuell:
His filth within being cast, he would appeare
A pond, as deepe as hell.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: The prenzie, Angelo?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Oh 'tis the cunning Liuerie of hell,
The damnest bodie to inuest, and couer
In prenzie gardes; dost thou thinke Claudio,
If I would yeeld him my virginitie
Thou might'st be freed?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Oh heauens, it cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Yes, he would giu't thee; from this rank offence
So to offend him still. This night's the time
That I should do what I abhorre to name,
Or else thou diest to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Thou shalt not do't.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: O, were it but my life,
I'de throw it downe for your deliuerance
As frankely as a pin.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Thankes deere Isabell.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Be readie Claudio, for your death to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Yes. Has he affections in him,
That thus can make him bite the Law by th' nose,
When he would force it? Sure it is no sinne,
Or of the deadly seuen it is the least.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Which is the least?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: If it were damnable, he being so wise,
Why would he for the momentarie tricke
Be perdurablie fin'de? Oh Isabell.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: What saies my brother?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Death is a fearefull thing.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: And shamed life, a hatefull.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I, but to die, and go we know not where,
To lie in cold obstruction, and to rot,
This sensible warme motion, to become
A kneaded clod; And the delighted spirit
To bath in fierie floods, or to recide
In thrilling Region of thicke-ribbed Ice,
To be imprison'd in the viewlesse windes
And blowne with restlesse violence round about
The pendant world: or to be worse then worst
Of those, that lawlesse and incertaine thought,
Imagine howling, 'tis too horrible.
The weariest, and most loathed worldly life
That Age, Ache, periury, and imprisonment
Can lay on nature, is a Paradise
To what we feare of death.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Alas, alas.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Sweet Sister, let me liue.
What sinne you do, to saue a brothers life,
Nature dispenses with the deede so farre,
That it becomes a vertue.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Oh you beast,
Oh faithlesse Coward, oh dishonest wretch,
Wilt thou be made a man, out of my vice?
Is't not a kinde of Incest, to take life
From thine owne sisters shame? What should I thinke,
Heauen shield my Mother plaid my Father faire:
For such a warped slip of wildernesse
Nere issu'd from his blood. Take my defiance,
Die, perish: Might but my bending downe
Repreeue thee from thy fate, it should proceede.
Ile pray a thousand praiers for thy death,
No word to saue thee.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Nay heare me Isabell.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Oh fie, fie, fie:
Thy sinn's not accidentall, but a Trade;
Mercy to thee would proue it selfe a Bawd,
'Tis best that thou diest quickly.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Oh heare me Isabella.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Vouchsafe a word, yong sister, but one word.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: What is your Will.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Might you dispense with your leysure, I would by and by haue some speech with you: the satisfaction I would require, is likewise your owne benefit.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: I haue no superfluous leysure, my stay must be stolen out of other affaires: but I will attend you a while.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Son, I haue ouer-heard what hath past between you & your sister. Angelo had neuer the purpose to corrupt her; onely he hath made an assay of her vertue, to practise his iudgement with the disposition of natures. She (hauing the truth of honour in her) hath made him that gracious deniall, which he is most glad to receiue: I am Confessor to Angelo, and I know this to be true, therfore prepare your selfe to death: do not satisfie your resolution with hopes that are fallible, to morrow you must die, goe to your knees, and make ready.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Let me ask my sister pardon, I am so out of loue with life, that I will sue to be rid of it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Hold you there: farewell: Prouost, a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What's your will (father?)

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: That now you are come, you wil be gone: leaue me a while with the Maid, my minde promises with my habit, no losse shall touch her by my company.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: In good time.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: The hand that hath made you faire, hath made you good: the goodnes that is cheape in beauty, makes beauty briefe in goodnes; but grace being the soule of your complexion, shall keepe the body of it euer faire: the assault that Angelo hath made to you, Fortune hath conuaid to my vnderstanding; and but that frailty hath examples for his falling, I should wonder at Angelo: how will you doe to content this Substitute, and to saue your Brother?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I am now going to resolue him: I had rather my brother die by the Law, then my sonne should be vnlawfullie borne. But (oh) how much is the good Duke deceiu'd in Angelo: if euer he returne, and I can speake to him, I will open my lips in vaine, or discouer his gouernment.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: That shall not be much amisse: yet, as the matter now stands, he will auoid your accusation: he made triall of you onelie. Therefore fasten your eare on my aduisings, to the loue I haue in doing good; a remedie presents it selfe. I doe make my selfe beleeue that you may most vprighteously do a poor wronged Lady a merited benefit; redeem your brother from the angry Law; doe no staine to your owne gracious person, and much please the absent Duke, if peraduenture he shall euer returne to haue hearing of this businesse.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Let me heare you speake farther; I haue spirit to do any thing that appeares not fowle in the truth of my spirit.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Vertue is bold, and goodnes neuer fearefull: Haue you not heard speake of Mariana the sister of Fredericke the great Souldier, who miscarried at Sea?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: I haue heard of the Lady, and good words went with her name.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Shee should this Angelo haue married: was affianced to her oath, and the nuptiall appointed: between which time of the contract, and limit of the solemnitie, her brother Fredericke was wrackt at Sea, hauing in that perished vessell, the dowry of his sister: but marke how heauily this befell to the poore Gentlewoman, there she lost a noble and renowned brother, in his loue toward her, euer most kinde and naturall: with him the portion and sinew of her fortune, her marriage dowry: with both, her combynate-husband, this well-seeming Angelo.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Can this be so? did Angelo so leaue her?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Left her in her teares, & dried not one of them with his comfort: swallowed his vowes whole, pretending in her, discoueries of dishonor: in few, bestow'd her on her owne lamentation, which she yet weares for his sake: and he, a marble to her teares, is washed with them, but relents not.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What a merit were it in death to take this poore maid from the world? what corruption in this life, that it will let this man liue? But how out of this can shee auaile?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: It is a rupture that you may easily heale: and the cure of it not onely saues your brother, but keepes you from dishonor in doing it.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Shew me how (good Father.)

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: This fore-named Maid hath yet in her the continuance of her first affection: his vniust vnkindenesse (that in all reason should haue quenched her loue) hath (like an impediment in the Current) made it more violent and vnruly: Goe you to Angelo, answere his requiring with a plausible obedience, agree with his demands to the point: onely referre your selfe to this aduantage; first, that your stay with him may not be long: that the time may haue all shadow, and silence in it: and the place answere to conuenience: this being granted in course, and now followes all: wee shall aduise this wronged maid to steed vp your appointment, goe in your place: if the encounter acknowledge it selfe heereafter, it may compell him to her recompence; and heere, by this is your brother saued, your honor vntainted, the poore Mariana aduantaged, and the corrupt Deputy scaled. The Maid will I frame, and make fit for his attempt: if you thinke well to carry this as you may, the doublenes of the benefit defends the deceit from reproofe. What thinke you of it?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: The image of it giues me content already, and I trust it will grow to a most prosperous perfection.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: It lies much in your holding vp: haste you speedily to Angelo, if for this night he intreat you to his bed, giue him promise of satisfaction: I will presently to S. Lukes, there at the moated-Grange recides this deiected Mariana; at that place call vpon me, and dispatch with Angelo, that it may be quickly.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I thank you for this comfort: fare you well good father.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Nay, if there be no remedy for it, but that you will needes buy and sell men and women like beasts, we shall haue all the world drinke browne & white bastard.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Oh heauens, what stuffe is heere.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Twas neuer merry world since of two vsuries the merriest was put downe, and the worser allow'd by order of Law; a fur'd gowne to keepe him warme; and furd with Foxe and Lamb-skins too, to signifie, that craft being richer then Innocency, stands for the facing.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Come your way sir: blesse you good Father Frier.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: And you good Brother Father; what offence hath this man made you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Marry Sir, he hath offended the Law; and Sir, we take him to be a Theefe too Sir: for wee haue found vpon him Sir, a strange Pick-lock, which we haue sent to the Deputie.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Fie, sirrah, a Bawd, a wicked bawd,
The euill that thou causest to be done,
That is thy meanes to liue. Do thou but thinke
What 'tis to cram a maw, or cloath a backe
From such a filthie vice: say to thy selfe,
From their abhominable and beastly touches
I drinke, I eate away my selfe, and liue:
Canst thou beleeue thy liuing is a life,
So stinkingly depending? Go mend, go mend.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Indeed, it do's stinke in some sort, Sir:
But yet Sir I would proue.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Nay, if the diuell haue giuen thee proofs for sin
Thou wilt proue his. Take him to prison Officer:
Correction, and Instruction must both worke
Ere this rude beast will profit.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: He must before the Deputy Sir, he ha's giuen him warning: the Deputy cannot abide a Whore-master: if he be a Whore-monger, and comes before him, he were as good go a mile on his errand.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: That we were all, as some would seeme to bee
From our faults, as faults from seeming free.

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: His necke will come to your wast, a Cord sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I spy comfort, I cry baile: Here's a Gentleman, and a friend of mine.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: How now noble Pompey? What, at the wheels of Caesar? Art thou led in triumph? What is there none of Pigmalions Images newly made woman to bee had now, for putting the hand in the pocket, and extracting clutch'd? What reply? Ha? What saist thou to this Tune, Matter, and Method? Is't not drown'd i' th last raine? Ha? What saist thou Trot? Is the world as it was Man? Which is the vvay? Is it sad, and few words? Or how? The tricke of it?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Still thus, and thus: still vvorse?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: How doth my deere Morsell, thy Mistris? Procures she still? Ha?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Troth sir, shee hath eaten vp all her beefe, and she is her selfe in the tub.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Why 'tis good: It is the right of it: it must be so. Euer your fresh Whore; and your pouder'd Baud, an vnshun'd consequence, it must be so. Art going to prison Pompey?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Yes faith sir.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Why 'tis not amisse Pompey: farewell: goe say I sent thee thether: for debt Pompey? Or how?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: For being a baud; for being a baud.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Well, then imprison him: If imprisonment be the due of a baud, why 'tis his right. Baud is he doubtlesse, and of antiquity too. Baud borne. Farwell good Pompey: Commend me to the prison Pompey, you will turne good husband now Pompey, you vvill keepe the house.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I hope Sir, your good Worship wil be my baile?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: No indeed vvil I not Pompey, it is not the wear: I will pray (Pompey) to encrease your bondage if you take it not patiently: Why, your mettle is the more: Adieu trustie Pompey. Blesse you Friar.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: And you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Do's Bridge^
paint still, Pompey? Ha?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Come your waies sir, come.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: You will not baile me then Sir?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Then Pompey, nor now: what newes abroad Frier? What newes?

speeches.speaker: Elb.
prose: Come your waies sir, come.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Goe to kennell (Pompey) goe:
What newes Frier of the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I know none: can you tell me of any?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Some say he is with the Emperor of Russia: other some, he is in Rome: but where is he thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I know not where: but wheresoeuer, I wish him well.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: It was a mad fantasticall tricke of him to steale from the State, and vsurpe the beggerie hee was neuer borne to: Lord Angelo Dukes it well in his absence: he puts transgression too't.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: He do's well in't.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: A little more lenitie to Lecherie would doe no harme in him: Something too crabbed that way, Frier.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: It is too general a vice, and seueritie must cure it.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Yes in good sooth, the vice is of a great kindred; it is vvell allied, but it is impossible to extirpe it quite, Frier, till eating and drinking be put downe. They say this Angelo vvas not made by Man and Woman, after this downe-right vvay of Creation: is it true, thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: How should he be made then?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Some report, a Sea-maid spawn'd him. Some, that he vvas begot betweene two Stock-fishes. But it is certaine, that when he makes water, his Vrine is congeal'd ice, that I know to bee true: and he is a motion generatiue, that's infallible.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: You are pleasant sir, and speake apace.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Why, what a ruthlesse thing is this in him, for the rebellion of a Cod-peece, to take away the life of a man? Would the Duke that is absent haue done this? Ere he vvould haue hang'd a man for the getting a hundred Bastards, he vvould haue paide for the Nursing a thousand. He had some feeling of the sport; hee knew the seruice, and that instructed him to mercie.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I neuer heard the absent Duke much detected for Women, he was not enclin'd that vvay.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Oh Sir, you are deceiu'd.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: 'Tis not possible.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Who, not the Duke? Yes, your beggar of fifty: and his vse was, to put a ducket in her Clack-dish; the Duke had Crochets in him. Hee would be drunke too, that let me informe you.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: You do him wrong, surely.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir, I vvas an inward of his: a shie fellow vvas the Duke, and I beleeue I know the cause of his vvithdrawing.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: What (I prethee) might be the cause?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: No, pardon: 'Tis a secret must bee looke within the teeth and the lippes: but this I can let you vnderstand, the greater file of the subiect held the Duke to be vvise.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Wise? Why no question but he was.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: A very superficiall, ignorant, vnweighing fellow

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Either this is Enuie in you, Folly, or mistaking: The very streame of his life, and the businesse he hath helmed, must vppon a warranted neede, giue him a better proclamation. Let him be but testimonied in his owne bringings forth, and hee shall appeare to the enuious, a Scholler, a Statesman, and a Soldier: therefore you speake vnskilfully: or, if your knowledge bee more, it is much darkned in your malice.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir, I know him, and I loue him.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Loue talkes with better knowledge, & knowledge with deare loue.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Come Sir, I know what I know.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I can hardly beleeue that, since you know not what you speake. But if euer the Duke returne (as our praiers are he may) let mee desire you to make your answer before him: if it bee honest you haue spoke, you haue courage to maintaine it; I am bound to call vppon you, and I pray you your name?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir my name is Lucio, wel known to the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: He shall know you better Sir, if I may liue to report you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I feare you not.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: O, you hope the Duke will returne no more: or you imagine me to vnhurtfull an opposite: but indeed I can doe you little harme: You'll for-sweare this againe?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Ile be hang'd first: Thou art deceiu'd in mee Friar. But no more of this: Canst thou tell if Claudio die to morrow, or no?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Why should he die Sir?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Why? For filling a bottle with a Tunne-dish: I would the Duke we talke of were return'd againe: this vngenitur'd Agent will vn-people the Prouince with Continencie. Sparrowes must not build in his houseeeues, because they are lecherous: The Duke yet would haue darke deeds darkelie answered, hee would neuer bring them to light: would hee were return'd. Marrie this Claudio is condemned for vntrussing. Farwell good Friar, I prethee pray for me: The Duke (I say to thee againe) would eate Mutton on Fridaies. He's now past it, yet (and I say to thee) hee would mouth with a beggar, though she smelt browne-bread and Garlicke: say that I said so: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: No might, nor greatnesse in mortality
Can censure scape: Back-wounding calumnie
The whitest vertue strikes. What King so strong,
Can tie the gall vp in the slanderous tong?
But who comes heere?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Go, away with her to prison.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: Good my Lord be good to mee, your Honor is accounted a mercifull man: good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Double, and trebble admonition, and still forfeite in the same kinde? This would make mercy sweare and play the Tirant.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: A Bawd of eleuen yeares continuance, may it please your Honor.

speeches.speaker: Bawd.
prose: My Lord, this is one Lucio's information against me, Mistris Kate Keepe-downe was with childe by him in the Dukes time, he promis'd her marriage: his Childe is a yeere and a quarter olde come Philip and Iacob: I haue kept it my selfe; and see how hee goes about to abuse me.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: That fellow is a fellow of much License: Let him be call'd before vs. Away with her to prison: Goe too, no more words. Prouost, my Brother Angelo will not be alter'd, Claudio must die to morrow: Let him be furnish'd with Diuines, and haue all charitable preparation. If my brother wrought by my pitie, it should not be so with him.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: So please you, this Friar hath beene with him, and aduis'd him for th' entertainment of death.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Good'euen, good Father.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Blisse, and goodnesse on you.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Of whence are you?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Not of this Countrie, though my chance is now
To vse it for my time: I am a brother
Of gracious Order, late come from the Sea,
In speciall businesse from his Holinesse.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: What newes abroad i' th World?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: None, but that there is so great a Feauor on goodnesse, that the dissolution of it must cure it. Noueltie is onely in request, and as it is as dangerous to be aged in any kinde of course, as it is vertuous to be constant in any vndertaking. There is scarse truth enough aliue to make Societies secure, but Securitie enough to make Fellowships accurst: Much vpon this riddle runs the wisedome of the world: This newes is old enough, yet it is euerie daies newes. I pray you Sir, of what disposition was the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
verse: One, that aboue all other strifes,
Contended especially to know himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: What pleasure was he giuen to?

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: Rather reioycing to see another merry, then merrrie at anie thing which profest to make him reioice. A Gentleman of all temperance. But leaue wee him to his euents, with a praier they may proue prosperous, & let me desire to know, how you finde Claudio prepar'd? I am made to vnderstand, that you haue lent him visitation.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: He professes to haue receiued no sinister measure from his Iudge, but most willingly humbles himselfe to the determination of Iustice: yet had he framed to himselfe (by the instruction of his frailty) manie deceyuing promises of life, which I (by my good leisure) haue discredited to him, and now is he resolu'd to die.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: You haue paid the heauens your Function, and the prisoner the verie debt of your Calling. I haue labour'd for the poore Gentleman, to the extremest shore of my modestie, but my brother-Iustice haue I found so seuere, that he hath forc'd me to tell him, hee is indeede Iustice.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: If his owne life,
Answere the straitnesse of his proceeding,
It shall become him well: wherein if he chance to faile he hath sentenc'd himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Esc.
prose: I am going to visit the prisoner, Fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Peace be with you.
He who the sword of Heauen will beare,
Should be as holy, as seueare:
Patterne in himselfe to know,
Grace to stand, and Vertue go:
More, nor lesse to others paying,
Then by selfe-offences weighing.
Shame to him, whose cruell striking,
Kils for faults of his owne liking:
Twice trebble shame on Angelo,
To vveede my vice, and let his grow.
Oh, what may Man within him hide,
Though Angel on the outward side?
How may likenesse made in crimes,
Making practise on the Times,
To draw with ydle Spiders strings
Most ponderous and substantiall things?
Craft against vice, I must applie.
With Angelo to night shall lye
His old betroathed (but despised:)
So disguise shall by th' disguised
Pay with falshood, falfe exacting,
And performe an olde contracting.
Take, oh take those lips away, that so sweetly were for sworne,
And those eyes: the breake of day lights that doe mislead the Morne;
But my kisses bring againe, bring againe,
Seales of loue, but seal'd in vaine, seal'd in vaine.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Breake off thy song, and haste thee quick away,
Here comes a man of comfort, whose aduice
Hath often still'd my brawling discontent.
I cry you mercie, Sir, and well could wish
You had not found me here so musicall.
Let me excuse me, and beleeue me so,
My mirth it much displeas'd, but pleas'd my woe.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: 'Tis good; though Musick oft hath such a charme
To make bad, good; and good prouoake to harme.
prose: I pray you tell me, hath any body enquir'd for mee here to day; much vpon this time haue I promis'd here to meete.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: You haue not bin enquir'd after: I haue sat here all day.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: I doe constantly beleeue you: the time is come euen now. I shall craue your forbearance a little, may be I will call vpon you anone for some aduantage to your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I am alwayes bound to you.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Very well met, and well come:
What is the newes from this good Deputie?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: He hath a Garden circummur'd with Bricke,
Whose westerne side is with a Vineyard back't;
And to that Vineyard is a planched gate,
That makes his opening with this bigger Key:
This other doth command a little doore,
Which from the Vineyard to the Garden leades,
There haue I made my promise, vpon the
Heauy midle of the night, to call vpon him.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: But shall you on your knowledge find this way?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I haue t'ane a due, and wary note vpon't,
With whispering, and most guiltie diligence,
In action all of precept, he did show me
The way twice ore.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Are there no other tokens
Betweene you 'greed, concerning her obseruance?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: No: none but onely a repaire ith' darke,
And that I haue possest him, my most stay
Can be but briefe: for I haue made him know,
I haue a Seruant comes with me along
That staies vpon me; whose perswasion is,
I come about my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: 'Tis well borne vp.
I haue not yet made knowne to Mariana
A word of this: what hoa, within; come forth,
I pray you be acquainted with this Maid,
She comes to doe you good.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I doe desire the like.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Do you perswade your selfe that I respect you?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Good Frier, I know you do, and haue found it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Take then this your companion by the hand
Who hath a storie readie for your eare:
I shall attend your leisure, but make haste
The vaporous night approaches.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Wilt please you walke aside.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Oh Place, and greatnes: millions of false eies
Are stucke vpon thee: volumes of report
Run with these false, and most contrarious Quest
Vpon thy doings: thousand escapes of wit
Make thee the father of their idle dreame,
And racke thee in their fancies. Welcome, how agreed?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Shee'll take the enterprize vpon her father,
If you aduise it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: It is not my consent,
But my entreaty too.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
verse: Little haue you to say
When you depart from him, but soft and low,
Remember now my brother.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Feare me not.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Nor gentle daughter, feare you not at all:
He is your husband on a pre-contract:
To bring you thus together 'tis no sinne,
Sith that the Iustice of your title to him
Doth flourish the deceit. Come, let vs goe,
Our Corne's to reape, for yet our Tithes to sow.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Come hither sirha; can you cut off a mans head?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: If the man be a Bachelor Sir, I can:
But is he be a married man, he's his wiues head,
And I can neuer cut off a womans head.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Come sir, leaue me your snatches, and yeeld mee a direct answere. To morrow morning are to die Claudio and Barnardine: heere is in our prison a common executioner, who in his office lacks a helper, if you will take it on you to assist him, it shall redeeme you from your Gyues: if not, you shall haue your full time of imprisonment, and your deliuerance with an vnpittied whipping; for you haue beene a notorious bawd.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir, I haue beene an vnlawfull bawd, time out of minde, but yet I will bee content to be a lawfull hang-man: I would bee glad to receiue some instruction from my fellow partner.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What hoa, Abhorson: where's Abhorson there?

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Doe you call sir?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Sirha, here's a fellow will helpe you to morrow in your execution: if you thinke it meet, compound with him by the yeere, and let him abide here with you, if not, vse him for the present, and dismisse him, hee cannot plead his estimation with you: he hath beene a Bawd.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: A Bawd Sir? fie vpon him, he will discredit our mysterie.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Goe too Sir, you waigh equallie: a feather will turne the Scale.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Pray sir, by your good fauor: for surely sir, a good fauor you haue, but that you haue a hanging look: Doe you call sir, your occupation a Mysterie?

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: I Sir, a Misterie.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Painting Sir, I haue heard say, is a Misterie; and your Whores sir, being members of my occupation, vsing painting, do proue my Occupation, a Misterie: but what Misterie there should be in hanging, if I should be hang'd, I cannot imagine.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Sir, it is a Misterie.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Proofe.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Euerie true mans apparrell fits your Theefe.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: If it be too little for your theefe, your true man thinkes it bigge enough. If it bee too bigge for your Theefe, your Theefe thinkes it little enough: So euerie true mans apparrell fits your Theefe.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Are you agreed?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir, I will serue him: For I do finde your Hang-man is a more penitent Trade then your Bawd: he doth oftner aske forgiuenesse.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: You sirrah, prouide your blocke and your Axe to morrow, foure a clocke.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Come on (Bawd) I will instruct thee in my Trade: follow.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I do desire to learne sir: and I hope, if you haue occasion to vse me for your owne turne, you shall finde me y' are. For truly sir, for your kindnesse, I owe you a good turne.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Call hether Barnardine and Claudio:
Th' one has my pitie; not a iot the other,
Being a Murtherer, though he were my brother.
Looke, here's the Warrant Claudio, for thy death,
'Tis now dead midnight, and by eight to morrow
Thou must be made immortall. Where's Barnardine?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: As fast lock'd vp in sleepe, as guiltlesse labour,
When it lies starkely in the Trauellers bones,
He will not wake.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Who can do good on him?
Well, go, prepare your selfe. But harke, what noise?
Heauen giue your spirits comfort: by, and by,
I hope it is some pardon, or repreeue
For the most gentle Claudio. Welcome Father.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: The best, and wholsomst spirits of the night,
Inuellop you, good Prouost: who call'd heere of late?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: None since the Curphew rung.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Not Isabell?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: They will then er't be long.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: What comfort is for Claudio?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: There's some in hope.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: It is a bitter Deputie.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Not so, not so: his life is paralel'd
Euen with the stroke and line of his great Iustice:
He doth with holie abstinence subdue
That in himselfe, which he spurres on his powre
To qualifie in others: were he meal'd with that
Which he corrects, then were he tirrannous,
But this being so, he's iust. Now are they come.
This is a gentle Prouost, sildome when
The steeled Gaoler is the friend of men:
How now? what noise? That spirit's possest with hast,
That wounds th' vnsisting Posterne with these strokes.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: There he must stay vntil the Officer
Arise to let him in: he is call'd vp.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Haue you no countermand for Claudio yet?
But he must die to morrow?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: None Sir, none.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: As heere the dawning Prouost, as it is,
You shall heare more ere Morning.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Happely
You something know: yet I beleeue there comes
No countermand: no such example haue we:
Besides, vpon the verie siege of Iustice,
Lord Angelo hath to the publike eare
Profest the contrarie.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: This is his Lords man.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: And heere comes Claudio's pardon.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: My Lord hath sent you this note,
And by mee this further charge;
That you swerue not from the smallest Article of it,
Neither in time, matter, or other circumstance.
Good morrow: for as I take it, it is almost day.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I shall obey him.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: This is his Pardon purchas'd by such sin,
For which the Pardoner himselfe is in:
Hence hath offence his quicke celeritie,
When it is borne in high Authority.
When Vice makes Mercie; Mercie's so extended,
That for the faults loue, is th' offender friended.
Now Sir, what newes?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I told you:
Lord Angelo (be-like) thinking me remisse
In mine Office, awakens mee
With this vnwonted putting on, methinks strangely:
For he hath not vs'd it before.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Pray you let's heare.

Whatsoeuer you may heare to the contrary, let Claudio be executed by foure of the clocke, and in the afternoone Bernardine: For my better satisfaction, let mee haue Claudios head sent me by fiue. Let this be duely performed with a thought that more depends on it, then we must yet deliuer. Thus faile not to doe your Office, as you will answere it at your perill.
What say you to this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: What is that Barnardine, who is to be executed in th' afternoone?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: A Bohemian borne: But here nurst vp & bred,
One that is a prisoner nine yeeres old.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: How came it, that the absent Duke had not either deliuer'd him to his libertie, or executed him? I haue heard it was euer his manner to do so.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: His friends still wrought Repreeues for him: And indeed his fact till now in the gouernment of Lord Angelo, came not to an vndoubtfull proofe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: It is now apparant?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Most manifest, and not denied by himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Hath he borne himselfe penitently in prison?
How seemes he to be touch'd?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: A man that apprehends death no more dreadfully, but as a drunken sleepe, carelesse, wreaklesse, and fearelesse of what's past, present, or to come: insensible of mortality, and desperately mortall.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: He wants aduice.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: He wil heare none: he hath euermore had the liberty of the prison: giue him leaue to escape hence, hee would not. Drunke many times a day, if not many daies entirely drunke. We haue verie oft awak'd him, as if to carrie him to execution, and shew'd him a seeming warrant for it, it hath not moued him at all.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: More of him anon: There is written in your brow Prouost, honesty and constancie; if I reade it not truly, my ancient skill beguiles me: but in the boldnes of my cunning, I will lay my selfe in hazard: Claudio, whom heere you haue warrant to execute, is no greater forfeit to the Law, then Angelo who hath sentenc'd him. To make you vnderstand this in a manifested effect, I craue but foure daies respit: for the which, you are to do me both a present, and a dangerous courtesie.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Pray Sir, in what?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: In the delaying death.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Alacke, how may I do it? Hauing the houre limited, and an expresse command, vnder penaltie, to deliuer his head in the view of Angelo? I may make my case as Claudio's, to crosse this in the smallest.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: By the vow of mine Order, I warrant you,
If my instructions may be your guide,
Let this Barnardine be this morning executed,
And his head borne to Angelo.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Angelo hath seene them both,
And will discouer the fauour.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Oh, death's a great disguiser, and you may adde to it; Shaue the head, and tie the beard, and say it was the desire of the penitent to be so bar'de before his death: you know the course is common. If any thing fall to you vpon this, more then thankes and good fortune, by the Saint whom I professe, I will plead against it with my life.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Pardon me, good Father, it is against my oath.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Were you sworne to the Duke, or to the Deputie?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: To him, and to his Substitutes.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: You will thinke you haue made no offence, if the Duke auouch the iustice of your dealing?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: But what likelihood is in that?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Not a resemblance, but a certainty; yet since I see you fearfull, that neither my coate, integrity, nor perswasion, can with ease attempt you, I wil go further then I meant, to plucke all feares out of you. Looke you Sir, heere is the hand and Seale of the Duke: you know the Charracter I doubt not, and the Signet is not strange to you?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I know them both.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: The Contents of this, is the returne of the Duke; you shall anon ouer-reade it at your pleasure: where you shall finde within these two daies, he wil be heere. This is a thing that Angelo knowes not, for hee this very day receiues letters of strange tenor, perchance of the Dukes death, perchance entering into some Monasterie, but by chance nothing of what is writ. Looke, th' vnfolding Starre calles vp the Shepheard; put not your selfe into amazement, how these things should be; all difficulties are but easie vvhen they are knowne. Call your executioner, and off with Barnardines head: I will giue him a present shrift, and aduise him for a better place. Yet you are amaz'd, but this shall absolutely resolue you: Come away, it is almost cleere dawne.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose:
I am as well acquainted heere, as I was in our house of profession: one would thinke it vvere Mistris Ouer-dons owne house, for heere be manie of her olde Customers. First, here's yong Mr
Rash, hee's in for a commoditie of browne paper, and olde Ginger, nine score and seuenteene pounds, of which hee made fiue Markes readie money: marrie then, Ginger was not much in request, for the olde Women vvere all dead. Then is there heere one Mr
Caper, at the suite of Master Three-Pile the Mercer, for some foure suites of Peach-colour'd Satten, which now peaches him a beggar. Then haue vve heere, yong Dizie, and yong Mr
Deepe-vow, and Mr
Copperspurre, and Mr
Starue-Lackey the Rapier and dagger man, and yong Drop-heire that kild lustie Pudding, and Mr
Forthlight the Tilter, and braue Mr
Shootie the great Traueller, and wilde Halfe-Canne that stabb'd Pots, and I thinke fortie more, all great doers in our Trade, and are now for the Lords sake.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Sirrah, bring Barnardine hether.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose:
Mr
Barnardine, you must rise and be hang'd, Mr
Barnardine.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: What hoa Barnardine.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: A pox o' your throats: who makes that noyse there? What are you?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Your friends Sir, the Hangman:
You must be so good Sir to rise, and be put to death.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Away you Rogue, away, I am sleepie.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
verse: Tell him he must awake,
And that quickly too.

speeches.speaker: Clo:
prose: Pray Master Barnardine, awake till you are executed, and sleepe afterwards.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: Go in to him, and fetch him out.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: He is comming Sir, he is comming: I heare his Straw russle.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Is the Axe vpon the blocke, sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Verie readie Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: How now Abhorson?
What's the newes vvith you?

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Truly Sir, I would desire you to clap into your prayers: for looke you, the Warrants come.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You Rogue, I haue bin drinking all night,
I am not fitted for't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Oh, the better Sir: for he that drinkes all night, and is hanged betimes in the morning, may sleepe the sounder all the next day.

speeches.speaker: Abh.
prose: Looke you Sir, heere comes your ghostly Father: do we iest now thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Sir, induced by my charitie, and hearing how hastily you are to depart, I am come to aduise you, Comfort you, and pray with you.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Friar, not I: I haue bin drinking hard all night, and I will haue more time to prepare mee, or they shall beat out my braines with billets: I will not consent to die this day, that's certaine.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Oh sir, you must: and therefore I beseech you
Looke forward on the iournie you shall go.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: I sweare I will not die to day for anie mans perswasion.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: But heare you:

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Not a word: if you haue anie thing to say to me, come to my Ward: for thence will not I to day.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Vnfit to liue, or die: oh grauell heart.
After him (Fellowes) bring him to the blocke.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Now Sir, how do you finde the prisoner?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: A creature vnpre-par'd, vnmeet for death,
And to transport him in the minde he is,
Were damnable.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Heere in the prison, Father,
There died this morning of a cruell Feauor,
One Ragozine, a most notorious Pirate,
A man of Claudio's yeares: his beard, and head
Iust of his colour. What if we do omit
This Reprobate, til he were wel enclin'd,
And satisfie the Deputie with the visage
Of Ragozine, more like to Claudio?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Oh, 'tis an accident that heauen prouides:
Dispatch it presently, the houre drawes on
Prefixt by Angelo: See this be done,
And sent according to command, whiles I
Perswade this rude wretch willingly to die.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: This shall be done (good Father) presently:
But Barnardine must die this afternoone,
And how shall we continue Claudio,
To saue me from the danger that might come,
If he were knowne aliue?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Let this be done,
Put them in secret holds, both Barnardine and Claudio,
Ere twice the Sun hath made his iournall greeting
To yond generation, you shal finde
Your safetie manifested.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: I am your free dependant.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Quicke, dispatch, and send the head to Angelo
Now wil I write Letters to Angelo.
(The Prouost he shal beare them) whose contents
Shal witnesse to him I am neere at home:
And that by great Iniunctions I am bound
To enter publikely: him Ile desire
To meet me at the consecrated Fount,
A League below, the Citie: and from thence,
By cold gradation, and weale-ballanc'd forme.
We shal proceed with Angelo.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Heere is the head, Ile carrie it my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Conuenient is it: Make a swift returne,
For I would commune with you of such things,
That want no eare but yours.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Ile make all speede.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Peace hoa, be heere.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: The tongue of Isabell. She's come to know,
If yet her brothers pardon be come hither:
But I will keepe her ignorant of her good,
To make her heauenly comforts of dispaire,
