speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Oh sir, I did not looke so low. To conclude, this drudge or Diuiner layd claime to mee, call'd mee Dromio, swore I was assur'd to her, told me what priuie markes I had about mee, as the marke of my shoulder, the Mole in my necke, the great Wart on my left arme, that I amaz'd ranne from her as a witch. And I thinke, if my brest had not beene made of faith, and my heart of steele, she had transform'd me to a Curtull dog, & made me turne i' th wheele.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
verse: Go hie thee presently post to the rode,
And if the winde blow any way from shore,
I will not harbour in this Towne to night.
If any Barke put forth, come to the Mart,
Where I will walke till thou returne to me:
If euerie one knowes vs, and we know none,
'Tis time I thinke to trudge, packe, and be gone.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
verse: As from a Beare a man would run for life,
So flie I from her that would be my wife.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
verse: There's none but Witches do inhabite heere,
And therefore 'tis hie time that I were hence:
She that doth call me husband, euen my soule
Doth for a wife abhorre. But her faire sister
Possest with such a gentle soueraigne grace,
Of such inchanting presence and discourse,
Hath almost made me Traitor to my selfe:
But least my selfe be guilty to selfe wrong,
Ile stop mine eares against the Mermaids song.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose:
Mr
Antipholus.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: I that's my name.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I know it well sir, loe here's the chaine,
I thought to haue tane you at the Porpentine,
The chaine vnfinish'd made me stay thus long.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: What is your will that I shal do with this?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: What please your selfe sir: I haue made it for you.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Made it for me sir, I bespoke it not.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Not once, nor twice, but twentie times you haue:
Go home with it, and please your Wife withall,
And soone at supper time Ile visit you,
And then receiue my money for the chaine.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
verse: I pray you sir receiue the money now,
For feare you ne're see chaine, nor mony more.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: You are a merry man sir, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What I should thinke of this, I cannot tell:
But this I thinke, there's no man is so vaine,
That would refuse so faire an offer'd Chaine.
I see a man heere needs not liue by shifts,
When in the streets he meetes such Golden gifts:
Ile to the Mart, and there for Dromio stay,
If any ship put out, then straight away.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You know since Pentecost the sum is due,
And since I haue not much importun'd you,
Nor now I had not, but that I am bound
To Persia, and want Gilders for my voyage:
Therefore make present satisfaction,
Or Ile attach you by this Officer.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: Euen iust the sum that I do owe to you,
Is growing to me by Antipholus,
And in the instant that I met with you,
He had of me a Chaine, at fiue a clocke
I shall receiue the money for the same:
Pleaseth you walke with me downe to his house,
I will discharge my bond, and thanke you too.

speeches.speaker: Offi.
prose: That labour may you saue: See where he comes.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: While I go to the Goldsmiths house, go thou
And buy a ropes end, that will I bestow
Among my wife, and their confederates,
For locking me out of my doores by day:
But soft I see the Goldsmith; get thee gone,
Buy thou a rope, and bring it home to me.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: I buy a thousand pound a yeare, I buy a rope.

speeches.speaker: Eph. Am.
verse: A man is well holpe vp that trusts to you,
I promised your presence, and the Chaine,
But neither Chaine nor Goldsmith came to me:
Belike you thought our loue would last too long
If it were chain'd together: and therefore came not.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: Sauing your merrie humor: here's the note
How much your Chaine weighs to the vtmost charect,
The finenesse of the Gold, and chargefull fashion,
Which doth amount to three odde Duckets more
Then I stand debted to this Gentleman,
I pray you see him presently discharg'd,
For he is bound to Sea, and stayes but for it.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
verse: I am not furnish'd with the present monie:
Besides I haue some businesse in the towne,
Good Signior take the stranger to my house,
And with you take the Chaine, and bid my wife
Disburse the summe, on the receit thereof,
Perchance I will be there as soone as you.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: Then you will bring the Chaine to her your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: No beare it with you, least I come not time enough.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: Well sir, I will? Haue you the Chaine about you?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And if I haue not sir, I hope you haue:
Or else you may returne without your money.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: Nay come I pray you sir, giue me the Chaine:
Both winde and tide stayes for this Gentleman,
And I too blame haue held him heere too long.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
verse: Good Lord, you vse this dalliance to excuse
Your breach of promise to the Porpentine,
I should haue chid you for not bringing it,
But like a shrew you first begin to brawle.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: The houre steales on, I pray you sir dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: You heare how he importunes me, the Chaine.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why giue it to my wife, and fetch your mony.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: Come, come, you know I gaue it you euen now.
Either send the Chaine, or send me by some token.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Fie, now you run this humor out of breath,
Come where's the Chaine, I pray you let me see it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: My businesse cannot brooke this dalliance,
Good sir say, whe'r you'l answer me, or no:
If not, Ile leaue him to the Officer.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I answer you? What should I answer you.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: The monie that you owe me for the Chaine.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I owe you none, till I receiue the Chaine.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: You know I gaue it you halfe an houre since.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: You gaue me none, you wrong mee much to say so.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: You wrong me more sir in denying it.
Consider how it stands vpon my credit.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Well Officer, arrest him army suite.

speeches.speaker: Offi.
prose: I do, and charge you in the Dukes name to obey me.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: This touches me in reputation.
Either consent to pay this sum for me,
Or I attach you by this Officer.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Consent to pay thee that I never had:
Arrest me foolish fellow if thou dar'st.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: Heere is thy fee, arrest him Officer.
I would not spare my brother in this case,
If he should scorne me so apparantly.

speeches.speaker: Off^i^.
prose: I do arrest you sir, you heare the suite.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I do obey thee, till I giue thee baile.
But sirrah, you shall buy this sport as deere,
As all the mettall in your shop will answer.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: Sir, sir, I shall haue Law in Ephesus,
To your notorious shame, I doubt it not.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
verse: Master, there's a Barke of Epidamium,
That staies but till her Owner comes aboord,
And then sir she beares away. Our fraughtage sir,
I haue conuei'd aboord, and I haue bought
The Oyle, the Balsamum, and Aqua-vitae.
The ship is in her trim, the merrie winde
Blowes faire from land: they stay for nought at all,
But for their Owner, Master, and your selfe.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: How now? a Madman? Why thou peeuish sheep
What ship of Epidamium staies for me.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: A ship you sent me too, to hier waftage.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Thou drunken slaue, I sent thee for a rope,
And told thee to what purpose, and what end.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
verse: You sent me for a ropes end as soone,
You sent me to the Bay sir, for a Barke.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I will debate this matter at more leisure
And teach your eares to list me with more heede:
To Adriana Villaine hie thee straight:
Giue her this key, and tell her in the Deske
That's couer'd o're with Turkish Tapistrie,
There is a purse of Duckets, let her send it:
Tell her, I am arrested in the streete,
And that shall baile me: hie thee slaue, be gone,
On Officer to prison, till it come.

speeches.speaker: S. Dromio.
verse: To Adriana, that is where we din'd,
Where Dowsabell did claime me for her husband,
She is too bigge I hope for me to compasse,
Thither I must, although against my will:
For seruants must their Masters mindes fulfill.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Ah Luciana, did he tempt thee so?
Might'st thou perceiue austeerely in his eie,
That he did plead in earnest, yea or no:
Look'd he or red or pale, or sad or merrily?
What obseruation mad'st thou in this case?
Oh, his hearts Meteors tilting in his face.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: First he deni'de you had in him no right.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: He meant he did me none: the more my spight

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Then swore he that he was a stranger heere.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: And true he swore, though yet forsworne hee were.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Then pleaded I for you.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: And what said he?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: That loue I begg'd for you, he begg'd of me.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: With what perswasion did he tempt thy loue?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: With words, that in an honest suit might moue.
First, he did praise my beautie, then my speech.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Did'st speake him faire?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Haue patience I beseech.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: I cannot, nor I will not hold me still,
My tongue, though not my heart, shall have his will.
He is deformed, crooked, old, and sere,
Ill-fac'd, worse bodied, shapelesse euery where:
Vicious, vngentle, foolish, blunt, vnkinde,
Stigmaticall in making worse in minde.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Who would be iealous then of such a one?
No euill lost is wail'd, when it is gone.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Ah but I thinke him better then I say:
And yet would herein others eies were worse:
Farre from her nest the Lapwing cries away:
My heart praies for him, though my tongue doe curse.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Here goe: the deske, the purse, sweet now make haste.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: How hast thou lost thy breath?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: By running fast.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Where is thy Master Dromio? Is he well?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
verse: No, he's in Tartar limbo, worse then hell:
A diuell in an euerlasting garment hath him;
On whose hard heart is button'd vp with steele:
A Feind, a Fairie, pittilesse and ruffe:
A Wolfe, nay worse, a fellow all in buffe.
A back friend, a shoulder-clapper, one that counterma~ds
The passages of allies, creekes, and narrow lands:
A hound that runs Counter, and yet draws drifoot well,
One that before the Iudgme~t carries poore soules to hel.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Why man, what is the matter?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: I doe not know the matter, hee is rested on the case.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: What is he arrested? tell me at whose suite?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: I know not at whose suite he is arested well; but is in a suite of buffe which rested him, that can I tell, will you send him Mistris redemption, the monie in his deske.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Go fetch it Sister: this I wonder at.
Thus he vnknowne to me should be in debt:
Tell me, was he arested on a band?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
verse: Not on a band, but on a stronger thing:
A chaine, a chaine, doe you not here it ring.

speeches.speaker: Adria.
prose: What, the chaine?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
verse: No, no, the bell, 'tis time that I were gone:
It was two ere I left him, and now the clocke strikes one.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: The houres come backe, that did I neuer here.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Oh yes, if any houre meete a Serieant, a turnes backe for verie feare.

speeches.speaker: Adri.
prose: As if time were in debt: how fondly do'st thou reason?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
verse: Time is a verie bankerout, and owes more then he's worth to season.
Nay, he's a theefe too: haue you not heard men say,
That time comes stealing on by night and day?
If I be in debt and theft, and a Serieant in the way,
Hath he not reason to turne backe an houre in a day?

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Go Dromio, there's the monie, beare it straight,
And bring thy Master home imediately.
Come sister, I am prest downe with conceit:
Conceit, my comfort and my iniurie.
There's not a man I meete but doth salute me
As if I were their well acquainted friend,
And euerie one doth call me by my name:
Some tender monie to me, some inuite me;
Some other giue me thankes for kindnesses;
Some offer me Commodities to buy.
Euen now a' tailor cal'd me in his shop,
And show'd me Silkes that he had bought for me,
And therewithall tooke measure of my body.
Sure these are but imaginarie wiles,
And lapland Sorcerers inhabite here.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Master, here's the gold you sent me for: what haue you got the picture of old Adam new apparel'd?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: What gold is this? What Adam do'st thou meane?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Not that Adam that kept the Paradise: but that Adam that keepes the prison; hee that goes in the calues-skin, that was kil'd for the Prodigall: hee that came behinde you sir, like an euill angel, and bid you forsake your libertie.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I vnderstand thee not.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: No? why 'tis a plaine case: he that went like a Base-Viole in a case of leather; the man sir, that when gentlemen are tired giues them a sob, and rests them: he sir, that takes pittie on decaied men, and giues them suites of durance: he that sets vp his rest to doe more exploits with his Mace, then a Moris Pike.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: What thou mean'st an officer?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: I sir, the Serieant of the Band: he that brings any man to answer it that breakes his Band: one that thinkes a man alwaies going to bed, and saies, God giue you good rest.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Well sir, there rest in your foolerie:
Is there any ships puts forth to night? may we be gone?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Why sir, I brought you word an houre since, that the Barke Expedition put forth to night, and then were you hindred by the Serieant to tarry for the Hoy Delay: Here are the angels that you sent for to deliuer you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: The fellow is distract, and so am I,
And here we wander in illusions:
Some blessed power deliuer vs from hence.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Well met, well met, Master Antipholous:
I see sir you haue found the Gold-smith now:
Is that the chaine you promis'd me to day.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Sathan auoide, I charge thee tempt me not.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Master, is this Mistris Sathan?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: It is the diuell.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Nay, she is worse, she is the diuels dam: And here she comes in the habit of a light wench, and thereof comes, that the wenches say God dam me, That's as much to say, God make me a light wench: It is written. they appeare to men like angels of light, light is an effect of fire, and fire will burne: ergo, light wenches will burne, come not neere her.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Your man and you are maruailous merrie sir.
Will you goe with me, wee'll mend our dinner here?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Master, if do expect spoon-meate, or bespeake a long spoone.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why Dromio?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Marrie he must haue a long spoone that must eate with the diuell.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Auoid then fiend, what tel'st thou me of supping?
Thou art, as you are all a sorceresse:
I coniure thee to leaue me, and be gon.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Giue me the ring of mine you had at dinner,
Or for my Diamond the Chaine you promis'd,
And Ile be gone sir, and not trouble you.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose:
Some diuels aske but the parings of ones naile,

a rush, a haire, a drop of blood, a pin, a nut, a cherriestone: but she more couetous, wold haue a chaine: Master be wise, and if you giue it her, the diuell will shake her Chaine, and fright vs with it.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: I pray you sir my Ring, or else the Chaine,
I hope you do not meane to cheate me so?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Auant thou witch: Come Dromio let vs go.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Flie pride saies the Pea-cocke, Mistris that you know.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Now out of doubt Antipholus is mad,
Else would he neuer so demeane himselfe,
A Ring he hath of mine worth fortie Duckets,
And for the same he promis'd me a Chaine,
Both one and other he denies me now:
The reason that I gather he is mad,
Besides this present instance of his rage,
Is a mad tale he told to day at dinner,
Of his owne doores being shut against his entrance.
Belike his wife acquainted with his fits,
On purpose shut the doores against his way:
My way is now to hie home to his house,
And tell his wife, that being Lunaticke,
He rush'd into my house, and tooke perforce
My Ring away. This course I fittest choose,
For fortie Duckets is too much to loose.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Feare me not man, I will not breake away,
Ile giue thee ere I leaue thee so much money
To warrant thee as I am rested for.
My wife is in a wayward moode to day,
And will not lightly trust the Messenger,
That I should be attach'd in Ephesus,
I tell you 'twill sound harshly in her eares.
Heere comes my Man, I thinke he brings the monie.
How now sir? Haue you that I sent you for?

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: Here's that I warrant you will pay them all.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: But where's the Money?

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: Why sir, I gaue the Monie for the Rope.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Fiue hundred Duckets villaine for a rope?

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: Ile serue you sir fiue hundred at the rate.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: To what end did I bid thee hie thee home?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: To a ropes end sir, and to that end am I return'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: And to that end sir, I will welcome you.

speeches.speaker: Offi.
prose: Good sir be patient.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: Nay 'tis for me to be patient, I am in aduersitie.

speeches.speaker: Offi.
prose: Good now hold thy tongue.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: Nay, rather perswade him to hold his hands.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Thou whoreson senselesse Villaine.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: I would I were senselesse sir, that I might not feele your blowes.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Thou art sensible in nothing but blowes, and so is an Asse.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: I am an Asse indeede, you may prooue it by my long eares. I haue serued him from the houre of my Natiuitie to this instant, and haue nothing at his hands for my seruice but blowes. When I am cold, he heates me with beating: when I am warme, he cooles me with beating: I am wak'd with it when I sleepe, rais'd with it when I sit, driuen out of doores with it when I goe from home, welcom'd home with it when I returne, nay I beare it on my shoulders, as a begger woont her brat: and I thinke when he hath lam'd me, I shall begge with it from doore to doore.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Come goe along, my wife is comming yonder.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: Mistris respice finem, respect your end, or rather the prophesie like the Parrat, beware the ropes end.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Wilt thou still talke?

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose: How say you now? Is not your husband mad?

speeches.speaker: Adri.
verse: His inciuility confirmes no lesse:
Good Doctor Pinch, you are a Coniurer,
Establish him in his true sence againe,
And I will please you what you will demand.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Alas how fiery, and how sharpe he lookes.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Marke, how he trembles in his extasie.

speeches.speaker: Pinch.
prose: Giue me your hand, and let mee feele your pulse.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: There is my hand, and let it feele your eare.

speeches.speaker: Pinch.
verse: I charge thee Sathan, hous'd within this man,
To yeeld possession to my holie praiers,
And to thy state of darknesse hie thee straight,
I coniure thee by all the Saints in heauen.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Peace doting wizard, peace; I am not mad.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Oh that thou wer't not, poore distressed soule.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
verse: You Minion you, are these your Customers?
Did this Companion with the saffron face
Reuell and feast it at my house to day,
Whil'st vpon me the guiltie doores were shut,
And I denied to enter in my house.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: O husband, God doth know you din'd at home
Where would you had remain'd vntill this time,
Free from these slanders, and this open shame.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Din'd at home? Thou Villaine, what sayest thou?

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Sir sooth to say, you did not dine at home.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Were not my doores lockt vp, and I shut out?

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Perdie, your doores were lockt, and you shut out.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: And did not she her selfe reuile me there?

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Sans Fable, she her selfe reuil'd you there.

speeches.speaker: Anti.
prose: Did not her Kitchen maide raile, taunt, and scorne me?

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Certis she did, the kitchin vestall scorn'd you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: And did not I in rage depart from thence?

speeches.speaker: Dro.
verse: In veritie you did, my bones beares witnesse,
That since haue felt the vigor of his rage.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Is't good to sooth him in these crontraries?

speeches.speaker: Pinch.
verse: It is no shame, the fellow finds his vaine,
And yeelding to him, humors well his frensie.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Thou hast subborn'd the Goldsmith to arrest mee.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Alas, I sent you Monie to redeeme you,
By Dromio heere, who came in hast for it.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
verse: Monie by me? Heart and good will you might,
But surely Master not a ragge of Monie.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Wentst not thou to her for a purse of Duckets.

speeches.speaker: Adri.
prose: He came to me, and I deliuer'd it.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: And I am witnesse with her that she did:

speeches.speaker: Dro.
verse: God and the Rope-maker beare me witnesse,
That I was sent for nothing but a rope.

speeches.speaker: Pinch.
verse: Mistris, both Man and Master is possest,
I know it by their pale and deadly lookes,
They must be bound and laide in some darke roome.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Say wherefore didst thou locke me forth to day,
And why dost thou denie the bagge of gold?

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: I did not gentle husband locke thee forth.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
verse: And gentle Mr I receiu'd no gold:
But I confesse sir, that we were lock'd out.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Dissembling Villain, thou speak'st false in both

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Dissembling harlot, thou art false in all,
And art confederate with a damned packe,
To make a loathsome abiect scorne of me:
But with these nailes, Ile plucke out these false eyes,
That would behold in me this shamefull sport.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Oh binde him, binde him, let him not come neere me.

speeches.speaker: Pinch.
prose: More company, the fiend is strong within him

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Aye me poore man, how pale and wan he looks.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What will you murther me, thou Iailor thou?
I am thy prisoner, wilt thou suffer them to make a rescue?

speeches.speaker: Offi.
prose: Masters let him go: he is my prisoner, and you shall not haue him.

speeches.speaker: Pinch.
prose: Go binde this man, for he is franticke too.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: What wilt thou do, thou peeuish Officer?
Hast thou delight to see a wretched man
Do outrage and displeasure to himselfe?

speeches.speaker: Offi.
verse: He is my prisoner, if I let him go,
The debt he owes will be requir'd of me.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: I will discharge thee ere I go from thee,
Beare me forthwith vnto his Creditor,
And knowing how the debt growes I will pay it.
Good Master Doctor see him safe conuey'd
Home to my house, oh most vnhappy day.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Oh most vnhappie strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Master, I am heere entred in bond for you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Out on thee Villaine, wherefore dost thou mad mee?

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Will you be bound for nothing, be mad good Master, cry the diuell.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: God helpe poore soules, how idlely doe they talke.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Go beare him hence, sister go you with me:
Say now, whose suite is he arrested at?

speeches.speaker: Off.
prose: One Angelo a Goldsmith, do you know him?

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: I know the man: what is the summe he owes?

speeches.speaker: Off.
prose: Two hundred Duckets.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Say, how growes it due.

speeches.speaker: Off.
prose: Due for a Chaine your husband had of him.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: He did bespeake a Chain for me, but had it not.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: When as your husband all in rage to day.
Came to my house, and tooke away my Ring,
The Ring I saw vpon his finger now,
Straight after did I meete him with a Chaine.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: It may be so, but I did neuer see it.
Come Iailor, bring me where the Goldsmith is,
I long to know the truth heereof at large.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: God for thy mercy, they are loose againe.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: And come with naked swords,
Let's call more helpe to haue them bound againe.

speeches.speaker: Off.
prose: Away, they'l kill vs.

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
prose: I see these Witches are affraid of swords.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: She that would be your wife, now ran from you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Come to the Centaur, fetch our stuffe from thence:
I long that we were safe and sound aboord.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: Faith stay heere this night, they will surely do vs no harme: you saw they speake vs faire, giue vs gold: me thinkes they are such a gentle Nation, that but for the Mountaine of mad flesh that claimes mariage of me, I could finde in my heart to stay heere still, and turne Witch.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I will not stay to night for all the Towne,
Therefore away, to get our stuffe aboord.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: I am sorry Sir that I haue hindred you,
But I protest he had the Chaine of me,
Though most dishonestly he doth denie it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: How is the man esteem'd heere in the Citie?

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: Of very reuerent reputation sir,
Of credit infinite, highly belou'd,
Second to none that liues heere in the Citie:
His word might beare my wealth at any t^me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Speake softly, yonder as I thinke he walkes.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: 'Tis so: and that selfe chaine about his necke,
Which he forswore most monstrously to haue.
Good sir draw neere to me, Ile speake to him:
Signior Antipholus, I wonder much
That you would put me to this shame and trouble,
And not without some scandall to your selfe,
With circumstance and oaths, so to denie
This Chaine, which now you weare so openly.
Beside the charge, the shame, imprisonment,
You haue done wrong to this my honest friend,
Who but for staying on our Controuersie,
Had hoisted saile, and put to sea to day:
This Chaine you had of me, can you deny it?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I thinke I had, I neuer did deny it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Yes that you did sir, and forswore it too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Who heard me to denie it or forsweare it?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: These eares of mine thou knowst did hear thee:
Fie on thee wretch, 'tis pitty that thou liu'st
To walke where any honest men resort.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Thou art a Villaine to impeach me thus,
Ile proue mine honor, and mine honestie
Against thee presently, if thou dar'st stand:

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I dare and do defie thee for a villaine.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Hold, hurt him not for God sake, he is mad,
Some get within him, take his sword away:
Binde Dromio too, and beare them to my house.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
verse: Runne master run, for Gods sake take a house,
This is some Priorie, in, or we are spoyl'd.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: Be quiet people, wherefore throng you hither?

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: To fetch my poore distracted husband hence,
Let vs come in, that we may binde him fast,
And beare him home for his recouerie.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: I knew he vvas not in his perfect wits.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I am sorry now that I did draw on him.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: How long hath this possession held the man.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: This weeke he hath beene heauie, sower sad,
And much different from the man he was:
But till this afternoone his passion
Ne're brake into extremity of rage.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
verse: Hath he not lost much wealth by wrack of sea,
Buried some deere friend, hath not else his eye
Stray'd his affection in vnlawfull loue,
A sinne preuailing much in youthfull men,
Who giue their eies the liberty of gazing.
Which of these sorrowes is he subiect too?

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: To none of these, except it be the last,
Namely, some loue that drew him oft from home.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: You should for that haue reprehended him.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Why so I did.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: I but not rough enough.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: As roughly as my modestie would let me.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: Haply in priuate.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: And in assemblies too.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: I, but not enough.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: It was the copie of our Conference.
In bed he slept not for my vrging it,
At boord he fed not for my vrging it:
Alone, it was the subiect of my Theame:
In company I often glanced it:
Still did I tell him, it was vilde and bad.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
verse: And thereof came it, that the man was mad.
The venome clamors of a iealous woman,
Poisons more deadly then a mad dogges tooth.
It seemes his sleepes were hindred by thy railing,
And thereof comes it that his head is light.
Thou saist his meate was sawc'd with thy vpbraidings,
Vnquiet meales make ill digestions,
Thereof the raging fire of feauer bred,
And what's a Feauer, but a fit of madnesse?
Thou sayest his sports were hindred by thy bralles.
Sweet recreation barr'd, what doth ensue
But moodie and dull melancholly,
Kinsman to grim and comfortlesse dispaire,
And at her heeles a huge infectious troope
Of pale distemperatures, and foes to life?
In food, in sport, and life-preseruing rest
To be disturb'd, would mad or man, or beast:
The consequence is then, thy iealous fits
Hath scar'd thy husband from the vse of wits.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: She neuer reprehended him but mildely,
When he demean'd himselfe, rough, rude, and wildly,
Why beare you these rebukes, and answer not?

speeches.speaker: Adri.
verse: She did betray me to my owne reproofe,
Good people enter, and lay hold on him.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: No, not a creature enters in my house.

speeches.speaker: Ad.
prose: Then let your seruants bring my husband forth

speeches.speaker: Ab.
verse: Neither: he tooke this place for sanctuary,
And it shall priuiledge him from your hands,
Till I haue brought him to his wits againe,
Or loose my labour in assaying it.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: I will attend my husband, be his nurse,
Diet his sicknesse, for it is my Office,
And will haue no atturney but my selfe,
And therefore let me haue him home with me.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
verse: Be patient, for I will not let him stirre,
Till I haue vs'd the approoued meanes I haue,
With wholsome sirrups, drugges, and holy prayers
To make of him a formall man againe:
It is a branch and parcell of mine oath,
A charitable dutie of my order,
Therefore depart, and leaue him heere with me.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: I will not hence, and leaue my husband heere:
And ill it doth beseeme your holinesse
To separate the husband and the wife.

speeches.speaker: Ab.
prose: Be quiet and depart, thou shalt not haue him.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Complaine vnto the Duke of this indignity.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Come go, I will fall prostrate at his feete,
And neuer rise vntill my teares and prayers
Haue won his grace to come in person hither,
And take perforce my husband from the Abbesse.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: By this I thinke the Diall points at fiue:
Anon I' me sure the Duke himselfe in person
Comes this way to the melancholly vale;
The place of depth, and sorrie execution,
Behinde the ditches of the Abbey heere.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: Vpon what cause?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To see a reuerent Siracusian Merchant,
Who put vnluckily into this Bay
Against the Lawes and Statutes of this Towne,
Beheaded publikely for his offence.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: See where they come, we wil behold his death.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Kneele to the Duke before he passe the Abbey.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Yet once againe proclaime it publikely,
If any friend will pay the summe for him,
He shall not die, so much we tender him.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Iustice most sacred Duke against the Abbesse.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: She is a vertuous and a reuerend Lady,
It cannot be that she hath done thee wrong.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: May it please your Grace, Antipholus my husba~d,
Who I made Lord of me, and all I had,
At your important Letters this ill day,
A most outragious fit of madnesse tooke him:
That desp'rately he hurried through the streete,
With him his bondman, all as mad as he,
Doing displeasure to the Citizens,
By rushing in their houses: bearing thence
Rings, Iewels, any thing his rage did like.
Once did I get him bound, and sent him home,
Whil'st to take order for the wrongs I went,
That heere and there his furie had committed,
Anon I wot not, by what strong escape
He broke from those that had the guard of him,
And with his mad attendant and himselfe,
Each one with irefull passion, with drawne swords
Met vs againe, and madly bent on vs
Chac'd vs away: till raising of more aide
We came againe to binde them: then they fled
Into this Abbey, whether we pursu'd them,
And heere the Abbesse shuts the gates on vs,
And will not suffer vs to fetch him out,
Nor send him forth, that we may beare him hence.
Therefore most gracious Duke with thy command,
Let him be brought forth, and borne hence for helpe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Long since thy husband seru'd me in my wars
And I to thee ingag'd a Princes word,
When thou didst make him Master of thy bed,
To do him all the grace and good I could.
Go some of you, knocke at the Abbey gate,
And bid the Lady Abbesse come to me:
I will determine this before I stirre.
Oh Mistris, Mistris, shift and saue your selfe,
My Master and his man are both broke loose,
Beaten the Maids a-row, and bound the Doctor,
Whose beard they haue sindg'd off with brands of fire,
And euer as it blaz'd, they threw on him
Great pailes of puddled myre to quench the haire;
My Mr preaches patience to him, and the while
His man with Cizers nickes him like a foole:
And sure (vnlesse you send some present helpe)
Betweene them they will kill the Coniurer.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Peace foole, thy Master and his man are here,
And that is false thou dost report to vs.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Mistris, vpon my life I tel you true,
I haue not breath'd almost since I did see it.
He cries for you, and vowes if he can take you,
To scorch your face, and to disfigure you:
Harke, harke, I heare him Mistris: flie, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Come stand by me, feare nothing: guard with Halberds.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: Ay me, it is my husband: witnesse you,
That he is borne about inuisible,
Euen now we hous'd him in the Abbey heere.
And now he's there, past thought of humane reason.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
verse: Iustice most gracious Duke, oh grant me iustice,
Euen for the seruice that long since I did thee,
When I be^rid thee in the warres, and tooke
Deepe scarres to saue thy life; euen for the blood
That then I lost for thee, now grant me iustice.

speeches.speaker: Mar. Fat.
prose: Vnlesse the feare of death doth make me dore, I see my sonne Antipholus and Dromio.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
verse: Iustice (sweet Prince) against yt Woman there:
She whom thou gau'st to me to be my wife;
That hath abused and dishonored me,
Euen in the strength and height of iniurie:
Beyond imagination is the wrong
That she this day hath shamelesse throwne on me.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Discouer how, and thou shalt finde me iust.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
verse: This day (great Duke) she shut the doores vpon me,
While she with Harlots feasted in my house.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: A greeuous fault: say woman, didst thou so?

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: No my good Lord. My selfe, he, and my sister,
To day did dine together: so befall my soule,
As this is false he burthens me withall.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Nere may I looke on day, nor sleepe on night,
But she tels to your Highnesse simple truth.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: O periur'd woman! They are both forsworne,
In this the Madman iustly chargeth them.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
verse: My Liege, I am aduised what I say,
Neither disturbed with the effect of Wine,
Nor headie-rash prouoak'd with raging ire,
Albeit my wrongs might make one wiser mad.
This woman lock'd me out this day from dinner;
That Goldsmith there, were he not pack'd with her,
Could witnesse it: for he was with me then,
Who parted with me to go fetch a Chaine,
Promising to bring it to the Porpentine,
Where Balthasar and I did dine together.
Our dinner done, and he not comming thither,
I went to seeke him. In the street I met him,
And in his companie that Gentleman.
There did this periur'd Goldsmith sweare me downe,
That I this day of him receiu'd the Chaine,
Which God he knowes, I saw not. For the which,
He did arrest me with an Officer.
I did obey, and sent my Pesant home
For certaine Duckets: he with none return'd.
Then fairely I bespoke the Officer
To go in person with me to my house.
By 'th 'way, we met my wife, her sister, and a rabble more
Of vilde Confederates: Along with them
They brought one Pinch, a hungry leane-fac'd Villaine;
A meere Anatomie, a Mountebanke,
A thred-bare Iugler, and a Fortune-teller,
A needy-hollow-ey'd-sharpe-looking-wretch;
A liuing dead man. This pernicious slaue,
Forsooth tooke on him as a Coniurer:
And gazing in mine eyes, feeling my pulse,
And with no-face (as 'twere) out-facing me,
Cries out, I was possest. Then altogether
They fell vpon me, bound me, bore me thence,
And in a darke and dankish vault at home
There left me and my man, both bound together,
Till gnawing with my teeth my bonds in sunder,
I gain'd my freedome; and immediately
Ran hether to your Grace, whom I beseech
To giue me ample satisfaction
For these deepe shames, and great indignities.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: My Lord, in truth, thus far I witnes with him:
That he din'd not at home, but was lock'd out.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: But had he such a Chaine of thee, or no?

speeches.speaker: Gold.
verse: He had my Lord, and when he ran in heere,
These people saw the Chaine about his necke.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Besides, I will be sworne these eares of mine,
Heard you confesse you had the Chaine of him,
After you first forswore it on the Mart,
And thereupon I drew my sword on you:
And then you fled into this Abbey heere,
From whence I thinke you are come by Miracle.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
verse: I neuer came within these Abbey wals,
Nor euer didst thou draw thy sword on me:
I neuer saw the Chaine, so helpe me heauen:
And this is false you burthen me withall.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Why what an intricate impeach is this?
I thinke you all haue drunke of Circes cup:
If heere you hous'd him, heere he would haue bin.
If he were mad, he would not pleade so coldly:
You say he din'd at home, the Goldsmith heere
Denies that saying. Sirra, what say you?

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: Sir he din'de with her there, at the Porpentine.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: He did, and from my finger snacht that Ring.

speeches.speaker: E. Anti.
prose: Tis true (my Liege) this Ring I had of her.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Saw'st thou him enter at the Abbey heere?

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose: As sure (my Liege) as I do see your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Why this is straunge: Go call the Abbesse hither.
I thinke you are all mated, or starke mad.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Most mighty Duke, vouchsafe me speak a word:
Haply I see a friend will saue my life,
And pay the sum that may deliuer me.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Speake freely Siracusian what thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Is not your name sir call'd Antipholus?
And is not that your bondman Dromio?

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
verse: Within this houre I was his bondman sir,
But he I thanke him gnaw'd in two my cords,
Now am I Dromio, and his man, vnbound.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
prose: I am sure you both of you remember me.

speeches.speaker: Dro.
verse: Our selues we do remember sir by you:
For lately we were bound as you are now.
You are not Pinches patient, are you sir?

speeches.speaker: Father.
prose: Why looke you strange on me? you know me well.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
prose: I neuer saw you in my life till now.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Oh! griefe hath chang'd me since you saw me last,
And carefull houres with times deformed hand,
Haue written strange defeatures in my face:
But tell me yet, dost thou not know my voice?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Neither.

speeches.speaker: Fat.
prose: Dromio, nor thou?

speeches.speaker: Dro.
prose: No trust me sir, nor I.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: I am sure thou dost?

speeches.speaker: E. Dromio.
prose: I sir, but I am sure I do not, and whatsoeuer a man denies, you are now bound to beleeue him.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Not know my voice, oh times e^tremity
Hast thou so crack'd and splitted my poore tongue
In seuen short yeares, that heere my onely sonne
Knowes not my feeble key of vntun'd cares?
Though now this grained face of mine be hid
In sap-consuming Winters drizled snow,
And all the Conduits of my blood froze vp:
Yet hath my night of life some memorie:
My wasting lampes some fading glimmer left;
My dull deafe eares a little vse to heare:
All these old witnesses, I cannot erre.
Tell me, thou art my sonne Antipholus.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I neuer saw my Father in my life.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: But seuen yeares since, in Siracusa boy
Thou know'st we parted, but perhaps my sonne,
Thou sham'st to acknowledge me in miserie.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: The Duke, and all that know me in the City,
Can witnesse with me that it is not so.
I ne're saw Siracusa in my life.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I tell thee Siracusian, twentie yeares
Haue I bin Patron to Antipholus,
During which time, he ne're saw Siracusa:
I see thy age and dangers make thee dote.

speeches.speaker: Abbesse.
prose: Most mightie Duke, behold a man much wrong'd.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: I see two husbands, or mine eyes deceiue me.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: One of these men is genius to the other:
And so of these, which is the naturall man,
And which the spirit? Who deciphers them?

speeches.speaker: S. Dromio.
prose: I Sir am Dromio, command him away.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: I Sir am Dromio, pray let me stay.

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
prose: Egeon art thou not? or else his ghost.

speeches.speaker: S. Drom.
prose: Oh my olde Master, who hath bound him heere?

speeches.speaker: Abb.
verse: Who euer bound him, I will lose his bonds,
And gaine a husband by his libertie:
Speake olde Egeon, if thou bee'st the man
That hadst a wife once call'd Aemilia,
That bore thee at a burthen two faire sonnes?
Oh if thou bee'st the same Egeon, speake:
And speake vnto the same Aemilia.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Why heere begins his Morning storie right:
These two Antipholus, these two so like,
And these two Dromio's, one in semblance:
Besides her vrging of her wracke at sea,
These are the parents to these children,
Which accidentally are met together.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: If I dreame not, thou art Aemilia,
If thou art she, tell me, where is that sonne
That floated with thee on the fatall rafte.

speeches.speaker: Abb.
verse: By men of Epidamium, he, and I,
And the twin Dromio, all were taken vp;
But by and by, rude Fishermen of Corinth
By force tooke Dromio, and my sonne from them,
And me they left with those of Epidamium.
What then became of them, I cannot tell:
I, to this fortune that you see mee in.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Antipholus thou cam'st from Corinth first.

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
prose: No sir, not I, I came from Siracuse.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Stay, stand apart, I know not which is which.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
prose: I came from Corinth my most gracious Lord

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: And I with him.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
verse: Brought to this Town by that most famous Warriour,
Duke Menaphon, your most renowned Vnckle.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: Which of you two did dine with me to day?

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
prose: I, gentle Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
prose: And are not you my husband?

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
prose: No, I say nay to that.

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
verse: And so do I, yet did she call me so:
And this faire Gentlewoman her sister heere
Did call me brother. What I told you then,
I hope I shall haue leisure to make good,
If this be not a dreame I see and heare.

speeches.speaker: Goldsmith.
prose: That is the Chaine sir, which you had of mee.

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
prose: I thinke it be sir, I denie it not.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
prose: And you sir for this Chaine arrested me.

speeches.speaker: Gold.
prose: I thinke I did sir, I deny it not.

speeches.speaker: Adr.
verse: I sent you monie sir to be your baile
By Dromio, but I thinke he brought it not.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: No, none by me.

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
verse: This purse of Duckets I receiu'd from you,
And Dromio my man did bring them me:
I see we still did meete each others man,
And I was tane for him, and he for me,
And thereupon these errors are arose.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
prose: These Duckets pawne I for my father heere.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: It shall not neede, thy father hath his life.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Sir I must haue that Diamond from you.

speeches.speaker: E. Ant.
prose: There take it, and much thanks for my good cheere.

speeches.speaker: Abb.
verse: Renowned Duke, vouchsafe to take the paines
To go with vs into the Abbey heere,
And heare at large discoursed all our fortunes,
And all that are assembled in this place:
That by this simpathized one daies error
Haue suffer'd wrong. Goe, keepe vs companie,
And we shall make full satisfaction.
Thirtie three yeares haue I but gone in trauaile
Of you my sonnes, and till this present houre
My heauie burthen are deliuered:
The Duke my husband, and my children both,
And you the Kalenders of their Natiuity,
Go to a Gossips feast, and go with mee,
After so long greefe such Natiuitie.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: With all my heart, Ile Gossip at this feast.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Mast. shall I fetch your stuffe from shipbord?

speeches.speaker: E. An.
prose: Dromio, what stuffe of mine hast thou imbarkt

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Your goods that lay at host sir in the Centaur.

speeches.speaker: S. Ant.
verse: He speakes to me, I am your master Dromio.
Come go with vs, wee'l looke to that anon,
Embrace thy brother there, reioyce with him.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
verse: There is a fat friend at your masters house,
That kitchin'd me for you to day at dinner:
She now shall be my sister, not my wife.

speeches.speaker: E.D.
verse: Me thinks you are my glasse, & not my brother:
I see by you, I am a sweet-fac'd youth,
Will you walke in to see their gossipping?

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Not I sir, you are my elder.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
prose: That's a question, how shall we trie it.

speeches.speaker: S. Dro.
prose: Wee'l draw Cuts for the Signior, till then, lead thou first.

speeches.speaker: E. Dro.
verse: Nay then thus:
We came into the world like brother and brother:
And now let's go hand in hand, not one before another.

plays.play_title: Much adoe about Nothing.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: I Learne in this Letter, that Don Peter of Arragon, comes this night to Messina.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: He is very neere by this: he was not three Leagues off when I left him.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: How many Gentlemen haue you lost in this action?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: But few of any sort, and none of name.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: A victorie is twice it selfe, when the atchieuer brings home full numbers: I finde heere, that Don Peter hath bestowed much honor on a yong Florentine, called Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: Much deseru'd on his part, and equally remembred by Don Pedro, he hath borne himselfe beyond the promise of his age, doing in the figure of a Lambe, the feats of a Lion, he hath indeede better bettred expectation, then you must expect of me to tell you how.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: He hath an Vnckle heere in Messina, wil be very much glad of it.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: I haue alreadie deliuered him letters, and there appeares much ioy in him, euen so much, that ioy could not shew it selfe modest enough, without a badg of bitternesse.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: Did he breake out into teares?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: In great measure.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: A kinde ouerflow of kindnesse, there are no faces truer, then those that are so wash'd, how much better is it to weepe at ioy, then to ioy at weeping?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
I pray you, is Signior Mountant^
return'd from the warres, or no?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: I know none of that name, Lady, there was none such in the armie of any sort.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: What is he that you aske for Neece?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: My cousin meanes Signior Benedick of Padua

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: O he's return'd, and as pleasant as euer he was.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: He set vp his bils here in Messina, & challeng'd Cupid at the Flight: and my Vnckles foole reading the Challenge, subscrib'd for Cupid, and challeng'd him at the Burbolt. I pray you, how many hath hee kil'd and eaten in these warres? But how many hath he kil'd? for indeed, I promis'd to eate all of his killing.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: 'Faith Neece, you taxe Signior Benedicke too much, but hee'l be meet with you, I doubt it not.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: He hath done good seruice Lady in these wars.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: You had musty victuall, and he hath holpe to ease it: he's a very valiant Trencher-man, hee hath an excellent stomacke.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: And a good souldier too Lady.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: And a good souldier to a Lady. But what is he to a Lord?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: A Lord to a Lord, a man to a man, stuft with all honourable vertues.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: It is so indeed, he is no lesse then a stuft man: but for the stuffing well, we are all mortall.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: You must not (sir) mistake my Neece, there is a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick, & her: they neuer meet, but there's a skirmish of wit between them.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: Alas, he gets nothing by that. In our last conflict, foure of his fiue wits went halting off, and now is the whole man gouern'd with one: so that if hee haue wit enough to keepe himselfe warme, let him beare it for a difference betweene himselfe and his horse: For it is all the wealth that he hath left, to be knowne a reasonable creature. Who is his companion now? He hath euery month a new sworne brother.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: I'st possible?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Very easily possible: he weares his faith but as the fashion of his hat, it euer changes with ye next block.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: I see (Lady) the Gentleman is not in your bookes.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: No, and he were, I would burne my study. But I pray you, who is his companion? Is there no young squarer now, that will make a voyage with him to the diuell?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: He is most in the company of the right noble Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: O Lord, he will hang vpon him like a disease: he is sooner caught then the pestilence, and the taker runs presently mad. God helpe the noble Claudio, if hee haue caught the Benedict, it will cost him a thousand pound ere he be cur'd.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: I will hold friends with you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: Do good friend.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: You'l ne're run mad Neece.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: No, not till a hot Ianuary.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: Don Pedro is approach'd.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Good Signior Leonato, you are come to meet your trouble: the fashion of the world is to auoid cost, and you encounter it.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Neuer came trouble to my house in the likenes of your Grace: for trouble being gone, comfort should remaine: but when you depart from me, sorrow abides, and happinesse takes his leaue.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: You embrace your charge too willingly: I thinke this is your daughter.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: Her mother hath many times told me so.

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: Were you in doubt that you askt her?

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: Signior Benedicke, no, for then were you a childe.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: You haue it full Benedicke, we may ghesse by this, what you are, being a man, truely the Lady fathers her selfe: be happie Lady, for you are like an honorable father.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: If Signior Leonato be her father, she would not haue his head on her shoulders for al Messina, as like him as she is.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I wonder that you will still be talking, signior Benedicke. no body markes you.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: What my deere Ladie Disdaine! are you yet liuing?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Is it possible Disdaine should die, while shee hath such meete foode to feede it, as Signior Benedicke? Curtesie it selfe must conuert to Disdaine, if you come in her presence.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Then is curtesie a turne-coate, but it is certaine I am loued of all Ladies, onely you excepted: and I would I could finde in my heart that I had not a hard heart, for truely I loue none.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: A deere happinesse to women, they would else haue beene troubled with a pernitious Su^er, I thanke God and my cold blood, I am of your humour for that, I had rather heare my Dog barke at a Crow, than a man sweare he loues me.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: God keepe your Ladiship still in that minde, so some Gentleman or other shall scape a predestinate scratcht face.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Scratching could not make it worse, and 'twere such a face as yours were.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Well, you are a rare Parrat teacher.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: A bird of my tongue, is better than a beast of your.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: I would my horse had the speed of your tongue, and so good a continuer, but keepe your way a Gods name, I haue done.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: You alwaies end with a Iades tricke, I know you of old.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: This is the summe of all: Leonato, signior Claudio, and signior Benedicke; my deere friend Leonato, hath inuited you all, I tell him we shall stay here, at the least a moneth, and he heartily praies some occasion may detaine vs longer: I dare sweare hee is no hypocrite, but praies from his heart.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: If you sweare, my Lord, you shall not be forsworne, let mee bid you welcome, my Lord, being reconciled to the Prince your brother: I owe you all duetie.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: I thanke you, I am not of many words, but I thanke you.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Please it your grace leade on?

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Your hand Leonato, we will goe together.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Benedicke, didst thou note the daughter of signior Leonato?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I noted her not, but I lookt on her.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Is she not a modest yong Ladie?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Doe you question me as an honest man should doe, for my simple true iudgement? or would you haue me speake after my custome, as being a professed tyrant to their sexe?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: No, I pray thee speake in sober iudgement.

speeches.speaker: Bene:
prose: Why yfaith me thinks shee's too low for a hie praise, too browne for a faire praise, and too little for a great praise, onely this commendation I can affoord her, that were shee other then she is, she were vnhandsome, and being no other, but as she is, I doe not like her.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Thou think'st I am in sport, I pray thee tell me truely how thou lik'st her.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Would you buie her, that you enquier after her?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Can the world buie such a iewell?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Yea, and a case to put it into, but speake you this with a sad brow? Or doe you play the flowting iacke, to tell vs Cupid is a good Hare-finder, and Vulcan a rare Carpenter: Come, in what key shall a man take you to goe in the song?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: In mine eie, she is the sweetest Ladie that euer I lookt on.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I can see yet without spectacles, and I see no such matter: there's her cosin, and she were not possest with a furie, exceedes her as much in beautie, as the first of Maie doth the last of December: but I hope you haue no intent to turne husband, haue you?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: I would scarce trust my selfe, though I had sworne the contrarie, if Hero would be my wife.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Ist come to this? in faith hath not the world one man but he will weare his cap with suspition? shall I neuer see a batcheller of three score againe? goe to yfaith, and thou wilt needes thrust thy necke into a yoke, weare the print of it, and sigh away sundaies: looke, don Pedro is returned to seeke you.

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
prose: What secret hath held you here, that you followed not to Leonatoes?

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: I would your Grace would constraine mee to tell.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: I charge thee on thy allegeance.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: You heare, Count Claudio, I can be secret as a dumbe man, I would haue you thinke so (but on my allegiance, marke you this, on my allegiance) hee is in loue, With who? now that is your Graces part: marke how short his answere is, with Hero, Leonatoes short daughter.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If this were so, so were it vttred.

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: Like the old tale, my Lord, it is not so, nor 'twas not so: but indeede, God forbid it should be so.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If my passion change not shortly, God forbid it should be otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Amen, if you loue her, for the Ladie is verie well worthie.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: You speake this to fetch me in, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
prose: By my troth I speake my thought.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: And in faith, my Lord, I spoke mine.

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: And by my two faiths and troths, my Lord, I speake mine.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: That I loue her, I feele.

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
prose: That she is worthie, I know.

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: That I neither feele how shee should be loued, nor know how shee should be worthie, is the opinion that fire cannot melt out of me, I will die in it at the stake.

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
prose: Thou wast euer an obstinate heretique in the despight of Beautie.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: And neuer could maintaine his part, but in the force of his will.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: That a woman conceiued me, I thanke her: that she brought mee vp, I likewise giue her most humble thankes: but that I will haue a ^echare winded in my forehead, or hang my bugle in an inuisible baldricke, all women shall pardon me: because I will not do them the wrong to mistrust any, I will doe my selfe the right to trust none: and the fine is, (for the which I may goe the finer) I will liue a Batchellor.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: I shall see thee ere I die, looke pale with loue.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: With anger, with sicknesse, or with hunger, my Lord, not with loue: proue that euer I loose more blood with loue, then I will get againe with drinking, picke out mine eyes with a Ballet-makers penne, and hang me vp at the doore of a brothel-house for the signe of blinde Cupid.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Well, if euer thou doost fall from this faith, thou wilt proue a notable argument.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: If I do, hang me in a bottle like a Cat, & shoot at me, and he that hit's me, let him be clapt on the shoulder, and cal'd Adam.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Well, as time shall trie: In time the sauage Bull doth beare the yoake.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: The sauage bull may, but if euer the sensible Benedicke beare it, plucke off the bulles hornes, and set them in my forehead, and let me be vildely painted, and in such great Letters as they write, heere is good horse to hire: let them signifie vnder my signe, here you may see Benedicke the married man.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If this should euer happen, thou wouldst bee horne mad.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Nay, if Cupid haue not spent all his Quiuer in Venice, thou wilt quake for this shortly.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I looke for an earthquake too then.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Well, you will temporize with the houres, in the meane time, good Signior Benedicke, repaire to Leonatoes, commend me to him, and tell him I will not faile him at supper, for indeede he hath made great preparation.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I haue almost matter enough in me for such an Embassage, and so I commit you.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: To the tuition of God. From my house, if I had it.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: The sixt of Iuly. Your louing friend, Benedick.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Nay mocke not, mocke not; the body of your discourse is sometime guarded with fragments, and the guardes are but slightly basted on neither, ere you flout old ends any further, examine your conscience, and so I leaue you.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: My Liege, your Highnesse now may doe mee good.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
verse: My loue is thine to teach, teach it but how,
And thou shalt see how apt it is to learne
Any hard Lesson that may do thee good.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Hath Leonato any sonne my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
verse: No childe but Hero, she's his onely heire.
Dost thou affect her Claudio?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: O my Lord,
When you went onward on this ended action,
I look'd vpon her with a souldiers eie,
That lik'd, but had a rougher taske in hand,
Than to driue liking to the name of loue:
But now I am return'd, and that warre-thoughts
Haue left their places vacant: in their roomes,
Come thronging soft and delicate desires,
All prompting mee how faire yong Hero is,
Saying I lik'd her ere I went to warres.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
verse: Thou wilt be like a louer presently,
And tire the hearer with a booke of words:
If thou dost loue faire Hero, cherish it,
And I will breake with her: wast not to this end,
That thou beganst to twist so fine a story?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: How sweetly doe you minister to loue,
That know loues griefe by his complexion!
But lest my liking might too sodaine seeme,
I would haue salu'd it with a longer treatise.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: What need ye bridge much broder then the flood?
The fairest graunt is the necessitie:
Looke what will serue, is fit: 'tis once, thou louest,
And I will fit thee with the remedie,
I know we shall haue reuelling to night,
I will assume thy part in some disguise,
And tell faire Hero I am Claudio,
And in her bosome Ile vnclaspe my heart,
And take her hearing prisoner with the force
And strong incounter of my amorous tale:
Then after, to her father will I breake,
And the conclusion is, shee shall be thine,
In practise let vs put it presently.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: How now brother, where is my cosen your son: hath he prouided this musicke?

speeches.speaker: Old.
prose: He is very busie about it, but brother, I can tell you newes that you yet dreamt not of.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
prose: Are they good?

speeches.speaker: Old.
prose: As the euents stamps them, but they haue ^ good couer: they. shew well outward, the Prince and Count Claudio walking in a thick pleached alley in my orchard, were thus ouer-heard by a man of mine: the Prince discouered to Claudio that hee loued my niece your daughter, and meant to acknowledge it this night in a dance, and if hee found her accordant, hee meant to take the present time by the top, and instantly breake with you of it.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: Hath the fellow any wit that told you this?

speeches.speaker: Old.
prose: A good sharpe fellow, I will send for him, and question him your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: No, no; wee will hold it as a dreame, till it appeare it selfe: but I will acquaint my daughter withall, that she may be the better prepared for an answer, if peraduenture this bee true: goe you and tell her of it: coosins, you know what you haue to doe, O I crie you mercie friend, goe you with mee and I will vse your skill, good cosin haue a care this busie time.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: What the good yeere my Lord, why are you thus out of measure sad?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
prose: There is no measure in the occasion that breeds, therefore the sadnesse is without limit.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: You should heare reason.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: And when I haue heard it, what blessing bringeth it?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: If not a present remedy, yet a patient sufferance.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
prose: I wonder that thou (being as thou saist thou art, borne vnder Saturne) goest about to apply a morall medicine, to a mortifying mischiefe: I cannot hide what I am: I must bee sad when I haue cause, and smile at no mans iests, eat when I haue stomacke, and wait for no mans leisure: sleepe when I am drowsie, and tend on no mans businesse, laugh when I am merry, and claw no man in his humor.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
Yea, but you must not make the ful show of this, till you may doe it without controllment, you haue of

late stood out against your brother, and hee hath tane you newly into his grace, where it is impossible you should take root, but by the faire weather that you make your selfe, it is needful that you frame the season for your owne haruest.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: I had rather be a canker in a hedge, then a rose in his grace, and it better fits my bloud to be disdain'd of all, then to fashion a carriage to rob loue from any: in this (though I cannot be said to be a flattering honest man) it must not be denied but I am a plaine dealing villaine, I am trusted with a mussell, and enfranchisde with a clog, therefore I haue decreed, not to sing in my cage: if I had my mouth, I would bite: if I had my liberty, I would do my liking: in the meane time, let me be that I am, and seeke not to alter me.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Can you make no vse of your discontent?

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
verse: I will make all vse of it, for I vse it onely.
Who comes here? what newes Borachio?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: I came yonder from a great supper, the Prince your brother is royally entertained by Leonato, and I can giue you intelligence of an intended marriage.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Will it serue for any Modell to build mischiefe on? What is hee for a foole that betrothes himselfe to vnquietnesse?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Mary it is your brothers right hand.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Who, the most exquisite Claudio?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Euen he.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: A proper squier, and who, and who, which way lookes he?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Mary on Hero, the daughter and Heire of Leonato.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: A very forward March-chicke, how came you to this?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Being entertain'd for a perfumer, as I was smoaking a musty roome, comes me the Prince and Claudio, hand in hand in sad conference: I whipt behind the Arras, and there heard it agreed vpon, that the Prince should wooe Hero for himselfe, and hauing obtain'd her, giue her to Count Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Come, come, let vs thither, this may proue food to my displeasure, that young start-vp hath all the glorie of my ouerthrow: if I can crosse him any way, I blesse my selfe euery way, you are both sure, and will assist mee?

speeches.speaker: Conr.
prose: To the death my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Let vs to the great supper, their cheere is the greater that I am subdued, would the Cooke were of my minde: shall we goe proue whats to be done?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Wee'll wait vpon your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: Was not Count Iohn here at supper?

speeches.speaker: Brother.
prose: I saw him not.

speeches.speaker: Beatrice.
prose: How tartly that Gentleman lookes, I neuer can see him, but I am heart-burn'd an howre after.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: He is of a very melancholy disposition.

speeches.speaker: Beatrice.
prose: Hee were an excellent man that were made iust in the mid-way betweene him and Benedicke, the one is too like an image and saies nothing, and the other too like my Ladies eldest sonne, euermore tatling.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Then halfe signior Benedicks tongue in Count Iohns mouth, and halfe Count Iohns melancholy in Signior Benedicks face.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: With a good legge, and a good foot vnckle, and money enough in his purse, such a man would winne any woman in the world, if he could get her good will.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: By my troth Neece, thou wilt neuer get thee a husband, if thou be so shrewd of thy tongue.

speeches.speaker: Brother.
prose: Infaith shee's too curst.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Too curst is more then curst, I shall lessen Gods sending that way: for it is said, God sends a curst Cow short hornes, but to a Cow too curst he sends none.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: So, by being too curst, God will send you no hornes.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Iust, if he send me no husband, for the which blessing, I am at him vpon my knees euery morning and euening: Lord, I could not endure a husband with a beard on his face, I had rather lie in the woollen.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: You may light vpon a husband that hath no beard.

speeches.speaker: Batrice.
prose: What should I doe with him? dresse him in my apparell, and make him my waiting gentlewoman? he that hath a beard, is more then a youth: and he that hath no beard, is lesse then a man: and hee that is more then a youth, is not for mee: and he that is lesse then a man, I am not for him: therefore I will euen take sixepence in earnest of the Berrord, and leade his Apes into hell.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Well then, goe you into hell.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: No, but to the gate, and there will the Deuill meete mee like an old Cuckold with hornes on his head, and say, get you to heauen Beatrice, get you to heauen, heere's no place for you maids, so deliuer I vp my Apes, and away to S. Peter: for the heauens, hee shewes mee where the Batchellers sit, and there liue wee as merry as the day is long.

speeches.speaker: Brother.
prose: Well neece, I trust you will be rul'd by your father.

speeches.speaker: Beatrice.
prose: Yes faith, it is my cosens dutie to make curtsie, and say, as it please you: but yet for all that cosin, let him be a handsome fellow, or else make an other cursie, and say, father, as it please me.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: Well neece, I hope to see you one day sitted with a husband.

speeches.speaker: Beatrice.
prose: Not till God make men of some other mettall then earth, would it not grieue a woman to be ouer-mastred with a peece of valiant dust? to make account of her life to a clod of waiward marle? no vnckle, ile none: Adams sonnes are my brethren, and truly I hold it a sinne to match in my kinred.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Daughter, remember what I told you, if the Prince doe solicit you in that kinde, you know your answere.

speeches.speaker: Beatrice.
prose: The fault will be in the musicke cosin, if you be not woed in good time: if the Prince bee too important, tell him there is measure in euery thing, & so dance out the answere, for heare me Hero, wooing, wedding, & repenting, is as a Scotch ijgge, a measure, and a cinque-pace: the first suite is hot and hasty like a Scotch ijgge (and full as fantasticall) the wedding manerly modest, (as a measure) full of state & aunchentry, and then comes repentance, and with his bad legs falls into the cinque-pace faster and faster, till he sinkes into his graue.

speeches.speaker: Leonata.
prose: Cosin you apprehend passing shrewdly.

speeches.speaker: Beatrice.
prose: I haue a good eye vnckle, I can see a Church by daylight.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: The reuellers are entring brother, make good roome.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Lady, will you walke about with your friend?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: So you walke softly, and looke sweetly, and say nothing, I am yours for the walke, and especially when I walke away.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: With me in your company.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: I may say so when I please.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: And when please you to say so?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: When I like your fauour, for God defend the Lute should be like the case.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: My visor is Philemons roofe, within the house is Loue.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Why then your visor should be thatcht.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Speake low if you speake Loue.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Well, I would you did like me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: So would not I for your owne sake, for I haue manie ill qualities.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Which is one?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I say my prayers alowd.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: I loue you the better, the hearers may cry Amen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: God match me with a good dauncer.

speeches.speaker: Balt.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And God keepe him out of my sight when the daunce is done: answer Clarke.

speeches.speaker: Balt.
prose: No more words the Clarke is answered.

speeches.speaker: Vrsula.
prose: I know you well enough, you are Signior Anthonio.

speeches.speaker: Anth.
prose: At a word, I am not.

speeches.speaker: Vrsula.
prose: I know you by the wagling of your head.

speeches.speaker: Anth.
prose: To tell you true, I counterfet him.

speeches.speaker: Vrsu.
prose: You could neuer doe him so ill well, vnlesse you were the very man: here's his dry hand vp & down, you are he, you are he.

speeches.speaker: Anth.
prose: At a word I am not.

speeches.speaker: ~rsula.
prose: Come, come, doe you thinke I doe not know you by your excellent wit? can vertue hide it selfe? goe to, mumme, you are he, graces will appeare, and there's an end.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Will you not tell me who told you so?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: No, you shall pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Nor will you not tell me who you are?

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: Not now.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: That I was disdainfull, and that I had my good wit out of the hundred merry tales: well, this was Signior Benedicke that said so.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: What's he?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I am sure you know him well enough.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Not I, beleeue me.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Did he neuer make you laugh?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I pray you what is he?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Why he is the Princes ieaster, a very dull foole, onely his gift is, in deuising impossible slanders, none but Libertines delight in him, and the commendation is not in his witte, but in his villanie, for hee both pleaseth men and angers them, and then they laugh at him, and beat him: I am sure he is in the Fleet, I would he had boorded me.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: When I know the Gentleman, Ile tell him what you say.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Do, do, hee'l but breake a comparison or two on me, which peraduenture (not markt, or not laugh'd at) strikes him into melancholly, and then there's a Partridge wing saued, for the foole will eate no supper that night. We must follow the Leaders.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: In euery good thing.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: Nay, if they leade to any ill, I will leaue them at the next turning.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Sure my brother is amorous on Hero, and hath withdrawne her father to breake with him about it: the Ladies follow her, and but one visor remaines.

speeches.speaker: Borachio.
prose: And that is Claudio, I know him by his bearing.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Are not you signior Benedicke?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: You know me well, I am hee.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Signior, you are verie neere my Brother in his loue, he is enamor'd on Hero, I pray you disswade him from her, she is no equall for his birth: you may do the part of an honest man in it.

speeches.speaker: Claudio.
prose: How know you he loues her?

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: I heard him sweare his affection,

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: So did I too, and he swore he would marrie her to night.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Come, let vs to the banquet.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Thus answere I in name of Benedicke,
But heare these ill newes with the eares of Claudio:
'Tis certaine so, the Prince woes for himselfe:
Friendship is constant in all other things,
Saue in the Office and affaires of loue:
Therefore all hearts in loue vse their owne tongues.
