Let euerie eye negotiate for it selfe,
And trust no Agent: for beautie is a witch,
Against whose charmes, faith melteth into blood:
This is an accident of hourely proofe,
Which I mistrusted not. Farewell therefore Hero.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Count Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Yea, the same.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Come, will you go with me?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Whither?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Euen to the next Willow, about your own businesse, Count. What fashion will you weare the Garland off? About your necke, like an Vsurers chaine? Or vnder your arme, like a Lieutenants scarfe? You must weare it one way, for the Prince hath got your Hero.

speeches.speaker: Clau:
prose: I wish him ioy of her.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Why that's spoken like an honest Drouier, so they sel Bullockes: but did you thinke the Prince wold haue serued you thus?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: I pray you leaue me.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Ho now you strike like the blindman, 'twas the boy that stole your meate, and you'l beat the post.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If it will not be, Ile leaue you.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Alas poore hurt fowle, now will he creepe into sedges: But that my Ladie Beatrice should know me, & not know me: the Princes foole! Hah? It may be I goe vnder that title, because I am merrie: yea but so I am apt to do my selfe wrong: I am not so reputed, it is the base (though bitter) disposition of Beatrice, that putt's the world into her person, and so giues me out: well, Ile be reuenged as I may.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Now Signior, where's the Count, did you see him?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Troth my Lord, I haue played the part of Lady Fame, I found him heere as melancholy as a Lodge in a Warren, I told him, and I thinke, told him true, that your grace had got the will of this young Lady, and I offered him my company to a willow tree, either to make him a garland, as being forsaken, or to binde him a rod, as being worthy to be whipt.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: To be whipt, what's his fault?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: The slat transgression of a Schoole-boy, who being ouer-ioyed with finding a birds nest, shewes it his companion, and he steales it.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Wilt thou make a trust, a transgression? the transgression is in the stealer.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Yet it had not beene amisse the rod had beene made, and the garland too, for the garland he might haue worne himselfe, and the rod hee might haue bestowed on you, who (as I take it) haue stolne his birds nest.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: I will but teach them to sing, and restore them to the owner.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: If their singing answer your saying. by my faith you say honestly.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: The Lady Beatrice hath a quarrell to you, the Gentleman that daunst with her, told her shee is much wrong'd by you.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: O she misusde me past the indurance of a block: an oake but with one greene leafe on it, would haue answered her: my very visor began to assume life, and scold with her: shee told mee, not thinking I had beene my selfe, that I was the Princes Iester, and that I was duller then a great thaw, hu^ling iest vpon iest, with such impossible conueiance vpon me, that I stood like a man at a marke, with a whole army shooting at me: shee speakes poynyards, and euery word stabbes: if her breath were as terrible as terminations, there were no liuing neere her, she would infect to the north starre: I would not marry her, though she were indowed with all that Adam had left him before he transgrest, she would haue made Hercules haue turnd spit, yea, and haue cleft his club to make the fire too: come, talke not of her, you shall finde her the infernall Ate in good apparell. I would to God some scholler would coniure her, for certainely while she is heere, a man may liue as quiet in hell, as in a sanctuary, and people sinne vpon purpose, because they would goe thither, so indeed all disquiet, horror, and perturbation followes her.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Looke heere she comes.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Will your Grace command mee any seruice to the worlds end? I will goe on the slightest arrand now to the Antypodes that you can deuise to send me on: I will fetch you a tooth-picker now from the furthest inch of Asia: bring you the length of Prester Iohns foot: fetch you a hayre off the great Chams beard: doe you any embassage to the Pigmies, rather then hould three words conference, with this Harpy: you haue no employment for me?

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: None, but to desire your good company.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: O God sir, heeres a dish I loue not, I cannot indure this Lady tongue.

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
prose: Come Lady, come, you haue lost the heart of Signior Benedicke.

speeches.speaker: Beatr.
prose: Indeed my Lord, hee lent it me a while, and I gaue him vse for it, a double heart for a single one, marry once before he wonne it of mee, with false dice, therefore your Grace may well say I haue lost it.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: You haue put him downe Lady, you haue put him downe.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: So I would not he should do me, my Lord, lest I should prooue the mother of fooles: I haue brought Count Claudio, whom you sent me to seeke.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Why how now Count, wherfore are you sad?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Not sad my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: How then? sicke?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Neither, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: The Count is neither sad, nor sicke, nor merry, nor well: but ciuill Count, ciuill as an Orange, and something of a iealous complexion.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Ifaith Lady, I thinke your blazon to be true, though Ile be sworne, if hee be so, his conceit is false: heere Claudio, I haue wooed in thy name, and faire Hero is won, I haue broke with her father, and his good will obtained, name the day of marriage, and God giue thee ioy.

speeches.speaker: Leona.
prose: Count, take of me my daughter, and with her my fortunes: his grace hath made the match, & all grace say, Amen to it.

speeches.speaker: Beatr.
prose: Speake Count, tis your Qu.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Silence is the perfectest Herault of ioy, I were but little happy if I could say, how much? Lady, as you are mine, I am yours, I giue away my selfe for you, and doat vpon the exchange.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Speake cosin, or (if you cannot) stop his mouth with a kisse, and let not him speake neither.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Infaith Lady you haue a merry heart.

speeches.speaker: Beatr.
prose: Yea my Lord I thanke it, poore foole it keepes on the windy side of Care, my coosin tells him in his eare that he is in my heart.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: And so she doth coosin.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Good Lord for alliance: thus goes euery one to the world but I, and I am sun-burn'd, I may sit in a corner and cry, heigh ho for a husband.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Lady Beatrice, I will get you one.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I would rather haue one of your fathers getting: hath your Grace ne're a brother like you? your father got excellent husbands, if a maid could come by them.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Will you haue me? Lady.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: No, my Lord, vnlesse I might haue another for working-daies, your Grace is too costly to weare euerie day: but I beseech your Grace pardon mee, I was borne to speake all mirth, and no matter.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Your silence most offends me, and to be merry, best becomes you, for out of question, you were born in a merry howre.

speeches.speaker: Beatr.
prose: No sure my Lord, my Mother cried, but then there was a starre daunst, and vnder that was I borne: cosins God giue you ioy.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: Neece, will you looke to those rhings I told you of?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I cry you mercy Vncle, by your Graces pardon.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: By my troth a pleasant spirited Lady.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: There's little of the melancholy element in her my Lord, she is neuer sad, but when she sleepes, and not euer sad then: for I haue heard my daughter say, she hath often dreamt of vnhappinesse, and wakt her selfe with laughing.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
prose: Shee cannot indure to heare tell of a husband.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: O, by no meanes, she mocks all her wooers out of suite.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: She were an excellent wife for Benedick.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose:
O Lord, my Lord, if they were but a weeke

married, they would talke themselues madde.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Counte Claudio, when meane you to goe to Church?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: To morrow my Lord, Time goes on crutches, till Loue haue all his rites.

speeches.speaker: Leonata.
prose: Not till monday, my deare sonne, which is hence a iust seuen night, and a time too briefe too, to haue all things answer minde.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Come, you shake the head at so long a breathing, but I warrant thee Claudio, the time shall not goe dully by vs, I will in the interim, vndertake one of Hercules labors, which is, to bring Signior Benedicke and the Lady Beatrice into a mountaine of affection, th' one with th' other, I would faine haue it a match, and I doubt not but to fashion it, if you three will but minister such assistance as I shall giue you direction.

speeches.speaker: Leonata.
prose: My Lord, I am for you, though it cost mee ten nights watchings.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: And I my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: And you to gentle Hero?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: I will doe any modest office, my Lord, to helpe my cosin to a good husband.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: And Benedick is not the vnhopefullest husband that I know: thus farre can I praise him, hee is of a noble straine, of approued valour, and confirm'd honesty, I will teach you how to humour your cosin, that shee shall fall in loue with Benedicke, and I, with your two helpes, will so practise on Benedicke, that in despight of his quicke wit, and his queasie stomacke, hee shall fall in loue with Beatrice: if wee can doe this, Cupid is no longer an Archer, his glory shall be ours, for wee are the onely loue-gods, goe in with me, and I will tell you my drift.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
prose: It is so, the Count Claudio shal marry the daughter of Leonato.

speeches.speaker: Bora.
prose: Yea my Lord, but I can crosse it.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Any barre, any crosse, any impediment, will be medicinable to me, I am sicke in displeasure to him, and whatsoeuer comes athwart his affection, ranges euenly with mine, how canst thou crosse this marriage?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Not honestly my Lord, but so couertly, that no dishonesty shall appeare in me.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Shew me breefely how.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: I thinke I told your Lordship a yeere since, how much I am in the fauour of Margaret, the waiting gentlewoman to Hero.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: I remember.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: I can at any vnseasonable instant of the night, appoint her to look out at her Ladies chamber window.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: What life is in that, to be the death of this marriage?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: The poyson of that lies in you to temper, goe you to the Prince your brother, spare not to tell him, that hee hath wronged his Honor in marrying the renowned Claudio, whose estimation do you mightily hold vp, to a contaminated stale, such a one as Hero.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: What proofe shall I make of that?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Proofe enough, to misuse the Prince, to vexe Claudio, to vndoe Hero, and kill Leonato, looke you for any other issue?

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Onely to despight them, I will endeauour any thing.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Goe then, finde me a meete howre, to draw on Pedro and the Count Claudio alone, tell them that you know that Hero loues me, intend a kinde of zeale both to the Prince and Claudio (as in a loue of your brothers honor who hath made this match) and his friends reputation, who is thus like to be cosen'd with the semblance of a maid, that you haue discouer'd thus: they will scarcely beleeue this without triall: offer them instances which shall beare no lesse likelihood, than to see mee at her chamber window, heare me call Margaret, Hero; heare Margaret terme me Claudio, and bring them to see this the very night before the intended wedding, for in the meane time, I will so fashion the matter, that Hero shall be absent, and there shall appeare such seeming truths of Heroes disloyaltie, that iealousie shall be cal'd assurance, and all the preparation ouerthrowne.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: Grow this to what aduerse issue it can, I will put it in practise: be cunning in the working this, and thy fee is a thousand ducates.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Be thou constant in the accusation, and my cunning shall not shame me.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
prose: I will presentlie goe learne their day of marriage.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Signior.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: In my chamber window lies a booke, bring it hither to me in the orchard.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I am heere already sir.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I know that, but I would haue thee hence, and heere againe. I doe much wonder, that one man seeing how much another man is a foole, when he dedicates his behauiours to loue, will after hee hath laught at such shallow follies in others, become the argument of his owne scorne, by falling in loue, & such a man is Claudio, I haue known when there was no musicke with him but the drum and the fife, and now had hee rather heare the taber and the pipe: I haue knowne when he would haue walkt ten mile afoot, to see a good armor, and now will he lie ten nights awake caruing the fashion of a new dublet: he was wont to speake plaine, & to the purpose (like an honest man & a souldier) and now is he turn'd orthography, his words are a very fantasticall banquet, iust so many strange dishes: may I be so conuerted, & see with these eyes? I cannot tell, I thinke not: I will not bee sworne, but loue may transforme me to an oyster, but Ile take my oath on it, till he haue made an oyster of me, he shall neuer make me such a foole: one woman is faire, yet I am well: another is wise, yet I am well: another vertuous, yet I am well: but till all graces be in one woman. one woman shall not come in my grace: rich shee shall be, that's certaine: wise, or Ile none: vertuous, or Ile neuer cheapen her: faire, or Ile neuer looke on her: milde, or come not neere me: Noble, or not for an Angell: of good discourse: an excellent Musitian, and her haire shal be of what colour it please God, hah! the Prince and Monsieur Loue, I will hide me in the Arbor.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Come, shall we heare this musicke?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Yea my good Lord: how still the euening is,
As husht on purpose to grace harmonie.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: See you where Benedicke hath hid himselfe?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: O very well my Lord: the musicke ended,
Wee'll fit the kid-foxe with a penny worth.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Come Balthasar, wee'll heare that song again.

speeches.speaker: Balth.
verse: O good my Lord, taxe not so bad a voyce,
To slander musicke any more then once.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: It is the witnesse still of excellency,
To slander Musicke any more then once.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
verse: It is the witnesse still of excellencie,
To put a strange face on his owne perfection,
I pray thee sing, and let me woe no more.

speeches.speaker: Balth.
verse: Because you talke of wooing, I will sing,
Since many a wooer doth commence his suit,
To her he thinkes not worthy, yet he wooes,
Yet will he sweare he loues.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
verse: Nay pray thee come,
Or if thou wilt hold longer argument,
Doe it in notes.

speeches.speaker: Balth.
verse: Note this before my notes,
Theres not a note of mine that's worth the noting.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
verse: Why these are very crotchets that he speaks,
Note notes forsooth, and nothing.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Now diuine aire, now is his soule rauisht, is it not strange that sheepes guts should hale soules out of mens bodies? well, a horne for my money when all's done.

verse: Sigh no more Ladies, sigh no more,
Men were deceiuers euer,
One foote in Sea and one on shore,
To one thing constant neuer,
Then sigh not so, but let them goe,
And be you blithe and bonnis,
Conuerting all your sounds of woe,
Into hey nony nony.
Sing no more ditties, sing no moe,
Of dumps so dull and heauy,
The fraud of men were euer so,
Since summer first was leauy,
Then sigh not so, &c.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: By my troth a good song.

speeches.speaker: Balth.
prose: And an ill singer, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Ha, no, no faith, thou singst well enough for a shift.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: And he had been a dog that should haue howld thus, they would haue hang'd him, and I pray God his bad voyce bode no mischiefe, I had as liefe haue heard the night-rauen, come what plague could haue come after it.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Yea marry, dost thou heare Balthasar? I pray thee get vs some excellent musick: for to morrow night we would haue it at the Lady Heroes chamber window.

speeches.speaker: Balth.
prose: The best I can, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Do so, farewell. Come hither Leonato, what was it you told me of to day, that your Niece Beatrice was in loue with signior Benedicke?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: O I, stalke on, stalke on, the foule sits. I did neuer thinke that Lady would haue loued any man.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: No nor I neither, but most wonderful, that she should so dote on Signior Benedicke, whom shee hath in all outward behauiours seemed euer to abhorre.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Is't possible? sits the winde in that corner?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: By my troth my Lord, I cannot tell what to thinke of it, but that she loues him with an inraged affection, it is past the infinite of thought.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: May be she doth but counterfeit.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Faith like enough.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: O God! counterfeit? there was neuer counterfeit of passion, came so neere the life of passion as she discouers it.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Why what effects of passion shewes she?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Baite the hooke well, this fish will bite.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: What effects my Lord? shee will sit you, you heard my daughter tell you how.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: She did indeed.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: How, how I pray you? you amaze me, I would haue thought her spirit had beene inuincible against all assaults of affection.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: I would haue sworne it had, my Lord, especially against Benedicke.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I should thinke this a gull, but that the white-bearded fellow speakes it: knauery cannot sure hide himselfe in such reuerence.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: He hath tane th' infection, hold it vp.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: Hath shee made her affection known to Benedicke?

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: No, and sweares she neuer will, that's her torment.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: 'Tis true indeed, so your daughter saies: shall I, saies she, that haue so oft encountred him with scorne, write to him that I loue him?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: This saies shee now when shee is beginning to write to him, for shee'll be vp twenty times a night, and there will she sit in her smocke, till she haue writ a sheet of paper: my daughter tells vs all.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Now you talke of a sheet of paper, I remember a pretty iest your daughter told vs of.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: O when she had writ it, & was reading it ouer, she found Benedicke and Beatrice betweene the sheete.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: That.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: O she tore the letter into a thousand halfpence, raild at her self, that she should be so immodest to write, to one that shee knew would flout her: I measure him, saies she, by my owne spirit, for I should flout him if hee writ to mee, yea though I loue him, I should.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Then downe vpon her knees she falls, weepes, sobs, beates her heart, teares her hayre, praies, curses, O sweet Benedicke, God giue me patience.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: She doth indeed, my daughter saies so, and the extasie hath so much ouerborne her, that my daughter is somtime afeard she will doe a desperate out-rage to her selfe, it is very true.

speeches.speaker: Princ.
prose: It were good that Benedicke knew of it by some other, if she will not discouer it.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: To what end? he would but make a sport of it, and torment the poore Lady worse.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: And he should, it were an almes to hang him, shee's an excellent sweet Lady, and (out of all suspition,) she is vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Claudio.
prose: And she is exceeding wise.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: In euery thing, but in louing Benedicke.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: O my Lord, wisedome and bloud combating in so tender a body, we haue ten proofes to one, that bloud hath the victory, I am sorry for her, as I haue iust cause, being her Vncle, and her Guardian.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: I would shee had bestowed this dotage on mee, I would haue daft all other respects, and made her halfe my selfe: I pray you tell Benedicke of it, and heare what he will say.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Were it good thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Hero thinkes surely she wil die, for she saies she will die, if hee loue her not, and shee will die ere shee make her loue knowne, and she will die if hee wooe her, rather than shee will bate one breath of her accustomed crossenesse.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose:
She doth well, if she should make tender of her

loue, 'tis very possible hee'l scorne it, for the man (as you know all) hath a contemptible spirit.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: He is a very proper man.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: He hath indeed a good outward happines.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: 'Fore God, and in my minde very wise.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: He doth indeed shew some sparkes that are like wit.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: And I take him to be valiant.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: As Hector, I assure you, and in the managing of quarrels you may see hee is wise, for either hee auoydes them with great discretion, or vndertakes them with a Christian-like feare.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: If hee doe feare God, a must necessarilie keepe peace, if hee breake the peace, hee ought to enter into a quarrell with feare and trembling.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: And so will he doe, for the man doth fear God, howsoeuer it seemes not in him, by some large ieasts hee will make: well, I am sorry for your niece, shall we goe see Benedicke, and tell him of her loue,

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Neuer tell him, my Lord, let her weare it out with good counsell.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Nay that's impossible, she may weare her heart out first.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Well, we will heare further of it by your daughter, let it coole the while, I loue Benedicke well, and I could wish he would modestly examine himselfe, to see how much he is vnworthy to haue so good a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: My Lord, will you walke? dinner is ready.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If he do not doat on her vpon this, I wil neuer trust my expectation.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Let there be the same Net spread for her, and that must your daughter and her gentlewoman carry: the sport will be, when they hold one an opinion of anothers dotage, and no such matter, that's the Scene that I would see, which will be meerely a dumbe shew: let vs send her to call him into dinner.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: This can be no tricke, the conference was sadly borne, they haue the truth of this from Hero, they seeme to pittie the Lady: it seemes her affections haue the full bent: loue me? why it must be requited: I heare how I am censur'd, they say I will beare my selfe proudly, if I perceiue the loue come from her: they say too, that she will rather die than giue any signe of affection: I did neuer thinke to marry, I must not seeme proud, happy are they that heare their detractions, and can put them to mending: they say the Lady is faire, 'tis a truth, I can beare them witnesse: and vertuous, tis so, I cannot reprooue it, and wise, but for louing me, by my troth it is no addition to her witte, nor no great argument of her folly; for I wil be horribly in loue with her, I may chance haue some odde quirkes and remnants of witte broken on mee, because I haue rail'd so long against marriage: but doth not the appetite alter? a man loues the meat in his youth, that he cannot indure in his age. Shall quips and sentences, and these paper bullets of the braine awe a man from the careere of his humour? No, the world must be peopled. When I said I would die a batcheler, I did not think I should liue till I were maried, here comes Beatrice: by this day, shee's a faire Lady, I doe spie some markes of loue in her.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Against my wil I am sent to bid you come in to dinner.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Faire Beatrice, I thanke you for your paines.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I tooke no more paines for those thankes, then you take paines to thanke me, if it had been painefull, I would not haue come.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: You take pleasure then in the message.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Yea iust so much as you may take vpon a kniues point, and choake a daw withall: you haue no stomacke signior, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Ha, against my will I am sent to bid you come into dinner: there's a double meaning in that: I tooke no more paines for those thankes then you tooke paines to thanke me, that's as much as to say, any paines that I take for you is as easie as thankes: if I do not take pitty of her I am a villaine, if I doe not loue her I am a Iew, I will goe get her picture.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Good Margaret runne thee to the parlour,
There shalt thou finde my Cosin Beatrice,
Proposing with the Prince and Claudio,
Whisper her eare, and tell her I and Vrsula,
Walke in the Orchard, and our whole discourse
Is all of her, say that thou ouer-heardst vs,
And bid her steale into the pleached bower,
Where hony-suckles ripened by the sunne,
Forbid the sunne to enter: like fauourites,
Made proud by Princes, that aduance their pride,
Against that power that bred it, there will she hide her,
To listen our purpose, this is thy office,
Beare thee well in it, and leaue vs alone.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
prose: Ile make her come I warrant you presently.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Now Vrsula, when Beatrice doth come,
As we do trace this alley vp and downe,
Our talke must onely be of Benedicke,
When I doe name him, let it be thy part,
To praise him more then euer man did merit,
My talke to thee must be how Benedicke
Is sicke in loue with Beatrice: of this matter,
Is little Cupids crasty arrow made,
That onely wounds by heare-say: now begin,
For looke where Beatrice like a Lapwing runs
Close by the ground, to heare our conference.

speeches.speaker: Vrs.
verse: The pleasant'st angling is to see the fish
Cut with her golden ores the siluer streame,
And greedily deuoure the treacherous baite:
So angle we for Beatrice, who euen now,
Is couched in the wood-bine couerture,
Feare you not my part of the Dialogue.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: Then go we neare her that her eare loose nothing,
Of the false sweete baite that we lay for it:
No truely Vrsula, she is too disdainfull,
I know her spirits are as coy and wilde,
As Haggerds of the rocke.

speeches.speaker: ~rsula.
verse: But are you sure,
That Benedicke loues Beatrice so intirely?

speeches.speaker: Her.
prose: So saies the Prince, and my new trothed Lord.

speeches.speaker: Vrs.
prose: And did they bid you tell her of it, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: They did intreate me to acquaint her of it,
But I perswaded them, if they lou'd Benedicke,
To wish him wrastle with affection,
And neuer to let Beatrice know of it.

speeches.speaker: Vrsula.
verse: Why did you so, doth not the Gentleman
Deserue as full as fortunate a bed,
As euer Beatrice shall couch vpon?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: O God of loue! I know he doth deserue,
As much as may be yeelded to a man:
But Nature neuer fram'd a womans heart,
Of prowder stuffe then that of Beatrice:
Disdaine and Scorne ride sparkling in her eyes,
Mis-prizing what they looke on, and her wit
Values it selfe so highly, that to her
All matter else seemes weake: she cannot loue,
Nor take no shape nor proiect of affection,
Shee is so selfe indeared.

speeches.speaker: Vrsula.
verse: Sure I thinke so,
And therefore certainely it were not good
She knew his loue, left she make sport at it.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Why you speake truth, I neuer yet saw man,
How wise, how noble, yong, how rarely featur'd.
But she would spell him backward: if faire fac'd,
She would sweare the gentleman should be her sister:
If blacke, why Nature drawing of an anticke,
Made a foule blot: if tall, a launce ill headed:
If low, an agot very vildlie cut:
If speaking, why a vane blowne with all windes:
If silent, why a blocke moued with none.
So turnes she euery man the wrong side out,
And neuer giues to Truth and Vertue, that
Which simplenesse and merit purchaseth.

speeches.speaker: Vrsu.
prose: Sure, sure, such carping is not commendable.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: No, not to be so odde, and from all fashions,
As Beatrice is, cannot be commendable,
But who dare tell her so? if I should speake,
She would mocke me into ayre, O she would laugh me
Out of my selfe, presse me to death with wit,
Therefore let Benedicke like couered fire,
Consume away in sighes, waste inwardly:
It were a better death, to die with mockes,
Which is as bad as die with tickling.

speeches.speaker: ~rsu.
prose: Yet tell her of it, heare what shee will say.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: No, rather I will goe to Benedicke,
And counsaile him to fight against his passion,
And truly Ile deuise some honest slanders,
To staine my cosin with, one doth not know,
How much an ill word may impoison liking.

speeches.speaker: ~rsu.
verse: O doe not doe your cosin such a wrong,
She cannot be so much without true iudgement,
Hauing so swift and excellent a wit
As she is prisde to haue, as to refuse
So rare a Gentleman as signior Benedicke.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: He is the onely man of Italy,
Alwaies excepted, my deare Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Vrsu.
verse: I pray you be not angry with me, Madame,
Speaking my fancy: Signior Benedicke,
For shape, for bearing argument and valour,
Goes formost in report through Italy.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Indeed he hath an excellent good name.

speeches.speaker: ~rsu.
verse: His excellence did earne it ere he had it:
When are you married Madame?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Why euerie day to morrow, come goe in,
Ile shew thee some attires, and haue thy counsell,
Which is the best to furnish me to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Vrsu.
verse: Shee's tane I warrant you,
We haue caught her Madame?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: If it proue so, then louing goes by haps,
Some Cupid kills with arrowes, some with traps.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
verse: What fire is in mine eares? can this be true?
Stand I condemn'd for pride and scorne so much?
Contempt, farewell, and maiden pride, adew,
No glory liues behinde the backe of such.
And Benedicke, loue on, I will requite thee,
Taming my wilde heart to thy louing hand:
If thou dost loue, my kindenesse shall incite thee
To binde our loues vp in a holy band.
For others say thou dost deserue, and I
Beleeue it better then reportingly.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: I doe but stay till your marriage be consummate, and then go I toward Arragon.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Ile bring you thither my Lord, if you'l vouchsafe me.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Nay, that would be as great a soyle in the new glosse of your marriage, as to shew a childe his new coat and forbid him to weare it, I will onely bee bold with Benedicke for his companie, for from the crowne of his head, to the sole of his foot, he is all mirth, he hath twice or thrice cut Cupids bow-string, and the little hang-man dare not shoot at him, he hath a heart as sound as a bell, and his tongue is the clapper, for what his heart thinkes, his tongue speakes.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Gallants, I am not as I haue bin.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: So say I, methinkes you are sadder.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: I hope he be in loue.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Hang him truant, there's no true drop of bloud in him to be truly toucht with loue, if he be sad, he wants money.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I haue the tooth-ach.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Draw it.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Hang it.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: You must hang it first, and draw it afterwards.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: What? sigh for the tooth-ach.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Where is but a humour or a worme.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Well, euery one cannot master a griefe, but hee that has it.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Yet say I, he is in loue.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: There is no appearance of fancie in him, vnlesse it be a fancy that he hath to strange disguises, as to bee a Dutchman to day, a Frenchman to morrow: vnlesse hee haue a fancy to this foolery, as it appeares hee hath, hee is no foole for fancy, as you would haue it to appeare he is.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If he be not in loue vvith some vvoman, there is no beleeuing old signes, a brushes his hat a mornings, What should that bode?

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Hath any man seene him at the Barbers?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: No, but the Barbers man hath beene seen with him, and the olde ornament of his cheeke hath alreadie stuft tennis balls.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Indeed he lookes yonger than hee did, by the losse of a beard.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Nay a rubs himselfe vvith Ciuit, can you smell him out by that?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: That's as much as to say, the sweet youth's in loue.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: The greatest note of it is his melancholy.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: And vvhen vvas he vvont to vvash his face?

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Yea, or to paint himselfe? for the which I heare vvhat they say of him.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Nay, but his iesting spirit, vvhich is now crept into a lute-string, and now gouern'd by stops.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Indeed that tels a heauy tale for him: conclude, he is in loue.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Nay, but I know who loues him.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: That would I know too, I warrant one that knowes him not.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Yes, and his ill conditions, and in despight of all, dies for him.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Shee shall be buried with her face vpwards.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Yet is this no charme for the tooth-ake, old signior, walke aside with mee, I haue studied eight or nine wise words to speake to you, which these hobby-horses must not heare.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: For my life to breake with him about Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: 'Tis euen so, Hero and Margaret haue by this played their parts with Beatrice, and then the two Beares will not bite one another when they meete.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: My Lord and brother, God saue you.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Good den brother.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: If your leisure seru'd, I would speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
prose: In priuate?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: If it please you, yet Count Claudio may heare, for what I would speake of, concernes him.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Basta.
prose: Meanes your Lordship to be married to morrow?

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: You know he does.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I know not that when he knowes what I know.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If there be any impediment, I pray you discouer it.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: You may thinke I loue you not, let that appeare hereafter, and ayme better at me by that I now will manifest, for my brother (I thinke, he holds you well, and in dearenesse of heart) hath holpe to effect your ensuing marriage: surely sute ill spent, and labour ill bestowed.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Why, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Bastard.
prose: I came hither to tell you, and circumstances shortned, (for she hath beene too long a talking of) the Lady is disloyall.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Who Hero?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Euen shee, Leonatoes Hero, your Hero, euery mans Hero.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Disloyall?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: The word is too good to paint out her wickednesse, I could say she were worse, thinke you of a worse title, and I will fit her to it: wonder not till further warrant: goe but with mee to night, you shal see her chamber window entred, euen the night before her wedding day, if you loue her, then to morrow wed her: But it would better fit your honour to change your minde.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: May this be so?

speeches.speaker: Princ.
prose: I will not thinke it.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: If you dare not trust that you see, confesse not that you know: if you will follow mee, I will shew you enough, and when you haue seene more, & heard more, proceed accordingly.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If I see any thing to night, why I should not marry her to morrow in the congregation, where I shold wedde, there will I shame her.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: And as I wooed for thee to obtaine her, I will ioyne with thee to disgrace her.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I will disparage her no farther, till you are my witnesses, beare it coldly but till night, and let the issue shew it selfe.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: O day vntowardly turned!

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: O mischiefe strangelie thwarting!

speeches.speaker: Bastard.
prose: O plague right well preuented! so will you say, when you haue seene the sequele.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: Are you good men and true?

speeches.speaker: Verg.
prose: Yea, or else it were pitty but they should suffer saluation body and soule.

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: Nay, that were a punishment too good for them, if they should haue any allegiance in them, being chosen for the Princes watch.

speeches.speaker: Verges.
prose: Well, giue them their charge, neighbour Dogbery.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: First, who thinke you the most desartlesse man to be Constable?

speeches.speaker: Watch. 1.
prose: Hugh Ote-cake sir, or George Sea-coale, for they can write and reade.

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: Come hither neighbour Sea-coale, God hath blest you with a good name: to be a wel-fauoured man, is the gift of Fortune, but to write and reade, comes by Nature.

speeches.speaker: Watch 2.
prose: Both which Master Constable

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: You haue: I knew it would be your answere: well, for your fauour sir, why giue God thankes, & make no boast of it, and for your writing and reading, let that appeare when there is no need of such vanity, you are thought heere to be the most senslesse and fit man for the Constable of the watch: therefore beare you the lanthorne: this is your charge: You shall comprehend all vagrom men, you are to bid any man stand in the Princes name.

speeches.speaker: Watch 2.
prose: How if a will not stand?

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: Why then take no note of him, but let him go, and presently call the rest of the Watch together, and thanke God you are ridde of a knaue.

speeches.speaker: ~erges.
prose: If he will not stand when he is bidden, hee is none of the Princes subiects.

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: True, and they are to meddle with none but the Princes subiects: you shall also make no noise in the streetes: for, for the Watch to babble and talke, is most tollerable, and not to be indured.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: We will rather sleepe than talke, wee know what belongs to a Watch.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: Why you speake like an ancient and most quiet watchman, for I cannot see how sleeping should offend: only haue a care that your bills be not stolne: well, you are to call at all the Alehouses, and bid them that are drunke get them to bed.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: How if they will not?

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: Why then let them alone till they are sober, if they make you not then the better answere, you may say, they are not the men you tooke them for.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: Well sir.

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: If you meet a theefe, you may suspect him, by vertue of your office, to be no true man. and for such kinde of men, the lesse you meddle or make with them, why the more is for your honesty.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: If wee know him to be a thiefe, shall wee not lay hands on him.

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: Truly by your office you may, but I think they that touch pitch will be defil'd: the most peaceable way for you, if you doe take a theefe, is, to let him shew himselfe what he is, and steale out of your company.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: You haue bin alwaies cal'd a merciful ma~ partner.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: Truely I would not hang a dog by my will, much more a man who hath anie honestie in him.

speeches.speaker: Verges.
prose: If you heare a child crie in the night you must call to the nurse, and bid her still it.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: How if the nurse be asleepe and will not heare vs?

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: Why then depart in peace, and let the childe wake her with crying, for the ewe that will not heare her Lambe when it baes, will neuer answere a calfe when he bleates.

speeches.speaker: Verges.
prose: 'Tis verie true.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: This is the end of the charge: you constable are to present the Princes owne person, if you meete the Prince in the night, you may staie him.

speeches.speaker: Verges.
prose: Nay birladie that I thinke a cannot.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: Fiue shillings to one on't with anie man that knowes the Statues, he may staie him, marrie not without the prince be willing, for indeed the watch ought to offend no man, and it is an offence to stay a man against his will.

speeches.speaker: ~erges.
prose: Birladie I thinke it be so.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: Ha, ah ha, well masters good night, and there be anie matter of weight chances, call vp me, keepe your fellowes counsailes, and your owne, and good night, come neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: Well masters, we heare our charge, let vs go sit here vpon the Church bench till two, and then all to bed.

speeches.speaker: Dog.
prose: One word more, honest neighbors. I pray you watch about signior Leonatoes doore, for the wedding being there to morrow, there is a great coyle to night, adiew, be vigitant I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: What, Conrade?

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: Peace, stir not.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Conrade I say.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Here man, I am at thy elbow.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Mas and my elbow itcht, I thought there would a scabbe follow.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: I will owe thee an answere. for that, and now forward with thy tale.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Stand thee close then vnder this penthouse, for it drissels raine, and I will, like a true drunkard, vtter all to thee.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: Some treason masters, yet stand close.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Therefore know, I haue earned of Don Iohn a thousand Ducates.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Is it possible that anie villanie should be so deare?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Thou should'st rather aske if it were possible anie villanie should be so rich? for when rich villains haue neede of poore ones, poore ones may make what price they will.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: I wonder at it.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: That shewes thou art vnconfirm'd, thou knowest that the fashion of a doublet, or a hat, or a cloake, is nothing to a man.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Yes, it is apparell.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: I meane the fashion.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Yes the fashion is the fashion.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Tush, I may as well say the foole's the foole, but seest thou not what a deformed theefe this fashion is?

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: I know that deformed, a has bin a vile theefe, this vii. yeares, a goes vp and downe like a gentle man: I remember his name.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Did'st thou not heare some bodie?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: No, 'twas the vaine on the house.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Seest thou not (I say) what a deformed thiefe this fashion is, how giddily a turnes about all the Hot-blouds, betweene foureteene & fiue & thirtie, sometimes fashioning them like Pharaoes souldiours in the rechie painting, sometime like god Bels priests in the old Church window, sometime like the shauen Hercules in the smircht worm eaten tapestrie, where his cod-peece seemes as massie as his club.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: All this I see, and see that the fashion weares out more apparrell then the man; but art not thou thy selfe giddie with the fashion too that thou hast shifted out of thy tale into telling me of the fashion?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Not so neither, but know that I haue to night wooed Margaret the Lady Heroes gentle-woman, by the name of Hero, she leanes me out at her mistris chamber-vvindow, bids me a thousand times good night: I tell this tale vildly. I should first tell thee how the Prince Claudio and my Master planted, and placed, and possessed by my Master Don Iohn, saw a far off in the Orchard this amiable incounter.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: And thought thy Margaret was Hero?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Two of them did, the Prince and Claudio, but the diuell my Master knew she was Margaret and partly by his oathes, which first possest them, partly by the darke night which did deceiue them, but chiefely, by my villanie, which did confirme any slander that Don Iohn had made, away vvent Claudio enraged, swore hee vvould meete her as he was apointed next morning at the Temple, and there, before the whole congregation shame her with vvhat he saw o're night, and send her home againe vvithout a husband.

speeches.speaker: Watch. 1.
prose: We charge you in the Princes name stand.

speeches.speaker: Watch. 2.
prose: Call vp the right master Constable, vve haue here recouered the most dangerous peece of lechery, that euer vvas knowne in the Common-wealth.

speeches.speaker: Watch. 1.
prose: And one Deformed is one of them, I know him, a vveares a locke.

speeches.speaker: Conr.
prose: Mast^ masters.

speeches.speaker: Watch. 2.
prose: Youre be made bring deformed forth I warrant you,

speeches.speaker: Conr.
prose: Masters, neuer speake, vve charge you, let vs obey you to goe vvith vs.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: We are like to proue a goodly commoditie, being taken vp of these mens bils.

speeches.speaker: Conr.
prose: A commoditie in question I warrant you, come vveele obey you.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Good Vrsula wake my cosin Beatrice, and desire her to rise.

speeches.speaker: ~rsu.
prose: I will Lady.

speeches.speaker: Her.
prose: And bid her come hither.

speeches.speaker: Vrs.
prose: Well.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Troth I thinke your other rebato were better.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
prose: No pray thee good Meg, Ile vveare this.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
prose: By my troth's not so good, and I vvarrant your cosin vvill say so.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
prose: My cosin's a foole, and thou art another, ile vveare none but this.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I like the new tire vvithin excellently, if the haire vvere a thought browner: and your gown's a most rare fashion yfaith, I saw the Dutchesse of Millaines gowne that they praise so.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
prose: O that exceedes they say.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: By my troth's but a night-gowne in respect of yours, cloth a gold and cuts and lac'd with siluer, set with pearles, downe sleeues, side sleeues, and skirts, round vnderborn with a blewish tinsel, but for a fine queint gracefull and excellent fashion, yours is worth ten on't.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: God giue mee ioy to weare it, for my heart is exceeding heauy.

speeches.speaker: Marga.
prose: 'Twill be heauier soone, by the waight of a man.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Fie vpon thee, art not asham'd?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
prose: Of what Lady? of speaking honourably? is not marriage honourable in a beggar? is not your Lord honourable without marriage? I thinke you would haue me say, sauing your reuerence a husband: and bad thinking doe not wrest true speaking, Ile offend no body, is there any harme in the heauier for a husband? none I thinke, and it be the right husband, and the right wife, otherwise 'tis light and not heauy, aske my Lady Beatrice else, here she comes.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Good morrow Coze.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Good morrow sweet Hero.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Why how now? do you speake in the sick tune?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I am out of all other tune, me thinkes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Claps into Light a loue, (that goes without a burden,) do you sing it and Ile dance it.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Ye Light aloue with your heeles, then if your husband haue stables enough, you'll looke he shall lacke no barnes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: O illegitimate construction! I scorne that with my heeles.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: 'Tis almost fiue a clocke cosin, 'tis time you were ready, by my troth I am exceeding ill, hey ho.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: For a hauke, a horse, or a husband?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: For the letter that begins them all, H.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Well, and you be not turn'd Turke, there's no more sayling by the starre.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: What meanes the foole trow?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Nothing I, but God send euery one rheir harts desire.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: These gloues the Count sent mee, they are an excellent perfume.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I am stuft cosin, I cannot smell.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: A maid and stuft! there's goodly catching of colde.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: O God helpe me, God help me, how long haue you profest apprehension?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Euer since you left it, doth not my wit become me rarely?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: It is not seene enough, you should weare it in your cap, by my troth I am sicke.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Get you some of this distill'd carduus benedictus and lay it to your heart, it is the onely thing for a qualm.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: There thou prickst her with a thissell.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Benedictus, why benedictus? you haue some morall in this benedictus.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Morall? no by my troth, I haue no morall meaning, I meant plaine holy thissell, you may thinke perchance that I thinke you are in loue, nay birlady I am not such a foole to thinke what I list, nor I list not to thinke what I can, nor indeed I cannot thinke, if I would thinke my hart out of thinking, that you are in loue, or that you will be in loue, or that you can be in loue: yet Benedicke was such another, and now is he become a man, he swore hee would neuer marry, and yet now in despight of his heart he eates his meat without grudging, and how you may be conuerted I know not, but me thinkes you looke with your eies as other women doe.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: What pace is this that thy tongue keepes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Not a false gallop.

speeches.speaker: Vrsula.
prose: Madam, withdraw, the Prince, the Count, signior Benedicke, Don Iohn, and all the gallants of the towne are come to fetch you to Church.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Helpe to dresse mee good coze, good Meg, good Vrsula.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: What would you with mee, honest neighbour?

speeches.speaker: Const. Dog.
prose: Mary sir I would haue some confidence with you, that decernes you nearely.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Briefe I pray you, for you see it is a busie time with me.

speeches.speaker: Const. Dog.
prose: Mary this it is sir.

speeches.speaker: Headb.
prose: Yes in truth it is sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: What is it my good friends?

speeches.speaker: Con. Do.
prose: Goodman Verges sir speakes a little of the matter, an old man sir, and his wits are not so blunt, as God helpe I would desire they were, but infaith honest as the skin betweene his browes.

speeches.speaker: Head.
prose: Yes I thank God, I am as honest as any man liuing, that is an old man, and no honester then I.

speeches.speaker: Con. Dog.
prose: Comparisons are odorous, palabras, neighbour Verges.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Neighbours, you are tedious.

speeches.speaker: Con. Dog.
prose: It pleases your worship to say so, but we are the poore Dukes officers, but truely for mine owne part, if I were as tedious as a King I could finde in my heart to bestow it all of your worship.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: All thy tediousnesse on me, ah?

speeches.speaker: Const. Dog.
prose: Yea, and 'twere a thousand times more than 'tis, for I heare as good exclamation on your Worship as of any man in the Citie, and though I bee but a poore man, I am glad to heare it.

speeches.speaker: Head.
prose: And so am I.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I would faine know what you haue to say.

speeches.speaker: Head.
prose: Marry sir our watch to night, excepting your worships presence, haue tane a couple of as arrant knaues as any in Messina.

speeches.speaker: Con. Dog.
prose: A good old man sir, hee will be talking as they say, when the age is in the wit is out, God helpe vs, it is a world to see: well said yfaith neighbour Verges, well, God's a good man, and two men ride of a horse, one must ride behinde, an honest soule yfaith sir, by my troth he is, as euer broke bread, but God is to bee worshipt, all men are not alike, alas good neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Indeed neighbour he comes too short of you.

speeches.speaker: Con. Do.
prose: Gifts that God giues.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I must leaue you.

speeches.speaker: Con. Dog.
prose: One word sir, our watch sir haue indeede comprehended two aspitious persons, & we would haue them this morning examined before your worship.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Take their examination your selfe, and bring it me, I am now in great haste, as may appeare vnto you.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: It shall be suffigance.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Drinke some wine ere you goe: fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Messenger.
prose: My Lord, they stay for you to giue your daughter to her husband.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Ile wait vpon them, I am ready.

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose: Goe good partner, goe get you to Francis Sea-coale, bid him bring his pen and inkehorne to the Gaole: we are now to examine those men.

speeches.speaker: Verges.
prose: And we must doe it wisely.

speeches.speaker: Dogb.
prose:
Wee will spare for no witte I warrant you:

heere's that shall driue some of them to a non-come, only get the learned writer to set downe our excommunication, and meet me at the Iaile.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: Come Frier Francis, be briefe, onely to the plaine forme of marriage, and you shal recount their particular duties afterwards.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: You come hither, my Lord, to marry this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: To be married to her: Frier, you come to marrie her.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
prose: Lady, you come hither to be married to this Count.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: I doe.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
prose: If either of you know any inward impediment why you should not be conioyned, I charge you on your soules to vtter it.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Know you anie, Hero?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: None my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
prose: Know you anie, Count?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I dare make his answer, None.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: O what men dare do! what men may do! what men daily do!

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: How now! interiections? why then, some be of laughing, as ha, ha, he.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Stand thee by Frier, father, by your leaue,
Will you with free and vnconstrained soule
Giue me this maid your daughter?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: As freely sonne as God did giue her me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And what haue I to giue you back, whose worth
May counterpoise this rich and precious gift?

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Nothing, vnlesse you render her againe.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Sweet Prince, you learn me noble thankfulnes:
There Leonato, take her backe againe,
Giue not this rotten Orenge to your friend,
Shee's but the signe and semblance of her honour:
Behold how like a maid she blushes heere!
O what authoritie and shew of truth
Can cunning sinne couer it selfe withall!
Comes not that bloud, as modest euidence,
To witnesse simple Vertue? would you not sweare
All you that see her, that she were a maide,
By these exterior shewes? But she is none:
She knowes the heat of a luxurious bed:
Her blush is guiltinesse, not modestie.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: What doe you meane, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Not to be married,
Not to knit my soule to an approued wanton.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Deere my Lord, if you in your owne proofe,
Haue vanquisht the resistance of her youth,
And made defeat of her virginitie.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: I know what you would say: if I haue knowne her,
You will say, she did imbrace me as a husband,
And so extenuate the forehand sinne: No Leonato,
I neuer tempted her with word too large,
But as a brother to his sister, shewed
Bashfull sinceritie and comely loue.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: And seem'd I euer otherwise to you?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Out on thee seeming, I will write against it,
You seeme to me as Diane in her Orbe,
As chaste as is the budde ere it be blowne:
But you are more intemperate in your blood,
Than Venus, or those pampred animalls,
That rage in sauage sensualitie.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: Is my Lord well, that he doth speake so wide?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Sweete Prince, why speake not you?

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: What should I speake?
I stand dishonour'd that haue gone about,
To linke my deare friend to a common stale.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Are these things spoken, or doe I but dreame?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Sir, they are spoken, and these things are true.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: This lookes not like a nuptiall.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: True, O God!

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Leonato, stand I here?
Is this the Prince? is this the Princes brother?
Is this face Heroes? are our eies our owne?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: All this is so, but what of this my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Let me but moue one question to your daughter,
And by that fatherly and kindly power,
That you haue in her, bid her answer truly.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: I charge thee doe, as thou art my childe.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: O God defend me how am I beset,
What kinde of catechizing call you this?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: To make you answer truly to your name.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Is it not Hero? who can blot that name
With any iust reproach?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Marry that can Hero,
Hero it selfe can blot out Heroes vertue.
What man was he, talkt with you yesternight,
Out at your window betwixt twelue and one?
Now if you are a maid, answer to this.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
prose: I talkt with no man at that howre my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
verse: Why then you are no maiden. Leonato,
I am sorry you must heare: vpon mine honor,
My selfe, my brother, and this grieued Count
Did see her, heare her, at that howre last night,
Talke with a ruffian at her chamber window,
Who hath indeed most like a liberall villaine,
Confest the vile encounters they haue had
A thousand times in secret.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
verse: Fie, fie, they are not to be named my Lord,
Not to be spoken of,
There is not chastitie enough in language,
Without offence to vtter them: thus pretty Lady
I am sorry for thy much misgouernment.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: O Hero! what a Hero hadst thou beene
If halfe thy outward graces had beene placed
About thy thoughts and counsailes of thy heart?
But fare thee well, most foule, most faire, farewell
Thou pure impiety, and impious puritie,
For thee Ile locke vp all the gates of Loue,
And on my eie-lids shall Coniecture hang,
To turne all beauty into thoughts of harme,
And neuer shall it more be gracious.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Hath no mans dagger here a point for me?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Why how now cosin, wherfore sink you down?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: Come, let vs go: these things come thus to light,
Smother her spirits vp.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: How doth the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
verse: Dead I thinke, helpe vncle,
Hero, why Hero, Vncle, Signor Benedicke, Frier.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
verse: O Fate! take not away thy heauy hand,
Death is the fairest couer for her shame
That may be wisht for.

speeches.speaker: Beatr.
prose: How now cosin Hero?

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: Haue comfort Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Dost thou looke vp?

speeches.speaker: Frier.
prose: Yea, wherefore should she not?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Wherfore? Why doth not euery earthly thing
Cry shame vpon her? Could she heere denie
The storie that is printed in her blood?
Do not liue Hero, do not ope thine eyes:
For did I thinke thou wouldst not quickly die,
Thought I thy spirits were stronger then thy shames,
My selfe would on the reward of reproaches
Strike at thy life. Grieu'd I, I had but one?
Chid I, for that at frugal Natures frame?
O one too much by thee: why had I one?
Why euer was't thou louelie in my eies?
Why had I not with charitable hand
Tooke vp a beggars issue at my gates,
Who smeered thus, and mir'd with infamie,
I might haue said, no part of it is mine:
This shame deriues it selfe from vnknowne loines,
But mine, and mine I lou'd, and mine I prais'd,
And mine that I was proud on mine so much,
That I my selfe, was to my selfe not mine:
Valewing of her, why she, O she is falne
Into a pit of Inke, that the wide sea
Hath drops too few to wash her cleane againe,
And salt too little, which may season giue
To her foule tainted flesh.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Sir, sir, be patient: for my part, I am so attired in wonder, I know not what to say.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: O on my soule my cosin is belied.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Ladie, were you her bedfellow last night?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
verse: No truly: not although vntill last night,
I haue this tweluemonth bin her bedfellow.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Confirm'd, confirm'd, O that is stronger made
Which was before barr'd vp with ribs of iron.
Would the Princes lie, and Claudio lie,
Who lou'd her so, that speaking of her foulnesse,
Wash'd it with teares? Hence from her, let her die.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: A thousand blushing apparitions,
To start into her face, a thousand innocent shames,
In Angel whitenesse beare away those blushes,
And in her eie there hath appear'd a fire
To burne the errors that these Princes hold
Against her maiden truth. Call me a foole,
Trust not my reading, nor my obseruations,
Which with experimental seale doth warrant
The tenure of my booke: trust not my age,
My reuerence, calling, nor diuinitie,
If this sweet Ladie lye not guiltlesse heere,
Vnder some biting error.
prose: Heare me a little, for I haue onely bene silent so long, and giuen way vnto this course of fortune, by noting of the Ladie, I haue markt.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Friar, it cannot be:
Thou seest that all the Grace that she hath left,
Is, that she wil not adde to her damnation,
A sinne of periury, she not denies it:
Why seek'st thou then to couer with excuse,
That which appeares in proper nakednesse?

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: Ladie, what man is he you are accus'd of?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: They know that do accuse me, I know none:
If I know more of any man aliue
Then that which maiden modestie doth warrant,
Let all my sinnes lacke mercy. O my Father,
Proue you that any man with me conuerst,
At houres vnmeete, or that I yesternight
Maintain'd the change of words with any creature,
Refuse me, hate me, torture me to death.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: There is some strange misprision in the Princes.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Two of them haue the verie bent of honor,
And if their wisedomes be misled in this:
The practise of it liues in Iohn the bastard,
Whose spirits toile in frame of villanies.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I know not: if they speake but truth of her,
These hands shall teare her: If they wrong her honour,
The proudest of them shall wel heare of it.
Time hath not yet so dried this bloud of mine,
Nor age so eate vp my inuention,
Nor Fortune made such hauocke of my meanes,
Nor my bad life rest me so much of friends,
But they shall finde, awak'd in such a kinde,
Both strength of limbe, and policie of minde,
Ability in meanes, and choise of friends,
To quit me of them throughly.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Pause awhile:
And let my counsell sway you in this case,
Your daughter heere the Princesse (left for dead)
Let her awhile be secretly kept in,
And publish it, that she is dead indeed:
Maintaine a mourning ostentation,
And on your Families old monument,
Hang mournfull Epitaphes, and do all rites,
That appertaine vnto a buriall.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: What shall become of this? What wil this do?

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Marry this wel carried, shall on her behalfe,
Change slander to remorse, that is some good,
But not for that dreame I on this strange course,
But on this trauaile looke for greater birth:
She dying, as it must be so maintain'd,
Vpon the instant that she was accus'd,
Shal be lamented, pittied, and excus'd
Of euery hearer: for it so fals out,
That what we haue, we prize not to the worth,
Whiles we enioy it; but being lack'd and lost,
Why then we racke the value, then we finde
The vertue that possession would not shew vs
Whiles it was ours, so will it fare with Claudio:
When he shal heare she dyed vpon his words,
Th' Idea of her life shal sweetly creepe
Into his study of imagination.
And euery louely Organ of her life,
Shall come apparel'd in more precious habite:
More mouing delicate, and ful of life,
Into the eye and prospect of his soule
Then when she liu'd indeed: then shal he mourne,
If euer Loue had interest in his Liuer,
And wish he had not so accused her:
No, though he thought his accusation true:
Let this be so, and doubt not but successe
Wil fashion the euent in better shape,
Then I can lay it downe in likelihood.
But if all ayme but this be leuelld false,
The supposition of the Ladies death,
Will quench the wonder of her infamie.
And if it sort not well, you may conceale her,
As best befits her wounded reputation,
In some reclusiue and religious life,
Out of all eyes, tongues, mindes and iniuries.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
verse: Signior Leonato, let the Frier aduise you,
And though you know my inwardnesse and loue
Is very much vnto the Prince and Claudio.
Yet, by mine honor, I will deale in this.
As secretly and iustlie, as your soule
Should with your bodie.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Being that I flow in greefe,
The smallest twine may lead me.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
verse: 'Tis well consented, presently away,
For to strange sores, strangely they straine the cure,
Come Lady, die to liue, this wedding day
Perhaps is but prolong'd, haue patience & endure.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Lady Beatrice, haue you wept all this while?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Yea, and I will weepe a while longer.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I will not desire that.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: You haue no reason, I doe it freely.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Surelie I do beleeue your fair cosin is wrong'd.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Ah, how much might the man deserue of mee that would right her!

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Is there any way to shew such friendship?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: A verie euen way, but no such friend.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: May a man doe it?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: It is a mans office, but not yours.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I doe loue nothing in the world so well as you, is not that strange?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: As strange as the thing I know not, it were as possible for me to say, I loued nothing so well as you, but beleeue me not, and yet I lie not, I confesse nothing, nor I deny nothing, I am sorry for my cousin.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: By my sword Beatrice thou lou'st me.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Doe not sweare by it and eat it.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I will sweare by it that you loue mee, and I will make him eat it that sayes I loue not you.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Will you not eat your word?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: With no sawce that can be deuised to it, I protest I loue thee.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Why then God forgiue me.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: What offence sweet Beatrice?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: You haue stayed me in a happy howre; I was about to protest I loued you.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: And doe it with all thy heart.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I loue you with so much of my heart, that none is left to protest.

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: Come, bid me doe any thing for thee.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Kill Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Ha, not for the wide world.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: You kill me to denie, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Tarrie sweet Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I am gone, though I am heere, there is no loue in you, nay I pray you let me goe.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Infaith I will goe.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Wee'll be friends first.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: You dare easier be friends with mee, than fight with mine enemy.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Is Claudio thine enemie?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Is a not approued in the height a villaine, that hath slandered, scorned, dishonoured my kinswoman? O that I were a man! what, beare her in hand vntill they come to take hands, and then with publike accusation vncouered slander, vnmittigated rancour? O God that I were a man! I would eat his heart in the market-place.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Heare me Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Talke with a man out at a window, a proper saying.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Nay but Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Sweet Hero, she is wrong'd, shee is slandered, she is vndone.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Beat?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Princes and Counties! surelie a Princely testimonie, a goodly Count, Comfect, a sweet Gallant surelie, O that I were a man for his sake! or that I had any friend would be a man for my sake! But manhood is melted into cursies, valour into complement, and men are onelie turned into tongue, and trim ones too: he is now as valiant as Hercules, that only tells a lie, and sweares it: I cannot be a man with wishing, therfore I will die a woman with grieuing.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Tarry good Beatrice, by this hand I loue thee.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Vse it for my loue some other way then swearing by it.

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: Thinke you in your soule the Count Claudio hath wrong'd Hero?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Yea, as sure as I haue a thought, or a soule.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Enough, I am engagde, I will challenge him, I will kisse your hand, and so leaue you: by this hand Claudio shall render me a deere account: as you heare of me, so thinke of me: goe comfort your coosin, I must say she is dead, and so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Keeper.
prose: Is our whole dissembly appeard?

speeches.speaker: Cowley.
prose: O a stoole and a cushion for the Sexton.

speeches.speaker: Sexton.
prose: Which be the malefactors?

speeches.speaker: Andrew.
prose: Marry that am I, and my partner.

speeches.speaker: Cowley.
prose: Nay that's certaine, wee haue the exhibition to examine.

speeches.speaker: Sexton.
prose: But which are the offenders that are to be examined, let them come before master Constable.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: Yea marry, let them come before mee, what is your name, friend?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Borachio.

speeches.speaker: Kem.
prose: Pray write downe Borachio. Yours sirra.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: I am a Gentleman sir, and my name is Conrade.

speeches.speaker: Kee.
prose:
Write downe Master gentleman Conrade^
: maisters, doe you serue God: maisters, it is proued alreadie that you are little better than false knaues, and it will goe neere to be thought so shortly, how answer you for your selues?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Marry sir, we say we are none.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: A maruellous witty fellow I assure you, but I will goe about with him: come you hither sirra, a word in your eare sir, I say to you, it is thought you are false knaues.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Sir, I say to you, we are none.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: Well, stand aside, 'fore God they are both in a tale: haue you writ downe that they are none?

speeches.speaker: Sext.
prose: Master Constable, you goe not the way to examine, you must call forth the watch that are their accusers.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: Yea marry, that's the eftest way, let the watch come forth: masters, I charge you in the Princes name, accuse these men.

speeches.speaker: Watch 1.
prose: This man said sir, that Don Iohn the Princes brother was a villaine.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: Write down, Prince Iohn a villaine: why this is flat periurie, to call a Princes brother villaine.

speeches.speaker: Bora.
prose: Master Constable.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: Pray thee fellow peace, I do not like thy looke I promise thee.

speeches.speaker: Sexton.
prose: What heard you him say else?

speeches.speaker: Watch 2.
prose: Mary that he had receiued a thousand Dukates of Don Iohn, for accusing the Lady Hero wrongfully.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: Flat Burglarie as euer was committed.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Yea by th' masse that it is.

speeches.speaker: Sexton.
prose: What else fellow?

speeches.speaker: Watch 1.
prose: And that Count Claudio did meane vpon his words, to disgrace Hero before the whole assembly, and not marry her.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: O villaine! thou wilt be condemn'd into euerlasting redemption for this.

speeches.speaker: Sexton.
prose: What else?

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: This is all.

speeches.speaker: Sexton.
prose: And this is more masters then you can deny, Prince Iohn is this morning secretly stolne away: Hero was in this manner accus'd, in this very manner refus'd, and vpon the griefe of this sodainely died: Master Constable, let these men be bound, and brought to Leonato, I will goe before, and shew him their examination.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Come, let them be opinion'd.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
prose: Let them be in the hands of Coxcombe.

speeches.speaker: Kem.
prose: Gods my life, where's the Sexton? let him write downe the Princes Officer Coxcombe: come, binde them thou naughty varlet.

speeches.speaker: Couley.
prose: Away, you are an asse, you are an asse.

speeches.speaker: Kemp.
prose: Dost thou not suspect my place? dost thou not suspect my yeeres? O that hee were heere to write mee downe an asse! but masters, remember that I am an asse: though it be not written down, yet forget not yt I am an asse: No thou villaine, yu art full of piety as shall be prou'd vpon thee by good witnesse, I am a wise fellow, and which is more, an officer, and which is more, a houshoulder, and which is more, as pretty a peece of flesh as any in Messina, and one that knowes the Law, goe to, & a rich fellow enough, goe to, and a fellow that hath had losses, and one that hath two gownes, and euery thing handsome about him: bring him away: O that I had been writ downe an asse!

speeches.speaker: Brother.
verse: If you goe on thus, you will kill your selfe,
And 'tis not wisedome thus to second griefe,
Against your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I pray thee cease thy counsaile,
Which falls into mine eares as profitlesse,
As water in a siue: giue not me counsaile,
Nor let no comfort delight mine eare,
But such a one whose wrongs doth sute with mine.
Bring me a father that so lou'd his childe,
Whose ioy of her is ouer-whelmed like mine,
And bid him speake of patience,
Measure his woe the length and bredth of mine,
And let it answere euery straine for straine,
As thus for thus, and such a griefe for such,
In euery lineament, branch, shape, and forme:
If such a one will smile and stroke his beard,
And sorrow, wagge, crie hem, when he should grone,
Patch griefe with prouerbs, make misfortune drunke,
With candle-wasters: bring him yet to me,
And I of him will gather patience:
But there is no such man for brother, men
Can counsaile, and speake comfort to that griefe,
Which they themselues not feele, but to sting it,
Their counsaile turnes to passion, which before,
Would giue preceptiall medicine to rage,
Fetter strong madnesse in a silken thred,
Charme ache with ayre, and agony with words,
No, no, 'tis all mens office, to speake patience
To those that wring vnder the load of sorrow:
But no mans vertue nor sufficiencie
To be so morall, when he shall endure
The like himselfe: therefore giue me no counsaile,
My griefs cry lowder then aduertisement.

speeches.speaker: Broth.
prose: Therein do men from children nothing differ.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
verse: I pray thee peace, I will be flesh and bloud,
For there was neuer yet Philosopher,
That could endure the tooth-ake patiently,
How euer they haue writ the stile of gods,
And made a push at chance and sufferance.

speeches.speaker: Brother.
verse: Yet bend not all the harme vpon your selfe,
Make those that doe offend you, suffer too.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
