verse: There thou speak'st reason, nay I will doe so,
My soule doth tell me, Hero is belied,
And that shall Claudio know, so shall the Prince,
And all of them that thus dishonour her.

speeches.speaker: Brot.
prose: Here comes the Prince and Claudio hastily.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Good den, good den.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Good day to both of you.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Heare you my Lords?

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: We haue some haste Leonato.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Some haste my Lord! wel, fareyouwel my Lord,
Are you so hasty now? well, all is one.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Nay, do not quarrell with vs, good old man.

speeches.speaker: Brot.
verse: If he could rite himselfe with quarrelling,
Some of vs would lie low.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Who wrongs him?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Marry yu dost wrong me, thou dissembler, thou:
Nay, neuer lay thy hand vpon thy sword,
I feare thee not.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Marry beshrew my hand,
If it should giue your age such cause of feare,
Infaith my hand meant nothing to my sword.

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
verse: Tush, tush, man, neuer fleere and iest at me,
I speake not like a do^ard, nor a foole,
As vnder priuiledge of age to bragge,
What I haue done being yong, or what would doe,
Were I not old, know Claudio to thy head,
Thou hast so wrong'd my innocent childe and me,
That I am forc'd to lay my reuerence by,
And with grey haires and bruise of many daies,
Doe challenge thee to triall of a man,
I say thou hast belied mine innocent childe.
Thy slander hath gone through and through her heart,
And she lies buried with her ancestors:
O in a tombe where neuer scandall slept,
Saue this of hers, fram'd by thy villanie.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: My villany?

speeches.speaker: Leonato.
prose: Thine Claudio, thine I say.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: You say not right old man.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: My Lord, my Lord,
Ile proue it on his body if he dare,
Despight his nice fence, and his actiue practise,
His Maie of youth, and bloome of lustihood.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Away, I will not haue to do with you.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Canst thou so daffe me? thou hast kild my child,
If thou kilst me, boy, thou shalt kill a man.

speeches.speaker: Bro.
verse: He shall kill two of vs, and men indeed,
But that's no matter, let him kill one first:
Win me and weare me, let him answere me,
Come follow me boy, come sir boy, come follow me
Sir boy, ile whip you from your foyning fence,
Nay, as I am a gentleman, I will.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Brother.

speeches.speaker: Brot.
verse: Content your self, God knows I lou'd my neece,
And she is dead, slander'd to death by villaines,
That dare as well answer a man indeede,
As I dare take a serpent by the tongue.
Boyes, apes, braggarts, Iackes, milke-sops.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Brother Anthony.

speeches.speaker: Brot.
verse: Hold you content, what man? I know them, yea
And what they weigh, euen to the vtmost scruple,
Scambling, out-facing, fashion-monging boyes,
That lye, and cog, and flout, depraue, and slander,
Goe antiquely, and show outward hidiousnesse,
And speake of halfe a dozen dang'rous words,
How they might hurt their enemies, if they durst.
And this is all.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: But brother Anthonie.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Come, 'tis no matter,
Do not you meddle, let me deale in this.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Gentlemen both, we will not wake your patience
My heart is sorry for your daughters death:
But on my honour she was charg'd with nothing
But what was true, and very full of proofe.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: My Lord, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: I will not heare you.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: No come brother, away, I will be heard.

speeches.speaker: Bro.
prose: And shall, or some of vs will smart for it.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: See, see, here comes the man we went to seeke.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Now signior, what newes?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Good day my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Welcome signior, you are almost come to part almost a fray.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Wee had likt to haue had our two noses snapt off with two old men without teeth.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Leonato and his brother, what think'st thou? had wee fought, I doubt we should haue beene too yong for them.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: In a false quarrell there is no true valour, I came to seeke you both.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: We haue beene vp and downe to seeke thee, for we are high proofe melancholly, and would faine haue it beaten away, wilt thou vse thy wit?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: It is in my scabberd, shall I draw it?

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Doest thou weare thy wit by thy side?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Neuer any did so, though verie many haue been beside their wit, I will bid thee drawe, as we do the minstrels, draw to pleasure vs.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: As I am an honest man he lookes pale, art thou sicke, or angrie?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: What, courage man: what though care kil'd a cat, thou hast mettle enough in thee to kill care.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Sir, I shall meete your wit in the careere, and you charge it against me, I pray you chuse another subiect.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Nay then giue him another staffe, this last was broke crosse.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: By this light, he changes more and more, I thinke he be angrie indeede.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: If he be, he knowes how to turne his girdle.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Shall I speake a word in your eare?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: God blesse me from a challenge.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: You are a villaine, I iest not, I will make it good how you dare, with what you dare, and when you dare: do me right, or I will protest your cowardise: you haue kill'd a sweete Ladie, and her death shall fall heauie on you, let me heare from you.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Well, I will meete you, so I may haue good cheare.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: What, a feast, a feast?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: I faith I thanke him, he hath bid me to a calues head and a Capon, the which if I doe not carue most curiously, say my knife's naught, shall I not finde a woodcocke too?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Sir, your wit ambles well, it goes easily.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Ile tell thee how Beatrice prais'd thy wit the other day: I said thou hadst a fine wit: true saies she, a fine little one: no said I, a great wit: right saies shee, a great grosse one: nay said I, a good wit: iust said she, it hurts no body: nay said I, the gentleman is wise: certain said she, a wise gentleman: nay said I, he hath the tongues: that I beleeue said shee, for hee swore a thing to me on munday night, which he forswore on tuesday morning: there's a double tongue, there's two tongues: thus did shee an howre together trans-shape thy particular vertues, yet at last she concluded with a sigh, thou wast the proprest man in Italie.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: For the which she wept heartily, and said shee car'd not.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Yea that she did, but yet for all that, and if shee did not hate him deadlie, shee would loue him dearely, the old mans daughter told vs all.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: All, all, and moreouer, God saw him vvhen he was hid in the garden.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: But when shall we set the sauage Bulls hornes on the sensible Benedicks head?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Yea and text vnder-neath, heere dwells Benedicke the married man.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Fare you well, Boy, you know my minde, I will leaue you now to your gossep-like humor, you breake iests as braggards do their blades, which God be thanked hurt not: my Lord, for your manie courtesies I thank you, I must discontinue your companie, your brother the Bastard is fled from Messina: you haue among you, kill'd a sweet and innocent Ladie: for my Lord Lackebeard there, he and I shall meete, and till then peace be with him.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: He is in earnest.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: In most profound earnest, and Ile warrant you, for the loue of Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: And hath challeng'd thee.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Most sincerely.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: What a prettie thing man is, when he goes in his doublet and hose, and leaues off his wit.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: He is then a Giant to an Ape, but then is an Ape a Doctor to such a man.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: But soft you, let me be, plucke vp my heart, and be sad, did he not say my brother was fled?

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Come you sir, if iustice cannot tame you, shee shall nere weigh more reasons in her ballance, nay, and you be a cursing hypocrite once, you must be lookt to.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: How now, two of my brothers men bound? Borachio one.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Harken after their offence my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Officers, what offence haue these men done?

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Marrie sir, they haue committed false report, moreouer they haue spoken vntruths, secondarily they are slanders, sixt and lastly, they haue belyed a Ladie, thirdly, they haue verified vniust things, and to conclude they are lying knaues.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: First I aske thee what they haue done, thirdlie I aske thee vvhat's their offence, sixt and lastlie why they are committed, and to conclude, what you lay to their charge.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Rightlie reasoned, and in his owne diuision, and by my troth there's one meaning vvell suted.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Who haue you offended masters, that you are thus bound to your answer? this learned Constable is too cunning to be vnderstood, vvhat's your offence?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Sweete Prince, let me go no farther to mine answere: do you heare me, and let this Count kill mee: I haue deceiued euen your verie eies: vvhat your wisedomes could not discouer, these shallow fooles haue brought to light, vvho in the night ouerheard me confessing to this man, how Don Iohn your brother incensed me to slander the Ladie Hero, how you were brought into the Orchard, and saw me court Margaret in Heroes garments, how you disgrac'd her vvhen you should marrie her: my villanie they haue vpon record, vvhich I had rather seale vvith my death, then repeate ouer to my shame: the Ladie is dead vpon mine and my masters false accusation: and briefelie, I desire nothing but the reward of a villaine.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Runs not this speech like yron through your bloud?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: I haue drunke poison whiles he vtter'd it.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: But did my Brother set thee on to this?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Yea, and paid me richly for the practise of it.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: He is compos'd and fram'd of treacherie,
And fled he is vpon this villanie.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Sweet Hero, now thy image doth appeare
In the rare semblance that I lou'd it first.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Come, bring away the plaintiffes, by this time our Sexton hath reformed Signior Leonato of the matter: and masters, do not forget to specifie when time & place shall serue, that I am an Asse.

speeches.speaker: Con. 2.
prose: Here, here comes master Signior Leonato, and the Sexton too.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Which is the villaine? let me see his eies,
That when I note another man like him,
I may auoide him: vvhich of these is he?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: If you vvould know your wronger, looke on me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Art thou thou the slaue that with thy breath hast kild mine innocent childe?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Yea, euen I alone.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: No, not so villaine, thou belieft thy selfe,
Here stand a paire of honourable men,
A third is fled that had a hand in it:
I thanke you Princes for my daughters death,
Record it with your high and worthie deedes,
'Twas brauely done, if you bethinke you of it.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: I know not how to pray your patience,
Yet I must speake, choose your reuenge your selfe,
Impose me to what penance your inuention
Can lay vpon my sinne, yee sinn'd I not,
But in mistaking.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: By my soule nor I,
And yet to satisfie this good old man,
I vvould bend vnder anie heauie vvaight,
That heele enioyne me to.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I cannot bid you bid my daughter liue,
That vvere impossible, but I praie you both,
Possesse the people in Messina here,
How innocent she died, and if your loue
Can labour aught in sad inuention,
Hang her an epitaph vpon her toomb,
And sing it to her bones, sing it to night:
To morrow morning come you to my house,
And since you could not be my sonne in law,
Be yet my Nephew: my brother hath a daughter,
Almost the copie of my childe that's dead,
And she alone is heire to both of vs,
Giue her the right you should haue giu'n her cosin,
And so dies my reuenge.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: O noble sir!
Your ouer kindnesse doth wring teares from me,
I do embrace your offer, and dispose
For henceforth of poore Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: To morrow then I will expect your comming,
To night I take my leaue, this naughtie man
Shall face to face be brought to Margaret,
Who I beleeue was packt in all this wrong,
Hired to it by your brother.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: No by my soule she was not,
Nor knew not what she did when she spoke to me,
But alwaies hath bin iust and vertuous,
In anie thing that I do know by her.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Moreouer sir, which indeede is not vnder white and black, this plaintiffe here, the offendour did call mee asse, I beseech you let it be remembred in his punishment, and also the vvatch heard them talke of one Deformed, they say he weares a key in his eare and a lock hanging by it, and borrowes monie in Gods name, the which he hath vs'd so long, and neuer paied, that now men grow hard-harted and will lend nothing for Gods sake: praie you examine him vpon that point.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I thanke thee for thy care and honest paines.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Your vvorship speakes like a most thankefull and reuerend youth, and I praise God for you.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: There's for thy paines.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: God saue the foundation.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Goe, I discharge thee of thy prisoner, and I thanke thee.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: I leaue an arrant knaue vvith your vvorship, which I beseech your worship to correct your selfe, for the example of others: God keepe your vvorship, I wish your worship vvell, God restore you to health, I humblie giue you leaue to depart, and if a merrie meeting may be wisht, God prohibite it: come neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Vntill to morrow morning, Lords, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Brot.
prose: Farewell my Lords, vve looke for you to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: We will not faile.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: To night ile mourne with Hero:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Bring you these fellowes on, weel talke vvith Margaret, how her acquaintance grew vvith this lewd fellow.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Praie thee sweete Mistris Margaret, deserue vvell at my hands, by helping mee to the speech of Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Will you then write me a Sonnet in praise of my beautie?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: In so high a stile Margaret, that no man liuing shall come ouer it, for in most comely truth thou deseruest it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: To haue no man come ouer me, why, shall I alwaies keepe below staires?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Thy wit is as quicke as the grey-hounds mouth, it catches.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And yours, as blunt as the Fencers foiles, which hit, but hurt not.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: A most manly wit Margaret, it will not hurt a woman: and so I pray thee call Beatrice, I giue thee the bucklers.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Giue vs the swords, wee haue bucklers of our owne.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: If you vse them Margaret, you must put in the pikes with a vice, and they are dangerous weapons for Maides.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Well, I will call Beatrice to you, who I thinke hath legges.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose:
And therefore will come. The God of loue that sits aboue, and knowes me, and knowes me, how pittifull I deserue. I meane in singing, but in louing, Leander the good swimmer, Tro^lous the first imploier of pandars, and a whole booke full of these quondam carpet-mongers, whose name yet runne smoothly in the euen rode of a blanke verse, why they were neuer so truely turned ouer and ouer as my poore selfe in loue: marrie I cannot shew it rime, I haue tried, I can finde out no rime to Ladie but babie, an innocent rime: for scorne, horne, a hard time: for schoole foole, a babling time: verie ominous endings, no, I was not borne vnder a riming Plannet, for I cannot wooe in festiuall tearmes:

sweete Beatrice would'st thou come when I cal'd thee?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Yea Signior, and depart when you bid me.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: O stay but till then.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Then, is spoken: fare you well now, and yet ere I goe, let me goe with that I came, which is, with knowing what hath past betweene you and Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Onely foule words, and thereupon I will kisse thee.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Foule words is but foule wind, and foule wind is but foule breath, and foule breath is noisome, therefore I will depart vnkist.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Thou hast frighted the word out of his right sence, so forcible is thy wit, but I must tell thee plainely, Claudio vndergoes my challenge, and either I must shortly heare from him, or I will subscribe him a coward, and I pray thee now tell me, for which of my bad parts didst thou first fall in loue with me?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: For them all together, which maintain'd so politique a state of euill, that they will not admit any good part to intermingle with them: but for which of my good parts did you first suffer loue for me?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Suffer loue! a good epithite, I do suffer loue indeede, for I loue thee against my will.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: In spight of your heart I think, alas poore heart, if you spight it for my sake, I will spight it for yours, for I will neuer loue that which my friend hates.

speeches.speaker: Bened.
prose: Thou and I are too wise to wooe peaceablie.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: It appeares not in this confession, there's not one wise man among twentie that will praise himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: An old, an old instance Beatrice, that liu'd in the time of good neighbours, if a man doe not erect in this age his owne tombe ere he dies, hee shall liue no longer in monuments, then the Bels ring, & the Widdow weepes.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: And how long is that thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Question, why an hower in clamour and a quarter in rhewme, therfore is it most expedient for the wife, if Don worme (his conscience) finde no impediment to the contrarie, to be the trumpet of his owne vertues, as I am to my selfe so much for praising my selfe, who I my selfe will beare witnesse is praise worthie, and now tell me, how doth your cosin?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Verie ill.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: And how doe you?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Verie ill too.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Serue God, loue me, and mend, there will I leaue you too, for here comes one in haste.

speeches.speaker: Vrs.
prose: Madam, you must come to your Vncle, yonders old coile at home, it is prooued my Ladie Hero hath bin falselie accusde, the Prince and Claudio mightilie abusde, and Don Iohn is the author of all, who is fled and gone: will you come presentlie?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Will you go heare this newes Signior?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: I will hue in thy heart, die in thy lap, and be buried in thy eies: and moreouer, I will goe with thee to thy Vncles.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Is this the monument of Leonato?

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: Done to death by slanderous tongues,
Was the Hero that here lies:
Death in guerdon of her wrongs,
Giues her fame which neuer dies:
So the life that dyed with shame,
Liues in death with glorious fame.
Hang thou there vpon the tombe,
Praising her when I am dombe.
prose: It is my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Pardon goddesse of the night,
Those that slew thy virgin knight,
For the which with songs of woe,
Round about her tombe they goe:
Midnight assist our mone, helpe vs to sigh and grone
Heauily, heauily.
Graues yawne and yeelde your dead,
Till death be vttered,
Heauenly, heauenly.
prose: Now musick sound & sing your solemn hymne

speeches.speaker: Lo.
prose: Now vnto thy bones good night, yeerely will I do this right.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: Good morrow masters, put your Torches out,
The wolues haue preied, and looke, the gentle day
Before the wheeles of Phoebus, round about
Dapples the drowsie East with spots of grey:
Thanks to you all, and leaue vs, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Good morrow masters, each his seuerall way.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: Come let vs hence, and put on other weedes,
And then to Leonatoes we will goe.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: And Hymen now with luckier issue speeds,
Then this for whom we rendred vp this woe.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
prose: Did I not tell you she was innocent?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: So are the Prince and Claudio who accus'd her,
Vpon the errour that you heard debated:
But Margaret was in some fault for this,
Although against her will as it appeares,
In the true course of all the question.

speeches.speaker: Old.
prose: Well, I am glad that all things sort so well.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
verse: And so am I, being else by faith enforc'd
To call young Claudio to a reckoning for it.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Well daughter, and you gentlewomen all,
Withdraw into a chamber by your selues,
And when I send for you, come hither mask'd:
The Prince and Claudio promis'd by this howre
To visit me, you know your office Brother,
You must be father to your brothers daughter,
And giue her to young Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Old.
prose: Which I will doe with confirm'd countenance.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Frier, I must intreat your paines, I thinke.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
prose: To doe what Signior?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
verse: To binde me, or vndoe me, one of them:
Signior Leonato, truth it is good Signior,
Your neece regards me with an eye of fauour.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: That eye my daughter lent her, 'tis most true.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: And I doe with an eye of loue require her.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: The sight whereof I thinke you had from me,
From Claudio, and the Prince, but what's your will?

speeches.speaker: Bened.
verse: Your answer sir is Enigmaticall,
But for my will, my will is, your good will
May stand with ours, this day to be conioyn'd,
In the state of honourable marriage,
In which (good Frier) I shall desire your helpe.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: My heart is with your liking.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
prose: And my helpe.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Good morrow to this faire assembly.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Good morrow Prince, good morrow Claudio:
We heere attend you, are you yet determin'd,
To day to marry with my brothers daughter?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
prose: Ile hold my minde were she an Ethiope.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: Call her forth brother, heres the Frier ready.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: Good morrow Benedike, why what's the matter?
That you haue such a Februarie face,
So full of frost, of storme, and clowdinesse.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: I thinke he thinkes vpon the sauage bull:
Tush, feare not man, wee'll tip thy hornes with gold,
And all Europa shall reioyce at thee,
As once Europa did at lusty Ioue,
When he would play the noble beast in loue.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Bull Ioue sir, had an amiable low,
And some such strange bull leapt your fathers Cow,
A got a Calfe in that same noble seat,
Much like to you, for you haue iust his b^eat.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: For this I owe you: here comes other recknings.
Which is the Lady I must seize vpon?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: This same is she, and I ^oe giue you her.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: Why thou she's mine, sweet let me see your face.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No that you shal not, till you take her hand,
Before this Frier, and sweare to marry her.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Giue me your hand before this holy Frier,
I am your husband if you like of me.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: And when I liu'd I was your other wife,
And when you lou'd, you were my other husband.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
prose: Another Hero?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Nothing certaine^.
One Hero died, but I doe liue,
And surely as I liue, I am a maid.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: The former Hero, Hero that is dead.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Shee died my Lord, but whiles her slander liu'd.

speeches.speaker: Frier.
verse: All this amazement can I qualifie,
When after that the holy rites are ended,
Ile tell you largely of faire Heroes death:
Meane time let wonder seeme familiar,
And to the chappell let vs presently.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Soft and faire Frier, which is Beatrice?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I answer to that name, what is your will?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Doe not you loue me?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Why no, no more then reason.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Why then your Vncle, and the Prince, & Claudio, haue beene deceiued, they swore you did.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: Doe not you loue mee?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Troth no, no more then reason.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
verse:
Why then my Cosin Margaret and
~rsula
Are much deceiu'd, for they did sweare you did.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: They swore you were almost sicke for me.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: They swore you were wel-nye dead for me.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Tis no matter, then you doe not loue me?

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: No truly, but in friendly recompence.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Come Cosin, I am sure you loue the gentlema~.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: And Ile be sworne vpon't, that he loues her,
For heres a paper written in his hand,
A halting sonnet of his owne pure braine,
Fashioned to Beatrice.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: And heeres another,
Writ in my cosins hand, stolne from her pocket,
Containing her affection vnto Benedicke.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: A miracle, here's our owne hands against our hearts: come I will haue thee, but by this light I take thee for pittie.

speeches.speaker: Beat.
prose: I would not denie you, but by this good day, I yeeld vpon great perswasion, & partly to saue your life, for I was told, you were in a consumption.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Peace I will stop your mouth.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: How dost thou Benedicke the married man?

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Ile tell thee what Prince: a Colledge of witte-crackers cannot flout mee out of my humour, dost thou think I care for a Satyre or an Epigram? no, if a man will be beaten with braines, a shall weare nothing handsome about him: in briefe, since I do purpose to marry, I will thinke nothing to any purpose that the world can say against it, and therefore neuer flout at me, for I haue said against it: for man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion: for thy part Claudio, I did thinke to haue beaten thee, but in that thou art like to be my kinsman, liue vnbruis'd, and loue my cousin.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: I had well hop'd yu wouldst haue denied Beatrice, yt I might haue cudgel'd thee out of thy single life, to make thee a double dealer, which out of questio~ thou wilt be, if my Cousin do not looke exceeding narrowly to thee.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Come, come, we are friends, let's haue a dance ere we are married, that we may lighten our own hearts, and our wiues heeles.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Wee'll haue dancing afterward.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: First, of my vvord, therfore play musick. Prince, thou art sad, get, thee a vvife, get thee a vvife, there is no staff more reuerend then one tipt with horn.

speeches.speaker: Messen.
verse: My Lord, your brother Iohn is tane in flight,
And brought with armed men backe to Messina.

speeches.speaker: Bene.
prose: Thinke not on him till to morrow, ile deuise thee braue punishments for him: strike vp Pipers.

plays.play_title: Loues Labour's lost.

speeches.speaker: Ferdinand.
verse: LEt Fame, that all hunt after in their liues,
Liue registred vpon our brazen Tombes,
And then grace vs in the disgrace of death:
when spight of cormorant deuouring Time,
Th' endeuour of this present breath may buy:
That honour which shall bate his sythes keene edge,
And make vs heyres of all eternitie:
Therefore braue Conquerours, for so you are,
That warre against your owne affections,
And the huge Armie of the worlds desires.
Our late edict shall strongly stand in force,
Nauar shall be the wonder of the world.
Our Court shall be a little Achademe,
Still and contemplatiue in liuing Art.
You three, Berowne, Dumaine, and Longauill,
Haue sworne for three yeeres terme, to liue with me:
My fellow Schollers, and to keepe those statutes
That are recorded in this scedule heere.
Your oathes are past, and now subscribe your names:
That his owne hand may strike his honour downe,
That violates the smallest branch heerein:
If you are arm'd to doe, as sworne to do,
Subscribe to your deepe oathes, and keepe it to.

speeches.speaker: Longauill.
verse: I am resolu'd, 'tis but a three yeeres fast:
The minde shall banquet, though the body pine,
Fat paunches haue leane pates: and dainty bits,
Make rich the ribs, but bankerout the wits.

speeches.speaker: Dumane.
verse: My louing Lord, Dumane is mortified,
The grosser manner of these worlds delights,
He throwes vpon the grosse worlds baser slaues:
To loue, to wealth, to pompe, I pine and die,
With all these liuing in Philosophie.

speeches.speaker: Berowne.
verse: I can but say their protestation ouer,
So much, deare Liege, I haue already sworne,
That is, to liue and study heere three yeeres.
But there are other strict obseruances:
As not to see a woman in that terme,
Which I hope well is not enrolled there.
And one day in a weeke to touch no foode:
And but one meale on euery day beside:
The which I hope is not enrolled there.
And then to sleepe but three houres in the night,
And not be seene to winke of all the day.
When I was wont to thinke no harme all night,
And make a darke night too of halfe the day:
Which I hope well is not enrolled there.
O, these are barren taskes, too hard to keepe,
Not to see Ladies, study, fast, not sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: Your oath is past, to passe away from these.

speeches.speaker: Berow.
verse: Let me say no my Liedge, and if you please,
I onely swore to study with your grace,
And stay heere in your Court for three yeeres space.

speeches.speaker: Longa.
prose: You swore to that Berowne, and to the rest.

speeches.speaker: Berow.
verse: By yea and nay sir, than I swore in iest.
What is the end of study, let me know?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: Why that to know which else wee should not know.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Things hid & bard (you meane) fro~ co~mon sense.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: I, that is studies god-like recompence.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
verse: Come on then, I will sweare to studie so,
To know the thing I am forbid to know:
As thus, to study where I well may dine,
When I to fast expressely am forbid.
Or studie where to meet some Mistresse fine,
When Mistresses from common sense are hid.
Or hauing sworne too hard a keeping oath,
Studie to breake it, and not breake my troth.
If studies gaine be thus, and this be so,
Studie knowes that which yet it doth not know,
Sweare me to this, and I will nere say no.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
verse: These be the stops that hinder studie quite,
And traine our intellects to vaine delight.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Why? all delights are vaine, and that most vaine
Which with paine purchas'd, doth inherit paine,
As painefully to poare vpon a Booke,
To seeke the light of truth, while truth the while
Doth falsely blinde the eye-sight of his looke:
Light seeeking light, doth light of light beguile:
So ere you finde where light in darkenesse lies,
Your light growes darke by losing of your eyes.
Studie me how to please the eye indeede,
By fixing it vpon a fairer eye,
Who dazling so, that eye shall be his heed,
And giue him light that it was blinded by.
Studie is like the heauens glorious Sunne,
That will not be deepe search'd with sawcy lookes:
Small haue continuall plodders euer wonne,
Saue base authoritie from others Bookes.
These earthly Godfathers of heauens lights,
That giue a name to euery fixed Starre,
Haue no more profit of their shining nights,
Then those that walke and wot not what they are.
Too much to know, is to know nought but fame.
And euery Godfather can giue a name.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: How well hee's read, to reason against reading.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Proceeded well, to stop all good proceeding.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: Hee weedes the corne, and still lets grow the weeding.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: The Spring is neare when greene geesse are a breeding.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: How followes that?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Fit in his place and time.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: In reason nothing.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Something then in rime.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
verse: Berowne is like an enuious sneaping Frost,
That bites the first borne infants of the Spring.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Wel, say I am, why should proud Summer boast,
Before the Birds haue any cause to sing?
Why should I ioy in any abortiue birth?
At Christmas I no more desire a Rose,
Then wish a Snow in Mayes new fangled showes:
But like of each thing that in season growes.
So you to studie now it is too late,
That were to clymbe ore the house to vnlocke the gate.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: Well, fit you out: go home Berowne: adue.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: No my good Lord, I haue sworn to stay with you.
And though I haue for barbarisme spoke more,
Then for that Angell knowledge you can say,
Yet confident Ile keepe what I haue sworne,
And bide the pennance of each three yeares day.
Giue me the paper, let me reade the same,
And to the strictest decrees Ile write my name.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: How well this yeelding rescues thee from shame.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Item. That no woman shall come within a mile of my Court.
Hath this bin proclaimed?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: Foure dayes agoe.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Let's see the penaltie.
On paine of loosing her tongue.
Who deuis'd this penaltie?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: Marry that did I.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Sweete Lord, and why?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: To fright them hence with that dread penaltie, A dangerous law against gentilitie. Item, If any man be seene to talke with a woman within the tearme of three yeares, hee shall indure such publique shame as the rest of the Court shall possibly deuise.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: This Article my Liedge your selfe must breake,
For well you know here comes is Embassie
The French Kings daughter, with your selfe to speake:
A Maide of grace and compleate maiestie,
About surrender vp of Aquitaine:
To her decrepit, sicke, and bed-rid Father.
Therefore this Article is made in vaine,
Or vainly comes th' admired Princesse hither.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: What say you Lords?
Why, this was quite forgot.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: So Studie euermore is ouershot,
While it doth study to haue what it would,
It doth forget to doe the thing it should:
And when it hath the thing it hunteth most,
'Tis won as townes with fire, so won, so lost.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: We must of force dispence with this Decree,
She must lye here on meere necessitie.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Necessity will make vs all forsworne
Three thousand times within this three yeeres space:
For euery man with his affects is borne,
Not by might mastred, but by speciall grace.
If I breake faith, this word shall breake for me,
I am forsworne on meere necessitie.
So to the Lawes at large I write my name,
And he that breakes them in the least degree,
Stands in attainder of eternall shame.
Suggestions are to others as to me:
But I beleeue although I seeme so loth,
I am the last that will last keepe his oth.
But is there no quicke recreation granted?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I that there is, our Court you know is hanted
With a refined trauailer of Spaine,
A man in all the worlds new fashion planted,
That hath a mint of phrases in his braine:
One, who the musicke of his owne vaine tongue,
Doth rauish like inchanting harmonie:
A man of complements whom right and wrong
Haue chose as vmpire of their mutinie.
This childe of fancie that Armado hight,
For interim to our studies shall relate,
In high-borne words the worth of many a Knight:
From tawnie Spaine lost in the worlds debate.
How you delight my Lords, I know not I,
But I protest I loue to heare him lie,
And I will vse him for my Minstrelsie.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
verse: Armado is a most illustrious wight,
A man of fire, new words, fashions owne Knight.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: Costard the swaine and he, shall be our sport,
And so to studie, three yeeres is but short.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Which is the Dukes owne person.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: This fellow, What would'st?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: I my selfe reprehend his owne person, for I am his graces Tharborough: But I would see his own person in flesh and blood.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: This is he.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Signeor Arme, Arme commends you:
Ther's villanie abroad, this letter will tell you more.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Sir the Contempts thereof are as touching mee.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: A letter from the magnificent Armado.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: How low soeuer the matter, I hope in God for high words.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: A high hope for a low heauen, God grant vs patience.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: To heare, or forbeare hearing.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: To heare meekely sir, and to laugh moderately, or to forbeare both.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Well sir, be it as the stile shall giue vs cause to clime in the merrinesse.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: The matter is to me sir, as concerning Iaquenetta.
The manner of it is, I was taken with the manner.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: In what manner?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: In manner and forme following sir all those three. I was seene with her in the Mannor house, sitting with her vpon the Forme, and taken following her into the Parke: which put to gether, is in manner and forme following. Now sir for the manner; It is the manner of a man to speake to a woman, for the forme in some forme.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: For the following sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: As it shall follow in my correction, and God defend the right.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: Will you heare this Letter with attention?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: As we would heare an Oracle.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Such is the simplicitie of man to harken after the flesh.

speeches.speaker: Ferdinand.
prose: GReat Deputie, the Welk^ns Vicegerent, and sole dominator of Nauar, my soules earths God, and bodies fostring patrone:

speeches.speaker: Cost.
prose: Not a vvord of Costard yet.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: So it is.

speeches.speaker: Cost.
prose: It may be so: but if he say it is so, he is in telling true: but so.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: Peace,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Be to me, and euery man that dares not fight.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: No words,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Of other mens secrets I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: So it is besieged with sable coloured melancholie, I did commend the blacke oppressing humour to the most wholesome Physicke of thy health-giuing ayre: And as I am a Gentleman, betooke my selfe to walke: the time When? about the sixt houre, When beasts most grase, birds best pecke, and men sit downe to that nourishment which is called supper: So much for the time When. Now for the ground Which? which I meane I walkt vpon, it is ycliped, Thy Parke. Then for the place Where? where I meane I did encounter that obscene and most preposterous euent that draweth from my snow-white pen the ebon coloured Inke, which heere thou viewest, beholdest, suruayest, or seest. But to the place Where? It standeth North North-east and by East from the West corner of thy curious knotted garden; There did I see that low spirited Swaine, that base Minow of thy myrth, (Clown. Mee?) that vnletered small knowing soule, (Clow Me?) that shallow vassall (Clow. Still mee?) which as I remember, hight Costard, (Clow. O me) sorted and consorted contrary to thy established proclaymed Edict and Continet, Cannon: Which with, ô with, but with this I passion to say wherewith:

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: With a Wench.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: With a childe of our Grandmother E^e, a female; or for thy more sweet vnderstanding a woman: him, I (as my euer esteemed dutie prickes me on) haue sent to thee, to receiue the meed of punishment by thy sweet Graces Officer Anthony Dull, a man of good repute, carriage, bearing, & estimation.

speeches.speaker: Anth.
prose: Me, an't shall please you? I am Anthony Dull.

speeches.speaker: Ferd.
prose: For Iaquenetta (so is the weaker vessell called) which I apprehended with the aforesaid Swaine, I keeper her as a vessell of thy Lawes furie, and shall at the least of thy sweet notice, bring her to triall. Thine in all complements of deuoted and heart-burning heat of dutie.
Don Adriana de Armado.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: This is not so well as I looked for, but the best that euer I heard.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: I the best, for the worst. But sirra, What say you to this?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir I confesse the Wench.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: Did you heare the Proclamation?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I doe confesse much of the hearing it, but little of the marking of it.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: It was proclaimed a yeeres imprisonment to bee taken with a Wench.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I was taken with none sir, I was taken vvith a Damosell.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: Well, it was proclaimed Damosell.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: This was no Damosell neyther sir, shee was a Virgin.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: It is so varried to, for it was proclaimed Virgin.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: If it were, I denie her Virginitie: I was taken with a Maide.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
prose: This Maid will not serue your turne sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: This Maide will serue my turne sir.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Sir I will pronounce your sentence: You shall fast a Weeke with Branne and water.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I had rather pray a Moneth with Mutton and Porridge.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: And Don Armado shall be your keeper.
My Lord Berowne, see him deliuer'd ore,
And goe we Lords to put in practice that,
Which each to other hath so strongly sworne.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
verse: Ile lay my head to any good mans hat,
These oathes and lawes will proue an idle scorne.
Sirra, come on.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I suffer for the truth sir: for true it is, I was taken with Iaquenetta, and Iaquenetta is a true girle, and therefore welcome the sowre cup of prosperitie, affliction may one day smile againe, and vntill then sit downe sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Arma.
prose: Boy, What signe is it when a man of great spirit growes melancholy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: A great signe sir, that he will looke sad.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Why? sadnesse is one and the selfe-same thing deare impe.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: No no, O Lord sir no.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: How canst thou part sadnesse and melancholy my tender Iuuenall?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: By a familiar demonstration of the working, my tough signeur.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Why tough signeur? Why tough signeur?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Why tender Iuuenall? Why tender Iuuenall?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I spoke it tender Iuuenall, as a congruent apathaton, appertaining to thy young daies, which we may nominate tender.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: And I tough signeur, as an appertinent title to your olde time, which we may name tough.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Pretty and apt.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: How meane you sir, I pretty, and my saying apt? or I apt, and my saying prettie?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Thou pretty because little.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Little pretty, because little: wherefore apt?

speeches.speaker: Brag
prose: And therefore apt, because quicke.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Speake you this in my praise Master?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: In thy condigne praise.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I will praise an Eele with the same praise.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: What? that an Eele is ingenuous.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: That an Eele is quicke.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I doe say thou art quicke in answeres. Thou heat'st my bloud.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I am answer'd sir.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I loue not to be crost.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: He speakes the meere contrary, crosses loue not him.

speeches.speaker: Br.
prose: I haue promis'd to study iij. yeres with the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: You may doe it in an houre sir.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Impossible.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: How many is one thrice told?

speeches.speaker: Bra.
prose: I am ill at reckning, it fits the spirit of a Tapster.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: You are a gentleman and a gamester fir.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I confesse both, they are both the varnish of a compleat man.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Then I am sure you know how much the grosse summe of deus-ace amounts to.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: It doth amount to one more then two.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Which the base vulgar call three.

speeches.speaker: Br.
prose: True.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Why sir is this such a peece of study? Now here's three studied, ere you'll thrice wink, & how easie it is to put yeres to the word three, and study three yeeres in two words, the dancing horse will tell you.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: A most fine Figure.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: To proue you a Cypher.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I will heereupon confesse I am in loue: and as it is base for a Souldier to loue; so am I in loue with a base wench. If drawing my sword against the humour of affection, would deliuer mee from the reprobate thought of it, I would take Desire priso^, and ransome him to any French Courtier for a n^ deuis'd curtsie. I thinke scorne to sigh, me thinkes I should out-sweare Cupid. Comfort me Boy, What great men haue beene in loue?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Hercules Master.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Most sweete Hercules: more authority deare Boy, name more; and sweet my childe let them be men of good repute and carriage.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sampson Master, he was a man of good carriage, great carriage: for hee carried the Towne-gates on his backe like a Porter: and he was in loue.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: O well-knit Sampson, strong ioynted Sampson; I doe excell thee in my rapier, as much as thou didst mee in carrying gates. I am in loue too. Who was Sampsons loue my deare Moth?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: A Woman, Master.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Of what complexion?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Of all the foure, or the three, or the two, or one of the foure.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Tell me precisely of what complexion?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Of the sea-water Greene sir.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Is that one of the foure complexions?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: As I haue read sir, and the best of them too.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Greene indeed is the colour of Louers: but to haue a Loue of that colour, methinkes Sampson had small reason for it. He surely affected her for her wit.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: It was so sir, for she had a greene wit.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: My Loue is most immaculate white and red.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Most immaculate thoughts Master, are mask'd vnder such colours.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Define, define, well educated infant.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: My fathers witte, and my mothers tongue assist mee.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Sweet inuocation of a childe, most pretty and patheticall.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: If shee be made of white and red,
Her faults will nere be knowne:
For blush-in cheekes by faults are bred,
And feares by pale white showne:
Then if she feare, or be to blame,
By this you shall not know,
For still her cheekes possesse the same,
Which natiue she doth owe:
A dangerous rime master against the reason of white and redde.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Is there not a ballet Boy, of the King and the Begger?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: The world was very guilty of such a Ballet some three ages since, but I thinke now 'tis not to be found: or if it were, it would neither serue for the writing, nor the tune.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I will haue that subiect newly writ ore, that I may example my digression by some mighty president. Boy, I doe loue that Countrey girle that I tooke in the Parke with the rationall hinde Costard: she deserues well.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: To bee whip'd: and yet a better loue then my Master.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Sing Boy, my spirit grows heauy in ioue.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: And that's great maruell, louing a light wench.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I say sing.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Forbeare till this company be past.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Sir, the Dukes pleasure, is that you keepe Costard safe, and you must let him take no delight, nor no penance, but hee must fast three daies a weeke: for this Damsell, I must keepe her at the Parke, shee is alowd for the Day-woman. Fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I do betray my selfe with blushing: Maide.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
prose: Man.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I wil visit thee at the Lodge.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
prose: That's here by.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I know where it is situate.

speeches.speaker: Mai.
prose: Lord how wise you are!

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I will tell thee wonders.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: With what face?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I loue thee.

speeches.speaker: Mai.
prose: So I heard you say.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: And so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Mai.
prose: Faire weather after you.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Come Iaquenetta, away.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Villaine, thou shalt fast for thy offences ere thou be pardoned.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Well sir, I hope when I doe it, I shall doe it on a full stomacke.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Thou shalt be heauily punished.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I am more bound to you then your fellowes, for they are but lightly rewarded.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Take away this villaine, shut him vp.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Come you transgressing slaue, away.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Let mee not bee pent vp sir, I will fast being loose.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: No sir, that were fast and loose: thou shalt to prison.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Well, if euer I do see the merry dayes of desolation that I haue seene, some shall see.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: What shall some see?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Nay nothing, Master Moth, but what they looke vpon. It is not for prisoners to be silent in then words, and therefore I will say nothing: I thanke God, I haue as little patience as another man, and therefore I can be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I doe affect the very ground (which is base) where her shooe (which is baser) guided by her foote (which is basest) doth tread. I shall be forsworn (which ia a great argument of falshood) if I loue. And how can that be true loue, which is falsly attempted? Loue is a familiar, Loue is a Diuell. There is no euill Angell but Loue, yet Sampson was so tempted, and he had an excellent strength: Yet was Salomon so seduced, and hee had a very good witte. Cupids But shaft is too hard for Hercules Clubbe, and therefore too much ods for a Spaniards Rapier: The first and second cause will not serue my turne: the Passado hee respects not, the Duello he regards not; his disgrace is to be called Boy, but his glorie is to subdue men. Adue Valour, rust Rapier, bee still Drum, for your manager is in loue; yea hee loueth. Assist me some extemporall god of Rime, for I am sure I shall turne Sonnet. Deuise Wit, write Pen, for I am for whole volumes in folio.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
verse: Now Madam summon vp your dearest spirits,
Consider who the King your father sends:
To whom he sends, and what's his Embassie.
Your selfe, held precious in the worlds esteeme,
To parlee with the sole inheritour
Of all perfections that a man may owe,
Matchlesse Nauarre, the plea of no lesse weight
Then Aquitaine, a Dowrie for a Queene.
Be now as prodigall of all deare grace,
As Nature was in making Graces deare,
When she did starue the generall world beside,
And prodigally gaue them all to you.

speeches.speaker: Queen.
verse: Good L. Boyet, my beauty though but mean,
Needs not the painted flourish of your praise:
Beauty is bought by iudgement of the eye,
Not vttred by base sale of chapmens tongues:
I am lesse proud to heare you tell my worth,
Then you much wiling to be counted wise,
In spending your wit in the praise of mine.
But now to taske the tasker, good Boyet,

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: You are not ignorant all-telling fame
Doth noyse abroad Nauar hath made a vow,
Till painefull studie shall out-weare three yeares,
No woman may approach his silent Court:
Therefore to's seemeth it a needfull course,
Before we enter his forbidden gates,
To know his pleasure, and in that behalfe
Bold of your worthinesse, we single you,
As our best mouing faire soliciter:
Tell him, the daughter of the King of France,
On serious businesse crauing quicke dispatch,
Importunes personall conference with his grace.
Haste, signifie so much while we attend,
Like humble visag'd suters his high will.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Proud of imployment, willingly I goe.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: All pride is willing pride, and yours is so:
Who are the Votaries my louing Lords, that are vow-fellowes with this vertuous Duke?

speeches.speaker: Lor.
prose: Longauill is one.

speeches.speaker: Princ.
prose: Know you the man?

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: I know him Madame at a marriage feast,
Betweene L. Perigort and the beautious heire
Of Iaques Fauconbridge solemnized.
In Normandie saw I this Longauill,
A man of soueraigne parts he is esteem'd:
Well fitted in Arts, glorious in Armes:
Nothing becomes him ill that he would well.
The onely soyle of his faire vertues glosse,
If vertues glosse will staine with any soile,
Is a sharp wit match'd with too blunt a Will:
Whose edge hath power to cut whose will still wills,
It should none spare that come within his power.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Some merry mocking Lord belike, ist so?

speeches.speaker: Lad. 1.
prose: They say so most, that most his humors know.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: Such short liu'd wits do wither as they grow.
Who are the rest?

speeches.speaker: 2. Lad.
verse: The yong Dumaine, a well accomplisht youth,
Of all that Vertue loue, for Vertue loued.
Most power to doe most harme, least knowing ill:
For he hath wit to make an ill shape good,
And shape to win grace though she had no wit.
I saw him at the Duke Alansoes once,
And much too little of that good I saw,
Is my report to his great worthinesse.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: Another of these Students at that time,
Was there with him, as I haue heard a truth.
Berowne they call him, but a merrier man,
Within the limit of becomming mirth,
I neuer spent an houres talke withall.
His eye begets occasion for his wit,
For euery obiect that the one doth catch,
The other turnes to a mirth-mouing iest.
Which his faire tongue (conceits expositor)
Deliuers in such apt and gracious words,
That aged eares play treuant at his tales,
And yonger hearings are quite rauished.
So sweet and voluble is his discourse.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: God blesse my Ladies, are they all in loue?
That euery one her owne hath garnished,
With such bedecking ornaments of praise.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Heere comes Boyet.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Now, what admittance Lord?

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
verse: Nauar had notice of your faire approach,
And he and his competitors in oath,
Were all addrest to meete you gentle Lady
Before I came: Marrie thus much I haue learnt,
He rather meanes to lodge you in the field,
Like one that comes heere to besiege his Court,
Then seeke a dispensation for his oath:
To let you enter his vnpeopled house.
Heere comes Nauar.

speeches.speaker: Nau.
prose: Faire Princesse, welcom to the Court of Nauar.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Faire I giue you backe againe, and welcome I haue not yet: the roofe of this Court is too high to bee yours, and welcome to the wide fields, too base to be mine.

speeches.speaker: Nau.
prose: You shall be welcome Madam to my Court.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: I wil be welcome then, Conduct me thither.

speeches.speaker: Nau.
prose: Heare me deare Lady, I haue sworne an oath.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Our Lady helpe my Lord, he'll be forsworne.

speeches.speaker: Nau.
prose: Not for the world faire Madam, by my will.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Why, will shall breake it will, and nothing els.

speeches.speaker: Nau.
prose: Your Ladiship is ignorant what it is.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: Were my Lord so, his ignorance were wise,
Where now his knowledge must proue ignorance.
I heare your grace hath sworne out Houseekeeping:
'Tis deadly sinne to keepe that oath my Lord,
And sinne to breake it:
But pardon me, I am too sodaine bold,
To teach a Teacher ill beseemeth me.
Vouchsafe to read the purpose of my comming,
And sodainly resolue me in my suite.

speeches.speaker: Nau.
prose: Madam, I will, if sodainly I may.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: You will the sooner that I were away,
For you'll proue periur'd if you make me stay.

speeches.speaker: Berow.
prose: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I know you did.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: How needlesse was it then to ask the question?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: You must not be so quicke.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: 'Tis long of you yt spur me with such questions.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Your wit's too hot, it speeds too fast, 'twill tire.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Not till it leaue the Rider in the mire.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: What time a day?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: The howre that fooles should aske.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Now faire befall your maske.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Faire fall the face it couers.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: And send you many louers.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Amen, so you be none.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Nay then will I be gone.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Madame, your father heere doth intimate,
The paiment of a hundred thousand Crownes,
Being but th' one halfe, of an intire summe,
Disbursed by my father in his warres.
But say that he, or we, as neither haue
Receiu'd that summe; yet there remaines vnpaid
A hundred thousand more: in surety of the which,
One part of Aquitaine is bound to vs,
Although not valued to the moneys worth.
If then the King your father will restore
But that one halfe which is vnsatisfied,
We will giue vp our right in Aquitaine,
And hold faire friendship with his Maiestie:
But that it seemes he little purposeth,
For here he doth demand to haue repaie,
An hundred thousand Crownes, and not demands
One paiment of a hundred thousand Crownes,
To haue his title liue in Aquitaine.
Which we much rather had depart withall,
And haue the money by our father lent,
Then Aquitane, so guelded as it is.
Deare Princesse, were not his requests so farre
From reasons yeelding, your faire selfe should make
A yeelding 'gainst some reason in my brest,
And goe well satisfied to France againe.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: You doe the King my Father too much wrong,
And wrong the reputation of your name,
In so vnseeming to confesse receyt
Of that which hath so faithfully beene paid.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I doe protest I neuer heard of it,
And if you proue it, Ile repay it backe,
Or yeeld vp Aquitaine.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: We arrest your word:
Boyet, you can produce acquittances
For such a summe, from speciall Officers,
Of Charles his Father.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Satisfie me so.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
verse: So please your Grace, the packet is not come
Where that and other specialties are bound,
To morrow you shall haue a sight of them.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: It shall suffice me; at which enterview,
All liberall reason would I yeeld vnto:
Meane time, receiue such welcome at my hand,
As Honour, without breach of Honour may
Make tender of, to thy true worthinesse.
You may not come faire Princesse in my gates,
But heere without you shall be so receiu'd,
As you shall deeme your selfe lodg'd in my heart,
Though so deni'd farther harbour in my house:
Your owne good thoughts excuse me, and farewell,
To morrow we shall visit you againe.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Sweet health & faire desires consort your grace.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Thy own wish wish I thee, in euery place.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Lady, I will commend you to my owne heart.

speeches.speaker: La. Ro.
verse: Pray you doe my commendations,
I would be glad to see it.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I would you heard it grone.

speeches.speaker: La. Ro.
prose: Is the soule sicke?.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sicke at the heart.

speeches.speaker: La. Ro.
prose: Alacke, let it bloud.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Would that doe it good?

speeches.speaker: La. Ro.
prose: My Phisicke saies I.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Will you prick't with your eye.

speeches.speaker: La. Ro.
prose: No poynt, with my knife.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Now God saue thy life.

speeches.speaker: La. Ro.
prose: And yours from long liuing.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I cannot stay thanks-giuing.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Sir, I pray you a word: What Lady is that same?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: The heire of Alanson, Rosalin her name.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: A gallant Lady, Mounsier fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I beseech you a word: what is she in the white?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: A woman somtimes, if you saw her in the light.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Perchance light in the light: I desire her name.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Shee hath but one for her selfe,
To desire that were a shame.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Pray you sir, whose daughter?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Her Mothers, I haue heard.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Gods blessing a your beard.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Good sir be not offended,
Shee is an heyre of Faulconbridge.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Nay, my choller is ended:
Shee is a most sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Not vnlike sir, that may be.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: What's her name in the cap.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Katherine by good hap.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Is she wedded, or no.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: To her will sir, or so.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: You are welcome sir, adiew.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Fare well to me sir, and welcome to you.

speeches.speaker: La. Ma.
verse: That last is Beroune, the mery mad-cap Lord.
Not a word with him, but a iest.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: And euery iest but a word.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
prose: It was well done of you to take him at his word.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I was as willing to grapple, as he was to boord.

speeches.speaker: La. Ma.
verse: Two hot Sheepes marie:
And wherefore not Ships?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: No Sheepe (sweet Lamb) vnlesse we feed on your lips.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: You Sheep & I pasture: shall that finish the iest?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: So you grant pasture for me.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Not so gentle beast.
My lips are no Common, though seuerall they be.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
prose: Belonging to whom?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: To my fortunes and me.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: Good wits wil be iangling, but gentles agree.
This ciuill warre of wits were much better vsed
On Nauar and his bookemen, for heere 'tis abus'd.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: If my obseruation (which very seldome lies
By the hearts still rhetoricke, disclosed with eyes)
Deceiue me not now, Nauar is infected.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: With what?

speeches.speaker: Bo.
prose: With that which we Louers intitle affected.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Your reason.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Why all his behauiours doe make their retire,
To the court of his eye, peeping thorough desire.
His hart like an Agot with your print impressed,
Proud with his forme, in his eie pride expressed.
His tongue all impatient to speake and not see,
Did stumble with haste in his eie-sight to be,
All sences to that sence did make their repaire,
To feele onely looking on fairest of faire:
Me thought all his sences were lockt in his eye,
As Iewels in Christall for some Prince to buy.
Who tendring their own worth from whence they were glast,
Did point out to buy them along as you past.
His faces owne margent did coate such amazes,
That all eyes saw his eies inchanted with gazes.
Ile giue you Aquitaine, and all that is his,
And you giue him for my sake, but one louing Kisse.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Come to our Pauillion, Boyet is disposde.

speeches.speaker: Bro.
verse: But to speak that in words, which his eie hath disclos'd.
I onelie haue made a mouth of his eie,
By adding a tongue, which I know will not lie.

speeches.speaker: Lad. Ro.
prose: Thou art an old Loue-monger, and speakest skilfully.

speeches.speaker: Lad. Ma.
prose: He is Cupids Grandfather, and learnes news of him.

speeches.speaker: Lad. 2.
prose: Then was Venus like her mother, for her father is but grim.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Do you heare my mad wenches?

speeches.speaker: La. 1.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: What then, do you see?

speeches.speaker: Lad. 2.
prose: I, our way to be gone.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: You are too hard for me.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
prose: Warble childe, make passionate my sense of hearing.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Concolinel.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Sweete Ayer, go tendernesse of yeares: take this Key, giue enlargement to the swaine, bring him festinatly hither: I must imploy him in a letter to my Loue.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Will you win your loue with a French braule?

speeches.speaker: Bra.
prose: How meanest thou, brauling in French?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: No my compleat master, but to Iigge off a tune at the tongues end, canarie to it with the feete, humour it with turning vp your eie: sigh a note and sing a note, sometime through the throate: if you swallowed loue with singing, loue sometime through: nose as if you snuft vp loue by smelling loue with your hat penthouse-like ore the shop of your eies, with your armes crost on your thinbellie doublet, like a Rabbet on a spit, or your hands in your pocket, like a man after the old painting, and keepe not too long in one tune, but a snip and away: these are complements, these are humours, these betraie nice wenches that would be betraied without these, and make them men of note: do you note men that most are affected to these?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: How hast thou purchased this experience?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: By my penne of obseruation.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: But O, but O.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: The Hobbie-horse is forgot.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
prose: Cal'st thou my loue Hobbi-horse.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: No Master, the Hobbie-horse is but a Colt, and and your Loue perhaps, a Hacknie:
But haue you forgot your Loue?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Almost I had.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Negligent student, learne her by heart.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: By heart, and in heart Boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: And out of heart Master: all those three I will proue.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: What wilt thou proue?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: A man, if I liue (and this) by, in, and without, vpon the instant: by heart you loue her, because your heart cannot come by her: in heart you loue her, because your heart is in loue with her: and out of heart you loue her, being out of heart that you cannot enioy her.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: I am all these three.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: And three times as much more, and yet nothing at all.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Fetch hither the Swaine, he must carrie mee a letter.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: A message well simpathis'd, a Horse to be embassadour for an Asse.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Ha, ha, What saiest thou?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Marrie sir, you must send the Asse vpon the Horse for he is verie slow gated: but I goe.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: The way is but short, away.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: As swift as Lead sir.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Thy meaning prettie ingenious, is not Lead a mettall heauie, dull, and slow?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Minnime honest Master, or rather Master no.

speeches.speaker: Brad.
prose: I say Lead is slow.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You are too swift sir to say so.
Is that Lead slow which is fir'd from a Gunne?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
verse: Sweete smoke of Rhetorike,
He reputes me a Cannon, and the Bullet that's he:
I shoote thee at the Swaine.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Thump then, and I flee.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: A most acute iuuenall, voluble and free of grace,
By thy fauour sweet Welkin, I must sigh in thy face.
Most rude melancholie, Valour giues thee place.
My Herald is return'd.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: A wonder Master, here's a Costard broken in a shin.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Some enigma, some riddle, come, thy Lenuoy begin.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No egma, no riddle, no lenuoy, no salue, in thee male sir. Or sir, Plantan, a plaine Plantan: no lenuoy, no lenuoy, no Salue sir, but a Plantan.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: By vertue thou inforcest laughter, thy sillie thought, my spleene, the heauing of my lunges prouokes me to rediculous smyling: O pardon me my stars, doth the inconsiderate take salue for lenuoy, and the word lenuoy for a salue?

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: Doe the wise thinke them other, is not lenuoy a salue?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No Page, it is an epilogue or discourse to make plaine,
Some obscure precedence that hath to fore bin faine.
Now will I begin your morrall, and do you follow with my lenuoy.
The Foxe, the Ape, and the Humble-Bee,
Were still at oddes, being but three.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Vntill the Goose came out of doore,
Staying the oddes by adding foure.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: A good Lenuoy, ending in the Goose: would you desire more?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: The Boy hath sold him a bargaine, a Goose, that's flat
Sir, your penny-worth is good, and your Goose be fat.
To sell a bargaine well is as cunning as fast and loose:
Let me see a fat Lenuoy, I that's a fat Goose.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Come hither, come hither:
How did this argument begin?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: By saying that a Costard was broken in a shin.
Then cal'd you for the Lenuoy.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: True, and I for a Plantan:
Thus came your argument in:
Then the Boyes fat Lenuoy, the Goose that you bought,
And he ended the market.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: But tell me: How was there a Costard broken in a shin?

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: I will tell you sencibly.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Thou hast no feeling of it Moth,
I will speake that Lenuoy.
I Costard running out, that was safely within,
Fell ouer the threshold, and broke my shin.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
prose: We will talke no more of this matter.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Till there be more matter in the shin.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
prose: Sirra Costard, I will infranchise thee.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: O, marrie me to one Francis, I smell some Lenuoy, some Goose in this.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
prose: By my sweete soule, I meane, setting thee at libertie. Enfreedoming thy person: thou wert emured, restrained, captiuated, bound.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: True, true, and now you will be my purgation, and let me loose.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
prose: I giue thee thy libertie, set thee from durance, and in lieu thereof, impose on thee nothing but this: Beare this significant to the countrey Maide Iaquenetta: there is remuneration, for the best ward of mine honours is rewarding my dependants. Moth, follow.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse: Like the sequell I.
Signeur Costard adew.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: My sweete ounce of mans flesh, my in-conie Iew: Now will I looke to his remuneration. Remuneration, O, that's the Latine word for three-farthings: Three-farthings remuneration, What's the price of this yncle? i.d. no, Ile giue you a remuneration: Why? It carries it remuneration: Why? It is a fairer name then a French-Crowne. I will neuer buy and sell out of this word.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: O my good knaue Costard, exceedingly well met.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Pray you sir, How much Carnation Ribbon may a man buy for a remuneration?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: What is a remuneration?

speeches.speaker: Cost.
prose: Marrie sir, halfe pennie farthing.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: O, Why then three farthings worth of Silke.

speeches.speaker: Cost.
prose: I thanke your worship, God be wy you.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O stay slaue, I must employ thee:
As thou wilt win my fauour, good my knaue,
Doe one thing for me that I shall intreate.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: When would you haue it done sir?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: O this after-noone.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Well, I will doe it sir: Fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: O thou knowest not what it is.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I shall know sir, when I haue done it.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Why villaine thou must know first.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I wil come to your worship to morrow morning.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: It must be done this after-noone,
Harke slaue, it is but this:
The Princesse comes to hunt here in the Parke,
And in her traine there is a gentle Ladie:
When tongues speak sweetly, then they name her name,
And Rosaline they call her, aske for her:
And to her white hand see thou do commend
This seal'd vp counsaile. Ther's thy guerdon: goe.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Gardon, O sweete gardon, better then remuneration, a leuenpence-farthing better: most sweete gardon. I will doe it sir in print: gardon, remuneration.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O, and I forsooth in loue,
I that haue beene loues whip?
A verie Beadle to a humerous sigh: A Criticke,
Nay, a night-watch Constable.
A domineering pedant ore the Boy,
Then whom no mortall so magnificent.
This wimpled, whyning, purblinde waiward Boy,
This signior Iunios gyant drawfe, don Cupid,
Regent of Loue-rimes, Lord of folded armes,
Th' annointed soueraigne of sighes and groanes:
Liedge of all loyterers and male contents:
Dread Prince of Placcats, King of Codpeeces.
Sole Emperator and great generall
Of trotting Parrators (O my little heart.)
And I to be a Corporall of his field,
And weare his colours like a Tumblers hoope.
What? I loue, I sue, I seeke a wife,
A woman that is like a Germane Cloake,
Still a repairing: euer out of frame,
And neuer going a right, being a Watch:
But being watcht, that it may still goe right.
Nay, to be periurde, which is worst of all:
And among three, to loue the worst of all,
A whitly wanton, with a veluet brow.
With two pitch bals stucke in her face for eyes.
I, and by heauen, one that will doe the deede,
Though Argus were her Eunuch and her garde.
And I to sigh for her, to watch for her,
To pray for her, go to: it is a plague
That Cupid will impose for my neglect,
Of his almighty dreadfull little might.
Well, I will loue, write, sigh, pray, shue, grone,
Some men must loue my Lady, and some lone.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Was that the King that spurd his horse so hard,
Against the steepe vprising of the hill?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I know not, but I thinke it was not he.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Who ere a was, a shew'd a mounting minde:
Well Lords, to day we shall haue our dispatch,
On Saterday we will returne to France.
Then Forrester my friend, Where is the Bush
That we must stand and play the murtherer in?

speeches.speaker: For.
verse: Hereby vpon the edge of yonder Coppice,
A Stand where you may make the fairest shoote.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: I thanke my beautie, I am faire that shoote,
And thereupon thou speak'st the fairest shoote.

speeches.speaker: For.
prose: Pardon me Madam, for I meant not so.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: What, what? First praise me, & then again say no.
O short liu'd pride. Not faire? alacke for woe.

speeches.speaker: For.
prose: Yes Madam faire.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Nay, neuer paint me now,
Where faire is not, praise cannot mend the brow.
Here (good my glasse) take this for telling true:
Faire paiment for foule words, is more then due.

speeches.speaker: For.
prose: Nothing but faire is that which you inherit.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: See, see, my beautie will be sau'd by merit.
O heresie in faire, fit for these dayes,
A giuing hand, though foule, shall haue faire praise.
But come, the Bow: Now Mercie goes to kill,
And shooting well, is then accounted ill:
Thus will I saue my credit in the shoote,
Not wounding, pittie would not let me do't:
If wounding, then it was to shew my skill,
That more for praise, then purpose meant to kill.
And out of question, so it is sometimes:
Glory growes guiltie of detested crimes,
