When for Fames sake, for praise an outward part,
We bend to that, the working of the hart.
As I for praise alone now seeke to spill
The poore Deeres blood, that my heart meanes no ill.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Do not curst wiues hold that selfe-soueraigntie
Onely for praise sake, when they striue to be
Lords ore their Lords?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Onely for praise and praise we may afford,
To any Lady that subdewes a Lord.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Here comes a member of the common-wealth.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: God dig-you-den all, pray you which is the head Lady?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Thou shalt know her fellow, by the rest that haue no heads.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Which is the greatest Lady, the highest?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: The thickest, and the tallest.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: The thickest, & the tallest: it is so, truth is truth.
And your waste Mistris, were as slender as my wit,
One a these Maides girdles for your waste should be fit.
Are not you the chiefe woma~? You are the thickest here?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: What's your will sir? What's your will?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I haue a Letter from Monsier Berowne,
To one Lady Rosaline.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: O thy letter, thy letter: He's a good friend of mine.
Stand a side good bearer.
Boyet, you can carue,
Breake vp this Capon.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
verse: I am bound to serue.
This Letter is mistooke: it importeth none here:
It is writ to Iaquenetta.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: We will reade it, I sweare.
Breake the necke of the Waxe, and euery one giue eare.
Thus dost thou heare the Nemean Lion roare,
Gainst thee thou Lambe, that standest as his pray:
Submissiue fall his princely feete before,
And he from forrage will incline to play.
But if thou striue (poore soule) what art thou then?
Foode for his rage, repasture for his den.
prose:
BY heauen, that thou art faire, is most infallible: true that thou art beauteous, truth it selfe that thou art louely: more fairer then faire, beautifull then beautious, truer then truth it selfe: haue comiseration on thy heroicall Vassall. The magnanimous and most illustrate King Cophetua set eie vpon the pernicious and indubitate Begger Zenelophon: and he it was that might rightly say, Veni, vidi, vici: Which to annothanize in the vulgar, O base and obscure vulgar; videliset, He came, See, and ouercame: hee came one; see, two; couercame three: Who came? the King. Why did he come? to see. Why did he see? to ouercome. To whom came he? to the Begger. What saw he? the Begger. Who ouercame he? the Begger. The conclusion is victorie: On whose side? the King: the captiue is inricht: On whose side? the Beggers. The catastrophe is a Nuptiall: on whose side? the Kings: no, on both in one, or one in both. I am the King (for so stands the comparison) thou the Begger, for so witnesseth thy lowlinesse. Shall I command thy loue? I may. Shall I enforce thy loue? I could. Shall I entreate thy loue? I will. What, shalt thou exchange for ragges, roabes: for tittles titles, for thy selfe mee. Thus expecting thy reply, I prophane my lips on thy foote, my eyes on thy picture, and my heart on thy euerie part.

Thine in the dearest designe of industrie,
Don Adriana de Armatho.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: What plume of feathers is hee that indited this Letter? What veine? What Wethercocke? Did you euer heare better?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I am much deceiued, but I remember the stile.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Else your memorie is bad, going ore it erewhile.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: This Armando is a Spaniard that keeps here in court
A Phantasime, a Monarcho, and one that makes sport
To the Prince and his Booke-mates.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Thou fellow, a word.
Who gaue thee this Letter?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I told you, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: To whom should'st thou giue it?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: From my Lord to my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: From which Lord, to which Lady?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: From my Lord Berowne, a good master of mine,
To a Lady of France, that he call'd Rosaline.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Thou hast mistaken his letter. Come Lords away.
Here sweete, put vp this, 'twill be thine another day.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Who is the shooter? Who is the shooter?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Shall I teach you to know.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I my continent of beautie.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Why she that beares the Bow. Finely put off.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: My Lady goes to kill hornes, but if thou marrie,
Hang me by the necke, if hornes that yeare miscarrie.
Finely put on.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Well then, I am the shooter.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: And who is your Deare?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: If we choose by the hornes, your selfe come not neare. Finely put on indeede.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
prose: You still wrangle with her Boyet, and shee strikes at the brow.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
verse: But she her selfe is hit lower:
Haue I hit her now.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Shall I come vpon thee with an old saying, that was a man when King Pippin of France was a little boy, as touching the hit it.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
prose: So I may answere thee with one as old that was a woman when Queene Guinouer of Brittaine was a little wench, as touching the hit it.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: Thou canst not hit it, hit it, hit it,
Thou canst not hit it my good man.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I cannot, cannot, cannot:
And I cannot, another can.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: By my troth most pleasant, how both did fit it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: A marke marueilous well shot, for they both did hit.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: A mark, O marke but that marke: a marke saies my Lady.
Let the mark haue a pricke in't, to meat at, if it may be.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Wide a' th bow hand. yfaith your hand is out.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Indeede a' must shoote nearer, or heele ne're hit the clout.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: And if my hand be out, then belike your hand is in.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Then will shee get the vpshoot by cleauing the is in.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Come, come, you talke greasely, your lips grow foule,

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: She's too hard for you at pricks, sir challenge her to boule.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I feare too much rubbing: good night my good Oule.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: By my soule a Swaine, a most simple Clowne.
Lord, Lord, how the Ladies and I haue put him downe.
O my troth most sweete iests, most inconie vulgar wit,
When it comes so smoothly off, so obscenely, as it were, so fit.
Armathor ath to the side, O a most dainty man.
To see him walke before a Lady, and to beare her Fan.
To see him kisse his hand, and how most sweetly a will sweare:
And his Page at other side, that handfull of wit,
Ah heauens, it is most patheticall nit.
Sowla, sowla.

speeches.speaker: Nat.
prose: Very reuerent sport truely, and done in the testimony of a good conscience.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: The Deare was (as you know) sanguis in blood, ripe as a Pomwater, who now hangeth like a Iewell in the eare of Celo the skie; the welken the heauen, and anon falleth like a Crab on the face of Terra, the soyle, the land, the earth.

speeches.speaker: Curat. Nath.
prose: Truely M. Holofernes, the epythithes are sweetly varied like a scholler at the least: but sir I assure ye, it was a Bucke of the first head.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Sir Nathaniel, haud credo.

speeches.speaker: Dul.
prose: 'Twas not a haud credo, 'twas a Pricket.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Most barbarous intimation: yet a kinde of insinuation, as it were in via, in way of explication facere: as it were replication, or rather ostentare, to show as it were his inclination after his vndressed, vnpolished, vneducated, vnpruned, vntrained, or rather vnlettered, or ratherest vnconfirmed fashion, to insert againe my haud credo for a Deare.

speeches.speaker: Dul.
prose: I said the Deare was not a haud credo, 'twas a Pricket.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Twice sod simplicitie, his coctus, O thou monster Ignorance, how deformed doost thou looke.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
verse: Sir hee hath neuer fed of the dainties that are bred in a booke.
He hath not eate paper as it were:
He hath not drunke inke.
For as it would ill become me to be vaine, indiscreet, or a foole;
So were there a patch set on Learning, to see him in a Schoole.
But omne bene say I, being of an old Fathers minde,
Many can brooke the weather, that loue not the winde.
prose: His intellect is not replenished, hee is onely an animall, onely sensible in the duller parts: and such barren plants are set before vs, that we thankfull should be: which we taste and feeling, are for those parts that doe fructifie in vs more then he.

speeches.speaker: Dul.
prose: You two are book-men: Can you tell by your wit, What was a month old at Cains birth, that's not fiue weekes old as yet?

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Dictisima goodman Dull, dictisima goodman Dull.

speeches.speaker: Dul.
prose: What is dictima?

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: A title to Phebe, to Luna, to the Moone.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
verse: The Moone was a month old when Adam was no more.
And wrought not to fiue-weekes when he came to fiuescore.
Th' allusion holds in the Exchange.

speeches.speaker: Dul.
prose: 'Tis true indeede, the Collusion holds in the Exchange.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: God comfort thy capacity, I say th' allusion holds in the Exchange.

speeches.speaker: Dul.
prose: And I say the polusion holds in the Exchange: for the Moone is neuer but a month old: and I say beside that, 'twas a Pricket that the Princesse kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Sir Nathaniel, will you heare an extemporall Epytaph on the death of the Deare, and to humour the ignorant call'd the Deare, the Princesse kill'd a Pricket.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: Perge, good M. Holofernes, perge, so it shall please you to abrogate scurilitie.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
verse: I will something affect the letter, for it argues facilitie.
The prayfull Princesse pearst and prickt a prettie pleasing Pricket,
Some say a Sore, but not a sore, till now made sore with shooting.
The Dogges did yell, put ell to Sore, then Sorell iumps from thicket:
Or Pricket-sore, or else Sorell, the people fall a hooting.
If Sore be sore, then ell to Sore, makes fiftie sores O sorell:
Of one sore I an hundred make by adding but one more L.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: A rare talent.

speeches.speaker: Dul.
prose: If a talent be a claw, looke how he clawes him with a talent.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: This is a gift that I haue simple: simple, a foolish extrauagant spirit, full of formes, figures, shapes, obiects, Ideas, apprehensions, motions, reuolutions. These are begot in the ventricle of memorie, nourisht in the wombe of primater, and deliuered vpon the mellowing of occasion: but the gift is good in those in whom it is acute, and I am thankfull for it.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Sir, I praise the Lord for you, and so may my parishioners, for their Sonnes are well tutor'd by you, and their Daughters profit very greatly vnder you: you are a good member of the common-wealth.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose:
Mehercle, If their Sonnes be ingennous, they

shall want no instruction: If their Daughters be capable, I will put it to them. But Vir sapis qui pauca loquitur, a soule Feminine saluteth vs.

speeches.speaker: Iaqu.
prose: God giue you good morrow M. Person.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: Master Person, quasi Person? And if one should be perst, Which is the one?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Marry M. Schoolemaster, hee that is likest to a hogshead.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: Of persing a Hogshead, a good luster of conceit in a curph of Earth, Fire enough for a Flint, Pearle enough for a Swine: 'tis prettie, it is well.

speeches.speaker: Iaqu.
prose: Good Master Parson be so good as reade mee this Letter, it was giuen mee by Costard, and sent mee from Don Armatho: I beseech you reade it.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: Facile procor gellida, quando pecas omnia sub vmbraruminat, and so forth. Ah good old Mantuan, I may speake of thee as the traueiler doth of Venice, vemchie, vencha, que non te vnde, que non te perreche. Old Mantuam, old Mantuan. Who vnderstandeth thee not, vt re sol la mi fa: Vnder pardon sir, What are the contents? or rather as Horrace sayes in his, What my soule verses.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: I sir, and very learned.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
verse: Let me heare a staffe, a stanze, a verse, Lege domine.
If Loue make me forsworne, how shall I sweare to loue?
Ah neuer faith could hold, if not to beautie vowed.
Though to my selfe forsworn, to thee Ile faithfull proue.
Those thoughts to mee were Okes, to thee like Osiers bowed.
Studie his byas leaues, and makes his booke thine eyes.
Where all those pleasures liue, that Art would comprehend.
If knowledge be the marke, to know thee shall suffice.
Well learned is that tongue, that well can thee co~mend.
All ignorant that soule, that sees thee without wonder.
Which is to me some praise, that I thy parts admire;
Thy eye Ioues lightning beares, thy voyce his dreadfull thunder.
Which not to anger bent, is musique, and sweet fire.
Celestiall as thou art, Oh pardon loue this wrong,
That sings heauens praise, with such an earthly tongue.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: You finde not the apostraphas, and so misse the accent. Let me superuise the cangenet.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: Here are onely numbers ratified, but for the elegancy, facility, & golden cadence of poesie caret: Ouiddius Naso was the man. And why in deed Naso, but for smelling out the odoriferous flowers of fancy? the ierkes of inuention imitarie is nothing: So doth the Hound his master, the Ape his keeper, the tyred Horse his rider: But Damosella virgin, Was this directed to you?

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
prose: I sir from one mounsier Berowne, one of the strange Queenes Lords.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: I will ouerglance the superscript.
To the snow-white hand of the most beautious Lady Rosaline.
I will looke againe on the intellect of the Letter, for the nomination of the partie written to the person written vnto.
Your Ladiships in all desired imployment, Berowne.

speeches.speaker: Per.
prose: Sir Holofernes, this Berowne is one of the Votaries with the King, and here he hath framed a Letter to a sequent of the stranger Queenes: which accidentally, or by the way of progression, hath miscarried. Trip and goe my sweete, deliuer this Paper into the hand of the King, it may concerne much: stay not thy complement, I forgiue thy duetie, adue.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Good Costard go with me:
Sir God saue your life.

speeches.speaker: Cost.
prose: Haue with thee my girle.

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Sir you haue done this in the feare of God very religiously: and as a certaine Father saith

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Sir tell not me of the Father, I do feare colourable colours. But to returne to the Verses, Did they please you sir Nathaniel?

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: Marueilous well for the pen.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: I do dine to day at the fathers of a certaine Pupill of mine, where if (being repast) it shall please you to gratifie the table with a Grace, I will on my priuiledge I haue with the parents of the foresaid Childe or Pupill, vndertake your bien vonuto, where I will proue those Verses to be very vnlearned, neither sauouring of Poetrie, Wit, nor Inuention. I beseech your Societie.

speeches.speaker: Nat.
prose: And thanke you to: for societie (saith the text) is the happinesse of life.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
verse: And certes the text most infallibly concludes it.
Sir I do inuite you too, you shall not say me nay: pauca verba.
Away, the gentles are at their game, and we will to our recreation.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
verse: The King he is hunting the Deare,
I am coursing my selfe.
prose: They haue pitcht a Toyle, I am toyling in a pytch, pitch that defiles; defile, a foule word: Well, set thee downe sorrow; for so they say the foole said, and so say I, and I the foole: Well proued wit. By the Lord this Loue is as mad as Aiax, it kils sheepe, it kils mee, I a sheepe: Well proued againe a my side. I will not loue; if I do hang me: yfaith I will not. O but her eye: by this light, but for her eye, I would not loue her; yes, for her two eyes. Well, I doe nothing in the world but lye, and lye in my throate. By heauen I doe loue, and it hath taught mee to Rime, and to be mallicholie: and here is part of my Rime, and heere my mallicholie. Well, she hath one a' my Sonnets already, the Clowne bore it, the Foole sent it, and the Lady hath it: sweet Clowne, sweeter Foole, sweetest Lady. By the world, I would not care a pin, if the other three were in. Here comes one with a paper, God giue him grace to grone.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Ay mee!

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Shot by heauen: proceede sweet Cupid, thou hast thumpt him with thy Birdbolt vnder the left pap: in faith secrets.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: So sweete a kisse the golden Sunne giues not,
To those fresh morning drops vpon the Rose,
As thy eye beames, when their fresh rayse haue smot.
The night of dew that on my cheekes downe flowes.
Nor shines the siluer Moone one halfe so bright,
Through the transparent bosome of the deepe,
As doth thy face through teares of mine giue light:
Thou shin'st in euery teare that I doe weepe,
No drop, but as a Coach doth carry thee:
So ridest thou triumphing in my woe.
Do but behold the teares that swell in me,
And they thy glory through my griefe will show:
But doe not loue thy selfe, then thou wilt keepe
My teares for glasses, and still make me weepe.
O Queene of Queenes, how farre dost thou excell,
No thought can thinke, nor tongue of mortall tell.
How shall she know my griefes? Ile drop the paper.
Sweet leaues shade folly. Who is he comes heere?
What Longauill, and reading: listen eare.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Now in thy likenesse, one more foole appeare.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Ay me, I am forsworne.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Why he comes in like a periure, wearing papers.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: In loue I hope, sweet fellowship in shame.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: One drunkard loues another of the name.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: Am I the first yt haue been periur'd so?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I could put thee in comfort, not by two that I know,
Thou makest the triumphery, the corner cap of societie,
The shape of Loues Tiburne, that hangs vp simplicitie.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: I feare these stubborn lines lack power to moue.
O sweet Maria, Empresse of my Loue,
These numbers will I teare, and write in prose.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O Rimes are gards on wanton Cupids hose,
Disfigure not his Shop.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: Did not the heauenly Rhetoricke of thine eye,
'Gainst whom the world cannot hold argument,
Perswade my heart to this false periurie?
Vowes for thee broke deserue not punishment.
A woman I forswore, but I will proue,
Thou being a Goddesse, I forswore not thee.
My Vow was earthly, thou a heauenly Loue.
Thy grace being gain'd, cures all disgrace in me.
Vowes are but breath; and breath a vapour is.
Then thou faire Sun, which on my earth doest shine,
Exhalest this vapor-vow, in thee it is:
If broken then, it is no fault of mine:
If by me broke, What foole is not so wise,
To loose an oath, to win a Paradise?
prose: This same shall goe.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: This is the liuer veine, which makes flesh a deity.
A greene Goose, a Coddesse, pure pure Idolatry.
God amend vs, God amend, we are much out o' th' way.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: By whom shall I send this (company?) Stay.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
verse: All hid, all hid, an old infant play,
Like a demie God, here sit I in the skie,
And wretched fooles secrets heedfully ore-eye.
More Sacks to the myll. O heauens I haue my wish,
Dumaine transform'd, foure Woodcocks in a dish.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: O most diuine Kate.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
prose: O most prophane coxcombe.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: By heauen the wonder of a mortall eye.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
prose: By earth she is not, corporall, there you lye.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Her Amber haires for foule hath amber coted.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: An Amber coloured Rauen was well noted.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: As vpright as the Cedar.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Stoope I say her shoulder is with-child.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: As faire as day.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I as some daies, but then no sunne must shine.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: O that I had my wish?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: And I had mine.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: And mine too good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Amen, so I had mine: Is not that a good word?

speeches.speaker: Dum.
verse: I would forget her, but a Feuer she
Raignes in my bloud, and will remembred be.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: A Feuer in your bloud, why then incision
Would let her out in Sawcers, sweet misprision.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Once more Ile read the Ode that I haue writ.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Once more Ile marke how Loue can varry Wit.

verse: This will I send, and something else more plaine.
That shall expresse my true-loues fasting paine.
O would the King, Berowne and Longauill,
Were Louers too, ill to example ill,
Would from my forehead wipe a periur'd note:
For none offend, where all alike doe dote.
prose:
On a day, alack the day:
Loue, whose Month is euery May,
Spied a blossome passing faire,
Playing in the wanton ayre:
Through the Veluet, leaues the winde,
All vnseene, can passage finde.
That the Louer sicke to death,
Wish himselfe the heauens breath.
Ayre (quoth he) thy cheekes may blowe,
Ayre, would I might triumph so.
But alacke my hand is sworne,
Nere to plucke thee from thy throne:
Vow alacke for youth vnmeete,
Youth so apt to plucke a sweet.
Doe not call it sinne in me,
That I am forsworne for thee.
Thou for whom loue would sweare,

Iuno but an Aethiop were,
And denie himselfe for Ioue.

Turning mortall for thy Loue.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: Dumaine, thy Loue is farre from charitie,
That in Loues griefe desir'st societie:
You may looke pale, but I should blush I know,
To be ore-heard, and taken napping so.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Come sir, you blush: as his, your case is such,
You chide at him, offending twice as much.
You doe not loue Maria? Longauile,
Did neuer Sonnet for her sake compile;
Nor neuer lay his wreathed armes athwart
His louing bosome, to keepe downe his heart.
I haue beene closely shrowded in this bush,
And markt you both, and for you both did blush.
I heard your guilty Rimes, obseru'd your fashion:
Saw sighes reeke from you, noted well your passion.
Aye me, sayes one! O Ioue, the other cries!
On her haires were Gold, Christall the others eyes.
You would for Paradise breake Faith and troth,
And Ioue for your Loue would infringe an oath.
What will Berowne say when that he shall heare
Faith infringed, which such zeale did sweare.
How will he scorne? how will he spend his wit?
How will he triumph, leape, and laugh at it?
For all the wealth that euer I did see,
I would not haue him know so much by me.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
verse: Now step I forth to whip hypocrisie.
Ah good my Liedge, I pray thee pardon me.
Good heart, What grace hast thou thus to reproue
These wormes for louing, that art most in loue?
Your eyes doe make no couches in your teares.
There is no certaine Princesse that appeares.
You'll not be periur'd, 'tis a hatefull thing:
Tush, none but Minstrels like of Sonnetting.
But are you not asham'd? nay, are you not
All three of you, to be thus much ore'shot?
You found his Moth, the King your Moth did see:
But I a Beame doe finde in each of three.
O what a Scene of fool'ry haue I seene.
Of sighes, of grones, of sorrow, and of teene:
O me, with what strict patience haue I sat,
To see a King transformed to a Gnat?
To see great Hercules whipping a Gigge,
And profound Salomon tuning a Iygge?
And Nestor play at push-pin with the boyes,
And Critticke Tymon laugh at idle toyes.
Where lies thy griefe? O tell me good Dumaine;
And gentle Longauill, where lies thy paine?
And where my Liedges? all about the brest:
A Candle hoa!

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Too bitter is thy iest.
Are wee betrayed thus to thy ouer-view?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Not you by me, but I betrayed to you.
I that am honest, I that hold it sinne
To breake the vow I am ingaged in.
I am betrayed by keeping company
With men, like men of inconstancie.
When shall you see me write a thing in rime?
Or grone for Ioane? or spend a minutes time,
prose: In pruning mee, when shall you heare that I will praise a hand, a foot, a face, an eye: a gate, a state, a brow, a brest, a waste, a legge, a limme.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Soft, Whither a-way so fast?
A true man, or a theefe, that gallops so.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I post from Loue, good Louer let me go.

speeches.speaker: Iaqu.
prose: God blesse the King.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: What Present hast thou there?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Some certaine treason.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: What makes treason heere?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Nay it makes nothing sir.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: If it marre nothing neither,
The treason and you goe in peace away together.

speeches.speaker: Iaqu.
verse: I beseech your Grace let this Letter be read,
Our person mis-doubts it: it was treason he said.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Berowne, read it ouer.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Where hadst thou it?

speeches.speaker: Iaqu.
prose: Of Costard.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Where hadst thou it?

speeches.speaker: Cost.
prose: Of Dun Adramadio, Dun Adramadio.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: How now, what is in you? why dost thou tear it?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: A toy my Liedge, a toy: your grace needes not feare it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: It did moue him to passion, and therefore let's heare it.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: It is Berowns writing, and heere is his name.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Ah you whoreson loggerhead, you were borne to doe me shame.
Guilty my Lord, guilty: I confesse, I confesse.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: What?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: That you three fooles, lackt mee foole, to make vp the messe.
He, he, and you: and you my Liedge, and I,
Are picke-purses in Loue, and we deserue to die.
O dismisse this audience, and I shall tell you more.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Now the number is euen.

speeches.speaker: Berow.
prose: True true, we are fowre: will these Turtles be gone?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Hence sirs, away.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Walk aside the true folke, & let the traytors stay.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Sweet Lords, sweet Louers, O let vs imbrace,
As true we are as flesh and bloud can be,
The Sea will ebbe and flow, heauen will shew his face:
Young bloud doth not obey an old decree.
We cannot crosse the cause why we are borne:
Therefore of all hands must we be forsworne.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: What, did these rent lines shew some loue of thine?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Did they, quoth you? Who sees the heauenly Rosaline,
That (like a rude and sauage man of Inde.)
At the first opening of the gorgeous East,
Bowes not his vassall head, and strooken blinde,
Kisses the base ground with obedient breast?
What peremptory Eagle-sighted eye
Dares looke vpon the heauen of her brow,
That is not blinded by her maiestie?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: What zeale, what furie, hath inspir'd thee now?
My Loue (her Mistres) is a gracious Moone,
Shee (an attending Starre) scarce seene a light.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: My eyes are then no eyes, nor I Berowne.
O, but for my Loue, day would turne to night,
Of all complexions the cul'd soueraignty,
Doe meet as at a faire in her faire cheeke,
Where seuerall Worthies make one dignity,
Where nothing wants, that want it selfe doth seeke.
Lend me the flourish of all gentle tongues,
Fie painted Rethoricke, O she needs it not,
To things of sale, a sellers praise belongs:
She passes prayse, then prayse too short doth blot.
A withered Hermite, fiuescore winters worne,
Might shake off fiftie, looking in her eye:
Beauty doth varnish Age, as if new borne,
And giues the Crutch the Cradles infancie.
O 'tis the Sunne that maketh all things shine.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: By heauen, thy Loue is blacke as Ebonie.

speeches.speaker: Berow.
verse: Is Ebonie like her? O word diuine?
A wife of such wood were felicitie.
O who can giue an oth? Where is a booke?
That I may sweare Beauty doth beauty lacke,
If that she learne not of her eye to looke:
No face is faire that is not full so blacke.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: O paradoxe, Blacke is the badge of hell,
The hue of dungeons, and the Schoole of night:
And beauties crest becomes the heauens well.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Diuels soonest tempt resembling spirits of light.
O if in blacke my Ladies browes be deckt,
It mournes, that painting vsurping haire
Should rauish doters with a false aspect:
And therfore is she borne to make blacke, faire.
Her fauour turnes the fashion of the dayes,
For natiue bloud is counted painting now:
And therefore red that would auoyd dispraise,
Paints it selfe blacke, to imitate her brow.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: To look like her are Chimny-sweepers blacke.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: And since her time, are Colliers counted bright.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: And Aethiops of their sweet complexion crake.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Dark needs no Candles now, for dark is light.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Your mistresses dare neuer come in raine,
For feare their colours should be washt away.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: 'Twere good yours did: for sir to tell you plaine,
Ile finde a fairer face not washt to day.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Ile proue her faire, or talke till dooms-day here.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: No Diuell will fright thee then so much as shee.

speeches.speaker: Duma.
prose: I neuer knew man hold vile stuffe so deere.

speeches.speaker: Lou.
prose: Looke, heer's thy loue, my foot and her face see.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O if the streets were paued with thine eyes,
Her feet were much too dainty for such tread.

speeches.speaker: Duma.
verse: O vile, then as she goes what vpward lyes?
The street should see as she walk'd ouer head.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: But what of this, are we not all in loue?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: O nothing so sure, and thereby all forsworne.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Then leaue this chat, & good Berown now proue
Our louing lawfull, and our fayth not torne.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: I marie there, some flattery for this euill.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: O some authority how to proceed,
Some tricks, some quillets, how to cheat the diuell.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Some salue for periurie.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O 'tis more then neede.
Haue at you then affections men at armes,
Consider what you first did sweare vnto:
To fast, to study, and to see no woman:
Flat treason against the Kingly state of youth.
Say, Can you fast? your stomacks are too young:
And abstinence ingenders maladies.
And where that you haue vow'd to studie (Lords)
In that each of you haue forsworne his Booke
Can you still dreame and pore, and thereon looke.
For when would you my Lord, or you, or you,
Haue found the ground of studies excellence,
Without the beauty of a womans face;
From womens eyes this doctrine I deriue,
They are the Ground, the Bookes, the Achadems,
From whence doth spring the true Promethean fire.
Why, vniuersall plodding poysons vp
The nimble spirits in the arteries,
As motion and long during action tyres
The sinnowy vigour of the trauailer.
Now for not looking on a womans face,
You haue in that forsworne the vse of eyes:
And studie too, the causer of your vow.
For where is any Author in the world,
Teaches such beauty as a womans eye:
Learning is but an adiunct to our selfe,
And where we are, our Learning likewise is.
Then when our selues we see in Ladies eyes,
With our selues.
Doe we not likewise see our learning there?
O we haue made a Vow to studie, Lords,
And in that vow we haue forsworne our Bookes:
For when would you (my Leege) or you, or you?
In leaden contemplation haue found out
Such fiery Numbers as the prompting eyes,
Of beauties tutors haue inrich'd you with:
Other slow Arts intirely keepe the braine:
And therefore finding barraine practizers,
Scarce shew a haruest of their heauy toyle.
But Loue first learned in a Ladies eyes,
Liues not alone emured in the braine:
But with the motion of all elements,
Courses as swift as thought in euery power,
And giues to euery power a double power,
Aboue their functions and their offices.
It addes a precious seeing to the eye:
A Louers eyes will gaze an Eagle blinde.
A Louers eare will heare the lowest sound.
When the suspicious head of theft is stopt.
Loues feeling is more soft and sensible,
Then are the tender hornes of Cockled Snayles.
Loues tongue proues dainty, Bachus grosse in taste,
For Valour, is not Loue a Hercules?
Still climing trees in the Hesporides.
Subtill as Sphinx, as sweet and musicall,
As bright Apollo's Lute, strung with his haire.
And when Loue speakes, the voyce of all the Gods,
Make heauen drowsie with the harmonie.
Neuer durst Poet touch a pen to write,
Vntill his Inke were tempred with Loues sighes:
O then his lines would rauish sauage eares,
And plant in Tyrants milde humilitie.
From womens eyes this doctrine I deriue.
They sparcle still the right promethean fire,
They are the Bookes, the Arts, the Achademes,
That shew, containe, and nourish all the world.
Else none at all in ought proues excellent.
Then fooles you were these women to forsweare:
Or keeping what is sworne, you will proue fooles,
For Wisedomes sake, a word that all men loue:
Or for Loues sake, a word that loues all men.
Or for Mens sake, the author of these Women:
Or Womens sake, by whom we men are Men.
Let's once loose our oathes to finde our selues,
Or else we loose our selues, to keepe our oathes.
It is religion to be thus forsworne.
For Charity it selfe fulfills the Law:
And who can seuer loue from Charity.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Saint Cupid then, and Souldiers to the field.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Aduance your standards, & vpon them Lords.
Pell, mell, downe with them: but be first aduis'd,
In conflict that you get the Sunne of them.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Now to plaine dealing, Lay these glozes by,
Shall we resolue to woe these girles of France?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: And winne them too, therefore let vs deuise,
Some entertainment for them in their Tents.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: First from the Park let vs conduct them thither,
Then homeward euery man attach the hand
Of his faire Mistresse, in the afternoone
We will with some strange pastime solace them:
Such as the shortnesse of the time can shape,
For Reuels, Dances, Maskes, and merry houres,
Fore-runne faire Loue, strewing her way with flowres.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Away, away, no time shall be omitted,
That will be time, and may by vs be fitted.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Alone, alone sowed Cockell, reap'd no Corne,
And Iustice alwaies whirles in equall measure:
Light Wenches may proue plagues to men forsworne,
If so, our Copper buyes no better treasure.

speeches.speaker: Pedant.
prose: Satis quid sufficit.

speeches.speaker: Curat.
prose: I praise God for you sir, your reasons at dinner haue beene sharpe & sententious: pleasant without scurrillity, witty without affection, audacious without impudency, learned without opinion, and strange without heresie: I did conuerse this quondam day with a companion of the Kings, who is intituled, nominated, or called, Don Adriano de Armatho.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Noui hominum tanquam te, His humour is lofty, his discourse peremptorie: his tongue filed, his eye ambitious, his gate maiesticall, and his generall behauiour vaine, ridiculous, and thrasonicall. He is too picked, too spruce, too affected, too odde, as it were, too peregrinat, as I may call it.

speeches.speaker: Curat.
prose: A most singular and choise Epithat,

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: He draweth out the thred of his verbositie, finer then the staple of his argument. I abhor such phanaticall phantasims, such insociable and poynt deuise companions, such rackers of ortagriphie, as to speake dout fine, when he should say doubt; det, when he shold pronounce debt; de^t, not det: he clepeth a Calf, Caufe: halfe, haufe: neighbour vocatur nebour; neigh abreuiated ne: this is abhominable, which he would call abhominable: it insinuateth me of infamie: ne inteligis domine, to make franti^ke, lunaticke?

speeches.speaker: Cura.
prose: Laus deo, bene intelligo.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Bome boon for boon prescian, a little scratcht, 'twil serue.

speeches.speaker: Curat.
prose: Vides ne quis venit?

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Video, & gaudio.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Chirra.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose:
Quar^
Chirra, not Sirra?

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Men of peace well incountred.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Most millitarie sir salutation.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: They haue beene at a great feast of Languages, and stolne the scraps.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: O they haue liu'd long on the almes-basket of words. I maruell thy M. hath not eaten thee for a word, for thou art not so long by the head as honorificabilitudinitatibus: Thou art easier swallowed then a flap dragon.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Peace, the peale begins.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Mounsier, are you not lettred?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Yes, yes, he ^eaches boyes the Horne-booke:
What is Abspeld backward with the horn on his head?

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Ba, puericia with a horne added.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: Ba most seely Sheepe, with a horne: you heare his learning.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Quis quis, thou Consonant?

speeches.speaker: Pag
prose: The last of the fiue Vowels if You repeat them, or the fift if I.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: I will repeat them: a e I.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: The She^pe, the other two concludes it o u.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Now by the salt waue of the mediteranium, a sweet tutch, a quicke vene we of wit, snip snap, quick & home, it reioyceth my intellect, true wit.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Offered by a childe to an olde man: which is wit-old.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: What is the figure? What is the figure?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: Hornes.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Thou disputes like an Infant: goe whip thy Gigge.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: Lend me your Horne to make one, and I will whip about your Infamie vnum cita a gigge of a Cuckolds horne.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: And I had but one penny in the world, thou shouldst haue it to buy Ginger bread: Hold, there is the very Remuneration I had of thy Maister, thou halfpenny purse of wit, thou Pidgeon-egge of discretion. O & the heauens were so pleased, that thou wert but my Bastard; What a ioyfull father wouldst thou make mee? Goe to, thou hast it ad dungil, at the fingers ends, as they say.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Oh I smell false Latine, dunghel for vnguem.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Arts-man preambulat, we will bee singled from the barbarous. Do you not educate youth at the Charghouse on the top of the Mountaine?

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Or Mons the hill.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: At your sweet pleasure, for the Mountaine.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: I doe sans question.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
prose: Sir, it is the Kings most sweet pleasure and affection, to congratulate the Princesse at her Pauilion, in the posteriors of this day, which the rude multitude call the after-noone.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: The posterior of the day, most generous sir, is liable, congruent, and measurable for the after-noone: the word is well culd, chose, sweet, and apt I doe assure you sir, I doe assure.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Sir, the King is a noble Gentleman, and my familiar, I doe assure ye very good friend: for what is inward betweene vs, let it passe. I doe beseech thee remember thy curtesie. I beseech thee apparell thy head: and among other importunate & most serious designes, and of great import indeed too: but let that passe, for I must tell thee it will please his Grace (by the world) sometime to leane vpon my poore shoulder, and with his royall finger thus dallie with my excrement, with my mustachio: but sweet heart let that passe. By the world I recount no fable, some certaine speciall honours it pleaseth his greatnesse to impart to Armado a Souldier, a man of trauell, that hath seene the world: but let that passe; the very all of all is: but sweet heart, I do implore secrecie, that the King would haue mee present the Princesse (sweet chucke) with some delightfull ostentation, or show, or pageant, or anticke, or fire-worke: Now, vnderstanding that the Curate and your sweet self are good at such eruptions, and sodaine breaking out of myrth ^. i^ were) I haue acquainted you withall, to the end to craue your assistance.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Sir, you shall present before her the Nine Worthies. Sir Holofernes, as concerning some entertainment of time, some show in the posterior of this day, to bee rendred by our assistants the Kings command: and this most gallant, illustrate and learned Gentleman, before the Princesse: I say none so sit as to present the Nine Worthies.

speeches.speaker: Curat.
prose: Where will you finde men worthy enough to present them?

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Iosua, your selfe: my selfe, and this gallant gentleman Iudas Machabeus; this Swaine (because of his great limme or ^oynt) shall passe Pompey the great, the Page Hercules.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Pardon sir, error: He is not quantitie enough for that Worthies thumb, hee is not so big as the end of his Club.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Shall I haue audience? he shall present Hercules in minoritie: his enter and exit shall bee strangling a Snake; and I will haue an Apologie for that purpose.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: An excellent deuice: so if any of the audience hisse, you may cry, Well done Hercules, now thou crushest the Snake; that is the way to make an offence gracious, though few haue the grace to doe it.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: For the rest of the Worthies?

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: I will play three my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: Thrice worthy Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Shall I tell you a thing?

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: We attend.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: We will haue, if this fadge not, an Antique. I beseech you follow.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Via good-man Dull, thou hast spoken no word all this while.

speeches.speaker: Dull.
prose: Nor vnderstood none neither sir.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Alone, we will employ thee.

speeches.speaker: Dull.
prose:
Ile make one in a dance, or so: or I will play

on the taber to the Worthies, & let them dance the hey.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Most Dull, honest Dull, to our sport away.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Sweet hearts we shall be rich ere we depart,
If fairings come thus plentifully in.
A Lady wal'd about with Diamonds: Look you, what I haue from the louing King.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Madam, came nothing else along with that?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Nothing but this yes as much loue in Rime,
As would be cram'd vp in a sheet of paper
Writ on both sides the lease, margent and all,
That he was faine to seale on Cupids name.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: That was the way to make his god-head wax:
For he hath beene fiue thousand yeeres a Boy.

speeches.speaker: Kath.
prose: I, and a shrewd vnhappy gallowes too.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: You'll nere be friends with him, a kild your sister.

speeches.speaker: Kath.
prose: He made her melancholy, sad, and heauy, and so she died: had she beene Light like you, of such a merrie nimble stirring spirit, she might a bin a Grandam ere she died. And so may you: For a light heart liues long.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: What's your darke meaning mouse, of this light word?

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: A light condition in a beauty darke.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: We need more light to finde your meaning out.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
verse: You'll marre the light by taking it in snuffe:
Therefore Ile darkely end the argument.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Look what you doe, you doe it stil i' th darke.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: So do not you, for you are a light Wench.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Indeed I waigh not you, and therefore light.

speeches.speaker: Ka.
prose: You waigh me not, O that's you care not for me.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Great reason: for past care, is still past cure.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Well bandied both, a set of Wit well played.
But Rosaline, you haue a Fauour too?
Who sent it? and what is it?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I would you knew.
And if my face were but as faire as yours.
My Fauour were as great, be witnesse this.
Nay, I haue Verses too, I thanke Berowne,
The numbers true, and were the numbring too,
I were the fairest goddesse on the ground.
I am compar'd to twenty thousand fairs.
O he hath drawne my picture in his letter.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Any thing like?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Much in the letters, nothing in the praise.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Beauteous as Incke: a good conclusion.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Faire as a text B. in a Coppie booke.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ware pensals. How? Let me not die your debtor,
My red Dominicall, my golden letter.
O that your face were full of Ocs.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: A Pox of that iest, and I beshrew all Shrowes:
But Katherine, what was sent to you
From faire Dumaine?

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Madame, this Gloue.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Did he not send you twaine?

speeches.speaker: Kat.
verse: Yes Madame: and moreouer,
Some thousand Verses of a faithfull Louer.
A huge translation of hypocrisie,
Vildly compiled, profound simplicitie.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: This, and these Pearls, to me sent Longauile.
The Letter is too long by halfe a mile.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: I thinke no lesse: Dost thou wish in heart
The Chaine were longer, and the Letter short.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I, or I would these hands might neuer part.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
prose: We are wise girles to mocke our Louers so.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: They are worse fooles to purchase mocking so.
That same Berowne ile torture ere I goe.
O that I knew he were but in by th' weeke,
How I would make him fawne, and begge, and seeke,
And wait the season, and obserue the times,
And spend his prodigall wits in booteles rimes.
And shape his seruice wholly to my deuice,
And make him proud to make me proud that iests.
So pertaunt like would I o' resway his state,
That he shold be my foole, and I his fate.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: None are so surely caught. when they are catcht,
As Wit turn'd foole, follie in Wisedome hatch'd:
Hath wisedoms warrant, and the helpe of Schoole,
And Wits owne grace to grace a learned Foole?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: The bloud of youth burns not with such excesse,
As grauities reuolt to wantons be.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Follie in Fooles beares not so strong a note,
As fool'ry in the Wise, when Wit doth dote:
Since all the power thereof it doth apply,
To proue by Wit, worth in simplicitie.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Heere comes Boyet, and mirth in his face.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: O I am stab'd with laughter, Wher's her Grace?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Thy newes Boyet?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Prepare Madame, prepare.
Arme Wenches arme, incounters mounted are,
Against your Peace, Loue doth approach, disguis'd:
Armed in arguments, you'll be surpriz'd.
Muster your Wits, stand in your owne defence,
Or hide your heads like Cowards, and flie hence.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Saint Dennis to S. Cupid: What are they,
That charge their breath against vs? Say scout say.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Vnder the coole shade of a Siccamore,
I thought to close mine eyes some halfe an houre:
When lo to interrupt my purpos'd rest,
Toward that shade I might behold addrest,
The King and his companions: warely
I stole into a neighbour thicket by,
And ouer-heard, what you shall ouer-heare:
That by and by disguis'd they will be heere.
Their Herald is a pretty knauish Page:
That well by heart hath con'd his embassage,
Action and accent did they teach him there.
Thus must thou speake, and thus thy body beare.
And euer and anon they made a doubt,
Presence maiesticall would put him out:
For quoth the King, an Angell shalt thou see:
Yet feare not thou, but speake audaciously.
The Boy reply'd, An Angell is not euill:
I should haue fear'd her, had she beene a deuill.
With that all laugh'd, and clap'd him on the shoulder,
Making the bold wagg by their praises bolder.
One rub'd his elboe thus, and fleer'd, and swore,
A better speech was neuer spoke before.
Another with his finger and his thumb,
Cry'd via, we will doo't, come what will come.
The third he caper'd and cried, All goes well.
The fourth turn'd on the toe, and downe he fell:
With that they all did tumble on the ground,
With such a zelous laughter so profound,
That in this spleene ridiculous appeares,
To checke their folly passions solemne teares.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
prose: But what, but what, come they to visit vs?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: They do, they do; and are apparel'd thus,
Like Muscouites, or Russians, as I gesse.
Their purpose is to parlee, to court, and dance,
And euery one his Loue-feat will aduance,
Vnto his seuerall Mistresse: which they'll know
By fauours seuerall, which they did bestow.

speeches.speaker: Queen.
verse: And will they so? the Gallants shall be taskt:
For Ladies; we will euery one be maskt,
And not a man of them shall haue the grace
Despight of sute, to see a Ladies face.
Hold Rosaline, this Fauour thou shalt weare,
And then the King will court thee for his Deare:
Hold, take thou this my sweet, and giue me thine,
So shall Berowne take me for Rosaline.
And change your Fauours too, so shall your Loues
Woo contrary, deceiu'd by these remoues.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Come on then, weare the fauours most in sight.

speeches.speaker: Kath.
prose: But in this changing, What is your intent?

speeches.speaker: Queen.
verse: The effect of my intent is to crosse theirs:
They doe it but in mocking merriment,
And mocke for mocke is onely my intent.
Their seuerall counsels they vnbosome shall,
To Loues mistooke, and so be mockt withall.
Vpon the next occasion that we meete,
With Visages displayd to talke and greete.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: But shall we dance, if they desire vs too't?

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: No, to the death we will not moue a foot,
Nor to their pen'd speech render we no grace:
But while 'tis spoke, each turne away his face.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Why that contempt will kill the keepers heart,
And quite diuorce his memory from his part.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Therefore I doe it, and I make no doubt,
The rest will ere come in, if he be out.
Theres no such sport, as sport by sport orethrowne:
To make theirs ours, and ours none but our owne.
So shall we stay mocking entended game,
And they well mockt, depart away with shame.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: The Trompet sounds, be maskt, the maskers come.

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: All haile, the richest Beauties on the earth.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Beauties no richer then rich Taffata.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: A holy parcell of the fairest dames that euer turn'd their backes to mortall viewes.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Their eyes villaine, their eyes.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse: That euer turn'd their eyes to mortall viewes.
Out

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: True, out indeed.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse: Out of your fauours heauenly spirits vouchsafe
Not to beholde.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Once to behold, rogue.

speeches.speaker: Pag
verse: Once to behold with your Sunne beamed eyes,
With your Sunne beamed eyes.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: They will not answer to that Epythite,
You were best call it Daughter beamed eyes.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
prose: They do not marke me, and that brings me out.

speeches.speaker: Bero.
prose: Is this your perfectnesse? be gon you rogue.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: What would these strangers?
Know their mindes Boyet.
If they doe speake our language, 'tis our will
That some plaine man recount their purposes.
Know what they would?

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
prose: What would you with the Princes?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Nothing but peace, and gentle visitation.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: What would they, say they?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Nothing but peace, and gentle visitation.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Why that they haue, and bid them so be gon.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: She saies you haue it, and you may be gon.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Say to her we haue measur'd many miles,
To tread a Measure with you on the grasse.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: They say that they haue measur'd many a mile,
To tread a Measure with you on this grasse.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: It is not so. Aske them how many inches
Is in one mile? If they haue measur'd manie,
The measure then of one is easlie told:

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: If to come hither, you haue measur'd miles,
And many miles: the Princesse bids you tell,
How many inches doth fill vp one mile?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Tell her we measure them by weary steps.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: She heares her selfe.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: How manie wearie steps,
Of many wearie miles you haue ore-gone,
Are numbred in the trauell of one mile?

speeches.speaker: Bero.
verse: We number nothing that we spend for you,
Our dutie is so rich, so infinite,
That we may doe it still without accompt.
Vouchsafe to shew the sunshine of your face,
That we (like sauages) may worship it.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: My face is but a Moone, and clouded too.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Blessed are clouds, to doe as such clouds do.
Vouchsafe bright Moone, and these thy stars to shine,
(Those clouds remooued) vpon our waterie eyne.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: O vaine peticioner, beg a greater matter,
Thou now requests but Mooneshine in the water.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Then in our measure, vouchsafe but one change.
Thou bidst me begge, this begging is not strange.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: Play musicke then: nay you must doe it soone.
Not yet no dance: thus change I like the Moone.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Will you not dance? How come you thus estranged?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: You tooke the Moone at full, but now shee's changed?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Yet still she is the Moone, and I the Man.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: The musick playes, vouchsafe some motion to it: Our eares vouchsafe it.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: But your legges should doe it.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Since you are strangers, & come here by chance,
Wee'll not be nice, take hands, we will not dance.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Why take you hands then?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: Onelie to part friends.
Curtsie sweet hearts, and so the Measure ends.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: More measure of this measure, be not nice.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: We can afford no more at such a price.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Prise your selues: What buyes your companie?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Your absence onelie.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: That can neuer be.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: Then cannot we be bought: and so adue,
Twice to your Visore, and halfe once to you.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: If you denie to dance, let's hold more chat.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: In priuate then.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: I am best pleas'd with that.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: White handed Mistris, one sweet word with thee.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Hony, and Milke, and Suger: there is three.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Nay then two treyes, an if you grow so nice
Methegline, Wort, and Malmsey; well runne dice:
There's halfe a dozen sweets.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Seuenth sweet adue, since you can cogg,
Ile play no more with you.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: One word in secret.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Let it not be sweet.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Thou greeu'st my gall.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Gall, bitter.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Therefore meete.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Will you vouchsafe with me to change a word?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Name it.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Faire Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Say you so? Faire Lord:
Take you that for your faire Lady.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Please it you,
As much in priuate, and Ile bid adieu.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: What, was your vizard made without a tong?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I know the reason Ladie why you aske.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: O for your reason, quickly sir, I long.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: You haue a double tongue within your mask.
And would affoord my speechlesse vizard halfe.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Veale quoth the Dutch-man: is not Veale a Calfe?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: A Calfe faire Ladie?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: No, a faire Lord Calfe.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Let's part the word.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No, Ile not be your halfe:
Take all and weane it, it may proue an Oxe.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Looke how you but your selfe in those sharpe mockes.
Will you giue hornes chast Ladie? Do not so.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Then die a Calfe before your horns do grow.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: One word in priuate with you ere I die.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Bleat softly then, the Butcher heares you cry.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
verse: The tongues of mocking wenches are as keen
As is the Razors edge, inuisible:
Cutting a smaller haire then may be seene,
Aboue the sense of sence so sensible:
Seemeth their conference, their conceits haue wings,
Fleeter then arrows, bullets wind, thoght, swifter things

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Not one word more my maides, breake off, breake off.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: By heauen, all drie beaten with pure scoffe.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Farewell madde Wenches, you haue simple wits.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Twentie adieus my frozen Muscouits.
Are these the breed of wits so wondred at?

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
prose: Tapers they are, with your sweete breathes puft out.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Wel-liking wits they haue, grosse, grosse, fat, fat.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: O pouertie in wit, Kingly poore flout.
Will they not (thinke you) hang themselues to night?
Or euer but in vizards shew their faces:
This pert Berowne was out of count'nance quite.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: They were all in lamentable cases.
The King was vveeping ripe for a good word.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Berowne did sweare himselfe out of all suite.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Dumaine was at my seruice, and his sword:
No point (quoth I:) my seruant straight vvas mute.

speeches.speaker: Ka.
verse: Lord Longauill said I came ore his hart:
And trow you vvhat he call'd me?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Qualme perhaps.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Yes in good faith.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Go sicknesse as thou art.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Well, better wits haue worne plain statute caps,
But vvil you heare; the King is my loue sworne.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: And quicke Berowne hath plighted faith to me.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: And Longauill was for my seruice borne.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Dumaine is mine as sure as barke on tree.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
verse: Madam, and prettie mistresses giue care,
Immediately they will againe be heere
In their owne shapes: for it can neuer be,
They will digest this harsh indignitie.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Will they returne?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: They will they will, God knowes,
And leape for ioy, though they are lame with blowes:
Therefore change Fauours, and when they repaire,
Blow like sweet Roses, in this summer aire.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: How blovv? how blovv? Speake to bee vnderstood.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Faire Ladies maskt, are Roses in their bud:
Dismaskt, their damaske sweet commixture showne,
Are Angels vailing clouds, or Roses blowne.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Auant perplexitie: What shall vve do,
If they returne in their owne shapes to wo?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: Good Madam, if by me you'l be aduis'd,
Let's mocke them still as well knowne as disguis'd:
Let vs complaine to them vvhat fooles were heare,
Disguis'd like Muscouites in shapelesse geare:
And wonder what they were, and to what end
Their shallow showes, and Prologue vildely pen'd:
And their rough carriage so ridiculous,
Should be presented at our Tent to vs.

speeches.speaker: Boyet.
prose: Ladies, withdraw: the gallants are at hand.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
prose: Whip to our Tents, as Roes runnes ore Land.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Faire sir, God saue you. Wher's the Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Gone to her Tent.
Please it your Maiestie command me any seruice to her?

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: That she vouchsafe me audience for one word.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I will, and so will she, I know my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: This fellow pickes vp wit as Pigeons pease,
And vtters it againe, when Ioue doth please.
He is Wits Pedler, and retailes his Wares,
At Wakes, and Wassels, Meetings, M^kets, Faires.
And we that sell by grosse, the Lord doth know,
Haue not the grace to grace it with such show.
This Gallant pins the Wenches on his sleeue.
Had he bin Adam, he had tempted Eue.
He can carue too, and lispe: Why this is he,
That kist away his hand in courtesie.
This is the Ape of Forme, Monsieur the nice,
That when he plaies at Tables, chides the Dice
In honorable tearmes: Nay he can sing
A meane most meanly, and in Vshering
Mend him who can: the Ladies call him sweete.
The staires as he treads on them kisse his feete.
This is the flower that smiles on euerie one,
To shew his teeth as white as Whales bone.
And consciences that wil not die in debt,
Pay him the dutie of honie-tongued Boyet.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: A blister on his sweet tongue with my hart,
That put Armathoes Page out of his part.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: See where it comes. Behauiour what wer't thou,
Till this madman shew'd thee? And what art thou now?

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: All haile sweet Madame, and faire time of day.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Faire in all Haile is foule, as I conceiue.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Construe my speeches better, if you may.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Then wish me better, I wil giue you leaue.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: We came to visit you, and purpose now
To leade you to our Court, vouchsafe it then.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: This field shal hold me, and so hold your vow:
Nor God, nor I, delights in periur'd men.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Rebuke me not for that which you prouoke:
The vertue of your eie must breake my oth.

speeches.speaker: Q.
verse: You nickname vertue: vice you should haue spoke:
For vertues office neuer breakes men troth.
Now by my maiden honor, yet as pure
As the vnsallied Lilly, I protest,
A world of torments though I should endure,
I would not yeeld to be your houses guest:
So much I hate a breaking cause to be
Of heauenly oaths, vow'd with integritie.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: O you haue liu'd in desolation heere,
Vnseene, vnuisited, much to our shame.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Not so my Lord, it is not so I sweare,
We haue had pastimes heere, and pleasant game,
A messe of Russians left vs but of late.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: How Madam? Russians?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: I in truth, my Lord.
Trim gallants, full of Courtship and of state.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: Madam speake true. It is not so my Lord:
My Ladie (to the manner of the daies)
In curtesie giues vndeseruing praise.
We foure indeed confronted were with foure
In Russia habit: Heere they stayed an houre,
And talk'd apace: and in that houre (my Lord)
They did not blesse vs with one happy word.
I dare not call them fooles; but this I thinke,
When they are thirstie, fooles would faine haue drinke.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: This iest is drie to me. Gentle sweete,
Your wits makes wise things foolish when we greete
With eies best seeing, heauens fierie eie:
By light we loose light; your capacitie
Is of that nature, that to your huge stoore,
Wise things seeme foolish, and rich things but poore.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: This proues you wise and rich: for in my eie

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I am a foole, and full of pouertie.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: But that you take what doth to you belong,
It were a fault to snatch words from my tongue.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: O, I am yours and all that I possesse.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: All the foole mine.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I cannot giue you lesse.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Which of the Vizards what it that you wore?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Where? when? What Vizard?
Why demand you this?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: There, then, that vizard, that superfluous case,
That hid the worse, and shew'd the better face.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: We are discried,
They'l mocke vs now downeright.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Let vs confesse, and turne it to a iest.

speeches.speaker: Que.
prose: Amaz'd my Lord? Why lookes your Highnes sadde?

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
verse: Helpe hold his browes, hee'l sound: why looke you pale?
Sea-sicke I thinke comming from Muscouie.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Thus poure the stars down plagues for periury.
Can any face of brasse hold longer out?
Heere stand I Ladie dart thy skill at me,
Bruise me with scorne, confound me with a flout.
Thrust thy sharpe wit quite through my ignorance.
Cut me to peeces with thy keene conceit:
And I will wish thee neuer more to dance,
Nor neuer more in Russian habit waite.
O! neuer will I trust to speeches pen'd,
Nor to the motion of a Schoole-boies tongue
Nor neuer come in vizard to my friend,
Nor woo in rime like a blind-harpers songue,
Taffata phrases, silken tearmes precise,
Three-pil'd Hyperboles, spruce affection;
Figures pedanticall, these summer flies,
Haue blowne me full of maggot ostentation.
I do forsweare them, and I heere protest,
By this white Gloue (how white the hand God knows)
Henceforth my woing minde shall be exprest
In russet yeas, and honest kersie noes.
And to begin Wench, so God helpe me law,
My loue to thee is sound, sans cracke or flaw.

speeches.speaker: Rosa.
prose: Sans, sans, I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Yet I haue a tricke
Of the old rage: beare with me, I am sicke.
Ile leaue it by degrees: soft, let vs see,
Write Lord haue mercie on vs, on those three,
They are infected, in their hearts it lies:
They haue the plague, and caught it of your eyes:
These Lords are visited, you are not free:
For the Lords tokens on you do I see.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: No, they are free that gaue these tokens to vs.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Our states are forfeit, seeke not to vndo vs.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: It is not so; for how can this be true,
That you stand forfeit, being those that sue.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Peace, for I will not haue to do with you.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Nor shall not, if I do as I intend.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Speake for your selues, my wit is at an end.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Teach vs sweete Madame, for our rude transgression, some faire excuse.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: The fairest is confession.
Were you not heere but euen now, disguis'd?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Madam, I was.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: And were you well aduis'd?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: I was faire Madam.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: When you then were heere,
What did you whisper in your Ladies eare?

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: That more then all the world I did respect her

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: When shee shall challenge this, you will reiect her.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Vpon mine Honor no.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Peace, peace, forbeare: your oath once broke, you force not to forsweare.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Despise me when I breake this oath of mine.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: I will, and therefore keepe it. Rosaline,
What did the Russian whisper in your eare?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Madam, he swore that he did hold me deare
As precious eye-sight, and did value me
Aboue this World: adding thereto moreouer,
That he vvould Wed me, or else die my Louer.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: God giue thee ioy of him: the Noble Lord Most honorably doth vphold his word.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What meane you Madame?
By my life, my troth,
I neuer swore this Ladie such an oth.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: By heauen you did; and to confirme it plaine, you gaue me this: But take it sir againe.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: My faith and this, the Princesse I did giue,
I knew her by this Iewell on her sleeue.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Pardon me sir, this Iewell did she weare,
And Lord Berowne (I thanke him) is my deare.
What? Will you haue me, or your Pearle againe?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Neither of either, I remit both twaine.
I see the tricke on't: Heere was a consent,
Knowing aforehand of our merriment,
To dash it like a Christmas Comedie.
Some carry-tale, some please-man, some slight Zanie,
Some mumble-newes, some trencher-knight, som Dick
That smiles his cheeke in yeares, and knowes the trick
To make my Lady laugh, when she's dispos'd;
Told our intents before: which once disclos'd,
The Ladies did change Fauours, and then we
Following the signes, woo'd but the signe of she.
Now to our periurie, to adde more terror,
We are againe forsworne in will and error.
Much vpon this tis: and might not you
Forestall our sport, to make vs thus vntrue?
Do not you know my Ladies foot by 'th squier?
And laugh vpon the apple of her eie?
And stand betweene her backe sir, and the fire,
Holding a trencher, iesting merrilie?
You put our Page out: go, you are alowd.
Die when you will, a smocke shall be your shrowd.
You leere vpon me, do you? There's an eie
Wounds like a Leaden sword.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Full merrily hath this braue manager, this carreere bene run.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Loe, he is tilting straight. Peace, I haue don.
Welcome pure wit, thou part'st a faire fray.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: O Lord sir, they would kno,
Whether the three worthies shall come in, or no.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: What, are there but three?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: No sir, but it is var^ fine,
For euerie one pursents three.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: And three times thrice is nine.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Not so sir, vnder correction sir, I hope it is not so. You cannot beg vs sir, I can assure you sir, we know what we know: I hope sir three times thrice sir.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Is not nine.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Vnder correction sir, wee know where-vntill it doth amount.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: By Ioue, I alwaies tooke three threes for nine.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: O Lord sir, it were pittie you should get your liuing by reckning sir.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: How much is it?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O Lord sir, the parties themselues, the actors sir will shew where-vntill it doth amount: for mine owne part, I am (as they say, but to perfect one man in one poore man) Pompion the great sir.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Art thou one of the Worthies?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: It pleased them to thinke me worthie of Pompey the great: for mine owne part, I know not the degree of the Worthie, but I am to stand for him.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Go, bid them prepare.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: We will turne it finely off sir, we wil take some care.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Berowne, they will shame vs:
Let them not approach.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: We are shame-proofe my Lord: and 'tis some policie, to haue one shew worse then the Kings and his companie.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: I say they shall not come.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Nay my good Lord, let me ore-rule you now;
That sport best pleases, that doth least know how.
Where Zeale striues to content, and the contents
Dies in the Zeale of that which it presents:
Their forme confounded, makes most forme in mirth,
When great things labouring perish in their birth.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: A right description of our sport my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: Annointed, I implore so much expence of thy royall sweet breath, as will vtter a brace of words.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Doth this man serue God?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Why aske you?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: He speak's not like a man of God's making.

speeches.speaker: Brag.
prose: That's all one my faire sweet honie Monarch: For I protest, the Schoolmaster is exceeding fantasticall: Too too vain, too too vaine. But we wil put it (as they say) to Fortuna delaguar, I wish you the peace of minde most royall cupplement.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Here is like to be a good presence of Worthies; He presents Hector of Troy, the Swaine Pompey ye great, the Parish Curate Alexander, Armadoes Page Hercules, the Pedant Iudas Machabeus: And if these foure Worthies in their first shew thriue, these foure will change habites, and present the other fiue.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: There is fiue in the first shew.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: You are deceiued, tis not so.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: The Pedant, the Braggart, the Hedge-Priest, the Foole, and the Boy,
Abate throw at Novum, and the whole world againe,
Cannot pricke out fiue such, take each one in's vaine.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: The ship is vnder saile, and here she coms amain.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I Pompey am.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: You lie, you are not he.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I Pompey am.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: With Libbards head on knee.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Well said old mocker,
I must needs be friends with thee.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I Pompey am, Pompey surnam'd the big.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: The great.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: It is great sir: Pompey surnam'd the great:
That oft in field, with Targe and Shield, did make my foe to sweat:
And trauailing along this coast, I heere am come by chance,
And lay my Armes before the legs of this sweet Lasse of France.
If your Ladiship would say thankes Pompey, I had done.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Great thankes great Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Tis not so much worth: but I hope I was perfect. I made a little fault in great.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: My hat to a halfe-penie, Pompey prooues the best Worthie.

speeches.speaker: Curat.
verse: When in the world I liu'd, I was the worldes Commander:
By East, West, North, & South, I spred my conquering might
My Scutcheon plaine declares that I am Alisander.

speeches.speaker: Boiet.
verse: Your nose saies no, you are not:
For it stands too right.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Your nose smels no, in this most tender smelling Knight.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: The Conqueror is dismaid:
Proceede good Alexander.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: When in the world I liued, I was the worldes Commander.

speeches.speaker: Boiet.
prose: Most true, 'tis right: you were so Alisander.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Pompey the great.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: your seruant and Costard.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Take away the Conqueror, take away Alisander

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose:
O sir, you haue ouerthrowne Alisander the conqueror: you will be scrap'd out of the painted cloth for

this: your Lion that holds his Pollax sitting on a close stoole, will be giuen to Aiax. He will be the ninth worthie. A Conqueror, and affraid to speake? Runne away for shame Alisander. There an't shall please you: a foolish milde man, an honest man, looke you, & soon dasht. He is a maruellous good neighbour insooth, and a verie good Bowler: but for Alisander, alas you see, how 'tis a little ore-parted. But there are Worthies a comming, will speake their minde in some other sort.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Stand aside good Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Great Hercules is presented by this Impe,
Whose Club kil'd Cerberus that three-headed Canus,
And when he was a babe, a childe, a shrimpe,
Thus did he strangle Serpents in his Manus:
Quoniam, he seemeth in minoritie,
Ergo, I come with this Apologie.
Keepe some state in thy exit, and vanish.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Iudas I am.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: A Iudas?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Not Iscariot sir.
Iudas I am, ycliped Machabeus.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: Iudas Machabeus clipt, is plaine Iudas.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: A kissing traitor. How art thou prou'd Iudas?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Iudas I am.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: The more shame for you Iudas.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: What meane you sir?

speeches.speaker: Boi.
prose: To make Iudas hang himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Begin sir, you are my elder.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Well follow'd, Iudas was hang'd on an Elder.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: I will not be put out of countenance.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Because thou hast no face.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: What is this?

speeches.speaker: Boi.
prose: A Citterne head.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: The head of a bodkin.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: A deaths face in a ring.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: The face of an old Roman coine, scarce seene.

speeches.speaker: Boi.
prose: The pummell of Caesars Faulchion.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: The caru'd-bone face on a Flaske.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: S. Georges halfe cheeke in a brooch.

speeches.speaker: Dum.
prose: I, and in a brooch of Lead.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I, and worne in the cap of a Tooth-drawer.
And now forward, for we haue put thee in countenance

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: You haue put me out of countenance.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: False, we haue giuen thee faces.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: But you haue out-fac'd them all.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: And thou wer't a Lion, we would do so.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Therefore as he is, an Asse, let him go:
And so adieu sweet Iude. Nay, why dost thou stay?
