speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Me Pardonato, gentle master mine:
I am in all affected as your selfe,
Glad that you thus continue your resolue,
To sucke the sweets of sweete Philosophie.
Onely (good master) while we do admire
This vertue, and this morall discipline,
Let's be no Stoickes, nor no stockes I pray,
Or so deuote to Aristotles checkes
As Ouid; be an out-cast quite abiur'd:
Balke Lodgicke with acquaintaince that you haue,
And practise Rhetoricke in your common talke,
Musicke and Poesie vse, to quicken you,
The Mathematickes, and the Metaphysickes
Fall to them as you finde your stomacke serues you:
No profit growes, where is no pleasure tane:
In briefe sir, studie what you most affect.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Gramercies Tranio, well dost thou aduise,
If Biondello thou wert come ashore,
We could at once put vs in readinesse,
And take a Lodging fit to entertaine
Such friends (as time) in Padua shall beget.
But stay a while, what companie is this?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Master some shew to welcome vs to Towne.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Gentlemen, importune me no farther,
For how I firmly am resolu^d you know:
That is, not to bestow my yongest daughter,
Before I haue a husband for the elder:
If either of you both loue Katherina,
Because I know you well, and loue you well,
Leaue shall you haue to court her at your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: To cart her rather. She's to rough for mee,
There, there Hortensio, will you any Wife?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: I pray you sir, is it your will
To make a stale of me amongst these mates?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Mates maid, how meane you that?
No mates for you,
Vnlesse you were of gentler milder mould.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: I' faith sir, you shall neuer neede to feare,
I-wis it is not halfe way to her heart:
But if it were, doubt not, her care should be,
To combe your noddle with a three-legg'd stoole,
And paint your face, and vse you like a foole.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: From all such diuels, good Lord deliuer vs.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: And me too, good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Husht master, heres some good pastime toward;
That wench is starke mad, or wonderfull froward.

speeches.speaker: Lucen.
verse: But in the others silence do I see,
Maids milde behauiour and sobrietie.
Peace Tranio.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Well said Mr, mum, and gaze your fill.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Gentlemen, that I may soone make good
What I haue said, Bianca get you in,
And let it not displease thee good Bianca,
For I will loue thee nere the lesse my girle.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: A pretty peate, it is best put finger in the eye, and she knew why.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Sister content you, in my discontent.
Sir, to your pleasure humbly I subscribe:
My bookes and instruments shall be my companie,
On them to looke, and practise by my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Harke Tranio, thou maist heare Minerua speak.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Signior Baptista, will you be so strange,
Sorrie am I that our good will effects
Bianca's greefe.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: Why will you mew her vp
(Signior Baptista) for this fiend of hell,
And make her beare the pennance of her tongue.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Gentlemen content ye: I am resould:
Go in Bianca.
And for I know she taketh most delight
In Musicke, Instruments, and Poetry,
Schoolemasters will I keepe within my house,
Fit to instruct her youth. If you Hortensio,
Or signior Gremio you know any such,
Preferre them hither: for to cunning men,
I will be very kinde and liberall,
To mine owne children, in good bringing vp,
And so farewell: Katherina you may stay,
For I haue more to commune with Bianca.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Why, and I trust I may go too, may I not?
What shall I be appointed houres, as though
(Belike) I knew not what to take,
And what to leaue? Ha.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: You may go to the diuels dam: your guifts are so good heere's none will holde you: Their loue is not so great Hortensio, but we may blow our nails together, and fast it fairely out. Our cakes dough on both sides. Farewell: yet for the loue I beare my sweet Bianca, if I can by any meanes light on a fit man to teach her that wherein she delights, I will wish him to her father.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: So will I signiour Gremio: but a word I pray: Though the nature of our quarrell yet neuer brook'd parle, know now vpon aduice, it toucheth vs both: that we may yet againe haue accesse to our faire Mistris, and be happie riuals in Bianca's loue, to labour and effect one thing specially.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: What's that I pray?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Marrie sir to get a husband for her Sister.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: A husband: a diuell.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I say a husband.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: I say, a diuell: Think'st thou Hortensio, though her father be verie rich, any man is so verie a foole to be married to hell?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Tush Gremio: though it passe your patience & mine to endure her lowd alarums, why man there bee good fellowes in the world, and a man could light on them, would take her with all faults, and mony enough.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: I cannot tell: but I had as lief take her dowrie with this condition; To be whipt at the hie crosse euerie morning.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Faith (as you say) there's small choise in rotten apples: but come, since this bar in law makes vs friends, it shall be so farre forth friendly maintain'd, till by helping Baptistas eldest daughter to a husband, wee set his yongest free for a husband, and then haue too t afresh: Sweet Bianca, happy man be his dole: hee that runnes fastest, gets the Ring: How say you signior Gremio?

speeches.speaker: Grem.
prose: I am agreed, and would I had giuen him the best horse in Padua to begin his woing that would thoroughly woe her, wed her, and bed her, and ridde the house of her. Come on.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I pray sir tel me, is it possible
That loue should of a sodaine take such hold.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Oh Tranio, till I found it to be true,
I neuer thought it possible or likely.
But see, while idely I stood looking on,
I found the effect of Loue in idlenesse,
And now in plainnesse do confesse to thee
That art to me as secret and as deere
As Anna to the Queene of Carthage was:
Tranio I burne, I pine, I perish Tranio,
If I atchieue not this yong modest gyrle:
Counsaile me Tranio, for I know thou canst:
Assist me Tranio, for I know thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Master, it is no time to chide you now,
Affection is not rated from the heart:
If loue haue touch'd you, naught remaines but so,
Redime te captam quam queas minimo.

speeches.speaker: Luc
verse: Gramercies Lad: Go forward, this contents,
The rest wil comfort, for thy counsels sound.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Master, you look'd so longly on the maide,
Perhaps you mark'd not what's the pith of all.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Oh yes, I saw sweet beautie in her face,
Such as the daughter of Agenor had,
That made great Ioue to humble him to her hand,
When with his knees he kist the Cretan strond.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Saw you no more? Mark'd you not how hir sister
Began to scold, and raise vp such a storme,
That mortal eares might hardly indure the din.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Tranio, I saw her corrall lips to moue,
And with her breath she did perfume the ayre,
Sacred and sweet was all I saw in her.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Nay, then 'tis time to stirre him fro~ his trance:
I pray awake sir: if you loue the Maide,
Bend thoughts and wits to atcheeue her. Thus it stands:
Her elder sister is so curst and shrew'd,
That til the Father rid his hands of her,
Master, your Loue must liue a maide at home,
And therefore has he closely mou'd her vp,
Because she will not be annoy'd with suters.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Ah Tranio, what a cruell Fathers he:
But art thou not aduis'd, he tooke some care
To get her cunning Schoolemasters to instruct her.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: I marry am I sir, and now 'tis plotted.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I haue it Tranio.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Master, for my hand,
Both our inuentions meet and iumpe in one.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Tell me thine first.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: You will be schoole-master,
And vndertake the teaching of the maid:
That's your deuice.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: It is: May it be done?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Not possible: for who shall beare your part,
And be in Padua heere Vincentio's sonne,
Keepe house, and ply his booke, welcome his friends,
Visit his Countrimen, and banquet them?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Basta, content thee: for I haue it full.
We haue not yet bin seene in any house,
Nor can we be distinguish'd by our faces,
For man or master: then it followes thus;
Thou shalt be master, Tranio in my sted:
Keepe house, and port, and seruants, as I should,
I will some other be, some Florentine,
Some Neapolitan, or meaner man of Pisa.
'Tis hatch'd, and shall be so: Tranio at once
Vncase thee: take my Conlord hat and cloake,
When Biondello comes, he waites on thee,
But I will charme him first to keepe his tongue.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: So had you neede:
In breese Sir, sith it your pleasure is,
And I am tyed to be obedient,
For so your father charg'd me at our parting:
Be seruiceable to my sonne (quoth he)
Although I thinke 'twas in another sence,
I am content to bee Lucentio,
Because so well I loue Lucentio.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Tranio be so, because Lucentio loues,
And let me be a slaue, t' atchieue that maide.
Whose sodaine sight hath thral'd my wounded eye.
Heere comes the rogue. Sirra, where haue you bin?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Where haue I beene? Nay how now, where are you? Maister, ha's my fellow Tranio stolne your cloathes, or you stolne his, or both? Pray what's the newes?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Sirra come hither, 'tis no time to iest,
And therefore frame your manners to the time
Your fellow Tranio heere to saue my life,
Puts my apparrell, and my count'nance on,
And I for my escape haue put on his:
For in a quarrell since I came a shore,
I kil'd a man, and feare I was descried:
Waite you on him, I charge you, as becomes:
While I make way from hence to saue my life:
You vnderstand me?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: I sir, ne're a whit.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: And not a iot of Tranio in your mouth,
Tranio is chang'd into Lucentio.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: The better for him, would I were so too.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: So could I 'faith boy, to haue the next wish after, that Lucentio indeede had Baptistas yongest daughter. But sirra, not for my sake, but your masters, I aduise you vse your manners discreetly in all kind of companies: When I am alone, why then I am Tranio: but in all places else, you master Lucentio.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Tranio let's go:
One thing more rests, that thy selfe execute,
To make one among these wooers: if thou ask me why,
Sufficeth my reasons are both good and waighty.

speeches.speaker: 1. Man.
prose: My Lord you nod, you do not minde the play.

speeches.speaker: Beg.
verse: Yes by Saint Anne do I, a good matter surely:
Comes there any more of it?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: My Lord, 'tis but begun.

speeches.speaker: Beg.
prose: 'Tis a verie excellent peece of worke, Madame Ladie: would 'twere done.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Verona, for a while I take my leaue,
To see my friends in Padua; but of all
My best beloued and approued friend
Hortensio: & I trow this is his house:
Heere sirra Grumio, knocke I say.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Knocke sir? whom should I knocke? Is there any man ha's rebus'd your worship?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Villaine I say, knocke me heere soundly.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Knocke you heere sir? Why sir, what am I sir, that I should knocke you heere sir.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Villaine I say, knocke me at this gate,
And rap me well, or Ile knocke your knaues pate.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
verse: My Mr is growne quarrelsome:
I should knocke you first,
And then I know after who comes by the worst.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Will it not be?
'Faith sirrah, and you'l not knocke, Ile ring it,
Ile trie how you can Sol, Fa, and sing it.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Helpe mistris helpe, my master is mad.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Now knocke when I bid you: sirrah villaine.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: How now, what's the matter? My olde friend Grumio, and my good friend Petruchio? How do you all at Verona?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Signior Hortensio, come you to part the fray?
Contutti le core bene trobatto, may I say.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Alla nostra casa bene venuto multo honorata signior mio Petruchio.
Rise Grumio rise, we will compound this quarrell.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Nay 'tis no matter sir, what he leges in Latine. If this be not a lawfull cause for me to leaue his seruice, looke you sir: He bid me knocke him, & rap him soundly sir. Well, was it fit for a seruant to vse his master so, being perhaps (for ought I see) two and thirty, a peepe out? Whom would to God I had well knockt at first, then had not Grumio come by the worst.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: A sencelesse villaine: good Hortensio,
I had the rascall knocke vpon your gate,
And could not get him for my heart to do it.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Knocke at the gate? O heauens: spake you not these words plaine? Sirra, Knocke me heere: rappe me heere: knocke me well, and knocke me soundly? And come you now with knocking at the gate?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Sirra be gone, or talke not I aduise you

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Petruchio patience, I am Grumio's pledge:
Why this a heauie chance twixt him and you,
Your ancient trustie pleasant seruant Grumio:
And tell me now (sweet friend) what happie gale
Blowes you to Padua heere, from old Verona?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Such wind as scatters yongmen throgh ye world,
To seeke their fortunes farther then at home,
Where small experience growes but in a few.
Signior Hortensio, thus it stands with me,
Antonio my father is deceast,
And I haue thrust my selfe into this maze,
Happily to wiue and thriue, as best I may:
Crownes in my purse I haue, and goods at home,
And so am come abroad to see the world.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Petruchio, shall I then come roundly to thee,
And wish thee to a shrew'd ill-fauour'd wife?
Thou'dst thanke me but a little for my counsell:
And yet Ile promise thee she shall be rich,
And verie rich: but th' art too much my friend,
And Ile not wish thee to her.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Signior Hortensio, 'twixt such friends as wee,
Few words suffice: and therefore, if thou know
One rich enough to be Petruchio's wife:
(As wealth is burthen of my woing dance)
Be she as foule as was Florentius Loue,
As old as Sibell, and as curst and shrow'd
As Socrates Zentippe, or a worse:
She moues me not, or not remoues at least
Affections edge in me. Were she is as rough
As are the swelling Adriaticke seas.
I come to wiue it wealthily in Padua:
If wealthily, then happily in Padua.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Nay looke you sir, hee tels you flatly what his minde is: why giue him Gold enough, and marrie him to a Puppet or an Aglet babie, or an old trot with ne're a tooth in her head, though she haue as manie diseases as two and fiftie horses. Why nothing comes amisse, so monie comes withall.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Petruchio, since we are stept thus farre in,
I will continue that I broach'd in iest,
I can Petruchio helpe thee to a wife
With wealth enough, and yong and beautious,
Brought vp as best becomes a Gentlewoman.
Her onely fault, and that is faults enough,
Is, that she is intollerable curst,
And shrow'd, and froward, so beyond all measure,
That were my state farre worser then it is,
I would not wed her for a mine of Gold.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Hortensio peace: thou knowst not golds effect,
Tell me her fathers name, and 'tis enough:
For I will boord her, though she chide as loud
As thunder, when the clouds in Autumne cracke.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Her father is Baptista Minola,
An affable and courteous Gentleman,
Her name is Katherina Minola,
Renown'd in Padua for her scolding tongue.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: I know her father, though I know not her,
And he knew my deceased father well:
I wil not sleepe Hortensio til I see her,
And therefore let me be thus bold with you,
To giue you ouer at this first encounter,
Vnlesse you wil accompanie me thither.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I pray you Sir let him go while the humor lasts. A my word, and she knew him as wel as I do, she would thinke scolding would doe little good vpon him. Shee may perhaps call him halfe a score Knaues, or so: Why that's nothing; and he begin once, hee'l raile in his rope trickes. Ile tell you what sir, and she stand him but a litle, he wil throw a figure in her face, and so disfigure hir with it, that shee shal haue no more eies to see withall then a Cat: you know him not sir.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Tarrie Petruchio, I must go with thee,
For in Baptistas keepe my treasure is:
He hath the Iewel of my life in hold,
His yongest daughter, beautiful Bianca,
And her with-holds from me. Other more
Suters to her, and riuals in my Loue:
Supposing it a thing impossible,
For those defects I haue before rehearst,
That euer Katherina wil be woo'd:
Therefore this order hath Baptista tane,
That none shal haue accesse vnto Bianca,
Til Katherine the Curst, haue got a husband.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
verse: Katherine the curst,
A title for a maide, of all titles the worst.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Now shal my friend Petruchio do me grace,
And offer me disguis'd in sober robes,
To old Baptista as a schoole-master
Well seene in Musicke, to instruct Bianca,
That so I may by this deuice at least
Haue leaue and leisure to make loue to her,
And vnsuspected court her by her selfe.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Heere's no knauerie. See, to beguile the olde-folkes, how the young folkes lay their heads together. Master, master, looke about you: Who goes there? ha.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Peace Grumio, it is the riuall of my Loue.
Petruchio stand by a while.

speeches.speaker: Grumio.
prose: A proper stripling, and an amorous.

speeches.speaker: Gremio.
verse: O very well, I haue perus'd the note:
Hearke you sir, Ile haue them verie fairely bound,
All bookes of Loue, see that at any hand,
And see you reade no other Lectures to her:
You vnderstand me. Ouer and beside
Signior Baptistas liberalitie,
Ile mend it with a Largesse. Take your paper too,
And let me haue them verie wel perfum'd;
For she is sweeter then perfume it selfe
To whom they go to: what wil you reade to her.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: What ere I reade to her, Ile pleade for you,
As for my patron, stand you so assur'd,
As firmely as your selfe were still in place,
Yea and perhaps with more successefull words
Then you; vnlesse you were a scholler sir.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Oh this learning, what a thing it is.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Oh this Woodcocke, what an Asse it is.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Peace sirra.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Grumio mum: God saue you signior Gremio.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: And you are wel met, Signior Hortensio.
Trow you whither I am going? To Baptista Minola,
I promist to enquire carefully
About a schoolemaster for the faire Bianca,
And by good fortune I haue lighted well
On this yong man: For learning and behauiour
Fit for her turne, well read in Poetrie
And other bookes, good ones, I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: 'Tis well: and I haue met a Gentleman
Hath promist me to helpe one to another,
A fine Musitian to instruct our Mistris,
So shal I no whit be behinde in dutie
To faire Bianca, so beloued of me.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Beloued of me, and that my deeds shal proue.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: And that his bags shal proue.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Gremio, 'tis now no time to vent our loue,
Listen to me, and if you speake me faire,
Ile tel you newes indifferent good for either.
Heere is a Gentleman whom by chance I met
Vpon agreement from vs to his liking,
Will vndertake to woo curst Katherine,
Yea, and to marrie her, if her dowrie please.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: So said, so done, is well:
Hortensio, haue you told him all her faults?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: I know she is an irkesome brawling scold:
If that be all Masters, I heare no harme.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: No, sayst me so, friend? What Countreyman?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Borne in Verona, old Butonios sonne:
My father dead, my fortune liues for me,
And I do hope, good dayes and long, to see.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: Oh sir, such a life with such a wife, were strange:
But if you haue a stomacke, too't a Gods name,
You shal haue me assisting you in all.
But will you woo this Wilde-cat?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Will I liue?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Wil he woo her? I: or Ile hang her.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Why came I hither, but to that intent?
Thinke you, a little dinne can daunt mine eares?
Haue I not in my time heard Lions rore?
Haue I not heard the sea, puft vp with windes,
Rage like an angry Boare, chafed with sweat?
Haue I not heard great Ordnance in the field?
And heauens Artillerie thunder in the skies?
Haue I not in a pitched battell heard
Loud larums, neighing steeds, & trumpets clangue.
And do you tell me of a womans tongue?
That giues not halfe so great a blow to heare,
As wil a Chesse-nut in a Farmers fire.
Tush, tush, feare boyes with bugs.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: For he feares none.

speeches.speaker: Grem.
verse: Hortensio hearke:
This Gentleman is happily arriu'd,
My minde presumes for his owne good, and yours.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: I promist we would be Contributors,
And beare his charge of wooing whatsoere.

speeches.speaker: Gremio.
prose: And so we wil, prouided that he win her.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I would I were as sure of a good dinner.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Gentlemen God saue you. If I may be bold
Tell me I beseech you, which is the readiest way
To the house of Signior Baptista Minola?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: He that ha's the two faire daughters: ist he you meane?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Euen he Biondello.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Hearke you sir, you meane not her to —

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Perhaps him and her sir, what haue you to do?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Not her that chides sir, at any hand I pray.

speeches.speaker: Tranio.
prose: I loue no chiders sir: Biondello, let's away.

speeches.speaker: Luc
prose: Well begun Tranio.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Sir, a word ere you go:
Are you a sutor to the Maid you talke of, yea or no?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: And if I be sir, is it any offence?

speeches.speaker: Gremio.
prose: No: if without more words you will get you hence.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Why sir, I pray are not the streers as free
For me, as for you?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: But so is not she.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: For what reason I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: For this reason if you'l kno,
That she's the choise loue of Signior Gremio.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: That she's the chosen of signior Hortensio.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Softly my Masters: If you be Gentlemen
Do me this right: heare me with patience,
Baptista is a noble Gentleman,
To whom my Father is not all vnknowne,
And were his daughter fairer then she is,
She may more sutors haue, and me for one.
Faire Laedaes daughter had a thousand wooers,
Then well one more may faire Bianca haue;
And so she shall: Lucentio shal make one,
Though Paris came, in hope to speed alone.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: What, this Gentleman will out-talke vs all.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir giue him head, I know hee'l proue a Iade.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Hortensio, to what end are all these words?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Sir, let me be so bold as aske you,
Did you yet euer see Baptistas daughter?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: No sir, but heare I do that he hath two:
The one, as famous for a scolding tongue,
As is the other, for beauteous modestie.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Sir, sir, the first's for me, let her go by.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: Yea, leaue that labour to great Hercules,
And let it be more then Alcides twelue.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Sir vnderstand you this of me (insooth)
The yongest daughter whom you hearken for,
Her father keepes from all accesse of sutors,
And will not promise her to any man,
Vntill the elder sister first be wed.
The yonger then is free, and nor before.

speeches.speaker: Tranio.
verse: If it be so sir, that you are the man
Must steed vs all, and me amongst the rest:
And if you breake the ice, and do this seeke,
Atchieue the elder: set the yonger free,
For our accesse, whose hap shall be to haue her,
Wil not so gracelesse be, to be ingrate.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Sir you say wel, and wel you do conceiue,
And since you do professe to be a sutor,
You must as we do, gratifie this Gentleman,
To whom we all rest generally beholding.

speeches.speaker: Tranio.
verse: Sir, I shal not be slacke, in signe whereof,
Please ye we may contriue this afternoone,
And quaffe carowses to our Mistresse health,
And do as aduersaries do in law,
Striue mightily, but eate and drinke as friends.

speeches.speaker: Gru. Bion.
prose: Oh excellent motion: fellowes let's be gon.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: The motions good indeed, and be it so,
Petruchio, I shal be your Been venuto.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Good sister wrong me not, nor wrong your self,
To make a bondmaide and a slaue of mee,
That I disdaine: but for these other goods,
Vnbinde my hands, Ile pull them off my selfe,
Yea all my raiment, to my petticoate,
Or what you will command me, wil I do,
So well I know my dutie to my elders.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Of all thy sutors heere I charge tel
Whom thou lou'st best: see thou dissemble not.

speeches.speaker: Bianca.
verse: Beleeue me sister, of all the men aliue,
I neuer yet beheld that speciall face,
Which I could fancie, more then any other.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Minion thou lyest: Is't not Hortensio?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: If you affect him sister, heere I sweare
Ile pleade for you my selfe, but you shal haue him.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Oh then belike you fancie riches more,
You wil haue Gremio to keepe you faire.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Is it for him you do enuie me so?
Nay then you iest, and now I wel perceiue
You haue but iested with me all this while:
I prethee sister Kate, vntie my hands.

speeches.speaker: Ka.
prose: If that be iest, then all the rest was so.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Why how now Dame, whence growes this insolence?
Bianca stand aside, poore gyrle she weepes:
Go ply thy Needle, meddle not with her.
For shame thou Hilding of a diuellish spirit,
Why dost thou wrong her, that did nere wrong thee?
When did she crosse thee with a bitter word?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Her silence flouts me, and Ile be reueng'd.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: What in my sight? Bianca get thee in.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: What will you not suffer me: Nay now I see
She is your treasure, she must haue a husband,
I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day,
And for your loue to her, leade Apes in hell.
Talke not to me, I will go sit and weepe,
Till I can finde occasion of reuenge.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Was euer Gentleman thus greeu'd as I?
But who comes heere.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Good morrow neighbour Baptista.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Good morrow neighbour Gremio: God saue you Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: And you good sir: pray haue you not a daughter, cal'd Katerina, faire and vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: I haue a daughter sir, cal'd Katerina.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: You are too blunt, go to it orderly.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: You wrong me signior Gremio, giue me leaue.
I am a Gentleman of Verona sir,
That hearing of her beautie, and her wit,
Her affability and bashfull modestie:
Her wondrous qualities, and milde behauiour,
Am bold to shew my selfe a forward guest
Within your house, to make mine eye the witnesse
Of that report, which I so oft haue heard,
And for an entrance to my entertainment,
I do present you with a man of mine
Cunning in Musicke, and the Mathematickes,
To instruct her fully in those sciences,
Whereof I know she is not ignorant,
Accept of him, or else you do me wrong,
His name is Litio, borne in Mantua.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Y' are welcome sir, and he for your good sake.
But for my daughter Katerine, this I know,
She is not for your turne, the more my greefe.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I see you do not meane to part with her,
Or else you like not of my companie.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Mistake me not, I speake but as I finde,
Whence are you sir? What may I call your name.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Petruchio is my name, Antonio's sonne,
A man well knowne throughout all Italy.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: I know him well: you are welcome for his sake.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Sauing your tale Petruchio, I pray let vs that are poore petitioners speake too? Bacare, you are meruaylous forward.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Oh, Pardon me signior Gremio, I would faine be doing.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: I doubt it not sir. But you will curse
Your wooing neighbors: this is a guift
Very gratefull, I am sure of it, to expresse
The like kindnesse my selfe, that haue beene
More kindely beholding to you then any:
Freely giue vnto this yong Scholler, that hath
Beene long studying at Rhemes, as cunning
In Greeke, Latine, and other Languages,
As the other in Musicke and Mathematickes:
His name is Cambio: pray accept his seruice.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: A thousand thankes signior Gremio:
Welcome good Cambio. But gentle sir,
Me thinkes you walke like a stranger,
May I be so bold, to know the cause of your comming?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Pardon me sir, the boldnesse is mine owne,
That being a stranger in this Cittie heere,
Do make my selfe a sutor to your daughter,
Vnto Bianca, faire and vertuous:
Nor is your firme resolue vnknowne to me,
In the preferment of the eldest sister.
This liberty is all that I request,
That vpon knowledge of my Parentage,
I may haue welcome 'mongst the rest that woo,
And free accesse and fauour as the rest.
And toward the education of your daughters:
I heere bestow a simple instrument,
And this small packet of Greeke and Latine bookes:
If you accept them, then their worth is great:

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Lucentio is your name, of whence I pray.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Of Pisa sir, sonne to Vincentio.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: A mightie man of Pisa by report,
I know him well: you are verie welcome sir:
Take you the Lute, and you the set of bookes,
You shall go see your Pupils presently.
Holla, within.
Sirrah, leade these Gentlemen
To my daughters, and tell them both
These are their Tutors, bid them vse them well,
We will go walke a little in the Orchard,
And then to dinner: you are passing welcome,
And so I pray you all to thinke your selues.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Signior Baptista, my businesse asketh haste,
And euerie day I cannot come to woo,
You knew my father well, and in him me,
Left solie heire to all his Lands and goods,
Which I haue bettered rather then decreast,
Then tell me, if I get your daughters loue,
What dowrie shall I haue with her to wife.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: After my death, the one halfe of my Lands,
And in possession twentie thousand Crownes.

speeches.speaker: Pet
verse: And for that dowrie, Ile assure her of
Her widdow-hood, be it that she suruiue me
In all my Lands and Leases whatsoeuer,
Let specialties be therefore drawne betweene vs,
That couenants may be kept on either hand.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I, when the speciall thing is well obtain'd,
That is her loue: for that is all in all.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why that is nothing: for I tell you father,
I am as peremptorie as she proud minded:
And where two raging fires meete together,
They do consume the thing that feedes their furie.
Though little fire growes great with little winde,
yet extreme gusts will blow out fire and all:
So I to her, and so she yeelds to me,
For I am rough, and woo not like a babe.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Well maist thou woo, and happy be thy speed:
But be thou arm'd for some vnhappie words.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I to the proofe, as Mountaines are for windes,
That shakes not, though they blow perpetually.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: How now my friend, why dost thou looke so pale?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: For feare I promise you, if I looke pale.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: What, will my daughter proue a good Musitian?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: I thinke she'l sooner proue a souldier,
Iron may hold with her, but neuer Lutes.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Why then thou canst not break her to the Lute?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Why no, for she hath broke the Lute to me:
I did but tell her she mistooke her frets,
And bow'd her hand to teach her fingering,
When (with a most impatient diuellish spirit)
Frets call you these? (quoth she) Ile fume with them:
And with that word she stroke me on the head,
And through the instrument my pate made way,
And there I stood amazed for a while,
As on a Pillorie, looking through the Lute,
While she did call me Rascall, Fidler,
And twangling lacke, with twentie such vilde tearmes,
As had she studied to misvse me so.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Now by the world, it is a lustie Wench,
I loue her ten times more then ere I did,
Oh how I long to haue some chat with her.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Wel go with me, and be not so discomfited.
Proceed in practise with my yonger daughter,
She's apt to learne, and thankefull for good turnes:
Signior Petruchio, will you go with vs,
Or shall I send my daughter Kate to you.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I pray you do. Ile attend her heere,
And woo her with some spirit when she comes,
Say that she raile, why then Ile tell her plaine,
She sings as sweetly as a Nightinghale:
Say that she frowne, Ile say she lookes as cleere
As morning Roses newly washt with dew:
Say she be mute, and will not speake a word,
Then Ile commend her volubility,
And say she vtcereth piercing eloquence:
If she do bid me packe, Ile giue her thankes,
As though she bid me stay by her a weeke:
If she denie to wed, Ile craue the day
When I shall aske the banes, and when be married.
But heere she comes, and now Petruchio speake.
Good morrow Kate, for thats your name I heare.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Well haue you heard, but something hard of hearing:
They call me Katerine, that do talke of me.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: You lye infaith, for you are call'd plaine Kate,
And bony Kate, and sometimes Kate the curst:
But Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendome,
Kate of Kate-hall, my super-daintie Kate,
For dainties are all Kates, and therefore Kate
Take this of me, Kate of my consolation,
Hearing thy mildnesse prais'd in euery Towne,
Thy vertues spoke of, and thy beautie sounded,
Yet not so deepely as to thee belongs,
My selfe am moou'd to woo thee for my wife.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Mou'd, in good time, let him that mou'd you hether
Remoue you hence: I knew you at the first
You were a mouable.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Why, what's a mouable?

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: A ioyn'd stoole.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Thou hast hit it: come sit on me.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Asses are made to beare, and so are you.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Women are made to beare, and so are you.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: No such Iade as you, if me you meane.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Alas good Kate, I will not burthen thee,
For knowing thee to be but yong and light.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Too light for such a swaine as you to catch,
And yet as heauie as my waight should be.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Shold be, should: buzze.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Well tane, and like a buzzard.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Oh slow-wing'd Turtle, shal a buzard take thee?

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: I for a Turtle, as he takes a buzard.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Come, come you Waspe, y' faith you are too angrie.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: If I be waspish, best beware my sting.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: My remedy is then to plucke it out.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I, if the foole could finde it where it lies.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Who knowes not where a Waspe does, weare his sting? In his taile.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: In his tongue?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Whose tongue.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Yours if you talke of tales, and so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: What with my tongue in your taile.
Nay, come againe, good Kate, I am a Gentleman,

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: That Ile trie.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: I sweare Ile cuffe you, if you strike againe.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: So may you loose your armes,
If you strike me, you are no Gentleman,
And if no Gentleman, why then no armes.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: A Herald Kate? Oh put me in thy bookes.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: What is your Crest, a Coxcombe?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: A comblesse Cocke, so Kate will be my Hen.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: No Cocke of mine, you crow too like a crauen

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Nay come Kate, come: you must not looke so sowre.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: It is my fashion when I see a Crab.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Why heere's no crab, and therefore looke not sowre.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: There is, there is.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Then shew it me.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Had I a glasse, I would.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: What, you meane my face.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Well aym'd of such a yong one.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Now by S. George I am too yong for you.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Yet you are wither'd.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: 'Tis with cares.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I care not.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Nay heare you Kate. Insooth you scape not so.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I chafe you if I tarrie. Let me go.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: No, not a whit, I finde you passing gentle:
'Twas told me you were rough, and coy, and sullen,
And now I finde report a very liar:
For thou art pleasant, g^mesome, passing courteous,
But slow in speech: yet sweet as spring-time flowers.
Thou canst not frowne, thou canst not looke a sconce,
Nor bite the lip, as angry wenches will,
Nor hast thou pleasure to be crosse in talke:
But thou with mildnesse entertain'st thy wooers,
With gentle conference, soft, and affable.
Why does the world report that Kate doth limpe?
Oh sland'rous world: Kate like the hazle twig
Is straight, and slender, and as browne in hue
As hazle nuts, and sweeter then the kernels:
Oh let me see thee walke: thou dost not halt.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Go foole, and whom thou keep'st command.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Did euer Dian so become a Groue
As Kate this chamber with her princely gate:
O be thou Dian, and let her be Kate,
And then let Kate be chaste, and Dian sportfull.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Where did you study all this goodly speech?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: It is extempore, from my mother wit.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: A witty mother, witlesse else her sonne.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Am I not wise?

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Yes, keepe you warme.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Marry so I meane sweet Katherine in thy bed:
And therefore setting all this chat aside,
Thus in plaine termes: your father hath consented
That you shall be my wife; your dowry greed on,
And will you, ^ill you, I will marry you.
Now Kate, I am a husband for your turne,
For by this light, whereby I see thy beauty,
Thy beauty that doth make me like thee well,
Thou must be married to no man but me,
For I am he am borne to tame you Kate,
And bring you from a wilde Kate to a Kate
Conformable as other houshold Kates:
Heere comes your father, neuer make deniall.
I must, and will haue Katherine to my wife.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Now Signior Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: How but well sir? how but well?
It were impossible I should speed amisse.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Why how now daughter Katherine, in your dumps?

speeches.speaker: Kat.
verse: Call you me daughter? now I promise you
You haue shewd a tender fatherly regard,
To wish me wed to one halfe Lunaticke,
A mad-cap ruffian, and a swearing lacke,
That thinkes with oathes to face the matter out.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Father, 'tis thus, your selfe and all the world
That talk'd of her, haue talk'd amisse of her:
If she be curst, it is for pollicie,
For shee's not froward, but modest as the Doue,
Shee is not hot, but temperate as the morne,
For patience shee will proue a second Grissell,
And Romane Lucrece for her chastitie:
And to conclude, we haue greed so well together,
That vpon sonday is the wedding day.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Ile see thee hang'd on sonday first.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Hark Petruchio, she saies shee'll see thee hang'd first.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Is this your speeding? nay the~ godnight our part.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Be patient gentlemen, I choose her for my selfe,
If she and I be pleas'd, what's that to you?
'Tis bargain'd twixt vs twaine being alone,
That she shall still be curst in company.
I tell you 'tis incredible to beleeue
How much she loues me: oh the kindest Kate,
Shee hung about my necke, and kisse on kisse
Shee vi'd so fast, protesting oath on oath,
That in a twinke she won me to her loue.
Oh you are nouices, 'tis a world to see
How tame when men and women are alone.
A meacocke wretch can make the curstest shrew:
Giue me thy hand Kate, I will vnto Venice
To buy apparell 'gainst the wedding day;
Prouide the feast father, and bid the guests,
I will be sure my Katherine shall be fine.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I know not what to say, but giue me your ha~ds,
God send you ioy, Petruchio, 'tis a match.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Tra. Amen say we, we will be witnesses.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Father, and wife, and gentlemen adieu,
I will to Venice, sonday comes apace,
We will haue rings, and things, and fine array,
And kisse me Kate, we will be married a sonday.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Was euer match clapt vp so sodainly?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Faith Gentlemen now I play a marchants part,
And venture madly on a desperate Mart.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Twas a commodity lay fretting by you,
'Twill bring you gaine, or perish on the seas.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: The gaine I seeke, is quiet me the match.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch:
But now Baptista, to your yonger daughter,
Now is the day we long haue looked for,
I am your neighbour, and was suter first.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: And I am one that loue Bianca more
Then words can witnesse, or your thoughts can guesse.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Yongling thou canst not loue so deare as I.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Gray-beard thy loue doth freeze.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: But thine doth frie,
Skipper stand backe, 'tis age that nourisheth.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: But youth in Ladies eyes that florisheth.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Content you gentlemen, I wil co~pound this strife
'Tis deeds must win the prize, and he of both
That can assure my daughter greatest dower,
Shall haue my Biancas loue.
Say signior Gremio, what can you assure her?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: First, as you know, my house within the City
Is richly furnished with plate and gold,
Basons and ewers to laue her dainty hands:
My hangings all of tirian tapestry:
In Iuory cofers I haue stuft my crownes:
In Cypros chests my arras counterpoints,
Costly apparell, tents, and Canopies,
Fine Linnen, Turky cushions bost with pearle,
Vallens of Venice gold, in needle worke:
Pewter and brasse, and all things that belongs
To house or house-keeping: then at my farme
I haue a hundred milch-kine to the pale,
Sixe-score fat Oxen standing in my stalls,
And all things answerable to this portion.
My selfe am strooke in yeeres I must confesse,
And if I die to morrow this is hers,
If whil'st I liue she will be onely mine.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: That only came well in: sir, list to me,
I am my fathers heyre and onely sonne,
If I may haue your daughter to my wife,
Ile leaue her houses three or foure as good
Within rich Pisa walls, as any one
Old Signior Gremio has in Padua,
Besides, two thousand Duckets by the yeere
Of fruitfull land, all which shall be her ioynter.
What, haue I pincht you Signior Gremio?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: Two thousand Duckets by the yeere of land,
My Land amounts not to so much in all:
That she shall haue, besides an Argosie
That now is lying in Marcellus roade:
What, haue I choakt you with an Argosie?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Gremio, 'tis knowne my father hath no lesse
Then three great Argosies, besides two Galliasses
And twelue tite Gallies, these I will assure her,
And twice as much what ere thou offrest next.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: Nay, I haue offred all, I haue no more,
And she can haue no more then all I haue,
If you like me, she shall haue me and mine.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Why then the maid is mine from all the world
By your firme promise, Gremio is out-vied.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I must confesse your offer is the best,
And let your father make her the assurance,
Shee is your owne, else you must pardon me:
If you should die before him, where's her dower?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: That's but a cauill: he is olde, I young.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: And may not yong men die as well as old?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Well gentlemen, I am thus resolu'd,
On sonday next, you know
My daughter Katherine is to be married:
Now on the sonday following, shall Bianca
Be Bride to you, if you make this assurance:
If not, to Signior Gremio:
And so I take my leaue, and thanke you both.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
verse: Adieu good neighbour: now I feare thee not:
Sirra, yong gamester, your father were a foole
To giue thee all, and in his wayning age
Set foot vnder thy table: tut, a toy,
An olde Italian foxe is not so kinde my boy.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: A vengeance on your crafty withered hide,
Yet I haue fac'd it with a card of ten:
'Tis in my head to doe my master good:
I see no reason but suppos'd Lucentio

Must get a father, call'd suppos'd
~incentio,
And that's a wonder: fathers commonly
Doe get their children: but in this case of woing,
A childe shall get a sire, if I faile not of my cunning.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Fidler forbeare you grow too forward Sir,
Haue you so soone forgot the entertainment
Her sister Katherine welcom'd you withall.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
verse: But wrangling pedant, this is
The patronesse of heauenly harmony:
Then giue me leaue to haue prerogatiue,
And when in Musicke we haue spent an houre,
Your Lecture shall haue leisure for as much.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Preposterous Asse that neuer read so farre,
To know the cause why musicke was ordain'd:
Was it not to refresh the minde of man
After his studies, or his vsuall paine?
Then giue me leaue to read Philosophy,
And while I pause, serue in your harmony.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Sirra, I will not beare these braues of thine.

speeches.speaker: Bianc.
verse: Why gentlemen, you doe me double wrong,
To striue for that which resteth in my choice:
I am no breeching scholler in the schooles,
Ile not be tied to howres, nor pointed times,
But learne my Lessons as I please my selfe,
And to cut off all strife: heere sit we downe,
Take you your instrument, play you the whiles,
His Lecture will be done ere you haue tun'd.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: You'll leaue his Lecture when I am in tune?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: That will be neuer, tune your instrument.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Where left we last?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Heere Madam: Hic Ibat Simois, hic est sigeria tellus, hic steterat Priamiregia Celsa senis.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Conster them.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Hic Ibat, as I told you before. Simois, I am Lucentio, hic est, sonne vnto Vincentio of Pisa, Sigeriatellus, disguised thus to get your loue, hic steterat, and that Lucentio that comes a wooing, priami, is my man Tranio, regia, bearing my port, celsa senis that we might beguile the old Pantalowne.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Madam, my Instrument's in tune.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Let's heare, oh fie, the treble iarres.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Spit in the hole man, and tune againe.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Now let mee see if I can conster it. Hic ibat simois, I know you not, hic est sigeria tellus, I trust you not, hic staterat priami, take heede he heare vs not, regia presume not, Celsa senis, despaire not.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Madam, tis now in tune.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: All but the base.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: The base is right, 'tis the base knaue that iars.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: How fiery and forward our Pedant is,
Now for my life the knaue doth court my loue,
Pedascule, Ile watch you better yet:
In time I may beleeue, yet I mistrust.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Mistrust it not, for sure Aeacides
Was Atax cald so from his grandfather.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
verse: I must beleeue my master, else I promise you,
I should be arguing still vpon that doubt,
But let it rest, now Litio to you:
Good master take it not vnkindly pray
That I haue beene thus pleasant with you both.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
verse: You may go walk, and giue me leaue a while,
My Lessons make no musicke in three parts.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Are you so formall sir, well I must waite
And watch withall, for but I be deceiu'd,
Our fine Musitian groweth amorous.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Madam, before you touch the instrument,
To learne the order of my fingering,
I must begin with rudiments of Art,
To teach you gamoth in a briefer sort,
More pleasant, pithy, and effectuall,
Then hath beene taught by any of my trade,
And there it is in writing fairely drawne.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Why, I am past my gamouth long agoe.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Yet read the gamouth of Hortentio.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Gamouth I am, the ground of all accord:
Are, to plead Hortensio's passion:
Beeme, Bianca take him for thy Lord
Cfavt, that loues with all affection:
D solre, one Cliffe, two notes haue I,
Elami, show pitty or I die.
Call you this gamouth? tut I like it not,
Old fashions please me best, I am not so nice
To charge true rules for old inuentions.

speeches.speaker: Nicke.
verse: Mistresse, your father prayes you leaue your books,
And helpe to dresse your sisters chamber vp,
You know to morrow is the wedding day.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Farewell sweet masters both, I must be gone.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Faith Mistresse then I haue no cause to stay.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: But I haue cause to pry into this pedant,
Methinkes he lookes as though he were in loue:
Yet if thy thoughts Bianca be so humble
To cast thy wandring eyes on euery stale:
Seize thee that List, if once I finde thee ranging,
Hortensio will be quit with thee by changing.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Signior Lucentio, this is the pointed day
That Katherine and Petruchio should be married,
And yet we heare not of our sonne in Law:
What will be said, what mockery will it be?
To want the Bride-groome when the Priest attends
To speake the ceremoniall rites of marriage?
What saies Lucentio to this shame of ours?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: No shame but mine, I must forsooth be forst
To giue my hand oppos'd against my heart
Vnto a mad-braine rudes by, full of spleene,
Who woo'd in haste, and meanes to wed at leysure:
I told you I, he was a franticke foole,
Hiding his bitter iests in blunt behauiour,
And to be noted for a merry man;
Hee'll wooe a thousand, point the day of marriage,
Make friends, inuite, and proclaime the banes,
Yet neuer meanes to wed where he hath woo'd:
Now must the world point at poore Katherine,
And say, loe, there is man Petruchio's wife
If it would please him come and marry her.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Patience good Katherine and Baptista too,
Vpon my life Petruchio meanes but well,
What euer fortune stayes him from his word,
Though he be blunt, I know him passing wise,
Though he be merry, yet withall he's honest.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Would Katherine had neuer seen him though.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Goe girle, I cannot blame thee now to weepe,
For such an iniurie would vexe a very saint,
Much more a shrew of impatient humour.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Master, master, newes, and such newes as you neuer heard of,

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Is it new and olde too? how may that be?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Why, is it not newes to heard of Petruchio's comming?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Is he come?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Why no sir.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: What then?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: He is comming.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: When will he be heere?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: When he stands where I am, and sees you there.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: But say, what to thine olde newes?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Why Petruchio is comming, in a new hat and an old ierkin, a paire of olde breeches thrice turn'd; a paire of bootes that haue beene candle-cases, one buckled, another lac'd: an olde rusty sword tane out of the Towne Armory, with a broken hilt, and chapelesse: with two broken points: his horse hip'd with an olde mothy saddle, and stirrops of no kindred: besides possest with the glanders, and like to mose in the chine, troubled with the Lampasse, infected with the fashions, full of Windegalls, sped with Spauins, raied with the Yellowes, past cure of the Fiues, starke spoyl'd with the Staggers, begnawne with the Bots, Waid in the backe, and shoulder-shotten, neere leg'd before, and with a halfe-chekt Bitte, & a headstall of sheepes leather, which being restrain'd to keepe him from stumbling, hath been often burst, and now repaired with knots: one girth sixe times peec'd, and a womans Crupper of velure, which hath two letters for her name, fairely set down in studs, and heere and there peec'd with packthred.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Who comes with him?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Oh sir, his Lackey, for all the world Caparison'd like the horse: with a linnen stock on one leg, and a kersey boot-hose on the other, gartred with a red and blew lift; an old hat, & the humor of forty fancies prickt in't for a feather: a monster, a very monster in apparell, & not like a Christian foot-boy, or a gentlemans Lacky.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: 'Tis some od humor pricks him to this fashion,
Yet oftentimes he goes but meane apparel'd.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: I am glad he's come, howsoere he comes.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Why sir, he comes not.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Didst thou not say hee comes?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Who, that Petruchio came?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: I, that Petruchio came.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: No sir, I say his horse comes with him on his backe.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Why that's all one.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Nay by S. Iamy, I hold you a penny, a horse and a man is more then one, and yet not many.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Come, where be these gallants? who's at home?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: You are welcome sir.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: And yet I come not well.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: And yet you halt not.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Not so well apparell'd as I wish you were.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Were it better I should rush in thus:
But where is Kate? where is my louely Bride?
How does my father? gentles methinkes you frowne,
And wherefore gaze this goodly company,
As if they saw some wondrous monument,
Some Commet, or vnusuall prodigie?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Why sir, you know this is your wedding day.
First were we sad, fearing you would not come,
Now sadder that you come so vnprouided:
Fie, doff this habit, shame to your estate,
An eye-sore to our solemne festiuall.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: And tell vs what occasion of import
Hath all so long detain'd you from your wife,
And sent you hither so vnlike your selfe?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Tedious it were to tell, and harsh to heare,
Sufficeth I am come to keepe my word.
Though in some part inforced to digresse,
Which at more leysure I will so excuse,
As you shall well be satisfied with all.
But where is Kate? I stay too long from her,
The morning weares, 'tis time we were at Church.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: See not your Bride in these vnreuerent robes,
Goe to my chamber, put on clothes of mine.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Not I, beleeue me, thus Ile visit her.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: But thus I trust you will not marry her.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Good sooth euen thus: therefore ha done with words,
To me she's married, not vnto my cloathes:
Could I repaire what she will weare in me,
As I can change these poore accoutrements,
'Twere well for Kate, and better for my selfe.
But what a foole am I to chat with you,
When I should bid good morrow to my Bride?
And seale the title with a louely kisse.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: He hath some meaning in his mad attire,
We will perswade him be it possible,
To put on better ere he goe to Church.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Ile after him, and see the euent of this.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: But sir, Loue concerneth vs to adde
Her fathers liking, which to bring to passe
As before imparted to your worship,
I am to get a man what ere he be,
It skills not much, weele fit him to our turne,
And he shall be Vincentio of Pisa,
And make assurance heere in Padua
Of greater summes then I haue promised,
So shall you quietly enioy your hope,
And marry sweet Bianca with consent.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Were it not that my fellow schoolemaster
Doth watch Bianca's steps so narrowly:
'Twere good me-thinkes to steale our marriage,
Which once perform'd, let all the world say no,
Ile keepe mine owne despite of all the world.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: That by degrees we meane to looke into,
And watch our vantage in this businesse,
Wee'll ouer-reach the grey-beard Gremio,
The narrow prying father Minola,
The quaint Musician, amorous Litio,
All for my Masters sake Lucentio.
Signior Gremio, came you from the Church?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: As willingly as ere I came from schoole.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: And is the Bride & Bridegroom coming home?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: A bridegroome say you? 'tis a groome indeed,
A grumlling groome, and that the girle shall finde.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Curster then she, why 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Why hee's a deuill, a deuill, a very fiend.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Why she's a deuill, a deuill, the deuils damme.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: Tut, she's a Lambe, a Doue, a foole to him:
Ile tell you sir Lucentio; when the Priest
Should aske if Katherine should be his wife,
I, by goggs woones quoth he, and swore so loud,
That all amaz'd the Priest let fall the booke,
And as he stoop'd againe to take it vp,
This mad-brain'd bridegroome tooke him such a cuffe,
That downe sell Priest and booke, and booke and Priest,
Now take them vp quoth he, if any list.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: What said the wench when he rose againe?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Trembled and shooke: for why, he stamp'd and swore, as if the Vicar meant to cozen him: but after many ceremonies done, hee calls for wine, a health quoth he, as if he had beene aboord carowsing to his Mates after a storme, quaft off the Muscadell, and threw the sops all in the Sextons face: hauing no other reason, but that his beard grew thinne and hungerly, and seem'd to aske him sops as hee was drinking: This done, hee tooke the Bride about the necke, and kist her lips with such a clamorous smacke, that at the parting all the Church did eccho: and I seeing this, came thence for very shame, and after mee I know the rout is comming, such a mad marryage neuer was before: harke, harke, I heare the minstrels play.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Gentlemen & friends, I thank you for your pains,
I know you thinke to dine with me to day,
And haue prepar'd great store of wedding cheere,
But so it is, my haste doth call me hence,
And therefore heere I meane to take my leaue.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Is't possible you will away to night?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I must away to day before night come,
Make it no wonder: if you knew my businesse,
You would intreat me rather goe then stay:
And honest company, I thanke you all,
That haue beheld me giue away my selfe
To this most patient, sweet, and vertuous wife,
Dine with my father, drinke a health to me,
For I must hence, and farewell to you all.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Let vs intreat you stay till after dinner.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: It may not be.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Let me intreat you.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: It cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Let me intreat you.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: I am content.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Are you content to stay?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I am content you shall entreat me stay,
But yet not stay, entreat me how you can.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Now if you loue me stay.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Grumio, my horse.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I sir, they be ready, the Oates haue eaten the horses.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Nay then,
Doe what thou canst, I will not goe to day,
No, nor to morrow, not till I please my selfe,
The dore is open sir, there lies your way,
You may be iogging whiles your bootes are greene:
For me, Ile not be gone till I please my selfe,
'Tis like you'll proue a iolly surly groome,
That take it on you at the first so roundly.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: O Kate content thee, prethee be not angry.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
verse: I will be angry, what hast thou to doe?
Father, be quiet, he shall stay my leisure.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: I marry sir, now it begins to worke.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
verse: Gentlemen, forward to the bridall dinner,
I see a woman may be made a foole
If she had not a spirit to resist.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: They shall goe forward Kate at thy command,
Obey the Bride you that attend on her.
Goe to the feast, reuell and domineere,
Carowse full measure to her maiden-head,
Be madde and merry, or goe hang your selues:
But for my bonny Kate, she must with me:
Nay, looke not big, nor stampe, nor stare, nor fret,
I will be master of what is mine owne,
Shee is my goods, my chattels, she is my house,
My houshold-stuffe, my field, my barne,
My horse, my oxe, my asse, my any thing,
And heere she stands, touch her who euer dare,
Ile bring mine action on the proudest he
That stops my way in Padua: Grumio
Draw forth thy weapon, we are beset with theeues,
Rescue thy Mistresse if thou be a man:
Feare not sweet wench, they shall not touch thee Kate,
Ile buckler thee against a Million.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Nay, let them goe, a couple of quiet ones.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Went they not quickly, I should die with laughing.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Of all mad matches neuer was the like.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Mistresse, what is your opinion of your sister?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: That being mad her selfe, she's madly mated.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: I warrant him Petruchio is Kated.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Neighbours and friends, though Bride & Bridegroom wants
For to supply the places at the table,
You know there wants no iunkets at the feast:
Lucentio, you shall supply the Bridegroomes place,
And let Bianca take her sisters roome.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Shall sweet Bianca practise how to bride it?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: She shall Lucentio: come gentlemen lets goe.

speeches.speaker: Gru.:
prose: Fie, fie on all tired Iades, on all mad Masters, & all foule waies: was euer man so beaten? was euer man so raide? was euer man so weary? I am sent before to make a fire, and they are comming after to warme them: now were not I a little pot, & soone hot; my very lippes might freeze to my teeth, my tongue to the roofe of my mouth, my heart in my belly, ere I should come by a fire to thaw me, but I with blowing the fire shall warme my selfe: for considering the weather, a taller man then I will take cold: Holla, hoa Curtis.

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose: Who is that calls so coldly?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose:
A piece of Ice: if thou doubt it, thou maist slide from my shoulder to my heele, with no

greater a run but my head and my necke. A fire good Curtis.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Is my master and his wife comming Grumio?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Oh I Curtis I, and therefore fire, fire, cast on no water.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Is she so hot a shrew as she's reported.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: She was good Curtis before this frost: but thou know'st winter tames man, woman, and beast: for it hath tam'd my old master, and my new mistris, and my selfe fellow Curtis.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Away you three inch foole, I am no beast.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Am I but three inches? Why thy horne is a foot and so long am I at the least. But wilt thou make a fire, or shall I complaine on thee to our mistris, whose hand (she being now at hand) thou shalt soone feele, to thy cold comfort, for being slow in thy hot office.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: I prethee good Grumio, tell me, how goes the world?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: A cold world Curtis in euery office but thine, & therefore fire: do thy duty, and haue thy dutie, for my Master and mistris are almost frozen to death.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: There's fire readie, and therefore good Grumio the newes.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Why Iacke boy, ho boy, and as much newes as wilt thou.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Come, you are so full of conicatching.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Why therefore fire, for I haue caught extreme cold. Where's the Cooke, is supper ready, the house trim'd, rushes strew'd, cobwebs swept, the seruingmen in their new fustian, the white stockings, and euery officer his wedding garment on? Be the Iackes faire within, the Gils fai^ without, the Carpets laide, and euerie thing in order?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: All readie: and therefore I pray thee newes.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: First know my horse is tired, my master & mistris falne out.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Out of their saddles into the durt, and thereby hangs a tale.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Let's ha't good Grumio.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Lend thine eare.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Heere.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: There.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: This 'tis to feele a tale, not to heare a tale.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: And therefore 'tis cal'd a sensible tale: and this Cuffe was but to knocke at your eare, and beseech listning: now I begin, Inprimis wee came downe a fowle hill, my Master riding behinde my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Both of one horse?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: What's that to thee?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Why a horse.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Tell thou the tale: but hadst thou not crost me, thou shouldst haue heard how her horse fel, and she vnder her horse: thou shouldst haue heard in how miery a place, how she was bemoil'd, how hee left her with the horse vpon her, how he beat me because her horse stumbled, how she waded through the durt to plucke him off me: how he swore, how she prai'd, that neuer prai'd before: how I cried, how the horses ranne away, how her bridle was burst: how I lost my crupper, with manie things of worthy memorie, which now shall die in obliuion, and thou returne vnexperienc'd to thy graue.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: By this reckning he is more shrew than she.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I, and that thou and the proudest of you all shall finde when he comes home. But what talke I of this? Call forth Nathaniel, Ioseph, Nicholas, Phillip, Walter, Sugersop and the rest: let their heads bee slickely comb'd, their blew coats brush'd, and their garters of an indifferent knit, let them curtsie with their left legges, and not presume to touch a haire of my Masters horse-taile, till they kisse their hands. Are they all readie?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: They are.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Call them forth.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Do you heare ho? you must meete my maister to countenance my mistris.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Why she hath a face of her owne.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Who knowes not that?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Thou it seemes, that cals for company to countenance her.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: I call them forth to credit her.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Why she comes to borrow nothing of them.

speeches.speaker: Nat.
prose: Welcome home Grumio.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: How now Grumio.

speeches.speaker: Ios.
prose: What Grumio.

speeches.speaker: Nick.
prose: Fellow Grumio.

speeches.speaker: Nat.
prose: How now old lad.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Welcome you: how now you: what you: fellow you: and thus much for greeting. Now my spruce companions, is all readie, and all things neate?

speeches.speaker: Nat.
prose: All things is readie, how neere is our master?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: E'ne at hand, alighted by this: and therefore be not—Cockes passion, silence, I heare my master.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Where be these knaues? What no man at doore
To hold my stirrop, nor to take my horse?
Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Phillip.

speeches.speaker: All ser.
prose: Heere, heere sir, heere sir.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Heere sir, heere sir, heere sir, heere sir.
You logger-headed and vnpollisht groomes:
What? no attendance? no regard? no dutie?
Where is the foolish knaue I sent before?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Heere sir, as foolish as I was before.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: You pezant, swain, you horson malt-horse drudg
Did I not bid thee meete me in the Parke,
And bring along these rascal knaues with thee?

speeches.speaker: Grumio.
verse: Nathaniels coate sir was not fully made,
And Gabrels pumpes were all vnpinkt i' th heele:
There was no Linke to colour Peters hat,
And Walters dagger was not come from sheathing:
There were none fine, but Adam, Rafe, and Gregory,
The rest were ragged, old, and beggerly,
Yet as they are, heere are they come to meete you.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Go rascals, go, and fetch my supper in.
Where is the life that late I led?
Where are those? Sit downe Kate,
And welcome. Soud, soud, soud, soud.
Why when I say? Nay good sweete Kate be merrie.
Off with my boots, you rogues: you villaines, when?
It was the Friar of Orders gray,
As he forth walked on his way.
Out you rogue, you plucke my foote awrie,
Take that, and mend the plucking of the other.
Be merrie Kate: Some water heere: what hoa.
Where's my Spaniel Troilus? Sirra, get you hence,
And bid my cozen Ferdinand come hither:
One Kate that you must kisse, and be acquainted with.
Where are my Slippers? Shall I haue some water?
Come Kate and wash, & welcome heartily:
you horson villaine, will you let it fall?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Patience I pray you, 'twas a fault vnwilling.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: A horson beetle-headed flap-ear'd knaue:
Come Kate sit downe, I know you haue a stomacke,
Will you giue thankes, sweete Kate, or else shall I?
What's this, Mutton?

speeches.speaker: 1. Ser.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Who brought it?

speeches.speaker: Peter.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Tis burnt, and so is all the meate:
What dogges are these? Where is the rascall Cooke?
How durst you villaines bring it from the dresser
And serue it thus to me that loue it not?
There, take it to you, trenchers, cups, and all:
You heedlesse iolt-heads, and vnmanner'd slaues.
What, do you grumble? Ile be with you straight.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: I pray you husband be not so disquiet,
The meate was well, if you were so contented.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I tell thee Kate, 'twas burnt and dried away,
And I expressely am forbid to touch it:
For it engenders choller, planteth anger,
And better 'twere that both of vs did fast,
Since of our selues, our selues are chollericke,
Then feede it with such ouer-rosted flesh:
Be patient, to morrow't shalbe mended,
And for this night we'l fast for companie.
Come I wil bring thee to thy Bridall chamber.

speeches.speaker: Nath.
prose: Peter didst euer see the like.

speeches.speaker: Peter.
prose: He kils her in her owne humor.

speeches.speaker: Grumio.
prose: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: In her chamber, making a sermon of continencie to her, and railes, and sweares, and rates, that shee (poore soule) knowes not which way to stand, to looke, to speake, and sits as one new risen from a dreame. Away, away, for he is comming hither.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Thus haue I politickely begun my reigne,
And 'tis my hope to end successefully:
My Faulcon now is sharpe, and passing emptie,
And til she stoope, she must not be full gorg'd,
For then she neuer lookes vpon her lure.
Another way I haue to man my Haggard,
To make her come, and know her Keepers call:
That is, to watch her, as we watch these Kites,
That baite, and beare, and will not be obedient:
She eate no meate to day, nor none shall eate.
Last night she slept not, nor to night she shall not:
As with the meate, some vndeserued fault
Ile finde about the making of the bed,
And heere Ile fling the pillow, there the boulster,
This way the Couerlet, another way the sheets:
I, and amid this hurlie I intend,
That all is done in reuerend care of her,
And in conclusion, she shal watch all night,
And if she chance to nod, Ile raile and brawle,
And with the clamor keepe her stil awake:
This is a way to kil a Wife with kindnesse,
And thus Ile curbe her mad and headstrong humor:
He that knowes better how to tame a shrew,
Now let him speake, 'tis charity to shew.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Is't possible friend Lisio, that mistris Bianca
Doth fancie any other but Lucentio,
I tel you sir, she beares me faire in hand.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Sir, to satisfie you in what I haue said,
Stand by, and marke the manner of his teaching.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Now Mistris, profit you in what you reade?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: What Master reade you first, resolue me that?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I reade, that I professe the Art to loue.

speeches.speaker: Bian
prose: And may you proue sir Master of your Art.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: While you sweet deere ptoue Mistresse of my heart.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Quicke proceeders marry, now tel me I pray, you that durst sweare that your mistris Bianca Lou'd me in the World so wel as Lucentio.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Oh despightful Loue, vnconstant womankind,
I tel thee Lisio this is wonderfull.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Mistake no more, I am not Lisio,
Nor a Musitian as I seeme to bee,
But one that scorne to liue in this disguise,
For such a one as leaues a Gentleman,
And makes a God of such a Cullion;
Know sir, that I am cal'd Hortensio.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Signior Hortensio, I haue often heard
Of your entire affection to Bianca,
And since mine eyes are witnesse of her lightnesse,
I wil with you, if you be so contented,
Forsweare Bianca, and her loue for euer.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: See how they kisse and court: Signior Lucentio,
Heere is my hand, and heere I firmly vow
Neuer to woo her more, but do forsweare her
As one vnworthie all the former fauours
That I haue fondly flatter'd them withall.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: And heere I take the like vnfained oath,
Neuer to marrie with her, though she would intreate,
Fie on her, see how beastly she doth court him.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Would all the world but he had quite forsworn
For me, that I may surely keepe mine oath.
I wil be married to a wealthy Widdow,
Ere three dayes passe, which hath as long lou'd me,
As I haue lou'd this proud disdainful Haggard,
And so farewel signior Lucentio,
Kindnesse in women, not their beauteous lookes
Shal win my loue, and so I take my leaue,
In resolution, as I swore before.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Mistris Bianca, blesse you with such grace,
As longeth to a Louers blessed case:
Nay, I haue tane you napping gentle Loue,
And haue forsworne you with Hortensio.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Tranio you iest, but haue you both forsworne mee?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Mistris we haue.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Then we are rid of Lisio.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I' faith hee'l haue a lustie Widdow now,
That shalbe woo'd, and wedded in a day.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: God giue him ioy.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: I, and hee'l tame her.

speeches.speaker: Bianca.
prose: He sayes so Tranio.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Faith he is gone vnto the taming schoole.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: The taming schoole: what is there such a place?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I mistris, and Petruchio is the master,
That teacheth trickes eleuen and twentie long,
To tame a shrew, and charme her chattering tongue.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
verse: Oh Master, master I haue watcht so long,
That I am dogge-wearie, but at last I spied
An ancient Angel comming downe the hill,
Wil serue the turne.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: What is he Biondello?

speeches.speaker: Bio.
verse: Master, a Marcantant, or a pedant,
I know not what, but formall in apparrell,
In gate and countenance surely like a Father.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: And what of him Tranio?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: If he be credulous, and trust my tale,
Ile make him glad to seeme Vincentio,
And giue assurance to Baptista Minola.

As if he were the right
~incentio.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Take me your loue, and then let me alone.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: God saue you sir.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: And you sir, you are welcome,
Trauaile you farre on, or are you at the farthest?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Sir at the farthest for a weeke or two,
But then vp farther, and as farre as Rome,
And so to Tripolie, if God lend me life.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: What Countreyman I pray?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Of Mantua.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Of Mantua Sir, marrie God forbid,
