And come to Padua carelesse of your life.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: My life sir? how I pray? for that goes hard.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: 'Tis death for any one in Mantua
To come to Padua, know you not the cause?
Your ships are staid at Venice, and the Duke
For priuate quarrel 'twixt your Duke and him,
Hath publish'd and proclaim'd it openly:
'Tis meruaile, but that you are but newly come,
you might haue heard it else proclaim'd about.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Alas sir, it is worse for me then so,
For I haue bils for monie by exchange
From Florence, and must heere deliuer them.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Wel sir, to do you courtesie,
This wil I do, and this I wil aduise you.
First tell me, haue you euer beene at Pisa?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I sir, in Pisa haue I often bin,
Pisa renowned for graue Citizens.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Among them know you one Vincentio?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I know him not, but I haue heard of him:
A Merchant of incomparable wealth.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: He is my father sir, and sooth to say,
In count'nance somewhat doth resemble you.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: As much as an apple doth an oyster, & all one.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: To saue your life in this extremitie,
This fauor wil I do you for his sake,
And thinke it not the worst of all your fortunes,
That you are like to Sir Vincentio.
His name and credite shal you vndertake,
And in my house you shal be friendly lodg'd,
Looke that you take vpon you as you should,
you vnderstand me sir: so shal you stay
Til you haue done your businesse in the Citie:
If this be court'sie sir, accept of it.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Oh sir I do, and wil repute you euer
The patron of my life and libertie.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Then go with me, to make the matter good,
This by the way I let you vnderstand,
My father is heere look'd for euerie day,
To passe assurance of a dowre in marriage
'Twixt me, and one Baptistas daughter heere:
In all these circumstances Ile instruct you,
Go with me to cloath you as becomes you.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: No, no forsooth I dare not for my life.

speeches.speaker: Ka.
verse: The more my wrong, the more his spite appears,
What, did he marrie me to famish me?
Beggers that come vnto my fathers doore,
Vpon intreatie haue a present almes,
If not, elsewhere they meete with charitie:
But I, who neuer knew how to intreat,
Nor neuer needed that I should intreate,
Am staru'd for meate. giddie for lacke of sleepe:
With oathes kept waking, and with brawling fed,
And that which spights me more then all these wants,
He does it vnder name of perfect loue:
As who should say. if I should sleepe or eate.
'Twere deadly sicknesse, or else present death.
I prethee go, and get me some repast,
I care not what, so it be holsome soode.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: What say you to a Neats foote?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: 'Tis passing good, I prethee let me haue it.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
verse: I feare it is too chollericke a meate.
How say you to a fat Tripe finely broyl'd?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I like it well, good Grumio fetch it me.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
verse: I cannot tell, I feare 'tis chollericke.
What say you to a peece of Beefe and Mustard?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: A dish that I do loue to feede vpon.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I, but the Mustard is too hot a little.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Why then the Beefe, and let the Mustard rest.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
verse: Nay then I wil not, you shal haue the Mustard
Or else you get no beefe of Grumio.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Then both or one, or any thing thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Why then the Mustard without the beefe.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Go get thee gone, thou false deluding slaue,
That feed'st me with the verie name of meate.
Sorrow on thee, and all the packe of you
That triumph thus vpon my misery:
Go get thee gone, I say.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: How fares my Kate, what sweeting all a-mort?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Mistris, what cheere?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Faith as cold as can be.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Plucke vp thy spirits, looke cheerfully vpon me.
Heere Loue, thou seest how diligent I am,
To dresse thy meate my selfe, and bring it thee.
I am sure sweet Kate, this kindnesse merites thankes.
What, not a word? Nay then, thou lou'st it not:
And all my paines is sorted to no proofe.
Heere take away this dish.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I pray you let it stand.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: The poorest seruice is repaide with thankes,
And so shall mine before you touch the meate.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Signior Petruchio, fie you are too blame:
Come Mistris Kate, Ile beare you companie.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Eate it vp all Hortensio, if thou louest mee:
Much good do it vnto thy gentle heart:
Kate eate apace; and now my honie Loue,
Will we returne vnto thy Fathers house,
And reuell it as brauely as the best,
With silken coats and caps, and golden Rings,
With Ruffes and Cuffes, and Fardingales, and things:
With Scarfes, and Fannes, & double change of brau'ry,
With Amber Bracelets, Beades, and all this knau'ry.
What hast thou din'd? The Tailor staies thy leasure,
To decke thy bodie with his ruffling treasure.
Come Tailor, let vs see these ornaments.
Lay forth the gowne. What newes with you sir?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Heere is the cap your Worship did bespeake.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why this was moulded on a porrenger,
A Veluet dish: Fie, fie, 'tis lewd and filthy,
Why 'tis a cockle or a walnut-shell,
A knacke, a toy, a tricke, a babies cap:
Away with it, come let me haue a bigger.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Ile haue no bigger, this doth fit the time,
And Gentlewomen weare such caps as these.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: When you are gentle, you shall haue one too,
And not till then.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: That will not be in hast.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Why sir I trust I may haue leaue to speake,
And speake I will. I am no childe, no babe,
Your betters haue indur'd me say my minde,
And If you cannot, best you stop your eares.
My tongue will tell the anger of my heart,
Or els my heart concealing it wil breake,
And rather then it shall, I will be free,
Euen to the vttermost as I please in words.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why thou saist true, it is paltrie cap,
A custard coffen, a bauble, a silken pie,
I loue thee well in that thou lik'st it not.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Loue me, or loue me not, I like the cap,
And it I will haue, or I will haue none.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Thy gowne, why I: come Tailor let vs see't.
Oh mercie God, what masking stuffe is heere?
Whats this? a sleeue? 'tis like demi cannon,
What, vp and downe caru'd like an apple Tart?
Heers snip, and nip, and cut, and slish and slash,
Like to a Censor in a barbers shoppe:
Why what a deuils name Tailor cal'st thou this?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I see shees like to haue neither cap nor gowne.

speeches.speaker: Tai.
verse: You bid me make it orderlie and well,
According to the fashion, and the time.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Marrie and did: but if you be remembred,
I did not bid you marre it to the time.
Go hop me ouer euery kennell home,
For you shall hop without my custome sir:
Ile none of it; hence, make your best of it.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: I neuer saw a better fashion'd gowne,
More queint, more pleasing, nor more commendable:
Belike you meane to make a puppet of me.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Why true, he meanes to make a puppet of thee.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
prose: She saies your Worship meanes to make a puppet of her.

speeches.speaker: Pet
verse: Oh monstrous arrogance:
Thou lyest, thou thred, thou thimble,
Thou yard three quarters, halfe yard, quarter, naile,
Thou Flea, thou Nit, thou winter cricket thou:
Brau'd in mine owne house with a skeine of thred:
Away thou Ragge, thou quantitie, thou remnant,
Or I shall so be-mete thee with thy yard,
As thou shalt thinke on prating whil'st thou liu'st:
I tell thee I, that thou hast marr'd her gowne.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
verse: Your worship is deceiu'd, the gowne is made
Iust as my master had direction:
Grumio gaue order how it should be done.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I gaue him no order, I gaue him the stuffe.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
prose: But how did you desire it should be made?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Marrie sir with needle and thred.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
prose: But did you not request to haue it cut?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Thou hast fac'd many things.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
prose: I haue.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Face not mee: thou hast brau'd manie men, braue not me; I will neither bee fac'd nor brau'd. I say vnto thee, I bid thy Master cut out the gowne, but I did not bid him cut it to peeces. Ergo thou liest.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
prose: Why heere is the note of the fashion to testify.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Reade it.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: The note lies in's throate if he say I said so.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
prose: Inprimis, a loose bodied gowne.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Master, if euer I said loose-bodied gowne, sow me in the skirts of it, and beate me to death with a bottome of browne thred: I said a gowne.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Proceede.

speeches.speaker: Tai.
prose: With a small compast cape.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I confesse the cape.

speeches.speaker: Tai.
prose: With a trunke sleeue.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I confesse two sleeues.

speeches.speaker: Tai.
prose: The sleeues curiously cut.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: I there's the villanie.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Error i' th bill sir, error i' th bill? I commanded the sleeues should be cut out, and sow'd vp againe, and that Ile proue vpon thee, though thy little finger be armed in a thimble.

speeches.speaker: Tail.
prose: This is true that I say, and I had thee in place where thou shouldst know it.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: I am for thee straight: take thou the bill, giue me thy meat-yard, and spare not me.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: God-a-mercie Grumio, then hee shall haue no oddes.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Well sir in breefe the gowne is not for me.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: You are i' th right sir, 'tis for my mistris.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Go take it vp vnto thy masters vse.

speeches.speaker: Gru.
prose: Villaine, not for thy life: Take vp my Mistresse gowne for thy masters vse.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Why sir, what's your conceit in that?

speeches.speaker: Gru.
verse: Oh sir, the conceit is deeper then you think for:
Take vp my Mistris gowne to his masters vse.
Oh fie, fie, fie.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Hortensio, say thou wilt see the Tailor paide:
Go take it hence, be gone, and say no more.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Tailor, Ile pay thee for thy gowne to morrow,
Take no vnkindnesse of his hastie words:
Away I say, commend me to thy master.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Well, come my Kate, we will vnto your fathers,
Euen in these honest meane habiliments:
Our purses shall be proud, our garments poore:
For 'tis the minde that makes the bodie rich.
And as the Sunne breakes through the darkest clouds,
So honor peereth in the meanest habit.
What is the Iay more precious then the Larke?
Because his feathers are more beautifull.
Or is the Adder better then the Eele.
Because his painted skin contents the eye.
Oh no good Kate: neither art thou the worse
For this poore furniture, and meane array.
If thou accountedst it shame, lay it on me,
And therefore frolicke, we will hence forthwith,
To feast and sport vs at thy fathers house,
Go call my men, and let vs straight to him,
And bring our horses vnto Long-lane end,
There wil we mount, and thither walke on foote,
Let's see, I thinke 'tis now some seuen a clocke,
And well we may come there by dinner time.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: I dare assure you sir, 'tis almost two,
And 'twill be supper time ere you come there.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: It shall be seuen ere I go to horse:
Looke what I speake, or do, or thinke to doe,
You are still crossing it, sirs let't alone,
I will not goe to day, and ere I doe,
It shall be what a clock I say it is.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Why so this gallant will command the sunne.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Sirs, this is the house, please it you that I call.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I what else, and but I be deceiued,
Signior Baptista may remember me
Neere twentie yeares a goe in Genoa.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Where we were lodgers, at the Pegasus,
Tis well, and hold your owne in any case
With such austeritie as longeth to a father.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I warrant you: but sir here comes your boy,
Twere good he were school'd.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Feare you not him: sirra Biondello,
Now doe your dutie throughlie I aduise you:
Imagine 'twere the right Vincentio.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Tut, feare not me.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: But hast thou done thy errand to Baptista.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
verse: I told him that your father was at Venice,
And that you look't for him this day in Padua.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Th' art a tall fellow, hold thee that to drinke,
Here comes Baptista: set your countenance sir.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Signior Baptista you are happilie met:
Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of,
I pray you stand good father to me now,
Giue me Bianca for my patrimony.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Soft son: sir by your leaue, hauing com to Padua
To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio
Made me acquainted with a waighty cause
Of loue betweene your daughter and himselfe:
And for the good report I heare of you,
And for the loue he beareth to your daughter,
And she to him: to stay him not too long,
I am content in a good fathers care
To haue him matcht, and if you please to like
No worse then I, vpon some agreement
Me shall you finde readie and willing
With one consent to haue her so bestowed:
For curious I cannot be with you
Signior Baptista, of whom I heare so well.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Sir, pardon me in what I haue to say,
Your plainnesse and your shortnesse please me well:
Right true it is your sonne Lucentio here
Doth loue my daughter, and she loueth him,
Or both dissemble deepely their affections:
And therefore if you say no more then this,
That like a Father you will deale with him,
And passe my daughter a sufficient dower,
The match is made, and all is done,
Your sonne shall haue my daughter with consent.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I thanke you sir, where then doe you know best
We be affied and such assurance tane,
As shall with either parts agreement stand.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Not in my house Lucentio, for you know
Pitchers haue eares, and I haue manie seruants,
Besides old Gremio is harkning still,
And happilie we might be interrupted.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Then at my lodging, and it like you,
There doth my father lie: and there this night
Weele passe the businesse priuately and well:
Send for your daughter by your seruant here,
My Boy shall fetch the Scriuener presentlie,
The worst is this that at so slender warning,
You are like to haue a thin and slender pittance.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: It likes me well:
Cambio hie you home, and bid Bianca make her readie straight:
And if you will tell what hath hapned,
Lucentios Father is arriued in Padua,
And how she's like to be Lucentios wife.

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: I praie the gods she may withall my heart.

speeches.speaker: Tran.
verse: Dallie not with the gods, but get thee gone.
Signior Baptista, shall I leade the way,
Welcome, one messe is like to be your cheere,
Come sir, we will better it in Pisa.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: I follow you.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Cambio.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: What saist thou Biondello.

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: You saw my Master winke and laugh vpon you?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Biondello, what of that?

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: Faith nothing: but has left mee here behinde to expound the meaning or morrall of his signes and tokens.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I pray thee moralize them.

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: Then thus: Baptista is safe talking with the deceiuing Father of a deceitfull sonne.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: And what of him?

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: And then.

speeches.speaker: Bio.
prose: The old Priest at Saint Lukes Church is at your command at all houres.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: And what of all this.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
verse: If this be not that you looke for, I haue no more to say,
But bid Bianca farewell for euer and a day.
prose: I cannot tell, expect they are busied about a counterfeit assurance: take you assurance of her, Cum preuilegio ad Impremendum solem, to th' Church take the Priest, Clarke, and some sufficient honest witnesses:

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Hear'st thou Biondello.

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: I cannot tarry: I knew a wench maried in an afternoone as shee went to the Garden for Parseley to stuffe a Rabit, and so may you sir: and so adew sir, my Master hath appointed me to goe to Saint Lukes to bid the Priest be readie to come against you come with your appendix.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I may and will, if she be so contented:
She will be pleas'd, then wherefore should I doubt:
Hap what hap may, Ile roundly goe about her:
It shall goe hard if Cambio goe without her.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Come on a Gods name, once more toward our fathers:
Good Lord how bright and goodly shines the Moone.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: The Moone, the Sunne: it is not Moonelight now.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: I say it is the Moone that shines so bright.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I know it is the Sunne that shines so bright.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Now by my mothers sonne, and that's my selfe,
It shall be moone, or starre, or what I list,
Or ere I iourney to your Fathers house:
Goe on, and fetch our horses backe againe,
Euermore crost and crost, nothing but crost.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Say as he saies, or we shall neuer goe.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Forward I pray, since we haue come so farre,
And be it moone, or sunne, or what you please:
And if you please to call it a rush Candle,
Henceforth I vowe it shall be so for me.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: I say it is the Moone.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: I know it is the Moone.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Nay then you lye: it is the blessed Sunne.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Then God be blest, it in the blessed sun,
But sunne it is not, when you say it is not.
And the Moone changes euen as your minde:
What you will haue it nam'd, euen that it is,
And so it shall be so for Katherine.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Petruchio, goe thy waies, the field is won.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Well, forward, forward, thus the bowle should run,
And not vnluckily against the Bias:
But soft, Company is comming here.
Good morrow gentle Mistris, where away:
Tell me sweete Kate, and tell me truely too,
Hast thou beheld a fresher Gentlewoman:
Such warre of white and red within her cheekes:
What stars do spangle heauen with such beautie,
As those two eyes become that heauenly face?
Faire louely Maide, once more good day to thee:
Sweete Kate embrace her for her beauties sake.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: A will make the man mad to make the woman of him.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Yong budding Virgin, faire, and fresh, & sweet,
Whether away, or whether is thy aboade?
Happy the Parents of so faire a childe;
Happier the man whom fauourable stars
A lots thee for his louely bedfellow.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Why how now Kate, I hope thou art not mad,
This is a man old, wrinckled, faded, withered,
And not a Maiden, as thou saist he is.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Pardon old father my mistaking eies,
That haue bin so bedazled with the sunne,
That euery thing I looke on seemeth greene:
Now I perceiue thou art a reuerent Father:
Pardon I pray thee for my mad mistaking.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Do good old grandsire, & withall make known
Which way thou trauellest, if along with vs,
We shall be ioyfull of thy companie.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
verse: Faire Sir, and you my merry Mistris,
That with your strange encounter much amasde me:
My name is call'd Vincentio, my dwelling Pisa,
And bound I am to Padua, there to visite
A sonne of mine, which long I haue not seene.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: What is his name?

speeches.speaker: Vinc.
prose: Lucentio gentle sir.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Happily met, the happier for thy sonne:
And now by Law, as well as reuerent age,
I may intitle thee my louing Father,
The sister to my wife, this Gentlewoman,
Thy Sonne by this hath married: wonder not,
Nor be not grieued, she is of good esteeme,
Her dowrie wealthie, and of worthie birth;
Beside, so qualified, as may beseeme
The Spouse of any noble Gentleman:
Let me imbrace with old Vincentio,
And wander we to see thy honest sonne,
Who will of thy arriuall be full ioyous.

speeches.speaker: Vinc.
verse: But is this true, or is it else your pleasure,
Like pleasant trauailors to breake a left
Vpon the companie you ouertake?

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: I doe assure thee father so it is.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Come goe along and see the truth hereof,
For our first merriment hath made thee iealous.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Well Petruchio, this has put me in heart;
Haue to my Widdow, and if she froward,
Then hast thou taught Hortentio to be vntoward.

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: Softly and swiftly sir, for the Priest is ready.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I flie Biondello; but they may chance to neede thee at home, therefore leaue vs.

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: Nay faith, Ile see the Church a your backe, and then come backe to my mistris as soone as I can.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: I maruaile Cambio comes not all this while.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Sir heres the doore, this is Lucentios house,
My Fathers beares more toward the Market-place,
Thither must I, and here I leaue you sir.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
verse: You shall not choose but drinke before you go,
I thinke I shall command your welcome here;
And by all likelihood some cheere is toward.

speeches.speaker: Grem.
prose: They're busie within, you were best knocke lowder.

speeches.speaker: Ped
prose: What's he that knockes as he would beat downe the gate?

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Is Signior Lucentio within sir?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: He's within sir, but not to be spoken withall.

speeches.speaker: Vinc.
prose: What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two to make merrie withall.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Keepe your hundred pounds to your selfe, hee shall neede none so long as I liue.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Nay, I told you your sonne was well beloued in Padua: doe you heare sir, to leaue friuolous circumstances, I pray you tell signior Lucentio that his Father is come from Pisa, and is here at the doore to speake with him.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Thou liest his Father is come from Padua, and here looking out at the window.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Art thou his father?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: I sir, so his mother saies, if I may beleeue her.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Why how now gentleman: why this is flat knauerie to take vpon you another mans name.

speeches.speaker: Peda.
prose: Lay hands on the villaine, I beleeue a meanes to cosen some bodie in this Citie vnder my countenance.

speeches.speaker: Bio.
prose:
I haue seene them in the Church together, God send'em good shipping: but who is here? mine old Master
~incentio: now wee are vndone and brough to nothing.

speeches.speaker: ~in.
prose: Come hither crackhempe.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: I hope I may choose Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Come hither you rogue, what haue you forgot mee?

speeches.speaker: Biond.
prose: Forgot you, no sir: I could not forget you, for I neuer saw you before in all my life.

speeches.speaker: ~inc.
prose: What, you notorious villaine, didst thou neuer see thy Mistris father, Vincentio?

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: What my old worshipfull old master? yes marie sir see where he lookes out of the window.

speeches.speaker: ~in.
prose: Ist so indeede.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Helpe, helpe, helpe, here's a mad man will murder me.

speeches.speaker: Pedan.
prose: Helpe, sonne, helpe signior Baptista.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Pree the Kate let's stand aside and see the end of this controuersie.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Sir, what are you that offer to beate my seruant?

speeches.speaker: Vinc.
prose: What am I sir: nay what are you sir: oh immortall Goddes: oh fine villaine, a silken doubtlet, a veluet hose, a scarlet cloake, and a copataine hat: oh I am vndone, I am vndone: while I plaie the good husband at home, my sonne and my seruant spend all at the vniuersitie.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: How now, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
prose: What is the man lunaticke?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Sir, you seeme a sober ancient Gentleman by your habit: but your words shew you a mad man: why sir, what cernes it you, if I weare Pearle and gold: I thank my good Father, I am able to maintaine it.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Thy father: oh villaine, he is a Saile-maker in Bergamo.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: You mistake sir, you mistake sir, praie what do you thinke is his name?

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: His name, as if I knew not his name: I haue brought him vp euer since he was three yeeres old, and his name is Tronio.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Awaie, awaie mad asse, his name is Lucentio, and he is mine onelie sonne and heire to the Lands of me signior Vincentio.

speeches.speaker: Ven.
prose: Lucentio: oh he hath murdred his Master; laie hold on him I charge you in the Dukes name: oh my sonne, my sonne: tell me thou villaine, where is my son Lucentio?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Call forth an officer: Carrie this mad knaue to the Iaile: father Baptista, I charge you see that hee be forth comming.

speeches.speaker: Vinc.
prose: Carrie me to the Iaile?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Staie officer, he shall not go to prison.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Talke not signior Gremio: I saie he shall goe to prison.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Take heede signior Baptista, least you be conicatcht in this businesse: I dare sweare this is the right Vincentio.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Sweare if thou dar'st.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Naie, I dare not sweare it.

speeches.speaker: Tran.
prose: Then thou wert best saie that I am not Lucentio.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Yes, I know thee to be signior Lucentio.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Awaie with the dotard, to the Iaile with him.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Thus strangers may be haild and abusd: oh monstrous villaine.

speeches.speaker: Bion.
prose: Oh we are spoil'd, and yonder he is, denie him, forsweare him, or else we are all vndone.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Pardon sweete father.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Liues my sweete sonne?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Pardon deere father.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: How hast thou offended, where is Lucentio?

speeches.speaker: Luc:
verse:
Here's Lucentio, right sonne to the right
~incentio,
That haue by marriage made thy daughter mine,
While counterfeit supposes bleer'd thine eine.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Here's packing with a witnesse to deceiue vs all.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
verse: Where is that damned villaine Tranio,
That fac'd and braued me in this matter so?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Why, tell me is not this my Cambio?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Cambio is chang'd into Lucentio.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Loue wrought these miracles. Biancas loue
Made me exchange my state with Tranio,
While he did beare my countenance in the towne,
And happilie I haue arriued at the last
Vnto the wished hauen of my blisse:
What Tranio did, my selfe enforst him to;
Then pardon him sweete Father for my sake.

speeches.speaker: ~in.
prose: Ile slit the villaines nose that would haue sent me to the Iaile.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: But doe you heare sir, haue you married my daughter without asking my good will?

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Feare not Baptista, we will content you, goe to: but I will in to be reueng'd for this villanie.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: And I to sound the depth of this knauerie.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Looke not pale Bianca, thy father will not frown.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: My cake is doug^h but Ile in among the rest,
Out of hope of all, but my share of the feast.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Husband let's follow, to see the end of this adoe.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: First kisse me Kate, and we will.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: What in the midst of the streete?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: What art thou asham'd of me?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Mo sir, God forbid, but asham'd to kisse.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Why then let's home againe: Come Sirra let's awaie.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: Nay, I will giue thee a kisse, now praie thee Loue staie.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Is not this well? come my sweete Kate.
Better once then neuer, for neuer to late.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: At last, though long, our iarring notes agree,
And time it is when raging warre is come,
To smile at scapes and perils ouerblowne:
My faire Bianca bid my father welcome,
While I with selfesame kindnesse welcome thine:
Brother Petruchio, sister Katerina,
And thou Hortentio with thy louing Widdow:
Feast with the best, and welcome to my house,
My Banket is to close our stomakes vp
After our great good cheere: praie you sit downe,
For now we sit to chat as well as eate.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Nothing but sit and sit, and eate and eate.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Padua affords this kindnesse, sonne Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Padua affords nothing but what is kinde.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: For both our sakes I would that word were true.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Now for my life Hortentio feares his Widow.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Then neuer trust me if I be affeard.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: You are verie sencible, and yet you misse my sence:
I meane Hortentio is afeard of you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: He that is giddie thinks the world turns round.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Roundlie replied.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: Mistris, how meane you that?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Thus I conceiue by him.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Conceiues by me, how likes Hortentio that?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: My Widdow saies, thus she conceiues her tale.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Verie well mended: kisse him for that good Widdow.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
verse: He that is giddie thinkes the world turnes round,
I praie you tell me what you meant by that.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: Your housband being troubled with a shrew,
Measures my husbands sorrow by his woe:
And now you know my meaning.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: A verie meane meaning.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Right, I meane you.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: And I am meane indeede, respecting you.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: To her Kate.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: To her Widdow.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: A hundred marks, my Kate does put her down.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: That's my office

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Spoke like an Officer: ha to the lad.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: How likes Cremio these quicke witted folkes?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: Beleeue me sir, they But together well.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Head, and but an hastie witted bodie,
Would say your Head and But were head and horne.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: I Mistris Bride, hath that awakened you?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: I, but not frighted me, therefore Ile sleepe againe.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Nay that you shall not since you haue begun:
Haue at you for a better iest or too.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Am I your Bird, I meane to shift my bush,
And then pursue me as you draw your Bow.
You are welcome all.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: She hath preuented me, here signior Tranio,
This bird you aim'd at, though you hit her not,
Therefore a health to all that shot and mist.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: Oh sir, Lucentio slipt me like his Gray-hound,
Which runs himselfe, and catches for his Master.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: A good swift simile, but something currish.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: 'Tis well sir that you hunted for your selfe:
'Tis thought your Deere does hold you at a baie.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Oh, oh Petruchio, Tranio hits you now.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I thanke thee for that gird good Tranio.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Confesse, confesse, hath he not hit you here?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: A has a little gald me I confesse:
And as the Iest did glaunce awaie from me,
'Tis ten to one it maim'd you too out right.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Now in good sadnesse sonne Petruchio,
I thinke thou hast the veriest shrew of all.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Well, I say no: and therefore sir assurance,
Let's each one send vnto his wife,
And he whose wife is most obedient,
To come at first when he doth send for her,
Shall win the wager which we will propose.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Content, what's the wager?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Twentie crownes.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Twentie crownes,
Ile venture so much of my Hawke or Hound,
But twentie times so much vpon my Wife.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: A hundred then.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Content.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: A match, 'tis done.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Who shall begin?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: That will I.
Goe Biondello, bid your Mistris come to me.

speeches.speaker: Bio.
prose: Igoe.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Sonne, Ile be your halfe, Bianca comes.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Ile haue no halues: Ile beare it all my selfe.
How now, what newes?

speeches.speaker: Bio.
verse: Sir, my Mistris sends you word
That she is busie, and she cannot come.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: How? she's busie, and she cannot come: is that an answere?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
verse: I, and a kinde one too:
Praie God sir your wife send you not a worse.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: I hope better.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Sirra Biondello, goe and intreate my wife to come to me forthwith.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Oh ho, intreate her, nay then shee must needes come.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Yours will not be entreated: Now, where's my wife?
prose: I am affraid sir, doe what you can

speeches.speaker: Bion.
verse: She saies you haue some goodly Iest in hand,
She will not come: she bids you come to her.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Worse and worse, she will not come:
Oh vilde, intollerable, not to be indur'd:
Sirra Grumio, goe to your Mistris.
Say I command her come to me.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I know her answere.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: What?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: She will not.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: The fouler fortune mine, and there an end.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Now by my hollidam here comes Katerina.

speeches.speaker: Kat.
prose: What is your will sir, that you send for me?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
prose: Where is your sister, and Hortensios wife?

speeches.speaker: Kate.
prose: They sit conferring by the Parler fire.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Goe fetch them hither, if they denie to come,
Swinge me them soundly forth vnto their husbands.
Away I say, and bring them hither straight.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Here is a wonder, if you talke of a wonder.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: And so it is: I wonder what it boads.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Marrie peace it boads, and loue, and quiet life,
An awfull rule, and right supremicie:
And to be short, what not, that's sweete and happie.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Now faire befall thee good Petruchio;
The wager thou hast won, and I will adde
Vnto their losses twentie thousand crownes,
Another dowrie to another daughter,
For she is chang'd as she had neuer bin.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Nay, I will win my wager better yet,
And show more signe of her obedience,
Her new built vertue and obedience.
See where she comes, and brings your froward Wiues
As prisoners to her womanlie perswasion:
Katerine, that Cap of yours becomes you not,
Off with that bable, throw it vnderfoote.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: Lord let me neuer haue a cause to sigh,
Till I be brought to such a sillie passe.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Fie what a foolish dutie call you this?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I would your dutie were as foolish too:
The wisdome of your dutie faire Bianca,
Hath cost me fiue hundred crownes since supper time.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: The more foole you for laying on my dutie.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Katherine I charge thee tell these head-strong women, what dutie they doe owe their Lords and husbands.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Come, come, your mocking: we will haue no telling.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Come on I say, and first begin with her.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: She shall not.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: I say she shall, and first begin with her.

speeches.speaker: Kate.
verse: Fie, fie, vnknit that thretaning vnkinde brow,
And dart not scornefull glances from those eies,
To wound thy Lord, thy King, thy Gouernour.
It blots thy beautie, as frosts doe bite the Meads,
Confounds thy fame, as whirlewinds shake faire budds,
And in no sence is meete or amiable.
A woman mou'd, is like a fountaine troubled,
Muddie, ill seeming, thicke, hereft of beautie,
And while it is so, none so dry or thirstie
Will daigne to sip, or touch one drop of it.
Thy husband is thy Lord, thy life, thy keeper,
Thy head, thy soueraigne: One that cares for thee,
And for thy maintenance. Commits his body
To painfull labour, both by sea and land:
To watch the night in stormes, the day in cold,
Whil'st thou ly'st warme at home, secure and safe,
And craues no other tribute at thy hands,
But loue, faire lookes, and true obedience;
Too little payment for so great a debt.
Such dutie as the subiect owes the Prince,
Euen such a woman oweth to her husband:
And when she is froward, peeuish, sullen, sowre,
And not obedient to his honest will,
What is she but a foule contending Rebell,
And gracelesse Traitor to her louing Lord?
I am asham'd that women are so simple,
To offer warre, where they should kneele for peace:
Or seeke for rule, supremacie, and sway,
When they are bound to serue, loue, and obay.
Why are our bodies soft, and weake, and smooth,
Vnapt to toyle and trouble in the world,
But that our soft conditions, and our harts,
Should well agree with our externall parts?
Come, come, you froward and vnable wormes,
My minde hath bin as bigge as one of yours,
My heart as great, my reason haplie more,
To bandie word for word, and frowne for frowne;
But now I see our Launces are but strawes:
Our strength as weake, our weakenesse past compare,
That seeming to be most, which we indeed least are.
Then vale your stomackes, for it is no boote,
And place your hands below your husbands foote:
In token of which dutie, if he please,
My hand is readie, may it do him ease.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Why there's a wench: Come on, and kisse mee Kate.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Well go thy waies olde Lad for thou shalt ha't.

speeches.speaker: Vin.
prose: Tis a good hearing, when children are toward.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: But a harsh hearing, when women are froward,

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Come Kate, weee'le to bed,
We three are married, but you two are sped.
'Twas I wonne the wager, though you hit the white,
And being a winner, God giue you good night.

speeches.speaker: Horten.
prose: Now goe thy wayes, thou hast tam'd a curst Shrow.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Tis a wonder, by your leaue, she wil be tam'd so.

plays.play_title: ALL'S Well, that Ends Well.

speeches.speaker: Mother.
prose: IN deliuering my sonne from me, I burie a second husband.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: And I in going Madam, weep ore my fathers death anew; but I must attend his maiesties command, to whom I am now in Ward, euermore in subiection.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: You shall find of the King a husband Madame, you sir a father. He that so generally is at all times good, must of necessitie hold his vertue to you, whose worthinesse would stirre it vp where it wanted rather then lack it where there is such abundance.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: What hope is there of his Maiesties amendment?

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: He hath abandon'd his Phisitions Madam, vnder whose practises he hath persecuted time with hope, and finds no other aduantage in the processe, but onely the loosing of hope by time.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: This yong Gentlewoman had a father, O that had, how sad a passage tis, whose skill was almost as great as his honestie, had it stretch'd so far, would haue made nature immortall, and death should haue play for lacke of worke. Would for the Kings sake hee were liuing, I thinke it would be the death of the Kings disease.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: How call'd you the man you speake of Madam?

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: He was famous sir in his profession, and it was his great right to be so: Gerard de Narbon.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: He was excellent indeed Madam, the King very latelie spoke of him admiringly, and mourningly: hee was skilfull enough to haue liu'd stil, if knowledge could be set vp against mortallitie.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: What is it (my good Lord) the King languishes of?

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: A Fistula my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ros
prose: I heard not of it before.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I would it were not notorious. Was this Gentlewoman the Daughter of Gerard de Narbon?

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: His sole childe my Lord, and bequeathed to my ouer looking. I haue those hopes of her good, that her education promises her dispositions shee inherits, which makes faire gifts fairer: for where an vncleane mind carries vertuous qualities, there commendations go with pitty, they are vertues and traitors too: in her they are the better for their simplenesse; she deriues her honestie, and atcheeues her goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Lafew.
prose: Your commendations Madam get from her teares.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: 'Tis the best brine a Maiden can season her praise in. The remembrance of her father neuer approches her heart, but the tirrany of her sorrowes takes all liuelihood from her cheeke. No more of this Helena, go too, no more least it be rather thought you affect a sorrow, then to haue—

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: I doe affect a sorrow indeed, but I haue it too.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Moderate lamentation is the right of the dead, excessiue greefe the enemie to the liuing.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: If the liuing be enemie to the greefe, the excesse makes it soone mortall.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Maddam I desire your holie wishes.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: How vnderstand we that?

speeches.speaker: Mo.
verse: Be thou blest Bertrame, and succeed thy father
In manners as in shape: thy blood and vertue
Contend for Empire in thee, and thy goodnesse
Share with thy birth-right. Loue all, trust a few,
Doe wrong to none: be able for thine enemie
Rather in power then vse: and keepe thy friend
Vnder thy owne lifes key. Be checkt for silence,
But neuer tax'd for speech. What heauen more wil,
That thee may furnish, and my prayers plucke downe,
Fall on thy head. Farwell my Lord,
'Tis an vnseason'd Courtier, good my Lord
Aduise him.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: He cannot want the best
That shall attend his loue.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: Heauen blesse him: Farwell Bertram.

speeches.speaker: Ro.
prose: The best wishes that can be forg'd in your thoghts be seruants to you: be comfortable to my mother, your Mistris, and make much of her.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Farewell prettie Lady, you must hold the credit of your father.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: O were that all, I thinke not on my father,
And these great teares grace his remembrance more
Then those I shed for him. What was he like?
I haue forgott him. My imagination
Carries no fauour in't but Bertrams.
I am vndone, there is no liuing, none,
If Bertram be away. 'Twere all one,
That I should loue a bright particuler starre,
And think to wed it, he is so aboue me
In his bright radience and colaterall light,
Must I be comforted, not in his sphere;
Th' ambition in my loue thus plagues it selfe:
The hind that would be mated by the Lion
Must die for loue. 'Twas prettie, though a plague
To see him euerie houre to sit and draw
His arched browes, his hawking eie, his curles
In our hearts table: heart too capeable
Of euerie line and tricke of his sweet fauour.
But now he's gone, and my idolatrous fancie
Must sanctifie his Reliques. Who comes heere?
One that goes with him: I loue him for his sake,
And yet I know him a notorious Liar,
Thinke him a great way foole, solie a coward,
Yet these fixt euils sit so fit in him,
That they take place, when Vertues steely bones
Lookes bleake i' th cold wind: withall, full ofte we see
Cold wisedome waighting on superfluous follie.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Saue you faire Queene.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: And you Monarch.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: And no.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Are you meditating on virginitie?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: If you haue some staine of souldier in you: Let mee aske you a question. Man is enemie to virginitie, how may we barracado it against him?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Keepe him out.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: But he assailes, and our virginitie though valiant, in the defence yet is weak: vnfold to vs some warlike resistance.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: There is none: Man setting downe before you, will vndermine you, and blow you vp.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Blesse our poore Virginity from vnderminers and blowers vp. Is there no Military policy how Virgins might blow vp men?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Virginity beeing blowne downe, Man will quicklier be blowne vp: marry in blowing him downe againe, with the breach your selues made, you lose your Citty. It is not politicke, in the Common-wealth of Nature, to preserue virginity. Losse of Virginitie, is rationall encrease, and there was neuer Virgin goe, till virginitie was first lost. That you were made of, is mettall to make Virgins. Virginitie, by beeing once lost, may be ten times found: by being euer kept, it is euer lost: 'tis too cold a companion: Away with't.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I will stand for't a little, though therefore I die a Virgin.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: There's little can bee saide in't, 'tis against the rule of Nature. To speake on the part of virginitie, is to accuse your Mothers; which is most infallible disobedience. He that hangs himselfe is a Virgin: Virginitie murthers it selfe, and should be buried in highwayes out of all sanctified limit, as a desperate Offendresse against Nature. Virginitie breedes mites, much like a Cheese, consumes it selfe to the very payring, and so dies with feeding his owne stomacke. Besides, Virginitie is peeuish, proud, ydle, made of selfe-loue, which is the most inhibited sinne in the Cannon. Keepe it not, you cannot choose but loose by't. Out with't: within ten yeare it will make it selfe two, which is a goodly increase, and the principall it selfe not much the worse. Away with't.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: How might one do sir, to loose it to her owne liking?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Let mee see. Marry ill, to like him that ne're it likes. 'Tis a commodity wil lose the glosse with lying: The longer kept, the lesse worth: Off with't while 'tis vendible. Answer the time of request, Virginitie like an olde Courtier, weares her cap out of fashion, richly suted, but vnsuteable, iust like the brooch & the toothpick, which were not now: your Date is better in your Pye and your Porredge, then in your cheeke: and your virginity, your old virginity, is like one of our French wither'd peares, it lookes ill, it eates drily, marry 'tis a wither'd peare: it was formerly better, marry yet 'tis a wither'd peare: Will you any thing with it?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Not my virginity yet:
There shall your Master haue a thousand loues,
A Mother, and a Mistresse, and a friend,
A Phenix, Captaine, and an enemy.
A guide, a Goddesse, and a Soueraigne,
A Counsellor, a Traitoresse, and a Deare:
His humble ambition, proud humility:
His iarring, concord: and his discord, dulcet:
His faith, his sweet disaster: with a world
Of pretty fond adoptious christendomes
That blinking Cupid gossips. Now shall he:
I know not what he shall, God send him well,
The Courts a learning place, and he is one.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: What one ifaith?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: That I wish well, 'tis pitty.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: What's pitty?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: That wishing well had not a body in't,
Which might be felt, that we the poorer borne,
Whose baser starres do shut vs vp in wishes,
Might vvith effects of them follow our friends,
And shew what vve alone must thinke, which neuer
Returnes vs thankes.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse: Monsieur Parrolles,
My Lord cals for you.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Little Hellen farewell, if I can remember thee, I will thinke of thee at Court.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Monsieur Parolles, you were borne vnder a charitable starre.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Vnder Mars I.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I especially thinke, vnder Mars.

speeches.speaker: Par
prose: Why vnder Mars?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: The warres hath so kept you vnder, that you must needes be borne vnder Mars.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: When he was predominant.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: When he was retrograde I thinke rather.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Why thinke you so?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: You go so much backward when you fight.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: That's for aduantage.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: So is running away,
When feare proposes the safetie:
prose: But the composition that your valour and feare makes in you, is a vertue of a good wing, and I like the weare well.

speeches.speaker: Paroll.
prose:
I am so full of businesses, I cannot answere thee acutely: I will returne perfect Courtier, in the which my instruction shall serue to naturalize thee, so thou wilt be capeable of a Courtiers councell, and vnderstand what aduice shall thrust vppon thee, else thou diest in thine vnthankfulnes, and thine ignorance makes thee away, farewell: When thou hast leysure, say thy praiers: when thou hast none, remember thy Friends:

Get thee a good husband, and vse him as he vses thee: So farewell.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Our remedies oft in our selues do lye,
Which we ascribe to heauen: the fated skye
Giues vs free scope, onely doth backward pull
Our slow designes, when we our selues are dull.
What power is it, which mounts my loue so hye,
That makes me see, and cannot feede mine eye?
The mightiest space in fortune, Nature brings
To ioyne like, likes; and kisse like natiue things.
Impossible be strange attempts to those
That weigh their paines in sence, and do suppose
What hath beene, cannot be. Who euer stroue
To shew her merit, that did misse her loue?
(The Kings disease) my proiect may deceiue me,
But my intents are fixt, and will not leaue me.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: The Florentines and Senoys are by th' eares,
Haue fought with equall fortune, and continue
A brauing warre.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
prose: So tis reported sir.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Nay tis most credible, we heere receiue it,
A certaintie vouch'd from our Cosin Austria,
With caution, that the Florentine will moue vs
For speedie ayde: wherein our deerest friend
Preiudicates the businesse, and would seeme
To haue vs make deniall.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
verse: His loue and wisedome
Approu'd so to your Maiesty, may pleade
For amplest credence.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: He hath arm'd our answer,
And Florence is deni'de before he comes:
Yet for our Gentlemen that meane to see
The Tuscan seruice, freely haue they leaue
To stand on either part.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
verse: It well may serue
A nursserie to our Gentrie, who are sicke
For breathing, and exploit.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: What's he comes heere.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lor. G.
verse: It is the Count Rosignoll my good Lord,
Yong Bertram.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Youth, thou bear'st thy Fathers face,
Franke Nature rather curious then in hast
Hath well compos'd thee: Thy Fathers morall parts
Maist thou inherit too: Welcome to Paris.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: My thankes and dutie are your Maiesties.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I would I had that corporall soundnesse now,
As when thy father, and my selfe, in friendship
First tride out souldiership: he did looke farre
Into the seruice of the time, and was
Discipled of the brauest. He lasted long,
But on vs both did haggish Age steale on,
And wore vs out of act: It much repaires me
To talke of your good father; in his youth
He had the wit, which I can well obserue
To day in our yong Lords: but they may iest
Till their owne scorne returne to them vnnoted
Ere they can hide their leuitie in honour:
So like a Courtier, contempt nor bitternesse
Were in his pride, or sharpnesse; if they were,
His equall had awak'd them, and his honour
Clocke to it selfe, knew the true minute when
Exception bid him speake: and at this time
His tongue obey d his hand. Who were below him,
He vs'd as creatures of another place,
And bow'd his eminent top to their low rankes,
Making them proud of his humilitie,
In their poore praise he humbled: Such a man
Might be a copie to these yonger times;
Which followed well, would demonstrate them now
But goers backward.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: His good remembrance sir
Lies richer in your thoughts, then on his tombe:
So in approofe liues not his Epitaph,
As in your royall speech.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Would I were with him he would alwaies say,
(Me thinkes I heare him now) his plausiue words
He scatter'd not in eares, but grafted them
To grow there and to beare: Let me not liue,
This his good melancholly oft began
On the Catastrophe and heele of pastime
When it was out: Let me not liue (quoth hee)
After my flame lackes oyle, to be the snuffe
Of yonger spirits, whose apprehensiue senses
All but new things disdaine; whose iudgements are
Meere fathers of their garments: whose constancies
Expire before their fashions: this he wish'd.
I after him, do after him wish too:
Since I nor wax nor honie can bring home,
I quickly were dissolued from my hiue
To giue some Labourers roome.

speeches.speaker: L. 2. E.
verse: You'r loued Sir,
They that least lend it you, shall lacke you first.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I fill a place I know't: how long ist Count
Since the Physitian at your fathers died?
He was much fam'd.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Some six moneths since my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: If he were liuing, I would try him yet.
Lend me an arme: the rest haue worne me out
With seuerall applications: Nature and sicknesse
Debate it at their leisure. Welcome Count,
My sonne's no deerer.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Thanke your Maiesty.

speeches.speaker: Coun.
prose: I will now heare, what say you of this gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Maddam the care I haue had to euen your content, I wish might be found in the Kalender of my past endeuours, for then we wound our Modestie, and make foule the clearnesse of our deseruings, whenof our selues we publish them.

speeches.speaker: Coun.
prose: What doe's this knaue heere? Get you gone sirra: the complaints I haue heard of you I do not all beleeue, 'tis my slownesse that I doe not: For I know you lacke not folly to commit them, & haue abilitie enough to make such knaueries yours.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: 'Tis not vnknown to you Madam, I am a poore fellow.

speeches.speaker: Coun.
prose: Well sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: No maddam,

'Tis not so well that I am poore, though manie

of the rich are damn'd, but if I may haue your Ladiships good will to goe to the world, Isbell the woman and w will doe as we may.

speeches.speaker: Coun.
prose: Wilt thou needes be a begger?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I doe beg your good will in this case.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: In what case?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: In Isbels case and mine owne: seruice is no heritage, and I thinke I shall neuer haue the blessing of God, till I haue issue a my bodie: for they say barnes are blessings.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Tell me thy reason why thou wilt marrie?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: My poore bodie Madam requires it, I am driuen onby the flesh, and hee must needes goe that the diuell driues.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Is this all your worships reason?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Faith Madam I haue other holie reasons, such as they are.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: May the world know them?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I haue beene Madam a wicked creature, as you and all flesh and blood are, and indeede I doe marrie that I may repent.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Thy marriage sooner then thy wickednesse.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I am out a friends Madam, and I hope to haue friends for my wiues sake.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Such friends are thine enemies knaue.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Y' are shallow Madam in great friends, for the knaues come to doe that for me which I am a wearie of: he that eres my Land, spares my teame, and giues mee leaue to Inne the crop: if I be his cuckold hee's my drudge; he that comforts my wife, is the cherisher of my flesh and blood; hee that cherishes my flesh and blood, loues my flesh and blood; he that loues my flesh and blood is my friend: ergo, he that kisses my wife is my friend: if men could be contented to be what they are, there were no feare in marriage, for yong Charbon the Puritan, and old Poysam the Papist, how somere their hearts are seuer'd in Religion, their heads are both one, they may ioule horns together like any Deare i' th Herd.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Wilt thou euer be a foule mouth'd and calumnious knaue?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: A Prophet I Madam, and I speake the truth the next waie, for I the Ballad will repeate, which men full true shall finde, your marriage comes by destinie, your Cuckow sings by kinde.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Get you gone sir, Ile talke with you more anon.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: May it please you Madam, that hee bid Hellen come to you, of her I am to speake.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Sirra tell my gentlewoman I would speake with her, Hellen I meane.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Was this faire face the cause, quoth she,
Why the Grecians sacked Troy,
Fond done, done, fond was this King Priams ioy,
With that she sighed as she stood, bis
prose: And gaue this sentence then, among nine bad if one be good, among nine bad if one be good, there's yet one good in ten.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: What, one good in tenne? you corrupt the song sirra.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: One good woman in ten Madam, which is a purifying ath' song: would God would serue the world so all the yeere, weed finde no fault with the tithe woman if I were the Parson, one in ten quoth a? and wee might haue a good woman borne but ore euerie blazing starre, or at an earthquake, 'twould mend the Lotterie well, a man may draw his heart out ere a plucke one.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Youle begone sir knaue. and doe as I command you?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: That man should be at womans command, and yet no hurt done, though honestie be no Puritan, yet it will doe no hurt, it will weare the Surplis of humilitie ouer the blacke-Gowne of a bigge heart: I am going forsooth, the businesse is for Helen to come hither.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Well now.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: I know Madam you loue your Gentlewoman intirely.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Faith I doe: her Father bequeath'd her to mee, and she her selfe without other aduantage, may lawfullie make title to as much loue as shee findes, there is more owing her then is paid, and more shall be paid her then sheele demand.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Madam, I was verie late more neere her then I thinke shee wisht mee, alone shee was, and did communicate to her selfe her owne words to her owne eares, shee thought, I dare vowe for her, they toucht not anie stranger sence, her matter was, shee loued your Sonne; Fortune shee said was no goddesse, that had put such difference betwixt their two estates: Loue no god, that would not extend his might onelie, where qualities were leuell, Queene of Virgins, that would suffer her poore Knight surpris'd without rescue in the first assault or ransome afterward: This shee deliuer'd in the most bitter touch of sorrow that ere I heard Virgin exclaime in, which I held my dutie speedily to acquaint you withall, sithence in the losse that may happen, it concernes you something to know it.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: You haue discharg'd this honestlie, keepe it to your selfe, manie likelihoods inform'd mee of this before, which hung so tottring in the ballance, that I could neither beleeue nor misdoubt: praie you leaue mee, stall this in your bosome, and I thanke you for your honest care: I will speake with you further anon.

speeches.speaker: Old. Cou.
verse: Euen so it vvas vvith me when I was yong:
If euer vve are natures, these are ours, this thorne
Doth to our Rose of youth righlie belong
Our bloud to vs, this to our blood is borne,
It is the show, and seale of natures truth,
Where loues strong passion is imprest in youth,
By our remembrances of daies forgon,
Such were our faults, or then we thought them none,
Her eie is sicke on't, I obserue her now.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: What is your pleasure Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ol. Cou.
prose: You know Hellen I am a mother to you.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: Mine honorable Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Cou.
verse: Nay a mother, why not a mother? when I sed a mother
Me thought you saw a serpent, what's in mother,
That you start at it? I say I am your mother,
And put you in the Catalogue of those
That were enwombed mine, 'tis often seene
Adoption striues vvith nature, and choise breedes
A natiue slip to vs from forraine seedes:
You nere opprest me with a mothers groane,
Yet I expresse to you a mothers care,
(Gods mercie maiden) dos it curd thy blood
To say I am thy mother? vvhat's the matter,
That this distempered messenger of wet?
The manie colour'd Iris rounds thine eye?
—Why, that you are my daughter?

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: That I am not.

speeches.speaker: Old. Cou.
prose: I say I am your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: Pardon Madam.
The Count Rosillion cannot be my brother:
I am from humble, he from honored name:
No note vpon my Parents, his all noble,
My Master, my deere Lord he is, and I
His seruant liue, and will his vassall die:
He must not be my brother.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Cou.
prose: Nor I your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: You are my mother Madam, would you were
So that my Lord your sonne were not my brother,
Indeede my mother, or were you both our mothers,
I care no more for, then I doe for heauen,
So I were not his sister, cant no other,
But I your daughter, he must be my brother.

speeches.speaker: Old. Cou.
verse: Yes Hellen, you might be my daughter in law,
God shield you meane it not, daughter and mother
So striue vpon your pulse; vvhat pale agen?
My feare hath catcht your fondnesse! now I see
The mistrie of your louelinesse, and finde
Your salt teares head, now to all sence 'tis grosse:
You loue my sonne, inuention is asham'd
Against the proclamation of thy passion
To say thou doost not: therefore tell me true,
But tell me then 'tis so, for looke, thy cheekes
Confesse it 'ton tooth to th' other, and thine eies
See it so grosely showne in thy behauiours,
That in their kinde they speake it, onely sinne
And hellish obstinacie tye thy tongue
That truth should be suspected, speake, ist so?
If it be so, you haue wound a goodly clewe:
If it be not, forsweare't how ere I charge thee,
As heauen shall worke in me for thine auaile
To tell me truelie.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: Good Madam pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Do you loue my Sonne?

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: Your pardon noble Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Loue you my Sonne?

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: Doe not you loue him Madam?

speeches.speaker: Cou.
verse: Goe not about; my loue hath in't a bond
Whereof the world takes note: Come, come, disclose:
The state of your affection, for your passions
Haue to the full appeach'd.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: Then I confesse
Here on my knee, before high heauen and you,
That before you, and next vnto high heauen, I loue your Sonne:
My friends were poore but honest, so's my loue:
Be not offended, for it hurts not him
That he is lou'd of me; I follow him not
By any token of presumptuous suite,
Nor would I haue him, till I doe deserue him,
Yet neuer know how that desert should be:
I know I loue in vaine, striue against hope:
Yet in this captious, and intemible Siue.
I still poure in the waters of my loue
And lacke not to loose still; thus Indian like
Religious in mine error, I adore
The Sunne that lookes vpon his worshipper,
But knowes of him no more. My deerest Madam,
Let not your hate incounter with my loue,
For louing where you doe; but if your selfe,
Whose aged honor cites a vertuous youth,
Did euer, in so true a flame of liking,
Wish chastly, and loue dearely, that your Dian
Was both her selfe and loue, O then giue pittie
To her whose state is such, that cannot choose
But lend and giue where she is sure to loose;
That seekes not to finde that, her search implies,
But riddle like, liues sweetely where she dies.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
verse: Had you not lately an intent, speake truely,
To goe to Paris?

speeches.speaker: Hell
prose: Madam I had.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Wherefore? tell true.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: I will tell truth. by grace it selfe I sweare:
You know my Father left me some prescriptions
Of rare and prou'd effects, such as his reading
And manifest experience, had collected
For generall soueraigntie: and that he wil'd me
In heedefull'st reseruation to bestow them,
As notes, whose faculties inclusiue were,
More then they were in note: Amongst the rest,
There is a remedie, approu'd, set downe,
To cure the desperate languishings whereof
The King is render'd lost.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: This was your motiue for Paris, was it, speake?

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: My Lord, your sonne, made me to think of this;
Else Paris, and the medicine, and the King,
Had from the conuersation of my thoughts,
Happily beene absent then.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
verse: But thinke you Hellen,
If you should tender your supposed aide,
He would receiue it? He and his Phisitions
Are of a minde, he, that they cannot helpe him:
They, that they cannot helpe, how shall they credit
A poore vnlearned Virgin, when the Schooles
Embowel'd of their doctrine, haue left off
The danger to it selfe.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: There's something in't
More then my Fathers skill, which was the great'st
Of his profession, that his good receipt,
Shall for my legacie be sanctified
By th' luckiest stars in heauen, and would your honor
But giue me leaue to trie successe, I'de venture
The well lost life of mine, on his Graces cure,
By such a day, an houre.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
prose: Doo'st thou beleeue't?

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: I Madam knowingly.

speeches.speaker: Cou.
verse: Why Hellen thou shalt haue my leaue and loue,
Meanes and attendants, and my louing greetings
To those of mine in Court, Ile staie at home
And praie Gods blessing into thy attempt:
Begon to morrow, and be sure of this,
What I can helpe thee to, thou shalt not misse.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Farewell yong Lords, these warlike principles
Doe not throw from you, and you my Lords farewell:
Share the aduice betwixt you, if both gaine, all
The guift doth stretch it selfe as 'tis receiu'd,
And is enough for both.

speeches.speaker: Lord. G.
verse: 'Tis our hope sir,
After well entred souldiers, to returne
And finde your grace in health.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: No, no, it cannot be; and yet my heart
Will not confesse he owes the mallady
That doth my life besiege: farwell yong Lords,
Whether I liue or die, be you the sonnes
Of worthy French men: let higher Italy
(Those bated that inherit but the fall
Of the last Monarchy) see that you come
Not to wooe honour, but to wed it, when
The brauest questant shrinkes: finde what you seeke,
That fame may cry you loud: I say farewell.

speeches.speaker: L.G.
prose: Health at your bidding serue your Maiesty.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Those girles of Italy, take heed of them,
They say our French, lacke language to deny
If they demand: beware of being Captiues
Before you serue.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
prose: Our hearts receiue your warnings.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Farewell, come hether to me.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
prose: Oh my sweet Lord yt you wil stay behind vs.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
prose: 'Tis not his fault the spark.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
prose: Oh 'tis braue warres.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
prose: Most admirable, I haue seene those warres.

speeches.speaker: Rossill.
verse: I am commanded here, and kept a coyle with,
Too young, and the next yeere, and 'tis too early.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
verse: And thy minde stand too't boy,
Steale away brauely.

speeches.speaker: Rossill.
verse: I shal stay here the for-horse to a smocke,
Creeking my shooes on the plaine Masonry,
Till honour be bought vp, and no sword worne
But one to dance with: by heauen, Ile steale away.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
prose: There's honour in the theft.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
prose: Commit it Count.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
prose: I am your accessary, and so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: I grow to you, & our parting is a tortur'd body.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
prose: Farewll Captaine.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
prose: Sweet Mounsier Parolles.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
prose: Noble Heroes; my sword and yours are kinne, good sparkes and lustrous, a word good mettals. You shall finde in the Regiment of the Spinij, one Captaine Spurio his sicatrice, with an Embleme of warre heere on his sinister cheeke; it was this very sword entrench'd it: say to him I liue, and obserue his reports for me.

speeches.speaker: Lo. G.
prose: We shall noble Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
prose: Mars doate on you for his nouices, what will ye doe?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose: Stay the King.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
prose: Vse a more spacious ceremonie to the Noble Lords, you haue restrain'd your selfe within the List of too cold an adieu: be more expressiue to them; for they weare themselues in the cap of the time, there do muster true gate; eat, speake, and moue vnder the influence of the most receiu'd starre, and though the deuill leade the measure, such are to be followed: after them, and take a more dilated farewell.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose: And I will doe so.

speeches.speaker: Parr.
prose: Worthy fellowes, and like to prooue most sinewie sword-men.

speeches.speaker: L. Laf.
prose: Pardon my Lord for mee and for my tidings.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Ile see thee to stand vp.

speeches.speaker: L. Laf.
verse: Then heres a man stands that has brought his pardon,
I would you had kneel'd my Lord to aske me mercy,
And that at my bidding you could so stand vp.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I would I had, so I had broke thy pate
And askt thee mercy for't.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: Good faith a-crosse, but my good Lord 'tis thus,
Will you be cur'd of your infirmitie?

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: O will you eat no grapes my royall foxe?
Yes but you will, my noble grapes, and if
My royall foxe could reach them: I haue seen a medicine
That's able to breath life into a stone,
Quicken a rocke, and make you dance Canari
With sprightly fire and motion, whose simple touch
Is powerfull to arayse King Pippen, nay
To giue great Charlemaine a pen in's hand
And write to her a loue-line.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: What her is this?

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: Why doctor she: my Lord, there's one arriu'd,
If you will see her: now by my faith and honour,
If seriously I may conuay my thoughts
In this my light deliuerance, I haue spoke
With one, that in her sexe, her yeeres, profession,
Wisedome and constancy, hath amaz'd mee more
Then I dare blame my weakenesse: will you see her?
For that is her demand, and know her businesse?
That done, laugh well at me.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Now good Lafew,
Bring in the admiration, that we with thee
May spend our wonder too, or take off thine
By wondring how thou tookst it.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: Nay, Ile fit you,
And not be all day neither.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Thus he his speciall nothing euer prologues.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Nay, come your waies.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: This haste hath wings indeed.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: Nay, come your waies,
This is his Maiestie, say your minde to him,
A Traitor you doe looke like, but such traitors
His Maiesty seldome feares, I am Cresseds Vncle,
That dare leaue two together, far you well.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Now faire one, do's your busines follow vs?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I my good Lord,
Gerard de Narbon was my father,
In what he did professe, well found.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: I knew him.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: The rather will I spare my praises towards him,
Knowing him is enough on's bed of death,
Many receits he gaue me, chieflie one,
Which as the dearest issue of his practice
And of his olde experience, th' onlie darling,
He bad me store vp, as a triple eye,
Safer then mine owne two: more deare I haue so,
And hearing your high Maiestie is toucht
With that malignant cause, wherein the honour
Of my deare fathers gift, stands cheefe in power,
I come to tender it, and my appliance,
With all bound humblenesse.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: We thanke you maiden,
But may not be so credulous of cure,
When our most learned Doctors leaue vs, and
The congregated Colledge haue concluded,
That labouring Art can neuer ransome nature
From her inaydible estate: I say we must not
So staine our iudgement, or corrupt our hope,
To prostitute our past-cure malladie
To empericks, or to disseuer so
Our great selfe and our credit, to esteeme
A sencelesse helpe, when helpe past sence we deeme.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: My dutie then shall pay me for my paines:
I will no more enforce mine office on you,
Humbly intreating from your royall thoughts,
A modest one to beare me backe againe.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I cannot giue thee lesse to be cal'd gratefull:
Thou thoughtst to helpe me, and such thankes I giue,
As one neere death to those that wish him liue:
But what at full I know, thou knowst no part,
I knowing all my perill, thou no Art.

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: What I can doe, can doe no hurt to try,
Since you set vp your rest 'gainst remedie:
He that of greatest workes is finisher,
Oft does them by the weakest minister:
So holy Writ, in babes hath iudgement showne,
When Iudges haue bin babes; great flouds haue flowne
From simple sources: and great Seas haue dried
When Miracles haue by the great'st beene denied.
Oft expectation failes, and most oft there
Where most it promises: and oft it hits,
Where hope is coldest, and despaire most shifts.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I must not heare thee, fare thee wel kind maide,
Thy paines not vs'd, must by thy selfe be paid,
Proffers not tooke, reape thanks for their reward.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Inspired Merit so by breath is bard,
It is not so with him that all things knowes
As 'tis with vs, that square our guesse by showes:
But most it is presumption in vs, when
The help of heauen we count the act of men.
Deare sir, to my endeauors giue consent,
Of heauen, not me, make an experiment.
I am not an Impostrue, that proclaime
My selfe against the leuill of mine aime,
But know I thinke, and thinke I know most sure,
My Art is not past power, nor you past cure.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Art thou so confident? Within what space
Hop'st thou my cure?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: The greatest grace lending grace,
Ere twice the horses of the sunne shall bring
Their fiery torcher his diurnall ring,
Ere twice in murke and occidentall dampe
Moist Hesperus, hath quench'd her sleepy Lampe:
Or foure and twenty times the Pylots glasse
Hath told the theeuish minutes, how they passe:
What is infirme, from your sound parts shall flie,
Health shall liue free, and sickenesse freely dye.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Vpon thy certainty and confidence,
What dar'st thou venter?

speeches.speaker: Hell.
verse: Taxe of impudence,
A strumpets boldnesse, a divulged shame
Traduc'd by odious ballads: my maidens name
Seard otherwise, ne worse of worst extended
With vildest torture, let my life be ended.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Methinks in thee some blessed spirit doth speak
His powerfull sound, within an organ weake:
And what impossibility would slay
In common sence, sence saues another way:
Thy life is deere, for all that life can rate
Worth name of life, in thee hath estimate:
Youth, beauty, wisedome, courage, all
That happines and prime, can happy call:
Thou this to hazard, needs must intimate
Skill infinite, or monstrous desperate,
Sweet practiser, thy Physicke I will try,
That ministers thine owne death if I die.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: If I breake time, or flinch in property
Of what I spoke, vnpittied let me die,
And well deseru'd: not helping, death's my see,
But if I helpe, what doe you promise me.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Make thy demand.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: But will you make it euen?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: I by my Scepter, and my hopes of helpe.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Then shalt thou giue me with thy kingly hand
What husband in thy power I will command:
Exempted be from me the arrogance
To choose from forth the royall bloud of France,
My low and humble name to propagate
With any branch or image of thy state:
But such a one thy vassall, whom I know
Is free for me to aske, thee to bestow.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Heere is my hand, the premises obseru'd,
Thy will by my performance shall be seru'd:
So make the choice of thy owne time, for I
Thy resolv'd Patient, on thee still relye:
More should I question thee, and more I must,
