Though more to know, could not be more to trust:
From whence thou can'st, how tended on, but rest
Vnquestion'd welcome, and vndoubted blest.
Giue me some helpe heere hoa, if thou proceed,
As high as word, my deed shall match thy deed.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Come on sir, I shall now put you to the height of your breeding.

speeches.speaker: Clown.
prose: I will shew my selfe highly fed, and lowly taught, I know my businesse is but to the Court.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: To the Court, why what place make you speciall, when you put off that with such contempt, but to the Court?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Truly Madam, if God haue lent a man any manners, hee may easilie put it off at Court: hee that cannot make a legge, put off's cap, kisse his hand, and say nothing, has neither legge, hands, lippe, nor cap; and indeed such a fellow, to say precisely, were not for the Court, But for me, I haue an answere will serue all men.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Marry that's a bountifull answere that fits all questions.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: It is like a Barbers chaire that fits all buttockes, the pin buttocke, the quatch-buttocke, the brawn buttocke, or any buttocke.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Will your answere serue fit to all questions?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: As fit as ten groats is for the hand of an Atturney, as your French Crowne for your taffety punke, as Tibs rush for Toms fore-finger, as a pancake for Shroue-tuesday, a Morris for May-day, as the naile to his hole, the Cuckold to his horne, as a scolding queane to a wrangling knaue, as the Nuns lip to the Friers mouth, nay as the pudding to his skin.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Haue you, I say, an answere of such fitnesse for all questions?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: From below your Duke, to beneath your Constable, it will fit any question.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: It must be an answere of most monstrous size, that must fit all demands.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: But a triflle neither in good faith, if the learned should speake truth of it: heere it is, and all that belongs to't. Aske mee if I am a Courtier, it shall doe you no harme to learne.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: To be young againe if we could: I will bee a foole in question, hoping to bee the wiser by your answer.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I pray you sir, are you a Courtier?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O Lord sir theres a simple putting off: more, more, a hundred of them.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Sir I am a poore freind of yours, that loues you.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O Lord sir, thicke, thicke, spare not me.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I thinke sir, you can eate none of this homely meate.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O Lord sir; nay put me too't, I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: You were lately whipt sir as I thinke.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O Lord sir, spare not me.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Doe you crie O Lord sir at your whipping, and spare not me? Indeed your O Lord sir, is very sequent to your whipping: you would answere very well to a whipping if you were but bound too't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I nere had worse lucke in my life in my O Lord sir: I see things may serue long, but not serue euer.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I play the noble huswife with the time, to entertaine it so merrily with a foole.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O Lord sir, why there't serues well agen.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: And end sir to your businesse: giue Hellen this,
And vrge her to a present answer backe,
Commend me to my kinsmen, and my sonne,
This is not much.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Not much commendation to them.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Not much imployement for you, you vnderstand me.

speeches.speaker: Clo
prose: Most fruitfully, I am there, before my legegs.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Hast you agen.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: They say miracles are past, and we haue our Philosophicall persons, to make moderne and familiar things supernaturall and causelesse. Hence is it, that we make trifles of terrours, ensconcing our selues into seeming knowledge, when we should submit our selues to an vnknowne feare.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Why 'tis the rarest argument of wonder, that hath shot out in our latter times.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: And so 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: To be relinquisht of the Artists.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: So I say both of Galen and Paracelsus.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: Of all the learned and authenticke fellowes.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Right so I say.

speeches.speaker: Ol Laf.
prose: That gaue him out incureable.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Why there 'tis, so say I too.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: Not to be help'd.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Right, as 'twere a man assur'd of a—

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: Vncertaine life, and sure death.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Iust, you say well: so would I haue said.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: I may truly say, it is a noueltie to the world.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: It is indeede if you will haue it in shewing, you shall reade it in what do ye call there.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: A shewing of a heauenly effect in an earthly Actor.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: That's it, I would haue said, the verie same.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
verse: Why your Dolphin is not lustier: fore mee
I speake in respect—

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Nay 'tis strange, 'tis very straunge, that is the breefe and the tedious of it, and he's of a most facinerious spirit, that will not acknowledge it to be the—

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: Very hand of heauen.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I, so I say.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: In a most weake—

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: And debile minister great power, grear trancendence, which should indeede giue vs a further vse to be made, then alone then recou'ry of the king, as to bee

speeches.speaker: Old Laf.
prose: Generally thankfull.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I would haue said it, you say well: heere comes the King.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: Lustique, as the Dutchman saies: Ile like a maide the Better whil'st I haue a tooth in my head: why he's able to leade her a Carranto.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Mor du vinager, is not this Helen?

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: Fore God I thinke so.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Goe call before mee all the Lords in Court,
Sit my preseruer by thy patients side,
And with this healthfull hand whose banisht sence
Thou hast repeal'd, a second time receyue
The confirmation of my promis'd guift,
Which but attends thy naming.
Faire Maide send forth thine eye, this youthfull parcell
Of Noble Batchellors, stand at my bestowing,
Ore whom both Soueraigne power, and fathers voice
I haue to vse; thy franke election make,
Thou hast power to choose, and they none to forsake.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: To each of you, one faire and vertuous Mistris;
Fall when loue please, marry to each but one.

speeches.speaker: Old Laf.
verse: I'de giue bay curtall, and his furniture
My mouth no more were broken then these boyes,
And writ as little beard.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Peruse them well:
Not one of those, but had a Noble father.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Gentlemen, heauen hath through me, restor'd the king to health.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: We vnderstand it, and thanke heauen for you.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I am a simple Maide, and therein wealthiest
That I protest, I simply am a Maide:
Please it your Maiestie, I haue done already:
The blushes in my cheekes thus whisper mee,
We blush that thou shouldst choose, but be refused;
Let the white death sit on thy cheeke for euer,
Wee'l nere come there againe.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Make choise and see,
Who shuns thy loue, shuns all his loue in mee.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Now Dian from thy Altar do I fly,
And to imperiall loue, that God most high
Do my sighes streame: Sir, wil you heare my suite?

speeches.speaker: 1. Lo
prose: And grant it.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Thankes sir, all the rest is mute.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: I had rather be in this choise, then throw Ames-ace for my life.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: The honor sir that flames in your faire eyes,
Before I speake too threatningly replies:
Loue make your fortunes twentie times aboue
Her that so vvishes, and her humble loue.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lo.
prose: No better if you please.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: My wish receiue,
Which great loue grant, and so I take my leaue.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Laf.
prose: Do all they denie her? And they were sons of mine, I'de haue them whip'd, or I would send them to 'th Turke to make Eunuches of.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Be not afraid that I your hand should take,
Ile neuer do you wrong for your owne sake:
Blessing vpon your vowes, and in your bed
Finde fairer fortune, if you euer wed.

speeches.speaker: Old Laf.
prose:
These boyes are boyes of Ice, they'le none

haue heere: sure they are bastards to the English, the French nere got em.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: You are too young, too happie, and too good
To make your selfe a sonne out of my blood.

speeches.speaker: 4. Lord.
prose: Faire one, I thinke not so.

speeches.speaker: Ol. Lord
prose: There's one grape yet, I am sure thy father drunke wine. But if thou best not an asse, I am a youth of fourteene: I haue knowne thee already.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I dare not say I take you, but I giue
Me and my seruice, euer whilst I liue
Into your guiding power: This is the man.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Why then young Bertram take her shee's thy wife.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: My wife my Leige? I shal beseech your highnes
In such a busines, giue me leaue to vse
The helpe of mine owne eies.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Know'st thou not Bertram what shee ha's done for mee?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Yes my good Lord, but neuer hope to know why I should marrie her.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Thou know'st shee ha's rais'd me from my sickly bed.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: But followes it my Lord, to bring me downe
Must answer for your raising? I knowe her well:
Shee had her breeding at my fathers charge:
A poore Physitians daughter my wife? Disdaine
Rather corrupt me euer.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Tis onely title thou disdainst in her, the which
I can build vp: strange is it that our bloods
Of colour, waight, and heat, pour'd all together,
Would quite confound distinction: yet stands off
In differences so mightie. If she bee
All that is vertuous (saue what thou dislik'st)
A poore Phisitians daughter, thou dislik'st
Of vertue for the name: but doe not so:
From lowest place, whence vertuous things proceed,
The place is dignified by th' doers deede.
Where great additions swell's, and vertue none,
It is a dropsied honour. Good a lone,
Is good without a name? Vilenesse is so:
The propertie by what is is, should go,
Not by the title. Shee is young, wise, faire,
In these, to Nature shee's immediate heire:
And these breed honour: that is honours scorne,
Which challenges it selfe as honours borne,
And is not like the fire: Honours thriue,
When rather from our acts we them deriue
Then our fore-goers: the meere words, a slaue
Debosh'd on euerie tombe, on euerie graue:
A lying Trophee, and as oft is dumbe,
Where dust, and damn'd obliuion is the Tombe.
Of honour'd bones-indeed, what should be saide?
If thou canst like this creature, as a maide,
I can create the rest: Vertue, and shee
Is her owne dower: Honour and wealth, from mee.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I cannot loue her, nor will striue to doo't.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Thou wrong'st thy selfe, if thou shold'st striue to choose.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: That you are well restor'd my Lord, I'me glad:
Let the rest go.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: My Honor's at the stake, which to defeate
I must produce my power. Heere, take her hand,
Proud scornfull boy, vnworthie this good gift,
That dost in vile misprision shackle vp
My loue, and her desert: that canst not dreame,
We poizing vs in her defectiue scale,
Shall weigh thee to the beame: That wilt not know,
It is in Vs to plant thine Honour, where
We please to haue it grow. Cheeke thy contempt:
Obey Our will, which trauailes in thy good:
Beleeue not thy disdaine, but presentlie
Do thine owne fortunes that obedient right
Which both thy dutie owes, and Our power claimes,
Or I will throw thee from my care for euer
Into the staggers, and the carelesse lapse
Of youth and ignorance: both my reuenge and hate
Loosing vpon thee, in the name of iustice,
Without all termes of pittie. Speake, thine answer.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Pardon my gracious Lord: for I submit
My fancie to your eies, when I consider
What great creation, and what dole of honour
Flies where you bid it: I finde that she which late
Was in my Nobler thoughts, most base: is now
The praised of the King, who so ennobled,
Is as 'twere borne so.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Take her by the hand,
And tell her she is thine: to whom I promise
A counterpoize: If not to thy estate,
A ballance more repleat.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I take her hand.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Good fortune, and the fauour of the King
Smile vpon this Contract: whose Ceremonie
Shall seeme expedient on the now borne briefe,
And be perform'd to night: the solemne Feast
Shall more attend vpon the coming space,
Expecting absent friends. As thou lou'st her,
Thy loue's to me Religious: else, do's erre.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Do you heare Monsieur? A word with you.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Your pleasure sir.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Your Lord and Master did well to make his recantation.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Recantation? My Lord? my Master?

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I: Is it not a Language I speake?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: A most harsh one, and not to bee vnderstoode without bloudie succeeding My Master.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Are you Companion to the Count Rosillion?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: To any Count, to all Counts: to what is man.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: To what is Counts man: Counts maister is of another stile.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: You are too old sir: Let it satisfie you, you are too old.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I must tell thee sirrah, I write Man: to which title age cannot bring thee.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: What I dare too well do, I dare not do.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I did thinke thee for two ordinaries: to bee a prettie wise fellow, thou didst make tollerable vent of thy trauell, it might passe: yet the scarffes and the bannerets about thee, did manifoldlie disswade me from beleeuing thee a vessell of too great a burthen. I haue now found thee, when I loose thee againe, I care not: yet art thou good for nothing but taking vp, and that th' ourt scarce worth.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Hadst thou not the priuiledge of Antiquity vpon thee.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Do not plundge thy selfe to farre in anger, least thou hasten thy triall: which if, Lord haue mercie on thee for a hen, so my good window of Lettice fare thee well, thy casement I neede not open, for I look through thee. Giue me thy hand.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: My Lord, you giue me most egregious indignity.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I with all my heart, and thou art worthy of it.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I haue not my Lord deseru'd it.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Yes good faith, eu'ry dramme of it, and I will not b^te thee a scruple.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Well, I shall be wiser.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Eu'n as soone as thou can'st, for thou hast to pull at a smacke a' th contrarie. If euer thou bee'st bound in thy skarfe and beaten, thou shall finde what it is to be proud of thy bondage, I haue a desire to holde my acquaintance with thee, or rather my knowledge, that I may say in the default, he is a man I know.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: My Lord you do me most insupportable vexation.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I would it were hell paines for thy sake, and my poore doing eternall: for doing I am past, as I will by thee, in what motion age will giue me leaue.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Well, thou hast a sonne shall take this disgrace off me; scuruy, old, filthy, scuruy Lord: Well, I must be patient, there is no fettering of authority. Ile beate him (by my life) if I can meete him with any conuenience, and he were double and double a Lord. Ile haue no more pittie of his age then I would haue of—Ile beate him, and if I could but meet him agen.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Sirra, your Lord and masters married, there's newes for you: you haue a new Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I most vnfainedly beseech your Lordshippe to make some reseruation of your wrongs. He is my good Lord, whom I serue aboue is my master.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Who? God.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I sir.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: The deuill it is, that's thy master. Why dooest thou garter vp thy armes a this fashion? Dost make hose of thy sleeues? Do other seruants so? Thou wert best set thy lower part where thy nose stands. By mine Honor, If I were but two houres yonger, I'de beate thee: meethink'st thou art a generall offence, and euery man shold beate thee: I thinke thou wast created for men to breath themselues vpon thee.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: This is hard and vndeserued measure my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Go too sir, you were beaten in Italy for picking a kernell out of a Pomgranat, you are a vagabond, and no true traueller: you are more sawcie with Lordes and honourable personages, then the Commission of your birth and vertue giues you Heraldry. You are not worth another word, else I'de call you knaue. I leaue you.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Good, very good, it is so then: good, very good, let it be conceal'd awhile.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Vndone, and forfeited to cares for euer.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: What's the matter sweet-heart?

speeches.speaker: Rossill.
prose: Although before the solemne Priest I haue sworne, I will not bed her.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: What? what sweet heart?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: O my Parrolles, they haue married me:
Ile to the Tuscan warres, and neuer bed her.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: France is a dog-hole, and it no more merits,
The tread of a mans foot: too 'th warres.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: There's letters from my mother: What th' import is, I know not yet.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: I that would be knowne: too 'th warrs my boy, too 'th warres:
He weares his honor in a boxe vnseene,
That hugges his kickie wickie heare at home,
Spending his manlie marrow in her armes
Which should sustaine the bound and high curuet
Of Marses fierie steed: to other Regions,
France is a stable, wee that dwell in't Iades,
Therefore too 'th warre.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: It shall be so, Ile send her to my house,
Acquaint my mother with my hate to her,
And wherefore I am fled: Write to the King
That which I durst not speake. His present gift
Shall furnish me to those Italian fields
Where noble fellowes strike: Warres is no strife
To the darke house, and the detected wife.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Will this Caprichio hold in thee, art sure?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Go with me to my chamber, and aduice me.
Ile send her straight away: To morrow,
Ile to the warres, she to her single sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: Why these bals bound, ther's noise in it. Tis hard
A yong man maried, is a man that's mard:
Therefore away, and leaue her brauely: go,
The King ha's done you wrong: but hush 'tis so.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: My mother greets me kindly, is she well?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: She is not well, but yet she has her health, she's very merrie, but yet she is not well: but thankes be giuen she's very well, and wants nothing i' th world: but yet she is not well.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: If she be verie wel, what do's she ayle, that she's not verie well?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Truly she's very well indeed, but for two things

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: What two things?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: One, that she's not in heauen, whether God send her quickly: the other, that she's in earth, from whence God send her quickly.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Blesse you my fortunate Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I hope sir I haue your good will to haue mine owne good fortune.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: You had my prayers to leade them on, and to keepe them on, haue them still. O my knaue, how do's my old Ladie?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: So that you had her wrinkles, and I her money,
I would she did as you say.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Why I say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Marry you are the wiser man: for many a mans tongue shakes out his masters vndoing: to say nothing, to do nothing, to know nothing, and to haue nothing, is to be a great part of your title, which is within a verie little of nothing.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Away, th' art a knaue.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: You should haue said sir before a knaue, th' art a knaue, that's before me th' art a knaue: this had beene truth sir.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Go too, thou art a wittie foole, I haue found thee.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Did you finde me in your selfe sir, or were you taught to finde me?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: The search sir was profitable, and much Foole may you find in you, euen to the worlds pleasure, and the encrease of laughter.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: A good knaue ifaith, and well fed.
Madam, my Lord will go awaie to night,
A verie serrious businesse call's on him:
The great prerogatiue and rite of loue,
Which as your due time claimes, he do's acknowledge,
But puts it off to a compell'd restraint:
Whose want, and whose delay. is strew'd with sweets
Which they distill now in the curbed time,
To make the comming houre oreflow with ioy,
And pleasure drowne the brim.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: What's his will else?

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: That you will take your instant leaue a' th king,
And make this hast as your owne good proceeding,
Strengthned with what Apologie you thinke
May make it probable neede.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: What more commands hee?

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: That hauing this obtain'd, you presentlie
Attend his further pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: In euery thing I waite vpon his will.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I shall report it so,

speeches.speaker: Hell.
prose: I pray you come sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: But I hope your Lordshippe thinkes not him a souldier.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Yes my Lord and of verie valiant approofe.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: You haue it from his owne deliuerance.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: And by other warranted testimonie.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Then my Diall goes not true, I tooke this Larke for a bunting.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I do assure you my Lord he is very great in knowledge, and accordinglie valiant.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I haue then sinn'd against his experience, and transgrest against his valour, and my state that way is dangerous, since I cannot yet find in my heart to repent: Heere he comes, I pray you make vs freinds, I will pursue the amitie.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: These things shall be done sir.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Pray you sir whose his Tailor?

speeches.speaker: Par
prose: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: O I know him well, I sir, hee sirs a good workeman, a verie good Tailor.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Is shee gone to the king?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Shee is.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Will shee away to night?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: As you'le haue her.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I haue writ my letters, casketted my treasure,
Giuen order for our horses, and to night,
When I should take possession of the Bride,
And ere I doe begin.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: A good Trauailer is something at the latter end of a dinner, but on that lies three thirds, and vses a known truth to passe a thousand nothings with, should bee once hard, and thrice beaten. God saue you Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Is there any vnkindnes betweene my Lord and you Monsieur?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I know not how I haue deserued to run into my Lords displeasure.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: You haue made shift to run into't, bootes and spurres and all: like him that leapt into the Custard, and out of it you'le runne againe, rather then suffer question for your residence.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: It may bee you haue mistaken him my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: And shall doe so euer, though I tooke him at's prayers. Fare you well my Lord, and beleeue this of me, there can be no kernell in this light Nut: the soule of this man is his cloathes: Trust him not in matter of heauie consequence: I haue kept of them tame, & know their natures. Farewell Monsieur, I haue spoken better of you, then you haue or will to deserue at my hand, but we must do good against euill.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: An idle Lord, I sweare.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I thinke so.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Why do you not know him?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Yes, I do know him well, and common speech
Giues him a worthy passe. Heere comes my clog.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I haue sir as I was commanded from you
Spoke with the King, and haue procur'd his leaue
For present parting, onely he desires
Some priuate speech with you.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I shall obey his will.
You must not meruaile Helen at my course,
Which holds not colour with the time, nor does
The ministration, and required office
On my particular. Prepar'd I was not
For such a businesse, therefore am I found
So much vnsetled: This driues me to intreate you,
That presently you take your way for home,
And rather muse then aske why I intreate you,
For my respects are better then they seeme,
And my appointments haue in them a neede
Greater then shewes it selfe at the first view,
To you that know them not. This to my mother,
'Twill be two daies ere I shall see you, so
I leaue you to your wisedome.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Sir, I can nothing say,
But that I am your most obedient seruant.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Come, come, no more of that.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: And euer shall
With true obseruance seeke to eeke out that
Wherein toward me my homely starres haue faild
To equall my great fortune.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Let that goe: my hast is verie great. Farwell:
Hie home.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Pray sir your pardon.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Well, what would you say?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I am not worthie of the wealth I owe,
Nor dare I say 'tis mine: and yet it is,
But like a timorous theefe, most faine would steale
What law does vouch mine owne.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: What would you haue?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Something, and scarse so much: nothing indeed,
I would not tell you what I would my Lord: Faith yes,
Strangers and foes do sunder, and not kisse.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I pray you stay not, but in hast to horse.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I shall not breake your bidding, good my Lord:
Where are my other men? Monsieur, farwell.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Go thou toward home, where I wil neuer come,
Whilst I can shake my sword, or heare the drumme:
Away, and for our flight.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Brauely, Coragio.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: So that from point to point, now haue you heard
The fundamentall reasons of this warre,
Whose great decision hath much blood let forth
And more thirsts after.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord.
verse: Holy seemes the quarrell
Vpon your Graces part: blacke and fearefull
On the opposer.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Therefore we meruaile much our Cosin France
Would in so iust a businesse, shut his bosome
Against our borrowing prayers.

speeches.speaker: French E.
verse: Good my Lord,
The reasons of our stare I cannot yeelde,
But like a common and an outward man,
That the great figure of a Counsaile frames,
By selfe vnable motion, therefore dare not
Say what I thinke of it, since I haue found
My selfe in my incertaine grounds to faile
As often as I guest.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Be it his pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Fren. G.
verse: But I am sure the yonger of our nature,
That surfet on their ease, will day by day
Come heere for Physicke.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Welcome shall they bee:
And all the honors that can flye from vs,
Shall on them settle: you know your places well,
When better fall, for your auailes they fell,
To morrow to 'th the field.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: It hath happen'd all, as I would haue had it, saue that he comes not along with her.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: By my troth I take my young Lord to be a verie melancholly man.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: By what obseruance I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why he will looke vppon his boote, and sing: mend the Ruffe and sing, aske questions and sing, picke his teeth, and sing: I know a man that had this tricke of melancholy hold a goodly Mannor for a song.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
prose: Let me see what he writes, and when he meanes to come.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I haue no minde to Isbell since I was at Court. Our old Lings, and our Isbels a' th Country, are nothing like your old Ling and your Isbels a' th Court: the brains of my Cupid's knock'd out, and I beginne to loue, as an old man loues money, with no stomacke.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
prose: What haue we heere?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: In that you haue there.
This is not well rash and vnbridled boy,
To flye the fauours of so good a King,
To plucke his indignation on thy head,
By the misprising of a Maide too vertuous
For the contempt of Empire.
prose:
I haue sent you a daughter-in-Law, shee hath recouered the King, and vndone me: I haue wedded her, not bedded her, and sworne to make the not eternall. You shall heare I am runne away, know it before the report come. If there bee bredth enough in the world, I will hold a long distance. My duty to you.



Your vnfortunate sonne, Bertram.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: O Madam, yonder is heauie newes within betweene two souldiers, and my yong Ladie.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: What is the matter.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Nay there is some comfort in the newes, some comfort, your sonne will not be kild so soone as I thoght he would.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Why should he be kill'd?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: So say I Madame, if he runne away, as I heare he does, the danger is in standing too't, that's the losse of men, though it be the getting of children. Heere they come will tell you more. For my part I onely heare your sonne was run away.

speeches.speaker: French E.
prose: Saue you good Madam.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Madam, my Lord is gone, for euer gone.

speeches.speaker: French G.
prose: Do not say so.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Thinke vpon patience, pray you Gentlemen,
I haue felt so many quirkes of ioy and greefe,
That the first face of neither on the start
Can woman me vntoo't. Where is my sonne I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Fren. G.
verse: Madam he's gone to serue the Duke of Florence,
We met him thitherward, for thence we came:
And after some dispatch in hand at Court,
Thither we bend againe.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Looke on his Letter Madam, here's my Pasport.
This is a dreadfull sentence.
prose: When thou canst get the Ring vpon my finger, which neuer shall come off, and shew mee a childe begotten of thy bodie, that I am father too, then call me husband: but in such a (then) I write a Neuer.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Brought you this Letter Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: 1. G.
prose: I Madam, and for the Contents sake are sorrie for our paines.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
verse: I prethee Ladie haue a better cheere,
If thou engrossest, all the greefes are thine,
Thou robst me of a moity: He was my sonne,
But I do wash his name out of my blood,
And thou art all my childe. Towards Florence is he?

speeches.speaker: Fren. G.
prose: I Madam.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: And to be a souldier.

speeches.speaker: Fren. G.
verse: Such is his noble purpose, and beleeu't
The Duke will lay vpon him all the honor
That good conuenience claimes.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Returne you thither.

speeches.speaker: Fren. E.
prose: I Madam, with the swiftest wing of speed.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Till I haue no wife, I haue nothing in France,
'Tis bitter.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Finde you that there?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I Madame.

speeches.speaker: Fren. E.
prose: 'Tis but the boldnesse of his hand haply, which his heart was not consenting too.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: Nothing in France, vntill he haue no wife:
There's nothing heere that is too good for him
But onely she, and she deserues a Lord
That twenty such rude boyes might tend vpon,
And call her hourely Mistris. Who was with him?

speeches.speaker: Fren. E.
prose: A seruant onely, and a Gentleman: whlch I haue sometime knowne.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Parolles was it not?

speeches.speaker: Fren. E.
prose: I my good Ladie, hee.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: A verie tainted fellow, and full of wickednesse,
My sonne corrupts a well deriued nature
With his inducement.

speeches.speaker: Fren. E.
prose: Indeed good Ladie the fellow has a deale of that, too much, which holds him much to haue.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose:
Y' are welcome Gentlemen, I will intreate you when you see my sonne, to tell him that his sword can neuer winne the honor that he looses: more Ile intreate

you written to beare along.

speeches.speaker: Fren. G.
prose: We serue you Madam in that and all your worthiest affaires.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Not so, but as we change our courtesies,
Will you draw neere?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Till I haue no wife I haue nothing in France.
Nothing in France vntill he has no wife:
Thou shalt haue none Rossillion, none in France,
Then hast thou all againe: poore Lord, is't I
That chase thee from thy Countrie, and expose
Those tender limbes of thine, to the euent
Of the none-sparing warre? And is it I,
That driue thee from the sportiue Court, where thou
Was't shot at with faire eyes, to be the marke
Of smoakie Musk^ts? O you leaden messengers,
That ride vpon the violent speede of fire,
Fly with false ayme, moue the still-peering aire
That sings with piercing, do not touch my Lord:
Who euer shoots at him, I set him there.
Who euer charges on his forward brest
I am the Caitiffe that do hold him too't,
And though I kill him not, I am the cause
His death was so effected: Better 'twere
I met the rauine Lyon when he roar'd
With sharpe constraint of hunger: better 'twere,
That all the miseries which nature owes
Were mine at once. No come thou home Rossillion,
Whence honor but of danger winnes a scarre,
As oft it looses all. I will be gone:
My being heere it is, that holds thee hence,
Shall I stay heere to doo't? No, no, although
The ayre of Paradise did fan the house,
And Angles offic'd all: I will be gone,
That pittifull rumour may report my flight
To consolate thine eare. Come night, end day,
For with the darke (poore theefe) Ile steale away.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: The Generall of our horse thou art, and we
Great in our hope, lay our best loue and credence
Vpon thy promising fortune.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Sir it is
A charge too heauy for my strength, but yet
Wee'l striue to beare it for your worthy sake,
To th' extreme edge of hazard.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Then go thou for^h,
And fortune play vpon thy prosperous helme
As thy auspicious mistris.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: This very day
Great Mars I put my selfe into thy file,
Make me but like my thoughts, and I shall proue
A louer of thy drumme, hater of loue.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Alas! and would you take the letter of her:
Might you not know she would do, as she has done,
By sending me a Letter. Reade it agen.
Ah what sharpe stings are in her mildest words?
Rynaldo, you did neuer lacke aduice so much,
As letting her passe so: had I spoke with her,
I could haue well diuerted her intents,
Which thus she hath preuented.
prose:
Letter.
I am S. Iaques Pilgrim, thither gone:
Ambitious loue hath so in me offended,
That bare-foot plod I the cold ground vpon
With sainted vow my faults to haue amended.
Write, write, that from the bloodie course of warre,
My deerest Master your deare sonne, may hie,
Blesse him at home in peace. Whilst I from farre,
His name with zealous feruour sanctifie:
His taken labours bid him me forgiue:
I his despightfull Iuno sent him forth,
From Courtly friends, with Camping foes to liue,
Where death and danger dogges the heeles of worth.
He is too good and faire for death, and mee,
Whom I my selfe embrace, to set him free.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: Pardon me Madam,
If I had giuen you this at ouer-night,
She might haue beene ore-tane: and yet she writes
Pursuite would be but vaine.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: What Angell shall
Blesse this vnworthy husband, he cannot thriue,
Vnlesse her prayers, whom heauen delights to beare
And loues to grant, repreeue him from the wrath
Of greatest Iustice. Write, write Rynaldo,
To this vnworthy husband of his wife,
Let euerie word waigh heauie of her worth,
That he does waigh too light: my greatest greefe,
Though little he do feele it, set downe sharpely.
Dispatch the most conuenient messenger,
When haply he shall heare that she is gone,
He will returne, and hope I may that shee
Hearing so much, will speede her foote againe,
Led hither by pure loue: which of them both
Is deerest to me, I haue no skill in sence
To make distinction: prouide this Messenger:
My heart is heauie, and mine age is weake,
Greefe would haue teares, and sorrow bids me speake.

speeches.speaker: Widdow.
verse: Nay come,
For if they do approach the Citty,
We shall loose all the sight.

speeches.speaker: Diana.
verse: They say, the French Count has done
Most honourable seruice.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: It is reported,
That he has taken their great'st Commander,
And that with his owne hand he slew
The Dukes brother: we haue lost our labour,
They are gone a contrarie way^ harke,
you may know by their Trumpets.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Come lets returne againe,
And suffice our selues with the report of it.
Well Diana, take heed of this French Earle,
The honor of a Maide is her name,
And no Legacie is so rich
As honestie.

speeches.speaker: Widdow.
verse: I haue told my neighbour
How you haue beene solicited by a Gentleman
His Companion.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
prose: I know that knaue, hang him, one Parolles, a filthy Officer he is in those suggestions for the young Earle, beware of them Diana; their promises, entisements, oathes, tokens, and all these engines of lust, are not the things they go vnder: many a maide hath beene seduced by them, and the miserie is example, that so terrible shewes in the wracke of maiden-hood, cannot for all that disswade succession, but that they are limed with the twigges that threatens them. I hope I neede not to aduise you further, but I hope your owne grace will keepe you where you are, though there were no further danger knowne, but the modestie which is so lost.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: You shall not neede to feare me.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I hope so: looke here comes a pilgrim, I know she will lye at my house, thither they send one another, Ile question her. God saue you pilgrim, whether are bound?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: To S. Iaques la grand.
Where do the Palmers lodge, I do beseech you?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: At the S. Francis heere beside the Port.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Is this the way?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: I marrie ist. Harke you, they come this way:
If you will tarrie holy Pilgrime
But till the troopes come by,
I will conduct you where you shall be lodg'd,
The rather for I thinke I know your hostesse
As ample as my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Is it your selfe?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: If you shall please so Pilgrime.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I thanke you, and will stay vpon your leisure.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: you came I thinke from France?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I did so.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: Heere you shall see a Countriman of yours
That has done worthy seruice.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: His name I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: The Count Rossillion: know you such a one?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: But by the eare that heares most nobly of him:
His face I know not.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: What somere he is
He's brauely taken heere. He stole from France
As 'tis reported: for the King had married him
Against his liking. Thinke you it is so?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I surely meere the truth, I know his Lady.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: There is a Gentleman that serues the Count,
Reports but coursely of her.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: What's his name?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: Monsieur Parrolles.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Oh I beleeue with him,
In argument of praise, or to the worth
Of the great Count himselfe, she is too meane
To haue her name repeated, all her deseruing
Is a reserued honestie, and that
I haue not heard examin'd.

speeches.speaker: Dian.
verse: Alas poore Ladie,
'Tis a hard bondage to become the wife
Of a detesting Lord.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: I write good creature, wheresoere she is,
Her hart waighes sadly: this yong maid might do her
A shrewd turne if she pleas'd.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: How do you meane?
May be the amorous Count solicites her
In the vnlawfull purpose.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: He does indeede,
And brokes with all that can in such a suite
Corrupt the tender honour of a Maide:
But she is arm'd for him, and keepes her guard
In honestest defence.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: The goddes forbid else.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: So, now they come:
That is Anthonio the Dukes eldest sonne,
That Escalus.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Which is the Frenchman?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: Hee,
That with the plume, 'tis a most gallant fellow,
I would he lou'd his wife: if he were honester
He were much goodlier. Is't not a handsom Gentleman

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I like him well.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: 'Tis pitty he is not honest: yonds that same knaue
That leades him to these places: were I his Ladie,
I would poison that vile Rascall.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Which is he?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: That Iacke an-apes with scarfes. Why is hee melancholly?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Perchance he^s hurt i' th battaile.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Loose our drum? Well.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: He's shrewdly vext at something. Looke he has spyed vs.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Marrie hang you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And your curtesie, for a ring-carrier.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: The troope is past: Come pilgrim, I wil bring you, Where you shall host: Of inioyn'd penitents
There's foure or fiue, to great S. Iaques bound,
Alreadie at my house.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I humbly thanke you:
Please it this Matron, and this gentle Maide
To eate with vs to night, the charge and thanking
Shall be for me. and to requite you further,
I will bestow some precepts of this Virgin,
Worthy the note.

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: Wee'l take your offer kindly.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Nay good my Lord put him too't: let him haue his way.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: If your Lordshippe finde him not a Hilding, hold me no more in your respect.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: On my life my Lord. a bubble.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Do you thinke I am so farre
Deceiued in him.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Beleeue it my Lord, in mine owne direct knowledge, without any malice, but to speake of him as my kinsman, hee's a most notable Coward, an infinite and endlesse Lyar, an hourely promise-breaker, the owner of no one good qualitie, worthy your Lordships entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: It were fit you knew him, least. reposing too farre in his vertue which he hath not, he might at some great and trustie businesse, in a maine daunger, fayle you.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I would I knew in what particular action to try him.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: None better then to let him fetch off his drumme, which you heare him so confidently vndertake to do.

speeches.speaker: C.E.
prose:
I with a troop of Florentines wil sodainly surprize

him; such I will haue whom I am sure he knowes not from the enemie: wee will binde and hoodwinke him so, that he shall suppose no other but that he is carried into the Leager of the aduersaries, when we bring him to our owne tents: be but your Lordship present at his examination, if he do not for the promise of his life, and in the highest compulsion of base feare, offer to betray you, and deliuer all the intelligence in his power against you, and that with the diuine forfeite of his soule vpon oath, neuer trust my iudgement in anie thing.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: O for the loue of laughter, let him fetch his drumme, he sayes he has a stratagem for't: when your Lordship sees the bottome of this successe in't, and to what mettle this counterfeyt lump of ours will be melted if you giue him not Iohn drummes entertainement, your inclining cannot be remoued. Heere he comes.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: O for the loue of laughter hinder not the honor of his designe, let him fetch off his drumme in any hand.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: How now Monsieur? This drumme sticks sorely in your disposition.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: A pox on't, let it go, 'tis but a drumme.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: But a drumme: Ist but a drumme? A drum so lost. There was excellent command, to charge in with our horse vpon our owne wings, and to rend our owne souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: That was not to be blam'd in the command of the seruice: it was a disaster of warre that Caesar him selfe could not haue preuented, if he had beene there to command.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Well, wee cannot greatly condemne our successe: some dishonor wee had in the losse of that drum, but it is not to be recouered.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: It might haue beene recouered.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: It might, but it is not now.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: It is to be recouered, but that the merit of seruice is sildome attributed to the true and exact performer, I would haue that drumme or another, or hic iacet.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Why if you haue a stomacke, too't Monsieur: if you thinke your mysterie in stratagem, can bring this instrument of honour againe into his natiue quarter, be magnanimious in the enterprize and go on, I wil grace the attempt for a worthy exploit: if you speede well in it, the Duke shall both speake of it, and extend to you what further becomes his greatnesse, euen to the vtmost syllable of your worthinesse.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: By the hand of a souldier I will vndertake it.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: But you must not now slumber in it.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Ile about it this euening, and I will presently pen downe my dilemma's, encourage my selfe in my certaintie, put my selfe into my mortall preparation: and by midnight looke to heare further from me.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: May I bee bold to acquaint his grace you are gone about it.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I know not what the successe wil be my Lord, but the attempt I vow.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I know th' art valiant,
And to the possibility of thy souldiership,
Will subscribe for thee: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I loue not many words.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: No more then a fish loues water. Is not this a strange fellow my Lord, that so confidently seemes to vndertake this businesse, which he knowes is not to be done, damnes himselfe to do, & dares better be damnd then to doo't.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: You do not know him my Lord as we doe, certaine it is that he will steale himselfe into a mans fauour, and for a weeke escape a great deale of discoueries, but when you finde him out, you haue him euer after.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Why do you thinke he will make no deede at all of this that so seriouslie hee dooes addresse himselfe vnto?

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: None in the world, but returne with an inuention, and clap vpon you two or three probable lies: but we haue almost imbost him, you shall see his fall to night; for indeede he is not for your Lordshippes respect.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Weele make you some sport with the Foxe ere we case him. He was first smoak'd by the old Lord Lafew, when his disguise and he is parted, tell me what a sprat you shall finde him, which you shall see this verie night.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
verse: I must go looke my twigges,
He shall be caught.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Your brother he shall go along with me.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: As't please your Lordship, Ile leaue you.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Now wil I lead you to the house, and shew you
The Lasse I spoke of.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: But you say she's honest.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: That's all the fault: I spoke with hir but once,
And found her wondrous cold, but I sent to her
By this same Coxcombe that we haue i' th winde
Tokens and Letters, which she did resend,
And this is all I haue done: She's a faire creature,
Will you go see her?

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: With all my heart my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: If you misdoubt me that I am not shee,
I know not how I shall assure you further,
But I shall loose the grounds I worke vpon.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: Though my estate be falne, I was well borne,
Nothing acquainted with these businesses,
And would not put my reputation now
In any staining act.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Nor would I wish you.
First giue me trust, the Count he is my husband,
And what to your sworne counsaile I haue spoken,
Is so from word to word: and then you cannot
By the good ayde that I of you shall borrow,
Erre in bestowing it.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: I should beleeue you,
For you haue shew'd me that which well approues
Y' are great in fortune.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Take this purse of Gold,
And let me buy your friendly helpe thus farre,
Which I will ouer-pay, and pay againe
When I haue found it. The Count he woes your daughter,
Layes downe his wanton siedge before her beautie,
Resolue to carrie her: let her in fine consent
As wee'l direct her how 'tis best to beare it:
Now his important blood will naught denie,
That shee'l demand: a ring the Countie weares,
That downward hath succeeded in his house
From sonne to sonne, some foure or fiue discents,
Since the first father wore it. This Ring he holds
In most rich choice: yet in his idle fire,
To buy his will, it would not seeme too deere,
How ere repented after.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Now I see the bottome of your purpose.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: You see it lawfull then, it is no more,
But that your daughter ere she seemes as wonne,
Desires this Ring; appoints him an encounter;
In fine, deliuers me to fill the time,
Her selfe most chastly absent: after
To marry her, Ile adde three thousand Crownes
To what is past already.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: I haue yeelded:
Instruct my daughter how she shall perseuer,
That time and place with this deceite so lawfull
May proue coherent. Euery night he comes
With Musickes of all sorts, and songs compos'd
To her vnworthinesse: It nothing steeds vs
To chide him from our eeues, for he persists
As if his life lay on't.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Why then to night
Let vs assay our plot, which if it speed,
Is wicked meaning in a lawfull deede;
And lawfull meaning in a lawfull act,
Where both not sinne, and yet a sinfull fact.
But let's about it.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord. E.
prose: He can come no other way but by this hedge corner: when you sallie vpon him, speake what terrible Language you will: though you vnderstand it not your selues, no matter: for we must not seeme to vnderstand him, vnlesse some one among vs, whom wee must produce for an Interpreter.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sol.
prose: Good Captaine, let me be th' Interpreter.

speeches.speaker: Lor. E.
prose: Art not acquainted with him? knowes he not thy voice?

speeches.speaker: 1. Sol.
prose: No sir I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: But what linsie wolsy hast thou to speake to vs againe.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sol.
prose: E'n such as you speake to me.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: He must thinke vs some band of strangers, i' th aduersaries entertainment. Now he hath a smacke of all neighbouring Languages: therefore we must euery one be a man of his owne fancie, not to know what we speak one to another: so we seeme to know, is to know straight our purpose: Choughs language, gabble enough, and good enough. As for you interpreter, you must seeme very politicke. But couch hoa, heere hee comes, to beguile two houres in a sleepe, and then to returne & swear the lies he forges.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Ten a clocke: Within these three houres 'twill be time enough to goe home. What shall I say I haue done? It must bee a very plausiue inuention that carries it. They beginne to smoake mee, and disgraces haue of late, knock'd too often at my doore: I finde my tongue is too foole-hardie, but my heart hath the feare of Ma^s before it, and of his creatures, not daring the reports of my tongue.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: This is the first truth that ere thine own tongue was guiltie of.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: What the diuell should moue mee to vndertake the recouerie of this drumme, being not ignorant of the impossibility, and knowing I had no such purpose? I must giue my selfe some hurts, and say I got them in exploit: yet slight ones will not carrie it. They will say, came you off with so little? And great ones I dare not giue, wherefore what's the instance. Tongue, I must put you into a Butter-womans mouth, and buy my selfe another of Baiazeths Mule, if you prattle mee into these perilles.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: Is it possible he should know what hee is, and be that he is.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I would the cutting of my garments wold serue the turne, or the breaking of my Spanish sword.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: We cannot affoord you so.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Or the baring of my beard, and to say it was in stratagem.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: 'Twould not do.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Or to drowne my cloathes, and say I was stript.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: Hardly serue.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Though I swore I leapt from the window of the Citadell.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: How deepe?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Thirty fadome.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: Three great oathes would scarse make that be beleeued.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I would I had any drumme of the enemies, I would sweare I recouer'd it.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: You shall heare one anon.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: A drumme now of the enemies.

speeches.speaker: Lo E.
prose: Throca movousus, cargo, cargo, cargo.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Cargo, cargo, cargo, villianda par corbo, cargo.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: O ransome, ransome,
Do not hide mine eyes.

speeches.speaker: Inter.
prose: Boskos thromuldo boskos.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: I know you are the Mu^kos Regiment,
And I shall loose my life for want of language.
If there be heere German or Dane, Low Dutch,
Italian, or French, let him speake to me,
Ile discouer that, which shal vndo the Florentine.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Boskos vauvado, I vnderstand thee, & can speake thy tongue: Kerelybonto sir, betake thee to thy faith, for seuenteene ponyards are at thy bosome.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Oh.

speeches.speaker: Inter.
verse: Oh pray, pray, pray,
Manka re^ania dulche.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: Oscorbidulchos voliuorc^.

speeches.speaker: Int.
verse: The Generall is content to spare thee yet,
And hoodwinkt as thou art, will leade thee on
To gather from thee. Haply thou mayst informe
Something to saue thy life.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: O let me liue,
And all the secrets of our campe Ile shew,
Their force, their purposes: Nay, Ile speake that,
Which you will wonder at.

speeches.speaker: Inter.
prose: But wilt thou faithfully?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: If I do not, damne me.

speeches.speaker: Inter.
verse: Acordo linta.
Come on, thou are granted space.

speeches.speaker: L.E.
verse: Go tell the Count Rossillion and my brother,
We haue caught the woodcocke, and will keepe him mufled
Till we do heare from them.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
prose: Captaine I will.

speeches.speaker: L.E.
verse: A will betray vs all vnto our selues,
Informe on that.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
prose: So I will sir.

speeches.speaker: L.E.
prose: Till then Ile keepe him darke and safely lockt.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: They told me that your name was Fontybell.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: No my good Lord, Diana.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Titled Goddesse,
And worth it with addition: but faire soule,
In your fine frame hath loue no qualitie?
If the quicke fire of youth light not your minde,
You are no Maiden but a monument
When you are dead you should be such a one
As you are now: for you are cold and sterne,
And now you should be as your mother was

When your sweet self^
. was got.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: She then was honest.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: So should you be.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: No:
My mother did but dutie, such (my Lord)
As you owe to your wife.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: No more a' that:
I prethee do not striue against my vowes:
I was compell'd to her, but I loue thee
By loues owne sweet constraint, and will for euer
Do thee all rights of seruice.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: I so you serue vs
Till we serue you: But when you haue our Roses,
You barely leaue our thornes to pricke our selues,
And mocke vs with our barenesse.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: How haue I sworne.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: Tis not the many oathes that makes the truth,
But the plaine single vow, that is vow'd true:
What is not holie, that we sweare not by,
But take the high'st to witnesse: then pray you tell me.
If I should sweare by Ioues great attributes,
I lou'd you deerely, would you beleeue my oathes,
When I did loue you ill? This ha's no holding
To sweare by him whom I protest to loue
That I will worke against him. Therefore your oathes
Are words and poore conditions, but vnseal'd
At lest in my opinion.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Change it, change it:
Be not so holy cruell: Loue is holie,
And my integritie ne're knew the crafts
That you do charge men with: Stand no more off,
But giue thy selfe vnto my sicke desires,
Who then recouers. Say thou art mine, and euer
My loue as it beginnes, shall so perseuer.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: I see that men make rope's in such a scarre,
That wee'l forsake our selues. Giue me that Ring.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Ile lend it thee my deere; but haue no power
To giue it from me.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: Will you not my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: It is an honour longing to our house,
Bequeathed downe from manie Ancestors,
Which were the greatest obloquie i' th world,
In me to loose.

speeches.speaker: Dian.
verse: Mine Honors such a Ring,
My chastities the Iewell of our house,
Bequeathed downe from many Ancestors,
Which were the greatest obloquie i' th world,
In mee to loose. Thus your owne proper wisedome
Brings in the Champion honor on my part,
Against your vaine assault.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Heere, take my Ring,
My house, mine honor, yea my life be thine,
And Ile be bid by thee.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: When midnight comes, knocke at my chamber window:
Ile order take, my mother shall not heare.
Now will I charge you in the band of truth,
When you haue conquer'd my yet maiden-bed,
Remaine there but an houre, nor speake to mee:
My reasons are most strong, and you shall know them,
When backe againe this Ring shall be deliuer'd:
And on your finger in the night, Ile put
Another Ring, that what in time proceeds,
May token to the future, our past deeds.
Adieu till then, then faile not: you haue wonne
A wife of me, though there my hope be done.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: A heauen on earth I haue won by wooing thee.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: For which, liue long to thank both heauen & me,
You may so in the end.
My mother told me iust how he would woo,
As if she sate in's heart. She sayes, all men
Haue the like oathes: He had sworne to marrie me
When his wife's dead: therfore Ile lye with him
When I am buried. Since Frenchmen are so braide,
Marry that will, I liue and die a Maid:
Onely in this disguise, I think't no sinne,
To cosen him that would vniustly winne.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: You haue not giuen him his mothers letter.

speeches.speaker: Cap E.
prose: I haue deliu'red it an houre since, there is som thing in't that stings his nature: for on the reading it, he chang'd almost into another man.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: He has much worthy blame laid vpon him, for shaking off so good a wife, and so sweet a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Especially, hee hath incurred the euerlasting displeasure of the King, who had euen tun'd his bounty to sing happinesse to him. I will tell you a thing, but you shall let it dwell darkly with you.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: When you haue spoken it 'tis dead, and I am the graue of it.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Hee hath peruerted a young Gentlewoman heere in Florence, of a most chaste renown, & this night he fleshes his will in the spoyle of her honour: hee hath giuen her his monumentall Ring, and thinkes himselfe made in the vnchaste composition.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Now God delay our rebellion as we are our selues, what things are we.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Meerely our owne traitours. And as in the common course of all treasons, we still see them reueale themselues, till they attaine to their abhorr'd ends: so he that in this action contriues against his owne Nobility in his proper streame, ore-flowes himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Is it not meant damnable in vs, to be Trumpeters of our vnlawfull intents? We shall not then haue his company to night?

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Not till after midnight: for hee is dieted to his houre.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose:
That approaches apace: I would gladly haue him see his company anathomiz'd, that hee might take

a measure of his owne iudgements, wherein so curiously he had set this counterfeit.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: We will not meddle with him till he come; for his presence must be the whip of the other.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: In the meane time, what heare you of these Warres?

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: I heare there is an ouerture of peace.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Nay, I assure you a peace concluded.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: What will Count Rossillion do then? Will he trauaile higher, or returne againe into France?

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: I perceiue by this demand, you are not altogether of his councell.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Let it be forbid sir, so should I bee a great deale of his act.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Sir, his wife some two months since fledde from his house, her pretence is a pilgrimage to Saint Iaques le grand; which holy vndertaking, with most austere sanctimonie she accomplisht: and there residing, the tendernesse of her Nature, became as a prey to her greefe: in fine, made a groane of her last breath, & now she sings in heauen.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: How is this iustified?

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: The stronger part of it by her owne Letters, which makes her storie true, euen to the poynt of her death: her death it selfe, which could not be her office to say, is come: was faithfully confirm'd by the Rector of the place.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Hath the Count all this intelligence?

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: I, and the particular confirmations, point from point, to the full arming of the veritie.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: I am heartily sorrie that hee'l bee gladde of this.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: How mightily sometimes, we make vs comforts of our losses.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: And how mightily some other times, wee drowne our gaine in teares, the great dignitie that his valour hath here acquir'd for him, shall at home be encountred with a shame as ample.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: The webbe of our life, is of a mingled yarne, good and ill together: our vertues would bee proud, if our faults whipt them not, and our crimes would dispaire if they were not cherish'd by our vertues.
How now? Where's your master?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: He met the Duke in the street sir, of whom hee hath taken a solemne leaue: his Lordshippe will next morning for France. The Duke hath offered him Letters of commendations to the King.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: They shall bee no more then needfull there, if they were more then they can commend.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: They cannot be too sweete for the Kings tartnesse, heere's his Lordship now. How now my Lord, i'st not after midnight?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I haue to night dispatch'd sixteene businesses, a moneths length a peece, by an abstract of successe: I haue congied with the Duke, done my adieu with his neerest; buried a wife, mourn'd for her. writ to my Ladie mother, I am returning, entertain'd my Conuoy, & betweene these maine parcels of dispatch, affected many nicer needs: the last was the greatest, but that I haue not ended yet.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: If the businesse bee of any difficulty, and this morning your departure hence, it requires hast of your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I meane the businesse is not ended, as fearing to heare of it hereafter: but shall we haue this dialogue betweene the Foole and the Soldiour. Come, bring forth this counterfet module, ha^s deceiu'd mee, like a double-meaning Prophesier.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Bring him forth, ha's sate i' th stockes all night poore gallant knaue.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: No matter, his heeles haue deseru'd it, in vsurping his spurres so long. How does he carry himselfe?

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: I haue told your Lordship alreadie: The stockes carrie him. But to answer you as you would be vnderstood, hee weepes like a wench that had shed her milke, he hath confest himselfe to Morgan, whom hee supposes to be a Friar, fro~ the time of his remembrance to this very instant disaster of his setting i' th stockes: and what thinke you he hath confest?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Nothing of me, ha's a?

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: His confession is taken, and it shall bee read to his face, if your Lordshippe be in't, as I beleeue you are, you must haue the patience to heare it.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: A plague vpon him, muffeld; he can say nothing of me: hush, hush.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Hoodman comes: Portotartarossa.

speeches.speaker: Inter.
prose: He calles for the tortures, what will you say without em.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: I will confesse what I know without constraint,
If ye pinch me like a Pasty, I can say no more.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Bosko Chimurcho.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Boblibindo chicurmurco.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: You are a mercifull Generall: Our Generall bids you answer to what I shall aske you out of a Note.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: And truly, as I hope to liue.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: First demand of him, how many horse the Duke is strong. What say you to that?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Fiue or sixe thousand, but very weake and vnseruiceable: the troopes are all scattered, and the Commanders verie poore rogues, vpon my reputation and credit, and as I hope to liue.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Shall I set downe your answer so?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Do, Ile take the Sacrament on't, how & which way you will: all's one to him.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: What a past-sauing slaue is this?

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Y'are deceiu'd my Lord, this is Mounsieur Parrolles the gallant militarist, that was his owne phrase that had the whole theoricke of warre in the knot of his scarfe, and the practise in the chape of his dagger.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: I will neuer trust a man againe, for keeping his sword cleane, nor beleeue he can haue euerie thing in him, by wearing his apparrell neatly.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Well, that's set downe.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Fiue or six thousand horse I sed, I will say true, or thereabouts set downe, for Ile speake truth.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: He's very neere the truth in this.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: But I con him no thankes for't in the nature he deliuers it.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Poore rogues, I pray you say.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Well, that's set downe.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I humbly thanke you sir, a truth's a truth, the Rogues are maruailous poore.

speeches.speaker: Interp.
prose: Demaund of him of what strength they are a foot. What say you to that?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose:
By my troth sir, if I were to liue this present houre, I will tell true. Let me see, Spurio a hundred &

fiftie, Sebastian so many, Corambus so many, Iaques so many: Guiltian, Cosmo, Lodowicke, and Gratij, two hundred fiftie each: Mine owne Company, Chitopher, ~aumond, Bentij, two hundred fiftie each: so that the muster file, rotten and sound, vppon my life amounts not to fifteene thousand pole, halfe of the which, dare not shake the snow from off their Cassockes, least they shake themselues to peeces.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: What shall be done to him?

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Nothing, but let him haue thankes. Demand of him my condition: and what credite I haue with the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Well that's set downe: you shall demaund of him, whether one Captaine Dumaine bee i' th Campe, a Frenchman: what his reputation is with the Duke, what his valour, honestie, and expertnesse in warres: or whether he thinkes it were not possible with well-waighing summes of gold to corrupt him to a reuolt. What say you to this? What do you know of it?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I beseech you let me answer to the particular of the intergatories. Demand them singly.

speeches.speaker: Int,
prose: Do you know this Captaine Dumaine?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I know him, a was a Botchers Prentize in Paris, from whence he was whipt for getting the Shrieues fool with childe, a dumbe innocent that could not say him nay.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Nay, by your leaue hold your hands, though I know his braines are forfeite to the next tile that fals.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Well, is this Captaine in the Duke of Florences campe?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Vpon my knowledge he is, and lowsie.

speeches.speaker: Cay. G.
prose: Nay looke not so vpon me: we shall heare of your Lord anon.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: What is his reputation with the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: The Duke knowes him for no other, but a poore Officer of mine, and writ to mee this other day, to turne him out a' th band. I thinke I haue his Letter in my pocket.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Marry we'll search.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: In good sadnesse I do not know, either it is there, or it is vpon a file with the Dukes other Letters, in my Tent.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Heere 'tis, heere's a paper, shall I reade it to you?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I do not know if it be it or no.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Our Interpreter do's it well.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Excellently.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Dian, the Counts a foole, and full of gold.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: That is not the Dukes letter sir: that is an aduertisement to a proper maide in Florence, one Diana, to take heede of the allurement of one Count Rossillion, a foolish idle boy: but for all that very ruttish. I pray you sir put it vp againe.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Nay, Ile reade it first by your fauour.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: My meaning in't I protest was very honest in the behalfe of the maid: for I knew the young Count to be a dangerous and lasciuious boy, who is a whale to Virginity and deuours vp all the fry it finds.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Damnable both-sides rogue.

speeches.speaker: Int Let.
verse: When he sweares oathes, hid him drop gold, and take it:
After he scores, he neuer payes the score:
Halfe won is match well made, match and well make it,
He nere payes after debts, take it before,
And say a souldier (Dian) told thee this:
Men are to mell with, boyes are not to kis.
For count of this, the Counts a Fool^ I know it,
Who payes before, but not when he does owe it.
Thine as he vow'd to thee in thine eare,

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: He shall be whipt through the Armie with this rime in's forehead.

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: This is your deuoted friend sir, the manifold Linguist, and the army-potent souldier.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: I could endure any thing before but a Cat, and now he's a Cat to me.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: I perceiue sir by your Generals lookes, wee shall be faine to hang you.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: My life sir in any case: Not that I am afraide to dye, but that my offences beeing many, I would repent out the remainder of Nature. Let me liue sir in a dungeon, i' th stockes, or any where, so I may liue.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Wee'le see what may bee done, so you confesse freely: therefore once more to this Captaine Dumaine: you haue answer'd to his reputation with the Duke, and to his valour. What is his honestie?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: He will steale sir an Egge out of a Cloister: for rapes and rauishments he paralels Nessus. Hee professes not keeping of oaths, in breaking em he is stronger then Hercules. He will lye sir, with such volubilitie, that you would thinke truth were a foole: drunkennesse is his best vertue, for he will be swine-drunke, and in his sleepe he does little harme, saue to his bed-cloathes about him: but they know his conditions, and lay him in straw. I haue but little more to say sir of his honesty, he ha's euerie thing that an honest man should not haue; what an honest man should haue, he has nothing.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: I begin to loue him for this.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: For this description of thine honestie? A pox vpon him for me, he's more and more a Cat.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: What say you to his expertnesse in warre?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Faith sir, ha's led the drumme before the English Tragedians: to belye him I will not, and more of his souldiership I know not, except in that Country, he had the honour to be the Officer at a place there called Mile-end, to instruct for the doubling of files. I would doe the man what honour I can, but of this I am not certaine.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: He hath out-villain'd villanie so farre, that the raritie redeemes him.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: A pox on him, he's a Cat still.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: His qualities being at this poore price. I neede not to aske you, if Gold will corrupt him to reuolt.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Sir, for a Cardceue he will sell the fee-simple of his saluation, the inheritance of it, and cut th' intaile from all remainders, and a perpetuall succession for it perpetually.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: What's his Brother, the other Captain Dumain?

speeches.speaker: Cap. E.
prose: Why do's he aske him of me?

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: What's he?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: E'ne a Crow a' th same nest: not altogether so great as the first in goodnesse, but greater a great deale in euill. He excels his Brother for a coward, yet his Brother is reputed one of the best that is. In a retreate hee outrunnes any Lackey; marrie in comming on, hee ha's the Crampe.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: If your life be saued, will you vndertake to betray the Florentine.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I, and the Captaine of his horse, Count Rossillion.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Ile whisper with the Generall, and knowe his pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose:
Ile no more drumming, a plague of all drummes, onely to seeme to deserue well, and to beguile the supposition

o' that lasciuious yong boy the Count, haue I run into this danger: yet who would haue suspected an ambush where I was taken?

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: There is no remedy sir, but you must dye: the Generall sayes, you that haue so traitorously discouerd the secrets of your army, and made such pestifferous reports of men very nobly held, can serue the world for no honest vse: therefore you must dye. Come headesman, off with his head.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: O Lord sir let me liue, or let me see my death.

speeches.speaker: Int.
verse: That shall you, and take your leaue of all your friends:
So, looke about you, know you any heere?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Good morrow noble Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: God blesse you Captaine Parolles.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: God saue you noble Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Lo. E.
prose: Captain, what greeting will you to my Lord Lafew? I am for France.

speeches.speaker: Cap. G.
prose: Good Captaine will you giue me a Copy of the sonnet you writ to Diana in behalfe of the Count Rossillion, and I were not a verie Coward, I'de compell it of you, but far you well.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: You are vndone Captaine all but your scarfe, that has a knot on't yet.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Who cannot be crush'd with a plot?

speeches.speaker: Inter.
prose: If you could finde out a Countrie where but women were that had receiued so much shame, you might begin an impudent Nation. Fare yee well sir, I am for France too, we shall speake of you there.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: Yet am I thankfull: if my heart were great
'Twould burst at this: Captaine Ile be no more,
But I will eate, and drinke, and sleepe as soft
As Captaine shall. Simply the thing I am
Shall make me liue: who knowes himselfe a braggart
Let him feare this; for it will come to passe,
That euery braggart shall be found an Asse.
Rust sword, coole blushes, and Parrolles liue
Safest in shame: being fool'd, by fool'rie thriue;
There's place and meanes for euery man aliue.
Ile after them.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: That you may well perceiue I haue not wrong'd you,
One of the greatest in the Christian world
Shall be my suretie: for whose throne 'tis needfull
Ere I can perfect mine intents, to kneele.
