Time was, I did him a desired office
Deere almost as his life, which gratitude
Through flintie Tartars bosome would peepe forth,
And answer thankes. I duly am inform'd,
His grace is at Marcellae, to which place
We haue conuenient conuoy: you must know
I am supposed dead, the Army breaking,
My husband hies him home, where heauen ayding,
And by the leaue of my good Lord the King,
Wee'l be before our welcome.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: Gentle Madam,
You neuer had a seruant to whose trust
Your busines was more welcome.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Nor your Mistris
Euer a friend, whose thoughts more truly labour
To recompence your loue: Doubt not but heauen
Hath brought me vp to be your daughters dower,
As it hath fated her to be my motiue
And helper to a husband. But O strange men,
That can such sweet vse make of what they hate,
When sawcie trusting of the cosin'd thoughts
Defiles the pitchy night, so lust doth play
With what it loathes, for that which is away,
But more of this heereafter: you Diana,
Vnder my poore instructions yet must suffer
Something in my behalfe.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: Let death and honestie
Go with your impositions, I am yours
Vpon your will to suffer.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Yet I pray you:
But with the word the time will bring on summer,
When Briars shall haue leaues as well as thornes,
And be as sweet as sharpe: we must away,
Our Wagon is prepar'd, and time reuiues vs,
All's well that ends well, still the fines the Crowne;
What ere the course, the end is the renowne.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: No, no, no, your sonne was misled with a snipt taffata fellow there, whose villanous saffron wold haue made all the vnbak'd and dowy youth of a nation in his colour: your daughter-in-law had beene aliue at this houre, and your sonne heere at home, more aduanc^d by the King, then by that red-tail'd humble Bee I speak of.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I would I had not knowne him, it was the death of the most vertuous gentlewoman, that euer Nature had praise for creating. If she had pertaken of my flesh and cost mee the deerest groanes of a mother, I could not haue owed her a more rooted loue.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Twas a good Lady, 'twas a good Lady. Wee may picke a thousand sallets ere wee light on such another hearbe.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Indeed sir she was the sweete Margerom of the sallet, or rather the hearbe of grace.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: They are not hearbes you knaue, they are nose-hearbes.

speeches.speaker: Clowne.
prose: I am no great Nabuchadnezar sir, I haue not much skill in grace.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Whether doest thou professe thy selfe, a knaue or a foole?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: A foole sir at a womans seruice, and a knaue at a mans.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Your distinction.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I would cousen the man of his wife, and do his seruice.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: So you were a knaue at his seruice indeed.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: And I would giue his wife my bauble sir to doe her seruice.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I will subscribe for thee, thou art both knaue and foole.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: At your seruice.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: No, no, no.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why sir, if I cannot serue you, I can serue as great a prince as you are.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Whose that, a Frenchman?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Faith sir a has an English maine, but his fisnomie is more hotter in France then there.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: What prince is that?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: The blacke prince sir, alias the prince of darkenesse, alias the diuell.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Hold thee there's my purse, I giue thee not this to suggest thee from thy master thou talk'st off, serue him still.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I am a woodland fellow sir, that alwaies loued a great fire, and the master I speak of euer keeps a good fire, but sure he is the Prince of the world, let his Nobilitie remaine in's Court. I am for the house with the narrow gate, which I take to be too little for pompe to enter: some that humble themselues may, but the manie will be too chill and tender, and theyle bee for the flowrie way that leads to the broad gate, and the great fire.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Go thy waies, I begin to bee a wearie of thee, and I tell thee so before, because I would not fall out with thee. Go thy wayes, let my horses be wel look'd too, without any trickes.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: If I put any trickes vpon em sir, they shall bee Iades trickes, which are their owne right by the law of Nature.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: A shrewd knaue and an vnhappie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: So a is. My Lord that's gone made himselfe much sport out of him, by his authoritie hee remaines heere, which he thinkes is a pattent for his sawcinesse, and indeede he has no pace, but runnes where he will.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I like him well, 'tis not amisse: and I was about to tell you, since I heard of the good Ladies death, and that my Lord your sonne was vpon his returne home. I moued the King my master to speake in the behalfe of my daughter, which in the minoritie of them both, his Maiestie out of a selfe gracious remembrance did first propose, his Highnesse hath promis'd me to doe it, and to stoppe vp the displeasure he hath conceiued against your sonne, there is no fitter matter. How do's your Ladyship like it?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: With verie much content my Lord, and I wish it happily effected.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: His Highnesse comes post from Marcellus, of as able bodie as when he number'd thirty, a will be heere to morrow, or I am deceiu'd by him that in such intelligence hath seldome fail'd.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Ir reioyces me, that I hope I shall see him ere I die. I haue letters that my sonne will be heere to night: I shall beseech your Lordship to remaine with mee, till they meete together.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Madam, I was thinking with what manners I might safely be admitted.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
prose: You neede but pleade your honourable priuiledge.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Ladie, of that I haue made a bold charter, but I thanke my God, it holds yet.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O Madam, yonders my Lord your sonne with a patch of veluet on's face, whether there bee a scar vnder't or no, the Veluet knowes, but 'tis a goodly patch of Veluet, his left cheeke is a cheeke of two pile and a halfe, but his right cheeke is worne bare.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: A scarre nobly got,
Or a noble scarre, is a good liu'rie of honor,
So belike is that.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: But it is your carbinado'd face.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: Let vs go see
your sonne I pray you, I long to talke
With the yong noble souldier.

speeches.speaker: Clowne.
prose: Faith there's a dozen of em, with delicate fine hats, and most courteous feathers, which bow the head, and nod at euerie man.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: But this exceeding posting day and night,
Must wear your spirits low, we cannot helpe it:
But since you haue made the daies and nights as one,
To weare your gentle limbes in my affayres,
Be bold you do so grow in my requitall,
As nothing can vnroote you. In happie time,
This man may helpe me to his Maiesties eare,
If he would spend his power. God saue you sir.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: And you.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Sir, I haue seene you in the Court of France.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: I haue beene sometimes there.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I do presume sir, that you are not falne
From the report that goes vpon your goodnesse,
And therefore goaded with most sharpe occasions,
Which lay nice manners by, I put you to
The vse of your owne vertues, for the which
I shall continue thankefull.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: What's your will?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: That it will please you
To giue this poore petition to the King,
And ayde me with that store of power you haue
To come into his presence.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
prose: The Kings not heere.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Not heere sir?

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Not indeed,
He hence remou'd last night, and with more hast
Then is his vse.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Lord how we loose our paines.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: All's well that ends well yet,
Though time seeme so aduerse, and meanes vnfit:
I do beseech you, whither is he gone?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Marrie as I take it to Rossillion,
Whither I am going.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: I do beseech you sir,
Since you are like to see the King before me,
Commend the paper to his gracious hand,
Which I presume shall render you no blame,
But rather make you thanke your paines for it,
I will come after you with what good speede
Our meanes will make vs meanes.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: This Ile do for you.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: And you shall finde your selfe to be well thankt what e're falles more. We must to horse againe, Go, go, prouide.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose:
Good Mr
Lauatch giue my Lord Lafew this letter, I haue ere now sir beene better knowne to you, when I haue held familiaritie with fresher cloathes: but I am now sir muddied in fortunes mood, and smell somewhat strong of her strong displeasure.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Truely, Fortunes displeasure is but sluttish if it smell so strongly as thou speak'st of: I will hencefoorth eate no Fish of Fortunes butt'ring. Pre thee alow the winde.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Nay you neede not to stop your nose sir: I spake but by a Metaphor.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Indeed sir, if your Metaphor stinke, I will stop my nose, or against any mans Metaphor. Prethe get thee further.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Pray you sir deliuer me this paper.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Foh, prethee stand away: a paper from fortunes close-stoole, to giue to a Nobleman. Looke heere he comes himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Heere is a purre of Fortunes sir, or of Fortunes Cat, but not a Muscat, that ha's falne into the vncleane fish-pond of her displeasure, and as he sayes is muddied withall. Pray you sir, vse the Carpe as you may, for he lookes like a poore decayed, ingenious, foolish, rascally knaue. I doe pittie his distresse in my smiles of comfort, and leaue him to your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: My Lord I am a man whom fortune hath cruelly scratch'd.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: And what would you haue me to doe? 'Tis too late to paire her nailes now. Wherein haue you played the knaue with fortune that she should scratch you, who of her selfe is a good Lady, and would not haue knaues thriue long vnder? There's a Cardecue for you: Let the Iustices make you and fortune friends; I am for other businesse.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I beseech your honour to heare mee one single word.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: you begge a single peny more: Come you shall ha^t, saue your word.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: My name my good Lord is Parrolles.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: You begge more then word then. Cox my passion, giue me your hand: How does your drumme?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: O my good Lord, you were the first that found mee.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Was I insooth? And I was the first that lost thee.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: It lies in you my Lord to bring me in some grace for you did bring me out.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Out vpon thee knaue, doest thou put vpon mee at once both the offiee of God and the diuel: one brings thee in grace, and the other brings thee out. The Kings comming I know by his Trumpets. Sirrah, inquire further after me, I had talke of you last night, though you are a foole and a knaue, you shall eate, go too, follow.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I praise God for you.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: We lost a Iewell of her, and our esteeme
Was made much poorer by it: but your sonne,
As mad in folly, lack'd the sence to know
Her estimation home.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
verse: 'Tis past my Liege,
And I beseech your Maiestie to make it
Naturall rebellion, done i' th blade of youth,
When oyle and fire, too strong for reasons force,
Ore-beares it, and burnes on.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: My honour'd Lady,
I haue forgiuen and forgotten all,
Though my reuenges were high bent vpon him,
And watch'd the time to shoote.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: This I must say,
But first I begge my pardon: the yong Lord
Did to his Maiesty, his Mother, and his Ladie,
Offence of mighty note; but to himselfe
The greatest wrong of all. He lost a wife,
Whose beauty did astonish the suruey
Of richest eies: whose words all eares tooke captiue,
Whose deere perfection, hearts that scorn'd to serue,
Humbly call'd Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Praising what is lost,
Makes the remembrance deere. Well, call him hither,
We are reconcil'd, and the first view shall kill
All repetition: Let him not aske our pardon,
The nature of his great offence is dead,
And deeper then obliuion, we do burie
Th' incensing reliques of it. Let him approach
A stranger, no offender; and informe him
So 'tis our will he should.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: I shall my Liege.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: What sayes he to your daughter,
Haue you spoke?

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: All that he is, hath reference to your Highnes.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Then shall we haue a match. I haue letters sent me, that sets him high in fame.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: He lookes well on't.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I am not a day of season,
For thou maist see a sun-shine, and a haile
In me at once: But to the brightest beames
Distracted clouds giue way, so stand thou forth,
The time is faire againe.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: My high repented blames
Deere Soueraigne pardon to me.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: All is whole,
Not one word more of the consumed time,
Let's take the instant by the forward top:
For we are old, and on our quick'st decrees
Th' inaudible, and noiselesse foot of time
Steales, ere we can effect them. You remember
The daughter of this Lord?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Admiringly my Liege, at first
I stucke my choice vpon her, ere my heart
Durst make too bold a herauld of my tongue:
Where the impression of mine eye enfixing,
Contempt his scornfull Perspectiue did lend me,
Which warpt the line, of euerie other fauour,
Scorn'd a faire colour, or exprest it stolne,
Extended or contracted all proportions
To a most hideous obiect. Thence it came,
That she whom all men prais'd, and whom my selfe,
Since I haue lost, haue lou'd; was in mine eye
The dust that did offend it.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Well excus'd:
That thou didst loue her, strikes some scores away
From the great compt: but loue that comes too late,
Like a remorsefull pardon slowly carried
To the great sender, turnes a sowre offence,
Crying, that's good that's gone: Our rash faults,
Make triuiall price of serious things we haue,
Not knowing them, vntill we know their graue,
Oft our displeasures to our selues vniust,
Destroy our friends, and after weepe their dust:
Our owne loue waking, cries to see what's don,e
While shamefull hate sleepes out the afternoone.
Be this sweet Helens knell, and now forget her.
Send forth your amorous token for faire Maudlin,
The maine consents are had, and heere wee'l stay
To see our widdowers second marriage day:
Which better then the first, O deere heauen blesse,
Or, ere they meete in me, O Nature cesse.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: Come on my sonne, in whom my houses name
Must be digested: giue a fauour from you
To sparkle in the spirits of my daughter,
That she may quickly come. By my old beard,
And eu'rie haire that's on't, Helen that's dead
Was a sweet creature: such a ring as this,
The last that ere I tooke her leaue at Court,
I saw vpon her finger.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: Hers it was not.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Now pray you let me see it. For mine eye,
While I was speaking, oft was fasten'd too't:
This Ring was mine, and when I gaue it Hellen,
I bad her if her fortunes euer stoode
Necessitied to helpe, that by this token
I would releeue her. Had you that craft to reaue her
Of what should stead her most?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: My gracious Soueraigne,
How ere it pleases you to take it so,
The ring was neuer hers.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
verse: Sonne, on my life
I haue seene her weare it, and she reckon'd it
At her liues rate.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I am sure I saw her weare it.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: You are deceiu'd my Lord, she neuer saw it:
In Florence was it from a casement throwne mee,
Wrap'd in a paper, which contain'd the name
Of her that threw it: Noble she was, and thought
I stood ingag'd. but when I had subscrib'd
To mine owne fortune, and inform'd her fully,
I could not answer in that course of Honour
As she had made the ouerture, she ceast
In heauie satisfaction, and would neuer
Receiue the Ring againe.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Platus himselfe,
That knowes the tinct and multiplying med'cine,
Hath not in natures mysterie more science,
Then I haue in this Ring. 'Twas mine, 'twas Helens,
Who euer gaue it you: then if you know
That you are well acquainted with your selfe,
Confesse 'twas hers, and by what rough enforcement
You got it from her. She call'd the Saints to suretie,
That she would neuer put it from her finger,
Vnlesse she gaue it to your selfe in bed,
Where you haue neuer come: or sent it vs
Vpon her great disaster.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: She neuer saw it.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Thou speak'st it falsely: as I loue mine Honor,
And mak'st connecturall feares to come into me,
Which I would faine shut out, if it should proue
That thou art so inhumane, 'twill not proue so:
And yet I know not, thou didst hate her deadly,
And she is dead, which nothing but to close
Her eyes my selfe, could win me to beleeue,
More then to see this Ring. Take him away,
My fore-past proofes, how ere the matter fall
Shall taze my feares of little vanitie,
Hauing vainly fear'd too little. Away with him,
Wee'l sift this matter further.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: If you shall proue
This Ring was euer hers, you shall as easie
Proue that I husbanded her bed in Florence,
Where yet she neuer was.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: I am wrap^d in dismall thinkings.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Gracious Soueraigne.
Whether I haue beene too blame or no, I know not,
Here's a petition from a Florentine,
Who hath for foure or fiue remoues come short,
To tender it her selfe. I vndertooke it,
Vanquish'd thereto by the faire grace and speech
Of the poore suppliant, who by this I know
Is heere attending: her businesse lookes in her
With an importing visage, and she told me
In a sweet verball breefe, it did concerne
Your Highnesse with her selfe.

prose:
~pon his many protestations to marrie mee when his wife was dead, I blush to say it, he wonne me. Now is the Count Rossillion a Widdower, his vowes are forfeited to mee, and my honors payed to him. Hee stole from Florence, taking no leaue, and I follow him to his Countrey for Iustice: Grant it me, O King, in you it best lies, otherwise a seducer flourishes, and a poore Maid is vndone.


Diana Capilet.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I will buy me a sonne in Law in a faire, and toule for this. Ile none of him.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: The heauens haue thought well on thee Lafew,
To bring forth this discou'rie, seeke these sutors:
Go speedily, and bring againe the Count.
I am a-feard the life of Hellen (Ladie)
Was fowly snatcht.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
prose: Now iustice on the doers.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I wonder sir, sir, wiues are monsters to you,
And that you flye them as you sweare them Lordship,
Yet you desire to marry. What woman's that?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: I am my Lord a wretched Florentine,
Deriued from the ancient Capilet,
My suite as I do vnderstand you know,
And therefore know how farre I may be pittied.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: I am her Mother sir, whose age and honour
Both suffer vnder this complaint we bring,
And both shall cease, without your remedie.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Come hether Count, do you know these Women?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: My Lord, I neither can nor will denie,
But that I know them, do they charge me further?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: Why do you looke so strange vpon your wife?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
prose: She's none of mine my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: If you shall marrie
You giue away this hand, and that is mine,
You giue away heauens vowes, and those are mine:
You giue away my selfe, which is knowne mine:
For I by vow am so embodied yours,
That she which marries you, must marrie me,
Either both or none.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: your reputation comes too short for my daughter, you are no husband for her.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: My Lord, this is a fond and desperate creature,
Whom sometime I haue laugh'd with: Let your highnes
Lay a more noble thought vpon mine honour,
Then for to thinke that I would sinke it heere.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Sir for my thoughts, you haue them il to friend,
Till your deeds gaine them fairer: proue your honor,
Then in my thought it lies.

speeches.speaker: Dian.
verse: Good my Lord,
Aske him vpon his oath, if hee do's thinke
He had not my virginity.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: What saist thou to her?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: She's impudent my Lord,
And was a common gamester to the Campe.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: He do's me wrong my Lord: If I were so,
He might haue bought me at a common price.
Do not beleeue him. O behold this Ring,
Whose high respect and rich validitie
Did lacke a Paralell: yet for all that
He gaue it to a Commoner a' th Campe
If I be one.

speeches.speaker: Coun.
verse: He blushes, and 'tis hit:
Of sixe preceding Ancestors, that Iemme
Confer'd by testament to 'th sequent issue
Hath it beene owed and worne. This is his wife,
That Ring's a thousand proofes.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Me thought you saide
You saw one heere in Court could witnesse it.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: I did my Lord, but loath am to produce
So bad an instrument, his names Parrolles.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: I saw the man to day, if man he bee.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Finde him, and bring him hether.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: What of him:
He's quoted for a most pe fidious slaue
With all the spots a' th world, taxt and debosh'd,
Whose nature sickens: but to speake a truth,
Am I, or that or this for what he'l vtter,
That will speake any thing.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: She hath that Ring of yours.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I thinke she has; certaine it is I lyk'd her,
And boorded her i' th wanton way of youth:
She knew her distance, and did angle for mee,
Madding my eagernesse with her restraint,
As all impediments in fancies course
Are motiues of more fancie, and in fine,
Her insuite comming with her moderne grace,
Subdu'd me to her rate, she got the Ring,
And I had that which any inferiour might
At Market price haue bought.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: I must be patient:
You that haue turn'd off a first so noble wife,
May iustly dyet me. I pray you yet,
(Since you lacke vertue, I will loose a husband)
Send for your Ring, I will returne it home,
And giue me mine againe.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: I haue it not.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: What Ring was yours I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Dian.
prose: Sir much like the same vpon your finger.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Know you this Ring, this Ring was his of late.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: And this was it I gaue him being a bed.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: The story then goes false, you threw it him
Out of a Casement.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: I haue spoke the truth.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: My Lord, I do confesse the ring was hers.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: You boggle shrewdly, euery feather starts you:
Is this the man you speake of?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: I, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Tell me sirrah, but tell me true I charge you,
Not fearing the displeasure of your master:
Which on your iust proceeding, Ile keepe off,
By him and by this woman heere, what know you?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: So please your Maiesty, my master hath bin an honourable Gentleman. Trickes hee hath had in him, which Gentlemen haue.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Come, come, to' th' purpose: Did hee loue this woman?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Faith sir he did loue her, but how.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: How I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: He did loue her sir, as a Gent. loues a Woman.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: How is that?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: He lou'd her sir, and lou'd her not.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: As thou art a knaue and no knaue, what an equiuocall Companion is this?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I am a poore man, and at your Maiesties command.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: Hee's a good drumme my Lord, but a naughtie Orator.

speeches.speaker: Dian.
prose: Do you know he promist me marriage?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Faith I know more then Ile speake.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: But wilt thou not speake all thou know'st?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Yes so please your Maiesty: I did goe betweene them as I said, but more then that he loued her, for indeede he was madde for her, and talkt of Sathan, and of Limbo, and of Furies, and I know not what: yet I was in that credit with them at that time, that I knewe of their going to bed, and of other motions, as promising her marriage, and things which would deriue mee ill will to speake of, therefore I will not speake what I know.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Thou hast spoken all alreadie, vnlesse thou canst say they are maried, but thou art too fine in thy euidence, therefore stand aside. This Ring you say was yours.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: I my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Where did you buy it? Or who gaue it you?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: It was not giuen me, nor I did not buy it.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Who lent it you?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: It was not lent me neither.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Where did you finde it then?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: I found it not.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: If it were yours by none of all these wayes,
How could you giue it him?

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: I neuer gaue it him.

speeches.speaker: Laf.
prose: This womans an easie gloue my Lord, she goes off and on at pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: This Ring was mine, I gaue it his first wife.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: It might be yours or hers for ought I know.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Take her away, I do not like her now,
To prison with her: and away with him,
Vnlesse thou telst me where thou hadst this Ring,
Thou diest within this houre.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: Ile neuer tell you.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Take her away.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: Ile put in baile my liedge.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: I thinke thee now some common Customer.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
prose: By Ioue if euer I knew man 'twas you.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Wherefore hast thou accusde him al this while.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: Because he's guiltie, and he is not guilty:
He knowes I am no Maid, and hee'l sweare too't:
Ile sweare I am a Maid, and he knowes not.
Great King I am no strumpet, by my life,
I am either Maid, or else this old mans wife.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: She does abuse our eares, to prison with her.

speeches.speaker: Dia.
verse: Good mother fetch my bayle. Stay Royall sir,
The Ieweller that owes the Ring is sent for,
And he shall surety me. But for this Lord,
Who hath abus'd me as he knowes himselfe,
Though yet he neuer harm'd me, heere I quit him.
He knowes himselfe my bed he hath defil'd,
And at that time he got his wife with childe:
Dead though she be, she feeles her yong one kicke:
So there's my riddle, one that's dead is quicke,
And now behold the meaning.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Is there no exorcist
Beguiles the truer Office of mine eyes?
Is't reall that I see?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: No my good Lord,
'Tis but the shadow of a wife you see,
The name, and not the thing.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Both, both, O pardon.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Oh my good Lord, when I was like this Maid,
I found you wondrous kinde, there is your Ring,
And looke you, heeres your letter: this it sayes,
When from my finger you can get this Ring,
And is by me with childe, &c. This is done,
Will you be mine now you are doubly wonne?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: If she my Liege can make me know this clearly,
Ile loue her dearely, euer, euer dearly.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: If it appeare not plaine, and proue vntrue,
Deadly diuorce step betweene me and you.
O my deere mother do I see you liuing?

speeches.speaker: Laf.
verse: Mine eyes smell Onions, I shall weepe anon:
Good Tom Drumme lend me a handkercher.
So I thanke thee, waite on me home, Ile make sport with thee: Let thy curtsies alone, they are scuruy ones.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: Let vs from point to point this storie know,
To make the euen truth in pleasure flow:
If thou beest yet a fresh vncropped flower,
Choose thou thy husband, and Ile pay thy dower.
For I can guesse, that by thy honest ayde,
Thou keptst a wife her selfe, thy selfe a Maide.
Of that and all the progresse more and lesse,
Resolduedly more leasure shall expresse:
All yet seemes well, and if it end so meete,
The bitter past, more welcome is the sweet.
THe Kings a Begger, now the Play is done,
All is well ended, if this suite be wonne,
That you expresse Content: which we will pay,
With strift to please you, day exceeding day:
Ours be your patience then, and yours our parts,
Your gentle hands lends vs, and take our hearts.

plays.play_title: Twelfe Night, Or what you will.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: IF Musicke be the food of Loue, play on,
Giue me excesse of it: that surfetting,
The appetite may sicken, and so dye.
That straine agen, it had a dying fall:
O, it came ore my eare, like the sweet sound
That breathes vpon a banke of Violets;
Stealing, and giuing Odour. Enough, no more,
'Tis not so sweet now, as it was before.
O spirit of Loue, how quicke and fresh art thou,
That notwithstanding thy capacitie,
Receiueth as the Sea. Nought enters there,
Of what validity, and pitch so ere,
But falles into abatement, and low price
Euen in a minute; so full of shapes is fancie,
That it alone, is high fantasticall.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
prose: Will you go hunt my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: What Curio?

speeches.speaker: Cu.
prose: The Hart.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why so I do, the Noblest that I haue:
O when mine eyes did see Oliuia first,
Me thought she purg'd the ayre of pestilence;
That instant was I turn'd into a Hart,
And my desires like fell and cruell hounds,
Ere since pursue me. How now what newes from her?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: So please my Lord, I might not be admitted,
But from her handmaid do returne this answer:
The Element it selfe, till seuen yeares heate,
Shall not behold her face at ample view:
But like a Cloystresse she will vailed walke,
And water once a day her Chamber round
With eye-offending brine: all this to season
A brothers dead loue, which she would keepe fresh
And lasting, in her sad remembrance.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O she that hath a heart of that fine frame
To pay this debt of loue but to a brother,
How will she loue, when the rich golden shaft
Hath kill'd the flocke of all affections else
That liue in her. When Liuer, Braine, and Heart,
These soueraigne thrones, are all supply'd and fill'd
Her sweete perfections with one selfe king:
Away before me, to sweet beds of Flowres,
Loue-thoughts lye rich, when canopy'd with bowres.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: What Country (Friends) is this?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: This is Illyria Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: And what should I do in Illyria?
My brother he is in Elizium,
Perchance he is not drown'd: What thinke you saylors?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: It is perchance that you your selfe were saued.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: O my poore brother, and so perchance may he be.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: True Madam, and to comfort you with chance,
Assure your selfe, after our ship did split,
When you, and those poore number saued with you,
Hung on our driuing boate: I saw your brother
Most prouident in perill, binde himselfe,
(Courage and hope both teaching him the practise)
To a strong Maste, that liu'd vpon the sea:
Where like Orion on the Dolphines backe,
I saw him hold acquaintance with the waues,
So long as I could see.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: For saying so, there's Gold:
Mine owne escape vnfoldeth to my hope,
Whereto thy speech serues for authoritie
The like of him. Know'st thou this Countrey?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: I Madam well, for I was bred and borne
Not three houres trauaile from this very place:

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Who gouernes heere?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: A noble Duke in nature, as in name.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: What is his name?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Orsino.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Orsino: I haue heard my father name him.
He was a Batchellor then.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: And so is now, or was so very late:
For but a month ago I went from hence,
And then 'twas fresh in murmure (as you know
What great ones do, the lesse will prattle of,)
That he did seeke the loue of faire Oliuia.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: What's shee?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: A vertuous maid, the daughter of a Count
That dide some tweluemonth since, then leauing her
In the protection of his sonne, her brother,
Who shortly also dide: for whose deere loue
(They say) she hath abiur'd the sight
And company of men.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: O that I seru'd that Lady,
And might not be deliuered to the world
Till I had made mine owne occasion mellow
What my estate is.

speeches.speaker: Cap
verse: That were hard to compasse,
Because she will admit no kinde of suite,
No not the Dukes.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: There is a faire behauiour in thee Captaine,
And though that nature, with a beauteous wall
Doth oft close in pollution: yet of thee
I will beleeue thou hast a minde that suites
With this thy faire and outward charracter.
I prethee (and Ile pay thee bounteously)
Conceale me what I am, and be my ayde,
For such disguise as haply shall become
The forme of my intent. Ile serue this Duke,
Thou shalt present me as an Eunuch to him,
It may be worth thy paines: for I can sing,
And speake to him in many sorts of Musicke,
That will allow me very worth his seruice.
What else may hap, to time I will commit,
Onely shape thou thy silence to my wit.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Be you his Eunuch, and your Mute Ile bee,
When my tongue blabs, then let mine eyes not see.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: I thanke thee: Lead me on.

speeches.speaker: Sir To.
prose: What a plague meanes my Neece to take the death of her brother thus? I am sure care's an enemie to life.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: By my troth sir Toby, you must come in earlyer a nights. your Cosin, my Lady, takes great exceptions to your ill houres.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Why let her except, before excepted.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: I, but you must confine your selfe within the modest limits of order.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Confine? Ile confine my selfe no finer then I am: these cloathes are good enough to drinke in, and so bee these boots too: and they be not, let them hang themselues in their owne straps.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: That quaffing and drinking will vndoe you: I heard my Lady talke of it yesterday: and of a foolish knight that you brought in one night here, to be hir woer

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Who, Sir Andrew Ague-cheeke?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: I he.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: He's as tall a man as any's in Illyria.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: What's that to th' purpose?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Why he ha's three thousand ducates a yeare.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: I, but hee'l haue but a yeare in all these ducates: He's a very foole, and a prodigall.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Fie, that you'l say so: he playes o' th Viol-de-ga^-boys, and speaks three or four languages word for word without booke, & hath all the good gifts of nature.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: He hath indeed, almost naturall: for besides that he's a foole, he's a great quarreller: and but that hee hath the gift of a Coward, to allay the gust he hath in quarrelling, 'tis thought among the prudent, he would quickely haue the gift of a graue.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
prose: By this hand they are scoundrels and substractor. that say so of him. Who are they?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: They that adde moreour, hee's drunke nightly in your company.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: With drinking healths to my Neece: Ile drinke to her as long as there is a passage in my throat, & drinke in Illyria: he's a Coward and a Coystrill that will not drinke to my Neece. till his braines turne o' th toe, like a parish top. What wench? Castiliano vulgo: for here coms Sir Andrew Agueface.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Sir Toby Belch. How now sir Toby Belch?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Sweet sir Andrew.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Blesse you faire Shrew.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And you too sir.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
prose: Accost Sir Andrew, accost.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: What's that?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: My Neeces Chamber-maid.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Good Mistris accost, I desire better acquaintance

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: My name is Mary sir.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Good mistris Mary, accost.

speeches.speaker: To,
prose: You mistake knight: Accost, is front her, boord her, woe her, assayle her.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: By my troth I would not vndertake her in this company. Is that the meaning of Accost?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Far you well Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: And thou let part so Sir Andrew, would thou mightst neuer draw sword agen.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And you part so mistris, I would I might neuer draw sword agen: Faire Lady, doe you thinke you haue fooles in hand?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Sir, I haue not you by 'th hand.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Marry but you shall haue, and heeres my hand.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Now sir. thought is free: I pray you bring your hand to 'th Buttry barre, and let it drinke.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Wherefore (sweet-heart?) What's your Metaphor?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: It's dry sir.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Why I thinke so: I am not such an asse, but I can keepe my hand dry. But what's your iest?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: A dry iest Sir.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Are you full of them?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: I Sir, I haue them at my fingers ends: marry now I let go your hand, I am barren.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: O knight, thou lack'st a cup of Canarie: when did I see thee so put downe?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Neuer in your life I thinke, vnlesse you see Canarie put me downe: mee thinkes sometimes I haue no more wit then a Christian, or an ordinary man ha's: but I am a great eater of beefe, and I beleeue that does harme to my wit.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: No question.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: And I thought that, I'de forsweare it. Ile ride home to morrow sir Toby.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Pur-quoy my deere knight?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: What is purquoy? Do, or not do? I would I had bestowed that time in the tongues, that I haue in fencing dancing, and beare-bayting; O had I but followed the Arts.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Then hadst thou had an excellent head of haire.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Why, would that haue mended my haire?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Past question, for thou seest it will not coole my nature

speeches.speaker: An
prose: But it becoms we wel enough, dost not?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Excellent, it hangs like flax on a distaffe: & I hope to see a huswife take thee between her legs, & spin it off.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Faith Ile home to morrow sir Toby, your niece wil not be seene, or if she be it's four to one, she'l none of me: the Count himselfe here hard by, wooes her,

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Shee'l none o' th Count, she'l not match aboue hir degree, neither in estate, yeares, nor wit: I haue heard her swear't. Tut there's life in't man.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Ile stay a moneth longer. I am a fellow o' th strangest minde i' th world: I delight in Maskes and Reuels sometimes altogether.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Art thou good at these kicke-chawses Knight?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: As any man in Illyria, whatsoeuer he be, vnder the degree of my betters, & yet I will not compare with an old man.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: What is thy excellence in a galliard, knight?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Faith, I can cut a caper.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: And I can cut the Mutton too't.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And I thinke I haue the backe-tricke, simply as strong as any man in Illyria.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Wherefore are these things hid? Wherefore haue these gifts a Curtaine before 'em? Are they like to take dust, like mistris Mals picture? Why dost thou not goe to Church in a Galliard, and come home in a Carranto? My verie walke should be a Iigge: I would not so much as make water but in a Sinke-a-pace: What dooest thou meane? Is it a world to hide vertues in? I did thinke by the excellent constitution of thy legge, it was form'd vnder the starre of a Galliard.

speeches.speaker: And,
prose: I, 'tis strong, and it does indifferent well in a dam'd colour'd stocke. Shall we sit about some Reuels?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: What shall we do else: were we not borne vnder Taurus?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Taurus? That sides and heart.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: No sir, it is leggs and thighes: let me see thee caper. Ha, higher: ha, ha, excellent.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: If the Duke continue these fauours towards you Cesario, you are like to be much aduanc'd, he hath known you but three dayes, and already you are no stranger.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: You either feare his humour, or my negligence, that you call in question the continuance of his loue. Is he inconstant sir, in his fauours.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: No beleeue me.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I thanke you: heere comes the Count.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Who saw Cesario hoa?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: On your attendance my Lord heere.

speeches.speaker: Du
verse: Stand you a-while aloofe. Cesario,
Thou knowst no lesse, but all: I haue vnclasp'd
To thee the booke euen of my secret soule.
Therefore good youth, addresse thy gate vnto her,
Be not deni'de accesse, stand at her doores,
And tell them, there thy fixed foot shall grow
Till thou haue audience.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Sure my Noble Lord,
If she be so abandon'd to her sorrow
As it is spoke, she neuer will admit me.

speeches.speaker: Du,
verse: Be clamorous, and leape all ciuill bounds,
Rather then make vnprofited returne,

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Say I do speake with her (my Lord) what then?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O then, vnfold the passion of my loue,
Surprize her with discourse of my deere faith;
It shall become thee well to act my woes:
She will attend it better in thy youth,
Then in a Nuntio's of more graue aspect.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I thinke not so, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Deere Lad, beleeue it;
For they shall yet belye thy happy yeeres,
That say thou art a man: Dianas lip
Is not more smooth, and rubious: thy small pipe
Is as the maidens organ, shrill, and sound,
And all is semblatiue a womans part.
I know thy constellation is right apt
For this affayre: some foure or fiue attend him,
All if you will: for I my selfe am best
When least in companie: prosper well in this,
And thou shalt liue as freely as thy Lord,
To call his fortunes thine.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Ile do my best
To woe your Lady: yet a barrefull strife,
Who ere I woe, my selfe would be his wife.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Nay, either tell me where thou hast bin, or I will not open my lippes so wide as a brissle may enter, in way of thy excuse: my Lady will hang thee for thy absence.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Let her hang me: hee that is well hang'de in this world, needs to feare no colours.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Make that good.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: He shall see none to feare.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: A good lenton answer: I can tell thee where yt saying was borne, of I feare no colours.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Where good mistris Mary?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: In the warrs, & that may you be bolde to say in your foolerie.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Well, God giue them wisedome that haue it: & those that are fooles, let them vse their talents.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Yet you will be hang'd for being so long absent, or to be turn'd away: is not that as good as a hanging to you?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Many a good hanging, preuents a bad marriage: and for turning away, let summer beare it out.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: You are resolute then?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Not so neyther, but I am resolu'd on two points

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: That if one breake, the other will hold: or if both breake, your gaskins fall.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Apt in good faith, very apt: well go thy way, if sir Toby would leaue drinking, thou wert as witty a piece of Eues flesh, as any in Illyria.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Peace you rogue, no more o' that: here comes my Lady: make your excuse wisely, you were best.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Wit, and't be thy will, put me into good fooling: those wits that thinke they haue thee, doe very oft proue fooles: and I that am sure I Iacke thee, may passe for a wise man. For what saies Quinapalus, Better a witty foole, then a foolish wit. God blesse thee Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Take the foole away.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Do you not heare fellowes, take away the Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Go too, y' are a dry foole: Ile no more of you: besides you grow dis-honest.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose:
Two faults Madona, that drinke & good counsell wil amend: for giue the dry foole drink, then is the foole not dry: bid the dishonest man mend himself, if he mend, he is no longer dishonest; if hee cannot, let the Botcher mend him: any thing that's mended, is but patch'd: vertu that transgresses, is but patcht with sinne, and sin that amends, is but patcht with vertue. If that this simple Sillogisme will serue, so: if it will not, vvhat remedy?

As there is no true Cuckold but calamity, so beauties a flower; The Lady bad take away the foole, therefore I say againe, take her away.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Sir, I bad them take away you.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Misprision in the highest degree. Lady, Cucullus non facit monachum: that's as much to say, as I weare not motley in my braine: good Madona, giue mee leaue to proue you a foole.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Can you do it?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Dexteriously, good Madona.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Make your proofe.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I must catechize you for it Madona, Good my Mouse of vertue answer mee.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Well sir, for want of other idlenesse, Ile bide your proofe.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Good Madona, why mournst thou?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Good foole, for my brothers death.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I thinke his soule is in hell, Madona.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: I know his soule is in heauen, foole.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: The more foole (Madona) to mourne for your Brothers soule, being in heauen. Take away the Foole, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What thinke you of this foole Maluolio, doth he not mend?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Yes, and shall do, till the pangs of death shake him: Infirmity that decaies the wise, doth euer make the better foole.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: God send you sir, a speedie Infirmity, for the better increasing your folly: Sir Toby will be sworn that I am no Fox, but he wil not passe his word for two pence that you are no Foole.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: How say you to that Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I maruell your Ladyship takes delight in such a barren rascall: I saw him put down the other day, with an ordinary foole, that has no more braine then a stone. Looke you now, he's out of his gard already: vnles you laugh and minister occasion to him, he is gag'd. I protest I take these Wisemen, that crow so at these set kinde of fooles, no better then the fooles Zanies.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: O you are ficke of selfe-loue Maluolio, and taste with a distemper'd appetite. To be generous, guitlesse, and of free disposition, is to take those things for Bird-bolts, that you deeme Cannon bullets: There is no slander in an allow'd foole, though he do nothing but rayle; nor no rayling, in a knowne discreet man, though hee do nothing but reproue.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Now Mercury indue thee with leasing, for thou speak'st well of fooles.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Madam, there is at the gate, a young Gentleman, much desires to speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: From the Count Orsino, is it?

speeches.speaker: Ma
prose: I know not (Madam) 'tis a faire young man, and well attended.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Who of my people hold him in delay.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Sir Toby Madam, your kinsman.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Fetch him off I pray you, he speakes nothing but madman: Fie on him. Go you Maluolio; If it be a^ suit from the Count, I am sicke, or not at home. What you will, to dismisse it.
Now you see sir, how your fooling growes old, & people dislike it.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Thou hast spoke for vs (Madona) as if thy eldest sonne should be a foole: whose scull, Ioue cramme with braines, for heere he comes.
One of thy kin has a most weake Pia-mater.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: By mine honor halfe drunke. What is he at the gate Cosin?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: A Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: A Gentleman? What Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: 'Tis a Gentleman heere. A plague o' these pickle herring: How now Sot.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Good Sir Toby.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Cosin, Cosin, how haue you come so earely by this Lethargie?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Letcherie, I defie Letchery: there's one at the gate.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: I marry, what is he?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Let him be the diuell and he will, I care not: giue me faith say I. Well, it's all one.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What's a drunken man like, foole?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Like a drown'd man, a foole, and a madde man:
One draught aboue heate, makes him a foole, the second maddes him, and a third drownes him.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Go thou and seeke the Crowner, and let him sitte o' my Coz: for he's in the third degree of drinke: hee's drown'd: go looke after him.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: He is but mad yet Madona, and the foole shall looke to the madman.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Madam, yond young fellow sweares hee will speake with you. I told him you were sicke, he takes on him to vnderstand so much, and therefore comes to speak with you. I told him you were asleepe, he seems to haue a fore knowledge of that too, and therefore comes to speake with you. What is to be said to him Ladie, hee's fortified against any deniall.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Tell him, he shall not speake with me.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Ha's beene told so: and hee sayes hee'l stand at your doore like a Sheriffes post, and be the supporter to a bench, but hee'l speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What kinde o' man is he?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Why of mankinde.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What manner of man?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Of verie ill manner: hee'l speake with you, will you, or no.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Of what personage, and yeeres is he?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Not yet old enough for a man, nor yong enough for a boy: as a squash is before tis a pescod, or a Codling when tis almost an Apple: Tis with him in standing water, betweene boy and man. He is verie well-fauour'd, and he speakes verie shrewishly: One would thinke his mothers milke were scarse out of him.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Let him approach: Call in my Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Gentlewoman, my Lady calles.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Giue me my vaile: come throw it ore my face,
Wee'l once more heare Orsinos Embassie.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: The honorable Ladie of the house, which is she?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Speake to me, I shall answer for her: your will.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Most radiant, exquisite, and vnmatchable beautie. I pray you tell me if this bee the Lady of the house, for I neuer saw her. I would bee loath to cast away my speech: for besides that it is excellently well pend, I haue taken great paines to con it. Good Beauties, let mee sustaine no scorne; I am very comptible, euen to the least sinister vsage.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Whence came you sir?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose:
I can say little more then I haue studied, & that question's out of my part. Good gentle one, giue mee modest assurance, if you be the Ladie of the house, that

may proceede in my speech.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Are you a Comedian?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: No my profound heart: and yet (by the verie phangs of malice, I sweare) I am not that I play. Are you the Ladie of the house?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: If I do not vsurpe my selfe, I am.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Most certaine, if you are she, you do vsurp your selfe: for what is yours to bestowe, is, not yours to reserue. But this is from my Commission: I will on with my speech in your praise, and then shew you the heart of my message.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Come to what is important in't: I forgiue you the praise.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Alas, I tooke great paines to studie it, and 'tis Poeticall.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: It is the more like to be feigned, I pray you keep it in. I heard you were sawcy at my gates, & allowd your approach rather to wonder at you, then to heare you. If you be not mad, be gone: if you haue reason, be breefe: 'tis not that time of Moone with me, to make one in so skipping a dialogue.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Will you hoyst sayle sir, here lies your way.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: No good swabber, I am to hull here a little longer. Some mollification for your Giant, sweete Ladie; tell me your minde, I am a messenger.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Sure you haue some hiddeous matter to deliuer, when the curtesie of it is so fearefull. Speake your office.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: It alone concernes your eare: I bring no ouerture of warre, no taxation of homage; I hold the Olyffe in my hand: my words are as full of peace, as matter.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Yet you began rudely. What are you? What would you?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: The rudenesse that hath appear'd in mee, haue I learn'd from my entertainment. What I am, and what I would, are as secret as maiden-head: to your eares, Diuinity; to any others, prophanation.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Giue vs the place alone,
We will heare this diuinitie. Now sir, what is your text?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Most sweet Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: A comfortable doctrine, and much may bee saide of it. Where lies your Text?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: In Orsinoes bosome.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: In his bosome? In what chapter of his bosome?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: To answer by the method in the first of his hart.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: O, I haue read it: it is heresie. Haue you no more to say?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Good Madam, let me see your face.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Haue you any Commission from your Lord, to negotiate with my face: you are now out of your Text: but we will draw the Curtain, and shew you the picture. Looke you sir, such a one I was this present: Ist not well done?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Excellently done, if God did all.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: 'Tis in graine sir, 'twill endure winde and weather.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Tis beauty truly blent, whose red and white,
Natures owne sweet, and cunning hand laid on:
Lady, you are the cruell'st shee aliue,
If you will leade these graces to the graue,
And leaue the world no copie.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: O sir, I will not be so hard-hearted: I will giue out diuers scedules of my beautie. It shalbe Inuentoried and euery particle and vtensile labell'd to my will: As, Item two lippes indifferent redde, Item two grey eyes, with lids to them: Item, one necke, one chin, & so forth. Were you sent hither to praise me?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I see you what you are, you are too proud:
But if you were the diuell, you are faire:
My Lord, and master loues you: O such loue
Could be but recompenc'd, though you were crown'd
The non-pareil of beautie.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: How does he loue me?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: With adorations, fertill teares,
With groanes that thunder loue, with sighes of fire.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Your Lord does know my mind, I cannot loue him
Yet I suppose him vertuous, know him noble,
Of great estate, of fresh and stainlesse youth;
In voyces well divulg'd, free, learn'd, and valiant,
And in dimension, and the shape of nature,
A gracious person; But yet I cannot loue him:
He might haue tooke his answer long ago.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: If I did loue you in my masters flame,
With such a suffring, such a deadly life:
In your deniall, I would finde no sence,
I would not vnderstand it.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Why, what would you?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Make me a willow Cabine at your gate,
And call vpon my soule within the house,
Write loyall Cantons of contemned loue,
And sing them lowd euen in the dead of night:
Hallow your name to the reuerberate hilles,
And make the babling Gossip of the aire,
Cry out Oliuia: O you should not rest
Betweene the elements of ayre, and earth,
But you should pittie me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: You might do much:
What is your Parentage?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Aboue my fortunes, yet my state is well:
I am a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Get you to your Lord:
I cannot loue him: let him send no more,
Vnlesse (perchance) you come to me againe,
To tell me how he takes it: Fare you well:
I thanke you for your paines: spend this for mee.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I am no feede poast, Lady; keepe your purse,
My Master, not my selfe, lackes recompence.
Loue make his heart of flint, that you shal loue,
And let your feruour like my masters be,
Plac'd in contempt: Farwell fayre crueltie.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: What is your Parentage?
Aboue my fortunes, yet my state is well;
I am a Gentleman. Ile be sworne thou art,
Thy tongue, thy face, thy limbes, actions, and spirit.
Do giue thee fiue-fold blazon: not too fast: soft, soft,
Vnlesse the Master were the man. How now?
Euen so quickly may one catch the plague?
Me thinkes I feele this youths perfections
With an inuisible, and subtle stealth
To creepe in at mine eyes. Well, let it be.
What hoa, Maluolio.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Heere Madam, at your seruice.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Run after that same peeuish Messenger
The Countes man: he left this Ring behinde him
Would I, or not: tell him, Ile none of it.
Desire him not to flatter with his Lord,
Nor hold him vp with hopes, I am not for him:
If that the youth will come this way to morrow,
Ile giue him reasons for't: hie thee Maluolio.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Madam, I will.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I do I know not what, and feare to finde
Mine eye too great a flatterer for my minde:
Fate, shew thy force, our selues we do not owe,
What is decreed, must be: and be this so.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: IF Musicke be the food of Loue, play on,
Giue me excesse of it: that surfetting,
The appetite may sicken, and so dye.
That straine agen, it had a dying fall:
O, it came ore my eare, like the sweet sound
That breathes vpon a banke of Violets;
Stealing, and giuing Odour. Enough, no more,
'Tis not so sweet now, as it was before.
O spirit of Loue, how quicke and fresh art thou,
That notwithstanding thy capacitie,
Receiueth as the Sea. Nought enters there,
Of what validity, and pitch so ere,
But falles into abatement, and low price
Euen in a minute; so full of shapes is fancie,
That it alone, is high fantasticall.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
prose: Will you go hunt my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: What Curio?

speeches.speaker: Cu.
prose: The Hart.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why so I do, the Noblest that I haue:
O when mine eyes did see Oliuia first,
Me thought she purg'd the ayre of pestilence;
That instant was I turn'd into a Hart,
And my desires like fell and cruell hounds,
Ere since pursue me. How now what newes from her?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: So please my Lord, I might not be admitted,
But from her handmaid do returne this answer:
The Element it selfe, till seuen yeares heate,
Shall not behold her face at ample view:
But like a Cloystresse she will vailed walke,
And water once a day her Chamber round
With eye-offending brine: all this to season
A brothers dead loue, which she would keepe fresh
And lasting, in her sad remembrance.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O she that hath a heart of that fine frame
To pay this debt of loue but to a brother,
How will she loue, when the rich golden shaft
Hath kill'd the flocke of all affections else
That liue in her. When Liuer, Braine, and Heart,
These soueraigne thrones, are all supply'd and fill'd
Her sweete perfections with one selfe king:
Away before me, to sweet beds of Flowres,
Loue-thoughts lye rich, when canopy'd with bowres.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Will you stay no longer: nor will you not that I go with you.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: By your patience, no: my starres shine darkely ouer me; the malignancie of my fate, might perhaps distemper yours; therefore I shall craue of you your leaue, that I may beare my euils alone. It were a bad recompence for your loue, to lay any of them on you.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Let me yet know of you, whither you are bound.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: No sooth sir: my determinate voyage is meere extrauagancie. But I perceiue in you so excellent a touch of modestie, that you will not extort from me, what I am willing to keepe in: therefore it charges me in manners, the rather to expresse my selfe: you must know of mee then Antonio, my name is Sebastian (which I call'd Rodorigo) my father was that Sebastian of Messaline, whom I know you haue heard of. He left behinde him, my selfe, and a sister, both borne in an houre: if the Heauens had beene pleas'd, would we had so ended. But you sir, alter'd that, for some houre before you tooke me from the breach of the sea, was my sister drown'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Alas the day.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: A Lady sir, though it was said shee much resembled me, was yet of many accounted beautiful: but ^hogh I could not with such estimable wonder ouer-farre beleeue that, yet thus farre I will boldly publish her, shee bore a minde that enuy could not but call faire: Shee is drown'd already sir with salt water, though I seeme to drowne her remembrance againe with more.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Pardon me sir, your bad entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: O good Antonio, forgiue me your trouble.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: If you will not murther me for my loue, let mee be your seruant.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: If you will not vndo what you haue done, that is kill him, whom you haue recouer'd, desire it not. Fare ye well at once, my bosome is full of kindnesse, and I am yet so neere the manners of my mother, that vpon the least occasion more, mine eyes will tell tales of me: I am bound to the Count Orsino's Court, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: The gentlenesse of all the gods go with thee:
I haue many enemies in Orsino's Court,
Else would I very shortly see thee there:
But come what may, I do adore thee so,
That danger shall seeme sport, and I will go.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Were not you eu'n now, with the Countesse Oliuia?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Euen now sir, on a moderate pace, I haue since ariu'd but hither.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: She returnes this Ring to you (sir) you might haue saued mee my paines, to haue taken it away your selfe. She adds moreouer, that you should put your Lord into a desperate assurance, she will none of him. And one thing more, that you be neuer so hardie: o come againe in his affaires, vnlesse it bee to report your Lords taking of this: receiue it so.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: She tooke the Ring of me, Ile none of it.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Come sir, you peeuishly threw it to her: and her will is, it should be so return'd: If it bee worth stooping for, there it lies, in your eye: if not, bee it his that findes it.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I left no Ring with her: what meanes this Lady?
Fortune forbid my out-side haue not charm'd her:
She made good view of me, indeed so much,
That me thought her eyes had lost her tongue,
For she did speake in starts distractedly.
She loues me sure, the cunning of her passion
Inuites me in this churlish messenger:
None of my Lords Ring? Why he sent her none;
I am the man, if it be so, as tis,
Poore Lady, she were better loue a dreame:
Disguise, I see thou art a wickednesse,
Wherein the pregnant enemie does much.
How easie is it, for the proper false
In womens waxen hearts to set their formes:
Alas, O frailtie is the cause, not wee,
For such as we are made, if such we bee:
How will this fadge? My master loues her deerely,
And I (poore monster) fond asmuch on him:
And she (mistaken) seemes to dote on me:
What will become of this? As I am man,
My state is desperate for my maisters loue:
As I am woman (now alas the day)
What thriftlesse sighes shall poore Oliuia breath?
O time, thou must vntangle this, not I,
It is too hard a knot for me t'vnty.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Approach Sir Andrew: not to bee a bedde after midnight, is to be vp betimes, and Deliculo surgere, thou know'st.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Nay by my troth I know not: but I know, to be vp late, is to be vp late.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: A false conclusion: I hate it as an vnfill'd Canne. To be vp after midnight, and to go to bed then is early: so that to go to bed after midnight, is to goe to bed betimes. Does not our liues consist of the foure Elements?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Faith so they say, but I thinke it rather consists of eating and drinking.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Th' art a scholler; let vs therefore eate and drinke Marian I say, a stoope of wine.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Heere comes the foole yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: How now my harts: Did you neuer see the Picture of we three?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Welcome asse, now let's haue a catch.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose:
By my troth the foole has an excellent breast. I had rather then forty shillings I had such a legge, and so sweet a breath to sing, as the foole has. Insooth thou wast in very gracious fooling last night, when thou spok'st of Pigrogromitus, of the
~apians passing the Equinoctial of Queubus: 'twas very good yfaith: I sent thee sixe pence

for thy Lemon, hadst it?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I did impeticos thy gratillity: for Maluolios nose is no Whip-stocke. My Lady has a white hand, and the Mermidons are no bottle-ale houses.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Excellent: Why this is the best fooling, when all is done. Now a song.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come on, there is sixe pence for you. Let's haue a song.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: There's a testrill of me too: if one knight giue a

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Would you haue a loue-song, or a song of good life?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: A loue song, a loue song.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: O Mistris mine where are you roming?
O stay and heare, your true loues coming,
That can sing both high and low.
Trip no further prettie sweeting.
Iourneys end in louers meeting,
Euery wise mans sonne doth know.
prose: I, I. I care not for good life.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Excellent good, ifaith.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Good, good.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: What is loue, tis not heereafter,
Present mirth, hath present laughter:
What's to come, is still vnsure.
In delay there lies no plentie,
Then come kisse me sweet and twentie:
Youths a stuffe will not endure.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: A mellifluous voyce, as I am true knight.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: A contagious breath.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Very sweet, and contagious ifaith.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: To heare by the nose, it is dulcet in contagion. But shall we make the Welkin dance indeed? Shall wee rowze the night-Owle in a Catch, that will drawe three soules out of one Weauer? Shall we do that?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And you loue me, let's doo't: I am dogge at a Catch.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Byrlady sir, and some dogs will catch well.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Most certaine: Let our Catch be, Thou Knaue.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Hold thy peace, thou Knaue knight. I shall be constrain'd in't, to call thee knaue, Knight.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: 'Tis not the first time I haue constrained one to call me knaue. Begin foole: it begins, Hold thy peace.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I shall neuer begin if I hold my peace.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Good ifaith: Come begin.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: What a catterwalling doe you keepe heere? If my Ladie haue not call'd vp her Steward Maluolio, and bid him turne you out of doores, neuer trust me.

speeches.speaker: To,
prose: My Lady's a Catayan, we are politicians, Maluolios a Peg-a-ramsie, and Three merry men be wee. Am not I consanguinious? Am I not of her blood: tilly vally. Ladie, There dwelt a man in Babylon, Lady, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Beshrew me, the knights in admirable fooling.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I, he do's well enough if he be dispos'd, and so do I too: he does it with a better grace, but I do it more naturall.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: O the twelfe day of December.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: For the loue o' God peace.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: My masters are you mad? Or what are you? Haue you no wit, manners, nor honestie, but to gabble like Tinkers at this time of night? Do yee make an Alehouse of my Ladies house, that ye squeak out your Coziers Catches without any mitigation or remorse of voice? Is there no respect of place, persons, nor time in you?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: We did keepe time sir in our Catches. Snecke vp.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir Toby, I must be round with you. My Lady bad me tell you, that though she harbors you as her kinsman, she's nothing ally'd to your disorders. If you can separate your selfe and your misdemeanors, you are welcome to the house: if not, and it would please you to take leaue of her, she is very willing to bid you farewell.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Farewell deere heart, since I must needs be gone.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Nay good Sir Toby.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: His eyes do shew his dayes are almost done.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Is't euen so?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: But I will neuer dye.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir Toby there you lye.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: This is much credit to you.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Shall I bid him go.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: What and if you do?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Shall I bid him go, and spare not?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O no, no, no, no, you dare not.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Out o' tune sir, ye lye: Art any more then a Steward? Dost thou thinke because thou art vertuous, there shall be no more Cakes and Ale?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Yes by S. Anne, and Ginger shall bee hotte y' th mouth too.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Th' art i' th right. Goe sir, rub your Chaine with crums. A stope of Wine Maria.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Mistris Mary, if you priz'd my Ladies sauour at any thing more then contempt, you would not giue meanes for this vnciuill rule; the shall know of it by this hand.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Go shake your eares.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: 'Twere as good a deede as to drink when a mans a hungrie, to challenge him the field, and then to breake promise with him, and make a foole of him.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Doo't knight, Ile write thee a Challenge: or Ile deliuer thy indignation to him by word of mouth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sweet Sir Toby be patient for to night: Since the youth of the Counts was to day with my Lady, she is much out of quiet. For Monsieur Maluolio, let me alone with him: If I do not gull him into an ayword, and make him a common recreation, do not thinke I haue witte enough to lye straight in my bed: I know I can do it.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Possesse vs, possesse vs, tell vs something of him.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Marrie sir, sometimes he is a kinde of Puritane.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: O, if I thought that, Ide beate him like a dogge.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: What for being a Puritan, thy exquisite reason, deere knight.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I haue no exquisite reason for't, but I haue reason good enough.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: The diu'll a Puritane that hee is, or any thing constantly but a time-pleaser, an affection'd Asse, that cons State without booke, and vtters it by great swarths. The best perswaded of himselfe: so cram'd (as he thinkes) with excellencies, that it is his grounds of faith, that all that looke on him, loue him: and on that vice in him, will my reuenge finde notable cause to worke.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: What wilt thou do?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I will drop in his way some obscure Epistles of loue, wherein by the colour of his beard, the shape of his legge, the manner of his gate, the expressure of his eye, forehead, and complection, he shall finde himselfe most feelingly personated. I can write very like my Ladie your Neece, on a forgotten matter wee can hardly make distinction of our hands.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Excellent, I smell a deuice.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I hau't in my nose too.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose:
He shall thinke by the Letters that thou wilt drop

that they come from my Neece, and that shee's in loue with him.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: My purpose is indeed a horse of that colour.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: And your horse now would make him an Asse.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Asse, I doubt not.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: O twill be admirable.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sport royall I warrant you: I know my Physicke will worke with him, I will plant you two, and let the Foole make a third, where he shall finde the Letter: obserue his construction of it: For this night to bed, and dreame on the euent: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Good night Penthisilea.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Before me she's a good wench.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: She's a beagle true bred, and one that adores me: what o' that?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I was ador'd once too.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Let's to bed knight: Thou hadst neede send for more money.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: If I cannot recouer your Neece, I am a foule way out.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Send for money knight, if thou hast her not i' th end, call me Cut.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: If I do not, neuer trust me, take it how you will.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come, come, Ile go burne some Sacke, tis too late to go to bed now: Come knight, come knight.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Giue me some Musick; Now good morow frends.
Now good Cesario, but that peece of song,
That old and Anticke song we heard last night;
Me thought it did releeue my passion much,
More then light ayres, and recollected termes
Of these most briske and giddy-paced times.
Come, but one verse.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: He is not heere (so please your Lordshippe) that should sing it?

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Who was it?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose:
Fest^
the lester my Lord, a foole that the Ladie Oliuiaes Father tooke much delight in. He is about the house.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come hither Boy, if euer thou shalt loue
In the sweet pangs of it, remember me:
For such as I am, all true Louers are,
Vnstaid and skittish in all motions else,
Saue in the constant image of the creature
That is belou'd. How dost thou like this tune?
prose: Seeke him out, and play the tune the while.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: It giues a verie eccho to the seate
Where loue is thron^d.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thou dost speake masterly,
My life vpon't, yong though thou art, thine eye
Hath staid vpon some fauour that it loues:
Hath it not boy?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: A little, by your fauour.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: What kinde of woman ist?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Of your complection.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: She is not worth thee then. What yeares ifaith?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: About your yeeres my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Too old by heauen: Let still the woman take
An elder then her selfe, so weares she to him;
So swayes she leuell in her husbands heart:
For boy, howeuer we do praise our seiues,
Our fancies are more giddie and vnfirme,
More longing, wauering, sooner lost and worne,
Then womens are.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: I thinke it well my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Then let thy Loue be yonger then thy selfe,
Or thy affection cannot hold the bent:
For women are as Roses, whose faire flowre
Being once displaid, doth fall that verie howre.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: And so they are: alas, that they are so:
To die, euen when they to perfection grow.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O fellow come, the song we had last night:
Marke it Cesario, it is old and plaine;
The Spinsters and the Knitters in the Sun,
And the free maides that weaue their thred with bones,
Do vse to chaunt it: it is silly sooth,
And dallies with the innocence of loue,
Like the old age.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Are you ready Sir?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I prethee sing.

verse: Come away, come away death,
And in sad cypresse let me be laide.
Fye away, fie away breath,
I am slaine by a faire cruell maide:
My shrowd of white, stuck all with Ew, O prepare it.
My part of death no one so true did share it.
Not a flower, not a flower sweete
On my blacke coffin, let there be strewne:
