Not a friend, not a friend greet
My poore corpes, where my bones shall be throwne:
A thousand thousand sighes to saue, lay me ô where
Sad true louer neuer find my graue, to weepe there.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: There's for thy paines.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No paines sir, I take pleasure in singing sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Ile pay thy pleasure then.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Truely sir, and pleasure will be paide one time, or another.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Giue me now leaue, to leaue thee.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Now the melancholly God protect thee, and the Tailor make thy doublet of changeable Taffata, for thy minde is a very Opall. I would haue men of such constancie put to Sea, that their businesse might be euery thing, and their intent euerie where, for that's it, that alwayes makes a good voyage of nothing. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Let all the rest giue place: Once more Cesario,
Get thee to yond same soueraigne crueltie:
Tell her my loue, more noble then the world
Prizes not quantitie of dirtie lands,
The parts that fortune hath bestow'd vpon her:
Tell her I hold as giddily as Fortune:
But 'tis that miracle, and Queene of Iems
That nature prankes her in, attracts my soule.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: But if she cannot loue you sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: It cannot be so answer'd.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Sooth but you must.
Say that some Lady, as perhappes there is,
Hath for your loue as great a pang of heart
As you haue for Oliuia: you cannot loue her:
You tel her so: Must she not then be answer'd?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: There is no womans sides
Can bide the beating of so strong a passion,
As loue doth giue my heart: no womans heart
So bigge, to hold so much, they lacke retention.
Alas, their loue may be call'd appetite,
No motion of the Liuer, but the Pallat,
That suffer surfet, cloyment, and reuolt,
But mine is all as hungry as the Sea,
And can digest as much, make no compare
Betweene that loue a woman can beare me,
And that I owe Oliuia.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: I but I know.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: What dost thou knowe?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Too well what loue women to men may owe:
In faith they are as true of heart, as we.
My Father had a daughter lou'd a man
As it might be perhaps, were I a woman
I should your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: And what's her history?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: A blanke my Lord: she neuer told her loue,
But let concealment like a worme i' th budde
Feede on her damaske cheeke: she pin'd in thought,
And with a greene and yellow melancholly,
She sate like Patience on a Monument,
Smiling at greefe. Was not this loue indeede?
We men may say more, sweare more, but indeed
Our shewes are more then will: for still we proue
Much in our vowes, but little in our loue.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: But di'de thy sister of her loue my Boy?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I am all the daughters of my Fathers house,
And all the brothers too: and yet I know not.
Sir, shall I to this Lady?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I that's the Theame,
To her in haste: giue her this Iewell: say,
My loue can giue no place, bide no denay.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come thy wayes Signior Fabian.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Nay Ile come: if I loose a scruple of this sport, let me be boyl'd to death with Melancholly.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Wouldst thou not be glad to haue the niggardly Rascally sheepe-biter, come by some notable shame?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: I would exult man: you know he brought me out o' fauour with my Lady, about a Beare-baiting heere.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: To anger him wee'l haue the Beare againe, and we will foole him blacke and blew, shall we not sir Andrew?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: And we do not, it is pittie of our liues.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Heere comes the little villaine: How now my Mettle of India?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Get ye all three into the box tree: Maluolio's comming downe this walke, he has beene yonder i' the Sunne practising behauiour to his own shadow this halfe houre: obserue him for the loue of Mockerie: for I know this Letter wil make a contemplatiue Ideot of him. Close in the name of ieasting, lye thou there: for heere comes the Trowt, that must be caught with tickling.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: 'Tis but Fortune, all is fortune. Maria once told me she did affect me, and I haue heard her self come thus neere, that should shee fancie, it should bee one of my complection. Besides she vses me with a more exalted respect, then any one else that followes her. What should I thinke on't?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Heere's an ouer-weening rogue.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Oh peace: Contemplation makes a rare Turkey Cocke of him, how he iets vnder his aduanc'd plumes.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Slight I could so beate the Rogue.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Peace I say.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: To be Count Maluolio.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Ah Rogue.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Pistoll him, pistoll him.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Peace, peace.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: There is example for't: The Lady of the Strachy, married the yeoman of the wardrobe.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Fie on him Iezabel.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: O peace, now he's deepely in: looke how imagination blowes him.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Hauing beene three moneths married to her, sitting in my state.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: O for a stone-bow to hit him in the eye.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Calling my Officers about me, in my branch'd Veluet gowne: hauing come from a day bedde, where I haue left Oliuia sleeping.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Fire and Brimstone.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: O peace, peace.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: And then to haue the humor of state: and after a demure trauaile of regard: telling them I knowe my place, as I would they should doe theirs: to aske for my kinsman Toby.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Boltes and shackles.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Oh peace, peace, peace, now, now.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Seauen of my people with an obedient start, make out for him: I frowne the while, and perchance winde vp my watch, or play with my some rich Iewell: Toby approaches; curtsies there to me.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Shall this fellow liue?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Though our silence be drawne from vs with cars, yet peace.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I extend my hand to him thus: quenching my familiar smile with an austere regard of controll.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: And do's not Toby take you a blow o' the lippes, then?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Saying, Cosine Toby, my Fortunes hauing cast me on your Neece, giue me this prerogatiue of speech.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: What, what?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: You must amend your drunkennesse.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Out scab.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Nay patience, or we breake the sinewes of our plot?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Besides you waste the treasure of your time, with a foolish knight.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: That's mee I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: One sir Andrew.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I knew 'twas I, for many do call mee foole.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: What employment haue we heere?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Now is the Woodcocke neere the gin.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Oh peace, and the spirit of humors intimate reading aloud to him.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose:
By my life this is my Ladies hand: these bee her very C's.
her
~'s, and her T's, and thus makes shee het great P's. It is in contempt of question her hand.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Her C's, her
~'s, and her T's: why that?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: To the vnknowne belou'd, this, and my good Wishes: Her very Phra^es: By your leaue wax. Soft, and the impressure her Lucrece, with which she vses to seale: tis my Lady: To whom should this be?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: This winnes him, Liuer and all.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Ioue knowes I loue, but who,
Lips do not mooue, no man must know.
No man must know. What followes?
The numbers alter^d: No man must know,
If this should be thee Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Marrie hang thee brocke.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: I may command where I adore, but silence like a Lucresse knife:
With bloodlesse stroke my heart doth gore, M.O.A.I. doth sway my life.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: A fustian riddle.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Excellent Wench, say I.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: M.O.A.I. doth sway my life. Nay but first let me see, let me see, let me see.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: What dish a poyson has she drest him?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: And with what wing the stallion checkes at it?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I may command, where I adore: Why shee may command me: I serue her, she is my Ladie. Why this is euident to any formall capacitie. There is no obstruction in this, and the end: What should that Alphabeticall position portend, if I could make that resemble something in me? Softly, M.O.A.I.

speeches.speaker: To
prose: O I, make vp that, he is now at a cold sent.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Sowter will cry vpon't for all this, though it bee as ranke as a Fox.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: M. Maluolio, M. why that begins my name.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Did not I say he would worke it out, the Curre is excellent at faults.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: M. But then there is no consonancy in the sequell that suffers vnder probation: A. should follow, but O. does.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: And O shall end, I hope.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I, or Ile cudgell him, and make him cry O.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: And then I. comes behind.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: I, and you had any eye behinde you, you^ might see more detraction at your heeles, then Fortunes before you.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: M, O, A, I. This simulation is not as the former: and yet to crush this a little, it would bow to mee, for euery one of these Letters are in my name. Soft, here followes prose: If this fall into thy hand, reuolue. In my stars I am aboue thee, but be not affraid of greatnesse: Some are become great, some atcheeues greatnesse, and some haue greatnesse thrust vppon em. Thy fates open theyr hands, let thy blood and spirit embrace them, and to invre thy selfe to what thou art like to be: cast thy humble slough, and appeare fresh. Be opposite with a kinsman, surly with seruants: Let thy tongue tang arguments of state; put thy selfe into the tricke of singularitie. Shee thus aduises thee, that sighes for thee. Remember who commended thy yellow stockings, and wish'd to see thee euer crosse garter'd: I say remember, goe too, thou art made if thou desir'st to be so: If not, let me see thee a steward still, the fellow of seruants, and not woorthie to touch Fortunes singers Farewell, Shee that would alter seruices with thee, tht fortunate vnhappy daylight and champian discouers not more: This is open, I will bee proud, I will reade pollticke Authours, I will baffle Sir Toby, I will wash off grosse acquaintance, I will be point deuise, the very man. I do not now foole my selfe, to let imagination iade mee; for euery reason excites to this, that my Lady loues me. She did commend my yellow stockings of late, shee did praise my legge being crosse-garter'd, and in this she manifests her selfe to my loue, & with a kinde of iniunction driues mee to these habites of her liking. I thanke my starres, I am happy: I will bee strange, stout, in yellow stockings, and crosse Garter'd, euen with the swiftnesse of putting on. Ioue, and my starres be praised. Heere is yet a postscript. Thou canst not choose but know who I am. If thou entertainst my loue, let it appeare in thy smiling, thy smiles become thee well. Therefore in my presence still smile, deero my sweete, I prethee. Ioue I thanke thee, I will smile, I wil do euery thing that thou wilt haue me.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: I will not giue my part of this sport for a pension of thousands to be paid from the Sophy.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I could marry this wench for this deuice.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: So could I too.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: And aske no other dowry with her, but such another iest.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Nor I neither.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Heere comes my noble gull catcher.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Wilt thou set thy foote o' my necke.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Or o' mine either?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Shall I play my freedome at tray-trip, and becom thy bondslaue?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Ifaith, or I either?

speeches.speaker: Tob.
prose: Why, thou hast put him in such a dreame, that when the image of it leaues him, he must run mad.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Nay but say true, do's it worke vpon him?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Like Aqua vite with a Midwife.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: If you will then see the fruites of the sport, mark his first approach before my Lady: hee will come to her in yellow stockings, and 'tis a colour she abhorres, and crosse garter'd, a fashion shee detests: and hee will smile vpon her, which will now be so vnsuteable to her disposition, being addicted to a melancholly, as shee is, that it cannot but turn him into a notable contempt: if you wil see it follow me.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: To the gates of Tartar, thou most excellent diuell of wit.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Ile make one too.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Saue thee Friend and thy Musick: dost thou liue by thy Tabor?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No sir, I liue by the Church.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Art thou a Churchman?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No such matter sir, I do liue by the Church: For, I do liue at my house, and my house dooth stand by the Church

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: So thou maist say the Kings lyes by a begger, if a begger dwell neer him: or the Church stands by thy Tabor, if thy Tabor stand by the Church.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: You haue said sir: To see this age: A sentence is but a cheu'rill gloue to a good witte, how quickely the wrong side may be turn'd outward.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Nay that's certaine: they that dally nicely with words, may quickely make them wanton.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I would therefore my sister had had no name Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Why man?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why sir, her names a word, and to dallie with that word, might make my sister wanton: But indeede, words are very Rascals, since bonds disgrac'd them.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Thy reason man?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Troth sir, I can yeeld you none without wordes, and wordes are growne so false, I am loath to proue reason with them.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I warrant thou art a merry fellow, and car'st for nothing.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Not so sir, I do care for something: but in my conscience sir, I do not care for you: if that be to care for nothing sir, I would it would make you inuisible.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Art not thou the Lady Oliuia's foole?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No indeed sir, the Lady Oliuia has no folly, shee will keepe no foole sir, till she be married, and fooles are as like husbands, as Pilchers are to Herrings, the Husbands the bigger, I am indeede not her foole, but hir corrupter of words.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I saw thee late at the Count Orsino's.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Foolery sir, does walke about the Orbe like the Sun, it shines euery where. I would be sorry sir, but the Foole should be as oft with your Master, as with my Mistris: I thinke I saw your wisedome there.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Nay, and thou passe vpon me, Ile no more with thee. Hold there's expences for thee.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Now Ioue in his next commodity of hayre, send thee a beard.

speeches.speaker:
Vi^
.
prose: By my troth Ile tell thee, I am almost sicke for one, though I would not haue it grow on my chinne. Is thy Lady within?

speeches.speaker: Clo
prose: Would not a paire of these haue bred sir?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Yes being kept together, and put to vse.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I would play Lord Pandarus of Phrygia sir, to bring a Cressida to this Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I vnderstand you sir, tis well begg'd.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: The matter I hope is not great sir; begging, but a begger: Cressida was a begger. My Lady is within sir. I will conster to them whence you come, who you are, and what you would are out of my welkin, I might say Element, but the word is ouer-worne.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: This fellow is wise enough to play the foole,
And to do that well, craues a kinde of wit:
He must obserue their mood on whom he iests,
The quality of persons, and the time:
And like the Haggard, checke at euery Feather
That comes before his eye. This is a practice,
As full of labour as a Wise-mans Art:
For folly that he wisely shewes, is fit;
But wisemens folly falne, quite taint their wit.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Saue you Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: And you sir.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Dieu vou guard Monsieur.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Et vouz ousie vostre seruiture.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I hope sir, you are, and I am yours.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Will you incounter the house, my Neece is desirous you should enter, if your trade be to her.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I am bound to your Neece sir, I meane she is the list of my voyage.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Taste your legges sir, put them to motion.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: My legges do better vnderstand me sir, then I vnderstand what you meane by bidding me taste my legs.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I meane to go sir, to enter.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I will answer you with gate and entrance, but we are preuented.
Most excellent accomplish'd Lady, the heauens raine Odours on you.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: That youth's a rare Courtier, raine odours, wel.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: My matter hath no voice Lady, but to your owne most pregnant and vouchsafed eare.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Odours, pregnant, and vouchsafed: Ile get 'em all three already.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Let the Garden doore be shut, and leaue mee to my hearing. Giue me your hand sir.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: My dutie Madam, and most humble seruice^

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What is your name?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Cesario is your seruants name, faire Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: My seruant sir? 'Twas neuer merry world, Since lowly feigning was call'd complement: y' are seruant to the Count Orsino youth.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: And he is yours, and his must needs be yours: your seruants seruant, is your seruant Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: For him, I thinke not on him: for his thoughts,
Would they were blankes, rather then fill'd with me.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Madam, I come to whet your gentle thoughts
On his behalfe.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: O by your leaue I pray you.
I bad you neuer speake againe of him;
But would you vndertake another suite
I had rather heare you, to solicit that,
Then Musicke from the spheares.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Deere Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Giue me leaue, beseech you: I did send,
After the last enchantment you did heare,
A Ring in chace of you. So did I abuse
My selfe, my seruant, and I feare me you:
Vnder your hard construction must I sit,
To force that on you in a shamefull cunning
Which you knew none of yours. What might you think?
Haue you not set mine Honor at the stake,
And baited it with all th' vnmuzled thoughts
That tyrannous heart can think? To one of your receiuing
Enough is shewne, a Cipresse, not a bosome,
Hides my heart: so let me heare you speake.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I pittie you.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: That's a degree to loue.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: No not a grize: for tis a vulgar proofe
That verie oft we pitty enemies.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Why then me thinkes 'tis time to smile agen:
O world, how apt the poore are to be proud?
If one should be a prey, how much the better
To fall before the Lion, then the Wolfe?
The clocke vpbraides me with the waste of time:
Be not affraid good youth, I will not haue you,
And yet when wit and youth is come to haruest,
your wife is like to reape a proper man:
There lies your way, due West.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Then Westward hoe:
Grace and good disposition attend your Ladyship:
you'l nothing Madam to my Lord, by me:

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Stay: I prethee tell me what thou thinkst of me?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: That you do thinke you are not what you are.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: If I thinke so, I thinke the same of you.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Then thinke you right: I am not what I am.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: I would you were, as I would haue you be.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Would it be better Madam, then I am?
I wish it might, for now I am your foole.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: O what a deale of scorne, lookes beautifull?
In the contempt and anger of his lip,
A murdrous guilt shewes not it selfe more soone,
Then loue that would seeme hid: Loues night, is noone.
Cesario, by the Roses of the Spring,
By maid-hood, honor, truth, and euery thing,
I loue thee so, that maugre all thy pride,
Nor wit, nor reason, can my passion hide:
Do not extort thy reasons from this clause,
For that I woo, thou therefore hast no cause:
But rather reason thus, with reason fetter;
Loue sought, is good: but giuen vnsought, is better.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: By innocence I sweare, and by my youth,
I haue one heart, one bosome, and one truth,
And that no woman has, nor neuer none
Shall mistris be of it, saue I alone.
And so adieu good Madam, neuer more,
Will I my Masters teares to you deplore.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Yet come againe: for thou perhaps mayst moue
That heart which now abhorres, to like his loue.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: No faith, Ile not stay a iot longer:

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Thy reason deere venom, giue thy reason.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: You must neede^ yeelde your reason, Sir Andrew?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Marry I saw your Neece do more fauours to the Counts Seruing-man, then euer she bestow'd vpon mee: I saw't i' th Orchard.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Did she see the while, old boy, tell me that.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: As plaine as I see you now.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: This was a great argument of loue in her toward you.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: S'light; will you make an Asse o'me.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: I will proue it legitimate sir, vpon the Oathes of iudgement, and reason.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: And they haue beene grand Iurie men, since before Noah was a Saylor.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Shee did shew fauour to the youth in your sight, onely to exasperate you, to awake your dormouse valour, to put fire in your Heart, and brimstone in your Liuer: you should then haue accosted her, and with some excellent iests, fire-new from the mint, you should haue bangd the youth into dumbenesse: this was look'd for at your hand, and this was b^ulkt: the double gilt of this opportunitie you let time wash off. and you are now sayld into the North of my Ladies opinion, where you will hang like an ysickle on a Dutchmans beard, vnlesse you do redeeme it, by some laudable attempt, either of valour or policie.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And't be any way, it must be with Valour, for policie I hate: I had as liefe be a Brownist, as a Politician.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Why then build me thy fortunes vpon the basis of valour. Challenge me the Counts youth to sight with him hurt him in eleuen places, my Neece shall take note of it, and assure thy selfe, there is no loue-Broker in the world, can more preuaile in mans commendation with woman, then report of valour.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: There is no way but this sir Andrew.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Will either of you beare me a challenge to him?

speeches.speaker: To
prose: ^o, write it in a martial hand, be curst and briefe: it is no matter how wittie, so it bee eloquent, and full of inuention: taunt hi^ with the license of Inke: if thou thou'st him some thrice, it shall not be amisse, and as many Lyes, as will lye in thy sheete of paper, although the sheete were bigge enough for the bedde of Ware in England, set 'em downe, go about it. Let there bee gaulle enough in thy inke, though thou write with a Goo^e-pen, no matter: about it.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Where shall I finde you?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Wee'l call thee at the Cubiculo: Go.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: This is a deere Manakin to you Sir Toby.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I haue beene deere to him lad, some two thousand strong, or so.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: We shall haue a rare Letter from him; but you'le not deliuer't.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Neuer trust me then: and by all meanes stirre on the youth to an answer. I thinke Oxen and waine-ropes cannot hale them together. For Andrew, if he were open'd and you finde so much blood in his Liuer, as will clog the foote of a flea, Ile eate the rest of th' anatomy.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: And his opposit the youth beares in his visage no great presage of cruelty.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Looke where the youngest Wren of mine comes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: If you desire the spleene, and will laughe your selues into stitches, follow me; yond gull Maluolio is turned Heathen, a verie Renegatho; for there is no christian that meanes to be saued by beleeuing rightly, can euer beleeue such impossible passages of grossenesse. Hee's in yellow stockings.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: And crosse garter'd?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Most villanously: like a Pedant that keepes a Schoole i' th Church: I haue dogg'd him like his murtherer. He does obey euery point of the Letter that I dropt, to betray him: He does smile his face into more lynes, then is in the new Mappe, with the augmentation of the Indies: you haue not seene such a thing as tis: I can hardly forbeare hu^ling things at him, I know my Ladie will strike him: if shee doe, hee'l smile, and take't for a great fauour.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come bring vs, bring vs where he is.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I would not by my will have troubled you,
But since you make your pleasure of your paines,
I will no further chide you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I could not stay behinde you: my desire
(More sharpe then filed steele) did spurre me forth,
And not all loue to see you (though so much
As might haue drawne one to a longer voyage)
But iealousie, what might befall your rrauell,
Being skillesse in these parts: which to a stranger,
Vnguided, and vnfriended, often proue
Rough, and vnhospitable. My willing loue,
The rather by these arguments of feare
Set forth in your pursuite.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: My kinde Anthonio,
I can no other answer make, but thankes,
And thankes: and euer oft good turnes,
Are shuffel'd off with such vncurrant pay:
But were my worth, as is my conscience firme,
You should finde better dealing: what's to do?
Shall we go see the reliques of this Towne?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: To morrow sir, best first go see your Lodging?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I am not weary, and 'tis long to night
I pray you let vs satisfie our eyes
With the memorials, and the things of fame
That do renowne this City.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Would youl'd pardon me:
I do not without danger walke these streetes.
Once in a sea-fight 'gainst the Count his gallies,
I did some seruice, of such note indeede,
That were I tane heere, it would scarse be answer'd.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Belike you slew great number of his people.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Th offence is not of such a bloody nature,
Albeit the quality of the time, and quarrell
Might well haue giuen vs bloody argument:
It might haue since bene answer'd in repaying
What we tooke from them, which for Traffiques sake
Most of our City did. Onely my selfe stood out,
For which if I be lapsed in this place
I shall pay deere.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Do not then walke too open.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It doth not fit me: hold sir, here's my purse,
In the South Suburbes at the Elephant
Is best to lodge: I will bespeake our dyet,
Whiles you beguile the time, and feed your knowledge
With viewing of the Towne, there shall you haue me.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Why I your purse?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Haply your eye shall light vpon some toy
You haue desire to purchase: and your store
I thinke is not for idle Markets, sir.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Ile be your purse-bearer, and leaue you
For an houre.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: To th' Elephant.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: I do remember.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I haue sent after him, he sayes hee'l come:
How shall I feast him? What bestow of him?
For youth is bought more oft, then begg'd, or borrow'd.
I speake too loud: Where's Maluolio, he is sad, and ciuill,
And suites well for a seruant with my fortunes,
Where is Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: He's comming Madame:
But in very strange manner. He is sure possest Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Why what's the matter, does he raue?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: No Madam, he does nothing but smile: your Ladyship were best to haue some guard about you, if hee come, for sure the man is tainted in's wits.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Go call him hither.
I am as madde as hee,
If sad and merry madnesse equall bee.
How now Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sweet Lady, ho, ho.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Smil'st thou? I sent for thee vpon a sad occasion.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Sad Lady, I could be sad:
This does make some obstruction in the blood:
This crosse-gartering, but what of that?
If it please the eye of one, it is with me as the very true
Sonnet is: Please one, and please all.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Why how doest thou man?
What is the matter with thee?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Not blacke in my minde, though yellow in my legges: It did come to his hands, and Commaunds shall be executed. I thinke we doe know the sweet Romane hand.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Wilt thou go to bed Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: To bed? I sweet heart, and Ile come to thee.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: God comfort thee: Why dost thou smile so, and kisse thy hand so oft?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: How do you Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Maluo.
verse: At your request:
Yes Nightingales answere Dawes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why appeare you with this ridiculous boldnesse before my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Be not afraid of greatnesse: 'twas well writ.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What meanst thou by that Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Some are borne great.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Some atcheeue greatnesse.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What sayst thou?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: And some haue greatnesse thrust vpon them.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Heauen restore thee.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Remember who commended thy yellow stockings.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Thy yellow stockings?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: And wish'd to see thee crosse garter'd.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Crosse garter'd?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Go too, thou art made, if thou desir'st to be so.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Am I made?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: If not, let me see thee a seruant still.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Why this is verie Midsommer madnesse.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Madame, the young Gentleman of the Count Orsino's is return'd, I could hardly entreate him backe: he attends your Ladyships pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Ile come to him.
prose: Good Maria, let this fellow be look^d too. Where's my Cosine Toby, let some of my people haue a speciall care of him, I would not haue him miscarrie for the halfe of my Dowry.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Oh ho, do you come neere me now: no worse man then sir Toby to looke to me. This concurres directly with the Letter, she sends him on purpose, that I may appeare stubborne to him: for she incites me to that in the Letter. Cast thy humble slough sayes she: be opposite with a Kinsman, surly with seruants, let thy tongue langer with arguments of state, put thy selfe into the tricke of singularity: and consequently setts downe the manner how: as a sad face, a reuerend carriage, a slow tongue, in the habite of some Sir of note, and so foorth. I haue lymde her, but it is Ioues doing, and Ioue make me thankefull. And when she went away now, let this Fellow be look'd too: Fellow? not Maluolio, nor after my degree, but Fellow. Why euery thing adheres togither, that no dramme of a scruple, no scruple of a scruple, no obstacle, no incredulous or vnsafe circumstance: What can be saide? Nothing that can be, can come betweene me, and the full prospect of my hopes. Well Ioue, not I, is the doer of this, and he is to be thanked.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Which way is hee in the name of sanctity. If all the diuels of hell be drawne in little, and Legion himselfe possest him, yet Ile speake to him.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Heere he is, heere he is: how ist with you sir?
How ist with you man?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Go off, I discard you: let me enioy my priuate: go off.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Lo, how hollow the s^end speakes within him; did not I tell you? Sir Toby, my Lady prayes you to haue a care of him.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Ah ha, does she so?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Go too, go too: peace, peace, wee must deale gently with him: Let me alone. How do you Maluolio? How ist with you? What man, defie the diuell: consider, he's an enemy to mankinde.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Do you know what you say?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: La you, and you speake ill of the diuell, how he takes it at heart Pray God he be not bewitch'd.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Carry his water to th' wise woman.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Marry and it shall be done to morrow morning if I liue. My Lady would not loose him for more then ile say.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: How now mistris?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Oh Lord.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Prethee hold thy peace, this is not the way: Doe you not see you moue him? Let me alone with him.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: No way but gentlenesse, gently, gently: the Fiend is rough, and will not be roughly vs'd.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Why how now my bawcock? how dost yu chuck?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I biddy, come with me. What man, tis not for grauity to play at cherrie pit with sathan Hang him foul Col^i^r.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Get him to say his prayers, good sir Toby gette him to pray.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: My prayers Minx.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: No I warrant you, he will not heare of godlynesse.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Go hang your selues all: you are ydle shallowe things, I am not of your element, you shall knowe more heereafter.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Ist possible?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: If this were plaid vpon a stage now, I could condemne it as an improbable fiction.

speeches.speaker: To
prose: His very genius hath taken the infection of the deuice man.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Nay pursue him now, least the deuice take ayre, and taint.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Why we shall make him mad indeede.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: The house will be the quieter.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come, wee'l haue him in a darke room & bound. My Neece is already in the beleefe that he's mad: we may carry it thus for our pleasure, and his pennance, til our very pastime tyred out of breath, prompt vs to haue mercy on him: at which time, we wil bring the deuice to the bar and crowne thee for a finder of madmen: but see, but see.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: More matter for a May morning.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Heere's the Challenge, reade it: I warrant there's vinegar and pepper in't.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Ist so sawcy?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I, ist? I warrant him: do but read.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Giue me.
Youth, whatsoeuer thou art, thou art but a scuruy fellow.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Good, and valiant.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Wonder not, nor admire not in thy minde why I doe call thee so, for I will shew thee no reason for't.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: A good note, that keepes you from the blow of ye Law

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Thou comst to the Lady Oliuia, and in my sight she vses thee kindly: but thou lyest in thy throat, that is not the matter I challenge thee for.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Very breefe, and to exceeding good sence-lesse.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I will way-lay thee going home, where if it be thy chance to kill me.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Good.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Thou kilst me like a rogue and a villaine.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Still you keepe o' th windie side of the Law: good.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
prose: Fartheewell, and God haue mercie vpon one of our soules. He may haue mercie vpon mine, but my hope is better, and so looke to thy selfe. Thy friend as thou vsest him, & thy sworne enemie, Andrew Ague-cheeke.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: If this Letter moue him not, his legges cannot:
Ile giu't him.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: You may haue verie sit occasion fot't: he is now in some commerce with my Ladie, and will by and by depart.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Go sir Andrew: scout mee for him at the corner of the Orchard like a bum-Baylie: so soone as euer thou seest him, draw, and as thou draw'st, sweare horrible: for ^t comes to passe oft, that a terrible oath, with a swaggering accent sharpely twang'd off, giues manhoode more approbation, then euer proofe it selfe would haue earn'd him. Away.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Nay let me alone for swearing.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Now will not I deliuer his Letter: for the behauiour of the yong Gentleman, giues him out to be of good capacity, and breeding: his employment betweene his Lord and my Neece, confirmes no lesse. Therefore, this Letter being so excellently ignorant, will breed no terror in the youth: he will finde it comes from a Clodde-pole. But sir, I will deliuer his Challenge by word of mouth; set vpon Ague-cheeke a notable report of valor, and driue the Gentleman (as I know his youth will aptly receiue it) into a most hideous opinion of his rage, skill, furie, and impetuositie. This will so fright them both, that they wil kill one another by the looke, like Cockatrices.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Heere he comes with your Neece, giue them way till he take leaue, and presently after him.

speeches.speaker: To
prose: I wil meditate the while vpon some horrid message for a Challenge.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I haue said too much vnto a hart of stone,
And laid mine honour too vnchary on't:
There's something in me that reproues my fault:
But such a head-strong potent fault it is,
That it but mockes reproofe.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: With the same hauiour that your passion beares,
Goes on my Masters greefes.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Heere, weare this Iewell for me, tis my picture:
Refuse it not, it hath no tongue, to vex you:
And I beseech you come againe to morrow.
What shall you aske of me that Ile deny,
That honour (sau'd) may vpon asking giue.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Nothing but this, your true loue for my master.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: How with mine honor may I giue him that,
Which I haue giuen to you.

speeches.speaker: Vio
prose: I will acquit you.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Well. come againe to morrow: far-thee-well,
A Fiend like thee might beare my soule to hell.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Gentleman, God saue thee.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: And you sir.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: That defence thou hast, betake the too't: of what nature the wrongs are thou hast done him, I knowe not: but thy intercepter full of despight, bloody as the Hunter, attends thee at the Orchard end: dismount thy tucke, be yare in thy preparation, for thy assaylant is quick, skilfull, and deadly.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: You mistake sir I am sure, no man hath any quarrell to me: my remembrance is very free and cleere from any image of offence done to any man.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: You'l finde it otherwise I assure you: therefore, if you hold your life at any price, betake you to your gard: for your opposite hath in him what youth, strength, skill, and wrath, can furnish man withall.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I pray you sir what is he?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: He is knight dubb'd with vnhatch'd Rapier, and on carpet consideration, but he is a diuell in priuate brall, soules and bodies hath he diuorc'd three, and his incensement at this moment is so implacable, that satisfaction can be none, but by pangs of death and sepulcher: Hob, nob, is his word: giu't or take't.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I will returne againe into the house, and desire some conduct of the Lady. I am no fighter, I haue heard of some kinde of men, that put quarrells purposely on others, to taste their valour: belike this is a man of that quirke.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Sir, no: his indignation deriues it selfe out of a very computent iniurie, therefore get you on, and giue him his desire. Backe you shall not to the house, vnlesse you vndertake that with me, which with as much safetie you might answer him: therefore on, or strippe your sword starke naked: for meddle you must that's certain, or forsweare to weare iron about you.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: This is as vnciuill as strange. I beseech you doe me this courteous office, as to know of the Knight what my offence to him is: it is something of my negligence, nothing of my purpose.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I will doe so. Signiour Fabian, stay you by this Gentleman, till my returne.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Pray you sir, do you know of this matter?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: I know the knight is incenst against you, euen to a mortall arbitrement, but nothing of the circumstance more.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I beseech you what manner of man is he?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Nothing of that wonderfull promise to read him by his forme, as you are like to finde him in the proofe of his valour. He is indeede sir, the most skilfull, bloudy, & fatall opposite that you could possibly haue found in anie part of Illyria: will you walke towards him, I will make your peace with him, if I can.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I shall bee much bound to you for't: I am one, that had rather go with sir Priest, then sir knight: I care not who knowes so much of my mettle.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Why man hee^s a verie diuell, I haue not seen such a firago: I had a passe with him, rapier, scabberd, and all: and he giues me the stucke in with such a mortall motion that it is ineuitable: and on the answer, he payes you as surely, as your feete hits the ground they step on. They say, he has bin Fencer to the Sophy.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Pox on't, Ile not meddle with him.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: I but he will not now be pacified,
Fabian can scarse hold him yonder.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Plague on't, and I thought he had beene vallant, and so cunning in Fence, I'de haue seene him damn'd ere I'de haue challeng'd him. Let him let the matter slip, and Ile giue him my horse, gray Capilet.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Ile make the motion: stand heere, make a good shew on't, this shall end without the perdition of soules, marry Ile ride your horse as well as I ride you.
I haue his horse to take vp the quarrell, I haue perswaded him the youths a diuell.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: He is as horribly conceited of him: and pants, & lookes pale, as if a Beare were at his heeles.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: There's no remedie sir, he will fight with you for's oath sake: marrie hee hath better bethought him of his quarrell, and hee findes that now scarse to bee worth talking of: therefore draw for the supportance of his vowe, he protests he will not hurt you.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Pray God defend me: a little thing would make me tell them how much I lacke of a man.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Giue ground if you see him furious.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come sir Andrew, there's no remedie, the Gentleman will for his honors sake haue one bowt with you: he cannot by the Duello auoide it: but hee has promised me, as he is a Gentleman and a Soldiour, he will not hurt you. Come on, too't.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Pray God he keepe his oath.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I do assure you tis against my will.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Put vp your sword: if this yong Gentleman
Haue done offence, I take the fault on me:
If you offend him, I for him defie you.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: You sir? Why, what are you?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: One sir, that for his loue dares yet do more
Then you haue heard him brag to you he will.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Nay, if you be an vndertaker, I am for you.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: O good sir Toby hold: heere come the Officers.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Ile be with you anon.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Pray sir, put your sword vp if you please.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Marry will I sir: and for that I promis'd you Ile be as good as my word. Hee will beare you easily, and raines well.

speeches.speaker: 1. Off.
prose: This is the man, do thy Office.

speeches.speaker: 2 Off.
prose: Anthonio, I arrest thee at the suit of Count Orsino

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: You do mistake me sir.

speeches.speaker: 1. Off.
verse: No sir, no iot: I know your fauour well:
Though now you haue no sea-cap on your head:
Take him away, he knowes I know him well.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I must obey. This comes with seeking you:
But there's no remedie, I shall answer it:
What will you do: now my necessitie
Makes me to aske you for my purse. It greeues mee
Much more, for what I cannot do for you,
Then what befals my selfe: you stand amaz'd,
But be of comfort.

speeches.speaker: 2 Off.
prose: Come sir away.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I must entreat of you some of that money.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: What money sir?
For the fayre kindnesse you haue shew'd me heere,
And part being prompted by your present trouble,
Out of my leane and low ability
Ile lend you some^hing: my hauing is not much,
Ile make diuision of my present with you:
Hold, there's halfe my Coffer.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Will you deny me now,
Ist possible that my deserts to you
Can lacke perswasion. Do not tempt my misery,
Least that it make me so vnsound a man
As to vpbraid you with those kindnesses
That I haue done for you.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I know of none,
Nor know I you by voyce, or any feature:
I hate ingratitude more in a man,
Then lying, vainnesse, babling drunkennesse,
Or any taint of vice, whose strong corruption
Inhabites our fraile blood.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Oh heauens themselues.

speeches.speaker: 2. Off.
prose: Come sir, I pray you go.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let me speake a little. This youth that you see heere,
I snatch'd one halfe out of the iawes of death,
Releeu'd him with such sanctitie of Ioue;
And to his image, which me thought did promise
Most venerable worth, did I deuotion.

speeches.speaker: 1. Off.
prose: What's that to vs, the time goes by: Away.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: But oh, how vilde an idoll proues this God:
Thou hast Sebastian done good feature, shame.
In Nature, there's no blemish but the minde:
None can be call'd deform'd, but the vnkinde.
Vertue is beauty, but the beauteous euill
Are empty trunkes, ore-flourish'd by the deuill.

speeches.speaker: 1. Off.
verse: The man growes mad, away with him:
Come, come sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Leade me on.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Me thinkes his words do from such passion flye
That he beleeues himselfe, so do not I:
Proue true imagination, oh proue true,
That I deere brother, be now tane for you.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come hither Knight, come hither Fabian: Weel whisper ore a couplet or two of most sage sawes.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: He nam'd Sebastian: I my brother know
Yet liuing in my glasse: euen such, and so
In fauour was my Brother, and he went
Still in this fashion, colour, ornament,
For him I imitate: Oh if it proue,
Tempests are kinde, and salt waues fresh in loue.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: A very dishonest paltry boy, and more a coward then a Hare, his dishonesty appeares, in leauing his frend heere in necessity, and denying him: and for his cowardship aske Fabian.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: A Coward, a most deuout Coward, religious in it.

speeches.speaker: And,
prose: Slid Ile after him againe, and beate him.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Do, cuffe him soundly, but neuer draw thy sword

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And I do not.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Come, let's see the euent.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: I dare lay any money, twill be nothing yet.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Will you make me beleeue, that I am not sent for you?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Go too, go too, thou art a foolish fellow,
Let me be cleere of thee.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Well held our yfaith: No, I do not know you, nor I am not sent to you by my Lady, to bid you come speake with her: nor your name is not Master C^sario, nor this is not my nose neyther: Nothing that is so, is so.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: I prethee vent thy folly some-where else, thou know'st not me.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Vent my folly: He has heard that word of some great man, and now applyes it to a foole. Vent my folly: I am affraid this great lubber the World will proue a Cockney: I prethee now vngird thy strangenes, and tell me what I shall vent to my Lady? Shall I vent to hir that thou art comming?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: I prethee foolish greeke depart from me, there's money for thee, if you tarry longer, I shall giue worse paiment.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: By my troth thou hast an open hand: these Wisemen that giue fooles money, get themselues a good report, after foureteene yeares purchase.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Now sir, haue I met you again: ther's for you.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Why there's for thee, and there, and there,
Are all the people mad?

speeches.speaker: To
prose: Hold sir, or Ile throw your dagger ore the house.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: This will I tell my Lady straight, I would not be in some of your coats for two pence.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come on sir, hold.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Nay let him alone, Ile go another way to worke with him: Ile haue an action of Battery against him, if there be any law in Illyria: though I stroke him first, yet it's no matter for that.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Let go thy hand.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Come sir, I will not let you go. Come my yong souldier put vp your yron: you are well flesh'd: Come on.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I will be free from thee. What wouldst yu now?
If thou dar'st tempt me further, draw thy sword.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: What, what? Nay then I must haue an Ounce or two of this malapert blood from you.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Hold Toby, on thy life I charge thee hold.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Will it be euer thus? Vngracious wretch,
Fit for the Mountaines, and the barbarous Caues,
Where manners nere were preach'd: out of my sight.
Be not offended, deere Cesario:
Rudesbey be gone. I prethee gentle friend,
Let thy fayre wisedome, not thy passion sway
In this vnciuill, and vniust extent
Against thy peace. Go with me to my house,
And heare thou there how many fruitlesse prankes
This Ruffian hath botch'd vp, that thou thereby
Mayst smile at this: Thou shalt not choose but goe:
Do not denie, beshrew his soule for mee,
He started one poore heart of mine, in thee.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: What rellish is in this? How runs the streame?
Or I am mad, or else this is a dreame:
Let fancie still my sense in Lethe sleepe,
If it be thus to dreame, still let me sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Nay come I prethee, would thoud'st be rul'd by me

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Madam, I will.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: O say so, and so be.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Nay, I prethee put on this gown, & this beard, make him beleeue thou art sir Topas the Curate, doe it quickly. Ile call sir Toby the whilst.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose:
Well, Ile put it on, and I will dissemble my selfe in't, and I would I were the first that euer dissembled in

such a gowne. I am not tall enough to become the function well, nor leane enough to bee thought a good Studient: but to be said an honest man and a good houskeeper goes as fairely, as to say, a carefull man, & a great scholler. The Competitors enter.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Ioue blesse thee M. Parson.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Bonos dies sir Toby: for as the old hermit of Prage that neuer saw pen and inke, very wittily sayd to a Neece of King Gorbodacke, that that is, is: so I being M. Parson, am M. Parson; for what is that, but that? and is, but is?

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: To him ^r Topas.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: What hoa, I say, Peace in this prison.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: The knaue counterfets well: a good knaue.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Who cals there?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Sir Topas the Curate, who comes to visit Maluolio the Lunaticke.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir Topas, sir Topas, good sir Topas goe to my Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Out hyperbolicall fiend, how vexest thou this man? Talkest thou nothing but of Ladies?

speeches.speaker: Tob.
prose: Well said M. Parson.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir Topas, neuer was man thus wronged, good sir Topas do not thinke I am mad: they haue layde mee heere in hideous darknesse.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Fye, thou dishonest sathan: I call thee by the most modest termes, for I am one of those gentle ones, that will vse the diuell himselfe with curtesie: sayst thou that house is darke?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: As hell sir Topas.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why it hath bay Windowes transparant as baricadoes, and the cleere stores toward the South north, are as lustrous as Ebony: and yet complainest thou of obstruction?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I am not mad sir Topas, I say to you this house is darke.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Madman thou errest: I say there is no darknesse but ignorance, in which thou art more puzel'd then the Aegyptians in their fogge.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I say this house is as darke as Ignorance, thogh Ignorance were as darke as hell; and I say there was neuer man thus abus'd, I am no more madde then you are, make the triall of it in any constant question.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: What is the opinion of Pythagoras concerning Wilde-fowle?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: That the soule of our grandam, might happily inhabite a bird.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: What thinkst thou of his opinion?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I thinke nobly of the soule, and no way aproue his opinion.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Fare thee well: remaine thou still in darkenesse, thou shalt hold th' opinion of Pythagoras, ere I will allow of thy wits, and feare to kill a Woodcocke, lest thou dispossesse the soule of thy grandam. Fare thee well.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir Topas, sir Topas.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
prose: My most exquisite sir Topas.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Nay I am for all waters.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Thou mightst haue done this without thy berd and gowne, he sees thee not.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: To him in thine owne voyce, and bring me word how thou findst him: I would we were well ridde of this knauery. If he may bee conueniently deliuer'd, I would he were, for I am now so farre in offence with my Niece, that I cannot pursue with any safety this sport the vppeshot. Come by and by to my Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Hey Robin, iolly Robin, tell me how thy Lady does.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Foole.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: My Lady is vnkind, perdie.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Foole.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Alas why is she so?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Foole, I say.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: She loues another. Who calles, ha?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Good foole, as euer thou wilt deserue well at my hand, helpe me to a Candle, and pen, inke, and paper: as I am a Gentleman, I will liue to bee thankefull to thee for't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: M. Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I good Foole.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Alas sir, how fell you besides your fiue witts?

speeches.speaker: Mall.
prose: Foole, there was neuer man so notoriouslie abus'd: I am as well in my wits (foole) as thou art.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: But as well: then you are mad indeede, if you be no better in your wits then a foole.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: They haue heere propertied me: keepe mee in darkenesse, send Ministers to me, Asses, and doe all they can to face me out of my wits.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Aduise you what you say: the Minister is heere. Maluolio, Maluolio, thy wittes the heauens restore: endeauour thy selfe to sleepe, and leaue thy vaine bibble babble.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir Topas.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Maintaine no words with him good fellow.
Who I sir, not I sir. God buy you good sir Topas: Marry Amen. I will sir, I will.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Foole, foole, foole I say.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Alas sir be patient. What say you sir, I am shent for speaking to you.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Good foole, helpe me to some light, and some paper, I tell thee I am as well in my wittes, as any man in Illyria.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Well-a-day, that you were sir.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: By this hand I am: good foole, some inke, paper, and light: and conuey what I will set downe to my Lady: it shall aduantage thee more, then euer the bearing of Letter did.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I will help you too't. But tel me true, are you not mad indeed, or do you but counterfeit.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Beleeue me I am not, I tell thee true.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Nay, Ile nere beleeue a madman till I see his brains
I will fetch you light, and paper, and inke.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Foole, Ile requite it in the highest degree:
I prethee be gone.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I am gone sir, and anon sir,
Ile be with you againe:
In a trice, like to the old vice,
your neede to sustaine.
Who with dagger of lath, in his rage and his wrath,
cries ah ha, to the diuell:
Like a mad lad, paire thy nayles dad,
Adieu good man diuell.
This is the ayre, that is the glorious Sunne,
This pearle she gaue me, I do feel't, and see't,
And though tis wonder that enwraps me thus,
Yet 'tis not madnesse. Where's Anthonio then,
I could not finde him at the Elephant,
Yet there he was, and there I found this credite,
That he did range the towne to seeke me out,
His councell now might do me golden seruice,
For though my soule disputes well with my sence,
That this may be some error, but no madnesse,
Yet doth this accident and flood of Fortune,
So farre exceed all instance, all discourse,
That I am readie to distrust mine eyes,
And wrangle with my reason that perswades me
To any other trust, but that I am mad,
Or else the Ladies mad; yet if 'twere so,
She could not sway her house, command her followers,
Take, and giue backe affayres, and their dispatch,
With such a smooth, discreet, and stable bearing
As I perceiue she do's: there's something in't
That is deceiueable. But heere the Lady comes.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Blame not this haste of mine: if you meane well
Now go with me, and with this holy man
Into the Chantry by: there before him,
And vnderneath that consecrated roofe,
Plight me the full assurance of your faith,
That my most iealious, and too doubtfull soule
May liue at peace. He shall conceale it,
Whiles you are willing it shall come to note,
What time we will our celebration keepe
According to my birth, what do you say?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Ile follow this good man, and go with you,
And hauing sworne truth, euer will be true.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Then lead the way good father, & heauens so shine,
That they may fairely note this acte of mine.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Now as thou lou'st me, let me see his Letter.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Good M. Fabian, grant me another request.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Any thing.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Do not desire to see this Letter.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: This is to giue a dogge, and in recompence desire my dogge againe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Belong you to the Lady Oliuia, friends?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I sir, we are some of her trappings.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I know thee well: how doest thou my good Fellow?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Truely sir, the better for my foes, and the worse for my friends.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Iust the contrary: the better for thy friends.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No sir, the worse.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: How can that be?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Marry sir, they praise me, and make an asse of me, now my foes tell me plainly, I am an Asse: so that by my foes sir, I profit in the knowledge of my selfe, and by my friends I am abused: so that conclusions to be as kisses, if your foure negatiues make your two affirmatiues, why then the worse for my friends, and the better for my foes.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Why this is excellent.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: By my troth sir, no: though it please you to be one of my friends.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Thou shalt not be the worse for me, there's gold.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: But that it would be double dealing sir, I would you could make it another.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: O you giue me ill counsell.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Put your grace in your pocket sir, for this once, and let your flesh and blood obey it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Well, I will be so much a sinner to be a double dealer: there's another.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Primo, secundo, tertio, is a good play, and the olde saying is, the third payes for all: the triplex sir, is a good tripping measure, or the belles of S. Bennet sir, may put you in minde, one, two, three.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: You can foole no more money out of mee at this throw: if you will let your Lady know I am here to speak with her, and bring her along with you, it may awake my bounty further.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Marry sir, lullaby to your bountie till I come agen. I go sir, but I would not haue you to thinke, that my desire of hauing is the sinne of couetousnesse: but as you say sir, let your bounty take a nappe, I will awake it anon.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Here comes the man sir, that did rescue mee.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: That face of his I do remember well,
yet when I saw it last, it was besmear'd
As blacke as Vulcan, in the smoake of warre:
A bawbling Vessell was he Captaine of,
For shallow draught and bulke vnprizable,
With which such scathfull grapple did he make,
With the most noble bottome of our Fleete,
That very enuy, and the tongue of losse
Cride fame and honor on him: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: 1 Offi.
verse: Orsino, this is that Anthonio
That tooke the Phoenix, and her fraught from Candy,
And this is he that did the Tiger boord,
When your yong Nephew Titus lost his legge;
Heere in the streets, desperate of shame and state,
In priuate brabble did we apprehend him.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: He did me kindnesse sir, drew on my side,
But in conclusion put strange speech vpon me,
I know not what 'twas, but distraction.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Notable Pyrate, thou salt-water Theefe,
What foolish boldnesse brought thee to their mercies,
Whom thou in termes so bloudie, and so deere
Hast made thine enemies?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Orsino: Noble sir,
Be pleas'd that I shake off these names you giue mee:
Anthonio neuer yet was Theefe, or Pyrate,
Though I confesse, on base and ground enough
Orsino's enemie. A witchcraft drew me hither:
That most ingratefull boy there by your side,
From the rude seas enrag'd and foamy mouth
Did I redeeme: a wracke past hope he was:
His life I gaue him, and did thereto adde
My loue without retention, or restraint,
All his in dedication. For his sake,
Did I expose my selfe (pure for his loue)
Into the danger of this aduerse Towne,
Drew to defend him, when he was beset:
Where being apprehended, his false cunning
(Not meaning to partake with me in danger)
Taught him to face me out of his acquaintance,
And grew a twentie yeeres remoued thing
While one would winke: denide me mine owne purse,
Which I had recommended to his vse,
Not halfe an houre before.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: How can this be?

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: When came he to this Towne?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: To day my Lord: and for three months before,
No intrim, not a minutes vacancie,
Both day and night did we keepe companie.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Heere comes the Countesse, now heauen walkes on earth:
But for thee fellow, fellow thy words are madnesse,
Three monthes this youth hath tended vpon mee,
But more of that anon. Take him aside.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: What would my Lord, but that he may not haue,
Wherein Oliuia may seeme seruiceable?
Cesario, you do not keepe promise with me.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Madam:

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Gracious Oliuia.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What do you say Cesario? Good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: My Lord would speake, my dutie hushes me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: If it be ought to the old tune my Lord,
It is as fat and fulsome to mine eare
As howling after Musicke.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Still so cruell?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Still so constant Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What to peruersenesse? you vnciuill Ladie
To whose ingrate, and vnauspicious Altars
My soule the faithfull'st offrings haue breath'd out
That ere deuotion tender'd. What shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Ol
prose: Euen what it please my Lord, that shal becom him

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why should I not, (had I the heart to do it)
Like to th' Egyptian theefe, at point of death
Kill what I loue: (a sauage iealousie,
That sometime sauours nobly) but heare me this:
Since you to non-regardance cast my faith,
And that I partly know the instrument
That screwes me from my true place in your fauour:
Liue you the Marble-brested Tirant still.
But this your Minion, whom I know you loue,
And whom, by heauen I sweare, I tender deerely,
Him will I teare out of that cruell eye,
Where he sits crowned in his masters spight.
Come boy with me, my thoughts are ripe in mischiefe:
Ile sacrifice the Lambe that I do loue,
To spight a Rauens heart within a Doue.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: And I most iocund, apt, and willinglie,
To do you rest, a thousand deaths would dye.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Where goes Cesario?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: After him I loue,
More then I loue these eyes, more then my life,
More by all mores, then ere I shall loue wife.
If I do feigne, you witnesses aboue
Punish my life, for tainting of my loue.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Aye me detested, how am I beguil'd?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Who does beguile you? who does do you wrong?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Hast thou forgot thy selfe? Is it so long?
Call forth the holy Father.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Come, away.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Whether my Lord? Cesario, Husband, stay.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Husband?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: I Husband. Can he that deny?

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Her husband, sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: No my Lord, not I.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Alas, it is the basenesse of thy feare,
That makes thee strangle thy propriety:
Feare not Cesario, take thy fortunes vp,
Be that thou know'st thou art, and then thou art
As great as that thou fear'st.
O welcome Father:
Father, I charge thee by thy reuerence
Heere to vnfold, though lately we intended
To keepe in darkenesse, what occasion now
Reueales before 'tis ripe: what thou dost know
Hath newly past, betweene this youth, and me.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: A Contract of eternall bond of loue,
Confirm'd by mutuall ioynder of your hands,
Attested by the holy close of lippes,
Strengthned by enterchangement of your rings,
And all the Ceremonie of this compact
Seal'd in my function, by my testimony:
Since when, my watch hath told me, toward my graue
I haue trauail'd but two houres.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O thou dissembling Cub: what wilt thou be
When time hath sow'd a grizzle on thy case?
Or will not else thy craft so quickely grow,
That thine owne trip shall be thine ouerthrow:
Farewell, and take her, but direct thy feete,
Where thou, and I (henceforth) may neuer meet.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: My Lord, I do protest.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: O do not sweare,
Hold little faith, though thou hast too much feare.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: For the loue of God a Surgeon, send one presently to sir Toby.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: H'as broke my head a-crosse, and has giuen Sir Toby a bloody Coxcombe too: for the loue of God your helpe, I had rather then forty pound I were at home.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Who has done this sir Andrew?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The Counts Gentleman, one Cesario: we tooke him for a Coward, but hee's the verie diuell incardinate.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: My Gentleman Cesario?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Odd's lifelings heere he is: you broke my head for nothing, and that that I did, I was set on to do't by sir Toby.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Why do you speake to me, I neuer hurt you:
you drew your sword vpon me without cause,
But I bespake you faire, and hurt you not.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: If a bloody coxcombe be a hurt, you haue hurt me: I thinke you set nothing by a bloody Coxecombe. Heere comes sir Toby halting, you shall heare more: but if he had not beene in drinke, hee would haue tickel'd you other gates then he did.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: How now Gentleman? how ist with you?

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: That's all one, has hurt me, and there's th' end on't:
Sot, didst see Dicke Surgeon, sot?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: O he's drunke sir Toby an houre agone: his eyes were set at eight i' th morning.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Then he's a Rogue, and a passy measures panyn: I hate a drunken rogue.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Away with him? Who hath made this hauocke with them?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Ile helpe you sir Toby, because we'll be drest together.

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: Will you helpe an Asse-head, and a coxcombe, & a knaue: a thin fac'd knaue, a gull?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Get him to bed, and let his hurt be look'd too.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I am sorry Madam I haue hurt your kinsman:
But had it beene the brother of my blood,
I must haue done no lesse with wit and safety.
You throw a strange regard vpon me, and by that
I do perceiue it hath offended you:
Pardon me (sweet one) euen for the vowes
We made each other, but so late ago.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: One face, one voice, one habit, and two persons,
A naturall Perspectiue, that is, and is not.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Anthonio: O my deere Anthonio,
How haue the houres rack'd, and tortur'd me,
Since I haue lost thee?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Sebastian are you?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: Fear'st thou that Anthonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How haue you made diuision of your selfe,
An apple cleft in two, is not more twin
Then these two creatures. Which is Sebastian?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Most wonderfull.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Do I stand there? I neuer had a brother:
Nor can there be that Deity in my nature
Of heere, and euery where. I had a sister,
Whom the blinde waues and surges haue deuour'd:
Of charity, what kinne are you to me?
What Countreyman? What name? What Parentage?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Of Messaline: Sebastian was my Father,
Such a Sebastian was my brother too:
So went he suited to his watery tombe:
If spirits can assume both forme and suite,
You come to fright vs.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: A spirit I am indeed,
But am in that dimension grossely clad,
Which from the wombe I did participate.
Were you a woman, a^ the rest goes euen,
I should my teares let fall vpon your cheeke,
And say, thrice welcome drowned Viola.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: My father had a moale vpon his brow.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
prose: And so had mine.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: And dide that day when Viola from her birth
Had numbred thirteene yeares.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: O that record is liuely in my soule,
He finished indeed his mortall acte
That day that made my sister thirteene yeares.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: If nothing lets to make vs happie both,
But this my masculine vsurp'd attyre:
Do not embrace me, till each circumstance,
Of place, time, fortune, do co-here and iumpe
That I am Viola, which to confirme,
Ile bring you to a Captaine in this Towne,
Where lye my maiden weeds: by whose gentle helpe,
I was preseru'd to serue this Noble Count:
All the occurrence of my fortune since
Hath beene betweene this Lady, and this Lord.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: So comes it Lady, you haue beene mistooke:
But Nature to her bias drew in that.
You would haue bin contracted to a Maid,
Nor are you therein (by my life) deceiu'd,
You are betroth'd both to a maid and man.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Be not amaz'd, right noble is his blood:
If this be so, as yet the glasse seemes true,
I shall haue share in this most happy wracke,
Boy, thou hast saide to me a thousand times,
Thou neuer should'st loue woman like to me.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: And all those sayings, will I ouer sweare,
And all those swearings keepe as true in soule,
As doth that Orbed Continent, the fire,
That seuers day ftom night.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Giue me thy hand,
And let me see thee in thy womans weedes.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: The Captaine that did bring me first on shore
Hath my Maides garments: he vpon some Action
Is now in durance, at Maluolio's suite,
A Gentleman, and follower of my Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: He shall inlarge him: fetch Maluolio hither,
And yet alas, now I remember me,
They say poore Gentleman, he's much distract.
A most extracting frensie of mine owne
From my remembrance, clearly banisht his.
How does he sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Cl.
prose: Truely Madam, he holds Belzebub at the staues end as well as a man in his case may do: has heere writ a letter to you, I should haue giuen't you to day morning. But as a madmans Epistles are no Gospels, so it skilles not much when they are deliuer'd.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Open't, and read it.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Looke then to be well edified, when the Foole deliuers the Madman. By the Lord Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: How now, art thou mad?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: No Madam, I do but reade madnesse: and your Ladyship will haue it as it ought to bee, you must allow Vox.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Prethee reade i' thy right wits.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: So I do Madona: but to reade his right wits, is to reade thus: therefore, perpend my Princesse, and giue eare.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Read it you, sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Reads. By the Lord Madam, you wrong me, and the world shall know it: Though you haue put mee into darkenesse, and giuen your drunken Cosine rule ouer me, yet haue I the benefit of my senses as well as your Ladieship. I haue your owne letter, that induced mee to the semblance I put on; with the which I doubt not, but to do my selfe much right, or you much shame: thinke of me as you please. I leaue my duty a little vnthought of, and speake out of my iniury.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Did he write this?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I Madame.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: This sauours not much of distraction.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: See him deliuer'd Fabian, bring him hither:
My Lord, so please you, these things further thought on,
To thinke me as well a sister, as a wife,
One day shall crowne th' alliance on't, so please you,
Heere at my house, and at my proper cost.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Madam, I am most apt t' embrace your offer:
Your Master quits you; and for your seruice done him,
So much against the mettle of your sex,
So farre beneath your soft and tender breeding,
And since you call'd me Master, for so long:
Heere is my hand, you shall from this time bee
your Masters Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: A sister, you are she.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Is this the Madman?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: I my Lord, this same: How now Maluolio?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Madam, you haue done me wrong,
Notorious wrong.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Haue I Maluolio? No.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Lady you haue, pray you peruse that Letter.
You must not now denie it is your hand,
Write from it if you can, in hand, or phrase,
Or say, tis not your seale, not your inuention:
You can say none of this. Well, grant it then,
And tell me in the modestie of honor,
Why you haue giuen me such cleare lights of fauour,
Bad me come smiling, and crosse-garter'd to you,
To put on yellow stockings, and to frowne
Vpon sir Toby, and the lighter people:
And acting this in an obedient hope,
Why haue you suffer'd me to be imprison'd,
Kept in a darke house, visited by the Priest,
And made the most notorious gecke and gull,
That ere inuention plaid on? Tell me why?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Alas Maluolio, this is not my writing,
Though I confesse much like the Charracter:
But out of question, tis Marias hand.
And now I do bethinke me, it was shee
First told me thou wast mad; then cam'st in smiling,
And in such formes, which heere were presuppos'd
Vpon thee in the Letter: prethee be content,
This practice hath most shrewdly past vpon thee:
But when we know the grounds, and authors of it,
Thou shalt be both the Plaintiffe and the Iudge
Of thine owne cause.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Good Madam heare me speake,
And let no quarrell, nor no braule to come,
Taint the condition of this present houre,
Which I haue wondred at. In hope it shall not,
Most freely I confesse my selfe, and Toby
Set this deuice against Maluolio heere,
Vpon some stubborne and vncourteous parts
