The merry Songs of Peace to all his Neighbours.
God shall be truely knowne, and those about her,
From her shall read the perfect way of Honour,
And by those claime their greatnesse; not by Blood.
Nor shall this peace sleepe with her: But as when
The Bird of Wonder dyes, the Mayden Phoenix,
Her Ashes new create another Heyre,
As great in admiration as her selfe.
So shall she leaue her Blessednesse to One,
(When Heauen shal call her from this clowd of darknes)
Who, from the sacred Ashes of her Honour
Shall Star-like rise, as great in fame as she was,
And so stand fix'd. Peace, Plenty, Loue, Truth, Terror,
That were the Seruants to this chosen Infant,
Shall then be his, and like a Vine grow to him;
Where euer the bright Sunne of Heauen shall shine,
His Honour, and the greatnesse of his Name,
Shall be, and make new Nations. He shall flourish,
And like a Mountaine Cedar, reach his branches,
To all the Plaines about him: Our Childrens Children
Shall see this, and blesse Heauen.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Thou speakest wonders.

speeches.speaker: Cran.
verse: She shall be to the happinesse of England,
An aged Princesse; many dayes shall see her,
And yet no day without a deed to Crowne it.
Would I had knowne no more: But she must dye,
She must, the Saints must haue her; yet a Virgin,
A most vnspotted Lilly shall she passe
To th' ground, and all the World shall mourne her.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: O Lord Archbishop
Thou hast made me now a man, neuer before
This happy Child, did I get any thing.
This Oracle of comfort, ha's so pleas'd me,
That when I am in Heauen, I shall desire
To see what this Child does, and praise my Maker.
I thanke ye all. To you my good Lord Maior,
And you good Brethren, I am much beholding:
I haue receiu'd much Honour by your presence,
And ye shall find me thankfull. Lead the way Lords,
Ye must all see the Queene, and she must thanke ye,
She will be sicke els. This day, no man thinke
'Has businesse at his house; for all shall stay:
This Little-One shall make it Holy-day.

plays.play_title: Mr. VVilliam Shakespeares comedies, histories, & tragedies Published according to the true originall copies.

segments.head: THE TRAGEDIE OF Troylus and Cressida. | Scoena Prima.

speeches.speaker: Troylus.
verse: CAll here my Varlet, Ile vnarme againe.
Why should I warre without the wals of Troy
That finde such cruell battell here within?
Each Troian that is master of his heart,
Let him to field, Troylus alas hath none.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Will this geere nere be mended?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: The Greeks are strong, & skilful to their strength,
Fierce to their skill, and to their fiercenesse Valiant:
But I am weaker then a womans teare;
Tamer then sleepe, fonder then ignorance;
Lesse valiant then the Virgin in the night,
And skillesse as vnpractis'd Infancie.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Well, I haue told you enough of this: For my part, Ile not meddle nor make no farther. Hee that will haue a Cake out of the Wheate, must needes tarry the grinding.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Haue I not tarried?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I the grinding; but you must tarry the bolting.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Haue I not tarried?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I the boulting; but you must tarry the leau'ing.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Still haue I tarried.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I, to the leauening: but heeres yet in the word hereafter, the Kneading, the making of the Cake, the heating of the Ouen, and the Baking; nay, you must stay the cooling too, or you may chance to burne your lips.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Patience her selfe, what Goddesse ere she be,
Doth lesser blench at sufferance, then I doe:
At Priams Royall Table doe I sit;
And when faire Cressid comes into my thoughts,
So (Traitor) then she comes, when she is thence.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Well:
She look'd yesternight fairer, then euer I saw her looke,
Or any woman else.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: I was about to tell thee, when my heart,
As wedged with a sigh, would riue in twaine,
Least Hector, or my Father should perceiue me:
I haue (as when the Sunne doth light a-scorne)
Buried this sigh, in wrinkle of a smile:
But sorrow, that is couch'd in seeming gladnesse,
Is like that mirth, Fate turnes to sudden sadnesse.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: And her haire were not somewhat darker then Helens, well go too, there were no more comparison betweene the Women. But for my part she is my Kinswoman, I would not (as they tearme it) praise it, but I wold some-body had heard her talke yesterday as I did: I will not dispraise your sister Cassandra's wit, but—

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Oh Pandarus! I tell thee Pandarus;
When I doe tell thee, there my hopes lye drown'd:
Reply not in how many Fadomes deepe
They lye indrench'd. I tell thee, I am mad
In Cressids loue. Thou answer'st she is Faire,
Powr'st in the open Vlcer of my heart,
Her Eyes, her Haire, her Cheeke, her Gate, her Voice,
Handlest in thy discourse. O that her Hand
(In whose comparison, all whites are Inke)
Writing their owne reproach; to whose soft seizure,
The Cignets Downe is harsh, and spirit of Sense
Hard as the palme of Plough-man. This thou tel'st me;
As true thou tel'st me, when I say I loue her:
But saying thus, instead of Oyle and Balme,
Thou lai'st in euery gash that loue hath giuen me,
The Knife that made it.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I speake no more then truth.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Thou do'st not speake so much.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Faith, Ile not meddle in't: Let her be as shee is, if she be faire, 'tis the better for her: and she be not, she ha's the mends in her owne hands.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Good Pandarus: How now Pandarus?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I haue had my Labour for my trauell, ill thought on of her, and ill thought on of you: Gone betweene and betweene, but small thankes for my labour.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: What art thou angry Pandarus? what with me?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Because she's Kinne to me, therefore shee's not so faire as Helen, and she were not kin to me, she would be as faire on Friday, as Helen is on Sunday. But what care I? I care not and she were a Black-a-Moore, 'tis all one to me.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Say I she is not faire?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: I doe not care whether you doe or no. Shee's a Foole to stay behinde her Father: Let her to the Greeks, and so Ile tell her the next time I see her: for my part, Ile meddle nor make no more i' th' matter.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Pandarus?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Not I.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Sweete Pandarus.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Pray you speake no more to me, I will leaue all as I found it, and there an end.

speeches.speaker: Tro.
verse: Peace you vngracious Clamors, peace rude sounds,
Fooles on both sides, Helen must needs be faire,
When with your bloud you daily paint her thus.
I cannot fight vpon this Argument:
It is too staru'd a subiect for my Sword,
But Pandarus: O Gods! How do you plague me?
I cannot come to Cressid but by Pandar,
And he's as teachy to be woo'd to woe,
As she is stubborne, chast, against all suite.
Tell me Apollo for thy Daphnes Loue
What Cressid is, what Pandar, and what we:
Her bed is India, there she lies, a Pearle.
Between our Ilium, and where shee recides
Let it be cald the wild and wandring flood,
Our selfe the Merchant, and this sayling Pandar,
Our doubtfull hope, our conuoy and our Barke.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: How now Prince Troylus?
Wherefore not a field?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Because not there; this womans answer sorts.
For womanish it is to be from thence:
What newes Aeneas from the field to day?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: That Paris is returned home, and hurt.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: By whom Aeneas?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Troylus by Menelaus.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Let Paris bleed, 'tis but a scar to scorne,
Paris is gor'd with Menelaus horne.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Harke what good sport is out of Towne to day.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Better at home, if would I might were may:
But to the sport abroad, are you bound thither?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: In all swift hast.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Come goe wee then togither.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Who were those went by?

speeches.speaker: Man.
prose: Queene Hecuba, and Hellen.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: And whether go they?

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Vp to the Easterne Tower,
Whose height commands as subiect all the vaile,
To see the battell: Hector whose pacience,
Is as a Vertue fixt, to day was mou'd:
He chides Andromache and strooke his Armorer,
And like as there were husbandry in Warre
Before the Sunne rose, hee was harnest lyte,
And to the field goe's he; where euery flower
Did as a Prophet weepe what it forsaw,
In Hectors wrath.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: What was his cause of anger?

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: The noise goe's this;
There is among the Greekes,
A Lord of Troian blood, Nephew to Hector,
They call him Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Good; and what of him?

speeches.speaker: Man.
prose: They say he is a very man per se and stands alone.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: So do all men, vnlesse they are drunke, sicke, or haue no legges.

speeches.speaker: Man.
prose: This man Lady, hath rob'd many beasts of their particular additions, he is as valiant as the Lyon, churlish as the Beare, slow as the Elephant: a man into whom nature hath so crowded humors, that his valour is crusht into folly, his folly sauced with discretion: there is no man hath a vertue, that he hath not a glimpse of, nor any man an attaint, but he carries some staine of it. He is melancholy without cause, and merry against the haire, hee hath the ioynts of euery thing, but euery thing so out of ioynt, that hee is a gowtie Briareus, many hands and no vse; or purblinded Argus, all eyes and no sight.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: But how should this man that makes me smile, make Hector angry?

speeches.speaker: Man.
prose: They say he yesterday cop'd Hector in the battell and stroke him downe, the disdaind & shame whereof, hath euer since kept Hector fasting and waking.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Who comes here?

speeches.speaker: Man.
prose: Madam your Vncle Pandarus.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Hectors a gallant man.

speeches.speaker: Man.
prose: As may be in the world Lady.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: What's that? what's that?

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Good morrow Vncle Pandarus.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Good morrow Cozen Cressid: what do you talke of? good morrow Alexander: how do you Cozen? when were you at Illium?

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: This morning Vncle.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: What were you talking of when I came? Was Hector arm'd and gon ere yea came to Illium? Hellen was not vp? was she?

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Hector was gone but Hellen was not vp?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: E'ene so; Hector was stirring early.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: That were we talking of, and of his anger.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Was he angry?

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: So he saies here.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: True he was so; I know the cause too, heele lay about him to day I can tell them that. and there's Troylus will not come farre behind him, let them take heede of Troylus; I can tell them that too.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: What is he angry too?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Who Troylus?
Troylus is the better man of the two.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Oh Iupiter; there's no comparison.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: What not betweene Troylus and Hector? do you know a man if you see him?

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: I, if I euer saw him before and knew him.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Well I say Troylus is Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
verse: Then you say as I say,
For I am sure he is not Hector.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: No not Hector is not Troylus in some degrees.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: 'Tis iust, to each of them he is himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Himselfe? alas poore Troylus I would he were.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: So he is.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Condition I had gone bare-foote to India.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: He is not Hector.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Himselfe? no? hee's not himselfe, would a were himselfe: well, the Gods are aboue, time must friend or end: well Troylus well, I would my heart were in her body; no, Hector is not a better man then Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Excuse me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: He is elder.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Pardon me, pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Th' others not come too't, you shall tell me another tale when th' others come too't: Hector shall not haue his will this yeare.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: He shall not neede it if he haue his owne.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Nor his qualities.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: No matter.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Nor his beautie.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: 'Twould not become him, his own's better.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You haue no iudgement Neece; Hellen her selfe swore th' other day, that Troylus for a browne fauour (for so 'tis I must confesse) not browne neither.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: No, but browne.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Faith to say truth, browne and not browne.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: To say the truth, true and not true.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: She prais'd his complexion aboue Paris.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Why Paris hath colour inough.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: So, he has.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose:
Then Troylus should haue too much, if she prasi'd him aboue, his complexion is higher then his, he hauing

colour enough, and the other higher, is too flaming a praise for a good complexion, I had as lieue Hellens golden tongue had commended Troylus for a copper nose.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I sweare to you,
I thinke Hellen loues him better then Paris.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Then shee's a merry Greeke indeed.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Nay I am sure she does, she came to him th' other day into the compast window, and you know he has not past three or foure haires on his chinne.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Indeed a Tapsters Arithmetique may soone bring his particulars therein, to a totall.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Why he is very yong, and yet will he within three pound lift as much as his brother Hector.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Is he is so young a man, and so old a lifter?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: But to prooue to you that Hellen loues him, she came and puts me her white hand to his clouen chin.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Iuno haue mercy, how came it clouen?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Why, you know 'tis dimpled,
I thinke his smyling becomes him better then any man in all Phrigia.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Oh he smiles valiantly.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Dooes hee not?

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Oh yes, and 'twere a clow'd in Autumne.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Why go to then, but to proue to you that Hellen loues Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
verse: Troylus wil stand to thee
Proofe, if youle prooue it so.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Troylus? why he esteemes her no more then I esteeme an addle egge.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: If you loue an addle egge as well as you loue an idle head, you would eate chickens i' th' shell.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I cannot chuse but laugh to thinke how she tickled his chin, indeed shee has a maruel's white hand I must needs confesse.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Without the racke.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: And shee takes vpon her to spie a white haire on his chinne.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Alas poore chin? many a wart is richer.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: But there was such laughing, Queene Hecuba laught that her eyes ran ore.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: With Milstones.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: And Cassandra laught.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: But there was more temperate fire vnder the pot of her eyes: did her eyes run ore too?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: And Hector laught.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: At what was all this laughing?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Marry at the white haire that Hellen spied on Troylus chin.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: And t' had beene a greene haire, I should haue laught too.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: They laught not so much at the haire, as at his pretty answere.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: What was his answere?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Quoth shee, heere's but two and fifty haires on your chinne; and one of them is white.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: This is her question.

speeches.speaker: Pand
prose: That's true, make no question of that, two and fiftie haires quoth hee, and one white, that white haire is my Father, and all the rest are his Sonnes. Iupiter quoth she, which of these haires is Paris my husband? The forked one quoth he, pluckt out and giue it him: but there was such laughing, and Hellen so blusht, and Paris so chaft, and all the rest so laught, that it past.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
verse: So let it now,
For is has beene a great while going by.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Well Cozen,
I told you a thing yesterday, think on't.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: So I does.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Ile be sworne 'tis true, he will weepe you an'twere a man borne in Aprill.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: And Ile spring vp in his teares, an'twere a nettle against May.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Harke they are comming from the field, shal we stand vp here and see them, as they passe toward Illium, good Neece do, sweet Neece Cressida.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: At your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Heere, heere, here's an excellent place, heere we may see most brauely, Ile tel you them all by their names, as they passe by, but marke Troylus aboue the rest.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Speake not so low'd.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: That's Aeneas, is not that a braue man, hee's one of the flowers of Troy I can you, but merke Troylus, you shal see anon.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: That's Antenor, he has a shrow'd wit I can tell you, and hee's a man good inough, hee's one o' th soundest iudgement in Troy whosoeuer, and a proper man of person: when comes Troylus? Ile shew you Troylus anon, if hee see me, you shall see him him nod at me.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Will he giue you the nod?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You shall see.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: If he do, the rich shall haue, more.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: That's Hector, that, that, looke you, that there's a fellow. Goe thy way Hector, there's a braue man Neece, O braue Hector! Looke how hee lookes? there's a countenance; ist not a braue man?

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: O braue man!

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Is a not? It dooes a mans heart good, looke you what hacks are on his Helmet, looke you yonder, do you see? Looke you there? There's no iesting, laying on, tak't off, who ill as they say, there be hacks.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Be those with Swords?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Swords, any thing he cares not, and the diuell come to him, it's all one, by Gods lid it dooes ones heart good. Yonder comes Paris, yonder comes Paris: looke yee yonder Neece, ist not a gallant man to, ist not? Why this is braue now: who said he came hurt home to day? Hee's not hurt, why this will do Hellens heart good now, ha? Would I could see Troylus now, you shall Troylus anon.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Whose that?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: That's Hellenus, I maruell where Troylus is, that's Helenus, I thinke he went not forth to day: that's Hellenus.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Can Hellenus fight Vncle?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Hellenus no: yes heele fight indifferent, well, I maruell where Troylus is; harke, do you not haere the people crie Troylus? Hellenus is a Priest.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: What sneaking fellow comes yonder?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Where? Yonder? That's Daphobus. 'Tis Troylus! Ther's a man Neece, hem. Braue Troylus, the Prince of Chiualrie.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
prose: Peace, for shame peace.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose:
Marke him, not him: O braue Troylus: looke well vpon him Neece, looke you how his Sword is bloudied, and his Helme more hackt then Hectors, and how he

lookes, and how he goes. O admirable youth! he ne're saw three and twenty. Go thy way Troylus, go thy way, had I a sister were a Grace, or a daughter a Goddesse, hee should take his choice. O admirable man! Paris? Paris is durt to him, and I warrant, Helen to change, would giue money to boot.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Heere come more.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Asses, fooles, dolts, chaffe and bran, chaffe and bran; porredge after meat. I could liue and dye i' th' eyes of Troylus. Ne're looke, ne're looke; the Eagles are gon, Crowes and Dawes, Crowes and Dawes: I had rather be such a man as Troylus, then Agamemnon, and all Greece.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: There is among the Greekes Achilles, a better man then Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Achilles? a Dray-man, a Porter, a very Camell.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Well, well.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Well, well? Why haue you any discretion? haue you any eyes? Do you know what a man is? Is not birth, beauty, good-shape, discourse, manhood, learning, gentlenesse, vertue, youth, liberality, and so forth: the Spice, and salt that seasons a man?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: I, a minc'd man, and then to be bak'd with no Date in the pye, for then the mans dates out.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You are such another woman, one knowes not at what ward you lye.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Vpon my backe, to defend my belly; vpon my wit, to defend my wiles; vppon my secrecy, to defend mine honesty; my Maske, to defend my beauty, and you to defend all these: and at all these wardes I lye at, at a thousand watches.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Say one of your watches.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Nay Ile watch you for that, and that's one of the cheefest of them too: If I cannot ward what I would not haue hit, I can watch you for telling how I took the blow, vnlesse it swell past hiding, and then it's past watching.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You are such another.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, my Lord would instantly speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Where?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: At your owne house.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Good Boy tell him I come, I doubt he bee hurt.
Fare ye well good Neece.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Adieu Vnkle.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Ile be with you Neece by and by.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: To bring Vnkle.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I, a token from Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: By the same token, you are a Bawd.
Words, vowes, gifts, teares, & loues full sacrifice,
He offers in anothers enterprise:
But more in Troylus thousand fold I see,
Then in the glasse of Pandar's praise may be;
Yet hold I off. Women are Angels wooing,
Things won are done, ioyes soule lyes in the dooing:
That she belou'd, knowes nought, that knowes not this;
Men prize the thing vngain'd, more then it is.
That she was neuer yet, that euer knew
Loue got so sweet, as when desire did sue:
Therefore this maxime out of loue I teach;
"Atchieuement, is command; vngain'd, beseech.
That though my hearts Contents firme loue doth beare,
Nothing of that shall from mine eyes appeare.

speeches.speaker: Agam.
verse: Princes:
What greefe hath set the Iaundies on your cheekes?
The ample proposition that hope makes
In all designes, begun on earth below
Fayles in the promist largenesse: checkes and disasters
Grow in the veines of actions highest rear'd.
As knots by the conflux of meeting sap,
Infect the sound Pine, and diuerts his Graine
Tortiue and erant from his course of growth.
Nor Princes, is it matter new to vs,
That we come short of our suppose so farre,
That after seuen yeares siege, yet Troy walles stand,
Sith euery action that hath gone before,
Whereof we haue Record, Triall did draw
Bias and thwart, not answering the ayme:
And that vnbodied figure of the thought
That gaue't surmised shape. Why then (you Princes)
Do you with cheekes abash'd, behold our workes,
And thinke them shame, which are (indeed) nought else
But the protractiue trials of great Ioue,
To finde persistiue constancie in men?
The finenesse of which Mettall is not found
In Fortunes loue: for then, the Bold and Coward,
The Wise and Foole, the Artist and vn-read,
The hard and soft, seeme all affin'd, and kin.
But in the Winde and Tempest of her frowne,
Distinction with a lowd and powrefull fan,
Puffing at all, winnowes the light away;
And what hath masse, or matter by it selfe,
Lies rich in Vertue, and vnmingled.

speeches.speaker: Nestor.
verse: With due Obseruance of thy godly seat,
Great Agamemnon, Nestor shall apply
Thy latest words.
In the reproofe of Chance,
Lies the true proofe of men: The Sea being smooth,
How many shallow bauble Boates dare saile
Vpon her patient brest, making their way
With those of Nobler bulke?
But let the Ruffian Boreas once enrage
The gentle Thetis, and anon behold
The strong ribb'd Barke through liquid Mountaines cut,
Bounding betweene the two moyst Elements
Like Perseus Horse. Where's then the sawcy Boate,
Whose weake vntimber'd sides but euen now
Co-riual'd Greatnesse? Either to harbour fled,
Or made a Toste for Neptune. Euen so,
Doth valours shew, and valours worth diuide
In stormes of Fortune.
For, in her ray and brightnesse,
The Heard hath more annoyance by the Brieze
Then by the Tyger: But, when the splitting winde
Makes flexible the knees of knotted Oakes,
And Flies fled vnder shade, why then
The thing of Courage,
As rowz'd with rage, with rage doth sympathize,
And with an accent tun'd in selfe-same key,
Retyres to chiding Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: Agamemnon.
Thou great Commander, Nerue, and Bone of Greece,
Heart of our Numbers, soule, and onely spirit,
In whom the tempers, and the mindes of all
Should be shut vp: Heare what Vlysses speakes,
Besides the applause and approbation
The which most mighty for thy place and sway,
And thou most reuerend for thy stretcht-out life,
I giue to both your speeches: which were such,
As Agamemnon and the hand of Greece
Should hold vp high in Brasse: and such againe
As venerable Nestor (hatch'd in Siluer)
Should with a bond of ayre, strong as the Axletree
In which the Heauens ride, knit all Greekes eares
To his experienc'd tongue: yet let it please both
(Thou Great, and Wise) to heare Vlysses speake.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Speak Prince of Ithaca, and be't of lesse expect:
That matter needlesse of importlesse burthen
Diuide thy lips; then we are confident
When ranke Thersites opes his Masticke iawes,
We shall heare Musicke, Wit, and Oracle.

speeches.speaker: ~lys.
verse: Troy yet vpon his basis had bene downe,
And the great Hectors sword had lack'd a Master
But for these instances.
The specialty of Rule hath beene neglected;
And looke how many Grecian Tents do stand
Hollow vpon this Plaine, so many hollow Factions.
When that the Generall is not like the Hiue,
To whom the Forragers shall all repaire,
What Hony is expected? Degree being vizarded,
Th' vnworthiest shewes as fairely in the Maske.
The Heauens themselues, the Planets, and this Center,
Obserue degree, priority, and place,
Insisture, course, proportion, season, forme,
Office, and custome, in all line of Order:
And therefore is the glorious Planet Sol
In noble eminence, enthron'd and sphear'd
Amid'st the other, whose med'cinable eye
Corrects the ill Aspects of Planets euill,
And postes like the Command'ment of a King,
Sans checke, to good and bad. But when the Planets
In euill mixture to disorder wander,
What Plagues, and what portents, what mutiny?
What raging of the Sea? shaking of Earth?
Commotion in the Windes? Frights, changes, horrors,
Diuert, and cracke, rend and deracinate
The vnity, and married calme of States
Quite from their fixure? O, when Degree is shak'd,
(Which is the Ladder to all high designes)
The enterprize is sicke. How could Communities,
Degrees in Schooles, and Brother-hoods in Cities,
Peacefull Commerce from diuidable shores,
The primogenitiue, and due of Byrth,
Prerogatiue of Age, Crownes, Scepters, Lawrels
(But by Degree) stand in Authentique place?
Take but Degree away, vn-tune that string,
And hearke what Discord followes: each thing meetes
In meere oppugnancie. The bounded Waters,
Should lift their bosomes higher then the Shores,
And make a soppe of all this solid Globe:
Strength should be Lord of imbecility,
And the rude Sonne should strike his Father dead:
Force should be right, or rather, right and wrong,
(Betweene whose endlesse iarre, Iustice recides)
Should loose her names, and so should Iustice too.
Then euery thing includes it selfe in Power,
Power into Will, Will into Appetite,
And Appetite (an vniuersall Wolfe,
So doubly seconded with Will, and Power)
Must make perforce an vniuersall prey,
And last, eate vp himselfe.
Great Agamemnon:
This Chaos, when Degree is suffocate,
Followes the choaking:
And this neglection of Degree, is it
That by a pace goes backward in a purpose
It hath to climbe. The Generall's disdain'd
By him one step below; he, by the next,
That next, by him beneath: so euery step
Exampled by the first pace that is sicke
Of his Superiour, growes to an enuious Feauer
Of pale, and bloodlesse Emulation.
And 'tis this Feauer that keepes Troy on foote,
Not her owne sinewes. To end a tale of length,
Troy in our weaknesse liues, not in her strength.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: Most wisely hath Vlysses heere discouer'd
The Feauer, whereof all our power is sicke.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: The Nature of the sicknesse found (~lysses)
What is the remedie?

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: The great Achilles, whom Opinion crownes,
The sinew, and the fore-hand of our Hoste,
Hauing his eare full of his ayery Fame,
Growes dainty of his worth, and in his Tent
Lyes mocking our designes. With him, Patroclus,
Vpon a lazie Bed, the liue-long day
Breakes scurrill Iests,
And with ridiculous and aukward action,
(Which Slanderer, he imitation call's)
He Pageants vs. Sometime great Agamemnon,
Thy toplesse deputation he puts on;
And like a strutting Player, whose conceit
Lies in his Ham-string, and doth thinke it rich
To heare the woodden Dialogue and sound
'Twixt his stretcht footing, and the Scaffolage,
Such to be pittied, and ore-rested seeming
He acts thy Greatnesse in: and when he speakes,
'Tis like a Chime a mending. With tearmes vnsquar'd,
Which from the tongue of roaring Typhon dropt,
Would seemes Hyperboles. At this fusty stuffe,
The large Achilles (on his prest-bed lolling)
From his deepe Chest, laughes out a lowd applause,
Cries excellent, 'tis Agamemnon iust.
Now play me Nestor; hum, and stroke thy Beard
As he, being drest to some Oration:
That's done, as neere as the extreamest ends
Of paralels; as like, as Vulcan and his wife,
Yet god Achilles still cries excellent,
'Tis Nestor right. Now play him (me) Patroclus,
Arming to answer in a night-Alarme,
And then (forsooth) the faint defects of Age
Must be the Scene of myrth, to cough, and spit,
And with a palsie fumbling on his Gorget,
Shake in and out the Riuet: and at this sport
Sir Valour dies; cries, O enough Patroclus,
Or, giue me ribs of Steele, I shall split all
In pleasure of my Spleene. And in this fashion,
All our abilities, gifts, natures, shapes,
Seuerals and generals of grace exact,
Atchieuments, plots, orders, preuentions,
Excitements to the field, or speech for truce,
Successe or losse, what is, or is not, serues
As stuffe for these two, to make paradoxes.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: And in the imitation of these twaine,
Who (as Vlysses sayes) Opinion crownes
With an Imperiall voyce, many are infect:
Aiax is growne selfe-will'd, and beares his head
In such a reyne, in full as proud a place
As broad Achilles, and keepes his Tent like him;
Makes factious Feasts, railes on our state of Warre
Bold as an Oracle, and sets Thersites
A slaue, whose Gall coines slanders like a Mint,
To match vs in comparisons with durt,
To weaken and discredit our exposure,
How ranke soeuer rounded in with danger.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: They taxe our policy, and call it Cowardice,
Count Wisedome as no member of the Warre,
Fore-stall prescience, and esteeme no acte
But that of hand: The still and mentall parts,
That do contriue how many hands shall strike
When fitnesse call them on, and know by measure
Of their obseruant toyle, the Enemies waight,
Why this hath not a singers dignity:
They call this Bed-worke, Mapp'ry, Closset-Warre:
So that the Ramme that batters downe the wall,
For the great swing and rudenesse of his poize,
They place before his hand that made the Engine,
Or those that with the finenesse of their soules,
By Reason guide his execution.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: Let this be granted, and Achilles horse
Makes many Thetis sonnes.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: What Trumpet? Looke Menelaus.

speeches.speaker: Men.
prose: From Troy.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: What would you 'fore our Tent?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Is this great Agamemnons Tent, I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Euen this.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: May one that is a Herald, and a Prince,
Do a faire message to his Kingly eares?

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: With surety stronger then Achilles arme,
'Fore all the Greekish heads, which with one voyce
Call Agamemnon Head and Generall.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Faire leaue, and large security. How may
A stranger to those most Imperial lookes,
Know them from eyes of other Mortals?

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: I: I aske, that I might waken reuerence,
And on the cheeke be ready with a blush
Modest as morning, when she coldly eyes
The youthfull Phoebus:
Which is that God in office guiding men?
Which is the high and mighty Agamemnon?

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: This Troyan scornes vs, or the men of Troy
Are ceremonious Courtiers.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Courtiers as free, as debonnaire; vnarm'd,
As bending Angels: that's their Fame, in peace:
But when they would seeme Souldiers, they haue galles,
Good armes, strong ioynts, true swords, & Ioues accord,
Nothing so full of heart. But peace Aeneas,
Peace Troyan, lay thy finger on thy lips,
The worthinesse of praise distaines his worth:
If that he prais'd himselfe, bring the praise forth.
But what the repining enemy commends,
That breath Fame blowes, that praise sole pure transce~ds.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Sir, you of Troy, call you your selfe Aeneas?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: I Greeke, that is my name.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: What's your affayre I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Sir pardon, 'tis for Agamemnons cares.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: He heares nought priuatly
That comes from Troy.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Nor I from Troy come not to whisper him,
I bring a Trumpet to awake his eare,
To set his sence on the attentiue bent,
And then to speake.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Speake frankely as the winde.
It is not Agamemnons sleeping houre;
That thou shalt know Troyan he is awake,
He tels thee so himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Trumpet blow loud,
Send thy Brasse voyce through all these lazie Tents,
And euery Greeke of mettle, let him know,
What Troy meanes fairely, shall be spoke alowd.
We haue great Agamemnon heere in Troy,
A Prince calld Hector, Priam is his Father:
Who in this dull and long-continew'd Truce
Is rusty growne. He bad me take a Trumpet,
And to this purpose speake: Kings, Princes, Lords,
If there be one among'st the fayr'st of Greece,
That holds his Honor higher then his ease,
That seekes his praise, more then he feares his perill,
That knowes his Valour, and knowes not his feare,
That loues his Mistris more then in confession,
(With truant vowes to her owne lips he loues)
And dare a vow her Beauty, and her Worth,
In other armes then hers: to him this Challenge.
Hector, in view of Troyans, and of Greekes,
Shall make it good, or do his best to do it.
He hath a Lady, wiser, fairer, truer,
Then euer Greeke did compasse in his armes,
And will to morrow with his Trumpet call,
Midway betweene your Tents, and walles of Troy,
To rowze a Grecian that is true in loue.
If any come, Hector shal honour him:
If none, hee'l say in Troy when he retyres,
The Grecian Dames are sun-burnt, and not worth
The splinter of a Lance: Euen so much.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: This shall be told our Louers Lord Aeneas,
If none of them haue soule in such a kinde,
We left them all at home: But we are Souldiers,
And may that Souldier a meere recreant proue,
That meanes not, hath not, or is not in loue:
If then one is, or hath, or meanes to be,
That one meets Hector; if none else, Ile be he.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: Tell him of Nestor, one that was a man
When Hectors Grandsire suckt: he is old now,
But if there be not in our Grecian mould,
One Noble man, that hath one spark^ of fire
To answer for his Loue; tell him from me,
Ile hide my Siluer beard in a Gold Beauer,
And in my Vantbrace put this wither'd brawne,
And meeting him, wil tell him, that my Lady
Was fayrer then his Grandame, and as chaste
As may be in the world: his youth in flood,
Ile pawne this truth with my three drops of blood.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Now heauens forbid such scarsitie of youth.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Faire Lord Aeneas,
Let me touch your hand:
To our Pauillion shal I leade you first:
Achilles shall haue word of this intent,
So shall each Lord of Greece from Tent to Tent:
Your selfe shall Feast with vs before you goe,
And finde the welcome of a Noble Foe.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
prose: Nestor.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: What sayes Vlysses?

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: I haue a young conception in my braine,
Be you my time to bring it to some shape.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: What is't?

speeches.speaker: ~lysses.
verse: This 'tis:
Blunt wedges riue hard knots: the seeded Pride
That hath to this maturity blowne vp
In ranke Achilles, must or now be cropt,
Or shedding breed a Nursery of like euil
To ouer-bulke vs all.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: Wel, and how?

speeches.speaker: ~lys.
verse: This challenge that the gallant Hector sends,
How euer it is spred in general name,
Relates in purpose onely to Achilles.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: The purpose is perspicuous euen as substance,
Whose grossenesse little charracters summe vp,
And in the publication make no straine,
But that Achilles, were his braine as barren
As bankes of Lybia, though (Apollo knowes)
'Tis dry enough, wil with great speede of iudgement,
I, with celerity, finde Hectors purpose
Pointing on him.

speeches.speaker: ~lys.
prose: And wake him to the answer, thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: Yes, 'tis most meet; who may you else oppose
That can from Hector bring his Honor off,
If not Achilles; though't be a sportfull Combate,
Yet in this triall, much opinion dwels.
For heere the Troyans taste our deer'st repute
With their fin'st Pallate: and trust to me Vlysses,
Our imputation shall be oddely poiz'd
In this wilde action. For the successe
(Although particular) shall giue a scantling
Of good or bad, vnto the Generall:
And in such Indexes, although small prickes
To their subsequent Volumes, there is seene
The baby figure of the Gyant-masse
Of things to come at large. It is suppos'd,
He that meets Hector, issues from our choyse;
And choise being mutuall acte of all our soules,
Makes Merit her election, and doth boyle
As 'twere, from forth vs all: a man distill'd
Out of our Vertues; who miscarrying,
What heart from hence receyues the conqu'ring part
To steele a strong opinion to themselues,
Which entertain'd, Limbes are in his instruments,
In no lesse working, then are Swords and Bowes
Directiue by the Limbes.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: Giue pardon to my speech:
Therefore 'tis meet, Achilles meet not Hector:
Let vs (like Merchants) shew our fowlest Wares,
And thinke perchance they'l sell: If not,
The luster of the better yet to shew,
Shall shew the better. Do not consent,
That euer Hector and Achilles meete:
For both our Honour, and our Shame in this,
Are dogg'd with two strange Followers.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: I see them not with my old eies: what are they?

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: What glory our Achilles shares from Hector,
(Were he not proud) we all should weare with him:
But he already is too insolent,
And we were better parch in Affricke Sunne,
Then in the pride and salt scorne of his eyes
Should he scape Hector faire. If he were foyld,
Why then we did our maine opinion crush
In taint of our best man. No, make a Lott'ry,
And by deuice let blockish Aiax draw
The sort to sight with Hector: Among our selues,
Giue him allowance as the worthier man,
For that will physicke the great Myrmidon
Who broyles in lowd applause, and make him fall
His Crest, that prouder then blew Iris bends.
If the dull brainlesse Aiax come safe off,
Wee'l dresse him vp in voyces: if he faile,
Yet go we vnder our opinion still,
That we haue better men. But hit or misse,
Our proiects life this shape of sence assumes,
Aiax imploy'd, pluckes downe Achilles Plumes.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: Now Vlysses, I begin to rellish thy aduice,
And I wil giue a taste of it forthwith
To Agamemnon, go we to him straight:
Two Curres shal tame each other, Pride alone
Must tarre the Mastiffes on, as 'twere their bone.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Thersites?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Agamemnon, how if he had Biles (ful) all ouer generally.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Thersites?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: And those Byles did runne, say so; did not the General run, were not that a botchy core?

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Dogge.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
verse: Then there would come some matter from him:
I see none now.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
verse: Thou Bitch-Wolfes-Sonne, canst yu not heare?
Feele then.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: The plague of Greece vpon thee thou Mungrel beefe-witted Lord.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Speake then you whinid'st leauen speake, I will beate thee into handsomnesse.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I shal sooner rayle thee into wit and holinesse: but I thinke thy Horse wil sooner con an Oration, then yu learn a prayer without booke: Thou canst strike, canst thou? A red Murren o' th thy Iades trickes.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Toads stoole, learne me the Proclamation.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Doest thou thinke I haue no sence thou strik'st me thus?

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: The Proclamation.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Thou art proclaim'd a foole, I thinke.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Do not Porpentine, do not; my fingers itch.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I would thou didst itch from head to foot, and I had the scratching of thee, I would make thee the lothsom'st scab in Greece.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: I say the Proclamation.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Thou grumblest & railest euery houre on Achilles, and thou art as ful of enuy at his greatnes, as Cerberus is at Proserpina's beauty. I, that thou barkst at him.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Mistresse Thersites.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Thou should'st strike him.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Coblofe.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: He would pun thee into shiuers with his fist, as a Sailor breakes a bisket.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: You horson Curre.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Do, do.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Thou stoole for a Witch.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I, do, do, thou sodden-witted Lord: thou hast no more braine then I haue in mine elbows: An Asinico may tutor thee. Thou scuruy valiant Asse, thou art heere but to thresh Troyans, and thou art bought and solde among those of any wit, like a Barbarian slaue. If thou vse to beat me, I wil begin at thy heele and tel what thou art by inches, thou thing of no bowels thou.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: You dogge.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: You scuruy Lord.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: You Curre.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Mars his Ideot: do rudenes, do Camell, do, do.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Why how now Aiax? wherefore do you this?
How now Thersites? what's the matter man?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: You see him there, do you?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: I, what's the matter.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Nay looke vpon him.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: So I do: what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Nay but regard him well.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Well, why I do so.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: But yet you looke not well vpon him: for who some euer you take him to be, he is Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: I know that foole.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I, but that foole knowes not himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: Therefore I beare thee.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Lo, lo, lo, lo, what modicums of wit he vtters: his euasions haue eares thus long. I haue bobb'd his Braine more then he has beate my bones: I will buy nine Sparrowes for a peny, and his Piamater is not worth the ninth part of a Sparrow. This Lord (Achilles) Aiax who wears his wit in his belly, and his guttes in his head, Ile tell you what I say of him.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: What?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I say this Aiax—

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Nay good Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Has not so much wit.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Nay, I must hold you.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: As will stop the eye of Helens Needle, for whom he comes to fight.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Peace foole.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I would haue peace and quietnes, but the foole will not: He there, that he, looke you there.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: O thou damn'd Curre, I shall—

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Will you set your wit to a Fooles.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: No I warrant you, for a fooles will shame it.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: Good words Thersites.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: What's the quarrell?

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: I bad thee vile Owle, goe learne me the tenure of the Proclamation, and he rayles vpon me.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I serue thee not.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: Well, go too, go too.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I serue heere voluntary.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Your last seruice was sufferance, 'twas not voluntary, no man is beaten voluntary: Aiax was heere the voluntary. and you as vnder an Impresse.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: E'neso, a great deale of your wit too lies in your sinnewes, or else there be Liars Hector shall haue a great catch, if he knocke out either of your braines, he were as good cracke a fustie nut with no kernell.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: What with me to Thersites?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: There's Vlysses, and old Nestor, whose Wit was mouldy ere their Grandsires had nails on their toes, yoke you like draft-Oxen, and make you plough vp the warre.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: What? what?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Yes good sooth, to Achilles, to Aiax, to—

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: I shall cut out your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: 'Tis no matter, I shall speake as much as thou afterwards.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: No more words Thersites.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I will hold my peace when Achilles Brooch bids me, shall I?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: There's for you Patroclus.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I wil see you hang'd like Clotpoles ere I come any more to your Tents; I will keepe where there is wit stirring, and leaue the faction of fooles.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: A good riddance.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Marry this Sin is proclaim'd through al our host,
That Hector by the sift houre of the Sunne,
Will with a Trumpet, 'twixt our Tents and Troy
To morrow morning call some Knight to Armes,
That hath a stomacke. and such a one that dare
Maintaine I know not what: 'tis trash. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: Farewell? who shall answer him?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: I know not, 'tis put to Lottry: otherwise
He knew his man.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: O meaning you, I wil go learne more of it.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: After so many houres, liues, speeches spent,
Thus once againe sayes Nestor from the Greekes,
Deliuer Helen, and all damage else
(As honour, losse of time, trauaile, expence,
Wounds, friends, and what els deere that is consum'd
In hot digestion of this comorant Warre)
Shall be stroke off. Hector, what say you too't.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Though no man lesser feares the Greeks then I,
As farre as touches my particular: yet dread Priam,
There is no Lady of more softer bowels,
More spungie, to sucke in the sense of Feare,
More ready to cry out, who knowes what followes
Then Hector is: the wound of peace is surety,
Surety secure: but modest Doubt is cal'd
The Beacon of the wise: the tent that searches
To' th' bottome of the worst. Let Helen go,
Since the first sword was drawne about this question,
Euery tythe soule 'mongst many thousand dismes,
Hath bin as deere as Helen: I meane of ours:
If we haue lost so many tenths of ours
To guard a thing not ours, nor worth to vs
(Had it our name) the valew of one ten;
What merit's in that reason which denies
The yeelding of her vp.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Fie, fie, my Brother;
Weigh you the worth and honour of a King
(So great as our dread Father) in a Scale
Of common Ounces? Wil you with Counters summe
The past proportion of his infinite,
And buckle in a waste most fathomlesse,
With spannes and inches so diminutiue,
As feares and reasons? Fie for godly shame?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: No maruel though you bite so sharp at reasons,
You are so empty of them, should not our Father
Beare the great sway of his affayres with reasons,
Because your speech hath none that tels him so.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: You are for dreames & slumbers brother Priest
You furre your gloues with reason: here are your reasons
You know an enemy intends you harme,
You know, a sword imploy'd is perillous,
And reason flyes the obiect of all harme.
Who maruels then when Helenus beholds
A Grecian and his sword, if he do set
The very wings of reason to his heeles:
Or like a Starre disorb'd. Nay, if we talke of Reason,
And flye like chidden Mercurie from Ioue,
Let's shut our gates and sleepe: Manhood and Honor
Should haue hard hearts, wold they but fat their thoghts
With this cramm'd reason: reason and respect,
Makes Liuers pale. and lustyhood deiect.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Brother, she is not worth
What she doth cost the holding.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: What's aught, but as 'tis valew'd?

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: But value dwels not in particular will,
It holds his estimate and dignitie
As well, wherein 'tis precious of it selfe,
As in the prizer: 'Tis made Idolatrie,
To make the seruice greater then the God,
And the will dotes that is inclineable
To what infectiously it selfe affects,
Without some image of th' affected merit.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: I take to day a Wife, and my election
Is led on in the conduct of my Will;
My Will enkindled by mine eyes and eares,
Two traded Pylots 'twixt the dangerous shores
Of Will, and Iudgement. How may I auoyde
(Although my will distaste what it elected)
The Wife I chose, there can be no euasion
To blench from this, and to stand firme by honour.
We turne not backe the Silkes vpon the Merchant
When we haue spoyl'd them; nor the remainder Viands
We do not throw in vnrespectiue same,
Because we now are full. It was thought meete
Paris should do some vengeance on the Greekes;
Your breath of full consent bellied his Sailes,
The Seas and Windes (old Wranglers) tooke a Truce,
And did him seruice; he touch'd the Ports desir'd,
And for an old Aunt whom the Greekes held Captiue,
He brought a Grecian Queen, whose youth & freshnesse
Wrinkles Apolloes, and makes stale the morning.
Why keepe we her? the Grecians keepe our Aunt:
Is she worth keeping? Why she is a Pearle,
Whose price hath launch'd aboue a thousand Ships,
And turn'd Crown'd Kings to Merchants.
If you'l auouch, 'twas wisedome Paris went,
(As you must needs, for you all cride, Go, go:)
If you'l confesse, he brought home Noble prize,
(As you must needs) for you all clapt your hands,
And cride inestimable; why do you now
The issue of your proper Wisedomes rate,
And do a deed that Fortune neuer did?
Begger the estimation which you priz'd,
Richer then Sea and Land? O Theft most base!
That we haue stolne what we do feare to keepe.
But Theeues vnworthy of a thing so stolne,
That in their Country did them that disgrace,
We feare to warrant in our Natiue place.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Cry Troyans, cry.

speeches.speaker: Priam.
prose: What noyse? what shreeke is this?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: 'Tis our mad sister, I do know her voyce.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Cry Troyans.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: It is Cassandra.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Cry Troyans cry; lend me ten thousand eyes,
And I will fill them with Propheticke teares.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Peace sister, peace.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Virgins, and Boyes; mid-age & wrinkled old,
Soft infancie, that nothing can but cry,
Adde to my clamour: let vs pay betimes
A moity of that masse of moane to come.
Cry Troyans cry, practise your eyes with teares,
Troy must not be, nor goodly Illion stand,
Our fire-brand Brother Paris burnes vs all.
Cry Troyans cry, a Helen and a woe;
Cry, cry, Troy burnes, or else let Helen goe.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Now youthfull Troylus, do not these hie strains
Of diuination in our Sister, worke
Some touches of remorse? Or is your bloud
So madly hot, that no discourse of reason,
Nor feare of bad successe in a bad cause,
Can qualifie the same?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Why Brother Hector,
We may not thinke the iustnesse of each acte
Such, and no other then euent doth forme it,
Not once deiect the courage of our mindes;
Because Cassandra's mad, her brainsicke raptures
Cannot distaste the goodnesse of a quarrell,
Which hath our seuerall Honours all engag'd
To make it gracious. For my priuate part,
I am no more touch'd, then all Priams sonnes,
And loue forbid there should be done among'st vs
Such things as might offend the weakest spleene,
To fight for, and maintaine.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: Else might the world conuince of leuitie,
As well my vnder-takings as your counsels:
But I attest the gods, your full consent
Gaue wings to my propension, and cut off
All feares attending on so dire a proiect.
For what (alas) can these my single armes?
What propugnation is in one mans valour
To stand the push and enmity of those
This quarrell would excite? Yet I protest,
Were I alone to passe the difficulties,
And had as ample power, as I haue will,
Paris should ne're retract what he hath done,
Nor faint in the pursuite.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Paris, you speake
Like one be-sotted on your sweet delights;
You haue the Hony still, but these the Gall,
So to be valiant, is no praise at all.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: Sir, I propose not meerely to my selfe,
The pleasures such a beauty brings with it:
But I would haue the soyle of her faire Rape
Wip'd off in honourable keeping her.
What Treason were it to the ransack'd Queene,
Disgrace to your great worths, and shame to me,
Now to deliuer her possession vp
On termes of base compulsion? Can it be,
That so degenerate a straine as this,
Should once set footing in your generous bosomes?
There's not the meanest spirit on our partie,
Without a heart to dare, or sword to draw,
When Helen is defended: nor none so Noble,
Whose life were ill bestow'd, or death vnfam'd,
Where Helen is the subiect. Then (I say)
Well may we fight for her, whom we know well,
The worlds large spaces cannot paralell.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Paris and Troylus, you haue both said well:
And on the cause and question now in hand,
Haue gloz'd, but superficially; not much
Vnlike young men, whom Aristotle thought
Vnfit to heare Morall Philosophie.
The Reasons you alledge. do more conduce
To the hot passion of distemp'red blood,
Then to make vp a free determination
'Twixt right and wrong: For pleasure, and reuenge,
Haue eares more deafe then Adders, to the voyce
Of any true decision. Nature craues
All dues be rendred to their Owners: now
What neerer debt in all humanity,
Then Wife is to the Husband? If this law
Of Nature be corrupted through affection,
And that great mindes of partiall indulgence,
To their benummed wills resist the same,
There is a Law in each well-ordred Nation,
To curbe those raging appetites that are
Most disobedient and refracturie.
If Helen then be wife to Sparta's King
(As it is knowne she is) these Morall Lawes
Of Nature, and of Nation, speake alowd
To haue her backe return'd. Thus to persist
In doing wrong, extenuates not wrong,
But makes it much more heauie. Hectors opinion
Is this in way of truth: yet nere the lesse,
My spritely brethren, I propend to you
In resolution to keepe Helen still;
For 'tis a cause that hath no meane dependance,
Vpon our ioynt and seuerall dignities.

speeches.speaker: Tro.
verse: Why? there you toucht the life of our designe:
Were it not glory that we more affected,
Then the performance of our heauing spleenes,
I would not wish a drop of Troian blood,
Spent more in her defence. But worthy Hector,
She is a theame of honour and renowne,
A spurre to valiant and magnanimous deeds,
Whose present courage may beate downe our foes,
And fame in time to come canonize vs.
For I presume braue Hector would not loose
So rich aduantage of a promis'd glory,
As smiles vpon the fore-head of this action,
For the wide worlds reuenew.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: I am yours,
You valiant off-spring of great Priamus,
I haue a roisting challenge sent among'st
The dull and factious nobles of the Greekes,
Will strike amazement to their drowsie spirits,
I was aduertiz'd, their Great generall slept,
Whil'st emulation in the armie crept:
This I presume will wake him.

prose: How now Thersites? what lost in the Labyrinth of thy furie? shall the Elephant Aiax carry it thus? he beates me, and I raile at him: O worthy satisfaction, would it were otherwise: that I could beate him, whil'st he rail'd at me: Sfoote, Ile learne to coniure and raise Diuels, but Ile see some issue of my spitefull execrations. Then ther's Achilles, a rare Enginer. If Troy be not taken till these two vndermine it, the wals will stand till they fall of themselues. O thou great thunder-darter of Olympus, forget that thou art Ioue the King of gods: and Mercury, loose all the Serpentine craft of thy Caduceus, if thou take not that little little lesse then little wit from them that they haue, which short-arm'd ignorance it selfe knowes, is so abundant scarse, it will not in circumuention deliuer a Flye from a Spider, without drawing the massie Irons and cutting the web: after this, the vengeance on the whole Camp, or rather the bone-ach, for that me thinkes is the curse dependant on those that warre for a placket. I haue said my prayers and diuell, enuie, say Amen: What ho? my Lord Achilles?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Who's there? Thersites. Good Thersites come in and raile.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: If I could haue remembred a guilt counterfeit, thou would'st not haue slipt out of my contemplation, but it is no matter, thy selfe vpon thy selfe. The common curse of mankinde, follie and ignorance be thine in great reuenew; heauen blesse thee from a Tutor, and Discipline come not neere thee. Let thy bloud be thy direction till thy death, then if she that laies thee out sayes thou art a faire coarse, Ile be sworne and sworne vpon't she neuer shrowded any but Lazars, Amen. Wher's Achilles?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: What art thou deuout? wast thou in a prayer?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: I, the heauens heare me.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Thersites, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Where, where, art thou come? why my cheese, my digestion, why hast thou not seru'd thy selfe into my Table, so many meales? Come, what's Agamemnon?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Thy Commander Achilles, then tell me Patroclus, what's Achilles?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Thy Lord Thersites: then tell me I pray thee, what's thy selfe?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Thy knower Patroclus: then tell me Patroclus, what art thou?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Thou maist tell that know'st.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: O tell, tell.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Ile declin the whole question: Agamemnon commands Achilles, Achilles is my Lord, I am Patroclus knower, and Patroclus is a foole.

speeches.speaker: Patro.
prose: You rascall.

speeches.speaker: Ter.
prose: Peace foole, I haue not done.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: He is a priuiledg'd man, proceede Thersites.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Agamemnon is a foole, Achilles is a foole, Thersites is a foole, and as aforesaid, Patroclus is a foole.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Deriue this? come?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Agamemnon is a foole to offer to command Achilles, Achilles is a foole to be commanded of Agamemon, Thersites is a foole to serue such a foole: and Patroclus is a foole positiue.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Why am I a foole?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Make that demand to the Creator, it suffises me thou art. Looke you, who comes here?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Patroclus, Ile speake with no body: come in with me Thersites.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Here is such patcherie, such iugling, and such knauerie: all the argument is a Cuckold and a Whore, a good quarrel to draw emulations, factions, and bleede to death vpon: Now the dry Suppeago on the Subiect, and Warre and Lecherie confound all.

speeches.speaker: Agam.
prose: Where is Achilles?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Within his Tent, but ill dispos'd my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Agam.
verse: Let it be knowne to him that we are here:
He sent out Messengers, and we lay by
Our appertainments, visiting of him:
Let him be told of, so perchance he thinke
We dare not moue the question of our place,
Or know not what we are.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: I shall so say to him.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
verse: We saw him at the opening of his Tent,
He is not sicke.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Yes, Lyon sicke, sicke of proud heart; you may call it Melancholly if will fauour the man, but by my head, it is pride; but why, why, let him show vs the cause? A word my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Nes.
prose: What moues Aiax thus to bay at him?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Achillis hath inueigled his Foole from him.

speeches.speaker: Nes.
prose: Who, Thersites?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: He.

speeches.speaker: Nes.
prose: Then will Aiax lacke matter, if he haue lost his Argument.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: No, you see he is his argument that has his argument Achilles.

speeches.speaker: Nes.
prose: All the better, their fraction is more our wish then their faction; but it was a strong counsell that a Foole could disunite.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Here comes Patroclus.
prose: The amitie that wisedome knits, not folly may easily vntie.

speeches.speaker: Nes.
prose: No Achilles with him?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: The Elephant hath ioynts, but none for curtesie:
His legge are legs for necessitie, not for slight.

speeches.speaker: Patro.
verse: Achilles bids me say he is much sorry:
If any thing more then your sport and pleasure,
Did moue your greatnesse, and this noble State,
To call vpon him; he hopes it is no other,
But for your health, and your digestion sake;
An after Dinners breath.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Heare you Patroclus:
We are too well acquainted with these answers:
But his euasion winged thus swift with scorne,
Cannot outflye our apprehensions.
Much attribute he hath, and much the reason,
Why we ascribe it to him, yet all his vertues,
Not vertuously of his owne part beheld,
Doe in our eyes, begin to loose their glosse;
Yea, and like faire Fruit in an vnholdsome dish,
Are like to rot vntasted: goe and tell him,
We came to speake with him; and you shall not sinne,
If you doe say, we thinke him ouer proud,
And vnder honest; in selfe-assumption greater
Then in the note of iudgement: & worthier then himselfe
Here tends the sauage strangenesse he puts on,
Disguise the holy strength of their command:
And vnder write in an obseruing kinde
His humorous predominance, yea watch
His pettish lines, his ebs, his flowes, as if
The passage and whole carriage of this action
Rode on his tyde. Goe tell him this, and adde,
That if he ouerhold his price so much,
Weele none of him; but let him, like an Engin
Not portable, lye vnder this report.
Bring action hither, this cannot goe to warre:
A stirring Dwarfe, we doe allowance giue,
Before a sleeping Gyant: tell him so.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: I shall, and bring his answere presently.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: In second voyce weele not be satisfied,

We come to speake with him,
~lisses enter you.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: What is he more then another?

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: No more then what he thinkes he is.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Is he so much, doe you not thinke, he thinkes himselfe a better man then I am?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
prose: No question.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: Will you subscribe his thought, and say he is?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
prose: No, Noble Aiax, you are as strong, as valiant, as wise, no lesse noble, much more gentle, and altogether more tractable

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: Why should a man be proud? How doth pride grow? I know not what it is.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Your minde is the cleerer Aiax, and your vertues the fairer; he that is proud, eates vp himselfe; Pride is his owne Glasse, his owne trumpet, his owne Chronicle, and what euer praises it selfe but in the deede, deuoures the deede in the praise.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: I do hate a proud man, as I hate the ingendring of Toades.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: Yet ^e ^oues himselfe: Is't not strange?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Achilles will not to the field to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
prose: What's his excuse?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: He doth relye on none,
But carries on the streame of his dispose,
Without obseruance or respect of any,
In will peculiar, and in selfe admission.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Why, will he not vpon our faire request,
Vntent his person, and share the ayre with vs?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Things small as nothing, for requests sake onely
He makes important; possest he is with greatnesse,
And speakes not to himselfe, but with a pride
That quarrels at selfe-breath. Imagin'd wroth
Holds in his bloud such swolne and hot discourse,
That twixt his mentall and his actiue parts,
Kingdom'd Achilles in commotion rages,
And batters gainst it selfe; what should I say?
He is so plaguy proud, that the death tokens of it,
Cry no recouery.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Let Aiax goe to him.
Deare Lord, goe you and greete him in his Tent;
'Tis said he holds you well, and will be led
At your request a little from himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: O Agamemnon, let it not be so.
Weele consecrate the steps that Aiax makes,
When they goe from Achilles; shall the proud Lord,
That bastes his arrogance with his owne seame,
And neuer suffers matter of the world,
Enter his thoughts: saue such as doe reuolue
And ruminate himselfe. Shall he be worshipt,
Of that we hold an Idoll, more then hee?
No, this thrice worthy and right valiant Lord,
Must not so staule his Palme, nobly acquir'd,
Nor by my will assubingate his merit,
As amply titled as Achilles is: by going to Achilles,
That were to enlard his fat already, pride,
And adde more Coles to Cancer, when he burnes
With entertaining great Hiperion.
This L. goe to him? Iupiter forbid,
And say in thunder, Achilles goe to him.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: O this is well, he rubs the veine of him.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: And how his silence drinkes vp this applause.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: If I goe to him, with my armed fist, Ile pash him ore the face.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
prose: O no, you shall not goe.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: And a be proud with me, ile phese his pride: let me goe to him.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: Not for the worth that hangs vpon our quarrel.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: A paultry insolent fellow.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: How he describes himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Can he not be sociable?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: The Rauen chides blacknesse.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Ile let his humours bloud.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
prose: He will be the Physitian that should be the patient.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: And all men were a my minde.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Wit would be out of fashion.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: A should not beare it so, a should eate Swords first: shall pride carry it?

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: And 'twould, you'ld carry halfe.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: A would haue ten shares.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: I will knede him, Ile make him supple, hee's not yet through warme.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: Force him with praises, poure in, poure in: his ambition is dry.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: My L. you feede too much on this dislike.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: Our noble Generall, doe not doe so.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
prose: You must prepare to fight without Achilles.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Why, 'tis this naming of him doth him harme.
Here is a man, but 'tis before his face,
I will be silent.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: Wherefore should you so?
He is not emulous, as Achilles is.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: 'Know the whole world, he is as valiant.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: A horson dog, that shal palter thus with vs, would he were a Troian.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: What a vice were it in Aiax now—

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: If he were proud.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Or couetous of praise.

speeches.speaker: Vlis
prose: I, or surley borne.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Or strange, or selfe affected.

speeches.speaker: Vl.
verse: Thank the heauens L. thou art of sweet composure;
Praise him that got thee, she that gaue thee sucke:
Fame by thy Tutor, and thy parts of nature
Thrice fam'd beyond, beyond all erudition;
But he that disciplin'd thy armes to fight,
Let Mars deuide Eternity in twaine,
And giue him halfe, and for thy vigour,
Bull-bearing Milo: his addition yeelde
To sinnowie Aiax: I will not praise thy wisdome,
Which like a bourne, a pale, a shore confines
Thy spacious and dilated parts; here's Nestor
Instructed by the Antiquary times:
He must, he is, he cannot but be wise.
But pardon Father Nestor, were your dayes
As greene as Aiax, and your braine so temper'd,
You should not haue the eminence of him,
But be as Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Shall I call you Father?

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: I my good Sonne.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Be rul'd by him Lord Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: There is no tarrying here, the Hart Achilles
Keepes thicker: please it our Generall,
To call together all his state of warre,
Fresh Kings are come to Troy; to morrow
We must with all our maine of power stand fast:
And here's a Lord, come Knights from East to West,
And cull their flowre, Aiax shall cope the best.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Goe we to Counsaile, let Achilles sleepe;
Light Botes may saile swift, though greater bulkes draw deepe.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Friend, you, pray you a word: Doe not you follow the yong Lord Paris?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I sir, when he goes before me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You depend vpon him I meane?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir, I doe depend vpon the Lord.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You depend vpon a noble Gentleman: I must needes praise him.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: The Lord be praised.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: You know me, doe you not?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Faith sir, superficially.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Friend know me better, I am the Lord Pandarus.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I hope I shall know your honour better.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: I doe desire it.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: You are in the state of Grace?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Grace, not so friend, honor and Lordship are my title: What Musique is this?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I doe but partly know sir: it is Musicke in parts.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Know you the Musitians.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Wholly sir.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Who play they to?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: To the hearers sir.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: At whose pleasure friend?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: At mine sir, and theirs that loue Musicke.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Command, I meane friend.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Who shall I command sir?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Friend, we vnderstand not one another: I am too courtly, and thou art too cunning. At whose request doe these men play?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: That's too't indeede sir: marry sir, at the request of Paris my L. who's there in person; with him the mortall Venus, the heart bloud of beauty, loues inuisible soule.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Who? my Cosin Cressida.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: No sir, Helen, could you not finde out that by her attributes?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: It should seeme fellow, that thou hast not seen the Lady Cressida. I come to speake with Paris from the Prince Troylus: I will make a complementall assault vpon him, for my businesse seethes.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sodden businesse, there's a stewed phrase indeede.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Faire be to you my Lord, and to all this faire company: faire desires in all faire measure fairely guide them, especially to you faire Queene, faire thoughts be your faire pillow.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Deere L. you are full of faire words.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You speake your faire pleasure sweete Queene: faire Prince, here is good broken Musicke.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: You haue broke it cozen: and by my life you shall make it whole againe, you shall peece it out with a peece of your performance. Nel, he is full of harmony.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Truely Lady no.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: O sir.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Rude in sooth, in good sooth very rude.

speeches.speaker: Paris.
prose: Well said my Lord: well, you say so in fits.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I haue businesse to my Lord, deere Queene: my Lord will you vouchsafe me a word.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Nay, this shall not hedge vs out, weele heare you sing certainely.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Well, sweete Queene you are pleasant with me, but, marry thus my Lord, my deere Lord, and most esteemed friend your brother Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: My Lord Pandarus, hony sweete Lord.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Go too sweete Queene, goe to.
Commends himselfe most affectionately to you.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: You shall not bob vs out of our melody:
If you doe, our melancholly vpon your head.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Sweete Queene, sweete Queene, that's a sweete Queene I faith—

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: And to make a sweet Lady sad, is a sower offence.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Nay, that shall not serue your turne, that shall it not in truth la. Nay, I care not for such words, no, no. And my Lord he desires you, that if the King call for him at Supper, you will make his excuse.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: My Lord Pandarus?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: What saies my sweete Queene, my very, very sweete Queene?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: What exploit's in hand, where sups he to night?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Nay but my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: What saies my sweere Queene? my cozen will fall out with you.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: You must not know where he sups.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: With my disposer Cressida.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: No, no; no such matter, you are wide, come your disposer is sicke.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Well, Ile make excuse.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I good my Lord: why should you say Cressida? no, your poore disposer's sicke.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I spie.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: You spie, what doe you spie: come, giue me an
Instrument now sweete Queene.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Why this is kindely done?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: My Neece is horrible in loue with a thing you haue sweete Queene.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: She shall haue it my Lord, if it be not my Lord Paris.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Hee? no, sheele none of him, they two are twaine.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Falling in after falling out, may make them three.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Come, come, Ile heare no more of this, Ile sing you a song now.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: I, I, prethee now: by my troth sweet Lord thou hast a fine fore-head.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I you may, you may.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: Let thy song be loue: this loue will vndoe vs al.
Oh Cupid Cupid. Cupid.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Loue? I that it shall yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: I, good now loue, loue, no thing but loue.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: In good troth it begins so.

Loue, loue, nothing but loue, still more:
For O loues Bow,
Shootes Bucke and Doe:
The Shaft confounds not that it wounds,
But tickles still the sore:
These Louers cry, oh ho they dye;
Yet that which seemes the wound to kill,
Doth turne oh ho, to ha ha he:
So dying loue liues still,
O ho a while, but ha ha ha,
O ho grones out for ha ha ha—hey ho.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: In loue yfaith to the very tip of the nose.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: He eates nothing but doues loue, and that breeds hot bloud, and hot bloud begets hot thoughts, and hot thoughts beget hot deedes, and hot deedes is loue.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Is this the generation of loue? Hot bloud, hot thoughts, and hot deedes, why they are Vipers, is Loue a generation of Vipers?
Sweete Lord whose a field to day?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Hector, Deiphoebus, Helenus, Anthenor, and all the gallantry of Troy. I would faine haue arm'd to day, but my Nell would not haue it so.
How chance my brother Troylus went not?

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: He hangs the lippe at something; you know all Lord Pandarus?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Not I hony sweete Queene: I long to heare how they sped to day:
Youle remember your brothers excuse?

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: To a hayre.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Farewell sweete Queene.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
prose: Commend me to your Neece.
