speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I will sweete Queene.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: They're come from fielde: let vs to Priams Hall
To greete the Warriors. Sweet Hellen, I must woe you,
To helpe vnarme our Hector: his stubborne Buckles,
With these your white enchanting fingers toucht,
Shall more obey then to the edge of Steele,
Or force of Greekish sinewes: you shall doe more
Then all the Iland Kings, disarme great Hector.

speeches.speaker: Hel.
verse: 'Twill make vs proud to be his seruant Paris:
Yea what he shall receiue of vs in duetie,
Giues vs more palme in beautie then we haue:
Yea ouershines our selfe.
Sweete aboue thought I loue thee.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: How now, where's thy Maister, at my Couzen Cressidas?

speeches.speaker: Man.
prose: No sir, he stayes for you to conduct him thither.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: O here he comes: How now, how now?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Sirra walke off.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Haue you seene my Cousin?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: No Pandarus: I stalke about her doore
Like a strange soule vpon the Stigian bankes
Staying for waftage. O be thou my Charon,
And giue me swift transportance to those fields,
Where I may wallow in the Lilly beds
Propos'd for the deseruer. O gentle Pandarus,
From Cupids shoulder plucke his painted wings,
And flye with me to Cressid.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Walke here ith' Orchard, Ile bring her straight.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: I am giddy; expectation whirles me round,
Th' imaginary relish is so sweete,
That it inchants my sence: what will it be
When that the watry pallats taste indeede
Loues thrice reputed Nectar? Death I feare me
Sounding distruction, or some ioy too fine,
Too subtile, potent, and too sharpe in sweetnesse,
For the capacitie of my ruder powers;
I feare it much, and I doe feare besides,
That I shall loose distinction in my ioyes,
As doth a battaile, when they charge on heapes
The enemy flying.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Shee's making her ready, sheele come straight; you must be witty now, she does so blush, & fetches her winde so short, as if she were fraid with a sprite: Ile fetch her; it is the prettiest villaine, she fetches her breath so short as a new tane Sparrow.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Euen such a passion doth imbrace my bosome:
My heart beates thicker then a feauorous pulse,
And all my powers doe their bestowing loose,
Like vass^lage at vnawares encountring
The eye of Maiestie.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Come, come, what neede you blush?

Shames a babie; here she is now, sweare the oathes now to her, that you haue sworne to me. What are you gone againe, you must be watcht ere you be made tame, must you? come your wayes, come your wayes, and you draw backward weele put you i' th fils: why doe you not speak to her? Come draw this curtaine, & let's see your picture. Alasse the day, how loath you are to offend day light? and 'twere darke you'ld close sooner: So, so. rub on, and kisse the mistresse; how now, a kisse in fee-farme? build there Carpenter, the ayre is sweete. Nay, you shall fight your hearts out ere I part you. The Faulcon, as the Tercell, for all the Ducks ith Riuer: go too. go too.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: You haue bereft me of all words Lady.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Words pay no debts; giue her deedes: but sheele bereaue you 'oth' deeds too, if shee call your actiuity in question: what billing againe? here's in witnesse whereof the Parties interchangeably. Come in, come in, Ile go get a fire?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Will you walke in my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: O Cressida, how often haue I wisht me thus?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Wisht my Lord? the gods grant? O my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: What should they grant? what makes this pretty abruption: what too curious dreg espies my sweete Lady in the fountaine of our loue?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: More dregs then water, if my eares haue eyes.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Feares make diuels of Cherubins, they neuer see truely.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Blinde feare, that seeing reason leads, findes safe footing, then blinde reason, stumbling without feare: to feare the worst, oft cures the worse.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Oh let my Lady apprehend no feare,
In all Cupids Pageant there is presented no monster.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Not nothing monstrous neither?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Nothing but our vndertakings, when we vowe to weepe seas, liue in fire, eate rockes, tame Tygers; thinking it harder for our Mistresse to deuise imposition inough, then for vs to vndergoe any difficultie imposed. This is the monstruositie in loue Lady, that the will is infinite, and the execution confin'd; that the desire is boundlesse, and the act a slaue to limit.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: They say all Louers sweare more performance then they are able, and yet reserue an ability that they neuer performe: vowing more then the perfection of ten; and discharging lesse then the tenth part of one. They that haue the voyce of Lyons, and the act of Hares: are they not Monsters?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Are there such? such are not we: Praise vs as we are tasted, allow vs as we proue: our head shall goe bare till merit crowne it: no perfection in reuersion shall haue a praise in present: wee will not name desert before his birth, and being borne his addition shall be humble: few words to faire faith. Troylus shall be such to Cressid, as what enuie can say worst, shall be a mocke for his truth; and what truth can speake truest, not truer then Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Will you walke in my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: What blushing still? haue you not done talking yet?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Well Vnckle, what folly I commit, I dedicate to you.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I thanke you for that: if my Lord get a Boy of you, youle giue him me: be true to my Lord, if he flinch, chide me for it.

speeches.speaker: Tro.
prose: You know now your hostages: your Vnckles word and my firme faith.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Nay, Ile giue my word for her too: our kindred though they be long ere they are wooed, they are constant being wonne: they are Burres I can tell you, they'le sticke where they are throwne.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Boldnesse comes to mee now, and brings mee heart: Prince Troylus, I haue lou'd you night and day, for many weary moneths.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Why was my Cressid then so hard to win?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Hard to seeme won: but I was won my Lord
With the first glance; that euer pardon me,
If I confesse much you will play the tyrant:
I loue you now, but not till now so much
But I might maister it; in faith I lye:
My thoughts were like vnbrideled children grow
Too head-strong for their mother: see we fooles,
Why haue I blab'd: who shall be true to vs
When we are so vnsecret to our selues?
But though I lou'd you well, I woed you not,
And yet good faith I wisht my selfe a man;
Or that we women had mens priuiledge
Of speaking first. Sweet, bid me hold my tongue,
For in this rapture I shall surely speake
The thing I shall repent: see, see, your silence
Comming in dumbnesse, from my weakenesse drawes
My soule of counsell from me. Stop my mouth.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: And shall, albeit sweete Musicke issues thence.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Pretty yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: My Lord, I doe beseech you pardon me,
'Twas not my purpose thus to beg a kisse:
I am asham'd; O Heauens, what haue I done!
For this time will I take my leaue my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Your leaue sweete Cressid?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Leaue: and you take leaue till to morrow morning.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Pray you content you.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: What offends you Lady?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Sir, mine owne company.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: You cannot shun your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Let me goe and try:
I haue a kinde of selfe recides with you:
But an vnkinde selfe, that it selfe will leaue,
To be anothers foole. Where is my wit?
I would be gone: I speake I know not what.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Well know they what they speake, that speakes so wisely.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
verse: Perchance my Lord, I shew more craft then loue,
And fell so roundly to a large confession,
To Angle for your thoughts: but you are wise,
Or else you loue not: for to be wise and loue,
Exceedes mans might, that dwels with gods aboue.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: O that I thought it could be in a woman:
As if it can, I will presume in you,
To feede for aye her lampe and flames of loue.
To keepe her constancie in plight and youth,
Out-liuing beauties outward, with a minde
That doth renew swifter then blood decaies:
Or that perswasion could but thus conuince me,
That my integritie and truth to you,
Might be affronted with the match and waight
Of such a winnowed puriritie in loue:
How were I then vp-lifted! but alas,
I am as true, as truths simplicitie,
And simpler then the infancie of truth.

speeches.speaker: Cr^s.
prose: In that Ile warre with you.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: O vertuous fight,
When right with right wars who shall be most right:
True swaines in loue, shall in the world to come
Approue their truths by Troylus, when their rimes,
Full of protest, of oath and big compare;
Wants similes, truth tir'd with iteration,
As true as steele, as plantage to the Moone:
As Sunne to day: as Turtle to her mate:
As Iron to Adamant: as Earth to th' Center:
Yet after all comparisons of truth,
(As truths authenticke author to be cited)
As true as Troylus, shall crowne vp the Verse,
And sanctifie the numbers.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Prophet may you be:
If I be false, or swerue a haire from truth,
When time is old and hath forgot it selfe:
When water drops haue worne the Stones of Troy;
And blinde obliuion swallow'd Cities vp;
And mightie States characterlesse are grated
To dustie nothing; yet let memory,
From false to false, among false Maids in loue,
Vpbraid my falsehood, when they'aue said as false,
As Aire, as Water, as Winde, as sandie earth;
As Foxe to Lambe; as Wolfe to Heifers Calfe;
Pard to the Hinde, or Stepdame to her Sonne;
Yea, let them say, to sticke the heart of falsehood,
As false as Cressid.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Go too, a bargaine made: seale it, seale it, Ile be the witnesse here I hold your hand: here my Cousins, feuer you proue false one to another, since I haue taken such paines to bring you together, let all pittifull goers betweene be cal'd to the worlds end after my name: call them all Panders; let all constant men be Troylusses, all false women Cressids, and all brokers betweene, Panders: say, Amen.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: And Cupid grant all tong-tide Maidens heere,
Bed, Chamber, and Pander, to prouide this geere.
prose: Amen.
Whereupon I will shew you a Chamber, which bed, because it shall not speake of your prettie encounters, presse it to death: away.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Now Princes for the seruice I haue done you,
Th' aduantage of the time promps me aloud,
To call for recompence: appeare it to your minde,
That through the sight I beare in things to loue,
I haue abandon'd Troy, left my possession,
Incur'd a Traitors name, expos'd my selfe,
From certaine and possest conueniences,
To doubtfull fortunes, sequestring from me all
That time, acquaintance, custome and condition,
Made tame, and most familiar to my nature:
And here to doe you seruice am become,
As new into the world, strange, vnacquainted.
I doe beseech you, as in way of taste,
To giue me now a little benefit:
Out of those many registred in promise,
Which you say, liue to come in my behalfe.

speeches.speaker: Agam.
prose: What would'st thou of vs Troian? make demand?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: You haue a Troian prisoner, cal'd Anthenor,
Yesterday tooke: Troy holds him very deere,
Oft haue you (often haue you, thankes therefore)
Desir'd my Cressid in right great exchange.
Whom Troy hath still deni'd: but this Anthenor,
I know is such a wrest in their affaires;
That their negotiations all must slacke,
Wanting his mannage: and they will almost,
Giue vs a Prince of blood, a Sonne of Priam,
In change of him. Let him be sent great Princes,
And he shall buy my Daughter: and her presence,
Shall quite strike off all seruice I haue done,
In most accepted paine.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Let Diomedes beare him,
And bring vs Cressid hither: Calcas shall haue
What he requests of vs: good Diomed
Furnish you fairely for this enterchange;
Withall bring word, if Hector will to morrow
Be answer'd in his challenge. Aiax is ready.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: This shall I vndertake, and 'tis a burthen
Which I am proud to beare.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Achilles stands i' th entrance of his Tent;
Please it our Generall to passe strangely by him,
As if he were forgot: and Princes all,
Lay negligent and loose regard vpon him;
I will come last, 'tis like heele question me,
Why such vnpla^siue eyes are bent? why turn'd on him?
If so, I haue derision medicinable,
To vse betweene your strangenesse and his pride,
Which his owne will shall haue desire to drinke;
It may doe good, pride hath no other glasse
To show it selfe, but pride: for supple knees,
Feede arrogance, and are the proud mans fees.

speeches.speaker: Agam.
verse: Weele execute your purpose, and put on
A forme of strangenesse as we passe along,
So doe each Lord, and either greete him not,
Or else disdainfully, which shall shake him more,
Then if not lookt on. I will lead the way.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: What comes the Generall to speake with me?
You know my minde, Ile fight no more 'gainst Troy.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: What saies Achilles, would he ought with vs?

speeches.speaker: Nes.
prose: Would you my Lord ought with the Generall?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Nes.
prose: Nothing my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: The better.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Good day, good day.

speeches.speaker: Men.
prose: How doe you? how doe you?

speeches.speaker: Achi.
prose: What, do's the Cuckold scorne me?

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: How now Patroclus?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Good morrow Aiax?

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: Ha.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: I, and good next day too.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: What meane these fellowes? know they not Achilles?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
verse: They passe by strangely: they were vs'd to bend
To send their smiles before them to Achilles:
To come as humbly as they vs'd to creepe to holy Altars.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: What am I poore of late?
'Tis certaine, greatnesse once falne out with fortune,
Must fall out with men too: what the declin'd is,
He shall as soone reade in the eyes of others,
As feele in his owne fall: for men like butter-flies,
Shew not their mealie wings, but to the Summer:
And not a man for being simply man,
Hath any honour; but honour'd for those honours
That are without him; as place, riches, and fauour,
Prizes of accident, as oft as merit:
Which when they fall, as being slippery standers;
The loue that leand on them as slippery too,
Doth one plucke downe another, and together
Dye in the fall. But 'tis not so with me;
Fortune and I are friends, I doe enioy
At ample point, all that I did possesse,
Saue these mens lookes: who do me thinkes finde out
Something not worth in me such rich beholding,

As they haue often giuen. Here is
~lisses,
Ile interrupt his reading: how now Vlisses?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Now great Thetis Sonne.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: What are you reading?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: A strange fellow here
Writes me, that man, how dearely euer parted,
How much in hauing, or without, or in,
Cannot make boast to haue that which he hath;
Nor feeles not what he owes, but by reflection:
As when his vertues shining vpon others,
Heate them, and they retort that heate againe
To the first giuer.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: This is not strange Vlisses:
The beautie that is borne here in the face,
The bearer knowes not, but commends it selfe,
Not going from it selfe: but eye to eye oppos'd
Salutes each other with each others forme:
For speculation turnes not to it selfe,
Till it hath trauail'd, and is married there
Where it may see it selfe: this is not strange at all.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
verse: I doe not straine it at the position,
It is familiar; but at the Authors drift,
Who in his circumstance, expresly proues
That no may is the Lord of any thing,
(Though in and of him there is much consisting,)
Till he communicate his parts to others:
Nor doth he of himselfe know them for ought,
Till he behold them formed in th' applause,
Where they are extended: who like an arch reuerb'rate
The voyce againe; or like a gate of steele,
Fronting the Sunne, receiues and renders backe
His figure, and his heate. I was much rapt in this,
And apprehended here immediately:
The vnknowne Aiax;
Heauens what a man is there? a very Horse,
That has he knowes not what. Nature, what things there are.
Most abiect in regard, and deare in vse.
What things againe most deere in the esteeme,
And poore in worth: now shall we see to morrow,
An act that very chance doth throw vpon him?
Aiax renown'd? O heauens, what some men doe,
While some men leaue to doe!
How some men creepe in skittish fortunes hall,
Whiles others play the Ideots in her eyes:
How one man eates into anothers pride,
While pride is feasting in his wantonnesse
To see these Grecian Lords; why, euen already,
They clap the lubber Aiax on the shoulder,
As if his foote were on braue Hectors brest,
And great Troy shrinking.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: I doe beleeue it:
For they past by me, as my sers doe by beggars,
Neither gaue to me good word, nor looke:
What are my deedes forgot?

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
verse: Time hath (my Lord) a wallet at his backe,
Wherein he puts almes for obliuion:
A great siz'd monster of ingratitudes:
Those scraps are good deedes past,
Which are deuour'd as fast as they are made,
Forgot as soone as done: perseuerance, deere my Lord,
Keepes honor bright, to haue done, is to hang
Quite out of fashion, like a rustie male,
In monumentall mockrie: take the instant way,
For honour trauels in a straight so narrow,
Where one but goes a breast, keepe then the path:
For emulation hath a thousand Sonnes,
That one by one pursue; if you giue way,
Or hedge aside from the direct forth right;
Like to an entred Tyde, they all rush by,
And leaue you hindmost:
Or like a gallant Horse falne in first ranke,
Lye there for pauement to the abiect, neere
Ore-run and trampled on: then what they doe in present,
Though lesse then yours in past, must ore-top yours:
For time is like a fashionable Hoste,
That slightly shakes his parting Guest by th' hand;
And with his armes out-stretcht, as he would flye,
Graspes in the commer: the welcome euer smiles,
And farewels goes out sighing: O let not vertue seeke
Remuneration for the thing it was: for beautie, wit,
High birth, vigor of bone, desert in seruice,
Loue, friendship, charity, are subiects all
To enuious and calumniating time:
One touch of nature makes the whole world kin:
That all with one consent praise new borne gaudes,
Though they are made and moulded of things past,
And goe to dust, that is a little guilt,
More laud then guilt ore dusted.
The present eye praises the pres^nt obiect:
Then maruell not thou great and compleat man,
That all the Greekes begin to worship Aiax;
Since things in motion begin to catch the eye,
Then what not sti^s: the cry went out on thee,
And still it might, and yet it may againe,
If thou would'st not entombe thy selfe aliue,
And case thy reputation in thy Tent;
Whose glorious deedes, but in these fields of late,
Made emulous missions 'mongst the gods themselues,
And draue great Mars to faction.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Of this my priuacie,
I haue strong reasons.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: But 'gainst your priuacie
The reasons are more potent and heroycall:
'Tis knowne Achilles, that you are in loue
With one of Priams daughters.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Ha? knowne?

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
verse: Is that a wonder?
The prouidence that's in a watchfull State,
Knowes almost euery graine of Plutoes gold;
Findes bottome in th' vncomprehensiue deepes;
Keepes place with thought; and almost like the gods,
Doe thoughts vnuaile in their dumbe cradles:
There is a mysterie (with whom relation
Durst neuer meddle) in the soule of State;
Which hath an operation more diuine,
Then breath or pen can giue expressure to:
All the commerse that you haue had with Troy,
As perfectly is ours, as yours, my Lord.
And better would it fit Achilles much,
To throw downe Hector then Polixena.
But it must grieue yong Pirhus now at home,
When fame shall in her Hand sound her trumpe;
And all the Greekish Girles shall tripping sing,
Great Hectors sister did Achilles winne;
But our great Aiax brauely beate downe him.
Farewell my Lord: I as your louer speake;
The foole slides ore the Ice that you should breake.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
verse: To this effect Achilles haue I mou'd you;
A woman impudent and mannish growne,
Is not more loth'd, then an effeminate man,
In time of action: I stand condemn'd for this;
They thinke my little stomacke to the warre,
And your great loue to me, restraines you thus:
Sweete, rouse your selfe; and the weake wanton Cupid
Shall from your necke vnloose his amorous fould,
And like a dew drop from the Lyons mane,
Be shooke to ayrie ayre.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Shall Aiax fight with Hector?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: I, and perhaps receiue much honor by him.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: I see my reputation is at stake,
My fame is shrowdly gored.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
verse: O then beware:
Those wounds heale ill, that men doe giue themselues:
Omission to doe what is necessary,
Seales a commission to a blanke of danger,
And danger like an ague subtly taints
Euen then when we sit idely in the sunne.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Goe call Thersites hither sweet Patroclus,
Ile send the foole to Aiax, and desire him
T' inuite the Troian Lords after the Combat
To see vs here vnarm'd: I haue a womans longing,
An appetite that I am sicke withall,
To see great Hector in his weedes of peace;
To talke with him, and to behold his visage,
Euen to my full of view. A labour sau'd.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: A wonder.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: What?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Aiax goes vp and downe the field, asking for himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: How so?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Hee must fight singly to morrow with Hector, and is so prophetically proud of an heroicall cudgelling, that he raues in saying nothing.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: How can that be?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Why he stalkes vp and downe like a Peacock, a stride and a stand: ruminates like an hostesse, that hath no Arithmatique but her braine to set downe her reckoning: bites his lip with a politique regard, as who should say, there were wit in his head and twoo'd out; and so there is: but it lyes as coldly in him, as fire in a flint, which will not shew without knocking. The mans vndone for euer; for if Hector breake not his necke i' th' combat, heele break't himselfe in vaine-glory. He knowes not mee: I said, good morrow Aiax; And he replyes, thankes Agamemnon, What thinke you of this man, that takes me for the Generall? Hee's growne a very land-fish, languagelesse, a monster: a plague of opinion, a man may weare it on both sides like a leather Ierkin.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Thou must be my Ambassador to him Thersites.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Who, I: why. heele answer no body: he professes not answering; speaking is for beggers: he weares his tongue in's armes: I will put on his presence; let Patroclus make his demands to me, you shall see the Pageant of Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: To him Patroclus; tell him, I humbly desire the valiant Aiax, to inuite the most valorous Hector, to come vnarm'd to my Tent, and to procure safe conduct for his person, of the magnanimious and most illustrious, sixe or feauen times honour'd Captaine, Generall of the Grecian Armie Agamemnon, &c. doe this.

speeches.speaker: Patro.
prose: Ioue blesse great Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Hum.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: I come from the worthy Achilles.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Who most humbly desires you to inuite Hector to his Tent.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Hum.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: And to procure safe conduct from Agamemnon.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Agamemnon?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: I my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: What say you too't.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: God buy you with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Your anfwer sir.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: If to morrow be a faire day, by eleuen a clocke it will goe one way or other; howsoeuer, he shall pay for me ere he has me.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Your answer sir.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Fare you well withall my heart.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Why, but he is not in this tune, is he?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: No, but he's out a tune thus: what musicke will be in him when Hector has knockt out his braines, I know not: but I am sure none, vnlesse the Fidler Apollo get his sinewes to make catlings on.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Come, thou shalt beare a Letter to him straight.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Let me carry another to his Horse; for that's the more capable creature.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: My minde is troubled like a Fountaine stir'd,
And I my selfe see not the bottome of it.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Would the Fountaine of your minde were cleere againe, that I might water an Asse at it: I had rather be a Ticke in a Sheepe, then such a valiant ignorance.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: See hoa, who is that there?

speeches.speaker: Dieph.
prose: It is the Lord Aeneas.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Is the Prince there in person?
Had I so good occasion to lye long
As you Prince Paris, nothing but heauenly businesse,
Should rob my bed-mate of my company.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
prose: That's my minde too: good morrow Lord Aeneas.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: A valiant Greeke Aeneas, take his hand,
Witnesse the processe of your speech within;
You told how Diomed, in a whole weeke by dayes
Did haunt you in the Field.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Health to you valiant sir,
During all question of the gentle truce:
But when I meete you arm'd, as blacke defiance,
As hea^t can thinke, or courage execute.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
verse: The one and other Diomed embraces,
Our blouds are now in calme; and so long health:
But when contention, and occasion meetes,
By Ioue, Ile play the hunter for thy life,
With all my force, pursuite and pollicy.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: And thou shalt hunt a Lyon that will flye
With his face backward, in humaine gentlenesse:
Welcome to Troy; now by Anchises life,
Welcome indeede: by Venus hand I sweare,
No man aliue can loue in such a sort,
The thing he meanes to kill, more excellently,

speeches.speaker: Diom.
verse: We simpathize. Ioue let Aeneas liue
(If to my sword his fate be not the glory)
A thousand compleate courses of the Sunne,
But in mine emulous honor let him dye:
With euery ioynt a wound, and that to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: We know each other well.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: We doe, and long to know each other worse.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: This is the most, despightful'st gentle greeting;
The noblest hatefull loue, that ere I heard of.
What businesse Lord so early?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: I was sent for to the King; but why, I know not.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: His purpose meets you; it was to bring this Greek
To Calcha's house; and there to render him,
For the enfreed Anthenor, the faire Cressid:
Lets haue your company; or if you please,
Haste there before vs. I constantly doe thinke
(Or rather call my thought a certaine knowledge)
My brother Troylus lodges there to night.
Rouse him, and giue him note of our approach,
With the whole quality whereof, I feare
We shall be much vnwelcome.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: That I assure you:
Troylus had rather Troy were borne to Greece,
Then Cressid borne from Troy.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: There is no helpe:
The bitter disposition of the time will haue it so.
On Lord, weele follow you.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Good morrow all.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: And tell me noble Diomed; faith tell me true,
Euen in the soule of sound good fellowship,
Who in your thoughts merits faire Helen most?
My selfe, or Menelaus?

speeches.speaker: Diom.
verse: Both alike.
He merits well to haue her, that doth seeke her,
Not making any scruple of her soylure,
With such a hell of paine, and world of charge.
And you as well to keepe her, that defend her,
Not pallating the taste of her dishonour,
With such a costly losse of wealth and friends:
He like a puling Cuckold, would drinke vp
The lees and dregs of a flat tamed peece:
You like a letcher, out of whorish loynes.
Are pleas'd to breede out your inheritors:
Both merits poyz'd, each weighs no lesse nor more,
But he as he, which heauier for a whore.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: You are too bitter to your country-woman.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Shee's bitter to her countrey: heare me Paris,
For euery false drop in her baudy veines,
A Grecians life hath sunke: for euery scruple
Of her contaminated carrion weight,
A Troian hath beene slaine. Since she could speake,
She hath not giuen so many good words breath,
As for her, Greekes and Troians suffred death.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: Faire Diomed, you doe as chapmen doe,
Dispraise the thing that you desire to buy:
But we in silence hold this vertue well;
Weele not commend, what we intend to sell.
Here lyes our way.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Deere trouble not your selfe: the morne is cold.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Then sweet my Lord, Ile call mine Vnckle down;
He shall vnbolt the Gates.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Trouble him not:
To bed, to bed: sleepe kill those pritty eyes,
And giue as soft attachment to thy sences,
As Infants empty of all thought.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Good morrow then.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: I prithee now to bed.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Are you a weary of me?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: O Cressida! but that the busie day
Wak't by the Larke, hath rouz'd the ribauld Crowes,
And dreaming night will hide our eyes no longer:
I would not from thee.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Night hath beene too briefe.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Beshrew the witch! with venemous wights she stayes,
As hidiously as hell; but flies the graspes of loue,
With wings more momentary, swift then thought:
You will catch cold, and curse me.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Prithee tarry, you men will neuer tarry;
O foolish Cressid, I might haue still held off,
And then you would haue tarried. Harke, ther's one vp?

speeches.speaker: Pand. within.
prose: What's all the doores open here?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: It is your Vnckle.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: A pestilence on him: now will he be mocking:
I shall haue such a life.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: How now, how now? how goe maiden-heads?
Heare you Maide: wher's my cozin Cressid?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Go hang your self, you naughty mocking Vnckle:
You bring me to doo—and then you floute me too.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: To do what? to do what? let her say what:
What haue I brought you to doe?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Come, come, beshrew your heart: youle nere be good, nor suffer others.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Ha, ha: alas poore wretch: a poore Chipochia, hast not slept to night? would he not (a naughty man) let it sleepe: a bug-beare take him.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: My Lord, come you againe into my Chamber:
You smile and mocke me, as if I meant naughtily.
prose: Did not I tell you? would he were knockt ith' head. Who's that at doore? good Vnckle goe and see.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Cre.
verse: Come you are deceiu'd, I thinke of no such thing.
How earnestly they knocke: pray you come in.
I would not for halfe Troy haue you seene here.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Who's there? what's the matter? will you beate downe the doore? How now, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Good morrow Lord, good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Who's there my Lord Aeneas? by my troth I knew you not: what newes with you so early?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Is not Prince Troylus here?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Here? what should he doe here?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Come he is here, my Lord, doe not deny him:
It doth import him much to speake with me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Is he here say you? 'tis more then I know, Ile be sworne: For my owne part I came in late: what should he doe here?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Who, nay then: Come, come, youle doe him wrong, ere y' are ware: youle be so true to him, to be false to him: Doe not you know of him, but yet goe fetch him hither, goe.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: How now, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: My Lord, I scarce haue leisure to salute you,
My matter is so rash: there is at hand,
Paris your brother, and Deiphoebus,
The Grecian Diomed, and our Anthenor
Deliuer'd to vs, and for him forth-with,
Ere the first sacrifice, within this houre,
We must giue vp to Diomeds hand
The Lady Cressida.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Is it concluded so?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: By Priam, and the generall state of Troy,
They are at hand, and ready to effect it.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: How my atchieuements mocke me;
I will goe meete them: and my Lord Aeneas,
We met by chance; you did not finde me here.

speeches.speaker: Aen.
verse: Good, good, my Lord, the secrets of nature
Haue not more gift in taciturnitie.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Is't possible? no sooner got but lost: the diuell take Anthenor; the yong Prince will goe mad: a plague vpon Anthenor; I would they had brok's necke.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: How now? what's the matter? who was here?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Ah, ha!

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Why sigh you so profoundly? wher's my Lord? gone? tell me sweet Vnckle, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Would I were as deepe vnder the earth as I am aboue.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: O the gods! what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Prythee get thee in: would thou had'st nere been borne; I knew thou would'st be his death. O poore Gentleman: a plague vpon Anthenor.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Good Vnckle I beseech you, on my knees, I beseech you what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Thou must be gone wench, thou must be gone; thou art chang'd for Anthenor: thou must to thy Father, and be gone from Troylus: 'twill be his death: 'twill be his baine, he cannot beare it.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: O you immortall gods! I will not goe.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Thou must.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: I will not Vnckle: I haue forgot my Father:
I know no touch of consanguinitie:
No kin, no loue, no bloud, no soule, so neere me,
As the sweet Troylus: O you gods diuine!
Make Cressids name the very crowne of falshood!
If euer she leaue Troylus: time, orce and death,
Do to this body what extremitie you can;
But the strong base and building of my loue,
Is as the very Center of the earth,
Drawing all things to it. I will goe in and weepe.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Doe, doe.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Teare my bright heire, and scratch my praised cheekes,
Cracke my cleere voyce with sobs, and breake my heart
With sounding Troylus. I will not goe from Troy.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: It is great morning, and the houre prefixt
Of her deliuerie to this valiant Greeke
Comes fast vpon: good my brother Troylus,
Tell you the Lady what she is to doe,
And hast her to the purpose.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Walke into her house:
Ile bring her to the Grecian presently;
And to his hand, when I deliuer her,
Thinke it an Altar, and thy brother Troylus
A Priest, there offring to it his heart.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: I know what 'tis to loue,
And would, as I shall pittie, I could helpe.
Please you walke in, my Lords.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Be moderate, be moderate.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Why tell you me of moderation?
The griefe is fine, full perfect that I taste,
And no lesse in a sense as strong
As that which causeth it. How can I moderate it?
If I could temporise with my affection,
Or brew it to a weake and colder pallat,
The like alaiment could I giue my griefe:
My loue admits no qualifying crosse;
No more my griefe, in such a precious losse.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Here, here, here, he comes, a sweet ducke.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: O Troylus, Troylus!

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: What a paire of spectacles is here? let me embrace too: oh hart, as the goodly saying is; O heart, heauie heart, why sighest thou without breaking? where he answers againe; because thou canst not ease thy smart by friendship, nor by speaking: there was neuer a truer rime; let vs cast away nothing, for we may liue to haue neede of such a Verse: we see it, we see it: how now Lambs?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Cressid: I loue thee in so strange a puritie;
That the blest gods, as angry with my fancie,
More bright in zeale, then the deuotion which
Cold lips blow to their Deities: take thee from me.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Haue the gods enuie?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I, I, I, I, 'tis too plaine a case.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: And is it true, that I must goe from Troy?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: A hatefull truth.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: What, and from Troylus too?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: From Troy, and Troylus.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Ist possible?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: And sodainely, where iniurie of chance
Puts backe leaue-taking, iustles roughly by
All time of pause; rudely beguiles our lips
Of all reioyndure: forcibly preuents
Our lockt embrasures; strangles our deare vowes,
Euen in the birth of our owne laboring breath.
We two, that with so many thousand sighes
Did buy each other, must poorely sell our selues,
With the rude breuitie and discharge of our
Iniurious time; now with a robbers haste
Crams his rich theeuerie vp, he knowes not how.
As many farwels as be stars in heauen,
With distinct breath, and consign'd kisses to them,
He fumbles vp into a loose adiew;
And scants vs with a single famisht kisse,
Distasting with the salt of broken teares.

speeches.speaker: Aeneus within.
prose: My Lord, is the Lady ready?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Harke, you are call'd: some say the genius so
Cries, come to him that instantly must dye.
Bid them haue patience: she shall come anon.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Where are my teares? raine, to lay this winde, or my heart will be blowne vp by the root.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: I must then to the Grecians?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: No remedy.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: A wofull Cressid 'mong'st the merry Greekes.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: When shall we see againe?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Here me my loue: be thou but true of heart.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: I true? how now? what wicked deeme is this?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Nay, we must vse expostulation kindely,
For it is parting from vs:
I speake not, be thou true, as fearing thee:
For I will throw my Gloue to death himselfe,
That there's no maculation in thy heart:
But be thou true, say I, to fashion in
My sequent protestation: be thou true,
And I will see thee.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: O you shall be expos'd, my Lord to dangers
As infinite, as imminent: but Ile be true.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: And Ile grow friend with danger;
Weare this Sleeue.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: And you this Gloue.
When shall I see you?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: I will corrupt the Grecian Centinels,
To giue thee nightly visitation.
But yet be true.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: O heauens: be true againe?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Heare why I speake it; Loue:
The Grecian youths are full of qualitie,
Their louing well compos'd, with guift of nature,
Flawing and swelling ore with Arts and exercise:
How nouelties may moue, and parts with person.
Alas, a kinde of godly iealousie;
Which I beseech you call a vertuous sinne:
Makes me affraid.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: O heauens, you loue me not!

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Dye I a villaine then:
In this I doe not call your faith in question
So mainely as my merit: I cannot sing,
Nor heele the high Lauolt; nor sweeten talke;
Nor play at subtill games; faire vertues all;
To which the Grecians are most prompt and pregnant:
But I can tell that in each grace of these,
There lurkes a still and dumb-discoursiue diuell,
That tempts most cunningly: but be not tempted.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Doe you thinke I will:

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: No, but something may be done that we wil not:
And sometimes we are diuels to our selues,
When we will tempt the frailtie of our powers,
Presuming on their changefull potencie.

speeches.speaker: Aeneas within.
prose: Nay, good my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Come kisse, and let vs part.

speeches.speaker: Paris within.
prose: Brother Troylus?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Good brother come you hither,
And bring Aeneas and the Grecian with you.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: My Lord, will you be true?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Who I? alas it is my vice, my fault:
Whiles others fish with craft for great opinion,
I, with great truth, catch meere simplicitie;
Whil'st some with cunning guild their copper crownes,
With truth and plainnesse I doe weare mine bare:
Feare not my truth; the morrall of my wit
Is plaine and true, ther's all the reach of it.
Welcome sir Diomed, here is the Lady
Which for Antenor, we deliuer you.
At the port (Lord) Ile giue her to thy hand,
And by the way possesse thee what she is.
Entreate her faire; and by my soule, faire Greeke,
If ere thou stand at mercy of my Sword,
Name Cressid, and thy life shall be as safe
As Priam is in Illion?

speeches.speaker: Diom.
verse: Faire Lady Cressid,
So please you saue the thankes this Prince expects:
The lustre in your eye, heauen in your cheeke,
Pleades your faire visage, and to Diomed
You shall be mistresse, and command him wholly.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Grecian, thou do'st not vse me curteously,
To shame the seale of my petition towards,
I praising her. I tell thee Lord of Greece:
Shee is as farre high soaring o're thy praises,
As thou vnworthy to be cal'd her seruant:
I charge thee vse her well, euen for my charge:
For by the dreadfull Pluto, if thou do'st not,
(Though the great bulke Achilles be thy guard)
Ile cut thy throate.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
verse: Oh be not mou'd Prince Troylus;
Let me be priuiledg'd by my place and message,
To be a speaker free? when I am hence,
Ile answer to my lust: and know my Lord;
Ile nothing doe on charge: to her owne worth
She shall be priz'd: but that you say, be't so;
Ile speake it in my spirit and honor, no.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Come to the Port. Ile tell thee Diomed,
This braue, shall oft make thee to hide thy head:
Lady, giue me your hand, and as we walke,
To our owne selues bend we our needefull talke.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: Harke, Hectors Trumpet.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: How haue we spent this morning
The Prince must thinke me tardy and remisse,
That swore to ride before him in the field.

speeches.speaker: Par.
prose: 'Tis Troylus fault: come, come, to field with him.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Let vs make ready straight.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Yea, with a Bridegroomes fresh alacritie
Let vs addresse to tend on Hectors heeles:
The glory of our Troy doth this day lye
On his faire worth, and single Chiualrie.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Here art thou in appointment fresh and faire,
Anticipating time. With starting courage,
Giue with thy Trumpet a loud note to Troy
Thou dreadfull Aiax, that the appauled aire
May pierce the head of the great Combatant,
And hale him hither.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
verse: Thou, Trumpet, ther's my purse;
Now cracke thy lungs, and split thy brasen pipe:
Blow villaine, till thy sphered Bias cheeke
Out-swell the collicke of puft Aquilon:
Come, stretch thy chest, and let thy eyes spout bloud:
Thou blowest for Hector.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: No Trumpet answers.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: 'Tis but early dayes.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Is not yong Diomed with Calcas daughter?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: 'Tis he, I ken the manner of his gate,
He rises on the toe: that spirit of his
In aspiration lifts him from the earth.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Is this the Lady Cressid?

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Euen she.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Most deerely welcome to the Greekes, sweete Lady.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: Our Generall doth salute you with a kisse.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: Yet is the kindenesse but particular; 'twere better she were kist in generall.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: And very courtly counsell: Ile begin. So much for Nestor.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Ile take that winter from your lips faire Lady Achilles bids you welcome.

speeches.speaker: Mene.
prose: I had good argument for kissing once.

speeches.speaker: Patro.
verse: But that's no argument for kissing now;
For thus pop't Paris in his hardiment.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Oh deadly gall, and theame of all our scornes,
For which we loose our heads, to gild his hornes.

speeches.speaker: Patro.
verse: The first was Menelaus kisse, this mine:
Patroclus kisses you.

speeches.speaker: Mene.
prose: Oh this is trim.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Paris and I kisse euermore for him.

speeches.speaker: Mene.
prose: Ile haue my kisse sir: Lady by your leaue.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: In kissing doe you render, or receiue.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Both take and giue.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Ile make my match to liue,
The kisse you take is better then you giue: therefore no kisse.

speeches.speaker: Mene.
prose: Ile giue you boote, Ile giue you three for one.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: You are an odde man, giue euen, or giue none.

speeches.speaker: Mene.
prose: An odde man Lady, euery man is odde.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: No, Paris is not; for you know 'tis true,
That you are odde, and he is euen with you.

speeches.speaker: Mene.
prose: You fillip me a' th' head.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: No, Ile be sworne.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: It were no match, your naile against his horne:
May I sweete Lady beg a kisse of you?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: You may.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: I doe desire it.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Why begge then?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Why then for Venus sake, giue me a kisse:
When Hellen is a maide againe, and his—

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: I am your debtor, claime it when 'tis due.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: Neuer's my day, and then a kisse of you.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
prose: Lady a word, Ile bring you to your Father.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: A woman of quicke sence.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Fie, fie, vpon her:
Ther's a language in her eye, her cheeke, her lip;
Nay, her foote speakes, her wanton spirites looke out
At euery ioynt, and motiue of her body:
Oh these encounterers so glib of tongue,
That giue a coasting welcome ete it comes;
And wide vnclaspe the tables of their thoughts,
To euery tickling reader: set them downe,
For sluttish spoyles of opportunitie;
And daughters of the game.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: The Troians Trumpet.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Yonder comes the troope.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Haile all you state of Greece: what shalbe done
To him that victory commands? or doe you purpose,
A victor shall be knowne: will you the Knights
Shall to the edge of all extremitie
Pursue each other. or shall be diuided
By any voyce, or order of the field: Hector bad aske?

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Which way would Hector haue it?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: He cares not, heele obey conditions.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: 'Tis done like Hector, but securely done,
A little proudly, and great deale disprising
The Knight oppos'd.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: If not Achilles sir, what is your name?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: If not Achilles, nothing.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: Therefore Achilles: but what ere, know this.
In the extremity of great and little:
Valour and pride excell themselues in Hector;
The one almost as infinite as all;
The other blanke as nothing: weigh him well:
And that which lookes like pride, is curtesie:
This Aiax is halfe made of Hectors bloud;
In loue whereof, halfe Hector staies at home:
Halfe heart, halfe hand, halfe Hector, comes to seeke
This blended Knight, halfe Troian, and halfe Greeke.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: A maiden battaile then? O I perceiue you.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Here is sir, Diomed: goe gentle Knight,
Stand by our Aiax: as you and Lord Aeneas
Consent vpon the order of their fight,
So be it: either to the vttermost,
Or else a breach: the Combatants being kin,
Halfe stints their strife, before their strokes begin.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: They are oppos'd already.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: What Troian is that same that lookes so heauy?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: The yongest Sonne of Priam;
A true Knight; they call him Troylus;
Not yet mature, yet matchlesse, firme of word,
Speaking in deedes, and deedelesse in his tongue;
Not soone prouok't, nor being prouok't, soone calm'd;
His heart and hand both open, and both free:
For what he has, he giues; what thinkes, he shewes;
Yet giues he not till iudgement guide his bounty,
Nor dignifies an impaire thought with breath:
Manly as Hector, but more dangerous;
For Hector in his blaze of wrath subscribes
To tender obiects; but he, in heate of action,
Is more vindecatiue then iealous loue.
They call him Troylus; and on him erect,
A second hope, as fairely built as Hector.
Thus saies Aeneas, one that knowes the youth,
Euen to his inches: and with priuate soule,
Did in great Illion thus translate him to me.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: They are in action.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: Now Aiax hold thine owne.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Hector, thou sleep'st, awake thee.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: His blowes are wel dispos'd there Aiax.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
prose: You must no more.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: Princes enough, so please you.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: I am not warme yet, let vs fight againe.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
prose: As Hector pleases.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Why then will I no more:
Thou art great Lord, my Fathers sisters Sonne;
A cousen german to great Priams seede:
The obligation of our bloud forbids
A gorie emulation 'twixt vs twaine:
Were thy commixion, Greeke and Troian so,
That thou could'st say, this hand is Grecian all,
And this is Troian: the sinewes of this Legge,
All Greeke, and this all Troy: my Mothers bloud
Runs on the dexter cheeke, and this sinister
Bounds in my fathers: by Ioue multipotent,
Thou should'st not beare from me a Greekish member
Wherein my sword had not impressure made
Of our ranke feud: but the iust gods gainsay,
That any drop thou borrwd'st from thy mother,
My sacred Aunt, should by my mortall Sword
Be drained. Let me embrace thee Aiax:
By him that thunders, thou hast lustie Armes;
Hector would haue them fall vpon him thus.
Cozen, all honor to thee.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
verse: I thanke thee Hector:
Thou art too gentle, and too free a man:
I came to kill thee Cozen, and beare hence
A great addition, earned in thy death.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Not Neoptolymus so mirable,
On whose bright crest, fame with her lowd'st (O yes)
Cries, This is he; could'st promise to himselfe,
A thought of added honor, torne from Hector.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: There is expectance here from both the sides,
What further you will doe?

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Weele answere it:
The issue is embracement: Aiax, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
verse: If I might in entreaties finde successe,
As seld I haue the chance; I would desire
My famous Cousin to our Grecian Tents.

speeches.speaker: Diom.
verse: 'Tis Agamemnons wish, and great Achilles
Doth long to see vnarm'd the valiant Hector.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Aeneas, call my brother Troylus to me:
And signifie this louing enterview
To the expecters of our Troian part:
Desire them home. Giue me thy hand, my Cousin:
I will goe eate with thee, and see your Knights.

speeches.speaker: Aia.
prose: Great Agamemnon comes to meete vs here.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: The worthiest of them, tell me name by name:
But for Achilles, mine owne serching eyes
Shall finde him by his large and portly size.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: Worthy of Armes: as welcome as to one.
That would be rid of such an enemie.
But that's no welcome: vnderstand more cleere
What's past, and what's to come, is strew'd with huskes
And formelesse ruine of obliuion:
But in this extant moment, faith and troth,
Strain'd purely from all hollow bias drawing:
Bids thee with most diuine integritie.
From heart of very heart, great Hector welcome.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: I thanke thee most imperious Agamemnon.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: My well-fam'd Lord of Troy, no lesse to you.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Let me confirme my Princely brothers greeting,
You brace of warlike Brothers, welcome hither.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Who must we answer?

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: The Noble Menelaus.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: O, you my Lord, by Mars his gauntlet thanks,
Mocke not, that I affect th' vntraded Oath,
Your quondam wife sweares still by Venus Gloue
Shee's well, but bad me not commend her to you.

speeches.speaker: Men.
prose: Name her not now sir, she's a deadly Theame.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: O pardon, I offend.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
verse: I haue (thou gallant Troyan) seene thee oft
Labouring for destiny, make cruell way
Through rankes of Greekish youth: and I haue seen thee
As hot as Perseus, spurre thy Phrygian Steed,
And seene thee scorning forfeits and subduments,
When thou hast hung thy aduanced sword i' th' ayre,
Not letting it decline, on the declined:
That I haue said vnto my standers by,
Loe Iupiter is yonder, dealing life.
And I haue seene thee pause, and take thy breath,
When that a ring of Greekes haue hem'd thee in,
Like an Olympian wrestling. This haue I seene,
But this thy countenance (still lockt in steele)
I neuer saw till now. I knew thy Grandsire,
And once fought with him; he was a Souldier good,
But by great Mars, the Captaine of vs all,
Neuer like thee. Let an oldman embrace thee,
And (worthy Warriour) welcome to our Tents.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
prose: 'Tis the old Nestor.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Let me embrace thee good old Chronicle,
That hast so long walk'd hand in hand with time:
Most reuerend Nestor, I am glad to claspe thee.

speeches.speaker: Ne.
verse: I would my armes could match thee in contention
As they contend with thee in courtesie.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: I would they could.

speeches.speaker: Nest.
prose: Ha? by this white beard I'ld fight with thee to morrow. Well, welcom, welcome: I haue seen the time.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: I wonder now, how yonder City stands,
When we haue heere her Base and pillar by vs.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: I know your fauour Lord Vlysses well.
Ah sir, there's many a Greeke and Troyan dead,
Since first I saw your selfe, and Diomed
In Illion, on your Greekish Embassie.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: Sir, I foretold you then what would ensue,
My prophesie is but halfe his iourney yet;
For yonder wals that pertly front your Towne,
Yond Towers, whose wanton tops do busse the clouds,
Must kisse their owne feet.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: I must not beleeue you:
There they stand yet: and modestly I thinke,
The fall of euery Phrygian stone will cost
A drop of Grecian blood: the end crownes all,
And that old common Arbitrator, Time,
Will one day end it.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: So to him we leaue it.
Most gentle, and most valiant Hector, welcome;
After the Generall, I beseech you next
To Feast with me, and see me at my Tent.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: I shall forestall thee Lord Vlysses, thou:
Now Hector I haue fed mine eyes on thee,
I haue with exact view perus'd thee Hector,
And quoted ioynt by ioynt.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Is this Achilles?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: I am Achilles.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Stand faire I prythee, let me looke on thee.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Behold thy fill.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Nay, I haue done already.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Thou art to breefe, I will the second time,
As I would buy thee, view thee, limbe by limbe.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: O like a Booke of sport thou'lt reade me ore:
But there's more in me then thou vnderstand'st.
Why doest thou so oppresse me with thine eye?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Tell me you Heauens, in which part of his body
Shall I destroy him? Whether there, or there, or there,
That I may giue the locall wound a name,
And make distinct the very breach, where-out
Hectors great spirit fl^w. Answer me heauens.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: It would discredit the blest Gods, proud man,
To answer such a question: Stand againe;
Think'st thou to catch my life so pleasantly,
As to prenominate in nice coniecture
Where thou wilt hit me dead?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: I tell thee yea.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Wert thou the Oracle to tell me so,
I'ld not beleeue thee: henceforth guard thee well,
For Ile not kill thee there, nor there, nor there,
But by the forge that stythied Mars his helme,
Ile kill thee euery where, yea, ore and ore.
You wisest Grecians, pardon me this bragge,
His insolence drawes folly from my lips,
But Ile endeuour deeds to match these words,
Or may I neuer—

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
verse: Do not chafe thee Cosin:
And you Achilles, let these threats alone
Till accident, or purpose bring you too't.
You may euery day enough of Hector.
If you haue stomacke. The generall state I feare,
Can scarse intreat you to be odde with him.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: I pray you let vs see you in the field,
We haue had pelting Warres since you refus'd
The Grecians cause.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Dost thou intreat me Hector?
To morrow do I meete thee fell as death,
To night, all Friends.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Thy hand vpon that match.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
verse: First, all you Peeres of Greece go to my Tent,
There in the full conuiue you: Afterwards,
As Hectors leysure, and your bounties shall
Concurre together, seuerally intreat him.
Beate lowd the Taborins, let the Trumpets blow,
That this great Souldier may his welcome know.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse:
My Lord
~lysses, tell me I beseech you,
In what place of the Field doth Calchas keepe?

speeches.speaker: ~lys.
verse: At Menelaus Tent, most Princely Troylus,
There Diomed doth feast with him to night,
Who neither lookes on heauen, nor on earth,
But giues all gaze and bent of amorous view
On the faire Cressid.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Shall I (sweet Lord) be bound to thee so much,
After we part from Agamemnons Tent,
To bring me thither?

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
verse: You shall command me sir:
As gentle tell me, of what Honour was
This Cressida in Troy, had she no Louer there
That wailes her absence?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: O sir, to such as boasting shew their scarres,
A mocke is due: will you walke on my Lord?
She was belou'd, she lou'd; she is, and dooth;
But still sweet Loue is food for Fortunes tooth.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Ile heat his blood with Greekish wine to night,
Which with my Cemitar Ile coole to morrow:
Patroclus, let vs Feast him to the hight.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: Heere comes Thersites.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: How now, thou core of Enuy?
Thou crusty batch of Nature, what's the newes?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Why thou picture of what thou seem'st, & I doll of Ideot-worshippers, here's a Letter for thee.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: From whence, Fragment?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Why thou full dish of Foole, from Troy.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: Who keepes the Tent now?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: The Surgeons box, or the Patients wound.

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Well said aduersity, and what need these tricks?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Prythee be silent boy, I profit not by thy talke, thou art thought to be Achilles male Varlot.

speeches.speaker: Patro.
prose: Male Varlot you Rogue? What's that?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Why his masculine Whore. Now the rotten diseases of the South, guts-griping Ruptures, Catarres, Loades a grauell i' th' backe, Lethargies, cold Palsies, and the like, take and take againe, such prepostrous discoueries.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: Why thou damnable box of enuy thou, what mean'st thou to curse thus?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Do I curse thee?

speeches.speaker: Patr.
prose: Why no, you ruinous But, you whorson indistinguishable Curre.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: No? why art thou then exasperate, thou idle, immateriall skiene of Sleyd silke; thou greene Sarcenet flap for a sore eye, thou tassell of a Prodigals purse thou:
Ah how the poore world is pestred with such water-flies, diminutiues of Nature.

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose: Out gall.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Finch Egge.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: My sweet Patroclus, I am thwarted quite
From my great purpose in to morrowes battell:
Heere is a Letter from Queene Hecuba,
A token from her daughter, my faire Loue,
Both taxing me, and gaging me to keepe
An Oath that I haue sworne. I will not breake it,
Fall Greekes, faile Fame, Honor or go, or stay,
My maior vow lyes heere; this Ile obay:
Come, come Thersites, helpe to trim my Tent,
This night in banquetting must all be spent.
Away Patroclus.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: With too much bloud, and too little Brain, these two may run mad: but if with too much braine, and too little blood, they do, Ile be a curer of madmen. Heere's Agamemnon, an honest fellow enough, and one that loues Quailes, but he has not so much Braine as eare-wax; and the goodly transformation of Iupiter there his Brother, the Bull, the primatiue Statue, and oblique memoriall of Cuckolds, a thrifty shooing-horne in a chaine, hanging at his Brothers legge, to what forme but that he is, shold wit larded with malice, and malice forced with wit, turne him too: to an Asse were nothing; hee is both Asse and Oxe; to an Oxe were nothing, hee is both Oxe and Asse: to be a Dogge, a Mule, a Cat, a Fitchew, a Toade, a Lizard, an Owle, a Puttocke, or a Herring without a Roe, I would not care: but to be Menelaus, I would conspire against Destiny. Aske me not what I would be, if I were not Thersites: sot I care not to bee the lowse of a Lazar, so I were not Menelaus. Hoy-day, spirits and fires.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: We go wrong, we go wrong.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: No yonder'tis, there where we see the light.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: I trouble you.

speeches.speaker: Aiax.
prose: No, not a whit.

speeches.speaker: Vlys.
prose: Heere comes himselfe to guide you?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Welcome braue Hector, welcome Princes all.

speeches.speaker: Agam.
verse: So now faire Prince of Troy, I bid goodnight,
Aiax commands the guard to tend on you.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Thanks, and goodnight to the Greeks general.

speeches.speaker: Men.
prose: Goodnight my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Goodnight sweet Lord Menelaus.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Sweet draught: sweet quoth-a? sweet sinke, sweet sure.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Goodnight and welcom, both at once, to those that go, or tarry.

speeches.speaker: Aga.
prose: Goodnight.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Old Nestor tarries, and you too Diomed,
Keepe Hector company an houre, or two.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: I cannot Lord, I haue important businesse,
The tide whereof is now, goodnight great Hector.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Giue me your hand.

speeches.speaker: ~lys.
verse: Follow his Torch, he goes to Chalcas Tent,
Ile keepe you company.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Sweet sir, you honour me.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: And so good night.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
prose: Come, come, enter my Tent.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: That same Diomed's a false-hearted Rogue, a most vniust Knaue; I will no more trust him when hee leeres, then I will a Serpent when he hisses: he will spend his mouth & promise, like Brabler the Hound; but when he performes, Astronomers foretell it, that it is prodigious, there will come some change; the Sunne borrowes of the Moone when Diomed keepes his word. I will rather leaue to see Hector, then not to dogge him: they say, he keepes a Troyan Drab, and vses the Traitour Chalcas his Tent. Ile after—Nothing but Letcherie? All incontinent Varlets.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: What are you vp here ho? speake?

speeches.speaker: Chal.
prose: Who cals?

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Diomed, Chalcas (I thinke) wher's you Daughter?

speeches.speaker: Chal.
prose: She comes to you.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Stand where the Torch may not discouer vs.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Cressid comes forth to him.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: How now my charge?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Now my sweet gardian: harke a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Yea, so familiar?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: She will sing any man at first sight.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: And any man may finde her, if he can take her life: she's noted.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Will you remember?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Remember? yes.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Nay, but doe then; and let your minde be coupled with your words.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: What should she remember?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: List?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Sweete hony Greek, tempt me no more to folly.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Roguery.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Nay then.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Ile tell you what.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Fo, fo, come tell a pin, you are a forsworne.—

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: In faith I cannot: what would you haue me do?

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: A iugling tricke, to be secretly open.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: What did you sweare you would bestow on me?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: I prethee do not hold me to mine oath,
Bid me doe not any thing but that sweete Greeke.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Good night.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Hold, patience.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: How now Troian?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Diomed.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: No, no, good night: Ile be your foole no more.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Thy better must.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Harke one word in your eare.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: O plague and madnesse!

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: You are moued Prince, let vs depart I pray you,
Lest your displeasure should enlarge it selfe
To wrathfull tearmes: this place is dangerous;
The time right deadly: I beseech you goe.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Behold, I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: Nay, good my Lord goe off:
You flow to great distraction; come my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: I pray thee stay?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: You haue not patience, come.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: I pray you stay? by hell and hell torments,
I will not speake a word.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: And so good night.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Nay, but you part in anger.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Doth that grieue thee? O withered truth!

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: Why, how now Lord?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: By Ioue I will be patient.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Gardian? why Greeke?

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Fo, fo, adew, you palter,

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: In faith I doe not: come hither once againe.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: You shake my Lord at something; will you goe? you will breake out.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: She stroakes his cheeke.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Come, come.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Nay stay, by Ioue I will not speake a word.
There is betweene my will, and all offences,
A guard of patience; stay a little while.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: How the diuell Luxury with his fat rumpe and potato finger, tickles these together: frye lechery, frye.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: But will you then?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: In faith I will lo; neuer trust me else.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Giue me some token for the surety of it.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Ile fetch you one.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: You haue sworne patience.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Feare me not sweete Lord.
I will not be my selfe, nor haue cognition
Of what I feele: I am all patience.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Now the pledge, now, now, now.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: Here Diomed, keepe this Sleeue.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: O beautie! where is thy Faith?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: I will be patient, outwardly I will.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: You looke vpon that Sleeue? behold it well:
He lou'd me: O false wench: giue't me againe.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Whose was't?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: It is no matter now I haue't againe.
I will not meete with you to morrow night:
I prythee Diomed visite me no more.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Now she sharpens: well said Whetstone.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: I shall haue it.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: What, this?

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: I that.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: O all you gods! O prettie, prettie pledge;
Thy Maister now lies thinking in his bed
Of thee and me, and sighes, and takes my Gloue,
And giues memoriall daintie kisses to it;
As I kisse thee.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Nay, doe not snatch it from me.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: He that takes that, rakes my heart withall.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: I had your heart before, this followes it.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: I did sweare patience.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: You shall not haue it Diomed; faith you shall not:
Ile giue you something else.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: I will haue this: whose was it?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: It is no matter.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Come tell me whose it was?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: 'Twas one that lou'd me better then you will.
But now you haue it, take it.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Whose was it?

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse:
By all Diana^
waiting women yond:
And by her selfe, I will not tell you whose.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: To morrow will I weare it on my Helme,
And grieue his spirit that dares not challenge it.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Wert thou the diuell, and wor'st it on thy horne.
It should be challeng'd.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Well, well, 'tis done, 'tis past; and yet it is not:
I will not keepe my word.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Why then farewell,
Thou neuer shalt mocke Diomed againe.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: You shall not goe: one cannot speake a word,
But it strait starts you.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: I doe not like this fooling.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Nor I by Pluto: but that that likes not me, pleases me best.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: What shall I come? the houre.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
prose: I, come: O Ioue! doe, come: I shall be plagu'd.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Farewell till then.

speeches.speaker: Cres.
verse: Good night: I prythee come:
Troylus farewell; one eye yet lookes on thee;
But with my heart, the other eye, doth see.
Ah poore our sexe; this fault in vs I finde:
The errour of our eye, directs our minde.
What errour leads, must erre: O then conclude,
Mindes swai'd by eyes, are full of turpitude.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
verse: A proofe of strength she could not publish more;
Vnlesse she say, my minde is now turn'd whore.

speeches.speaker: ~lis.
prose: Al's done my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: It is.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Why stay we then?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: To make a recordation to my soule
Of euery syllable that here was spoke:
But if I tell how these two did coact;
Shall I not lye, in publishing a truth?
Sith yet there is a credence in my heart:
An esperance so obstinately strong,
That doth inuert that test of eyes and eares;
As if those organs had deceptious functions,
Created onely to calumniate.
Was Cressed here?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: I cannot coniure Troian.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: She was not sure.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Most sure she was.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Why my negation hath no taste of madnesse?

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: Nor mine my Lord: Cressid was here but now.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Let it not be beleeu'd for womanhood:
Thinke we had mothers; doe not giue aduantage
To stubborne Criticks, apt without a theame
For deprauation, to square the generall sex
By Cressids rule. Rather thinke this not Cressid.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
prose: What hath she done Prince, that can soyle our mothers?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Nothing at all, vnlesse that this were she.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Will he swagger himselfe out on's owne eyes?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse:
This she? no, this is Diomids Cressid^
:
If beautie haue a soule, this is not she:
If soules guide vowes; if vowes are sanctimonie;
If sanctimonie be the gods delight:
If there be rule in vnitie it selfe,
This is not she: O madnesse of discourse
That cause sets vp, with, and against thy selfe
By foule authoritie: where reason can reuolt
Without perdition, and losse assume all reason,
Without reuolt. This is, and is not Cressid:
Within my soule, there doth conduce a fight
Of this strange nature, that a thing inseperate,
Diuides more wider then the skie and earth:
And yet the spacious bredth of this diuision.
Admits no Orifex for a point as subtle,
As Ariachnes broken woofe to enter:
Instance, O instance! strong as Plutoes gates:
Cressid is mine, tied with the bonds of heauen;
Instance, O instance, strong as heauen it selfe:
The bonds of heauen are slipt, dissolu'd, and loos'd,
And with another knot fiue finger tied,
The fractions of her faith, orts of her loue:
The fragments, scraps, the bits, and greazie reliques,
Of her ore-eaten faith, are bound to Diomed

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: May worthy Troylus be halfe attached
With that which here his passion doth expresse?

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: I Greeke: and that shall be divulged well
In Characters, as red as Mars his heart

Inflam'd with
~enus: neuer did yong man fancy
With so eternall, and so fixt a soule.
Harke Greek: as much I doe Cressida loue;
So much by weight, hate I her Diomed,
That Sleeue is mine, that heele beare in his Helme:
Were it a Caske compos'd by Vulcans skill,
My Sword should bite it: Not the dreadfull spout,
Which Shipmen doe the Hurricano call,
Constring'd in masse by the almighty Fenne,
Shall dizzie with more clamour Neptunes eare
In his discent; then shall my prompted sword,
Falling on Diomed.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Heele tickle it for his concupie.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: O Cressid! O false Cressid! false, false, false:
Let all vntruths stand by thy stained name,
And theyle seeme glorious.

speeches.speaker: Vlis.
verse: O containe your selfe:
Your passion drawes eares hither.

speeches.speaker: Aene.
verse: I haue beene seeking you this houre my Lord:
Hector by this is arming him in Troy.
Aiax your Guard, staies to conduct you home.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Haue with you Prince: my curteous Lord adew:
Farewell reuolted faire: and Diomed,
Stand fast, and weare a Castle on thy head.

speeches.speaker: Vli.
prose: Ile bring you to the Gates.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
prose: Accept distracted thankes.

speeches.speaker: Ther.
prose: Would I could meete that roague Diomed, I would croke like a Rauen: I would bode, I would bode: Patroclus will giue me any thing for the intelligence of this whore: the Parrot will not doe more for an Almond, then he for a commodious drab: Lechery, lechery, still warres and lechery, nothing else holds fashion. A burning diuell take them.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: When was my Lord so much vngently temper'd,
To stop his eares against admonishment?
Vnarme, vnarme, and doe not fight to day.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: You traine me to offend you: get you gone.
By the euerlasting gods, Ile goe.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: My dreames will sure proue ominous to the day.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: No more I say.

speeches.speaker: Cassa.
prose: Where is my brother Hector?

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Here sister, arm'd, and bloudy in intent:
Consort with me in loud and deere petition:
Pursue we him on knees: for I haue dreampt
Of bloudy turbulence; and this whole night
Hath nothing beene but shapes, and formes of slaughter.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
prose: O, 'tis true.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Ho? bid my Trumpet sound.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
prose: No notes of sallie, for the heauens, sweet brother.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
prose: Begon I say: the gods haue heard me sweare.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: The gods are deafe to hot and peeuish vowes;
They are polluted offrings, more abhord
Then spotted Liuers in the sacrifice.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: O be perswaded, doe not count it holy,
To hurt by being iust; it is as lawfull:
For we would count giue much to as violent thefts,
And rob in the behalfe of charitie.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: It is the purpose that makes strong the vowe;
But vowes to euery purpose must not hold:
Vnatme sweete Hector.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: Hold you still I say;
Mine honour keepes the weather of my fate:
Life euery man holds deere, but the deere man
Holds honor farre more precious, deere, then life.
How now yong man? mean'st thou to fight to day?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Cassandra, call my father to perswade.

speeches.speaker: Hect.
verse: No faith yong Troylus; doffe thy harnesse youth:
I am to day ith' vaine of Chiualrie:
Let grow thy Sinews till their knots be strong;
And tempt nor yet the brushes of the warre.
Vnarme thee, goe; and doubt thou not braue boy,
Ile stand to day, for thee, and me, and Troy.

speeches.speaker: Troy.
verse: Brother, you haue a vice of mercy in you;
