prose: True, and therefore women being the weaker Vessels, are euer thrust to the wall: therefore I will push Mountagues men from the wall, and thrust his Maides to the wall.

speeches.speaker: Greg.
prose: The Quarrell is betweene our Masters, and vs their men.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
prose: 'Tis all one, I will shew my selfe a tyrant: when I haue fought with the men, I will bee ciuill with the Maids, and cut off their heads.

speeches.speaker: Greg.
prose: The heads of the Maids?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I, the heads of the Maids, or their Maiden-heads,
Take it in what sence thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Greg.
prose: They must take it sence, that feele it.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: Me they shall feele while I am able to stand:
And 'tis knowne I am a pretty peece of flesh.

speeches.speaker: Greg.
prose: 'Tis well thou art not Fish: If thou had'st, thou had'st beene poore Iohn. Draw thy Toole, here comes of the House of the Mountagues.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
prose: My naked weapon is out: quarrel, I wil back thee

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: How? Turne thy backe, and run.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
prose: Feare me not.

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: No marry: I feare thee.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
prose: Let vs take the Law of our sides. let them begin.

speeches.speaker: Gr.
prose: I wil frown as I passe by, & let the~ take it as they list

speeches.speaker: Sam.
prose: Nay, as they dare. I wil bite my Thumb at them, which is a disgrace to them, if they beare it.

speeches.speaker: Abra.
prose: Do you bite your Thumbe at vs sir?

speeches.speaker: Samp.
prose: I do bite my Thumbe, sir.

speeches.speaker: Abra.
prose: Do you bite your Thumb at vs, sir?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
prose: Is the Law of our side, if I say I?

speeches.speaker: Gre.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Sam,
prose: No sir, I do not bite my Thumbe at you sir: but I bite my Thumbe sir.

speeches.speaker: Greg.
prose: Do you quarrell sir?

speeches.speaker: Abra.
prose: Quarrell sir? no sir.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
prose: If you do sir, I am for you, I serue as good a man as you

speeches.speaker: Abra.
prose: No better?

speeches.speaker: Samp.
prose: Well sir.

speeches.speaker: Gr.
prose: Say better: here comes one of my masters kinsmen.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
prose: Yes, better.

speeches.speaker: Abra.
prose: You Lye.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
prose: Draw if you be men. Gregory, remember thy washing blow.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Part Fooles, put vp your Swords, you know not what you do.

speeches.speaker: Tyb.
prose: What art thou drawne, among these heartlesse Hindes? Turne thee Benuolio, looke vpon thy death.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: I do but keepe the peace, put vp thy Sword,
Or manage it to part these men with me.

speeches.speaker: Tyb.
verse: What draw, and talke of peace? I hate the word
As I hate hell, all Mountagues, and thee:
Haue at thee Coward.

speeches.speaker: Offi.
verse: Clubs, Bils, and Partisons, strike, beat them down
Downe with the Capulets, downe with the Mountagues.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: What noise is this? Giue me my long Sword ho.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: A crutch, a crutch: why call you for a Sword?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: My Sword I say: Old Mountague is come,
And flourishes his Blade in spight of me.

speeches.speaker: Moun.
prose:
Thou villaine.
Capulet. Hold me not, let me go

speeches.speaker: 2. Wife.
prose: Thou shalt not stir a foote to seeke a Foe.

speeches.speaker: Prince.
verse: Rebellious Subiects, Enemies to peace,
Prophaners of this Neighbor-stained Steele,
Will they not heare? What hoe, you Men, you Beasts,
That quench the fire of your pernitious Rage,
With purple Fountaines issuing from your Veines:
On paine of Torture, from those bloody hands
Throw your mistemper'd Weapons to the ground,
And heare the Sentence of your mooued Prince.
Three ciuill Broyles, bred of an Ayery word,
By thee old Capulet and Mountague,
Haue thrice disturb'd the quiet of our streets,
And made Verona's ancient Citizens
Cast by their Graue beseeming Ornaments,
To wield old Partizans, in hands as old,
Cankred with peace, to part your Cankred hate,
If euer you disturbe our streets againe,
Your liues shall pay the forfeit of the peace.
For this time all the rest depart away:
You Capulet shall goe along with me,
And Mountague come you this afternoone,
To know our Fathers pleasure in this case:
To old Free-towne, our common iudgement place:
Once more on paine of death, all men depart.

speeches.speaker: Moun.
verse: Who set this auncient quarrell new abroach?
Speake Nephew, were you by, when it began:

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Heere were the seruants of your aduersarie,
And yours close fighting ere I did approach,
I drew to part them, in the instant came
The fiery Tibalt, with his sword prepar'd,
Which as he breath'd defiance to my eares,
He swong about his head, and cut the windes,
Who nothing hurt withall, hist him in scorne.
While we were enterchanging thrusts and blowes,
Came more and more, and fought on part and part,
Till the Prince came, who parted either part.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: O where is Romeo, saw you him to day?
Right glad am I, he was not at this fray.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Madam, an houre before the worshipt Sun
Peer'd forth the golden window of the East,
A troubled mind draue me to walke abroad,
Where vnderneath the groue of Sycamour,
That West-ward rooteth from this City side:
So earely walking did I see your Sonne:
Towards him I made, but he was ware of me,
And stole into the couert of the wood,
I measuring his affections by my owne,
Which then most sought, wher most might not be found:
Being one too many by my weary selfe,
Pursued my Honour, not pursuing his
And gladly shunn'd, who gladly fled from me.

speeches.speaker: Mount.
verse: Many a morning hath he there beene seene,
With teares augmenting the fresh mornings deaw,
Adding to cloudes, more cloudes with his deepe sighes,
But all so soone as the all-cheering Sunne,
Should in the farthest East begin to draw
The shadie Curtaines from Auroras bed,
Away from light-steales home my heauy Sonne,
And priuate in his Chamber pennes himselfe,
Shuts vp his windowes, lockes faire day-light out,
And makes himselfe an artificiall night:
Blacke and portendous must this humour proue,
Vnlesse good counsell may the cause remoue.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: My Noble Vncle doe you know the cause?

speeches.speaker: Moun.
prose: I neither know it, nor can learne of him.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Haue you importun'd him by any meanes?

speeches.speaker: Moun.
verse: Both by my selfe and many others Friends,
But he his owne affections counseller,
Is to himselfe (I will not say how true)
But to himselfe so secret and so close,
So farre from sounding and discouery,
As is the bud bit with an enuious worme,
Ere he can spread his sweete leaues to the ayre,
Or dedicate his beauty to the same.
Could we but learne from whence his sorrowes grow,
We would as willingly giue cure, as know.

speeches.speaker: Ben
verse: See where he comes, so please you step aside,
Ile know his greeuance, or be much denide.

speeches.speaker: Moun.
verse: I would thou wert so happy by thy stay,
To heare true shrift. Come Madam let's away.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Good morrow Cousin.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Is the day so young?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: But new strooke nine.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Aye me, sad houres seeme long:
Was that my Father that went henec so fast?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: It was: what sadnes lengthens Romeo's houres?

speeches.speaker: Ro.
prose: Not hauing that, which hauing, makes them short

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: In loue.

speeches.speaker: Romeo.
prose: Out.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Of loue.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Out of her fauour where I am in loue.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Alas that loue so gentle in his view,
Should be so tyrannous and rough in proofe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Alas that loue, whose view is muffled still,
Should without eyes, see path-wayes to his will:
Where shall we dine? O me: what fray was heere?
Yet tell me not, for I haue heard it all:
Heere's much to do with hate, but more with loue:
Why then, O brawling loue, O louing hate,
O any thing, of nothing first created:
O heauie lightnesse, serious vanity,
Mishapen Chaos of welseeing formes,
Feather of lead, bright smoake, cold fire, sicke health,
Still waking sleepe, that is not what it is:
This loue feele I, that feele no loue in this.
Doest thou not laugh?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: No Coze, I rather weepe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Good heart, at what?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: At thy good hearts oppression.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Why such is loues transgression.
Griefes of mine owne lie heauie in my breast,
Which thou wilt propagate to haue it preast
With more of thine, this loue that thou hast showne,
Doth adde more griefe, to too much of mine owne.
Loue, is a smoake made with the fume of sighes,
Being purg'd, a fire sparkling in Louers eyes,
Being vext, a Sea nourisht with louing teares,
What is it else? a madnesse, most discreet,
A choking gall, and a preseruing sweet:
Farewell my Coze.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Soft I will goe along.
And if you leaue me so, you do me wrong.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Tut I haue lost my selfe, I am not here,
This is not Romeo, hee's some other where.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Tell me in sadnesse, who is that you loue?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: What shall I grone and tell thee?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Grone, why no: but sadly tell me who.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: A sicke man in sadnesse makes his will:
A word ill vrg'd to one that is so ill:
In sadnesse Cozin, I do loue a woman.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: I aym'd so neare, when I suppos'd you lou'd.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: A right good marke man, and shee's faire I loue

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: A right faire marke, faire Coze, is soonest hit.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Well in that hit you misse, sheel not be hit
With Cupids arrow, she hath Dians wit:
And in strong proofe of chastity well arm'd:
From loues weake childish Bow, she liues vncharm'd.
Shee will not stay the siege of louing tearmes,
Nor bid th' incounter of assailing eyes.
Nor open her lap to Sainct-seducing Gold:
O she is rich in beautie, onely poore,
That when she dies, with beautie dies her store.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Then she hath sworne, that she will still liue chast?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: She hath, and in that sparing make huge wast?
For beauty steru'd with her seuerity,
Cuts beauty off from all posteritie.
She is too faire, too wisewi: sely too faire,
To merit blisse by making me dispaire:
She hath forsworne to loue, and in that vow
Do I liue dead, that liue to tell it now.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Be rul'd by me, forget to thinke of her.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: O teach me how I should forget to thinke.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: By giuing liberty vnto thine eyes,
Examine other beauties,

speeches.speaker: Ro.
verse: 'Tis the way to cal hers (exquisit) in question more,
These happy maskes that kisse faire Ladies browes,
Being blacke, puts vs in mind they hide the faire:
He that is strooken blind, cannot forget
The precious treasure of his eye-sight lost:
Shew me a Mistresse that is passing faire,
What doth her beauty serue but as a note,
Where I may read who past that passing faire.
Farewell thou can'st not teach me to forget,

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Ile pay that doctrine, or else die in debt.

speeches.speaker: Capu.
verse: Mountague is bound as well as I,
In penalty alike, and 'tis not hard I thinke,
For men so old as wee, to keepe the peace.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: Of Honourable reckoning are you both,
And pittie 'tis you liu'd at ods so long:
But now my Lord, what say you to my sute?

speeches.speaker: Capu.
verse: But saying ore what I haue said before,
My Child is yet a stranger in the world,
Shee hath not seene the change of fourteene yeares,
Let two more Summers wither in their pride,
Ere we may thinke her ripe to be a Bride.

speeches.speaker: Pari.
prose: Younger then she, are happy mothers made.

speeches.speaker: Capu.
verse: And too soone mar'd are those so early made:
Earth hath swallowed all my hopes but she,
Shee's the hopefull Lady of my earth:
But wooe her gentle Paris, get her heart,
My will to her consent, is but a part,
And shee agree, within her scope of choise,
Lyes my consent, and faire according voice:
This night I hold an old accustom'd Feast,
Whereto I haue inuited many a Guest,
Such as I loue, and you among the store,
One more, most welcome makes my number more:
At my poore house, looke to behold this night,
Earth-treading starres, that make darke heauen light,
Such comfort as do lusty young men feele,
When well apparrel'd Aprill on the heele
Of limping Winter treads, euen such delight
Among fresh Fennell buds shall you this night
Inherit at my house: heare all, all see:
And like her most, whose merit most shall be:
Which one more veiw, of many, mine being one,
May stand in number, though in reckning none.
Come, goe with me: goe sirrah trudge about,
Through faire Verona, find those persons out,
Whose names are written there, and to them say,
My house and welcome, on their pleasure stay.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Find them out whose names are written. Heere it is written, that the Shoo-maker should meddle with his Yard, and the Tayler with his Last, the Fisher with his Pensill, and the Painter with his Nets. But I am sent to find those persons whose names are writ, & can neuer find what names the writing person hath here writ (I must to the learned) in good time.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Tut man, one fire burnes out anothers burning,
One pai^e is lesned by anothers anguish:
Turne giddie, and be holpe by backward turning:
One desparate greefe, cures with anothers languish:
Take thou some new infection to the eye,
And the rank poyson of the old wil die.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Your Plantan leafe is excellent for that.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: For what I pray thee?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: For your broken shin.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Why Romeo art thou mad?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Not mad, but bound more then a mad man is:
Shut vp in prison, kept without my foode,
Whipt and tormented: and Godden good fellow,

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Godgigoden, I pray sir can you read?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I mine owne fortune in my miserie.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Perhaps you haue learn'd it without booke:
But I pray can you read any thing you see?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I, if I know the Letters and the Language.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Ye say honestly, rest you merry.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Stay fellow, I can read.
A faire assembly, whither should they come?
prose: SEigneur Martino, and his wife and daughter: County Ans:elme and his beautious sisters: the Lady widdow of ~truuio, Seigneur Placentio, and his louely Neeces: Mercutio and his brother Valentine: mine vncle Capulet his wife and daughters: my faire Neece Rosaline, Liuia, Seigneur Valentio, & his Cosen Tybalt: Lucio and the liuely Helena.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Vp.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Whither? to supper?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: To our house.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Whose house?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: My Maisters.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Indeed I should haue askt you that before.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Now Ile tell you without asking. My maister is the great rich Capulet, and if you be not of the house of Mountagues I pray come and crush a cup of wine. Rest you merry.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: At this same auncient Feast of Capulets
Sups the faire Rosaline, whom thou so loues:
With all the admired Beauties of Verona,
Go thither and with vnattainted eye,
Compare her face with some that I shall show,
And I will make thee thinke thy Swan a Crow.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: When the deuout religion of mine eye
Maintaines such falshood, then turne teares to fire:
And these who often drown'd could neuer die,
Transparent Heretiques be burnt for liers.
One fairer then my loue: the all-seeing Sun
Nere saw her match, since first the world begun.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Tut, you saw her faire, none else being by,
Herselfe poys'd with herselfe in either eye:
But in that Christall scales, let there be waid,
Your Ladies loue against some other Maid
That I will show you, shining at this Feast,
And she shew scant shell, well, that now shewes best.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Ile goe along, no such sight to be showne,
But to reioyce in splendor of mine owne.

speeches.speaker: Wife
prose: Nurse wher's my daughter? call her forth to me.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: Now by my Maidenhead, at twelue yeare old
I bad her come, what Lamb: what Ladi-bird, God forbid,
Where's this Girle? what Iuliet?

speeches.speaker: Iuliet.
prose: How now, who calls?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Iuliet.
prose: Madam I am heere, what is your will?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose:
This is the matter: Nurse giue leaue awhile, we

must talke in secret. Nurse come backe againe, I haue remembred me, thou'se heare our counsell. Thou knowest my daughter's of a prety age.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: Faith I can tell her age vnto an houre.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Shee's not fourteene.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: Ile lay fourteene of my teeth,
And yet to my teene be it spoken,
I haue but foure, shee's not fourteene.
How long is it now to Lammas tide?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: A fortnight and odde dayes.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: Euen or odde, of all daies in the yeare come Lammas Eue at night shall she be fourteene. Susan & she, God rest all Christian soules, were of an age. Well Susan is with God, she was too good for me. But as I said, on Lamas Eue at night shall she be fourteene, that shall she marie, I remember it well. 'Tis since the Earth-quake now eleuen yeares, and she was wean'd I neuer shall forget it, of all the daies of the yeare, vpon that day: for I had then laid Worme-wood to my Dug sitting in the Sunne vnder the Douehouse wall, my Lord and you were then at Mantua, nay I doe beare a braine. But as I said, when it did tast the Worme-wood on the nipple of my Dugge, and felt it bitter, pretty foole, to see it teachie, and fall out with the Dugge, Shake quoth the Doue-house, 'twas no neede I trow to bid mee trudge: and since that time it is a eleuen yeares, for then she could stand alone, nay bi' th' roode she could haue runne, & wadled all about: for euen the day before she broke her brow, & then my Husband God be with his soule, a was a merrie man, tooke vp the Child, yea quoth hee, doest thou fall vpon thy face? thou wilt fall backeward when thou hast more wit, wilt thou not Iule? And by my holy-dam, the pretty wretch lefte crying, & said I: to see now how a Iest shall come about. I warrant, & I shall liue a thousand yeares, I neuer should forget it: wilt thou not Iulet quoth he? and pretty foole it stinted, and said I.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
prose: Inough of this, I pray thee hold thy peace.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: Yes Madam, yet I cannot chuse but laugh, to thinke it should leaue crying, & say I: and yet I warrant it had vpon it brow, a bumpe as big as a young Cockrels stone? A perilous knock, and it cryed bitterly. Yea quoth my husband, fall'st vpon thy face, thou wilt fall backward when thou commest to age: wilt thou not Iule? It stinted: and said I.

speeches.speaker: Iule.
prose: And stint thou too. I pray thee Nurse, say I.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Peace I haue done: God marke thee too his grace thou wast the prettiest Babe that ere I nurst, and I might liue to see thee married once, I haue my wish.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
verse: Marry that marry is the very theame
I came to talke of, tell me daughter Iuliet,
How stands your disposition to be Married?

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
prose: It is an houre that I dreame not of.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: An houre, were not I thine onely Nurse, I would say thou had'st suckt wisedome from thy teat.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
verse: Well thinke of marriage now, yonger then you
Heere in Verona, Ladies of esteeme,
Are made already Mothers. By my count
I was your Mother, much vpon these yeares
That you are now a Maide, thus then in briefe:
The valiant Paris seekes you for his loue.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: A man young Lady, Lady, such a man as all the world. Why hee's a man of waxe.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
prose: Veronas Summer hath not such a flower.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: Nay hee's a flower, infaith a very flower.

speeches.speaker: Old La:
verse: What say you, can you loue the Gentleman?
This night you shall behold him at our Feast,
Read ore the volume of young Paris face,
And find delight, writ there with Beauties pen:
Examine euery seuerall liniament,
And see how one another lends content:
And what obscur'd in this faire volume lies,
Find written in the Margent of his eyes.
This precious Booke of Loue, this vnbound Louer,
To Beautifie him, onely lacks a Couer.
The fish liues in the Sea, and 'tis much pride
For faire without, the faire within to hide:
That Booke in manies eyes doth share the glorie,
That in Gold claspes, Lockes in the Golden storie:
So shall you share all that he doth possesse,
By hauing him, making your selfe no lesse.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: No lesse, nay bigger: women grow by men.

speeches.speaker: Old La.
prose: Speake briefly, can you like of Paris loue?

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
verse: Ile looke to like, if looking liking moue.
But no more deepe will I endart mine eye,
Then your consent giues strength to make flye.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Madam, the guests are come, supper seru'd vp, you cal'd, my young Lady askt for, the Nurse cur'st in the Pantery, and euery thing in extremitie: I must hence to wait, I beseech you follow straight.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: We follow thee, Iuliet, the Countie staies.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: Goe Gyrle, seeke happ^e nights to happy daies.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: What shall this speeh be spoke for our excuse?
Or shall we on without Apologie?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: The date is out of such prolixitie,
Weele haue no Cupid, hood winkt with a skarfe,
Bearing a Tartars painted Bow of lath,
Skaring the Ladies like a Crow-keeper.
But let them measure vs by what they will,
Weele measure them a Measure, and be gone.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Giue me a Torch, I am not for this ambling.
Being but heauy I will beare the light.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nay gentle Romeo, we must haue you dance.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Not I beleeue me, you haue dancing shooes
With nimble soles, I haue a soale of Lead
So stakes me to the ground, I cannot moue.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: You are a Louer, borrow Cupids wings,
And soare with them aboue a common bound.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: I am too sore enpearced with his shaft,
To soare with his light feathers, and to bound:
I cannot bound a pitch aboue dull woe,
Vnder loues heauy burthen doe I sinke.

speeches.speaker: Hora.
verse: And to sinke in it should you burthen loue,
Too great oppression for a tender thing.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Is loue a tender thing? it is too rough,
Too rude, too boysterous, and it pricks like thorne.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: If loue be rough with you, be rough with loue,
Pricke loue for pricking, and you beat loue downe,
Giue me a Case to put my visage in,
A Visor for a Visor, what care I
What curious eye doth quote deformities:
Here are the Beetle-browes shall blush for me.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Come knocke and enter, and no sooner in,
But euery man betake him to his legs.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: A Torch for me, let wantons light of heart
Tickle the sencelesse rushes with their heeles:
For I am prouerb'd with a Grandsier Phrase,
Ile be a Candle-holder and looke on,
The game was nere so faire, and I am done.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Tut, duns the Mouse, the Constables owne word,
If thou art dun, weele draw thee from the mire.
Or saue your reuerence loue, wherein thou stickest
Vp to the eares, come we burne day-light ho.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Nay that's not so.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I meane sir I delay,
We wast our lights in vaine, lights, lights, by day;
Take our good meaning, for our Iudgement sits
Fiue times in that, ere once in our fine wits.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: And we meane well in going to this Maske,
But 'tis no wit to go.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why may one aske?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I dreampt a dreame to night.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: And so did I.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Well what was yours?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: That dreamers often lye.

speeches.speaker: Ro.
prose: In bed a sleepe while they do dreame things true.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: This is the hag, when Maides lie on their backs,
That presses them, and learnes them first to beare,
Making them women of good carriage:
This is she.
prose: O then I see Queene Mab hath beene with you: She is the Fairies Midwife, & she comes in shape no bigger then Agat-stone, on the fore-finger of an Alderman, drawne with a teeme of little Atomies, ouer mens noses as they lie asleepe: her Waggon Spokes made of long Spinners legs: the Couer of the wings of Grashoppers, her Traces of the smallest Spiders web, her coullers of the Moonshines watry Beames, her Whip of Crickets bone, the Lash of Philome, her Waggoner, a small gray-coated Gnat, not halfe so bigge as a round little Worme, prickt from the Lazie-finger of a man. Her Chariot is an emptie Haselnut, made by the Ioyner Squirrel or old Grub, time out a mind, the Faries Coach-makers: & in this state she gallops night by night, through Louers braines: and then they dreame of Loue. On Courtiers knees, that dreame on Cursies strait: ore Lawyers fingers, who strait dreamt on Fees, ore Ladies lips, who strait on kisses dreame, which oft athe angry Mab with blisters plagues, because their breath with Sweet meats tainted are. Sometime she gallops ore a Courtiers nose, & then dreames he of smelling out asute: & somtime comes she with Tith pigs tale, tickling a Parsons nose as a lies asleepe, then he dreames of another Benefice. Sometime she driueth ore a Souldiers necke, & then dreames he of cutting Forraine throats, of Breaches, Ambuscados, Spanish Blades: Of Healths fiue Fadome deepe, and then anon drums in his eares, at which he startes and wakes; and being thus frighted, sweares a prayer or two & sleepes againe: this is that very Mab that plats the manes of Horses in the night: & bakes the Elk-locks in foule sluttish haires, which once vntangled, much misfortune bodes,

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Peace, peace, Mercutio peace,
Thou talk'st of nothing.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: True, I talke of dreames:
Which are the children of an idle braine,
Begot of nothing, but vaine phantasie,
Which is as thin of substance as the ayre,
And more inconstant then the wind, who wooes
Euen now the frozen bosome of the North:
And being anger'd, puffes away from thence,
Turning his side to the dew dropping South.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: This wind you talke of blowes vs from our selues,
Supper is done, and we shall come too late.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: I feare too early, for my mind misgiues,
Some consequence yet hanging in the starres,
Shall bitterly begin his fearefull date
With this nights reuels, and expire the tearme
Of a despised life clos'd in my brest:
By some vile forfeit of vntimely death.
But he that hath the stirrage of my course,
Direct my sute: on lustie Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Strike Drum.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Where's Potpan, that he helpes not to take away?
He shift a Trencher? he scrape a Trencher?

prose: When good manners, shall lie in one or two mens hands, and they vnwasht too, 'tis a foule thing.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Away with the Ioynstooles, remoue the Courtcubbord, looke to the Plate: good thou, saue mee a piece of Marchpane, and as thou louest me, let the Porter let in Susan Grindstone, and Nell, Anthonie and Potpan.
I Boy readie.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: You are lookt for, and cal'd for, askt for, & sought for, in the great Chamber.

verse: We cannot be here and there too, chearly Boyes,
Be brisk awhile, and the longer liuer take all.

speeches.speaker: 1. Capu.
verse: Welcome Gentlemen,
Ladies that haue their toes
Vnplagu'd with Cornes, will walke about with you:
Ah my Mistresses, which of you all
Will now deny to dance? She that makes dainty,
She Ile sweare hath Cornes: am I come neare ye now?
Welcome Gentlemen, I haue seene the day
That I haue worne a Visor, and could tell
A whispering tale in a faire Ladies eare:
Such as would please: 'tis gone, 'tis gone, 'tis gone,
You are welcome Gentlemen, come Musitians play:
A Hall, Hall, giue roome, and foote it Girles,
More light you knaues, and turne the Tables vp:
And quench the fire, the Roome is growne too hot.
Ah sirrah, this vnlookt for sport comes well:
Nay sit, nay sit, good Cozin Capulet,
For you and I are past our dauncing daies:
How long 'ist now since last your selfe and I
Were in a Maske?

speeches.speaker: 2. Capu.
prose: Berlady thirty yeares.

speeches.speaker: 1. Capu.
verse: What man: 'tis not so much, 'tis not so much,
'Tis since the Nuptiall of Lucentio,
Come Pentycost as quickely as it will,
Some fiue and twenty yeares, and then we Maskt.

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: 'Tis more, 'tis more, his Sonne is elder sir:
His Sonne is thirty.

speeches.speaker: 3. Cap.
verse: Will you tell me that?
His Sonne was but a Ward two yeares agoe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: What Ladie is that which dothni rich the hand
Of yonder Knight?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I know not sir.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: O she doth teach the Torches to burne bright:
It seemes she hangs vpon the cheeke of night,
As a rich Iewel in an Aethiops eare:
Beauty too rich for vse, for earth too deare:
So shewes a Snowy Doue trooping with Crowes,
As yonder Lady ore her fellowes showes;
The measure done, Ile watch her place of stand,
And touching hers, make blessed my rude hand.
Did my heart loue till now, forsweare it sight,
For I neuer saw true Beauty till this night.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: This by his voice, should be a Mountague.
Fetch me my Rapier Boy, what dares the slaue
Come hither couer'd with an antique face,
To fleere and scorne at our Solemnitie?
Now by the stocke and Honour of my kin,
To strike him dead I hold it not a sin.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Why how now kinsman,
Wherefore storme you so?

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Vncle this is a Mountague, our foe:
A Villaine that is hither come in spight,
To scorne at our Solemnitie this night.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Young Romeo is it?

speeches.speaker: Tib.
prose: 'Tis he, that Villaine Romeo.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Content thee gentle Coz, let him alone,
A beares him like a portly Gentleman:
And to say truth, Verona brags of him,
To be a vertuous and well gouern'd youth:
I would not for the wealth of all the towne,
Here in my house do him disparagement:
Therfore be patient, take no note of him,
It is my will, the which if thou respect,
Shew a faire presence, and put off these frownes,
An ill beseeming semblance for a Feast.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: It fits when such a Villaine is a guest,
Ile not endure him.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: He shall be endu'rd.
What goodman boy, I say he shall, go too,
Am I the Maister here or you? go too,
Youle not endure him, God shall mend my soule,
Youle make a Mutinie among the Guests:
You will set cocke a hoope, youle be the man.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
prose: Why Vncle, 'tis a shame.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Go too, go too,
You are a sawcy Boy, 'ist so indeed?
This tricke may chance to scath you, I know what,
You must contrary me, marry 'tis time.
Well said my hearts, you are a Princox, goe,
Be quiet, or more light, more light for shame,
Ile make you quiet. What, chearely my hearts.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Patience perforce, with wilfull choler meeting,
Makes my flesh tremble in their different greeting:
I will withdraw, but this intrusion shall
Now seeming sweet, conuert to bitter gall.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: If I prophane with my vnworthiest hand,
This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this,
My lips to blushing Pilgrims did ready stand,
To smooth that rough touch, with a tender kisse.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Good Pilgrime,
You do wrong your hand too much.
Which mannerly deuotion shewes in this,
For Saints haue hands, that Pilgrims hands do tuch,
And palme to palme, is holy Palmers kisse.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Haue not Saints lips, and holy Palmers too?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I Pilgrim, lips that they must vse in prayer.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: O then deare Saint, let lips do what hands do,
They pray (grant thou) least faith turne to dispaire.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Saints do not moue,
Though grant for prayers sake.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Then moue not while my prayers effect I take:
Thus from my lips, by thine my sin is purg'd.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Then haue my lips the sin that they haue tooke.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Sin from my lips? O trespasse sweetly vrg'd:
Giue me my sin againe.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: You kisse by' th' booke.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Madam your Mother craues a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: What is her Mother?

speeches.speaker: Nurs.
verse: Marrie Batcheler,
Her Mother is the Lady of the house,
And a good Lady, and a wise, and Vertuous,
I Nur'st her Daughter that you talkt withall:
I tell you, he that can lay hold of her,
Shall haue the chincks.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Is she a Capulet?
O deare account! My life is my foes debt.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Away, be gone, the sport is at the best.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I so I feare, the more is my vnrest.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Nay Gentlemen prepare not to be gone,
We haue a trifling foolish Banquet towards:
Is it e'ne so? why then I thanke you all.
I thanke you honest Gentlemen, good night:
More Torches here: come on, then let's to bed.
Ah sirrah, by my faie it waxes late,
Ile to my rest.

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
verse: Come hither Nurse,
What is yond Gentleman:

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: The Sonne and Heire of old Tyberio.

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
prose: What's he that now is going out of doore?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Marrie that I thinke be young Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: What's he that follows here that would not dance?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: I know not.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Go aske his name: if he be married,
My graue is like to be my wedded bed.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: His name is Romeo, and a Mountague,
The onely Sonne of your great Enemie.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: My onely Loue sprung from my onely hate,
Too early seene, vnknowne, and knowne too late,
Prodigious birth of Loue it is to me,
That I must loue a loathed Enemie.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: What's this? whats this?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: A rime, I learne euen now
Of one I dan'st withall.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Anon, anon:
Come let's away, the strangers all are gone.
Now old desire doth in his death bed lie,
And yong affection gapes to be his Heire,
That faire, for which Loue gron'd for and would die,
With tender Iuliet matcht, is now not faire.
Now Romeo is beloued, and Loues againe,
A like bewitched by the charme of lookes:
But to his foe suppos'd he must complaine,
And she steale Loues sweet bait from fearefull hookes:
Being held a foe, he may not haue accesse
To breath such vowes as Louers vse to sweare,
And she as much in Loue, her meanes much lesse,
To meete her new Beloued any where:
But passion lends them Power, time, meanes to meete,
Temp'ring extremities with extreame sweete.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Can I goe forward when my heart is here?
Turne backe dull earth, and find thy Center out.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Romeo, my Cozen Romeo, Romeo.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: He is wise,
And on my life hath stolne him home to bed.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: He ran this way and leapt this Orchard wall.
Call good Mercutio:
Nay, Ile coniure too.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Romeo, Humours, Madman, Passion, Louer,
Appeare thou in the likenesse of a sigh,
Speake but one rime, and I am satisfied:
Cry me but ay me, Prouant, but Loue and day,
Speake to my goship Venus one faire word,
One Nickname for her purblind Sonne and her,
Young Abraham Cupid he that shot so true,
When King Cophet^a lou'd the begger Maid,
He heareth not, he stirreth not, he moueth not,
The Ape is dead, I must coniure him,
I coniure thee by Rosalines bright eyes,
By her High forehead, and her Scarlet lip,
By her Fine foote, Straight leg, and Quiuering thigh,
And the Demeanes, that there Adiacent lie,
That in thy likenesse thou appeare to vs.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: And if he heare thee thou wilt anger him.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: This cannot anger him, t' would anger him
To raise a spirit in his Mistresse circle,
Of some strange nature, letting it stand
Till she had laid it, and coniured it downe,
That were some spight.
My inuocation is faire and honest, & in his Mistris name,
I coniure onely but to raise vp him.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Come, he hath hid himselfe among these Trees
To be consorted with the Humerous night:
Blind is his Loue, and best befits the darke.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: If Loue be blind, Loue cannot hit the marke,
Now will he sit vnder a Medler tree,
And wish his Mistresse were that kind of Fruite,
As Maides call Medlers when they laugh alone,
O Romeo that she were, O that she were
An open, or thou a Poprin Peare,
Romeo goodnight, Ile to my Truckle bed,
This Field-bed is to cold for me to sleepe,
Come shall we go?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Go then, for 'tis in vaine to seeke him here
That meanes not to be found.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: He ieasts at Scarres that neuer felt a wound,
But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?
It is the East, and Iuliet is the Sunne,
Arise faire Sun and kill the enuious Moone,
Who is already sicke and pale with griefe,
That thou her Maid art far more faire then she:
Be not her Maid since she is enuious,
Her Vestal liuery is but sicke and greene,
And none but fooles do weare it, cast it off:
It is my Lady, O it is my Loue, O that she knew she were,
She speakes, yet she sayes nothing, what of that?
Her eye discourses, I will answere it:
I am too bold 'tis not to me she speakes:
Two of the fairest starres in all the Heauen,
Hauing some businesse do entreat her eyes,
To twinckle in their Spheres till they returne.
What if her eyes were there, they in her head,
The brightnesse of her cheeke would shame those starres,
As day-light doth a Lampe, her eye in heauen,
Would through the ayrie Region streame so bright,
That Birds would sing, and thinke it were not night:
See how she leanes her cheeke vpon her hand.
O that I were a Gloue vpon that hand,
That I might touch that cheeke.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Ay me.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: She speakes.
Oh speake againe bright Angell, for thou art
As glorious to this night being ore my head,
As is a winged messenger of heauen
Vnto the white vpturned wondring eyes
Of mortalls that fall backe to gaze on him,
When he bestrides the lazie puffing Cloudes,
And sailes vpon the bosome of the ayre.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?
Denie thy Father and refuse thy name:
Or if thou wilt not, be but sworne my Loue,
And Ile no longer be a Capulet.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Shall I heare more, or shall I speake at this?

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: 'Tis but thy name that is my Enemy:
Thou art thy selfe, though not a Mountague,
What's Mountague? it is nor hand nor foote,
Nor arme, nor face, O be some other name
Belonging to a man.
What? in a names that which we call a Rose,
By any other word would smell as sweete,
So Romeo would, were he not Romeo cal'd,
Retaine that deare perfection which he owes,
Without that title Romeo, doffe thy name,
And for thy name which is no part of thee,
Take all my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: I take thee at thy word:
Call me but Loue, and Ile be new baptiz'd,
Hence foorth I neuer will be Romeo.

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
verse: What man art thou, that thus bescreen'd in night
So stumblest on my counsell?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: By a name,
I know not how to tell thee who I am:
My name deare Saint, is hatefull to my selfe,
Because it is an Enemy to thee,
Had I it written, I would teare the word.

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
verse: My eares haue yet not drunke a hundred words
Of thy tongues vttering, yet I know the sound.
Art thou not Romeo, and a Montague?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Neither faire Maid, if either thee dislike.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: How cam'st thou hither.
Tell me, and wherefore?
The Orchard walls are high, and hard to climbe,
And the place death, considering who thou art,
If any of my kinsmen find thee here,

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: With Loues light wings
Did I ore-perch these Walls,
For stony limits cannot hold Loue out,
And what Loue can do, that dares Loue attempt:
Therefore thy kinsmen are no stop to me.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: If they do see thee, they will murther thee.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Alacke there lies more perill in thine eye,
Then twenty of their Swords, looke thou but sweete,
And I am proofe against their enmity.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I would not for the world they saw thee here.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: I haue nights cloake to hide me from their eyes
And but thou loue me, let them finde me here,
My life were better ended by their hate,
Then death proroged wanting of thy Loue.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: By whose direction found'st thou out this place?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: By Loue that first did promp me to enquire,
He lent me counsell, and I lent him eyes,
I am no Pylot, yet wert thou as far
As that vast-shore-washet with the farthest Sea,
I should aduenture for such Marchandise.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Thou knowest the maske of night is on my face,
Else would a Maiden blush be paint my cheeke,
For that which thou hast heard me speake to night,
Faine would I dwell on forme, faine, faine, denie
What I haue spoke, but farewell Complement,
Doest thou Loue? I know thou wilt say I,
And I will take thy word, yet if thou swear'st,
Thou maiest proue false: at Louers periuries
They say Ioue laught, oh gentle Romeo,
If thou dost Loue, pronounce it faithfully:
Or if thou thinkest I am too quickly wonne,
Ile frowne and be peruerse, and say thee nay,
So thou wilt wooe: But else not for the world.
In truth saire Mountague I am too fond:
And therefore thou maiest thinke my behauiour light,
But trust me Gentleman, Ile proue more true,
Then those that haue coying to be strange,
I should haue beene more strange, I must confesse,
But that thou ouer heard'st ere I was ware
My true Loues passion, therefore pardon me,
And not impute this yeelding to light Loue,
Which the darke night hath so discouered.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Lady, by yonder Moone I vow,
That tips with siluer all these Fruite ^ree tops.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: O sweare not by the Moone, th' inconstant Moone,
That monethly changes in her circled Orbe,
Least that thy Loue proue likewise variable.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: What shall I sweare by?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Do not sweare at all:
Or if thou wilt sweare by thy gratious selfe,
Which is the God of my Idolatry,
And Ile beleeue thee.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: If my hearts deare loue.

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
verse: Well do not sweare, although I ioy in thee:
I haue no ioy of this contract to night,
It is too rash, too vnaduis'd, too sudden,
Too like the lightning which doth cease to be
Ere, one can say, it lightens, Sweete good night:
This bud of Loue by Summers ripening breath,
May proue a beautious Flower when next we meete:
Goodnight, goodnight, as sweete repose and rest,
Come to thy heart, as that within my brest.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: O wilt thou leaue me so vnsatisfied?

speeches.speaker: Iuli.
verse: What satisfaction can'st thou haue to night?

speeches.speaker: Ro.
prose: Th' exchange of thy Loues faithfull vow for mine.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I gaue thee mine before thou did'st request it:
And yet I would it were to giue againe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Would'st thou withdraw it,
For what purpose Loue?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: But to be franke and giue it thee againe,
And yet I wish but for the thing I haue,
My bounty is as boundlesse as the Sea,
My Loue as deepe, the more I giue to thee
The more I haue, for both are Infinite:
I heare some noyse within deare Loue adue:
Anon good Nurse, sweet Mountague be true:
Stay but a little, I will come againe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: O blessed blessed night, I am afear'd
Being in night, all this is but a dreame,
Too flattering sweet to be substantiall.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Three words deare Romeo,
And goodnight indeed,
If that thy bent of Loue be Honourable,
Thy purpose marriage, send me word to morrow,
By one that Ile procure to come to thee,
Where and what time thou wilt performe the right,
And all my Fortunes at thy foote Ile lay,
And follow thee my Lord throughout the world.
I come, anon: but if thou meanest not well,
I do beseech theee
(By and by I come)
To cease thy strife, and leaue me to my griefe,
To morrow will I send.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: So thriue my soule.

speeches.speaker: Iu.
prose: A thousand times goodnight.

speeches.speaker: Rome.
verse: A thousand times the worse to want thy light,
Loue goes toward Loue as school-boyes fro~ thier books
But Loue fro~ Loue, towards schoole with heauie lookes.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Hist Romeo hist: O for a Falkners voice,
To lure this Tassell gentle backe againe,
Bondage is hoarse, and may not speake aloud,
Else would I teare the Caue where Eccho lies,
And make her ayrie tongue more hoarse, then
With repetition of my Romeo.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: It is my soule that calls vpon my name.
How siluer sweet, sound Louers tongues by night,
Like softest Musicke to attending eares.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Romeo.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: My Neece.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: What a clock to morrow
Shall I send to thee?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: By the houre of nine.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I will not faile, 'tis twenty yeares till then,
I haue forgot why I did call thee backe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Let me stand here till thou remember it.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I shall forget, to haue thee still stand there,
Remembring how I Loue thy company.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: And Ile still stay, to haue thee still forget,
Forgetting any other home but this.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: 'Tis almost morning, I would haue thee gone,
And yet no further then a wantons Bird,
That let's it hop a little from his hand,
Like a poore prisoner in his twisted Gyues,
And with a silken thred plucks it backe againe,
So louing Iealous of his liberty.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I would I were thy Bird.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Sweet so would I,
Yet I should kill thee with much cherishing:
Good night, good night.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Parting is such sweete sorrow,
That I shall say goodnight, till it be morrow.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Sleepe dwell vpon thine eyes, peace in thy brest.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Would I were sleepe and peace so sweet to rest,
The gray ey'd morne smiles on the frowning night,
Checkring the Easterne Clouds with streakes of light,
And darknesse fleckel'd like a drunkard reeles,
From forth dayes pathway, made by Titans wheeles.
Hence will I to my ghostly Fries close Cell,
His helpe to craue, and my deare hap to tell.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: The gray ey'd morne smiles on the frowning night,
Checkring the Easterne Cloudes with streaks of light.
And fleckled darknesse like a drunkard reeles,
From forth daies path, and Titans burning wheeles:
Now ere the Sun aduance his burning eye,
The day to cheere, and nights danke dew to dry,
I must vpfill this Osier Cage of ours,
With balefull weedes, and precious Iuiced flowers,
The earth that's Natures mother, is her Tombe,
What is her burying graue that is her wombe:
And from her wombe children of diuers kind
We sucking on her naturall bosome find:
Many for many vertues excellent:
None but for some, and yet all different.
Omickle is the powerfull grace that lies
In Plants, Hearbs, stones, and their true qualities:
For nought so vile, that on the earth doth liue,
But to the earth some speciall good doth giue.
Nor ought so good, but strain'd from that faire vse,
Reuolts from true birth, stumbling on abuse.
Vertue it selfe turnes vice being misapplied,
And vice sometime by action dignified.
Within the infant rin'd of this weake flower,
Poyson hath residence, and medicine power:
For this being smelt, with that part cheares each part,
Being tasted slayes all sences with the heart.
Two such opposed Kings encampe them still,
In man as well as Hearbes, grace and rude will:
And where the worser is predominant,
Full soone the Canker death eates vp that Plant.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Good morrow Father.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Benedecite.
What early tongue so sweet saluteth me?
Young Sonne, it argues a distempered head,
So soone to bid goodmorrow to thy bed;
Care keepes his watch in euery old mans eye,
And where Care lodges, sleepe will neuer lye:
But where vnbrused you^h with vnstuft braine
Doth couch his lims, there, golden sleepe doth raigne;
Therefore thy earlinesse doth me assure,
Thou art vprous'd with some diftemprature;
Or if not so, then here I hit it right.
Our Romeo hath not beene in bed to night.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: That last is true, the sweeter rest was mine.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: God pardon sin: wast thou with Rosaline?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: With Rosaline, my ghostly Father? No,
I haue forgot that name, and that names woe.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: That's my good Son, but wher hast thou bin then?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Ile tell thee ere thou aske it me agen:
I haue beene feasting with mine enemie,
Where on a s^dden one hath wounded me,
That's by me wounded: both our remedies
Within thy helpe and holy phisicke lies:
I beare no hatred, blessed man: for loe
My intercession likewise steads my foe.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Be plaine good Son, rest homely in thy drift,
Ridling confession, findes but ridling shrift.

speeches.speaker: Rom
verse: Then plainly know my hearts deare Loue is set,
On the faire daughter of rich Capulet:
As mine on hers, so hers is set on mine;
And all combin'd, saue what thou must combine
By holy marriage: when and where, and how,
We met, we wooed, and made exchange of vow:
Ile tell thee as we passe, but this I pray,
That thou consent to marrie vs to day.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Holy S. Francis, what a change is heere?
Is Rosaline that thou didst Loue so deare
So soone forsaken? young mens Loue then lies
Not truely in their hearts, but in their eyes.
Iesu Maria, what a deale of brine
Hath washt thy sallow cheekes for Rosaline?
How much salt water throwne away in wast,
To season Loue that of it doth not tast.
The Sun not yet thy sighes, from heauen cleares,
Thy old grones yet ringing in my auncient eares:
Lo here vpon thy cheeke the staine doth sit,
Of an old teare that is not washt off yet.
If ere thou wast thy selfe, and these woes thine,
Thou and these woes, were all for Rosaline.
And art thou chang'd? pronounce this sentence then,
Women may fall, when there's no strength in men.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Thou chid'st me oft for louing Rosaline.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: For doting not for louing pupill mine.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: And bad'st me bury Loue.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Not in a graue,
To lay one in, another out to haue.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: I pray thee chide me not, her I Loue now
Doth grace for grace, and Loue for Loue allow:
The other did not so.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: O she knew well,
Thy Loue did read by rote, that could not spell:
But come young wauerer, come goe with me,
In one respect, Ile thy assistant be:
For this alliance may so happy proue,
To turne your houshould rancor to pure Loue.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: O let vs hence, I stand on sudden hast.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: Wisely and slow, they stumble that run fast.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Where the deu^le should this Romeo be? came he not home to night?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Not to his Fathers, I spoke with his man.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why that same pale hard-harted wench, that Rosaline torments him so, that he will sure run mad.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Tibalt, the kinsman to old Capulet, hath sent a Letter to his Fathers house.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: A challenge on my life.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Romeo will answere it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Any man that can write, may answere a Letter.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Nay, he will answere the Letters Maister how he dares, being dared.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Alas poore Romeo, he is already dead stab'd with a white wenche^ blacke eye, runne through the eare with a Loue song, the very pinne of his heart, cleft with the blind Bowe-boyes but-shaft, and is he a man to encounter Tybalt?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Why what is Tibalt?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: More then Prince of Cats. Oh hee's the Couragious Captaine of Complements: he fights as you sing pricksong, keeps time, distance, and proportion, he rests his minum, one, two, and the third in your bosom: the very butcher of a silk button, a Dualist, a Dualist: a Gentleman of the very first house of the first and second cause: ah the immortall Passado, the Punto reuerso, the Hay.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: The what?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The Pox of such antique lisping affecting phantacies, these new tuners of accent: Iesu a very good blade, a very tall man, a very good whore. Why is not this a lamentable thing Grandsire, that we should be thus afflicted with these strange flies: these fashion Mongers, these pardon-mee's, who stand so much on the new form, that they cannot sit at ease on the old bench. O their bones, their bones.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose:
Without his Roe, like a dryed Hering. O flesh, flesh, how art thou fishified? Now is he for the numbers that Petrarch flowed in: Laura to his Lady, was a kitchen wench, marrie she had a better Loue to be rime her: Dido a dowdie, Cleopatra a Gipsie, Hellen and Hero, hildinsgs and Harlots: Thisbie a gray eie or so, but not to the purpose. Signior Romeo, Bon iour, there's a French salutation to your

French slop: you gaue vs the the counterfait fairely last night.

speeches.speaker: Romeo.
prose: Good morrow to you both, what counterfeit did I giue you?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The slip sir, the slip, can you not conceiue?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Pardon Mercutio, my businesse was great, and in such a case as mine, a man may straine curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: That's as much as to say, such a case as yours constrains a man to bow in the hams.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Meaning to cursie.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Thou hast most kindly hit it.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: A most curteous exposition.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nay, I am the very pinck of curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Pinke for flower.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Right.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Why then is my Pump well flowr'd.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Sure wit, follow me this ieast, now till thou hast worne out thy Pump, that when the single sole of it is worne, the ieast may remaine after the wearing, sole-singular.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: O single sol'd ieast,
Soly singular for the singlenesse.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Come betweene vs good Benuolio, my wits faints.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Swits and spurs,
Swits and spurs, or Ile crie a match.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nay, if our wits run the Wild-Goose chase, I am done: For thou hast more of the Wild-Goose in one of thy wits, then I am sure I haue in my whole fiue. Was I with you there for the Goose?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Thou wast neuer with mee for any thing, when thou wast not there for the Goose.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I will bite thee by the eare for that iest.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Nay, good Goose bite not.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Thy wit is a very Bitter-sweeting,
It is a most sharpe sawce.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: And is it not well seru'd into a Sweet-Goose?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Oh here's a wit of Cheuerell, that stretches from an ynch narrow, to an ell broad.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I stretch it out for that word, broad, which added to the Goose, proues thee farre and wide, abroad Goose.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why is not this better now, then groning for Loue, now art thou sociable, now art thou Romeo: now art thou what thou art, by Art as well as by Nature, for this driueling Loue is like a great Naturall, that runs lolling vp and downe to hid his bable in a hole.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Stop there, stop there.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Thou desir'st me to stop in my tale against the haire.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Thou would'st else haue made thy tale large.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: O thou art deceiu'd, I would haue made it short, or I was come to the whole depth of my tale, and meant indeed to occupie the argument no longer.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Here's goodly geare.
A sayle, a sayle.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Two, two: a Shirt and a Smocke.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Peter?

speeches.speaker: Peter.
prose: Anon.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: My Fan Peter?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Good Peter to hide her face?
For her Fans the fairer face?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: God ye good morrow Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: God ye gooden faire Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Is it gooden?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: 'Tis no lesse I tell you: for the bawdy hand of the Dyall is now vpon the pricke of Noone.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Out vpon you: what a man are you?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: One Gentlewoman,
That God hath made, himselfe to mar.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: By my troth it is said, for himselfe to, mar quatha: Gentlemen, can any of you tel me where I may find the young Romeo?

speeches.speaker: Romeo.
prose: I can tell you: but young Romeo will be older when you haue found him, then he was when you sought him: I am the youngest of that name, for fault of a worse.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: You say well.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Yea is the worst well,
Very well tooke: I faith, wisely, wisely.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: If you be he sir,
I desire some confidence with you?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: She will endite him to some Supper.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: A baud, a baud, a baud. So no.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: What hast thou found?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: No Hare sir, vnlesse a Hare sir in a Lenten pie, that is something stale and hoare ere it be spent.
An old Hare hoare, and an old Hare hoare is very good meat in Lent.
But a Hare that is hoare is too much for a score. when it hoares ere it be spent,
Romeo will you come to your Fathers? Weele to dinner thither.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I will follow you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Farewell auncient Lady:
Farewell Lady, Lady, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: I pray you sir, what sawcie Merchant was this that was so full of his roperie?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: A Gentleman Nurse, that loues to heare himselfe talke, and will speake more in a minute, then he will stand to in a Moneth.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: And a speake any thing against me, Ile take him downe, & a were lustier then he is, and twentie such Iacks: and if I cannot, Ile finde those that shall: scuruie knaue, I am none of his flurt-gils, I am none of his skaines mates, and thou must stand by too and suffer euery knaue to vse me at his pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: I saw no man vse you at his pleasure: if I had, my weapon should quickly haue beene out, I warrant you, I dare draw assoone as another man, if I see occasion in a good quarrell, and the law on my side.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Now afore God, I am so vext, that euery part about me quiuers, skuruy knaue: pray you sir a word: and as I told you, my young Lady bid me enquire you out, what she bid me say, I will keepe to my selfe: but first let me tell ye, if ye should leade her in a fooles paradise, as they say, it were a very grosse kind of behauiour, as they say: for the Gentlewoman is yong: & therefore, if you should deale double with her, truely it were an ill thing to be offered to any Gentlewoman, and very weake dealing.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Nurse commend me to thy Lady and Mistresse, I protest vnto thee.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Good heart, and yfaith I will tell her as much:
Lord, Lord she will be a ioyfull woman.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: What wilt thou tell her Nurse? thou doest not marke me?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: I will tell her sir, that you do protest, which as I take it, is a Gentleman-like offer.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Bid her deuise some meanes to come to shrift this afternoone,
And there she shall at Frier Lawrence Cell
Beshriu'd and married: here is for thy paines.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: No truly sir not a penny.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Go too, I say you shall.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: This afternoone sir? well she shall be there.

speeches.speaker: Ro.
verse: And stay thou good Nurse behind the Abbey wall,
Within this houre my man shall be with thee,
And bring thee Cords made like a tackled staire.
Which to the high top gallant of my ioy,
Must be my conuoy in the secret night.
Farewell, be trustie and Ile quite thy paines:
Farewell, commend me to thy Mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Now God in heauen blesse thee: harke you sir,

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: What saist thou my deare Nurse?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
prose: Is your man secret, did you nere heare say two may keepe counsell putting one away.

speeches.speaker: Ro.
prose: Warrant thee my man as true as steele.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Well sir, my Mistresse is the sweetest Lady, Lord, Lord, when 'twas a little pra^ing thing. O there is a Noble man in Towne one Paris, that would faine lay knife aboard: but she good soule had as leeue a see Toade, a very Toade as see him: I anger her sometimes, and tell her that Paris is the propere^ man, but Ile warrant you, when I say so, shee lookes as pale as any clout in the versall world. Doth not Rosemarie and Romeo begin both with a letter?

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I Nurse, what of that? Both with an R

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: A mocker that's the dogs name, R. is for the no, I know it begins with some other letter, and she hath the prettiest sententious of it, of you and Rosemary, that it would do you good to heare it.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Commend me to thy Lady.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: I a thousand times. Peter?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: Anon.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Before and apace.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: The clocke strook nine, when I did send the Nurse,
In halfe an houre she promised to returne,
Perchance she cannot meete him: that's not so:
Oh she is lame, Loues Herauld should be thoughts,
Which ten times faster glides then the Sunnes beames,
Driuing backe shadowes ouer lowring hils.
Therefore do nimble Pinion'd Doues draw Loue,
And therefore hath the wind-swift Cupid wings:
Now is the Sun vpon the highmost hill
Of this daies iourney, and from nine till twelue,
I three long houres, yet she is not come.
Had she affections and warme youthfull blood,
She would be as swift in motion as a ball,
My words would bandy her to my sweete Loue,
And his to me, but old folkes,
Many faine as they were dead,
Vnwieldie, slow, heauy, and pale as lead.
O God she comes, O hony Nurse what newes?
Hast thou met with him? send thy man away.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Peter stay at the gate.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Now good sweet Nurse:
O Lord, why lookest thou sad?
Though newes, be sad, yet tell them merrily.
If good thou sham'st the musicke of sweet newes,
By playing it to me, with so sower a face.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: I am a weary, giue me leaue awhile,
Fie how my bones ake, what a iaunt haue I had?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I would thou had'st my bones, and I thy newes:
Nay come I pray thee speake, good good Nurse speake.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Iesu what hast? can you not stay a while?
Do you not see that I am out of breath?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: How art thou out of breath, when thou hast breth
To say to me, that thou art out of breath?
The excuse that thou dost make in this delay,
Is longer then the tale thou dost excuse.
Is thy newes good or bad? answere to that,
Say either, and Ile stay the circustance:
Let me be satisfied, ist good or bad?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Well, you haue made a simple choice, you know not how to chuse a man: Romeo, no not he though his face be better then any mans, yet his legs excels all mens, and for a hand, and a foote, and a body, though they be not to be talkt on, yet they are past compare: he is not the flower of curtesie, but Ile warrant him as gentle a Lambe: go thy waies wench, serue God. What haue you din'd at home?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: No no: but all this this did I know before
What saies he of our marriage? what of that?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Lord how my head akes, what a head haue I?
It beates as it would fall in twenty peeces.
My backe at other side: o my backe, my backe:
Beshrew your heart for sending me about
To catch my death with iaunting vp and downe.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Ifaith: I am sorrie that that thou art so well.
Sweet sweet, sweet Nurse, tell me what saies my Loue?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Your Loue saies like an honest Gentleman,
And a courteous, and a kind, and a handsome,
And I warrant a vertuous: where is your Mother?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Where is my Mother?
Why she is within, where should she be?
How odly thou repli'st:
Your Loue saies like an honest Gentleman
Where is your Mother?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: O Gods Lady deare,
Are you so hot? marrie come vp I trow,
Is this the Poultis for my aking bones?
Henceforward do your messages your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Heere's such a coile, come what saies Romeo?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
prose: Haue you got leaue to go to shrift to day?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: I haue.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Then high you hence to Frier Lawrence Cell,
There staies a Husband to make you a wife:
Now comes the wanton bloud vp in your cheekes,
The^'le be in Scarlet straight at any newes:
Hie you to Church, I must an other way,
To fetch a Ladder by the which your Loue
Must climde a birds nest Soone when it is darke:
I am the drudge, and toile in your delight:
But you shall beare the burthen soone at night.
Go Ile to dinner, hie you to the Cell.

speeches.speaker: Iui.
prose: Hie to high Fortune, honest Nurse, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: So smile the heauens vpon this holy act,
That after houres, with sorrow chide vs not.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Amen, amen, but come what sorrow can,
It cannot counteruaile the exchange of ioy
That one short minute giues me in her sight:
Do thou but close our hands with holy words,
Then Loue-deuouring death do what he dare,
It is inough. I may but call her mine.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: These violent delights haue violent endes,
And in their triumph: die like fire and powder;
Which as they kisse consume. The sweetest honey
Is loathsome in his owne deliciousnesse,
And in the taste confoundes the appetite.
Therefore Loue moderately, long Loue doth so,
Too swift arriues as tardie as too slow.
Here comes the Lady. Oh so light a foot
Will nere weare out the euerlasting flint,
A Louer may bestride the Gossamours,
That ydles in the wanton Summer ayre,
And yet not fall, so light is vanitie.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Good euen to my ghostly Confessor.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
prose: Romeo shall thanke thee Daughter for vs both.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: As much to him, else in his thanks too much.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Ah Iuliet, if the measure of thy ioy
Be heapt like mine, and that thy skill be more
To blason it, then sweeten with thy breath
This neighbour ayre, and let rich musickes tongue.
Vnfold the imagin'd happinesse that both
Receiue in either, by this deere encounter.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Conceit more rich in matter then in words,
Brags of his substance, not of Ornament:
They are but beggers that can count their worth,
But my true Loue is growne to such such excesse,
I cannot sum vp some of halfe my wealth.

speeches.speaker: Fri.
verse: Come, come with me, & we will make short worke,
For by your leaues, you shall not stay alone,
Till holy Church incorporate two in one.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: I pray thee good Mercutio lets retire,
The day is hot, the Capulets abroad:
And if we meet, we shal not scape a brawle, for now these hot dayes, is the mad blood stirring.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Thou art like one of these fellowes, that when he enters the confines of a Tauerne, claps me his Sword vpon the Table, and sayes, God send me no need of thee: and by the operation of the second cup, drawe^ him on the Drawer, when indeed there is no need.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Am I like such a Fellow?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Come, come, thou art as hot a Iacke in thy mood, as any in Italie: and assoone moued to be moodie, and assoone moodie to be mou'd.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: And what too?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nay, and there were two such, we should haue none shortly, for one would kill the other: thou, why thou wilt quarrell with a man that hath a haire more, or a haire lesse in his beard, then thou hast: thou wilt quarrell with a man for cracking Nuts, hauing no other reason, but because thou hast hasell eyes: what eye, but such an eye, would spie out such a quarrell? thy head is as full of quarrels, as an egge is full of meat, and yet thy head hath bin beaten as addle as an egge for quarreling: thou hast quarrel'd with a man for coffing in the street, because he hath wakened thy Dog that hath laine asleepe in the Sun. Did'st thou not fall out with a Tailor for wearing his new Doublet before Easter? with another, for tying his new shooes with old Riband, and yet thou wilt Tutor me from quarrelling?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: And I were so apt to quarell as thou art, any man should buy the Fee-simple of my life, for an houre and a quarter.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The Fee-simple? O simple.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: By my head here comes the Capulets.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: By my heele I care not.

speeches.speaker: Tyb.
verse: Follow me close, for I will speake to them.
Gentlemen, Good den, a word with one of you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: And but one word with one of vs? couple it with something, make it a word and a blow.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
prose: You shall find me apt inough to that sir, and you will giue me occasion.

speeches.speaker: Mercu.
prose: Could you not take some occasion without giuing?

speeches.speaker: Tib.
prose: Mercutio thou consort'st with Romeo.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Consort? what dost thou make vs Minstrels? & thou make Minstrels of vs, looke to heare nothing but discords: heere's my fiddlesticke, heere's that shall make you daunce. Come consort.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: We talke here in the publike haunt of men:
Either withdraw vnto some priuate place,
Or reason coldly of your greeuances:
Or else depart, here all eies gaze on vs.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Mens eyes were made to looke, and let them gaze.
I will not budge for no mans pleasure I.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
prose: Well peace be with you sir, here comes my man.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: But Ile be hang'd sir if he weare your Liuery.
Marry go before to field, heele be your follower,
Your worship in that sense, may call him man.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Romeo, the loue I beare thee, can affoord
No better terme then this: Thou art a Villaine.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Tibalt, the reason that I haue to loue thee,
Doth much excuse the appertaining rage
To such a greeting: Villaine am I none;
Therefore farewell, I see thou know'st me not.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Boy, this shall not excuse the iniuries
That thou hast done me, therefore turne and draw.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: I do protest I neuer iniur'd thee,
But lou'd thee better then thou can'st deuise:
Till thou shalt know the reason of my loue,
And so good Capulet, which name I tender
As dearely as my owne, be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: O calme, dishonourable, vile submission:
Alla stucatho carries it away.
Tybalt, you Rat-catcher, will you walke?

speeches.speaker: Tib.
prose: What woulds thou haue with me?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good King of Cats, nothing but one of your nine liues, that I meane to make bold withall, and as you shall vse me hereafter dry beate the rest of the eight. Will you pluck your Sword out of his Pilcher by the eares? Make hast, least mine be about your eares ere it be out.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
prose: I am for you.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Gentle Mercutio, put thy Rapier vp.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Come sir, your Passado.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: Draw Benuolio, beat downe their weapons:
Gentlemen, for shame forbeare this outrage,
Tibalt, Mercutio, the Prince expresly hath
Forbidden bandying in Verona streetes.
Hold Tybalt, good Mercutio.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I am hurt.
A plague a both the Houses, I am sped:
Is he gone and hath nothing?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: What art thou hurt?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I, I, a scratch, a scratch, marry 'tis inough,
Where is my Page? go Villaine fetch a Surgeon.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: Courage man, the hurt cannot be much.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No: 'tis not so deepe as a well, nor so wide as a Church doore, but 'tis inough, 'twill serue: aske for me to morrow, and you shall find me a graue man. I am pepper'd I warrant, for this world: a plague a both your houses. What, a Dog, a Rat, a Mouse, a Cat to scratch a man to death: a Braggart, a Rogue, a Villaine, that fights by the booke of Arithmeticke, why the deu'le came you betweene vs? I was hurt vnder your arme.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: I thought all for the best.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Helpe me into some house Benuolio,
Or I shall faint: a plague a both your houses.
They haue made wormes meat of me,
I haue it, and soundly to your Houses.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: This Gentleman the Princes neere Alie,
My very Friend hath got his mortall hurt
In my behalfe, my reputation stain'd
With Tibalts slaunder, Tybalt that an houre
Hath beene my Cozin: O Sweet Iuliet,
Thy Beauty hath made me Effeminate,
And in my temper softned Valours steele.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: O Romeo, Romeo, braue Mercutio's is dead,
That Gallant spirit hath aspir'd the Cloudes,
Which too vntimely here did scorne the earth.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: This daies blacke Fate, on mo daies doth depend,
This but begins, the wo others must end.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Here comes the Furious Tybalt backe againe.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: He gon in triumph, and Mercutio slaine?
Away to heauen respectiue Lenitie,
And fire and Fury, be my conduct now.
Now Tybalt take the Villaine backe againe
That late thou gau'st me, for Mercutios soule
Is but a little way aboue our heads,
Staying for thine to keepe him companie:
Either thou or I, or both, must goe with him.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Thou wretched Boy that didst consort him here,
Shalt with him hence.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: This shall determine that.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Romeo, away be gone:
The Citizens are vp, and Tybalt slaine,
Stand not amaz'd, the Prince will Doome thee death
If thou art taken: hence, be gone, away.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
prose: O! I am Fortunes foole.

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: Why dost thou stay?

speeches.speaker: Citi.
verse: Which way ran he that kild Mercutio?
Tibalt that Murtherer, which way ran he?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
prose: There lies that Tybalt.

speeches.speaker: Citi.
verse: Vp sir go with me:
I charge thee in the Princes names obey.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Where are the vile beginners of this Fray?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: O Noble Prince, I can discouer all
The vnluckie Mannage of this fatall brall:
There lies the man slaine by young Romeo,
That slew thy kinsman braue Mercutio.

speeches.speaker: Cap. Wi.
verse: Tybalt, my Cozin? O my Brothers Child,
O Prince, O Cozin, Husband, O the blood is spild
Of my deare kinsman. Prince as thou art true,
For bloud of ours, shed bloud of Mountague.
O Cozin, Cozin.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
prose: Benuolio, who began this Fray?

speeches.speaker: Ben.
verse: Tybalt here slaine, whom Romeo's hand did slay,
Romeo that spoke him faire, bid him bethinke
How nice the Quarrell was, and vrg'd withall
Your high displeasure: all this vttered,
With gentle breath, calme looke, knees humbly bow'd
Could not take truce with the vnruly spleene
Of Tybalts deafe to peace, but that he Tilts
With Peircing steele at bold Mercutio's breast,
Who all as hot, turnes deadly point to point,
And with a Martiall scorne, with one hand beates
Cold death aside, and with the other sends
It back to Tybalt, whose dexterity
Retorts it: Romeo he cries aloud,
Hold Friends, Friends part, and swifter then his tongue,
His aged arme beats downe their fatall points,
And twixt them rushes, vnderneath whose arme,
An enuious thrust from Tybalt, hit the life
Of stout Mercutio, and then Tybalt fled.
But by and by comes backe to Romeo,
Who had but newly entertained Reuenge,
And too't they goe like lightning, for ere I
Could draw to part them, was stout Tybalt slaine:
And as he fell, did Romeo turne and flie:
This is the truth, or let Benuolio die.

speeches.speaker: Cap. Wi.
verse: He is a kinsman to the Mountague,
Affection makes him false, he speakes not true
Some twenty of them fought in this blacke strife,
And all those twenty could but kill one life.
I beg for Iustice, which thou Prince must giue:
Romeo slew Tybalt, Romeo must not liue.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: Romeo slew him, he slew Mercutio,
Who now the price of his deare blood doth owe.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Not Romeo Prince, he was Mercutios Friend,
His fault concludes, but what the law should end,
The life of Tybalt.

speeches.speaker: Prin.
verse: And for that offence,
