speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Humbly I thanke your Lordship, neuer may
That state or Fortune fall into my keeping,
Which is not owed to you.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
verse: Vouchsafe my Labour,
And long liue your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I thanke you, you shall heare from me anon:
Go not away. What haue you there, my Friend?

speeches.speaker: Pain.
verse: A peece of Painting, which I do beseech
Your Lordship to accept.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Painting is welcome.
The Painting is almost the Naturall man:
For since Dishonor Traffickes with mans Nature,
He is but out-side: These Pensil'd Figures are
Euen such as they giue out. I like your worke,
And you shall finde I like it; Waite attendance
Till you heare further from me.

speeches.speaker: Pain.
prose: The Gods preserue ye.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Well fare you Gentleman: giue me your hand.
We must needs dine together: sir your Iewell
Hath suffered vnder praise.

speeches.speaker: Iewel.
prose: What my Lord, dispraise?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: A meere saciety of Commendations,
If I should pay you for't as 'tis extold,
It would vnclew me quite.

speeches.speaker: Iewel.
verse: My Lord, 'tis rated
As those which sell would giue: but you well know,
Things of like valew differing in the Owners,
Are prized by their Masters. Beleeu't deere Lord,
You mend the Iewell by the wearing it.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Well mock'd.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: No my good Lord, he speakes ye common toong
Which all men speake with him.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Looke who comes heere, will you be chid?

speeches.speaker: Iewel.
prose: Wee'l beare with your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Hee'l spare none.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Good morrow to thee,
Gentle Apermantus.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: Till I be gentle, stay thou for thy good morrow.
When thou art Timons dogge, and these Knaues honest.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Why dost thou call them Knaues, thou know'st them not?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Are they not Athenians?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Then I repent not.

speeches.speaker: Iew.
prose: You know me, Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Thou know'st I do, I call'd thee by thy name.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Thou art proud Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Of nothing so much, as that I am not like Timon

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Whether art going?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: To knocke out an honest Athenians braines.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: That's a deed thou't dye for.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Right, if doing nothing be death by th' Law.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: How lik'st thou this picture Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: The best. for the innocence.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Wrought he not well that painted it.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: He wrought better that made the Painter, and yet he's but a filthy peece of worke.

speeches.speaker: Pain.
prose: Y' are a Dogge.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Thy Mothers of my generation: what's she, if I be a Dogge?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Wilt dine with me Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: No: I eate not Lords.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: And thou should'st, thoud'st anger Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: O they eate Lords;
So they come by great bellies.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: That's a lasciuious apprehension.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: So, thou apprehend'st it,
Take it for thy labour.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: How dost thou like this Iewell, Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Not so well as plain-dealing, which wil not cast a man a Doit.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What dost thou thinke 'tis worth?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: Not worth my thinking.
How now Poet?

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: How now Philosopher?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Thou lyest.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: Art not one?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: Then I lye not.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Art not a Poet?

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: Then thou lyest:
Looke in thy last worke, where thou hast fegin'd him a worthy Fellow.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: That's not feign'd, he is so.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Yes he is worthy of thee, and to pay thee for thy labour. He that loues to be flattered, is worthy o' th flatterer. Heauens, that I were a Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What wouldst do then Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: E'ne as Apemantus does now, hate a Lord with my heart.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What thy selfe?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Wherefore?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: That I had no angry wit to be a Lord.
Art not thou a Merchant?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I Apemantus.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Traffick confound thee, if the Gods will not.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If Trafficke do it, the Gods do it.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: Traffickes thy God, & thy God confound thee.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What Trumpets that?

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: 'Tis Alcibiades, and some twenty Horse
All of Companionship.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Pray entertaine them, giue them guide to vs.
You must needs dine with me: go not you hence
Till I haue thankt you: when dinners done
Shew me this peece. I am ioyfull of your sights.
Most welcome Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: So, so; their Aches contract, and sterue your supple ioynts: that there should bee small loue amongest these sweet Knaues, and all this Curtesie. The straine of mans bred out into Baboon and Monkey.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Sir, you haue sau'd my longing, and I feed
Most hungerly on your sight.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Right welcome Sir:
Ere we depart, wee'l share a bounteous time
In different pleasures.
Pray you let vs in.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord
prose: What time a day is't Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Time to be honest.
That time serues still.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: The most accursed thou that still omitst it.
Thou art going to Lord Timons Feast.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: I, to see meate fill Knaues, and Wine heat fooles.
Farthee well, farthee well.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Thou art a Foole to bid me farewell twice.
Why Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Should'st haue kept one to thy selfe, for I meane to giue thee none.
Hang thy selfe.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: No I will do nothing at thy bidding:
Make thy requests to thy Friend.
Away vnpeaceable Dogge,
Or Ile spurne thee hence.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: I will flye like a dogge, the heeles a' th' Asse.

verse: Hee's opposite to humanity.
Comes shall we in,
And ^aste Lord Timons bountie: he out-goes
The verie heart of kindnesse.
He powres it out: Plutus the God of Gold
Is but his Steward: no meede but he repayes
Seuen-fold aboue it selfe: No guift to him,
But breeds the giuer a returne: exceeding
All vse of quittance.
The Noblest minde he carries,
That euer gouern'd man.
Long may he liue in Fortunes. Shall we in?
Ile keepe you Company.

speeches.speaker: Ventig.
verse: Most honoured Timon,
It hath pleas'd the Gods to remember my Fathers age,
And call him to long peace:
He is gone happy and has left me rich:
Then, as in gratefull Vertue I am bound
To your free heart, I do returne those Talents
Doubled with thankes and seruice, from whose helpe
I deriu'd libertie.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: O by no meanes,
Honest Ventigius: You mistake my loue,
I gaue it freely euer, and ther's none
Can truely say he giues, if he receiues:
If our betters play at that game, we must not dare
To imitate them: faults that are rich are faire.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
prose: A Noble spirit.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Nay my Lords, Ceremony was but deuis'd at first
To set a glosse on faint deeds, hollow welcomes,
Recanting goodnesse, sorry ere 'tis showne:
But where there is true friendship, there needs none,
Pray sit, more welcome are ye to my Fortunes,
Then my Fortunes to me.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord.
prose: My Lord, we alwaies haue confest it.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
prose: Ho ho, confest it? Handg'd it? Haue you not?

speeches.speaker: Timo.
prose: O Apermantus, you are welcome.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
verse: No: You shall not make me welcome:
I come to haue thee thrust me out of doores.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Fie, th' art a churle, ye' haue got a humour there
Does not become a man, 'tis much too blame:
They say my Lords, Irafuror breuis est,
But yond man is verie angrie.
Go, let him haue a Table by himselfe:
For he does neither affect companie,
Nor is he fit for't indeed.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
verse: Let me stay at thine apperill Timon,
I come to obserue, I giue thee warning on't.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I take no heede of thee: Th' art an Athenian, therefore welcome: I my selfe would haue no power, prythee let my meate make thee silent.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
verse: I wonder men dare trust themselues with men.
Me thinks they should enuite them without kniues,
Good for there meate, and safer for their liues.
prose: I scorne thy meate, 'twould choake me: for I should nere flatter thee. Oh you Gods! What a number of men eats Timon, and he sees 'em not? It greeues me to see so many dip there meate in one mans blood, and all the madnesse is, he cheeres them vp too.

There's much example for't, the fellow that sits next him, now parts bread with him, pledges the breath of him in a diuided draught: is the readiest man to kill him, 'Tas beene. proued, if I were a huge man I should feare to drinke at meales, least they should spie my wind-pipes dangerous noates, great men should drinke with harnesse on their throates.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: My Lord in heart: and let the health go round.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lord.
prose: Let it flow this way my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
verse: Heere's that which is too weake to be a sinner,
Honest water, which nere left man i' th' mire:
This and my food are equals, there's no ods,
Feasts are to proud to giue thanks to the Gods.
So fall too't:
Richmen sin, and I eat root.
Much good dich thy good heart, Apermantus
prose: Flow this way? A braue fellow. He keepes his tides well, those healths will make thee and thy state looke ill, Timon.

Apermantus Grace.
Immortall Gods, I craue no pelfe,
I pray for no man but my selfe,
Graunt I may neuer proue so fond,
To trust man on his Oath or Bond.
Or a Harlot for her weeping,
Or a Dogge that seemes asleeping,
Or a keeper with my freedome,
Or my friends if I should need 'em.
Amen.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Captaine, Alcibiades, your hearts in the field now.

speeches.speaker: Alci.
prose: My heart is euer at your seruice, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: You had rather be at a breakefast of Enemies, then a dinner of Friends.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: So they were bleeding new my Lord, there's no meat like 'em, I could wish my best friend at such a Feast.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
prose: Would all those Flatterers were thine Enemies then, that then thou might'st kill 'em: & bid me to 'em.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord.
prose: Might we but haue that happinesse my Lord, that you would once vse our hearts, whereby we might expresse some part of our zeales, we should thinke our selues for euer perfect.

speeches.speaker: Timon.
prose: Oh no doubt my good Friends, but the Gods themselues haue prouided that I shall haue much helpe from you: how had you beene my Friends else. Why haue you that charitable title from thousands? Did not you chiefely belong to my heart? I haue told more of you to my selfe, then you can with modestie speake in your owne behalfe. And thus farre I confirme you. Oh you Gods (thinke I,) what need we haue any Friends; if we should nere haue need of' em? They were the most needlesse Creatures liuing; should we nere haue vse for 'em? And would most resemble sweete Instruments hung vp in Cases, that keepes there sounds to themselues. Why I haue often wisht my selfe poorer, that I might come neerer to you: we are borne to do benefits. And what better or properer can we call our owne, then the richer of our Friends? Oh what a pretious comfort 'tis, to haue so many like Brothers commanding one anothers Fortunes. Oh ioyes, e'ne made away er't can be borne: mine eies cannot hold out wate^me thinks. to forget their Faults. I drinke to you.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
prose: Thou weep'st to make them drinke, Timon.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lord.
verse: Ioy had the like conception in our eies,
And at that instant, like a babe sprung vp.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
prose: Ho, ho: I laugh to thinke that babe a bastard.

speeches.speaker: 3. Lord.
prose: I promise you my Lord you mou'd me much.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
prose: Much.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What meanes that Trumpe? How now?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Please you my Lord, there are certaine Ladies
Most desirous of admittance.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Ladies? what are their wils?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: There comes with them a fore-runner my Lord, which beares that office, to signifie their pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I pray let them be admitted.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: There tast, touch all pleas'd from thy Table rise:
They onely now come but to Feast thine eies.
prose: Haile to thee worthy Timon and to all that of his Bounties taste: the fiue best Sencesa cknowledge thee their Patron, and come freely to gratulate thy plentiou^ bosome.

speeches.speaker: Timo.
prose: They'r wecome all, let 'em haue kind admittance. Musicke make their welcome.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: You see my Lord, how ample y' are belou'd.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
verse: Hoyday,
What a sweepe of vanitie comes this way.
They daunce? They are mad women,
Like Madnesse is the glory of this life,
As this pompe shewes to a little oyle and roote.
We make our selues Fooles, to disport our selues,
And spend our Flatteries, to drinke those men,
Vpon whose Age we voyde it vp agen
With poysonous Spight and Enuy.
Who liues, that's not depraued, or depraues;
Who dyes, that beares not one spurne to their graues
Of their Friends guift:
I should feare, those that dance before me now,
Would one day stampe vpon me: 'Tas bene done,
Men shut their doores against a setting Sunne.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: You haue done our pleasures
Much grace (faire Ladies)
Set a faire fashion on our entertainment,
Which was not halfe so beautifull, and kinde:
You haue added worth vntoo't, and luster,
And entertain'd me with mine owne deuice.
I am to thanke you for't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
prose: My Lord you take vs euen at the best.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
prose: Faith for the worst is filthy, and would not hold taking, I doubt me.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Ladies, there is an idle banquet attends you,
Please you to dispose your selues.

speeches.speaker: All La.
prose: Most thankfully, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Flauius.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: The little Casket bring me hither.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: Yes, my Lord. More Iewels yet?
There is no crossing him in's humor,
Else I should tell him well, y faith I should;
When all's spent, hee'ld be crost then, and he could:
'Tis pitty Bounty had not eyes behinde,
That man might ne're be wretched for his minde.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
prose: Where be our men?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Heere my Lord, in readinesse.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lord.
prose: Our Horses.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: O my Friends:
I haue one word to say to you: Looke you, my good L.
I must intreat you honour me so much,
As to aduance this Iewell, accept it, and weare it,
Kinde my Lord.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
prose: I am so farre already in your guifts.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: So are we all.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: My Lord, there are certaine Nobles of the Senate newly alighted, and come to visit you.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: They are fairely welcome.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose: I beseech your Honor, vouchsafe me a word, it does concerne you neere.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Neere? why then another time Ile heare thee.
I prythee let's be prouided to shew them entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose: I scarse know how.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: May it please your Honor, Lord Lucius^
(Out of his free loue) hath presented to you
Foure Milke-white Horses, trapt in Siluer.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I shall accept them fairely: let the Presents
Be worthily entertain'd.
How now? What newes?

speeches.speaker: 3. Ser.
prose: Please you my Lord, that honourable Gentleman Lord Lucullus, entreats your companie to morrow, to hunt with him, and ha's sent your Honour two brace of Grey-hounds.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Ile hunt with him,
And let them be receiu'd, not without faire Reward.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: What will this come to?
He commands vs to prouide, and giue great guifts, and all out of an empty Coffer:
Nor will he know his Purse, or yeeld me this,
To shew him what a Begger his heart is,
Being of no power to make his wishes good.
His promises flye so beyond his state,
That what he speaks is all in debt, he ows for eu'ry word:
He is so kinde, that he now payes interest for't;
His Land's put to their Bookes. Well, would I were
Gently put out of Office, before I were forc'd out:
Happier is he that has no friend to feede,
Then such that do e'ne Enemies exceede.
I bleed inwardly for my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: You do your selues much wrong,
You bate too much of your owne merits.
Heere my Lord, a trifle of our Loue.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lord.
verse: With more then common thankes
I will receyue it.

speeches.speaker: 3. Lord.
prose: O he's the very soule of Bounty.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: And now I remember my Lord, you gaue good words the other day of a Bay Courser I rod on. Tis yours because you lik'd it.

speeches.speaker: 1 L.
prose: Oh, I beseech you pardon mee, my Lord, in that.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: You may take my word my Lord: I know no man can iustly praise, but what he does affect. I weighe my Friends affection with mine owne: Ile tell you true, Ile call to you.

speeches.speaker: All Lor.
prose: O none so welcome.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I take all, and your seuerall visitations
So kinde to heart, 'tis not enough to giue:
Me thinkes, I could deale Kingdomes to my Friends,
And nere be wearie. Alcibiades,
Thou art a Soldiour, therefore sildome rich,
It comes in Charitie to thee: for all thy liuing
Is mong'st the dead: and all the Lands thou hast
Lye in a pitcht field.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: I, defil'd Land, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord.
prose: We are so vertuously bound.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: And so am I to you.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lord.
prose: So infinitely endeer'd.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: All to you. Lights, more Lights.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord.
verse: The best of Happines, Honor, and Fortunes
Keepe with you Lord Timon.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Ready for his Friends.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
verse: Friendships full of dregges,
Me thinkes false hearts, should neuer haue sound legges.
Thus honest Fooles lay out their wealth on Curtsies.
prose: What a coiles heere, seruing of beckes, and iutting out of bummes. I doubt whether their Legges be worth the summes that are giuen for 'em.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Now Apermantus (if thou wert not sullen)
I would be good to thee.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
prose: No, Ile nothing; for if I should be brib'd too, there would be none left to raile vponthee, and then thou wouldst sinne the faster. Thou giu'st so long Timon (I feare me) thou wilt giue away thy selfe in paper shortly. What needs these Feasts, pompes, and Vaine-glories?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Nay, and you begin to raile on Societie once, I am sworne not to giue regard to you. Farewell, & come with better Musicke.

speeches.speaker: Aper.
verse: So: Thou wilt not heare mee now, thou shalt not then. Ile locke thy heauen from thee:
Oh that mens eares should be
To Counsell deafe, but not to Flatterie.

speeches.speaker: Sen.
verse: And late fiue thousand: to Varro and to Isidore
He owes nine thousand, besides my former summe,
Which makes it fiue and twenty. Still in motion
Of raging waste? It cannot hold, it will not.
If I want Gold, steale but a beggers Dogge,
And giue it Timon, why the Dogge coines Gold.
If I would sell my Horse, and buy twenty moe
Better then he; why giue my Horse to Timon.
Aske nothing, giue it him, it Foles me straight
And able Horses: No Porter at his gate,
But rather one that smiles, and still inuites
All that passe by. It cannot hold, no reason
Can sound his state in safety. Caphis hoa,
Caphis I say.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: Heere sir, what is your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Sen.
verse: Get on your cloake, & hast you to Lord Timon,
Importune him for my Moneyes, be not ceast
With slight deniall; nor then silenc'd, when
Commend me to your Master, and the Cap
Playes in the right hand, thus: but tell him,
My Vses cry to me; I must serue my turne
Out of mine owne, his dayes and times are past,
And my reliances on his fracted dates
Haue smit my credit. I loue, and honour him,
But must not breake my backe, to heale his finger.
Immediate are my needs, and my releefe
Must not be tost and turn'd to me in words,
But finde supply immediate. Get you gone,
Put on a most importunate aspect,
A visage of demand: for I do feare
When euery Feather stickes in his owne wing,
Lord Timon will be left a naked gull,
Which flashes now a Phoenix, get you gone.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: I go sir.

speeches.speaker: Sen.
verse: I go sir?
Take the Bonds along with you,
And haue the dates in. Come.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
prose: I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sen.
prose: Go.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: No care, no stop, so senselesse of expence,
That he will neither know how to maintaine it,
Nor cease his flow of Riot. Takes no accompt
How things go from him, nor resume no care
Of what is to continue: neuer minde,
Was to be so vnwise, to be so kinde.
What shall be done, he will not heare, till feele:
I must be round with him, now he comes from hunting.
Fye, fie, fie, fie.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Good euen Varro: what, you come for money?

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: Is't not your businesse too?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: It is, and yours too, Isidore?

speeches.speaker: Isid.
prose: It is so.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Would we were all discharg'd.

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: I feare it,

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Heere comes the Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: So soone as dinners done, wee'l forth againe
My Alcibiades. With me, what is your will?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: My Lord, heere is a note of certaine dues.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Dues? whence are you?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Of Athens heere, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Go to my Steward.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Please it your Lordship, he hath put me off
To the succession of new dayes this moneth:
My Master is awak'd by great Occasion,
To call vpon his owne, and humbly prayes you,
That with your other Noble parts, you'l suite,
In giuing him his right.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Mine honest Friend,
I prythee but repaire to me next morning.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Nay, good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Containe thy selfe, good Friend.

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: One Varroes seruant, my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Isid.
prose: From Isidore, he humbly prayes your speedy payment.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: If you did know my Lord, my Masters wants.

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: 'Twas due on forfeyture my Lord, sixe weekes, and past.

speeches.speaker: Isi.
verse: Your Steward puts me off my Lord, and I
Am sent expressely to your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Giue me breath:
I do beseech you good my Lords keepe on,
Ile waite vpon you instantly. Come hither: pray you
How goes the world, that I am thus encountred
With clamorous demands of debt, broken Bonds,
And the detention of long since due debts
Against my Honor?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: Please you Gentlemen,
The time is vnagreeable to this businesse:
Your importunacie cease, till after dinner,
That I may make his Lordship vnderstand
Wherefore you are not paid.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Do so my Friends, see them well entertain'd.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Pray draw neere.

speeches.speaker: Caph.
prose: Stay, stay, here comes the Foole with Apemantus, let's ha some sport with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: Hang him, hee'l abuse vs.

speeches.speaker: Isid.
prose: A plague vpon him dogge.

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: How dost Foole?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Dost Dialogue with thy shadow?

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: I speake not to thee.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: No 'tis to thy selfe. Come away.

speeches.speaker: Isi.
prose: There's the Foole hangs on your backe already.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: No thou stand'st single, th' art not on him yet.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Where's the Foole now?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: He last ask'd the question. Poore Rogues, and Vsurers men, Bauds betweene Gold and want.

speeches.speaker: Al.
prose: What are we Apemantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Asses.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Ape,
prose: That you ask me what you are, & do not know your selues. Speake to 'em Foole.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: How do you Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Gramercies good Foole:
How does your Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: She's e'ne setting on water to scal'd such Chickens as you are. Would we could see you at Corinth.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Good, Gramercy.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Looke you, heere comes my Masters Page.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Why how now Captaine? what do you in this wise Company.
How dost thou Apermantus?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Would I had a Rod in my mouth, that I might answer thee profitably.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Prythee Apemantus reade me the superscription of these Letters, I know not which is which.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Canst not read?

speeches.speaker: Page.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: There will litle Learning dye then that day thou art hang'd. This is to Lord Timon, this to Alcibiades. Go thou was't borne a Bastard, and thou't dye a Bawd.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Thou was't whelpt a Dogge, and thou shalt famish a Dogges death.
Answer not, I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: E'ne so thou out-runst Grace,
Foole I will go with you to Lord Timons.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Will you leaue me there?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: If Timon stay at home.
You three serue three Vsurers?

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: I would they seru'd vs.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: So would I:
As good a tricke as euer Hangman seru'd Theefe.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Are you three Vsurers men?

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: I Foole.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: I thinke no Vsurer, but ha's a Foole to his Seruant. My Mistris is one, and I am her Foole: when men come to borrow of your Masters, they approach sadly, and go away merry: but they enter my Masters house merrily, and go away sadly. The reason of this?

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: I could render one.

speeches.speaker: Ap.
prose: Do it then, that we may account thee a Whoremaster, and a Knaue, which notwithstanding thou shalt be no lesse esteemed.

speeches.speaker: Varro.
prose: What is a Whoremaster Foole?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: A Foole in good cloathes, and something like thee. 'Tis a spirit, sometime t' appeares like a Lord, somtime like a Lawyer, sometime like a Philosopher, with two stones moe then's artificiall one. Hee is verie often like a Knight; and generally, in all shapes that man goes vp and downe in, from fourescore to thirteen, this spirit walkes in.

speeches.speaker: Var.
prose: Thou art not altogether a Foole.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Nor thou altogether a Wise man,
As much foolerie as I haue, so much wit thou lack'st.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: That answer might haue become Apemantus.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Aside, aside, heere comes Lord Timon.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Come with me (Foole) come.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: I do not alwayes follow Louer, elder Brother, aad Woman, sometime the Philosopher.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: Pray you walk en eere,
Ile speake with you anon.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: You make me meruell wherefore ere this time
Had you not fully laide my state before me,
That I might so haue rated my expence
As I had leaue of meanes.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: You would not heare me:
At many leysures I propose.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Go too:
Perchance some single vantages you tooke,
When my indisposition put you backe,
And that vnaptnesse made your minister
Thus to excuse your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: O my good Lord,
At many times I brought in my accompts,
Laid them before you, you would throw them off,
And say you sound them in mine honestie,
When for some trifling present you haue bid me
Returne so much, I haue shooke my head, and wept:
Yea 'gainst th' Authoritie of manners, pray'd you
To hold your hand more close: I did indure
Not sildome, nor no flight checkes, when I haue
Prompted you in the ebbe of your estate,
And your great flow of debts; my lou'd Lord,
Though you heare now (too late) yet nowes a time,
The greatest of your hauing, lackes a halfe,
To pay your present debts.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Let all my Land be sold.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: 'Tis all engag'd, some forfeyted and gone,
And what remaines will hardly stop the mouth
Of present dues; the future comes apace:
What shall defend the interim, and at length
How goes our reck'ning?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: To Lacedemon did my Land extend.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: O my good Lord, the world is but a word,
Were it all yours, to giue it in a breath,
How quickely were it gone.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: You tell me true.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: If you suspect my Husbandry or Falshood,
Call me before th' exactest Auditors,
And set me on the proofe. So the Gods blesse me,
When all our Offices haue beene opprest
With riotous Feeders, when our Vaults haue wept
With drunken spilth of Wine; when euery roome
Hath blaz'd with Lights, and braid with Minstrelsie,
I haue retyr'd me to a wastefull cocke,
And set mine eyes at flow.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Prythee no more.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: Heauens haue I said the bounty of this Lord:
How many prodigall bits haue Slaues and Pezants
This night englutted: who is not Timons,
What heart, head, sword, force, meanes, but is L. Timons:
Great Timon, Noble, Worthy, Royall Timon:
Ah, when the meanes are gone, that buy this praise,
The breath is gone, whereof this praise is made:
Feast won, fast lost; one cloud of Winter showres,
These flyes are coucht.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Come sermon me no further.
No villanous bounty yet hath past my heart;
Vnwisely, not ignobly haue I giuen.
Why dost thou weepe, canst thou the conscience lacke,
To thinke I shall lacke friends: secure thy heart,
If I would broach the vessels of my loue,
And try the argument of hearts, by borrowing,
Men, and mens fortunes could I frankely vse
As I can bid thee speake.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Assurance blesse your thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: And in some sort these wants of mine are crown'd,
That I account them blessings. For by these
Shall I trie Friends. You shall perceiue
How you mistake my Fortunes:
I am wealthie in my Friends.
Within there, Flauius, Seruilius?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: My Lord, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I will dispatch you seuerally.

You to Lord Lucius, to Lord Lucullus you, I hunted with his Honor to day; you to Sempronius; commend me to their loues; and I am proud say, that my occasions haue found time to vse 'em toward a supply of mony: let the request be fifty Talents.

speeches.speaker: Flam.
prose: As you haue said, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Lord Lucius and Lucullus? Humh.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Go you sir to the Senators;
Of whom, euen to the States best health; I haue
Deseru'd this Hearing: bid 'em send o' th' instant
A thousand Talents to me.

speeches.speaker: Ste,
verse: I haue beene bold
(For that I knew it the most generall way)
To them, to vse your Signet, and your Name,
But they do shake their heads, and I am heere
No richer in returne.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Is't true? Can't be?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: They answer in a ioynt and corporate voice,
That now they are at fall, want Treature cannot
Do what they would, are sorrie: you are Honourable,
But yet they could haue wisht, they know not,
Something hath beene amisse; a Noble Nature
May catch a wrench; would all were well; tis pitty,
And so intending other serious matters,
After distastefull lookes; and these hard Fractions
With certaine halfe-caps, and cold mouing nods,
They froze me into Silence.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: You Gods reward them:
Prythee man looke cheerely. These old Fellowes
Haue their ingratitude in them Hereditary:
Their blood is cak'd, 'tis cold, it sildome flowes,
'Tis lacke of kindely warmth, they are not kinde;
And Nature, as it growes againe toward earth,
Is fashion'd for the iourney, dull and heauy.

Go to
~entiddius (prythee be not sad,
Thou art true, and honest; Ingeniously I speake,
No blame belongs to thee:) Ventiddius lately
Buried his Father, by whose death hee's stepp'd
Into a great estate: When he was poore,
Imprison'd, and in scarsitie of Friends,
I cleer'd him with fiue Talents: Greet him from me,
Bid him suppose, some good necessity
Touches his Friend, which craues to be remembred
With those fiue Talents; that had, giue't these Fellowes
To whom 'tis instant due. Neu'r speake, or thinke,
That Timons fortunes 'mong his Friends can sinke.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: I would I could not thinke it:
That thought is Bounties Foe;
Being free it selfe, it thinkes all others so.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I haue told my Lord of you, he is comming down to you.

speeches.speaker: Flam.
prose: I thanke you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Heere's my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: One of Lord Timons men? A Guift I warrant. Why this hits right: I dreampt of a Siluer Bason & Ewre to night. Flaminius, honest Flaminius, you are verie respectiuely welcome sir. Fill me some Wine. And how does that Honourable, Compleate, Free-hearted Gentleman of Athens, thy very bountifull good Lord and Mayster?

speeches.speaker: Flam.
prose: His health is well sir.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I am right glad that his health is well sir: and what hast thou there vnder thy Cloake, pretty Flaminius?

speeches.speaker: Flam.
prose: Faith, nothing but an empty box Sir, which in my Lords behal^ I come to intreat your Honor to supply: who hauing great and instant occasion to vse fiftie Talents, hath sent to your Lordship to furnish him: nothing doubting your present assistance therein.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: La, la, la, la: Nothing doubting sayes hee? Alas good Lord, a Noble Gentleman 'tis, if he would not keep so good a house. Many a time and often I ha din'd with him, and told him on't, and come againe to supper to him of purpose, to haue him spend lesse, and yet he wold embrace no counsell, take no warning by my comming, euery man has his fault, and honesty is his. I ha told him on't, but I could nere get him from't.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Please your Lordship, heere is the Wine.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Flaminius, I haue noted thee alwayes wise.
Heere's to thee.

speeches.speaker: Flam.
prose: Your Lordship speakes your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I haue obserued thee alwayes for a towardlie prompt spirit, giue thee thy due, and one that knowes what belongs to reason; and canst vse the time wel, if the time vse thee well. Good parts in thee; get you gone sirrah. Draw neerer honest Flaminius. Thy Lords a bountifull Gentleman, but thou art wise, and thou know'st well enough (although thou com'st to me) that this is no time to lend money, especially vpon bare friendshippe without securitie. Here's three Solidares for thee, good Boy winke at me, and say thou saw'st mee not. Fare thee well.

speeches.speaker: Flam.
verse: Is't possible the world should so much differ,
And we aliue that liued? Fly damned basenesse
To him that worships thee.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Ha? Now I see thou art a Foole, and sit for thy Master.

speeches.speaker: Flam
verse: May these adde to the number yt may scald thee:
Let moulten Coine be thy damnation,
Thou disease of a friend, and not himselfe:
Has friendship such a faint and milkie heart,
It turnes in lesse then two nights? O you Gods!
I feele my Masters passion. This Slaue vnto his Honor,
Has my Lords meate in him:
Why should it thriue, and turne to Nutriment,
When he is turn'd to poyson?
O may Diseases onely worke vpon't:
And when he's sicke to death, let not that part of Nature
Which my Lord payd for, be of any power
To expell sicknesse, but prolong his hower.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Who the Lord Timon? He is my very good friend and an Honourable Gentleman.

We know him for no lesse, thogh we are but strangers to him. But I can tell you one thing my Lord, and which I heare from common rumours, now Lord Timons happie howres are done and past, and his estate shrinkes from him.

speeches.speaker: Lucius.
prose: Fye no, doe not beleeue it: hee cannot want for money.

But beleeue you this my Lord, that not long agoe, one of his men was with the Lord Lucullus, to borrow so many Talents, nay vrg'd extreamly for't, and shewed

what necessity belong'd too't, and yet was deny'de.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: How?
I tell you, deny'de my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: What a strange case was that? Now before the Gods I am asham'd on't. Denied that honourable man? There was verie little Honour shew'd in't. For my owne part, I must needes confesse, I haue receyued some small kindnesses from him, as Money, Plate, Iewels, and such like Trifles; nothing comparing to his: yet had hee mistooke him, and sent to me, I should ne're haue denied his Occasion so many Talents.

speeches.speaker: Seruil.
prose: See, by good hap yonders my Lord, I haue swet to see his Honor. My Honor'd Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lucil.
prose: Seruilius? You are kindely met sir. Farthewell, commend me to thy Honourable vertuous Lord, my very exquisite Friend.

speeches.speaker: Seruil.
prose: May it please your Honour, my Lord hath sent—

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: Ha? what ha's he sent? I am so much endeered to that Lord; hee's euer sending: how shall I thank him think'st thou? And what has he sent now?

speeches.speaker: Seruil.
prose: Has onely sent his present Occasion now my Lord: requesting your Lordship to supply his instant vse with so many Talents.

speeches.speaker: Lucil.
verse: I know his Lordship is but merry with me,
He cannot want fifty fiue hundred Talents.

speeches.speaker: Seruil.
verse: But in the mean time he wants lesse my Lord.
If his occasion were not vertuous,
I should not vrge it halfe so faithfully.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Dost thou speake seriously Seruilius?

speeches.speaker: Seruil.
prose: Vpon my soule, 'tis true Sir.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose:
What a wicked Beast was I to disfurnish my self against such a good time, when I might ha shewn my selfe Honourable? How vnluckily it hapned, that I shold Purchase the day before for a little part, and vndo a great deale of Honour? Seruilius.
now before the Gods I am not able to do (the more beast I say) I was sending to vse Lord Timon my selfe, these Gentlemen can witnesse; but I would not for the wealth of Athens I had done't now. Commend me bountifully to his good Lordship, and I hope his Honor will conceiue the fairest of mee, because I haue no power to be kinde. And tell him this from me, I count it one of my greatest afflictions say, that I cannot pleasure such an Honourable Gentleman. Good Seruilius, will you befriend mee so farre, as to vse mine owne words to him?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Yes sir, I shall.

speeches.speaker: Lucil.
verse: Ile looke you out a good turne Seruilius.
True as you said, Timon is shrunke indeede,
And he that's once deny'de, will hardly speede.

prose: Do you obserue this Hostilius?
I, to well.

verse: Why this is the worlds soule,
And iust of the same peece
Is euery Flatterers sport: who can call him his Friend
That dips in the same dish? For in my knowing
Timon has bin this Lords Father,
And kept his credit with his purse:
Supported his estate, nay Timons money
Has paid his men their wages. He ne're drinkes,
But Timons Siluer treads vpon his Lip,
And yet, oh see the monstrousnesse of man,
When he lookes out in an vngratefull shape;
He does deny him (in respect of his)
What charitable men affoord to Beggers.

prose: Religion grones at it.

verse: For mine owne part, I neuer tasted Timon in my life
Nor came any of his bounties ouer me,
To marke me for his Friend. Yet I protest,
For his right Noble minde, illustrious Vertue,
And Honourable Carriage,
Had his necessity made vse of me,
I would haue put my wealth into Donation,
And the best halfe should haue return'd to him,
So much I loue his heart: But I perceiue,
Men must learne now with pitty to dispence,
For Policy sits aboue Conscience.

speeches.speaker: Semp.
verse: Must he needs trouble me in't? Hum.
'Boue all others?
He might haue tried Lord Lucius, or Lucullus,
And now Ventidgius is wealthy too,
Whom he redeem'd from prison. All these
Owes their estates vnto him.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: My Lord,
They haue all bin touch'd, and found Base-Mettle,
For they haue all denied him.

speeches.speaker: Semp.
verse: How? Haue they deny'de him?
Has Ventidgius and Lucullus deny'de him,
And does he send to me? Three? Humh?
It shewes but little loue, or iudgement in him.
Must I be his last Refuge? His Friends (like Physitians)
Thriue, giue him ouer: Must I take th' Cure vpon me?
Has much disgrac'd me in't, I'me angry at him,
That might haue knowne my place. I see no sense for't,
But his Occasions might haue wooed me first:
For in my conscience, I was the first man
That ere receiued guift from him.
And does he thinke so backwardly of me now,
That Ile requite it last? No:
So it may proue an Argument of Laughter
To th' rest, and 'mong'st Lords be thought a Foole:
I'de rather then the worth of thrice the summe,
Had sent to me first, but for my mindes sake:
I'de such a courage to do him good. But now returne,
And with their faint reply, this answer ioyne;
Who bates mine Honor, shall not know my Coyne.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: This was my Lords best hope, now all are fled
Saue onely the Gods. Now his Friends are dead,
Doores that were ne're acquainted with their Wards
Many a bounteous yeere, must be imploy'd
Now to guard sure their Master:
And this is all a liberall course allowes,
Who cannot keepe his wealth, must keep his house.
prose: Excellent: Your Lordships a goodly Villain: the diuell knew not what he did, when hee made man Politicke; he crossed himselfe by't: and I cannot thinke, but in the end, the Villanies of man will set him cleere. How fairely this Lord striues to appeare foule? Takes Vertuous Copies to be wicked: like those, that vnder hotte ardent zeale, would set whole Realmes on fire, of such a nature is his politike loue.

speeches.speaker: ~ar. man.
prose: Well met, goodmorrow Titus & Hortensius

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: The like to you kinde Varro.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Lucius, what do we meet together?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I, and I think one businesse do's command vs all.
For mine is money.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: So is theirs, and ours.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: And sir Philotus too.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: Good day at once.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Welcome good Brother.
What do you thinke the houre?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: Labouring for Nine.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: So much?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: Is not my Lord seene yet?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: Not yet.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: I wonder on't, he was wont to shine at seauen.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I, but the dayes are waxt shorter with him:
You must consider, that a Prodigall course
Is like the Sunnes, but not like his recouerable, I feare:
'Tis deepest Winter in Lord Timons purse, that is:
One may reach deepe enough, and yet finde little.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: I am of your feare, for that.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
verse: Ile shew you how t' obserue a strange euent:
Your Lord sends now for Money?

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Most true, he doe's.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
verse: And he weares Iewels now of Timons guift,
For which I waite for money.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: It is against my heart.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Marke how strange it showes,
Timon in this, should pay more then he owes:
And e'ne as if your Lord should weare rich Iewels,
And send for money for 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
verse: I'me weary of this Charge,
The Gods can witnesse:
I know my Lord hath spent of Timons wealth,
And now Ingratitude, makes it worse then stealth.

speeches.speaker: Varro.
verse: Yes, mine's three thousand Crownes:
What's yours?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: Fiue thousand mine.

speeches.speaker: Varro.
verse: 'Tis much deepe, and it should seem by th' sum
Your Masters confidence was aboue mine,
Else surely his had equall'd.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: One of Lord Timons men.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Flaminius? Sir, a word: Pray is my Lord readie to come forth?

speeches.speaker: Flam.
prose: No, indeed he is not.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: We attend his Lordship: pray signifie so much.

speeches.speaker: Flam.
prose: I need not tell him that, he knowes you are too diligent.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Ha: is not that his Steward muffled so?
He goes away in a Clowd: Call him, call him.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: Do you heare, sir?

speeches.speaker: 2. Varro.
prose: By your leaue, sir.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: What do ye aske of me, my Friend.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: We waite for certaine Money heere, sir.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: I, if Money were as certaine as your waiting,
'Twere sure enough.
Why then preferr'd you not your summes and Billes
When your false Masters eate of my Lords meat?
Then they could smile, and fawne vpon his debts.
And take downe th' Intrest into their glutt'nous Mawes.
You do your selues but wrong, to stirre me vp,
Let me passe quietly:
Beleeue't, my Lord and I haue made an end,
I haue no more to reckon, he to spend.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: I, but this answer will not serue.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: If't 'twill not serue, 'tis not so base as you,
For you serue Knaues.

speeches.speaker: 1. Varro.
prose: How? What does his casheer'd Worship mutter?

speeches.speaker: 2. Varro.
prose: No matter what, hee's poore, and that's reuenge enough. Who can speake broader, then hee that has no house to put his head in? Such may rayle against great buildings.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: Oh heere's Seruilius: now wee shall know some answere.

speeches.speaker: Seru.
prose: If I might beseech you Gentlemen, to repayre some other houre, I should deriue much from't. For tak't of my soule, my Lord leanes wondrously to discontent: His comfortable temper has forsooke him, he's much out of health, and keepes his Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Many do keepe their Chambers, are not sicke:
And if it be so farre beyond his health,
Me thinkes he should the sooner pay his debts,
And make a cleere way to the Gods.

speeches.speaker: Seruil.
prose: Good Gods.

speeches.speaker: Titus.
verse: We cannot take this for answer, sir.

speeches.speaker: Flaminius within.
prose: Seruilius helpe, my Lord, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: What, are my dores oppos'd against my passage?
Haue I bin euer free, and must my house
Be my retentiue Enemy? My Gaole?
The place which I haue Feasted, does it now
(Like all Mankinde) shew me an Iron heart?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: Put in now Titus.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: My Lord, heere is my Bill.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: Here's mine.

speeches.speaker: 1. Var.
prose: And mine, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: 2. Var.
prose: And ours, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Philo.
prose: All our Billes.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Knocke me downe with 'em, cleaue mee to the Girdle.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Alas, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Cut my heart in summes.

speeches.speaker: Tit.
prose: Mine, fifty Talents.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Tell out my blood.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Fiue thousand Crownes, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Fiue thousand drops payes that.
What yours? and yours?

speeches.speaker: 1. Var.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: 2. Var.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Teare me, take me, and the Gods fall vpon you.

speeches.speaker: Hort.
prose: Faith I perceiue our Masters may throwe their caps at their money, these debts may well be call'd desperate ones, for a madman owes 'em.

speeches.speaker: Timon.
prose: They haue e'ene put my breath from mee the slaues. Creditors? Diuels.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: My deere Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What if it should be so?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Ile haue it so. My Steward?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Heere my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: So fitly? Go, bid all my Friends againe,
Lucius, Lucullus, and Sempronius Vllorxa: All,
Ile once more feast the Rascals.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: O my Lord, you onely speake from your distracted soule; there's not so much left to, furnish out a moderate Table.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Be it not in thy care:
Go I charge thee, inuite them all, let in the tide
Of Knaues once more: my Cooke and Ile prouide.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sen.
verse: My Lord, you haue my voyce, too't,
The faults Bloody:
'Tis necessary he should dye:
Nothing imboldens sinne so much, as Mercy.

prose: Most true; the Law shall bruise 'em.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: Honor, health, and compassion to the Senate.
Now Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: I am an humble Sutor to your Vertues;
For pitty is the vertue of the Law,
And none but Tyrants vse it cruelly.
It pleases time and Fortune to lye heauie
Vpon a Friend of mine, who in hot blood
Hath stept into the Law: which is past depth
To those that (without heede) do plundge intoo't.
He is a Man (setting his Fate aside) of comely Vertues,
Nor did he soyle the fact with Cowardice,
(And Honour in him, which buyes out his fault)
But with a Noble Fury, and faire spirit,
Seeing his Reputation touch'd to death,
He did oppose his Foe:
And with such sober and vnnoted passion
He did behooue his anger ere 'twas spent,
As if he had but prou'd an Argument.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sen.
verse: You vndergo too strict a Paradox,
Striuing to make an vgly deed looke faire:
Your words haue tooke such paines, as if they labour'd
To bring Man-slaughter into forme, and set Quarrelling
Vpon the head of Valour; which indeede
Is Valour mis-begot, and came into the world,
When Sects, and Factions were newly borne.
Hee's truly Valiant, that can wisely suffer
The worst that man can breath,
And make his Wrongs, his Out-sider,
To weare them like his Rayment, carelessely,
And ne're preferre his iniuries to his heart,
To bring it into danger.
If Wrongs be euilles, and inforce vs kill,
What Folly 'tis, to hazard life for Ill.

speeches.speaker: Alci.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sen.
verse: You cannot make grosse sinnes looke cleare,
To reuenge is no Valour, but to beare.

speeches.speaker: Alci.
verse: My Lords, then vnder fauour, pardon me,
If I speake like a Captaine.
Why do fond men expose themselues to Battell,
And not endure all threats? Sleepe vpon't,
And let the Foes quietly cut their Throats
Without repugnancy? If there be
Such Valour in the bearing, what make wee
Abroad? Why then, Women are more valiant
That stay at home, if Bearing carry it:
And the Asse, more Captaine then the Lyon?
The fellow loaden with Irons, wiser then the Iudge?
If Wisedome be in suffering, Oh my Lords,
As you are great, be pittifully Good,
Who cannot condemne rashnesse in cold blood?
To kill, I grant, is sinnes extreamest Gust,
But in defence, by Mercy, 'tis most iust.
To be in Anger, is impietie:
But who is Man, that is not Angrie.
Weigh but the Crime with this.

speeches.speaker: 2. Sen.
prose: You breath in vaine.

speeches.speaker: Alci.
verse: In vaine?
His seruice done at Lacedemon, and Bizantium,
Were a sufficient briber for his life.

prose: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Why say my Lords ha's done faire seruice,
And slaine in fight many of your enemies:
How full of valour did he beare himselfe
In the last Conflict, and made plenteous wounds?
He has made too much plenty with him:
He's a sworne Riotor, he has a sinne
That often drownes him, and takes his valour prisoner.
If there were no Foes, that were enough
To ouercome him. In that Beastly furie,
He has bin knowne to commit outrages,
And cherrish Factions. 'Tis inferr'd to vs,
His dayes are foule, and his drinke dangerous.

prose: He dyes.

speeches.speaker: Alci.
verse: Hard fate: he might haue dyed in warre.
My Lords, if not for any parts in him,
Though his right arme might purchase his owne time,
And be in debt to none: yet more to moue you,
Take my deserts to his, and ioyne 'em both.
And for I know, your reuerend Ages loue Security,
Ile pawne my Victories, all my Honour to you
Vpon his good returnes.
If by this Crime, he owes the Law his life,
Why let the Warre receiue't in valiant gore,
For Law is strict, and Warre is nothing more.
We are for Law, he dyes, vrge it no more
On height of our displeasure: Friend, or Brother,
He forfeits his owne blood, that spilles another.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Must it be so? It must not bee:
My Lords, I do beseech you know mee.

prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: Call me to your remembrances.
What.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: I cannot thinke but your Age has forgot me,
It could not else be, I should proue so bace,
To sue and be deny'de such common Grace.
My wounds ake at you.
Do you dare our anger?
'Tis in few words, but spacious in effect:
We banish thee for euer.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Banish me?
Banish your dotage, banish vsurie,
That makes the Senate vgly.
If after two dayes shine, Athens containe thee,
Attend our waightier Iudgement.
And not to swell our Spirit,
He shall be executed presently.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Now the Gods keepe you old enough,
That you may liue
Onely in bone, that none may looke on you.
I'm worse then mad: I haue kept backe their Foes
While they haue told their Money, and let out
Their Coine vpon large interest. I my selfe,
Rich onely in large hurts. All those, for this?
Is this the Balsome, that the vsuring Senat
Powres into Captaines wounds? Banishment.
It comes not ill: I hate not to be banisht,
It is a cause worthy my Spleene and Furie,
That I may strike at Athens. Ile cheere vp
My discontented Troopes, and lay for hearts;
'Tis Honour with most Lands to be at ods,
Souldiers should brooke as little wrongs as Gods.

prose: The good time of day to you, sir.
I also wish it to you: I thinke this Honorable Lord did but try vs this other day.
Vpon that were my thoughts tyring when wee encountred. I hope it is not so low with him as he made it seeme in the triall of his seuerall Friends.
It should not be, by the perswasion of his new Feasting.
I should thinke so. He hath sent mee an earnest inuiting, which many my neere occasions did vrge mee to put off: but he hath coniur'd mee beyond them, and I must needs appeare.
In like manner was I in debt to my importunat businesse, but he would not heare my excuse. I am sorrie, when he sent to borrow of mee, that my Prouision was out.
I am sicke of that greefe too, as I vnderstand how all things go.
Euery man heares so: what would hee haue borrowed of you?
A thousand Peeces.
A thousand Peeces?
What of you?
He sent to me sir—Heere he comes.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: With all my heart Gentlemen both; and how fare you?
Euer at the best, hearing well of your Lordship.
The Swallow followes not Summer more willing, then we your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Nor more willingly leaues Winter, such Summer Birds are men. Gentlemen, our dinner will not recompence this long stay: Feast your eares with the Musicke awhile: If they will fare so harshly o' th' Trumpets sound: we shall too't presently.
I hope it remaines not vnkindely with your Lordship, that I return'd you an empty Messenger.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: O sir, let it not trouble you.
My Noble Lord.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Ah my good Friend, what cheere?
My most Honorable Lord, I am e'ne sick of shame, that when your Lordship this other day sent to me, I was so vnfortunate a Beggar.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Thinke not on't, sir.
If you had sent but two houres before.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Let it not cumber your better remembrance.
Come bring in all together.

prose: All couer'd Dishes.
Royall Cheare, I warrant you.
Doubt not that, if money and the season can yeild it
How do you? What's the newes?
Alcibiades is banish'd: heare you of it?

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: Alcibiades banish'd?
'Tis so, be sure of it.
How? How?
I pray you vpon what?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: My worthy Friends, will you draw neere?
Ile tell you more anon. Here's a Noble feast toward
This is the old man still.
Wilt hold? Wilt hold?
It do's: but time will, and so.
I do conceyue.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Each man to his stoole, with that spurre as hee would to the lip of his Mistris: your dyet shall bee in all places alike. Make not a Citie Feast of it, to let the meat coole, ere we can agree vpon the first place. Sit, sit. The Gods require our Thankes.

You great Benefactors, sprinkle our Society with Thankefulnesse. For your owne guifts, make your selues prais'd: But reserue still to giue, least your Deities be despised. Lend to each man enough, that one neede not lend to another. For were your Godheads to borrow of men, men would forsake the Gods. Make the Meate be beloued, more then the Man that giues it. Let no Assembly of Twenty, be without a score of Villaines. If there sit twelue Women at the Table, let a dozen of them bee as they are. The rest of your Fees, O Gods, the Senators of Athens, together with the common legge of People, what is amisse in them, you Gods, make suteable for destruction. For these my present Friends, as they are to mee nothing, so in nothing blesse them, and to nothing are they welcome.
Vncouer Dogges, and lap.

speeches.speaker: Some speake.
prose: What do's his Lordship meane?

speeches.speaker: Some other.
prose: I know not.

speeches.speaker: Timon.
verse: May you a better Feast neuer behold
You knot of Mouth-Friends: Smoke, & lukewarm water
Is your perfection. This is Timons last,
Who stucke and spangled you with Flatteries,
Washes it off, and sprinkles in your faces
Your reeking villany. Liue loath'd, and long
Most smiling, smooth, detested Parasites,
Curteous Destroyers, affable Wolues, meeke Beares:
You Fooles of Fortune, Trencher-friends, Times Flyes,
Cap and knee-Slaues, vapours, and Minute Iackes.
Of Man and Beast, the infinite Maladie
Crust you quite o're. What do'st thou go?
Soft, take thy Physicke first; thou too, and thou:
Stay I will lend thee money, borrow none.
What? All in Motion? Henceforth be no Feast,
Whereat a Villaine's not a welcome Guest.
Burne house, sinke Athens, henceforth hated be
Of Timon Man, and all Humanity.

prose: How now, my Lords?
Know you the quality of Lord Timons fury?
Push, did you see my Cap?
I haue lost my Gowne.
He's but a mad Lord, & nought but humors swaies him. He gaue me a Iewell th' other day, and now hee has beate it out of my hat.
Did you see my Iewell?
Did you see my Cap.
Heere 'tis.
Heere lyes my Gowne.
Let's make no stay.
Lord Timons mad.
I feel't vpon my bones.
One day he giues vs Diamonds, next day stones.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Let me looke backe vpon thee. O thou Wall
That girdles in those Wolues, diue in the earth,
And fence not Athens. Matrons, turne incontinent,
Obedience fayle in Children: Slaues and Fooles
Plucke the graue wrinkled Senate from the Bench,
And minister in their steeds, to generall Filthes.
Conuert o' th' Instant greene Virginity,
Doo't in your Parents eyes. Bankrupts, hold fast
Rather then render backe; out with your Kniues,
And cut your Trusters throates. Bound Seruants, steale,
Large-handed Robbers your graue Masters are,
And pill by Law. Maide, to thy Masters bed,
Thy Mistris is o' th' Brothell. Some of sixteen,
Plucke the lyn'd Crutch from thy old limping Sire,
With it, beate out his Braines, Piety, and Feare,
Religion to the Gods, Peace, Iustice, Truth,
Domesticke awe, Night-rest, and Neighbour-hood,
Instruction, Manners, Mysteries, and Trades,
Degrees, Obseruances, Customes, and Lawes,
Decline to your confounding contraries.
And yet Confusion liue: Plagues incident to men,
Your potent and infectious Feauors, heape
On Athens ripe for stroke. Thou cold Sciatica,
Cripple our Senators, that their limbes may halt
As lamely as their Manners. Lust, and Libertie
Creepe in the Mindes and Marrowes of our youth,
That 'gainst the streame of Vertue they may striue,
And drowne themselues in Riot. Itches, Blaines,
So we all th' Athenian bosomes, and their crop
Be generall Leprosie: Breath, infect breath,
That their Society (as their Friendship) may
Be meerely poyson. Nothing Ile beare from thee
But nakednesse, thou detestable Towne,
Take thou that too, with multiplying Bannes:
Timon will to the Woods, where he shall finde
Th' vnkindest Beast, more kinder then Mankinde.
The Gods confound (heare me you good Gods all)
Th' Athenians both within and out that Wall:
And graunt as Timon growes, his hate may grow
To the whole race of Mankinde, high and low.
Amen.
Heare you M. Steward, where's our Master?
Are we vndone, cast off, nothing remaining?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: Alack my Fellowes, what should I say to you?
Let me be recorded by the righteous Gods,
I am as poore as you.
Such a House broke?
So Noble a Master falne, all gone, and not
One Friend to take his Fortune by the arme,
And go along with him.
As we do turne our backes
From our Companion, throwne into his graue,
So his Familiars to his buried Fortunes
Slinke all away leaue their false vowes with him
Like empty purses pickt; and his poore selfe
A dedicated Beggar to the Ayre,
With his disease, of all shunn'd pouerty,
Walkes like contempt alone. More of our Fellowes.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: All broken Implements of a ruin'd house.

verse: Yet do our hearts weare Timons Liuery,
That see I by our Faces: we are Fellowes still,
Seruing alike in sorrow: Leak'd is our Barke,
And we poore Mates, stand on the dying Decke,
Hearing the Surges threat: we must all part
Into this Sea of Ayre.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: Good Fellowes all,
The latest of my wealth Ile share among'st you.
Where euer we shall meete, for Timons sake,
Let's yet be Fellowes. Let's shake our heads, and say
As 'twere a Knell vnto our Masters Fortunes,
We haue seene better dayes. Let each take some:
Nay put out all your hands: Not one word more,
Thus part we rich in sorrow, parting poore.
Oh the fierce wretchednesse that Glory brings vs!
Who would not wish to be from wealth exempt,
Since Riches point to Misery and Contempt?
Who would be so mock'd with Glory, or to liue
But in a Dreame of Friendship,
To haue his pompe, and all what state compounds,
But onely painted like his varnisht Friends:
Poore honest Lord, brought lowe by his owne heart,
Vndone by Goodnesse: Strange vnvsuall blood,
When mans worst sinne is, He do's too much Good.
Who then dares to be halfe so kinde agen?
For Bounty that makes Gods, do still marre Men.
My deerest Lord, blest to be most accurst,
Rich onely to be wretched; thy great Fortunes
Are made thy cheefe Afflictions. Alas (kinde Lord)
Hee's flung in Rage from this ingratefull Seate
Of monstrous Friends:
Nor ha's he with him to supply his life,
Or that which can command it:
Ile follow and enquire him out.
Ile euer serue his minde, with my best will,
Whilst I haue Gold, Ile be his Steward still.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: O blessed breeding Sun, draw from the earth
Rotten humidity: below thy Sisters Orbe
Infect the ayre. Twin'd Brothers of one wombe,
Whose procreation, residence, and birth,
Scarse is diuidant; touch them with seuerall fortunes,
The greater scornes the lesser. Not Nature
(To whom all sores lay siege) can beare great Fortune
But by contempt of Nature,
Raise me this Begger, and deny't that Lord,
The Senators shall beare contempt Hereditary,
The Begger Natiue Honor.
It is the Pastour Lards, the Brothers sides,
The want that makes him leaue: who dares? who dares
In puritie of Manhood stand vpright
And say, this mans a Flatterer. If one be,
So are they all: for euerie grize of Fortune
Is smooth'd by that below. The Learned pate
Duckes to the Golden Foole. All's obliquie:
There's nothing leuell in our cursed Natures
But direct villanie. Therefore be abhorr'd,
All Feasts, Societies, and Throngs of men.
His semblable, yea himselfe Timon disdaines,
Destruction phang mankinde; Earth yeeld me Rootes,
Who seekes for better of thee, sawce his pallate
With thy most operant Poyson. What is heere?
Gold? Yellow, glittering, precious Gold?
No Gods, I am no idle Votarist,
Roots you cleere Heauens. Thus much of this will make
Blacke, white; fowle, faire; wrong, right;
Base, Noble; Old, young; Coward, valiant.
Ha you Gods! why this? what this, you Gods? why this
Will lugge your Priests and Seruants from your sides:
Plucke stout mens pillowes from below their heads.
This yellow Slaue,
Will knit and breake Religions, blesse th' accurst,
Make the hoare Leprosie ador'd, place Theeues,
And giue them Title, knee, and approbation
With Senators on the Bench: This is it
That makes the wappen'd Widdow wed againe;
Shee, whom the Spittle-house, and vlcerous sores,
Would cast the gorge at. This Embalmes and Spices
To' th' Aprill day againe. Come damn'd Earth,
Thou common whore of Mankinde, that puttes oddes
Among the rout of Nations, I will make thee
Do thy right Nature.
Ha? A Drumme? Th' art quicke,
But yet Ile bury thee: Thou't go (strong Theefe)
When Gowty keepers of thee cannot stand:
Nay stay thou out for earnest.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: What art thou there? speake.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: A Beast as thou art. The Canker gnaw thy hart
For shewing me againe the eyes of Man.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: What is thy name? Is man so hatefull to thee,
That art thy selfe a Man?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I am Misantropos, and hate Mankinde,
For thy part, I do wish thou wert a dogge,
That I might loue thee something.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: I know thee well:
But in thy Fortunes am vnlearn'd, and strange.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I know thee too, and more then that I know thee
I not desire to know. Follow thy Drumme,
With mans blood paint the ground Gules, Gules:
Religious Cannons, ciuill Lawes are cruell,
Then what should warre be? This fell whore of thine,
Hath in her more destruction then thy Sword,
For all her Cherubin looke.

speeches.speaker: Phrin.
prose: Thy lips rot off.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I will not kisse thee, then the rot returnes
To thine owne lippes againe.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: How came the Noble Timon to this change?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: As the Moone do's, by wanting light to giue:
But then renew I could not like the Moone,
There were no Sunnes to borrow of.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: Noble Timon, what friendship may I do thee?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: None, but to maintaine my opinion.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: What is it Timon?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Promise me Friendship, but performe none. If thou wilt not promise, the Gods plague thee, for thou art a man: if thou do'st performe, confound thee, for thou art a man.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: I haue heard in some sort of thy Miseries.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Thou saw'st them when I had prosperitie.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: I see them now, then was a blessed time.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: As thine is now, held with a brace of Harlots.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
prose: Is this th' Athenian Minion, whom the world Voic'd so regardfully?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Art thou Timandra?

speeches.speaker: Timan.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Be a whore still, they loue thee not that vse thee, giue them diseases, leauing with thee their Lust. Make vse of thy salt houres, season the slaues for Tubbes and Bathes, bring downe Rose-checkt youth to the Pubfast, and the Diet.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
prose: Hang thee Monster.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse:
Pardon him sweet Timandra.
for his wits
Are drown'd and lost in his Calamities.
I haue but little Gold of late, braue Timon,
The want whereof, doth dayly make reuolt
In my penurious Band. I haue heard and greeu'd
How cursed Athens, mindelesse of thy worth,
Forgetting thy great deeds, when Neighbour states
But for thy Sword and Fortune trod vpon them.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I prythee beate thy Drum, and get thee gone.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: I am thy Friend, and pitty thee deere Timon.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: How doest thou pitty him whom yu dost troble,
I had rather be alone.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Why fare thee well:
Heere is some Gold for thee.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Keepe it, I cannot eate it.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: When I haue laid proud Athens on a heape.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Warr'st thou 'gainst Athens.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: I Timon, and haue cause.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: The Gods confound them all in thy Conquest,
And thee after, when thou hast Conquer'd.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: Why me, Timon?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: That by killing of Villaines
Thou was't borne to conquer my Country.
Put vp thy Gold. Go on, heeres Gold, go on;
Be as a Plannetary plague, when Ioue
Will o're some high-Vic'd City, hang his poyson
In the sicke ayre: let not thy sword skip one:
Pitty not honour'd Age for his white Beard,
He is an Vsurer. Strike me the counterfet Matron,
It is her habite onely, that is honest,
Her selfe's a Bawd. Let not the Virgins cheeke
Make soft thy trenchant Sword: for those Milke pappes
That through the window Barne bore at mens eyes,
Are not within the Leafe of pitty writ,
But set them down horrible Traitors. Spare not the Babe
Whose dimpled smiles from Fooles exhaust their mercy;
Thinke it a Bastard, whom the Oracle
Hath doubtfully pronounced, the throat shall cut,
And mince it sans remorse. Sweare against Obiects,
Put Armour on thine eares, and on thine eyes,
Whose proofe, nor yels of Mothers, Maides, nor Babes,
Nor sight of Priests in holy Vestments bleeding,
Shall pierce a iot. There's Gold to pay thy Souldiers,
Make large confusion: and thy fury spent,
Confounded be thy selfe. Speake not, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: Hast thou Gold yet, Ile take the Gold thou giuest me, not all thy Counsell.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Dost thou or dost thou not, Heauens curse vpon thee.

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: Giue vs some Gold good Timon, hast yu more?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Enough to make a Whore forsweare her Trade,
And to make Whores, a Bawd. Hold vp you Sluts
Your Aprons mountant; you are not Othable,
Although I know you'l sweare, terribly sweare
Into strong shudders, and to heauenly Agues
Th' immortall Gods that heare you. Spare your Oathes:
Ile trust to your Conditions, be whores still.
And he whose pious breath seekes to conuert you,
Be strong in Whore, allure him, burne him vp,
Let your close fire predominate his smoke,
And be no turne-coats: yet may your paines six months
Be quite contrary, And Thatch
Your poore thin Roofes with burthens of the dead,
(Some that were hang'd) no matter:
Weare them, betray with them; Whore still,
Paint till a horse may myre vpon your face:
A pox of wrinkles.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: Well, more Gold, what then?
Beleeue't that wee'l do any thing for Gold.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Consumptions sowe
In hollow bones of man, strike their sharpe shinnes,
And marre mens spurring. Cracke the Lawyers voyce,
That he may neuer more false Title pleade,
Nor sound his Quillers shrilly: Hoare the Flamen,
That scold'st against the quality of flesh,
And not beleeues himselfe. Downe with the Nose,
Downe with it flat, take the Bridge quite away
Of him, that his particular to foresee
Smels from the generall weale. Make curld'pate Ruffians bald
And let the vnscarr'd Braggerts of the Warre
Deriue some paine from you. Plague all,
That your Actiuity may defeate and quell
The sourse of all Erection. There's more Gold.
Do you damne others, and let this damne you,
And ditches graue you all.

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: More counsell with more Money, bounteous Timon.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: More whore, more Mischeefe first, I haue giuen you earnest.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: Strike vp the Drum towardes Athens, farewell Timon: if I thriue well, Ile visit thee againe.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: If I hope well, Ile neuer see thee more.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: I neuer did thee harme.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Yes, thou spok'st well of me.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: Call'st thou that harme?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Men dayly finde it. Get thee away,
And take thy Beagles with thee.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
prose: We but offend him, strike.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: That Nature being sicke of mans vnkindnesse
Should yet be hungry: Common Mother, thou
Whose wombe vnmeasureable, and infinite brest
Teemes and feeds all: whose selfesame Mettle
Whereof thy proud Childe (arrogant man) is puft,
Engenders the blacke Toad, and Adder blew,
The gilded Newt, and eyelesse venom'd Worme,
With all th' abhorred Births below Crispe Heauen,
Whereon Hyperions quickning fire doth shine:
Yeeld him, who all the humane Sonnes do hate,
From foorth thy plenteous bosome, one poore roote:
Enseare thy Fertile and Conceptious wombe,
Let it no more bring out ingratefull man.
Goe great with Tygers, Dragons, Wolues, and Beares,
Teeme with new Monsters, whom thy vpward face
Hath to the Marbled Mansion all aboue
Neuer presented. O, a Root, deare thankes:
Dry vp thy Marrowes, Vines, and Plough-torne Leas,
Whereof ingratefull man with Licourish draughts
And Morsels Vnctious, greases his pure minde,
That from it all Consideration slippes —
More man? Plague, plague.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: I was directed hither. Men report,
Thou dost affect my Manners, and dost vse them.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: 'Tis then, because thou dost not keepe a dogge
Whom I would imitate. Consumption catch thee.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: This is in thee a Nature but infected,
A poore vnmanly Melancholly sprung
From change of future. Why this Spade? this place?
This Slaue-like Habit, and these lookes of Care?
Thy Flatterers yet weare Silke, drinke Wine, lye soft,
Hugge their diseas'd Perfumes, and haue forgot
That euer Timon was. Shame not these Woods,
By pa^cing on the cunning of a Carper.
Be thou a Flatterer now, and seeke to thriue
By that which ha's vndone thee; hindge thy knee,
And let his very breath whom thou'lt obserue
Blow off thy Cap: praise his most vicious straine,
And call it excellent: thou wast told thus:
Thou gau'st thine eares (like Tapsters, that bad welcom)
To Knaues, and all approachers: 'Tis most iust
That thou turne Rascall, had'st thou wealth againe,
Rascals should haue't. Do not assume my likenesse.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Were I like thee, I'de throw away my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: Thou hast cast away thy selfe, being like thy self
A Madman so long, now a Foole: what think'st
That the bleake ayre, thy boysterous Chamberlaine
Will put thy shirt on warme? Will these moyst Trees,
That haue out-liu'd the Eagle, page thy heeles
And skip when thou point'st out? Will the cold brooke
Candied with Ice, Cawdle thy Morning taste
To cure thy o're-nights surfet? Call the Creatures,
Whose naked Natures liue in all the spight
Of wrekefull Heauen, whose bare vnhoused Trunkes.
To the conflicting Elements expos'd
Answer meere Nature: bid them flatter thee.
O thou shalt finde.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: A Foole of thee: depart.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: I loue thee better now, then ere I did.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I hate thee worse.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Thou flatter'st misery.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: I flatter not, but say thou art a Caytiffe.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Why do'st thou seeke me out?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: To vex thee.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Alwayes a Villaines Office, or a Fooles.
Dost please thy selfe in't?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What, a Knaue too?

speeches.speaker: Ape.
verse: If thou did'st put this sowre cold habit on
To castigate thy pride, 'twere well: but thou
Dost it enforcedly: Thou'dst Courtier be againe
Wert thou not Beggar: willing misery
Out-liues: incertaine pompe, is crown'd before:
The one is filling still, neuer compleat:
The other, at high wish: best state Contentlesse,
Hath a distracted and most wretched being,
Worse then the worst, Content.
Thou should'st desire to dye, being miserable.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Not by his breath, that is more miserable.
Thou art a Slaue, whom Fortunes tender arme
With fauour neuer claspt: but bred a Dogge.
Had'st thou like vs from our first swath proceeded,
The sweet degrees that this breefe world affords,
To such as may the passiue drugges of it
Freely command'st: thou would'st haue plung'd thy self
In generall Riot, melted downe thy youth
In different beds of Lust, and neuer learn'd
The Icie precepts of respect, but followed
The Sugred game before thee. But my selfe,
Who had the world as my Confectionarie,
The mouthes, the tongues, the eyes, and hearts of men,
At duty more then I could frame employment;
That numberlesse vpon me stucke, as leaues
Do on the Oake, haue with one Winters brush
Fell from their boughes, and left me open, bare,
For euery storme that blowes. I to beare this,
That neuer knew but better, is some burthen:
Thy Nature, did commence in sufferance, Time
Hath made thee hard in't. Why should'st yu hate Men?
They neuer flatter'd thee. What hast thou giuen?
If thou wilt curse; thy Father (that poore ragge)
Must be thy subiect; who in spight put stuffe
To some shee-Begger, and compounded thee
Poore Rogue, hereditary. Hence, be gone,
If thou hadst not bene borne the worst of men,
Thou hadst bene a Knaue and Flatterer.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: Art thou proud yet?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I, that I am not thee.

speeches.speaker: Ape.
prose: I, that I was no Prodigall.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I, that I am one now.
Were all the wealth I haue shut vp in thee,
