speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: How cheerefully on the false Traile they cry,
Oh this is Counter you false Danish Dogges.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: The doores are broke.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Where is the King, sirs? Stand you all without.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: No, let's come in.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: I pray you giue me leaue.

speeches.speaker: Al.
prose: We will, we will.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: I thanke you: Keepe the doore.
Oh thou vilde King, giue me my Father.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Calmely good Laertes.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: That drop of blood, that calmes
Proclaimes me Bastard:
Cries Cuckold to my Father, brands the Harlot
Euen heere betweene the chaste vnsmirched brow
Of my true Mother.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What is the cause Laertes,
That thy Rebellion lookes so Gyant-like?
Let him go Gertrude: Do not feare our person:
There's such Diuinity doth hedge a King,
That Treason can but peepe to what it would,
Acts little of his will. Tell me Laertes,
Why thou art thus Incenst? Let him go Gertrude.
Speake man.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Where's my Father?

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Dead.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: But not by him.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Let him demand his fill.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: How came he dead? Ile not be Iuggel'd with.
To hell Allegeance: Vowes, to the blackest diuell.
Conscience and Grace, to the profoundest Pit.
I dare Damnation: to this point I stand,
That both the worlds I giue to negligence,
Let come what comes: onely Ile be reueng'd
Most throughly for my Father.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Who shall stay you?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: My Will, not all the world,
And for my meanes, Ile husband them so well,
They shall go farre with little.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Good Laertes:
If you desire to know the certaintie
Of your deere Fathers death, if writ in your reuenge,
That Soop-stake you will draw both Friend and Foe,
Winner and Looser.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: None but his Enemies.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Will you know them then.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: To his good Friends, thus wide Ile ope my Armes:
And like the kinde Life-rend'ring Politician,
Repast them with my blood.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Why now you speake
Like a good Childe, and a true Gentleman.
That I am guiltlesse of your Fathers death,
And am most sensible in greefe for it,
It shall as leuell to your Iudgement pierce
As day do's to your eye.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: How now? what noise is that?
Oh heate drie vp my Braines, teares seuen times salt,
Burne out the Sence and Vertue of mine eye.
By Heauen, thy madnesse shall be payed by waight,
Till our Scale turnes the beame. Oh Rose of May,
Deere Maid, kinde Sister, sweet Ophelia:
Oh Heauens, is't possible, a yong Maids wits,
Should be as mortall as an old mans life?
Nature is fine in Loue, and where 'tis fine,
It sends some precious instance of it selfe
After the thing it loues.

speeches.speaker: Ophe.
verse: They bore him bare fac'd on the Beer,
Hey non nony, nony, hey nony:
And on his graue raines many a teare,
Fare you well my Doue.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Had'st thou thy wits, and did'st perswade Reuenge, it could not moue thus.

speeches.speaker: Ophe.
prose: You must sing downe a-downe, and you call him a-downe-a. Oh, how the wheele becomes it? It is the false Steward that stole his masters daughter.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: This nothings more then matter.

speeches.speaker: Ophe.
verse: There's Rosemary, that's for Remembraunce.
Pray loue remember: and there is Paconcies, that's for Thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: A document in madnesse, thoughts & remembrance fitted.

speeches.speaker: Ophe.
prose: There's Fennell for you, and Columbines: ther's Rew for you, and heere's some for me. Wee may call it Herbe-Grace a Sundaies: Oh you must weare your Rew with a difference. There's a Daysie, I would giue you some Violets, but they wither'd all when my Father dyed: They say, he made a good end;

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: Thought, and Affliction, Passion, Hell it selfe:
She turnes to Fauour, and to prettinesse.

speeches.speaker: Ophe.
verse: And will he not come againe,
And will he not come againe:
No, no, he is dead, go to thy Death-bed,
He neuer wil come againe.
His Beard as white as Snow,
All Flaxen was his Pole:
He is gone, he is gone, and we cast away mone,
Gramercy on his Soule.
And of all Christian Soules, I pray God.
God buy ye.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Do you see this, you Gods?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Laertes, I must common with your greefe,
Or you deny me right: go but apart,
Make choice of whom your wisest Friends you will,
And they shall heare and iudge 'twixt you and me;
If by direct or by Colaterall hand
They finde vs touch'd, we will our Kingdome giue,
Our Crowne, our Life, and all that we call Ours
To you in satisfaction. But if not,
Be you content to lend your patience to vs,
And we shall ioyntly labour with your soule
To giue it due content.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: Let this be so:
His meanes of death, his obscure buriall;
No Trophee, Sword, nor Hatchment o're his bones,
No Noble rite, nor formall ostentation,
Cry to be heard, as 'twere from Heauen to Earth,
That I must call in question.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: So you shall:
And where th' offence is, let the great Axe fall.
I pray you go with me.

speeches.speaker: Hora.
prose: What are they that would speake with me?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Saylors sir, they say they haue Letters for you.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Let them come in,
I do not know from what part of the world
I should be greeted, if not from Lord Hamlet.

speeches.speaker: Say.
prose: God blesse you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Let him blesse thee too.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Come, I will giue you way for these your Letters,
And do't the speedier, that you may direct me
To him from whom you brought them.
prose: Hee shall Sir, and't please him. There's a Letter for you Sir: It comes from th' Ambassadours that was bound for England, if your name be Horatio, as I am let to know it is.

HOratio,

When thou shalt haue ouerlook'd this, giue these Fellowes some meanes to the King: They haue Letters for him. Ere we were two dayes old at Sea, a Pyrate of very Warlicke appointment gaue vs Chace. Finding our selues too slow of Saile, we put on a compelled Valour. In the Grapple, I boorded them: On the instant they got cleare of our Shippe, so I alone became their Prisoner. They haue dealt with mee, like Theeues of Mercy, but they knew what they did. I am to doe a good turne for them. Let the King haue the Letters I haue sent, and repaire thou to me with as much hast as thou wouldest flye death. I haue words to speake in your eare, will make thee-dumbe, yet are they much too light for the bore of the Matter. These good Fellowes will bring thee where I am. Rosincrance and Guildensterne, hold their course for England. Of them I haue much to tell thee, Farewell.


He that thou knowest thine, Hamlet.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Now must your conscience my acquittance seal,
And you must put me in your heart for Friend,
Sith you haue heard, and with a knowing eare,
That he which hath your Noble Father slaine,
Pursued my life.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: It well appeares. But tell me,
Why you proceeded not against these feates,
So crimefull, and so Capitall in Nature,
As by your Safety, Wisedome, all things else,
You mainly were stirr'd vp?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O for two speciall Reasons,
Which may to you (perhaps) seeme much vnsinnowed,
And yet to me they are strong. The Queen his Mother,
Liues almost by his lookes: and for my selfe,
My Vertue or my Plague, be it either which,
She's so coniunctiue to my life and soule;
That as the Starre moues not but in his Sphere,
I could not but by her. The other Motiue,
Why to a publike count I might not go,
Is the great loue the generall gender beare him,
Who dipping all his Faults in their affection,
Would like the Spring that turneth Wood to Stone,
Conuert his Gyues to Graces. So that my Arrowes
Too slightly timbred for so loud a Winde,
Would haue reuerted to my Bow againe,
And not where I had arm'd them.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: And so haue I a Noble Father lost,
A Sister driuen into desperate tearmes,
Who was (if praises may go backe againe)
Stood Challenger on mount of all the Age
For her perfections. But my reuenge will come.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Breake not your sleepes for that,
You must not thinke
That we are made of stuffe, so flat, and dull,
That we can let our Beard be shooke with danger,
And thinke it pastime. You shortly shall heare more,
I lou'd your Father, and we loue our Selfe,
And that I hope will teach you to imagine—
How now? What Newes?

speeches.speaker: Mes.
prose: Letters my Lord from Hamlet. This to your Maiesty: this to the Queene.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: From Hamlet? Who brought them?

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: Saylors my Lord they say, I saw them not:
They were giuen me by Claudio, he receiu'd them.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Laertes you shall heare them:
Leaue vs.
What should this meane? Are all the rest come backe?
Or is it some abuse? Or no such thing?
prose:
High and Mighty, you shall know I am set naked on your Kingdome. To morrow shall I begge leaue to see your Kingly Eyes. When I shall (first asking your Pardon thereunto) recount th' Occasions of my sodaine, and more strange returne.


Hamlet.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Know you the hand?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: 'Tis Hamlets Character, naked and in a Postscript here he sayes alone: Can you aduise me?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: I'm lost in it my Lord; but let him come,
It warmes the very sicknesse in my heart,
That I shall liue and tell him to his teeth;
Thus diddest thou.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: If it be so Laertes, as how should it be so:
How otherwise will you be rul'd by me?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: If so you'l not o're rule me to a peace.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: To thine owne peace: if he be now return'd,
As checking at his Voyage, and that he meanes
No more to vndertake it; I will worke him
To an exployt now ripe in my Deuice,
Vnder the which he shall not choose but fall;
And for his death no winde of blame shall breath,
But euen his Mother shall vncharge the practice,
And call it accident: Some two Monthes hence
Here was a Gentleman of Normandy,
I'ue seene my selfe, and seru'd against the French,
And they ran well on Horsebacke; but this Gallant
Had witchcraft in't; he grew into his Seat,
And to such wondrous doing brought his Horse,
As had he beene encorps't and demy-Natur'd
With the braue Beast, so farre he past my thought,
That I in forgery of shapes and trickes,
Come short of what he did.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: A Norman was't?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: A Norman.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Vpon my life Lamound.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: The very same.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: I know him well, he is the Brooch indeed,
And Iemme of all our Nation.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Hee mad confession of you,
And gaue you such a Masterly report,
For Art and exercise in your defence;
And for your Rapier most especiallye,
That he cryed out, t' would be a sight indeed,
If one could match you Sir. This report of his
Did Hamlet so envenom with his Enuy,
That he could nothing doe but wish and begge,
Your sodaine comming ore to play with him;
Now out of this.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Why out of this, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Kin
verse: Laertes was your Father deare to you?
Or are you like the painting of a sorrow,
A face without a heart?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Why aske you this?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Not that I thinke you did not loue your Father,
But that I know Loue is begun by Time:
And that I see in passages of proofe,
Time qualifies the sparke and fire of it:
Hamlet comes backe: what would you vndertake,
To show your selfe your Fathers sonne indeed,
More then in words?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: To cut his throat i' th' Church.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: No place indeed should murder Sancturize;
Reuenge should haue no bounds: but good Laertes
Will you doe this, keepe close within your Chamber,
Hamlet return'd, shall know you are come home:
Wee'l put on those shall praise your excellence,
And set a double varnish on the fame
The Frenchman gaue you, bring you in fine together,
And wager on your heads, he being remisse,
Most generous, and free from all contriuing,
Will not peruse the Foiles? So that with ease,
Or with a little shuffling, you may choose
A Sword vnbaited, and in a passe of practice,
Requit him for your Father.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: I will doo't,
And for that purpose Ile annoint my Sword:
I bought an Vnction of a Mountebanke
So mortall, I but dipt a knife in it,
Where it drawes blood, no Cataplasme so rare,
Collected from all Simples that haue Vertue
Vnder the Moone, can saue the thing from death,
That is but scratcht withall: Ile touch my point,
With this contagion, that if I gall him slightly,
It may be death.

speeches.speaker: Kin
verse: Let's further thinke of this,
Weigh what conuenience both of time and meanes
May fit vs to our shape, if this should faile;
And that our drift looke through our bad performance,
'Twere better not assaid; therefore this Proiect
Should haue a backe or second, that might hold,
If this should blast in proofe: Soft, let me see
Wee'l make a solemne wager on your commings,
I ha't: when in your motion you are hot and dry,
As make your bowts more violent to the end,
And that he cals for drinke; Ile haue prepar'd him
A Challice for the nonce; whereon but sipping,
If he by chance escape your venom'd stuck,
Our purpose may hold there; how sweet Queene.

speeches.speaker: Queen.
verse: One woe doth tread vpon anothers heele,
So fast they'l follow: your Sister's drown'd Laertes.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Drown'd! O where?

speeches.speaker: Queen.
verse: There is a Willow growes aslant a Brooke,
That shewes his hore leaues in the glassie streame:
There with fantasticke Garlands did she come,
Of Crow-slowers, Nettles, Daysies, and long Purples,
That liberall Shepheards giue a grosser name;
But our cold Maids doe Dead Mens Fingers call them:
There on the pendant boughes, her Coronet weeds
Clambring to hang; an enuious sliuer broke,
When downe the weedy Trophies, and her selfe,
Fell in the weeping Brooke, her cloathes spred wide,
And Mermaid-like, a while they bore her vp,
Which time she chaunted snatches of old tunes,
As one incapable of her owne distresse,
Or like a creature Natiue, and indued
Vnto that Element: but long it could not be,
Till that her garments, heauy with her drinke,
Pul'd the poore wretch from her melodious buy,
To muddy death.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Alas then, is she drown'd?

speeches.speaker: Queen,
prose: Drown'd, drown'd.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: Too much of water hast thou poore Ophelia,
And therefore I forbid my teares: but yet
It is our tricke, Nature her custome holds,
Let shame say what it will; when these are gone
The woman will be out: Adue my Lord,
I haue a speech of fire, that faine would blaze,
But that this folly doubts it.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Let's follow, Gertrude:
How much I had to doe to calme his rage?
Now feare I this will giue it start againe;
Therefore let's follow.

speeches.speaker: Clown.
prose: Is she to bee buried in Christian buriall, that wilfully seekes her owne saluation?

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: I tell thee she is, and therefore make her Graue straight, the Crowner hath sate on her, and finds it Christian buriall.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: How can that be, vnlesse she drowned her selfe in her owne defence?

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Why 'tis found so.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: It must be Se offendendo, it cannot bee else: for heere lies the point; If I drowne my selfe wittingly, it argues an Act: and an Act hath three branches. It is an Act to doe and to performe; argall she drown'd her selfe wittingly.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Nay but heare you Goodman Deluer.

speeches.speaker: Clown.
prose: Giue me leaue; heere lies the water; good: heere stands the man; good: If the man goe to this water and drowne himsele; it is will he nill he, he goes; marke you that? But if the water come to him & drowne him; hee drownes not himselfe. Argall, hee that is not guilty of his owne death, shortens not his owne life.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: But is this law?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I marry is't, Crowners Quest Law.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Will you ha the truth on't: if this had not beene a Gentlewoman, shee should haue beene buried out of Christian Buriall.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why there thou say'st. And the more pitty that great folke should haue countenance in this world to drowne or hang themselues, more then their euen Christian. Come, my Spade; there is no ancient Gentlemen, but Gardiners, Ditchers and Graue-makers; they hold vp Adams Profession.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Was he a Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: He was the first that euer bore Armes.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Why he had none.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: What, ar't a Heathen? how dost thou vnderstand the Scripture? the Scripture sayes Adam dig'd; could hee digge without Armes? Ile put another question to thee; if thou answerest me not to the purpose, confesse thy selfe—

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Go too.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: What is he that builds stronger then either the Mason, the Shipwright, or the Carpenter?

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: The Gallowes maker; for that Frame outliues a thousand Tenants.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I like thy wit well in good faith, the Gallowes does well; but how does it well? it does well to those that doe ill: now, thou dost ill to say the Gallowes is built stronger then the Church: Argall, the Gallowes may doe well to thee. Too't againe, Come.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Who builds stronger then a Mason, a Shipwright, or a Carpenter?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I, tell me that, and vnyoake.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Marry, now I can tell.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Too't.

speeches.speaker: Other.
prose: Masse, I cannot tell.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: In youth when I did loue, did loue,
me thought it was very sweete:
To contract O the time for a my behoue,
O me thought there was nothing meete.
prose: Cudgell thy braines no more about it; for your dull Asse will not mend his pace with beating; and when you are ask't this question next, say a Graue-maker: the Houses that he makes, lasts till Doomesday: go, get thee to Yaughan, fetch me a stoupe of Liquor.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Ha's this fellow no feeling of his businesse, that he sings at Graue-making?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Custome hath made it in him a property of easinesse.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: 'Tis ee'n so; the hand of little Imployment hath the daintier sense.

verse: But Age with his stealing steps
hath caught me in his clutch:
And hath shipped me intill the Land,
as if I had neuer beene such.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: That Scull had a tongue in it, and could sing once: how the knaue iowles it to th' grownd as if it were Caines Iaw-bone, that did the first murther: It might be the Pate of a Polititian which this Asse o're Offices: one that could circumuent God, might it not?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: It might, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Or of a Courtier, which could say, Good Morrow sweet Lord: how dost thou, good Lord? this might be my Lord such a one, that prais'd my Lord such a ones Horse, when he meant to begge it; might it not?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Why ee'n so: and now my Lady Wormes, Chaplesse, and knockt about the Mazard with a Sextons Spade; heere's fine Reuolution, if wee had the tricke to see't. Did these bones cost no more the breeding. but to play at Loggets with 'em? mine ake to thinke on't.

verse: A Pickhaxe and a Spade, a Spade,
for and a shrowding-Sheete:
O a Pit of Clay for to be made,
for such a Guest is meete.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: There's another: why might not that bee the Scull of of a Lawyer? where be his Quiddits now? his Quillets? his Cases? his Tenures, and his Tricks? why doe's he suffer this rude knaue now to knocke him about the Sconce with a dirty Shouell, and will not tell him of his Action of Battery? hum. This fellow might be in's time a great buyer of Land, with his Statutes, his Recognizances, his Fines, his double Vouchers, his Recoueries: Is this the fine of his Fines, and the recouery of his Recoueries, to haue his fine Pate full of fine Dirt? will his Vouchers vouch him no more of his Purchases, and double ones too, then the length and breadth of a paire of Indentures? the very Conueyances of his Lands will hardly lye in this Boxe; and must the Inheritor himselfe haue no more? ha?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Not a iot more, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Is not Parchment made of Sheep-skinnes?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I my Lord, and of Calue-skinnes too.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: They are Sheepe and Calues that seek out assurance in that. I will speake to this fellow: whose Graue's this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Mine Sir:
O a Pit of Clay for to be made,
for such a Guest is meete.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: I thinke it be thine indeed: for thou liest in't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: You lye out on't Sir, and therefore it is not yours: for my part, I doe not lye in't; and yet it is mine.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Thou dost lye in't, to be in't and say 'tis thine: 'tis for the dead, not for the quicke, therefore thou lyest.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: 'Tis a quicke lye Sir, 'twill a way againe from me to you.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: What man dost thou digge it for?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: For no man Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: What woman then?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: For none neither.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Who is to be buried in't?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: One that was a woman Sir; but rest her Soule, shee's dead.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: How absolute the knaue is? wee must speake by the Carde, or equiuocation will vndoe vs: by the Lord Horatio, these three yeares I haue taken note of it, the Age is growne so picked, that the toe of the Pesant comes so neere the heeles of our Courtier, hee galls his Kibe. How long hast thou been a Graue-maker?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Of all the dayes i' th' yeare, I came too't that day that our last King Hamlet o're came Fortinbras.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: How long is that since?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Cannot you tell that? euery foole can tell that: It was the very day, that young Hamlet was borne, hee that was mad, and sent into England.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: I marry, why was he sent into England?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why, because he was mad; hee shall recouer his wits there; or if he do not, it's no great matter there.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: 'Twill not be seene in him, there the men are as mad as he.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: How came he mad?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Very strangely they say.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: How strangely?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Faith e'ene with loosing his wits.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Vpon what ground?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why heere in Denmarke: I haue bin sixeteene heere, man and Boy thirty yeares.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: How long will a man lie 'i th' earth ere he rot?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I faith, if he be not rotten before he die (as we haue many pocky Coarses now adaies, that will scarce hold the laying in) he will last you some eight yeare, or nine yeare. A Tanner will last you nine yeare.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Why he, more then another?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why sir, his hide is so tan'd with his Trade, that he will keepe out water a great while. And your water, is a sore Decayer of your horson dead body. Heres a Scull now: this Scul, has laine in the earth three & twenty years.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Whose was it?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: A whoreson mad Fellowes it was;
Whose doe you thinke it was?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Nay, I know not.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: A pestlence on him for a mad Rogue, a pou'rd a Flaggon of Renish on my head once. This same Scull Sir, this same Scull sir, was Yoricks Scull, the Kings Iester.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: This?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: E'ene that.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Let me see. Alas poore Yorick, I knew him Horatio, a fellow of infinite Iest; of most excellent fancy, he hath borne me on his backe a thousand times: And how abhorred my Imagination is, my gorge rises at it. Heere hung those lipps, that I haue kist I know not how oft. VVhere be your libes now? Your Gambals? Your Songs? Your flashes of Merriment that were wont to set the Table on a Rore? No one now to mock your own Ieering? Quite chopfalne? Now get you to my Ladies Chamber, and tell her, let her paint an inch thicke, to this fauour she must come. Make her laugh at that: prythee Horatio tell me one thing.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: What's that my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Dost thou thinke Alexander lookt o' this fashion i' th' earth?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: E'ene so.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: And smelt so? Puh.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: E'ene so, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: To what base vses we may returne Horatio. Why may not Imagination trace the Noble dust of Alexander, till he find it stopping a bunghole.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: 'Twere to consider: to curiously to consider so.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Imperiall Caesar, dead and turn'd to clay,
Might stop a hole to keepe the winde away.
Oh, that that earth, which kept the world in awe,
Should patch a Wall, t' expell the winters flaw.
But soft, but soft, aside; heere comes the King.
The Queene, the Courtiers. Who is that they follow,
And with such maimed rites? This doth betoken,
The Coarse they follow, did with disperate hand,
Fore do it owne life; 'twas some Estate.
Couch we a while, and mark.
prose: No faith, not a iot. But to follow him thether with modestie enough, & likeliehood to lead it; as thus. Alexander died: Alexander was buried: Alexander returneth into dust; the dust is earth; of earth we make Lome, and why of that Lome (whereto he was conuerted) might they not stopp a Beere-barrell?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: What Cerimony else?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: That is Laertes, a very Noble youth: Marke.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: What Cerimony else?

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Her Obsequies haue bin as farre inlarg'd.
As we haue warrantis, her death was doubtfull,
And but that great Command, o're-swaies the order,
She should in ground vnsanctified haue lodg'd,
Till the last Trumpet. For charitable praier,
Shardes, Flints, and Peebles, should be throwne on her:
Yet heere she is allowed her Virgin Rites,
Her Maiden strewments, and the bringing home
Of Bell and Buriall.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Must there no more be done?

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: No more be done:
We should prophane the seruice of the dead,
To sing sage Requiem, and such rest to her
As to peace-parted Soules.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: Lay her i' th' earth,
And from her faire and vnpolluted flesh,
May Violets spring. I tell thee (churlish Priest)
A Ministring Angell shall my Sister be,
When thou liest howling?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: What, the faire Ophelia?

speeches.speaker: Queene.
verse: Sweets, to the sweet farewell.
I hop'd thou should'st haue bin my Hamlets wife:
I thought thy Bride-bed to haue deckt (sweet Maid)
And not t' haue strew'd thy Graue.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: Oh terrible woer,
Fall ten times trebble, on that cursed head
Whose wicked deed. thy most Ingenious sence
Depriu'd thee of. Hold off the earth a while,
Till I haue caught her once more in mine armes:
Now pile your dust, vpon the quicke, and dead,
Till of this flat a Mountaine you haue made,
To o're top old Pelion, or the skyish head
Of blew Olympus.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: What is he, whose griefes
Beares such an Emphasis? whose phrase of Sorrow
Coniure the wandring Starres, and makes them stand
Like wonder-wounded hearers? This is I,
Hamlet the Dane.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: The deuill take thy soule.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Thou prai'st not well,
I prythee take thy fingers from my throat;
Sir though I am not Spleenatiue, and rash,
Yet haue I something in me dangerous,
Which let thy wisenesse feare. Away thy hand.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Pluck them asunder.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Hamlet, Hamlet.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
prose: Good my Lord be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Why I will fight with him vppon this Theme.
Vntill my eielids will no longer wag.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Oh my Sonne, what Theame?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: I lou'd Ophelia; fortie thousand Brothers
Could not (with all there quantitie of Loue)
Make vp my summe. What wilt thou do for her?

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Oh he is mad Laertes,

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: For loue of God forbeare him.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Come show me what thou'lt doe.
Woo't weepe? Woo't fight? Woo't teare thy selfe?
Woo't drinke vp Esile, eate a Crocodile?
Ile doo't. Dost thou come heere to whine;
To outface me with leaping in her Graue?
Be buried quicke with her, and so will I.
And if thou prate of Mountaines; let them throw
Millions of Akers on vs; till our ground
Sindging his pate against the burning Zone,
Make Ossa like a wart. Nay, and thoul't mouth,
Ile rant as well as thou.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: This is meere Madnesse:
And thus awhile the fit will worke on him:
Anon as patient as the female Doue,
When that her golden Cuplet are disclos'd;
His silence will sit drooping.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Heare you Sir:
What is the reason that you vse me thus?
I loud you euer; but it is no matter:
Let Hercules himselfe doe what he may,
The Cat will Mew, and Dogge will haue his day.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I pray you good Horatio wait vpon him,
Strengthen you patience in our last nights speech,
Wee'l put the matter to the present push:
Good Gertrude set some watch ouer your Sonne,
This Graue shall haue a liuing Monument:
An houre of quiet shortly shall we see;
Till then, in patience our proceeding be.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: So much for this Sir; now let me see the other,
You doe remember all the Circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Remember it my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Sir, in my heart there was a kinde of fighting,
That would not let me sleepe; me thought I lay
Worse then the mutines in the Bilboes, rashly,
(And praise be rashnesse for it) let vs know,
Our indiscretion sometimes serues vs well,
When our deare plots do paule, and that should teach vs,
There's a Diuinity that shapes our ends,
Rough-hew them how we will.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: That is most certaine.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Vp from my Cabin
My sea-gowne scarft about me in the darke,
Grop'd I to finde out them; had my desire,
Finger'd their Packet, and in fine, withdrew
To mine owne roome againe, making so bold,
(My feares forgetting manners) to vnseale
Their grand Commission, where I found Horatio,
Oh royall knauery: An exact command,
Larded with many seuerall sorts of reason;
Importing Denmarks health, and Englands too,
With hoo, such Bugges and Goblins in my life,
That on the superuize no leasure bated,
No not to stay the grinding of the Axe,
My head shoud be struck off.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Ist possible?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Here's the Commission, read it at more leysure:
But wilt thou heare me how I did proceed?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Being thus benetted round with Villaines,
Ere I could make a Prologue to my braines,
They had begun the Play. I sate me downe,
Deuis'd a new Commission, wrote it faire,
I once did hold it as our Statists doe,
A basenesse to write faire; and laboured much
How to forget that learning: but Sir now,
It did me Yeomans seruice: wilt thou know
The effects of what I wrote?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: I, good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: An earnest Coniuration from the King,
As England was his faithfull Tributary,
As loue betweene them, as the Palme should flourish,
As Peace should still her wheaten Garland weare,
And stand a Comma 'tweene their amities,
And many such like Assis of great charge,
That on the view and know of these Contents,
Without debatement further, more or lesse,
He should the bearers put to sodaine death,
Not shriuing time allowed.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: How was this seal'd?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Why, euen in that was Heauen ordinate;
I had my fathers Signet in my Purse,
Which was the Modell of that Danish Seale:
Folded the Writ vp in forme of the other,
Subscrib'd it, gau't th' impression, plac't it safely,
The changeling neuer knowne: Now, the next day
Was our Sea Fight, and what to this was sement,
Thou know'st already.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: So Guildensterne and Rosincrance, go too't.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Why man, they did make loue to this imployment
They are not neere my Conscience; their debate
Doth by their owne insinuation grow:
'Tis dangerous, when the baser nature comes
Betweene the passe, and fell incensed points
Of mighty opposites.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Why, what a King is this?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Does it not, thinkst thee, stand me now vpon
He that hath kil'd my King, and whor'd my Mother,
Popt in betweene th' election and my hopes,
Throwne out his Angle for my proper life,
And with such coozenage; is't not perfect conscience,
To quit him with this arme? And is't not to be damn'd
To let this Canker of our nature come
In further euill.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: It must be shortly knowne to him from England
What is the issue of the businesse there.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: It will be short,
The interim's mine, and a mans life's no more
Then to say one: but I am very sorry good Horatio,
That to Laertes I forgot my selfe;
For by the image of my Cause, I see
The Portraiture of his; Ile count his fauours:
But sure the brauery of his griefe did put me
Into a Towring passion.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Peace, who comes heere?

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: Your Lordship is right welcome back to Denmarke.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: I humbly thank you Sir, dost know this waterflie?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: No my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Thy state is the more gracious; for 'tis a vice to know him: he hath much Land, and fertile; let a Beast be Lord of Beasts, and his Crib shall stand at the Kings Messe; 'tis a Chowgh; but as I saw spacious in the possession of dirt.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
verse: Sweet Lord, if your friendship were at leysure,
I should impart a thing to you from his Maiesty.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: I will receiue it with all diligence of spirit; put your Bonet to his right vse, 'tis for the head.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: I thanke your Lordship, 'tis very hot.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: No, beleeue mee 'tis very cold, the winde is Northerly.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: It is indifferent cold my Lord indeed.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Mee thinkes it is very soultry, and hot for my Complexion.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: Exceedingly, my Lord, it is very soultry, as 'twere I cannot tell how: but my Lord, his Maiesty bad me signifie to you, that he ha's laid a great wager on your head: Sir, this is the matter.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: I beseech you remember.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: Nay, in good faith, for mine ease in good faith: Sir, you are not ignorant of what excellence Laertes is at his weapon.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: What's his weapon?

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: Rapier and dagger.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: That's two of his weapons; but well.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: The sir King ha's wag'd with him six Barbary Horses, against the which he impon'd as I take it, sixe French Rapiers and Poniards, with their assignes, as Girdle, Hangers or so: three of the Carriages infaith are very deare to fancy, very responsiue to the hilts, most delicate carriages, and of very liberall conceit.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: What call you the Carriages?

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: The Carriages Sir, are the hangers.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: The phrase would bee more Germaine to the matter: If we could carry Cannon by our sides; I would it might be Hangers till then; but on sixe Barbary Horses against sixe French Swords: their Assignes, and three liberall conceited Carriages, that's the French but against the Danish; why is this impon'd as you call it?

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: The King Sir, hath laid that in a dozen passes betweene you and him, hee shall not exceed you three hits; He hath one twelue for mine, and that would come to imediate tryall, if your Lordship would vouchsafe the Answere.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: How if I answere no?

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: I meane my Lord, the opposition of your person in tryall.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Sir, I will walke heere in the Hall; if it please his Maiestie, 'tis the breathing time of day with me; let the Foyles bee brought, the Gentleman willing, and the King hold his purpose; I will win for him if I can: if not, Ile gaine nothing but my shame, and the odde hits.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: Shall I redeliuer you ee'n so?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: To this effect Sir, after what flourish your nature will.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: I commend my duty to your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Yours, yours; hee does well to commend it himselfe, there are no tongues else for's tongue.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: This Lapwing runs away with the shell on his head.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: He did Complie with his Dugge before hee suck't it: thus had he and mine more of the same Beauy that I know the drossie age dotes on; only got the tune of the time, and outward habite of encounter, a kinde of yesty collection, which carries them through & through the most fond and winnowed opinions; and doe but blow them to their tryalls: the Bubbles are out.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: You will lose this wager, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: I doe not thinke so, since he went into France, I haue beene in continuall practice; I shall winne at the oddes: but thou wouldest not thinke how all heere about my heart: but it is no matter.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: Nay, good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: It is but foolery; but it is such a kinde of gain-giuing as would perhaps trouble a woman.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
prose: If your minde dislike any thing, obey. I will forestall their repaire hither, and say you are not fit.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Not a whit, we defie Augury; there's a speciall Prouidence in the fall of a sparrow. If it be now, 'tis not to come: if it bee not to come, it will bee now: if it be not now; yet it will come; the readinesse is all, since no man ha's ought of what he leaues. What is't to leaue betimes?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
prose: Come Hamlet, come, and take this hand from me.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Giue me your pardon Sir, I'ue done you wrong,
But pardon't as you are a Gentleman.
This presence knowes,
And you must needs haue heard how I am punisht
With sore distraction? What I haue done
That might your nature honour, and exception
Roughly awake, I heere proclaime was madnesse:
Was^t Hamlet wrong'd Laertes? Neuer Hamlet.
If Hamlet from himselfe be tane away:
And when he's not himselfe, do's wrong Laertes,
Then Hamlet does it not, Hamlet denies it:
Who does it then? His Madnesse? If't be so,
Hamlet is of the Faction that is wrong'd,
His madnesse is poore Hamlets Enemy.
Sir, in this Audience,
Let my disclaiming from a purpos'd euill,
Free me so farre in your most generous thoughts,
That I haue shot mine Arrow o're the house,
And hurt my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: I am satisfied in Nature,
Whose motiue in this case should stirre me most
To my Reuenge. But in my termes of Honor
I stand aloofe, and will no reconcilement,
Till by some elder Masters of knowne Honor,
I haue a voyce, and president of peace
To keepe my name vngorg'd. But till that time,
I do receiue your offer'd loue like loue,
And wil not wrong it.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: I do embrace it freely,
And will this Brothers wager frankely play.
Giue vs the Foyles: Come on.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Come one for me.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Ile be your foile Laertes, in mine ignorance,
Your Skill shall like a Starre i' th' darkest night,
Sticke fiery off indeede.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: You mocke me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: No by this hand.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Giue them the Foyles yong Osricke,
Cousen Hamlet, you know the wagot.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Verie well my Lord,
Your Grace hath laide the oddes a' th' weaker side.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I do not feare it,
I haue seene you both:
But since he is better'd, we haue therefore oddes.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: This is too heauy,
Let me see another.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: This likes me well,
These Foyles haue all a length.

speeches.speaker: Osricke.
prose: I my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Set me the Stopes of wine vpon that Table:
If Hamlet giue the first, or second hit,
Or quit in answer of the third exchange,
Let all the Battlements their Ordinance fire,
The King shal drinke to Hamlets better breath,
And in the Cup an vnion shal he throw
Richer then that, which foure successiue Kings
In Denmarkes Crowne haue worne.
Giue me the Cups,
And let the Kettle to the Trumpets speake,
The Trumpet to the Cannoneer without,
The Cannons to the Heauens, the Heauen to Earth,
Now the King drinkes to Hamlet. Come, begin,
And you the Iudges beare a wary eye.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Come on sir.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Come on sir.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: One.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Iudgement.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: A hit, a very palpable hit.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Well: againe.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Stay, giue me drinke.
Hamlet, this Pearle is thine,
Here's to thy health. Giue him the cup,

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Ile play this bout first, set by a-while.
Come: Another hit; what say you?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: A touch, a touch, I do confesse.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Our Sonne shall win.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: He's fat, and scant of breath.
Heere's a Napkin, rub thy browes,
The Queene Carowses to thy fortune, Hamlet.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Good Madam.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Gertrude, do not drinke.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: I will my Lord;
I pray you pardon me.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: It is the poyson'd Cup, it is too late.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: I dare not drinke yet Madam,
By and by.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
prose: Come, let me wipe thy face.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: My Lord, Ile hit him now.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: I do not thinke't.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: And yet 'tis almost 'gainst my conscience.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Come for the third.
Laertes, you but daily,
I pray you passe with your best violence,
I am affear'd you make a wanton of me.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Say you so? Come on.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: Nothing neither way.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
prose: Haue at you now.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Part them, they are incens'd.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Nay come, againe.

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: Looke to the Queene there hoa.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: They bleed on both sides. How is't my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Osr.
prose: How is't Laertes?

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: Why as a Woodcocke
To mine Sprindge, Osricke,
I am iustly kill'd with mine owne Treacherie.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: How does the Queene?

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: She sounds to see them bleede.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: No, no, the drinke, the drinke.
Oh my deere Hamlet, the drinke, the drinke,
I am poyson'd.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Oh Villany! How? Let the doore be lock'd.
Treacherie, seeke it out.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: It is heere Hamlet.
Hamlet, thou art slaine,
No Medicine in the world can do thee good.
In thee, there is not halfe an houre of life;
The Treacherous Instrument is in thy hand.
Vnbated and envenom'd: the foule practise
Hath turn'd it selfe on me. Loe, heere I lye,
Neuer to rise againe: Thy Mothers poyson'd:
I can no more, the King, the King's too blame.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: The point envenom'd too,
Then venome to thy worke.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Treason, Treason.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: O yet defend me Friends, I am but hurt.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Heere thou incestuous, murdrous,
Damned Dane,
Drinke off this Potion: Is thy Vnion heere?
Follow my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Laer.
verse: He is ^ustly seru'd.
It is a poyson temp'red by himselfe:
Exchange forgiuenesse with me, Noble Hamlet;
Mine and my Fathers death come not vpon thee,
Nor thine on me.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: Heauen make thee free of it, I follow thee.
I am dead Horatio, wretched Queene adiew,
You that looke pale, and tremble at this chance,
That are but Mutes or audience to this acte:
Had I but time (as this fell Sergeant death
Is strick'd in his Arrest) oh I could tell you.
But let it be: Horatio, I am dead,
Thou liu'st, report me and my causes right.
To the vnsatisfied.

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Neuer beleeue it.
I am more an Antike Roman then a Dane:
Heere's yet some Liquor left.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: As th' art a man, giue me the Cup.
Let go, by Heauen Ile haue't.
Oh good Horatio, what a wounded name,
(Things standing thus vnknowne) shall liue behind me.
If thou did'st euer hold me in thy heart,
Absent thee from felicitie awhile,
And in this harsh world draw thy breath in paine,
To tell my Storie.
What warlike noyse is this?

speeches.speaker: Osr.
verse: Yong Fortinbras, with conquest come fro~ Poland
To th' Ambassadors of England giues this warlike volly.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
verse: O I dye Horatio:
The potent poyson quite ore-crowes my spirit,
I cannot liue to heare the Newes from England,
But I do prophesie th' election lights
On Fortinbras, he ha's my dying voyce,
So tell him with the occurrents more and lesse,
Which haue solicited. The rest is silence.

speeches.speaker: Hora.
verse: Now cracke a Noble heart:
Goodnight sweet Prince,
And flights of Angels sing thee to thy rest,
Why do's the Drumme come hither?

speeches.speaker: Fortin.
prose: Where is this sight?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: What is it ye would see;
If ought of woe, or wonder, cease your search.

speeches.speaker: For.
verse: His quarry cries on hauocke. Oh proud death,
What feast is toward in thine eternall Cell.
That thou so many Princes, at a shoote,
So bloodily hast strooke.

speeches.speaker: Amb.
verse: The sight is dismall,
And our affaires from England come too late,
The eares are senselesse that should giue vs hearing,
To tell him his command'ment is fulfill'd,
That Rosincrance and Guildensterne are dead:
Where should we haue our thankes?

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Not from his mouth,
Had it th' abilitie of life to thanke you:
He neuer gaue command'ment for their death.
But since so iumpe vpon this bloodie question,
You from the Polake warres, and you from England
Are heere arriued. Giue order that these bodies
High on a stage be placed to the view,
And let me speake to th' yet vnknowing world,
How these things came about. So shall you heare
Of carnall, bloudie, and vnnaturall acts,
Of accidentall iudgements, casuall slaughters
Of death's put on by cunning, and forc'd cause,
And in this vpshot, purposes mistooke,
Falne on the Inuentors heads. All this can I
Truly deliuer.

speeches.speaker: For.
verse: Let vs hast to heare it,
And call the Noblest to the Audience.
For me, with sorrow, I embrace my Fortune,
I haue some Rites of memory in this Kingdome,
Which are ro claime, my vantage doth
Inuite me,

speeches.speaker: Hor.
verse: Of that I shall haue alwayes cause to speake,
And from his mouth
Whose voyce will draw on more:
But let this same be presently perform'd,
Euen whiles mens mindes are wilde,
Lest more mischance
On plots, and errors happen.

speeches.speaker: For.
verse: Let foure Captaines
Beare Hamlet like a Soldier to the Stage,
For he was likely, had he beene put on
To haue prou'd most royally:
And for his passage,
The Souldiours Musicke, and the rites of Warre
Speake lowdly for him.
Take vp the body; Such a sight as this
Becomes the Field, but heere shewes much amis.
Go, bid the Souldiers shoote.

plays.play_title: THE TRAGEDIE OF KING LEAR.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I Thought the King had more affected the Duke of Albany, then Cornwall.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: It did alwayes seeme so to vs: But now in the diuision of the Kingdome, it appeares not which of the Dukes hee valewes most, for qualities are so weigh'd, that curiosity in neither, can make choise of eithers moity.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Is not this your Son, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: His breeding Sir, hath bin at my charge. I haue so often blush'd to acknowledge him, that now I am braz'd too't.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I cannot conceiue you.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Sir, this yong Fellowes mother could; wherevpon she grew round womb'd, and had indeede (Sir) a Sonne for her Cradle, ere she had a husband for her bed. Do you smell a fault?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I cannot wish the fault vndone, the issue of it, being so proper.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: But I haue a Sonne, Sir, by order of Law, some yeere elder then this; who, yet is no deerer in my account, though this Knaue came somthing sawcily to the world before he was sent for: yet was his Mother fayre, there was good sport at his making, and the horson must be acknowledged. Doe you know this Noble Gentleman, Edmond?

speeches.speaker: Edm.
prose: No, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: My Lord of Kent:
Remember him heereafter, as my Honourable Friend.

speeches.speaker: Edm.
prose: My seruices to your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I must loue you, and sue to know you better.

speeches.speaker: Edm.
prose: Sir, I shall study deseruing.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: He hath bin out nine yeares, and away he shall againe. The King is comming.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Attend the Lords of France & Burgundy, Gloster.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: I shall, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Meane time we shal expresse our darker purpose.
Giue me the Map there. Know, that we haue diuided
In three our Kingdome: and 'tis our fast intent,
To shake all Cares and Businesse from our Age,
Conferring them on yonger strengths, while we
Vnburthen'd crawle toward death. Our son of Cornwal,
And you our no lesse louing Sonne of Albany,
We haue this houre a constant will to publish
Our daughters seuerall Dowers, that future strife
May be preuented now. The Princes, France & Burgundy,
Great Riuals in our yongest daughters loue,
Long in our Court, haue made their amorous soiourne,
And heere are to be answer'd. Tell me my daughters
(Since now we will diuest vs both of Rule,
Interest of Territory, Cares of State)
Which of you shall we say doth loue vs most,
That we, our largest bountie may extend
Where Nature doth with merit challenge.
Our eldest borne, speake first.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Sir, I loue you more then word can weild ye matter,
Deerer then eye-sight, space, and libertie,
Beyond what can be valewed, rich or rare,
No lesse then life, with grace, health, beauty, honor:
As much as Childe ere lou'd, or Father found.
A loue that makes breath poore, and speech vnable,
Beyond all manner of so much I loue you.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: What shall Cordelia speake? Loue, and be silent.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Of all these bounds euen from this Line, to this,
With shadowie Forrests, and with Champains rich'd
With plenteous Riuers, and wide-skirted Meades
We make thee Lady. To thine and Albanies issues
Be this perpetuall. What sayes our second Daughter?
Our deerest Regan, wife of Cornwall?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: I am made of that selfe-mettle as my Sister,
And prize me at her worth. In my true heart,
I finde she names my very deede of loue:
Onely she comes too short, that I professe
My selfe an enemy to all other ioyes,
Which the most precious square of sense professes,
And finde I am alone felicitate
In your deere Highnesse loue.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Then poore Cordelia,
And yet not so, since I am sure my loue's
More ponderous then my tongue.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: To thee, and thine hereditarie euer,
Remaine this ample third of our faire Kingdome,
No lesse in space, validitie, and pleasure
Then that confeir'd on Gonerill. Now our Ioy,
Although our last and least; to whose yong loue.
The Vines of France, and Milke of Burgundie,
Striue to be interest. What can you say, to draw
A third, more opilent then your Sisters? speake.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Nothing my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Nothing?

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Nothing.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Nothing will come of nothing, speake againe.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Vnhappie that I am, I cannot heaue
My heart into my mouth: I loue your Maiesty
According to my bond, no more nor lesse.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: How, how Cordelia? Mend your speech a little,
Least you may marre your Fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Good my Lord,
You haue begot me, bred me, lou'd me.
I returne those duties backe as are right fit,
Obey you, Loue you, and most Honour you.
Why haue my Sisters Husbands, if they say
They loue you all? Happily when I shall wed,
That Lord, whose hand must take my plight, shall carry
Halfe my loue with him, halfe my Care, and Dutie,
Sure I shall neuer marry like my Sisters.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: But goes thy heart with this?

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: I my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: So young, and so vntender?

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: So young my Lord, and true.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Let it be so, thy truth then be thy dowre:
For by the sacred radience of the Sunne,
The miseries of Heccat and the night:
By all the operation of the Orbes,
From whom we do exist, and cease to be,
Heere I disclaime all my Paternall care,
Propinquity and property of blood,
And as a stranger to my heart and me,
Hold thee from this for euer. The barbarous Scythian,
Or he that makes his generation messes
To gorge his appetite, shall to my bosome
Be as well neighbour'd, pittied, and releeu'd,
As thou my sometime Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Good my Liege.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Peace Kent,
Come not betweene the Dragon and his wrath,
I lou'd her most, and thought to set my rest
On her kind nursery. Hence and avoid my sight:
So be my graue my peace, as here I giue
Her Fathers heart from her; call France, who stirres?
Call Burgundy, Cornwall, and Albanie,
With my two Daughters Dowres, digest the third,
Let pride, which she cals plainnesse, marry her:
I doe inuest you ioyntly with my power,
Preheminence, and all the large effects
That troope with Maiesty. Our selfe by Monthly course,
With reseruation of an hundred Knights.
By you to be sustain'd, shall our abode
Make with you by due turne, onely we shall retaine
The name, and all th' addition to a King: the Sway,
Reuennew Execution of the rest,
Beloued Sonnes be yours, which to confirme,
This Coronet part betweene you.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Royall Lear,
Whom I haue euer honor'd as my King.
Lou'd as my Father, as my Master follow'd,
As my great Patron thought on in my praiers.

speeches.speaker: Le.
prose: The bow is bent & drawne, make from the shaft.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Let it fall rather, though the forke inuade
The region of my heart, be Kent vnmannerly,
When Lear is mad, what wouldest thou do old man?
Think'st thou that dutie shall haue dread to speake,
When power to flattery bowes?
To plainnesse honour's bound,
When Maiesty falls to folly, reserue thy state,
And in thy best consideration checke
This hideous rashnesse, answere my life, my iudgement:
Thy yongest Daughter do's not loue thee least,
Nor are those empty hearted, whose low founds
Reuerbe no hollownesse.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Kent, on thy life no more.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: My life I neuer held but as pawne
To wage against thine enemies, nere feare to loose it,
Thy safety being motiue.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Out of my sight.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: See better Lear, and let me still remaine
The true blanke of thine eie.

speeches.speaker: Kear.
prose: Now by Apollo,

speeches.speaker: Lent.
verse: Now by Apollo, King
Thou swear.st thy Gods in vaine.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: O Vassall! Miscreant.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
prose: Cor. Deare Sir forbeare.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Kill thy Physition, and thy see bestow
Vpon the foule disease, reuoke thy guift,
Or whil'st I can vent clamour from my throate,
Ile tell thee thou dost euill.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Heare me recreant, on thine allegeance heare me;
That thou hast sought to make vs breake our vowes,
Which we durst neuer yet; and with strain'd pride,
To come betwixt our sentences, and our power.
Which, nor our nature, nor our place can beare;
Our potencie made good, take thy reward.
Fiue dayes we do allot thee for prouision,
To shield thee from disasters of the world,
And on the sixt to turne thy hated backe
Vpon our kingdome; if on the tenth day following,
Thy banisht trunke be found in our Dominions,
The moment is thy death, away. By Iupiter,
This shall not be reuok'd,

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Fare thee well King, sith thus thou wilt appeare,
Freedome liues hence, and banishment is here;
The Gods to their deere shelter take thee Maid,
That iustly think'st, and hast most rightly said:
And your large speeches, may your deeds approue,
That good effects may spring from words of loue:
Thus Kent, O Princes, bids you all adew,
Hee'l shape his old course, in a Country new.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Heere's France and Burgundy, my Noble Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: My Lord of Bugundie,
We first addresse toward you, who with this King
Hath riuald for our Daughter; what in the least
Will you require in present Dower with her,
Or cease your quest of Loue?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Most Royall Maiesty,
I craue no more then hath your Highnesse offer'd,
Nor will you tender lesse?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Right Noble Burgundy,
When she was deare to vs, we did hold her so,
But now her price is fallen: Sir, there she stands,
If ought within that little seeming substance,
Or all of it with our displeasure piec'd,
And nothing more may fitly like your Grace,
Shee's there, and she is yours.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
prose: I know no answer.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Will you with those infirmities she owes,
Vnfriended, new adopted to our hate,
Dow'rd with our curse, and stranger'd with our oath,
Take her or, leaue her.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Pardon me Royall Sir,
Election makes not vp in such conditions.

speeches.speaker: Le.
verse: Then leaue her sir, for by the powre that made me,
I tell you all her wealth. For you great King,
I would not from your loue make such a stray,
To match you where I hate, therefore beseech you
T' auert your liking a more worthier way,
Then on a wretch whom Nature is asham'd
Almost t' acknowledge hers.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: This is most strange,
That she whom euen but now, was your obiect.
The argument of your praise. balme of your age,
The best, the deerest, should in this trice of time
Commit a thing so monstrous, to dismantle
So many folds of fauour: sure her offence
Must be of such vnnaturall degree,
That monsters it: Or your fore-voucht affection
Fall into taint, which to beleeue of her
Must be a faith that reason without miracle
Should neuer plant in me.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: I yet beseech your Maiesty.
If for I want that glib and oylie Art,
To speake and purpose not, since what I will intend,
Ile do't before I speake, that you make knowne
It is no vicious blot, murther, or foulenesse,
No vnchaste action or dishonoured step
That hath depriu'd me of your Grace and fauour,
But euen for want of that, for which I am richer,
A still soliciting eye, and such a tongue,
That I am glad I haue not, though not to haue it,
Hath loft me in your liking.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Better thou had'st.
Not beene borne, then not t haue pleas'd me better.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Is it but this? A tardinesse in nature,
Which often leaues the history vnspoke
That it intends to do: my Lord of Burgundy,
What say you to the Lady? Loue's not loue
When it is mingled with regards, that stands
Aloofe from th' intire point, will you haue her?
She is herselfe a Dowrie.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Royall King,
Giue but that portion which your selfe propos'd,
And here I take Cordelia by the hand,
Dutchesse of Burgundie.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Nothing, I haue sworne, I am firme.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I am sorry then you haue so lost a Father,
That you must loose a husband.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Peace be with Burgundie,
Since that respect and Fortunes are his loue,
I shall not be his wife.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Fairest Cordelia, that art most rich being poore,
Most choise forsaken, and most lou'd despis'd,
Thee and thy vertues here I seize vpon,
Be it lawfull I take vp what's cast away.
Gods, Gods! 'Tis strange, that from their cold'st neglect
My Loue should kindle to enflam'd respect.
Thy dowrelesse Daughter King, throwne to my chance,
Is Queene of vs, of ours, and our faire France:
Not all the Dukes of watrish Burgundy,
Can buy this vnpriz'd precious Maid of me.
Bid them farewell Cordelia, though vnkinde,
Thou loosest here a better where to finde.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Thou hast her France, let her be thine, for we
Haue no such Daughter, nor shall euer see
That face of hers againe, therfore be gone,
Without our Grace, our Loue, our Benizon:
Come Noble Burgundie.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Bid farwell to your Sisters.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: The Iewels of our Father, with wash'd eies
Cordelia leaues you, I know you what you are,
And like a Sister am most loth to call
Your faults as they are named. Loue well our Father:
To your professed bosomes I commit him,
But yet alas, stood I within his Grace,
I would prefer him to a better place,
So farewell to you both.

speeches.speaker: Regn.
prose: Prescribe not vs our dutie.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Let your study
Be to content your Lord, who hath receiu'd you
At Fortunes almes, you haue obedience scanted,
And well are worth the want that you haue wanted.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Time shall vnfold what plighted cunning hides,
Who couers faults, at last with shame derides:
Well may you prosper.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Come my faire Cordelia.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Sister, it is not little I haue to say,
Of what most neerely appertaines to vs both,
I thinke our Father will hence to night.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: That's most certaine, and with you: next moneth with vs.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: You see how full of changes his age is, the obseruation we haue made of it hath beene little: he alwaies lou'd our Sister most, and with what poore iudgement he hath now cast her off, appeares too grossely.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: 'Tis the infirmity of his age, yet he hath euer but slenderly knowne himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: The best and soundest of his time hath bin but rash, then must we looke from his age, to receiue not alone the imperfections of long ingrafted condition, but therewithall the vnruly way wardnesse, that infirme and cholericke yeares bring with them.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Such vnconstant starts are we like to haue from him, as this of Kents banishment.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: There is further complement of leaue-taking betweene France and him, pray you let vs sit together, it our Father carry authority with such disposition as he beares, this last surrender of his will but offend vs.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: We shall further thinke of it.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: We must do something, and i' th' heate.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: Thou Nature art my Goddesse, to thy Law
My seruices are bound, wherefore should I
Stand in the plague of custome, and permit
The curiosity of Nations, to depriue me?
For that I am some twelue, or fourteene Moonshines
Lag of a Brother? Why Bastard? Wherefore base?
When my Dimensions are as well compact,
My minde as generous, and my shape as true
As honest Madams issue? Why brand they vs
With Base? With basenes Barstadie? Base, Base?
Who in the lustie stealth of Nature, take
More composition, and fierce qualitie,
Then doth within a dull stale tyred bed
Goe to th' creating a whole tribe of Fops
Got 'tweene a sleepe, and wake? Well then,
Legitimate Edgar, I must haue your land,
Our Fathers loue, is to the Bastard Edmond,
As to th' legitimate: fine word: Legitimate.
Well, my Legittimate, if this Letter speed,
And my inuention thriue, Edmond the base
Shall to' th' Legitimate: I grow, I prosper:
Now Gods, stand vp for Bastards.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: Kent banish'd thus? and France in choller parted?
And the King gone to night? Prescrib'd his powre,
Confin'd to exhibition? All this done
Vpon the gad? Edmond, how now? What newes?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: So please your Lordship, none.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Why so earnestly seeke you to put vp yt Letter?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I know no newes, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: What Paper were you reading?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Nothing my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: No? what needed then that terrible dispatch of it into your Pocket? The quality of nothing, hath not such neede to hide it selfe. Let's see: come, if it bee nothing, I shall not neede Spectacles.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I beseech you Sir, pardon mee; it is a Letter from my Brother, that I haue not all ore-read; and for so much as I haue perus'd, I finde it not fit for your ore-looking.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Giue me the Letter, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: I shall offend, either to detaine, or giue it:
The Contents, as in part I vnderstand them.
Are too blame.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Let's see, let's see.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I hope for my Brothers iustification, hee wrote this but as an essay, or taste of my Vertue.

This policie, and reuerence of Age, makes the world bitter to the best of our times: keepes our Fortunes from vs, till our oldnesse cannot rellish them. I begin to finde an idle and fond bondage, in the oppression of aged tyranny, who swayes not as it hath power, but as it is suffer'd. Come to me, that of this I may speake more. If our Father would sleepe till I wak'd him, you should enioy halfe his Reuennew for euer, and liue the beloued of your Brother.


Edgar.
Hum? Conspiracy? Sleepe till I wake him, you should enioy halfe his Reuennew: my Sonne Edgar, had hee a hand to write this? A heart and braine to breede it in? When came you to this? Who brought it?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: It was not brought mee, my Lord; there's the cunning of it. I found it throwne in at the Casement of my Closset.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: You know the character to be your Brothers?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: If the matter were good my Lord, I durst swear it were his: but in respect of that, I would faine thinke it were not.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: It is his.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: It is his hand, my Lord: but I hope his heart is not in the Contents.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Has he neuer before sounded you in this busines?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Neuer my Lord. But I haue heard him oft maintaine it to be fit, that Sonnes at perfect age, and Fathers declin'd, the Father should bee as Ward to the Son, and the Sonne manage his Reuennew.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: O Villain, villain: his very opinion in the Letter. Abhorred Villaine, vnnaturall, detested, brutish Villaine; worse then brutish: Go sirrah, seeke him: Ile apprehend him. Abhominable Villaine, where is he?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I do not well know my L. If it shall please you to suspend your indignation against my Brother, til you can deriue from him better testimony of his intent, you shold run a certaine course: where, if you violently proceed against him, mistaking his purpose, it would make a great gap in your owne Honor, and shake in peeces, the heart of his obedience. I dare pawne downe my life for him, that he hath writ this to feele my affection to your Honor, & to no other pretence of danger.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Thinke you so?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: If your Honor iudge it meere, I will place you where you shall heare vs conferre of this, and by an Auricular assurance haue your satisfaction, and that without any further delay, then this very Euening.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: He cannot bee such a Monster. Edmond seeke him out: winde me into him, I pray you: frame the Businesse after your owne wisedome. I would vnstate my selfe, to be in a due resolution.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I will seeke him Sir, presently: conuey the businesse as I shall find meanes, and acquaint you withall.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose:
These late Eclipses in the Sun and Moone portend no good to vs: though the wisedome of Nature can reason it thus, and thus, yet Nature finds it selfe scourg'd by the sequent effects. Loue cooles, friendship falls off, Brothers diuide. In Cities, mutinies; in Countries, discord; in Pallaces, Treason; and the Bond crack'd, 'twixt Sonne and Father. This villaine of mine comes vnder the prediction; there's Son against Father, the King fals from by as of Nature, there's Father against Childe. We haue seene the best of our time. Machinations, hollownesse, treacherie, and all ruinous disorders follow vs disquietly to our Graues. Find out this Villain.
Edmond, it shall lose thee nothing, do it carefully: and the Noble & true-harted Kent banish'd; his offence, honesty. 'Tis strange.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: This is the excellent foppery of the world, that when we are sicke in fortune, often the surfers of our own behauiour, we make guilty of our disasters, the Sun, the Moone, and Starres, as if we were villaines on necessitie, Fooles by heauenly compulsion, Knaues, Theeues, and Treachers by Sphericall predominance. Drunkards, Lyars, and Adulterers by an inforc'd obedience of Planatary influence; and all that we are euill in, by a diuine thrust^ng on. An admirable euasion of Whore-master-man, to lay his Goatish disposition on the charge of a Starre, My father compounded with my mother vnder the Dragons taile, and my Natiuity was vnder Vrsa Maior, so that it followes, I am rough and Leacherous. I should haue bin that I am, had the maidenlest Starre in the Firmament twinkled on my bastardizing.
Pat: he comes like the Catastrophe of the old Comedie: my Cue is villanous Melancholly, with a sighe like Tom o' Bedlam. — O these Eclipses do portend these diuisions. Fa, Sol, La, Me.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: How now Brother Edmond, what serious contemplation are you in?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I am thinking Brother of a prediction I read this other day, what should follow these Eclipses.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Do you busie your selfe with that?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: I promise you, the effects he writes of, succeede vnhappily.
When saw you my Father last?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: The night gone by.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Spake you with him?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: I, two houres together.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Parted you in good termes? Found you no displeasure in him, by word, nor countenance?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: None at all,

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose:
Bethink your selfe wherein you may haue offended him: and at my entreaty forbeare his presence, vntill some little time hath qualified the heat of his displeasure, which at this instant so rageth in him, that with the mischiefe

of your person, it would scarsely alay.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Some Villaine hath done me wrong.

speeches.speaker: Edm.
prose: That's my feare, I pray you haue a continent forbearance till the speed of his rage goes slower: and as I say, retire with me to my lodging, from whence I will fitly bring you to heare my Lord speake: pray ye goe, there's my key: if you do stirre abroad, goe arm'd.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Arm'd, Brother?

speeches.speaker: Edm.
prose: Brother, I aduise you to the best, I am no honest man, if ther be any good meaning toward you: I haue told you what I haue seene, and heard: But faintly, Nothing like the image, and horror of it, pray you away.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Shall I heare from you anon?

speeches.speaker: Edm.
verse: I do serue you in this businesse:
A Credulous Father, and a Brother Noble,
Whose nature is so farre from doing harmes,
That he suspects none: on whose foolish honestie
My practises ride easie: I see the businesse.
Let me, if not by birth, haue lands by wit,
All with me's meete, that I can fashion fit.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Did my Father strike my Gentleman for chiding of his Foole?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: I Madam.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: By day and night, he wrongs me, euery howre
He flashes into one grosse crime, or other,
That sets vs all at ods: Ile not endure it;
His Knights grow riotous, and himselfe vpbraides vs
On euery trifle. When he returnes from hunting,
I will not speake with him, say I am sicke,
If you come slacke of former seruices,
You shall do well, the fault of it Ile answer.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: He's comming Madam, I heare him.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Put on what weary negligence you please,
You and your Fellowes: I'de haue it come to question;
If he distaste it, let him to my Sister,
Whose mind and mine I know in that are one,
Remember what I haue said.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Well Madam.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: And let his Knights haue colder lookes among you: what growes of it no matter, aduise your fellowes so, Ile write straight to my Sister to hold my course; prepare for dinner.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: If but as will I other accents borrow,
That can my speech defuse, my good intent
May carry through it selfe to that full issue
For which I raiz'd my likenesse. Now banisht Kent,
If thou canst serue where thou dost stand condemn'd,
So may it come, thy Master whom thou Iou'st,
Shall find thee full of labours.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Let me not stay a iot for dinner, go get it ready: how now, what art thou?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: A man Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What dost thou professe? What would'st thou with vs?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I do professe to be no lesse then I seeme; to serue him truely that will put me in trust, to loue him that is honest, to conuerse with him that is wise and saies little, to feare iudgement, to fight when I cannot choose, and to eate no fish.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What art thou?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: A very honest hearted Fellow, and as poore as the King.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: If thou be'st as poore for a subiect, as hee's for a King, thou art poore enough. What wouldst thou?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Seruice.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Who wouldst thou serue?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: You.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Do'st thou know me fellow?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: No Sir, but you haue that in your countenance, which I would faine call Master.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Authority.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What seruices canst thou do?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I can keepe honest counsaile, ride, run, marre a curious tale in telling it, and deliuer a plaine message bluntly: that which ordinary men are fit for, I am quallified in, and the best of me, is Dilligence.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: How old art thou?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Not so young Sir to loue a woman for singing, nor so old to dote on her for any thing. I haue yeares on my backe forty eight.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Follow me, thou shalt serue me, if I like thee no worse after dinner, I will not part from thee yet. Dinner ho, dinner, where's my knaue? my Foole? Go you and call my Foole hither. You you Sirrah, where's my Daughter?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: So please you —

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What saies the Fellow there? Call the Clot-pole backe: wher's my Foole? Ho, I thinke the world's asleepe, how now? Where's that Mungrell?

speeches.speaker: Knigh.
prose: He saies my Lord, your Daughters is not well.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Why came not the slaue backe to me when I call'd him?

speeches.speaker: Knigh.
prose: Sir, he answered me in the roundest manner, he would not.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: He would not?

speeches.speaker: Knight.
prose: My Lord, I know not what the matter is, but to my iudgement your Highnesse is not entertain'd with that Ceremonious affection as you were wont, theres a great abatement of kindnesse appeares as well in the generall dependants, as in the Duke himselfe also, and your Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Ha? Saist thou so?

speeches.speaker: Knigh.
prose: I beseech you pardon me my Lord, if I bee mistaken, for my duty cannot be silent, when I thinke your Highnesse wrong'd.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Thou but remembrest me of mine owne Conception, I haue perceiued a most faint neglect of late, which I haue rather blamed as mine owne iealous curiositie, then as a very pretence and purpose of vnkindnesse; I will looke further intoo't^: but where's my Foole? I haue not seene him this two daies.

speeches.speaker: Knight.
verse: Since my young Ladies going into France
Sir, the Foole hath much pined away.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: No more of that, I haue noted it well, goe you and tell my Daughter, I would speake with her. Goe you call hither my Foole; Oh you Sir, you, come you hither Sir, who am I Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: My Ladies Father.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: My Ladies Father? my Lords knaue, you whorson dog, you slaue, you curre.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: I am none of these my Lord,
I beseech your pardon.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Do you bandy lookes with me, you Rascall?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Ile not be strucken my Lord.
