speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Nor tript neither, you base Foot-ball plaier.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: I thanke thee fellow.
Thou seru'st me, and Ile loue thee.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Come sir, arise, away, Ile teach you differences: away, away, if you will measure your lubbers length againe, tarry, but away, goe too, haue you wisedome, so.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Now my friendly knaue I thanke thee, there's earnest of thy seruice.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Let me hire him too, here's my Coxcombe.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: How now my pretty knaue, how dost thou?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Sirrah, you were best take my Coxcombe.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Why my Boy?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Why? for taking ones part that's out of fauour, nay, & thou canst not smile as the wind sits, thou'lt catch colde shortly, there take my Coxcombes why this fellow ha's banish'd two on's Daughters, and did the third a blessing against his will, if thou follow him, thou must needs weare my Coxcombe. How now Nunckle? would I had two Coxcombes and two Daughters.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Why my Boy?

speeches.speaker: Fool.
prose: If I gaue them all my liuing, I'ld keepe my Coxcombes my selfe, there's mine, beg another of thy Daughters.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Take heed Sirrah, the whip.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Truth's a dog must to kennell, hee must bee whipt out, when the Lady Brach may stand by' th' fire and stinke.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: A pestilent gall to me.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Sirha, Ile teach thee a speech.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Do.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Marke it Nuncle;
Haue more then thou showest,
Speake lesse then thou knowest,
Lend lesse then thou owest,
Ride more then thou goest,
Learne more then thou trowest,
Set lesse then thou throwest;
Leaue thy drinke and thy whore,
And keepe in a dore,
And thou shalt haue more,
Then two tens to a score.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: This is nothing Foole.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Then 'tis like the breath of an vnfeed Lawyer, you gaue me nothing for't, can you make no vse of nothing Nuncle?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Why no Boy,
Nothing can be made out of nothing.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Prythee tell him, so much the rent of his land comes to, he will not beleeue a Foole.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: A bitter Foole.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Do'st thou know the difference my Boy, betweene a bitter Foole, and a sweet one.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: No Lad, teach me.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Nunckle, giue me an egge, and Ile giue thee two Crownes.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What two Crownes shall they be?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Fooles had nere lesse grace in a yeere,
For wisemen are growne foppish,
And know not how their wits to weare,
Their manners are so apish.
prose: Why after I haue cut the egge i' th' middle and eate vp the meate, the two Crownes of the egge: when thou clouest thy Crownes i' th' middle, and gau'st away both parts, thou boar'st thine Asse on thy backe o're the durt, thou had'st little wit in thy bald crowne, when thou gau'st thy golden one away; if I speake like my selfe in this, let him be whipt that first findes it so.

speeches.speaker: Le.
prose: When were you wont to be so full of Songs sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: For sodaine ioy did weepe,
And I for sorrow sung,
That such a King should play bo-peepe,
And goe the Foole among.
Pry' thy Nunckle keepe a Schoolemaster that can teach
thy Foole to lie, I would faine learne to lie.
prose: I haue vsed it Nunckle, ere since thou mad'st thy Daughters thy Mothers, for when thou gau'st them the rod, and put'st downe thine owne breeches, then they

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: And you lie sirrah, wee'l haue you whipt.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: I maruell what kin thou and thy daughters are, they'l haue me whipt for speaking true: thou'lt haue me whipt for lying; and sometimes I am whipt for holding my peace. I had rather be any kind o' thing then a foole, and yet I would not be thee Nunckle, thou hast pared thy wit o' both sides, and left nothing i' th' middle; heere comes one o' the parings.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: How now Daughter? what makes that Frontlet on? You are too much of late i' th' frowne.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Mum, mum, he that keepes nor crust, not crum,
Weary of all, shall want some. That's a sheal'd Pescod.
prose: Thou wast a pretty fellow when thou hadst no need to care for her frowning, now thou art an O without a figure, I am better then thou art now, I am a Foole, thou art nothing. Yes forsooth I will hold my tongue, so your face bids me, though you say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Not only Sir this, your all-lycenc'd Foole,
But other of your insolent retinue
Do hourely Carpe and Quarrell, breaking forth
In ranke, and (not to be endur'd) riots Sir.
I had thought by making this well knowne vnto you,
To haue found a safe redresse, but now grow fearefull
By what your selfe too late haue spoke and done,
That you protect this course, and put it on
By your allowance, which if you should, the fault
Would not scape censure, nor the redresses sleepe,
Which in the tender of a wholesome weale,
Might in their working do you that offence,
Which else were shame, that then necessitie
Will call discreet proceeding.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: For you know Nunckle, the Hedge-Sparrow fed the Cuckoo so long, that it's had it head bit off by it young, so out went the Candle, and we were left darkling.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Are you our Daughter?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: I would you would make vse of your good wisedome
(Whereof I know you are fraught) and put away
These dispositions, which of late transport you
From what you rightly are.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: May not an Asse know, when the Cart drawes the Horse?
Whoop Iugge I loue thee.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Do's any heere know me?
This is not Lear:
Do's Lear walke thus? Speake thus? Where are his eies?
Either his Notion weakens, his Discernings
Are Lethargied. Ha! Waking? 'Tis not so?
Who is it that can tell me who I am?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Lears shadow.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Your name, faire Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: This admiration Sir, is much o' th' sauour
Of other your new prankes. I do beseech you
To vnderstand my purposes aright:
As you are Old, and Reuerend, should be Wise.
Heere do you keepe a hundred Knights and Squires,
Men so disorder'd, so debosh'd, and bold,
That this our Court infected with their manners,
Shewes like a riotous Inne; Epicurisme and Lust
Makes it more like a Tauerne, or a Brothell,
Then a grac'd Pallace. The shame it selfe doth speake
For instant remedy. Be then desir'd
By her, that else will take the thing she begges,
A little to disquantity your Traine,
And the remainders that shall still depend,
To be such men as may besort your Age,
Which know themselues, and you.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Darknesse, and Diuels.
Saddle my horses: call my Traine together.
Degenerate Bastard, Ile not trouble thee;
Yet haue I left a daughter.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: You strike my people, and your disorder'd rable, make Seruants of their Betters.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Woe, that too late repents:
Is it your will, speake Sir? Prepare my Horses.
Ingratitude! thou Marble-hearted Fiend,
More hideous when thou shew'st thee in a Child,
Then the Sea-monster.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
prose: Pray Sir be patient.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Detested Kite, thou lyest.
My Traine are men of choice, and rarest parts,
That all particulars of dutie know,
And in the most exact regard, support
The worships of their name. O most small fault,
How vgly did'st thou in Cordelia shew?
Which like an Engine, wrencht my frame of Nature
From the fixt place: drew from my heart all loue,
And added to the gall. O Lear, Lear, Lear!
Beate at this gate that let thy Folly in,
And thy deere Iudgement out. Go, go, my people.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: My Lord, I am guiltlesse, as I am ignorant
Of what hath moued you.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: It may be so, my Lord.
Heare Nature, heare deere Goddesse, heare:
Suspend thy purpose, if thou did'st intend
To make this Creature fruitfull:
Into her Wombe conuey stirrility,
Drie vp in her the Organs of increase,
And from her derogate body, neuer spring
A Babe to honor her. If she must teeme,
Create her childe of Spleene, that it may liue
And be a thwart disnatur'd torment to her.
Let it stampe wrinkles in her brow of youth,
With cadent Teares fret Channels in her cheekes,
Turne all her Mothers paines, and benefits
To laughter, and contempt: That she may feele,
How sharper then a Serpents tooth it is,
To haue a thanklesse Childe. Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Now Gods that we adore,
Whereof comes this?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Neuer afflict your selfe to know more of it:
But let his disposition haue that scope
As dotage giues it.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: What fiftie of my Followers at a clap?
Within a fortnight?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
prose: What's the matter, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Ile tell thee:
Life and death, I am asham'd
That thou hast power to shake my manhood thus,
That these hot teares, which breake from me perforce
Should make thee worth them.
Blastes and Fogges vpon thee:
Th' vntented woundings of a Fathers curse
Pierce euerie sense about thee. Old fond eyes,
Beweepe this cause againe, Ile plucke ye out,
And cast you with the waters that you loose
To temper Clay. Ha? Let it be so.
I haue another daughter,
Who I am sure is kinde and comfortable:
When she shall heare this of thee, with her nailes
Shee'l flea thy Woluish visage. Thou shalt finde,
That Ile resume the shape which thou dost thinke
I haue cast off for euer.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Do you marke that?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: I cannot be so partiall Gonerill,
To the great loue I beare you.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Pray you content. What Oswald, hoa?
You Sir, more Knaue then Foole, after your Master.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Nunkle Lear, Nunkle Lear,
Tarry, take the Foole with thee:
A Fox, when one has caught her.
And such a Daughter,
Should sure to the Slaughter,
If my Cap would buy a Halter,
So the Foole followes after.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: This man hath had good Counsell,
A hundred Knights?
'Tis politike, and safe to let him keepe
At point a hundred Knights: yes, that on euerie dreame,
Each buz, each fancie, each complaint, dislike,
He may enguard his dotage with their powres,
And hold our liues in mercy. Oswald, I say.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
prose: Well, you may feare too farre.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Safer then trust too farre;
Let me still take away the harmes I feare,
Not feare still to be taken. I know his heart,
What he hath vtter'd I haue writ my Sister:
If she sustaine him, and his hundred Knights
When I haue shew'd th' vnfitnesse.
How now Oswald?
What haue you writ that Letter to my Sister?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: I Madam.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Take you some company, and away to horse,
Informe her full of my particular feare,
And thereto adde such reasons of your owne,
As may compact it more. Get you gone,
And hasten your returne; no, no, my Lord,
This milky gentlenesse, and course of yours
Though I condemne not, yet vnder pardon
Your are much more at task for want of wisedome,
Then prai'sd for harmefull mildnesse.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: How farre your eies may pierce I cannot tell;
Striuing to better, oft we marre what's well.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Nay then —

speeches.speaker: Alb.
prose: Well, well, the'uent.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Go you before to Gloster with these Letters; acquaint my Daughter no further with any thing you know, then comes from her demand out of the Letter, if your Dilligence be not speedy, I shall be there afore you.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I will not sleepe my Lord, till I haue deliuered your Letter.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: If a mans braines were in's heeles, wert not in danger of kybes?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: I Boy.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Then I prythee be merry, thy wit shall not go slip-shod.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
prose: Shalt see thy other Daughter will vse thee kindly, for though she's as like this, as a Crabbe's like an Apple, yet I can tell what I can tell.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What can'st tell Boy?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: She will taste as like this as, a Crabbe do's to a Crab: thou canst tell why ones nose stands i' th' middle on's face?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Why to keepe ones eyes of either side's nose, that what a man cannot smell out, he may spy into.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: I did her wrong.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Can'st tell how an Oyster makes his shell?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Nor I neither; but I can tell why a Snaile ha's a house.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Why to put's head in, not to giue it away to his daughters, and leaue his hornes without a case.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: I will forget my Nature, so kind a Father? Be my Horsses ready?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Thy Asses are gone about 'em; the reason why the seuen Starres are no mo then seuen, is a pretty reason.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Because they are not eight.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Yes indeed, thou would'st make a good Foole.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: To tak't againe perforce; Monster Ingratitude!

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: If thou wert my Foole Nunckle, Il'd haue thee beaten for being old before thy time.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Thou shouldst not haue bin old, till thou hadst bin wise.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: O let me not be mad, not mad sweet Heauen. keepe me in temper, I would not be mad. How now are the Horses ready?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: Ready my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Come Boy.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: She that's a Maid now, & laughs at my departure,
Shall not be a Maid long, vnlesse things be cut shorter.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Saue thee Curan.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: And your Sir, I haue bin
With your Father, and giuen him notice
That the Duke of Cornwall, and Regan his Duchesse
Will be here with him this night.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: How comes that?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Nay I know not, you haue heard of the newes abroad, I meane the whisper'd ones, for they are yet but ear^-kissing arguments.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Not I: pray you what are they?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Haue you heard of no likely Warres toward,
'Twixt the Dukes of Cornwall, and Albany?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Not a word.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: You may do then in time,
Fare you well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: The Duke be here to night? The better best,
This weaues it selfe perforce into my businesse,
My Father hath set guard to take my Brother,
And I haue one thing of a queazie question
Which I must act, Briefenesse, and Fortune worke.
Brother, a word, discend; Brother I say,
My Father watches: O Sir, fly this place,
Intelligence is giuen where you are hid;
You haue now the good aduantage of the night,
Haue you not spoken 'gainst the Duke of Cornewall?
Hee's comming hither, now i' th' night, i' th' haste,
And Regan with him, haue you nothing said
Vpon his partie 'gainst the Duke of Albany?
Aduise your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: I am sure on't, not a word.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: I heare my Father comming, pardon me:
In cunning, I must draw my Sword vpon you:
Draw, seeme to defend your selfe,
Now quit you well.
Yeeld, come before my Father, light hoa, here,
Fly Brother, Torches, Torches, so farewell.
Some blood drawne on me, would beget opinion
Of my more fierce endeauour. I haue seene drunkards
Do more then this in sport. Father, Father,
Stop, stop, no helpe?

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Now Edmund, where's the villaine?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: Here stood he in the dark, his sharpe Sword out,
Mumbling of wicked charmes, coniuring the Moone
To stand auspicious Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: But where is he?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Looke Sir, I bleed.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Where is the villaine, Edmund?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Fled this way Sir, when by no meanes he could.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Pursue him, ho: go after. By no meanes, what?

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: Perswade me to the murther of your Lordship,
But that I told him the reuenging Gods,
'Gainst Paricides did all the thunder bend,
Spoke with how manifold, and strong a Bond
The Child was bound to' th' Father; Sir in fine,
Seeing how lothly opposite I stood
To his vnnaturall purpose, in fell motion
With his prepared Sword, he charges home
My vnprouided body, latch'd mine arme;
And when he saw my best alarum'd spirits
Bold in the quarrels right, rouz'd to th' encounter,
Or whether gasted by the noyse I made,
Full sodainely he fled.

speeches.speaker: Glost.
verse: Let him fly farre:
Not in this Land shall he remaine vncaught
And found; dispatch, the Noble Duke my Master,
My worthy Arch and Patron comes to night,
By his authoritie I will proclaime it,
That he which finds him shall deserue our thankes,
Bringing the murderous Coward to the stake:
He that conceales him death.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: When I disswaded him from his intent,
And found him pight to doe it, with curst speech
I threaten'd to discouer him; he replied,
Thou vnpossessing Bastard, dost thou thinke,
If I would stand against thee, would the reposall
Of any trust, vertue, or worth in thee
Make thy words faith'd? No, what should I denie,
(As this I would, though thou didst produce
My very Character) I'ld turne it all
To thy suggestion, plot, and damned practise:
And thou must make a dullard of the world,
If they not thought the profits of my death
Were very pregnant and potentiall spirits
To make thee seeke it.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: O strange and fastned Villaine,
Would he deny his Letter, said he?
Harke, the Dukes Trumpets, I know not wher he comes;
All Ports Ile barre, the villaine shall not scape,
The Duke must grant me that: besides, his picture
I will send farre and neere, that all the kingdome
May haue due note of him, and of my land,
(Loyall and naturall Boy) Ile worke the meanes
To make thee capable.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: How now my Noble friend, since I came hither
(Which I can call but now,) I haue heard strangenesse.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: If it be true; all vengeance comes too short
Which can pursue th' offender; how dost my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: O Madam, my old heart is crack'd, it's crack'd.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: What, did my Fathers Godsonne seeke your life?
He whom my Father nam'd, your Edgar?

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: O Lady, Lady, shame would haue it hid.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Was he not companion with the riotous Knights
That tended vpon my Father?

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: I know not Madam, 'tis too bad, too bad.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Yes Madam, he was of that consort.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: No maruaile then, though he were ill affected,
'Tis they haue put him on the old mans death,
To haue th' expence and wast of his Reuenues:
I haue this present euening from my Sister
Beene well inform'd of them, and with such cautions,
That if they come to soiourne at my house,
Ile not be there.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Nor I, assure thee Regan;
Edmund, I heare that you haue shewne your Father
A Child-like Office.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: It was my duty Sir.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: He did bewray his practise, and receiu'd
This hurt you see, striuing to apprehend him.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Is he pursued?

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: I my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: If he be taken, he shall neuer more
Be fear'd of doing harme, make your owne purpose,
How in my strength you please: for you Edmund,
Whose vertue and obedience doth this instant
So much commend it selfe, you shall be ours,
Nature's of such deepe trust, we shall much need:
You we first seize on.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: I shall serue you Sir truely, how euer else.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: For him I thanke your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: You know not why we came to visit you?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Thus out of season, thredding darke ey'd night,
Occasions Noble Gloster of some prize,
Wherein we must haue vse of your aduise.
Our Father he hath writ, so hath our Sister,
Of differences, which I best though it fit
To answere from our home: the seuerall Messengers
From hence attend dispatch, our good old Friend,
Lay comforts to your bosome, and bestow
Your needfull counsaile to our businesses,
Which craues the instant vse.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: I serue you Madam,
Your Graces are right welcome.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Good dawning to thee Friend, art of this house?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Where may we set our horses?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I' th' myre.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Prythee, if thou lou'st me, tell me.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I loue thee not.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Why then I care not for thee.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: If I had thee in Lipsbury Pinfold, I would make thee care for me.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Why do'st thou vse me thus? I know thee not.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Fellow I know thee.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: What do'st thou know me for?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: A Knaue, a Rascall, an eater of broken meates, a base, proud, shallow, beggerly, three-suited-hundred pound, filthy woosted-stocking knaue, a Lilly-liuered, action-taking, whoreson glasse-gazing super-seruiceable finicall Rogue, one Trunke-inheriting slaue, one that would'st be a Baud in way of good seruice, and art nothing but the composition of a Knaue, Begger, Coward, Pandar, and the Sonne and Heire of a Mungrill Bitch, one whom I will beate into clamours whining, if thou deny'st the least sillable of thy addition.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Why, what a monstrous Fellow art thou, thus to raile on one, that is neither knowne of thee, nor knowes thee?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose:
What a brazen-fac'd Varlet art thou, to deny thou knowest me? Is it two dayes since I tript vp thy heeles, and beate thee before the King? Draw you rogue,

for though it be night, yet the Moone shines, Ile make a sop oth' Moonshine of you, you whoreson Cullyenly Barber-monger, draw.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Away, I haue nothing to do with thee.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Draw you Rascall, you come with Letters against the King, and take Vanitie the puppets part, against the Royaltie of her Father: draw you Rogue, or Ile so carbonado your shanks, draw you Rascall, come your waies.

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: Helpe, ho, murther, helpe.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Strike you slaue: stand rogue, stand you neat slaue, strike.

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: Helpe hoa, murther, murther.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: How now, what's the matter? Part.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: With you goodman Boy, if you please, come,
Ile flesh ye, come on yong Master.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Weapons? Armes? what's the matter here?

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Keepe peace vpon your liues, he dies that strikes againe, what is the matter?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: The Messengers from our Sister, and the King?

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: What is your difference, speake?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
prose: I am scarce in breath my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: No Maruell, you haue so bestir'd your valour, you cowardly Rascall, nature disclaimes in thee: a Taylor made thee.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Thou art a strange fellow, a Taylor make a man?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: A Taylor Sir, a Stone-cutter, or a Painter, could not haue made him so ill, though they had bin but two yeares oth' trade.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Speake yet, how grew your quarrell?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
prose: This ancient Ruffian Sir, whose life I haue spar'd at sute of his gray-beard.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Thou whoreson Zed, thou vnnecessary letter: my Lord, if you will giue me leaue, I will tread this vnboulted villaine into morter, and daube the wall of a Iakes with him. Spare my gray-beard, you wagtaile?

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Peace sirrah,
You beastly knaue, know you no reuerence?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Yes Sir, but anger hath a priuiledge.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Why art thou angrie?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: That such a slaue as this should weare a Sword,
Who weares no honesty: such smiling rogues as these,
Like Rats oft bite the holy cords a twaine,
Which are t' intrince, t' vnloose: smooth euery passion
That in the natures of their Lords rebell,
Being oile to fire, snow to the colder moodes,
Reuenge, affirme, and turne their Halcion beakes
With euery gall, and varry of their Masters,
Knowing naught (like dogges) but following:
A plague vpon your Epilepticke visage,
Smoile you my speeches, as I were a Foole?
Goose, if I had you vpon Sarum Plaine,
I'ld driue ye cackling home to Camelot.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: What art thou mad old Fellow?

speeches.speaker: Glost.
prose: How fell you out, say that?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: No contraries hold more antipathy,
Then I, and such a knaue.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: Why do'st thou call him Knaue?
What is his fault?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: His countenance likes me not.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: No more perchance do's mine, not his, nor hers.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Sir, 'tis my occupation to be plaine,
I haue seene better faces in my time,
Then stands on any shoulder that I see
Before me, at this instant.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: This is some Fellow,
Who hauing beene prais'd for bluntnesse, doth affect
A saucy roughnes, and constraines the garb
Quite from his Nature. He cannot flatter he,
An honest mind and plaine, he must speake truth,
And they will take it so, if not, hee's plaine.
These kind of Knaues I know, which in this plainnesse
Harbour more craft, and more corrupter ends,
Then twenty silly-ducking obseruants,
That stretch their duties nicely.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Sir, in good faith, in sincere verity,
Vnder th' allowance of your great aspect,
Whose influence like the wreath of radient fire
On flicking Phoebus front.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: What mean'st by this?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: To go out of my dialect, which you discommend so much; I know Sir, I am no flatterer, he that beguild you in a plaine accent, was a plaine Knaue, which for my part I will not be, though I should win your displeasure to entreat me too't.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: What was th' offence you gaue him?

speeches.speaker: Ste.
verse: I neuer gaue him any:
It pleas'd the King his Master very late
To strike at me vpon his misconstruction,
When he compact, and flattering his displeasure
Tript me behind: being downe, insulted, rail'd,
And put vpon him such a deale of Man,
That worthied him, got praises of the King,
For him attempting, who was selfe-subdued,
And in the fleshment of this dead exploit,
Drew on me here againe.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: None of these Rogues, and Cowards
But Aiax is there Foole.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: Fetch forth the Stocks?
You stubborne ancient Knaue, you reuerent Bragart,
Wee'l teach you.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Sir, I am too old to learne:
Call not your Stocks for me, I serue the King.
On whose imployment I was sent to you,
You shall doe small respects, show too bold malice
Against the Grace, and Person of my Master,
Stocking his Messenger.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: Fetch forth the Stocks;
As I haue life and Honour, there shall he sit till Noone.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Till noone? till night my Lord, and all night too.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Why Madam, if I were your Fathers dog,
You should not vse me so.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Sir, being his Knaue, I will.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: This is a Fellow of the selfe same colour,
Our Sister speakes of. Come, bring away the Stocks.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: Let me beseech your Grace, not to do so,
The King his Master, needs must take it ill
That he so slightly valued in his Messenger,
Should haue him thus restrained.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
prose: Ile answere that.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: My Sister may recieue it much more worsse,
To haue her Gentleman abus'd, assaulted.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Come my Lord, away.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: I am sorry for thee friend, 'tis the Duke pleasure,
Whose disposition all the world well knowes
Will not be rub'd nor stopt, Ile entreat for thee.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Pray do not Sir, I haue watch'd and trauail'd hard,
Some time I shall sleepe out, the rest Ile whistle:
A good mans fortune may grow out at heeles:
Giue you good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: The Duke's too blame in this,
'Twill be ill taken.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Good King, that must approue the common saw,
Thou out of Heauens benediction com'st
To the warme Sun.
Approach thou Beacon to this vnder Globe,
That by thy comfortable Beames I may
Peruse this Letter. Nothing almost sees miracles
But miserie. I know 'tis from Cordelia,
Who hath most fortunately beene inform'd
Of my obscured course. And shall finde time
From this enormous State, seeking to giue
Losses their remedies. All weary and o're-watch'd,
Take vantage heauie eyes, not to behold
This shamefull lodging. Fortune goodnight,
Smile once more, turne thy wheele.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: I heard my selfe proclaim'd,
And by the happy hollow of a Tree,
Escap'd the hunt. No Port is free, no place
That guard, and most vnusall vigilance
Do's not attend my taking. Whiles I may scape
I will preserue myselfe: and am bethought
To take the basest, and most poorest shape
That euer penury in contempt of man,
Brought neere to beast; my face Ile grime with filth,
Blanket my loines, else all my haires in knots,
And with presented nakednesse out-face
The Windes, and persecutions of the skie;
The Country giues me proofe, and president
Of Bedlam beggers, who with roaring voices,
Strike in their num'd and mortified Armes,
Pins, Wodden-prickes, Nayles, Sprigs of Rosemarie:
And with this horrible obiect, from low Farmes,
Poore pelting Villages, Sheeps-Coates, and Milles,
Sometimes with Lunaticke bans, sometime with Praiers
Inforce their charitie: poore Turlygod, poore Tom,
That's something yet: Edgar I nothing am.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: 'Tis strange that they should so depart from home,
And not send backe my Messengers.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: As I learn'd,
The night before, there was no purpose in them
Of this remoue.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Haile to thee Noble Master.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Ha? Mak'st thou this shame ahy pastime?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: No my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Hah, ha, he weares Cruell Garters Horses are tide by the heads, Dogges and Beares by' th' necke, Monkies by' th' loynes, and Men by' th' legs: when a man ouerlustie at legs, then he weares wodden nether-stocks.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: What's he.
That hath so much thy place mistooke
To set thee heere?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: It is both he and she,
Your Son, and Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: No I say.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I say yea.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: By Iupiter I sweare no.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: By Iuno, I sweare I.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: They durst not do't:
They could not, would not do't: 'tis worse then murther,
To do vpon respect such violent outrage:
Resolue me with all modest haste, which way
Thou might'st deserue, or they impose this vsage,
Comming from vs.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: My Lord, when at their home
I did commend your Highnesse Letters to them,
Ere I was risen from the place, that shewed
My dutie kneeling, came there a reeking Poste,
Stew'd in his haste, halfe breathlesse, painting forth
From Gonerill his Mistris, salutations;
Deliuer'd Letters spight of intermission,
Which presently they read; on those contents
They summon'd vp their meiney, straight tooke Horse,
Commanded me to follow, and attend
The leisure of their answer, gaue me cold lookes,
And meeting heere the other Messenger,
Whose welcome I perceiu'd had poison'd mine,
Being the very fellow which of late
Displaid so sawcily against your Highnesse,
Hauing more man then wit about me, drew;
He rais'd the house, with loud and coward cries,
Your Sonne and Daughter found this trespasse worth
The shame which heere it suffers.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Winters not gon yet, if the wil'd Geese fly that way,
Fathers that weare rags, do make their Children blind,
But Fathers that beare bags, shall see their children kind.
Fortune that arrant whore, nere turns the key to th' poore.
But for all this thou shalt haue as many Dolors for thy
Daughters, as thou canst tell in a yeare.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Oh how this Mother swels vp toward my heart!
Historica passio, downe thou climing sorrow,
Thy Elements below where is this Daughter?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Wirh the Earle Sir, here within.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Follow me not, stay here.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Made you no more offence,
But what you speake of?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: None:
How chance the the King comes with so small a number?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: And thou hadst beene set i' th' Stockes for that question, thoud'st well deseru'd it.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Why Foole?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Wee'l set thee to schoole to an Ant, to teach thee ther's no labouring i' th' winter. All that follow their noses, are led by their eyes, but blinde men, and there's not a nose among twenty, but can smell him that's stinking; let go thy hold, when a great wheele runs downe a hill, least it breake thy necke with following. But the great one that goes vpward, let him draw thee after: when a wiseman giues thee better counsell giue me mine againe, I would hause none but knaues follow it, since a Foole giues it.
That Sir, which serues and seekes for gaine,
And followes but for forme;
Will packe, when it begins to raine,
And leaue thee in the storme,
But I will tarry, the Foole will stay,
And let the wiseman flie:
The knaue turnes Foole that runnes away,
The Foole no knaue perdie.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Where learn'd you this Foole?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Not i' th' Stocks Foole.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Deny to speake with me?
They are sicke, they are weary,
They haue trauail'd all the night? meere fetches,
The images of reuolt and flying off.
Fetch me a better answer.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: My deere Lord,
You know the fiery quality of the Duke,
How vnremoueable and fixt he is
In his owne course.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Vengeance, Plague, Death, Confusion:
Fiery? What quality? Why Gloster. Gloster,
I'ld speake with the Duke of Cornewall, and his wife.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Well my good Lord, I haue inform'd them so.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Inform'd them? Do'st thou vnderstand me man.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: I my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: The King would speake with Cornwall,
The deere Father
Would with his Daughter speake, commands, tends, seruice,
Are they inform'd of this? My breath and blood:
Fiery? The fiery Duke, tell the hot Duke that —
No, but not yet, may be he is not well,
Infirmity doth still neglect all office,
Whereto our health is bound, we are not our selues,
When Nature being opprest, commands the mind
To suffer with the body; Ile forbeare,
And am fallen out with my more headier will,
To take the indispos'd and sickly fit,
For the sound man. Death on my state: wherefore
Should he sit heere? This act perswades me,
That this emotion of the Duke and her
Is practise only. Giue me my Seruant forth;
Goe tell the Duke, and's wife, Il'd speake with them:
Now, presently: bid them come forth and heare me,
Or at their Chamber doore Ile beate the Drum,
Till it crie sleepe to death.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: I would haue all well betwixt you.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Oh me my heart! My rising heart! But downe.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Cry to it Nunckle, as the Cockney did to the Ecles, when she put 'em i' th' Paste aliue, she knapt 'em o' th' coxcombs with a sticke, and cryed downe wantons, downe; 'twas her Brother, that in pure kindnesse to his Horse buttered his Hay.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Good morrow to you both.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Haile to your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Reg
prose: I am glad to see your Highnesse.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Regan, I thinke your are. I know what reason
I haue to thinke so, if thou should'st not be glad,
I would diuorce me from thy Mother Tombe,
Sepulchring an Adultresse. O are you free?
Some other time for that. Beloued Regan,
Thy Sisters naught: oh Regan, she hath tied
Sharpe-tooth'd vnkindnesse, like a vulture heere,
I can scarce speake to thee, thou'lt not beleeue
With how deprau'd a quality. Oh Regan.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: I pray you Sir, take patience, I haue hope
You lesse know how to value her desert,
Then she to scant her dutie.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Say? How is that?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: I cannot thinke my Sister in the least
Would faile her Obligation. If Sir perchance
She haue restrained the Riots of your Followres,
'Tis on such ground, and to such wholesome end,
As cleeres her from all blame.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: My curses on her.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: O Sir, you are old,
Nature in you stands on the very Verge
Of his confine: you should be rul'd, and led
By some discretion, that discernes your state
Better then you your selfe: therefore I pray you,
That to our Sister, you do make returne,
Say you haue wrong'd her.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Aske her forgiuenesse?
Do you but marke how this becomes the house?
Deere daughter, I confesse that I am old;
Age is vnnecessary: on my knees I begge,
That you'l vouchsafe me Rayment, Bed, and Food.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Good Sir, no more: these are vnsightly trickes:
Returne you to my Sister.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Neuer Regan:
She hath abated me of halfe my Traine;
Look'd blacke vpon me, strooke me with her Tongue
Most Serpent-like, vpon the very Heart.
All the stor'd Vengeances of Heauen, fall
On her ingratefull top: strike her yong bones
You taking Ayres, with Lamenesse.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Fye sir. fie.

speeches.speaker: Le.
verse: You nimble Lightnings, dart your blinding flames
Into her scornfull eyes: Infect her Beauty,
You Fen-suck'd Fogges, drawne by the powrfull Sunne,
To fall, and blister.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: O the blest Gods!
So will you wish on me, when the rash moode is on.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: No Regan, thou shalt neuer haue my curse:
Thy tender-hefted Nature shall not giue
Thee o're to harshnesse: Her eyes are fierce, but thine
Do comfort, and not burne. 'Tis not in thee
To grudge my pleasures, to cut off my Traine,
To bandy hasty words, to scant my sizes,
And in conclusion, to oppose the bolt
Against my comming in. Thou better know'st
The Offices of Nature, bond of Childhood,
Effects of Curtesie, dues of Gratitude:
Thy halfe o' th' Kingdome hast thou not forgot,
Wherein I thee endow'd.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Good Sir, to' th' purpose.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Who put my^ an i' th' Stockes?

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: What Trumpet's that?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: I know't, my Sisters: this approues her Letter,
That she would soone be heere. Is your Lady come?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: This is a Slaue, whose easie borrowed pride
Dwels in the fickly grace of her he followes.
Out Varlet, from my sight.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: What meanes your Grace?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Who stockt my Seruant? Regan, I haue good hope
Thou did'st not know on't.
Who comes here? O Heauens!
If you do loue old men; if your sweet sway
Allow Obedience; if you your selues are old,
Make it your cause: Send downe, and take my part.
Art not asham'd to looke vpon this Beard?
O Regan, will you take her by the hand?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Why not by' th' hand Sir? How haue I offended?
All's not offence that indiscretion findes,
And dotage termes so.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: O sides, you are too tough!
Will you yet hold?
How came my man i' th' Stockes?

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: I set him there, Sir: but his owne Disorders
Deseru'd much lesse aduancement.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: You? Did you?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: I pray you Father being weake, seeme so.
If till the expiration of your Moneth
You will returne and soiourne with my Sister,
Dismissing halfe your traine, come then to me,
I am now from home, and out of that prouision
Which shall be needfull for your entertainement.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Returne to her? and fifty men dismiss'd?
No, rather I abiure all roofes, and chuse
To wage against the enmity oth' ayre,
To be a Comrade with the Wolfe, and Owle,
Necessities sharpe pinch. Returne with her?
Why the hot-bloodied France, that dowerlesse tooke
Our yongest borne, I could as well be brought
To knee his Throne, and Squire-like pension beg,
To keepe base life a foote; returne with her?
Perswade me rather to be slaue and sumpter
To this detested groome.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: At your choice Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: I prythee Daughter do not make me mad,
I will not trouble thee my Child: farewell:
Wee'l no more meete, no more see one another.
But yet thou art my flesh, my blood, my Daughter,
Or rather a disease that's in my flesh,
Which I must needs call mine. Thou art a Byle,
A plague sore, or imbossed Carbuncle
In my corrupted blood. But Ile not chide thee,
Let shame come when it will, I do not call it,
I do not bid the Thunder-bearer shoore,
Nor tell tales of thee to high-iudging Ioue,
Mend when thou can'st, be better at thy leisure,
I can be patient, I can stay with Regan,
I and my hundred Knights.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Not altogether so,
I look'd not for you yet, nor am prouided
For your fit welcome, giue eare Sir to my Sister,
For those that mingle reason with your passion,
Must be content to thinke you old, and so,
But she knowes what she doe's.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Is this well spoken?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: I dare auouch it Sir, what fifty Followers?
Is it not well? What should you need of more?
Yea, or so many? Sith that both charge and danger,
Speake 'gainst so great a number? How in one house
Should many people, vnder two commands
Hold amity? 'Tis hard, almost impossible.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Why might not you my Lord, receiue attendance
From those that she cals Seruants, or from mine?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Why not my Lord?
If then they chanc'd to slacke ye,
We could comptroll them; if you will come to me,
(For now I spi^ danger) I entreate you
To bring but fiue and twentie, to no more
Will I giue place or notice.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: I gaue you all.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: And in good time you gaue it.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Made you my Guardians, my Depositaries,
But kept a reseruation to be followed
With such a number? What, must I come to you
With fiue and twenty? Regan, said you so?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: And speak't againe my Lord, no more with me.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Those wicked Creatures yet do look wel fauor'd
When others are more wicked, not being the worst
Stands in some ranke of praise, Ile go with thee,
Thy fifty yet doth double fiue and twenty,
And thou art twice her Loue.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Heare me my Lord;
What need you fiue and twenty? Ten? Or fiue?
To follow in a house, where twice so many
Haue a command to tend you?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: What need one?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: O reason not the need: our basest Beggers
Are in the poorest thing superfluous,
Allow not Nature, more then Nature needs:
Mans life is cheape as Beastes. Thou art a Lady;
If onely to go warme were gorgeous,
Why Nature needs not what thou gorgeous wear'st,
Which scarcely keepes thee warme, but for true need:
You Heauens, giue me that patience, patience I need,
You see me heere (you Gods) a poore old man,
As full of griefe as age, wretched in both,
If it be you that stirres these Daughters hearts
Against their Father, foole me not so much,
To beare it tamely: touch me with Noble anger,
And let not womens weapons, water drops,
Staine my mans cheekes. No you vnnaturall Hags,
I will haue such reuenges on you both,
That all the world shall — I will do such things,
What they are yet, I know not, but they shalbe
The terrors of the earth? you thinke Ile weepe,
No, Ile not weepe, I haue full cause of weeping.
But this heart shal break into a hundred thousand flawes
Or ere Ile weepe: O Foole, I shall go mad.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Let vs withdraw, 'twill be a Storme.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: This house is little, the old man an'ds people,
Cannot be well bestow'd.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: 'Tis his owne blame hath put himselfe from rest,
And must needs taste his folly.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: For his particular, Ile receiue him gladly,
But not one follower.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: So am I purpos'd,
Where is my Lord of Gloster?

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Followed the old man forth, he is return'd.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: The King is in high rage.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Whether is he going?

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: He cals to Horse, but will I know not whether.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: 'Tis best to giue him way, he leads himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: My Lord, entreate him by no meanes to stay.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: Alacke the night comes on, and the high windes
Do sorely ruffle, for many Miles about
There's scarce a Bush.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: O Sir, to wilfull men,
The iniuries that they themselues procure,
Must be their Schoole-Masters: shut vp your doores,
He is attended with a desperate traine,
And what they may incense him too, being apt,
To haue his eare abus'd, wisedome bids feare.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Shut vp your ^ores my Lord, 'tis a wil'd night,
My Regan counsels well^: come out oth' storme.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Who's there besides foule weather?

speeches.speaker: Gen.
prose: One minded like the weather, most vnquietly.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: I know you: Where's the King?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Contending with the fretfull Elements;
Bids the winde blow the Earth into the Sea,
Or swell the curled Waters 'boue the Maine,
That things might change, or cease.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: But who is with him?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: None but the Foole, who labours to out-iest
His heart-strooke iniuries.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Sir, I do know you,
And dare vpon the warrant of my note
Commend a deere thing to you. There is diuision
(Although as yet the face of it is couer'd
With mutuall cunning) 'twixt Albany, and Cornwall:
Who haue, as who haue not, that their great Starres
Thron'd and set high; Seruants, who seeme no lesse,
Which are to France the Spies and Speculations
Intelligent of our State. What hath bin seene,
Either in snuffes, and packings of the Dukes,
Or the hard Reine which both of them hath borne
Against the old kinde King; or something deeper,
Whereof (perchance) these are but furnishings.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: I will talke further with you.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: No, do not:
For confirmation that I am much more
Then my out-wall; open this Purse, and take
What it containes. If you shall see Cordel^a,
(As feare not but you shall) shew her this Ring,
And she will tell you who that Fellow is
That yet you do not know. Fye on this Storme,
I will go seeke the King.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Giue me your hand,
Haue you no more to say?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Few words, but to effect more then all yet;
That when we haue found the King, in which your pain
That way, Ile this: He that first lights on him,
Holla the other.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Blow windes, & crack your cheeks; Rage, blow
You Cataracts, and Hyrricano's spout,
Till you haue drench'd our Steeples, drown the Cockes.
You Sulph'rous and Thought-executing Fires,
Vaunt-curriors of Oake-cleauing Thunder-bolts,
Sindge my white head. And thou all-shaking Thunder,
Strike flat the thicke Rotundity o' th' world,
Cracke Natures moulds, all germaines spill at once
That makes ingratefull Man.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: O Nunkle, Court holy-water in a dry house, is better then this Rain-water out o' doore. Good Nunkle, in, aske thy Daughters blessing, heere's a night pitties neither Wisemen, nor Fooles.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Rumble thy belly full: spit Fire, spowt Raine:
Nor Raine, Winde, Thunder, Fire are my Daughters;
I taxe not you, you Elements with vnkindnesse.
I neuer gaue you Kingdome, call'd you Children;
You owe me no subscription. Then let fall
Your horrible pleasure. Heere I stand your Slaue,
A poore, infirme, weake, and dispis'd old man:
But yet I call you Seruile Ministers,
That will with two pernicious Daughters ioyne
Your high-engender'd Battailes, 'gainst a head
So old, and white as this. O, ho! 'tis foule.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: He that has a house to put's head in, has a good Head-peece:
The Codpiece that will house, before the head has any;
The Head, and he shall Lowse: so Beggers marry many.
The man yt makes his Toe, what he his Hart shold make,
Shall of a Corne cry woe, and turne his sleepe to wake.
For there was neuer yet faire woman, but shee made mouthes in a glasse.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: No, I will be the patterne of all patience,
I will say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Marry here's Grace, and a Codpiece, that's a Wiseman, and a Foole.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Alas Sir are you here? Things that loue night,
Loue not such nights as these: The wrathfull Skies
Gallow the very wanderers of the darke
And make them keepe their Caues: Since I was man,
Such sheets of Fire, such bursts of horrid Thunder,
Such groanes of roaring Winde, and Raine, I neuer
Remember to haue heard. Mans Nature cannot carry
Th' affliction, nor the feare.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Let the great Goddes
That keepe this dreadfull pudder o're our heads,
Finde out their enemies now. Tremble thou Wretch,
That hast within thee vndivulged Crimes
Vnwhipt of Iustice. Hide thee, thou Bloudy hand;
Thou Periur'd, and thou Simular of Vertue
That art Incestuous. Caytiffe, to peeces shake
That vnder couert, and conuenient seeming
Ha's practis'd on mans life. Close pent-vp guilts,
Riue your concealing Continents, and cry
These dreadfull Summoners grace. I am a man,
More sinn'd against, then sinning.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Alacke, bare-headed?
Gracious my Lord, hard by heere is a Houell,
Some friendship will it lend you 'gainst the Tempest:
Repose you there, while I to this hard house,
(More harder then the stones whereof 'tis rais'd,
Which euen but now, demanding after you,
Deny'd me to come in) returne, and force
Their scanted curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: My wits begin to turne.
Come on my boy. How dost my boy? Art cold?
I am cold my selfe. Where is this straw, my Fellow?
The Art of our Necessities is strange,
And can make vilde things precious. Come, your Houel;
Poore Foole, and Knaue, I haue one part in my heart
That's sorry yet for thee.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: He that has and a little-tyne wit,
With heigh-ho, the Winde and the Raine,
Must make content with his Fort ^es fit,
Though the Raine it raineth euery day.

speeches.speaker: Le.
prose: True Boy: Come bring vs to this Houell.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: This is a braue night to coole a Curtizan:
Ile speake a Prophesie ere I go:
When Priests are more in word, then matter;
When Brewers marre their Malt with water;
When Nobles are their Taylors Tutors,
No Heretiques burn'd, but wenches Sutors;
When euery Case in Law, is right;
No Squire in debt, nor no poore Knight;
When Slanders do not liue in Tongues;
Nor Cut-purses come not to throngs;
When Vsurers tell their Gold i' th' Field,
And Baudes, and whores, do Churches build,
Then shal the Realme of Albion, come to great confusion:
Then comes the time, who liues to see't,
That going shalbe vs'd with feet.
This prophecie Merlin shall make, for I liue before his time.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Alacke, alacke Edmund, I like not this vnnaturall dealing; when I desired their leaue that I might pity him, they tooke from me the vse of mine owne house, charg'd me on paine of perpetuall displeasure, neither to spea^e of him entreat for him, or any way sustaine him.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Most sauage and vnnaturall.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
prose: Go too; say you nothing. There is diuision betweene the Dukes, and a worsse matter then that: I haue receiued a Letter this night, 'tis dangerous to be spoken, I haue lock'd the Letter in my Closset, these iniuries the King now beares, will be reuenged home; ther is part of a Power already footed, we must incline to the King, I will looke him, and priuily relieue him; goe you and maintaine talke with the Duke, that my charity be not of him perceiued; If he aske for me, I am ill, and gone to bed, if I die for it, (as no lesse is threatned me) the King my old Master must be relieued. There is strange things toward Edmund, pray you be carefull.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
verse: This Curtesie forbid thee, shall the Duke
Instantly know, and of that Letter too;
This seemes a faire deseruing, and must draw me.
That which my Father looses: no lesse then all,
The yonger rises, when the old doth fall.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Here is the place my Lord, good my Lord enter,
The tirrany of the open night's too rough
For Nature to endure.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Let me alone.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Good my Lord enter heere.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Wilt breake my heart?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: I had rather breake mine owne,
Good my Lord enter.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Thou think'st 'tis much that this contentious storme
Inuades vs to the skinso: 'tis to thee,
But where the greater malady is fixt,
The lesser is scarce felt. Thou'dst shun a Beare,
But if they flight lay toward the roaring Sea,
Thou'dst meete the Beare i' th' mouth, when the mind's free,
The bodies delicate: the tempest in my mind,
Doth from my sences take all feeling else,
Saue what beates there, Filliall ingratitude,
Is it not as this mouth should teare this hand
For lifting food too't? But I will punish home;
No, I will weepe no more; in such a night,
To shut me out? Poure on, I will endure:
In such a night as this? O Regan, Gonerill,
Your old kind Father, whose franke heart gaue all,
O that way madnesse lies, let me shun that:
No more of that.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Good my Lord enter here.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Prythee go in thy selfe, seeke thine owne ease,
This tempest will not giue me leaue to ponder
On things would hurt me more, but Ile goe in,
In Boy, go first. You houselesse pouertie,
Nay get thee in; Ile pray, and then Ile sleepe.
Poore naked wretches, where so ere you are
That bide the pelting of this pittilesse storme,
How shall your House-lesse heads, and vnfed sides,
Your lop'd, and window'd raggednesse defend you
From seasons such as these? O I haue tane
Too little care of this: Take Physicke, Pompe,
Expose thy selfe to feele what wretches feele,
That thou maist shake the superflux to them,
And shew the Heauens more iust.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Fathom, and halfe, Fathom and halfe; poore Tom.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Come not in heere Nuncle, here's a spirit, helpe me, helpe me.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Giue me thy hand, who's there?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: A spirite, a spirite, he sayes his name's poore Tom.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: What art thou that dost grumble there i' th' straw? Come forth.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Away, the foule Fiend followes me, through the sharpe Hauthorne blow the windes. Humh, goe to thy bed and warme thee.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Did'st thou giue all to thy Daughters? And art thou come to this?

speeches.speaker: Edgar.
prose: Who giues any thing to poore Tom? Whom the foule fiend hath led though Fire, and through Flame, through Sword, and Whirle-Poole, o're Bog, and Quagmire, that hath laid Kniues vnder his Pillow, and Halters in his Pue, set Rats-bane by his Porredge, made him Proud of heart, to ride on a Bay trotting Horse, ouer foure incht Bridges, to course his owne shadow for a Traitor. Blisse thy fiue Wits, Toms a cold. O do, de, do, de, do de, blisse thee from Whirle-Windes, Starre-blasting, and taking, do poore Tom some charitie, whom the foule Fiend vexes. There could I haue him now, and there, and there againe, and there.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Ha's his Daughters brought him to this passe?
Could'st thou saue nothing? Would'st thou giue 'em all?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Nay, he reseru'd a Blanket, else we had bin all sham'd.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Now all the plagues that in the pendulous ayre
Hang fated o're mens faults, light on thy Daughters.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: He hath no Daughters Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Death Traitor, nothing could haue subdu'd Nature
To such a lownesse, but his vnkind Daughters.
Is it the fashion, that discarded Fathers,
Should haue thus little mercy on their flesh:
Iudicious punishment, 'twas this flesh begot
Those Pelicane Daughters.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Pillicock sat on Pillicock hill, alow: alow, loo, loo.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: This cold night will turne vs all to Fooles, and Madmen.

speeches.speaker: Edgar.
prose:
Take heed o' th' foole Fiend, obey thy Parents, keepe thy words Iustice, sweare not, commit not,

with mans sworne Spouse: set not thy Sweet-heart on proud array. Tom^s a cold.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What hast thou bin?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: A Seruingman? Proud in heart, and minde; that curl'd my haire, wore Gloues in my cap; seru'd the Lust of my Mistris heart, and did the acte of darkenesse with her. Swore as many Oathes as I spake words, & broke them in the sweet face of Heauen. One, that slept in the contriuing of Lust, and wak'd to doe it. Wine lou'd I deerely, Dice deerely; and in Woman, out-Paramour'd the Turke. False of heart, light of eare, bloody of hand; Hog in sloth, Foxe in stealth, Wolfe in greedinesse, Dog in madnes, Lyon in prey. Let not the creaking of shooes, Nor the rustling of Silkes, betray thy poore heart to woman. Keepe thy foote out of Brothels, thy hand out of Plackets, thy pen from Lenders Bookes, and defye the foule Fiend. Still through the Hauthorne blowes the cold winde: Sayes suum, mun, nonny, Dolphin my Boy, Boy Sesey: let him trot by.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Thou wert better in a Graue, then to answere with thy vncouer'd body, this extremitie of the Skies. Is man no more then this? Consider him well. Thou ow'st the Worme no Silke; the Beast, no Hide; the Sheepe, no Wooll; the Cat, no perfume. Ha? Here's three on's are sophisticated. Thou art the thing it selfe; vnaccommodated man. is no more but such a poore, bare, forked Animall as thou art. Off, off you Lendings: Come, vnbutton heere.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Prythee Nunckle be contented, 'tis a naughtie night to swimme in. Now a little fire in a wilde Field, were like an old Letchers heart, a small spark, all the rest on's body, cold: Looke, heere comes a walking fire.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: This is the foule Flibbertigibbet; hee begins at Curfew, and walkes at first Cocke: Hee giues the Web and the Pin, squints the eye, and makes the Hare-lippe; Mildewes the white Wheate, and hurts the poore Creature of earth.
Swithold footed thrice the old,
He met the Night-Mare, and her nine-fold;
Bid her a-light, and her troth-plight,
And aroynt thee Witch, aroynt thee.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: How fares your Grace?

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: What's he?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Who's there? What is't you seeke?

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: What are you there? Your Names?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: Poore Tom, that eates the swimming Frog, the Toad, the Tod-pole, the wall-Neut, and the water: that in the furie of his heart, when the foule Fiend rages, eats Cow-dung for Sallets; swallowes the old Rat, and the ditch-Dogge; drinkes the green Mantle of the standing Poole: who is whipt from Tything to Tything, and stockt, punish'd, and imprison'd: who hath three Suites to his backe, sixe shirts to his body:
Horse to ride, and weapon to weare:
But Mice, and Rats, and such small Deare,
Haue bin Toms food, for seuen long yeare:
Beware my Follower. Peace Smulkin, peace thou Fiend.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: What, hath your Grace no better company?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: The Prince of Darkenesse is a Gentleman. Modo he's call'd, and Mahu.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Our flesh and blood, my Lord, is growne so vilde, that it doth hate what gets it.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Poore Tom's a cold.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Go in with me; my duty cannot suffer
T' obey in all your daughters hard commands:
Though their Iniunction be to barre my doores,
And let this Tyrannous night take hold vpon you,
Yet haue I ventured to come seeke you out,
And bring you where both fire, and food is ready.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: First let me talke with this Philosopher,
What is the cause of Thunder?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Good my Lord take his offer,
Go into th' house.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: Ile talke a word with this same lerned Theban:
What is your study?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: How to preuent the Fiend, and to kill Vermine.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Let me aske you one word in priuate.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Importune him once more to go my Lord,
His wits begin t' vnsettle.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Canst thou blame him?
His Daughters seeke his death: Ah, that good Kent,
He said it would be thus: poore banish'd man:
Thou sayest the King growes mad, Ile tell thee Friend
I am almost mad my selfe. I had a Sonne,
Now out-law'd from my blood: he sought my life
But lately: very late: I lou'd him (Friend)
No Father his Sonne deerer: true to tell thee,
The greefe hath craz'd my wits. What a night's this?
I do beseech your grace.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: O cry you mercy, Sir:
Noble Philosopher, your company.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Tom's a cold.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: In fellow there, into th' Houel; keep thee warm.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Come, let's in all.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: This way, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: With him;
I will keepe still with my Philosopher.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: Good my Lord, sooth him:
Let him take the Fellow.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Take him you on.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Sirra, come on: go along with vs.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Come, good Athenian.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: No words, no words, hush.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: Childe Rowland to the darke Tower came,
His word was still, fie, foh, and fumme,
I smell the blood of a Brittish man.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: I will haue my reuenge, ere I depart his house.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: How my Lord, I may be censured, that Nature thus giues way to Loyaltie, something feares mee to thinke of.

speeches.speaker: Cornw.
prose: I now perceiue, it was not altogether your Brothers euill disposition made him seeke his death: but a prouoking merit set a-worke by a reprouable badnesse in himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: How malicious is my fortune, that I must repent to be iust? This is the Letter which hee spoake of; which approues him an intelligent partie to the aduantages of France. O Heauens! that this Treason were not; or not I the detector.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Go with me to the Dutchesse.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: If the matter of this Paper be certain, you haue mighty businesse in hand.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: True or false, it hath made thee Earle of Gloucester: seeke out where thy Father is, that hee may bee ready for our apprehension.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: If I finde him comforting the King, it will stuffe his suspition more fully. I will perseuer in my course of Loyalty, though the conflict be sore betweene that, and my blood.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: I will lay trust vpon thee: and thou shalt finde a deere Father in my loue.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Heere is better then the open ayre. take it thankfully: I will peece out the comfort with what addition I can: I will not be long from you.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: All the powre of his wits, haue giuen way to his impatience: the Gods reward your kindnesse.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Fraterretto cals me, and tells me Nero is an Angler in the Lake of Darknesse: pray Innocent, and beware the foule Fiend.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Prythee Nunkle tell me, whether a madman be a Gentleman, or a Yeoman.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: A King, a King.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: No, he's a Yeoman, that ha's a Gentleman to his Sonne: for hee's a mad Yeoman that sees his Sonne a Gentleman before him.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: To haue a thousand with red burning spits
Come hizzing in vpon 'em.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Blesse thy fiue wits.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
verse: O pitty: Sir, where is the patience now
That you so oft haue boasted to retaine?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: My teares begin to take his part so much,
They marre my counterfetting.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
verse: The little dogges, and all;
Trey, Blanch, and Sweet-heart: see, they barke at me.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: Tom, will throw his head at them: Auaunt you
Curres, be thy mouth or blacke or white:
Tooth that poysons if it bite:
Mastiffe, Grey-hound, Mongrill, Grim,
Hound or Spaniell, Brache, or Hym:
Or Bobtaile tight, or Troudle taile,
Tom will make him weepe and waile,
For with throwing thus my head;
Dogs leapt the hatch, and all are fled.
Do, de, de, de: sese: Come, march to Wakes and Fayres,
And Market Townes: poore Tom thy horne is dry,

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Then let them Anatomize Regan: See what breeds about her heart. Is there any cause in Nature that make these hard-hearts. You sir, I entertaine for one of my hundred; only, I do not like the fashion of your garments. You will say they are Persian; but let them bee chang'd.

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Now good my Lord, lye heere, and rest awhile.

speeches.speaker: Lear.
prose: Make no noise, make no noise, draw the Curtaines: so, so, wee'l go to Supper i' th' morning.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: And Ile go to bed at noone.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Come hither Friend:
Where is the King my Master?

speeches.speaker: Kent.
prose: Here Sir, but trouble him not, his wits are gon.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Good friend, I prythee take him in thy armes;
I haue ore-heard a plot of death vpon him:
There is a Litter ready, lay him in't,
And driue toward Douer friend, where thou shalt meete
Both welcome, and protection. Take vp thy Master,
If thou should'st dally halfe an houre, his life
With thine, and all that offer to defend him,
Stand in assured losse. Take vp, take vp,
And follow me, that will to some prouision
Giue thee quicke conduct. Come, come, away.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Poste speedily to my Lord your husband, shew him this Letter, the Army of France is landed: seeke out the Traitor Glouster.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Hang him instantly.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Plucke out his eyes.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Leaue him to my displeasure. Edmond, keepe you our Sister company: the reuenges wee are bound to take vppon your Traitorous Father, are not fit for your beholding. Aduice the Duke where you are going, to a most festiuate preparation: we are bound to the like. Our Postes shall be swift, and intelligent betwixt vs. Farewell deere Sister, farewell my Lord of Glouster.
How now? Where's the King?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: My Lord of Glouster hath conuey'd him hence
Some fiue or six and thirty of his Knights
Hot Questrists after him, met him at gate,
Who, with some other of the Lords, dependants,
Are gone with him toward Douer; where they boast
To haue well armed Friends.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Get horses for your Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
prose: Farewell sweet Lord, and Sister.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: Edmund farewell: go seek the Traitor Gloster,
Pinnion him like a Theefe, bring him before vs:
Though well we may not passe vpon his life
Without the forme of Iustice: yet our power
Shall do a curt'sie to our wrath, which men
May blame, but not comptroll.
Who's there? the Traitor?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Ingratefull Fox, 'tis he.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Binde fast his corky armes.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: What meanes your Graces?
Good my Friends consider you are my Ghests:
Do me no foule play, Friends.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Binde him I say.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Hard, hard: O filthy Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Vnmercifull Lady, as you are, I'me none.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: To this Chaire binde him,
Villaine, thou shalt finde.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: By the kinde Gods, 'tis most ignobly done
To plucke me by the Beard.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: So white, and such a Traitor?

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Naughty Ladie,
These haires which thou dost rauish from my chin
Will quicken and accuse thee. I am your Host,
With Robbers hands, my hospitable fauours
You should not ruffle thus. What will you do?

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: Come Sir.
What Letters had you late from France?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Be simple answer'd, for we know the truth.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: And what confederacie haue you with the Traitors, late footed in the Kingdome?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: To whose hands
You haue sent the Lunaticke King: Speake.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: I haue a Letter guessingly set downe
Which came from one that's of a newtrall heart,
And not from one oppos'd.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Cunning.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: And false.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Where hast thou sent the King?

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: To Douer.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Wherefore to Douer?
Was't thou not charg'd at perill.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: Wherefore to Douer? Let him answer that.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: I am tyed to' th' Stake,
And I must stand the Course.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Wherefore to Douer?

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Because I would not see thy cruell Nailes
Plucke out his poore old eyes: nor thy fierce Sister,
In his Annointed flesh, sticke boarish phangs.
The Sea, with such a storme as his bare head,
In Hell-blacke-night indur'd, would haue buoy'd vp
And quench'd the Stelled fires:
Yet poore old heart, he holpe the Heauens to raine.
If Wolues had at thy Gate howl'd that sterne time,
Thou should'st haue said, good Porter turne the Key:
All Cruels else subscribe: but I shall see
The winged Vengeance ouertake such Children.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: See't shalt thou neuer. Fellowes hold ye Chaire,
Vpon these eyes of thine, Ile set my foote.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: He that will thinke to liue, till he be old,
Giue me some helpe. — O cruell! O you Gods.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: One side will mocke another: Th' other too.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: If you see vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Seru.
verse: Hold your hand, my Lord:
I haue seru'd you euer since I was a Childe:
But better seruice haue I neuer done you,
Then now to bid you hold.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: How now, you dogge?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: If you did weare a beard vpon your chin,
I'ld shake it on this quarrell. What do you meane?

speeches.speaker: Corn.
prose: My Villaine?

speeches.speaker: Seru.
prose: Nay then come on, and take the chance of anger.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
prose: Giue me thy Sword. A pezant stand vp thus?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Oh I am slaine: my Lord, you haue one eye left
To see some mischefe on him. Oh.

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: Lest it see more, preuent it; Out vilde gelly:
Where is thy luster now?

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: All darke and comfortlesse?
Where's my Sonne Edmund?
Edmund, enkindle all the sparkes of Nature
To quit this horrid acte.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Out treacherous Villaine,
Thou call'st on him, that hates thee. It was be
That made the ouerture of thy Treasons to vs:
Who is too good to pitty thee.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: O my Follies! then Edgar was abus'd,
Kinde Gods, forgiue me that, and prosper him.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Go thrust him out at gates, and let him smell
His way to Douer.
How is't my Lord? How looke you?

speeches.speaker: Corn.
verse: I haue receiu'd a hurt: Follow me Lady;
Turne out that eyelesse Villaine: throw this Slaue
Vpon the Dunghill: Regan, I bleed apace,
Vntimely comes this hurt. Giue me your arme.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: Yet better thus, and knowne to be contemn'd,
Then still contemn'd and flatter'd, to be worst:
The lowest, and most deiected thing of Fortune,
Stands still in esperance, liues not in feare:
The lamentable change is from the best,
The worst returnes to laughter. Welcome then,
Thou vnsubstantiall ayre that I embrace:
The Wretch that thou hast blowne vnto the worst,
Owes nothing to thy blasts.
But who comes heere? My Father poorely led?
World, World, O world!
But that thy strange mutations make vs hate thee,
Life would not yeelde to age.

speeches.speaker: Oldm.
verse: O my good Lord, I haue bene your Tenant,
And your Fathers Tenant, these fourescore yeares.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Away, get thee away: good Friend be gone,
Thy comforts can do me no good at all,
Thee, they may hurt.

speeches.speaker: Oldm.
prose: You cannot see your way.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: I haue no way, and therefore want no eyes:
I stumbled when I saw. Full oft 'tis seene,
Our meanes secure vs, and our meere defects
Proue our Commodities. Oh deere Sonne Edgar,
The food of thy abused Fathers wrath:
Might I but liue to see thee in my touch,
I'ld say I had eyes againe.

speeches.speaker: Oldm.
prose: How now? who's there?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: O Gods! Who is't can say I am at the worst?
I am worse then ere I was.

speeches.speaker: Old.
prose: 'Tis poore mad Tom.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: And worse I may be yet: the worst is not,
So long as we can say this is the worst.

speeches.speaker: Oldm.
prose: Fellow, where goest?

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Is it a Beggar-man?

speeches.speaker: Oldm.
prose: Madman, and beggar too.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: He has some reason, else he could not beg.
I' th' last nights storme, I such a fellow saw;
Which made me thinke a Man, a Worme. My Sonne
Came then into my minde, and yet my minde
Was then scarse Friends with him.
I haue heard more since:
As Flies to wanton Boyes, are we to th' Gods,
They kill vs for their sport.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: How should this be?
Bad is the Trade that must play Foole to sorrow,
Ang'ring it selfe, and others. Blesse thee Master.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Is that the naked Fellow?

speeches.speaker: Oldm.
prose: I, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Get thee away: If for my sake
Thou wilt ore-take vs hence a mile or twaine
I' th' way toward Douer, do it for ancient loue,
And bring some couering for this naked Soule,
Which Ile intreate to leade me.

speeches.speaker: Old.
prose: Alacke sir, he is mad.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: 'Tis the times plague,
When Madmen leade the blinde:
Do as I bid thee, or rather do thy pleasure:
Aboue the rest, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Oldm.
verse: He bring him the best Parrell that I haue
Come on't, what will.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Sirrah, naked fellow.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Poore Tom's a cold. I cannot daub it further.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Come hither fellow.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: And yet I must:
Blesse thy sweete eyes, they bleede.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
prose: Know'st thou the way to Douer?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: Both style, and gate; Horseway, and foot-path: poore Tom hath bin scarr'd out of his good wits. Blesse thee good mans sonne, from the foule Fiend.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: Here take this purse, yu whom the heau'ns plagues
Haue humbled to all strokes: that I am wretched
Makes thee the happier: Heauens deale so still:
Let the superfluous, and Lust-dieted man,
That slaues your ordinance, that will not see
Because he do's not feele, feele your powre quickly:
So distribution should vndoo excesse,
And each man haue enough. Dost thou know Douer?

speeches.speaker: Edg.
prose: I Master.

speeches.speaker: Glou.
verse: There is a Cliffe, whose high and bending head
Lookes fearfully in the confined Deepe:
Bring me but to the very brimme of it,
And Ile repayre the misery thou do'st beare
With something rich about me: from that place,
I shall no leading neede.

speeches.speaker: Edg.
verse: Giue me thy arme;
Poore Tom shall leade thee.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Welcome my Lord. I meruell our mild husband
Not met vs on the way. Now, where's your Master?

speeches.speaker: Stew.
verse: Madam within, but neuer man so chang'd:
I told him of the Army that was Landed:
He smil'd at it. I told him you were comming,
His answer was, the worse. Of Glosters Treachery,
And of the loyall Seruice of his Sonne
When I inform'd him, then he call'd me Sot,
And told me I had turn'd the wrong side out:
What most he should dislike, seemes pleasant to him;
What like, offensiue.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Then shall you go no further.
It is the Cowish terror of his spirit
That dares not vndertake: Hee'l not feele wrongs
Which tye him to an answer: our wishes on the way
May proue effects. Backe Edmond to my Brother,
Hasten his Musters, and conduct his powres.
I must change names at home, and giue the Distaffe
Into my Husbands hands. This trustie Seruant
Shall passe betweene vs: ere long you are like to heare
(If you dare venture in your owne behalfe)
A Mistresses command. Weare this; spare speech,
Decline your head. This kisse, if it durst speake
Would stretch thy Spirits vp into the ayre:
Conceiue, and fare thee well.

speeches.speaker: Bast.
prose: Yours in the rankes of death.
