speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Ile be with thee betimes.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Go too, farewell. Do you heare Rodorigo?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Ile sell all my Land.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Thus do I euer make my Foole, my purse:
For I mine owne gain'd knowledge should prophane
If I would time expend with such Snpe,
But for my Sport, and Profit: I hate the Moore,
And it is thought abroad, that 'twixt my sheets
She ha's done my Office. I know not if't be true,
But I, for meere suspition in that kinde,
Will do, as if for Surety. He holds me well,
The better shall my purpose worke on him:
Cassio's a proper man: Let me see now,
To get his Place, and to plume vp my will
In double Knauery. How? How? Let's see.
After some time, to abuse Othello's eares,
That he is too familiar with his wife:
He hath a person, and a smooth dispose
To be suspected: fram'd to make women false.
The Moore is of a free, and open Nature,
That thinkes men honest, that but seeme to be so,
And will as tenderly be lead by' th' Nose
As Asses are:
I haue't: it is engendred: Hell, and Night,
Must bring this monstrous Birth, to the worlds light.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: What from the Cape, can you discerne at Sea?

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
verse: Nothing at all, it is a high wrought Flood:
I cannot 'twixt the Heauen, and the Maine,
Descry a Saile.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Me thinks, the wind hath spoke aloud at Land,
A fuller blast ne're shooke our Battlements:
If it hath ruffiand so vpon the Sea,
What ribbes of Oake, when Mountaines melt on them,
Can hold the Morties. What shall we heare of this?
A Segregation of the Turkish Fleet:
For do but stand vpon the Foaming Shore,
The chidden Billow seemes to pelt the Clowds,
The winde-shak'd-Surge, with high & monstrous Maine
Seemes to cast water on the burning Beare,
And quench the Guards of th' euer-fixed Pole:
I neuer did like mollestation view
On the enchafed Flood.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: If that the Turkish Fleete
Be not enshelter'd, and embay'd, they are drown'd,
It is impossible to beare it out.
Newes Laddes: our warres are done:
The desperate Tempest hath so bang'd the Turkes,
That their designement halts. A Noble ship of Venice,
Hath seene a greeuous wracke and sufferance
On most part of their Fleet.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: How? Is this true?

verse: The Ship is heere put in: A Verennessa, Michael Cassio
Lieutenant to the warlike Moore, Othello,
Is come on Shore. the Moore himselfe at Sea,
And is in full Commission heere for Cyprus.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: I am glad on't:
'Tis a worthy Gouernour.
But this same Cassio, though he speake of comfort,
Touching the Turkish losse, yet he lookes sadly,
And praye the Moore be safe; for they were ^ted
With fowle and violent Tempest.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Pray Heauens he be:
For I haue seru'd him, and the man commands
Like a full Soldier. Let's to the Sea-side (hoa)
As well to see the Vessell that's come in,
As to throw-out our eyes for braue Othello,
Euen till we make the Maine, and th' Eriall blew,
An indistinct regard.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Come, let's do so;
For euery Minute is expectancie
Of more Arriuancie.

speeches.speaker: Cassi.
verse: Thankes you, the valiant of the warlike Isle,
That so approoue the Moore: Oh let the Heauens
Giue him defence against the Elements,
For I haue lost him on a dangerous Sea.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: Is he well ship'd?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: His Barke is stoutly Timber'd, and his Pylot
Of verie expert, and approu'd Allowance;
Therefore my hope's (not surfetted to death)
Stand in bold Cure.

speeches.speaker: Within.
prose: A Saile, a Saile, a Saile.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: What noise?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: The Towne is empty; on the brow o' th' Sea
Stand rankes of People, and they cry, a Saile.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: My hopes do shape him for the Gouernor.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: They do discharge their Shot of Courtesie,
Our Friends, at least.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: I pray you Sir, go forth,
And giue vs truth who 'tis that is arriu'd.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: I shall.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: But good Lieutenant, is your Generall wiu'd?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Most fortunately: he hath atchieu'd a Maid
That paragons description, and wilde Fame:
One that excels the quirkes of Blazoning pens,
And in th' essentiall Vesture of Creation,
Do's tyre the Ingeniuer.
How now? Who ha's put in?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: 'Tis one Iago, Auncient to the Generall.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Ha's had most fauourable, and happie speed:
Tempests themselues, high Seas, and howling windes,
The gutter'd-Rockes, and Congregated Sands,
Traitors ensteep'd, to enclogge the guiltlesse Keele,
As hauing sence of Beautie, do omit
Their mortall Natures, letting go safely by
The Diuine Desdemona.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: What is she?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: She that I spake of:
Our great Captains Captaine,
Left in the conduct of the bold Iago,
Whose footing heere anticipates our thoughts,
A Senights speed. Great Ioue, Othello guard,
And swell his Saile with thine owne powrefull breath,
That he may blesse this Bay with his tall Ship,
Make loues quicke pants in Desdemonaes Armes,
Giue renew'd fire to our extincted Spirits.
Oh behold,
The Riches of the Ship is come on shore:
You men of Cyprus, let her haue your knees.
Haile to thee Ladie: and the grace of Heauen,
Before, behinde thee, and on euery hand
Enwheele thee round.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I thanke you, Valiant Cassio,
What tydings can you tell of my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: He is not yet arriu'd, nor know I ought
But that he's well, and will be shortly heere.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Oh, but I feare:
How lost you company?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: The great Contention of Sea, and Skies
Parted our fellowship. But hearke, a Saile.

speeches.speaker: Within.
prose: A Saile, a Saile.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: They giue this greeting to the Cittadell:
This likewise is a Friend.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: See for the Newes:
Good Ancient, you are welcome. Welcome Mistris:
Let it not gaule your patience (good Iago)
That I extend my Manners. 'Tis my breeding,
That giues me this bold shew of Curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Sir, would she giue you so much of her lippes,
As of her tongue she oft bestowes on me,
You would haue enough.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Alas: she ha's no speech.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Infaith too much:
I finde it still, when I haue leaue to sleepe.
Marry before your Ladyship, I grant,
She puts het tongue a little in her heart,
And chides with thinking.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: You haue little cause to say so.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Come on, come on: you are Pictures out of doore: Bells in your Parlours: Wilde-Cats in your Kitchens: Saints in your Iniuries: Diuels being offended: Players in your Huswiferie, and Huswiues in your Beds.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Oh, fie vpon thee, Slanderer.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Nay, it is true: or else I am a Turke,
You rise to play, and go to bed to worke.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: You shall not write my praise.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: No, let me not.

speeches.speaker: Desde.
prose: What would'st write of me, if thou should'st praise me?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Oh, gentle Lady, do not put me too't,
For I am nothing, if not Criticall.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Come on, assay.
There's one gone to the Harbour?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I Madam.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I am not merry: but I do beguile
The thing I am, by seeming otherwise.
Come, how would'st thou praise me?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I am about it, but indeed my inuention comes from my pate, as Birdlyme do's from Freeze, it pluckes out Braines and all. But my Muse labours, and thus she is deliuer'd.
If she be faire, and wise: fairenesse, and wit,
The ones for vse, the other vseth it.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Well prais'd:
How if she be Blacke and Witty?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: If she be blacke, and thereto haue a wit,
She'le find a white, that shall her blacknesse fit.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Worse, and worse.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: How if Faire, and Foolish?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: She neuer yet was foolish that was faire,
For euen her folly helpt her to an heire.

speeches.speaker: Desde.
prose: These are old fond Paradoxes, to make Fooles laugh i' th' Alehouse. What miserable praise hast thou for her that's Foule, and Foolish.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: There's none so foule and foolish thereunto,
But do's foule pranks, which faire, and wise-ones do.

speeches.speaker: Desde.
prose: Oh heauy ignorance: thou praisest the worst best. But what praise could'st thou bestow on a deseruing woman indeed? One, that in the authorithy of her merit, did iustly put on the vouch of very malice it selfe.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: She that was euer faire, and neuer proud,
Had Tongue at will, and yet was neuer loud:
Neuer lackt Gold, and yet went neuer gay,
Fled from her wish, and yet said now I may.
She that being angred, her reuenge being nie,
Bad her wrong stay, and her displeasure flie:
She that in wisedome neuer was so fraile,
To change the Cods-head for the Salmons taile:
She that could thinke, and neu'r disclose her mind,
See Suitors following, and not looke behind:
She was a wight, (if euer such wightes were)

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: To do what?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: To suckle Fooles, and chronicle small Beere.

speeches.speaker: Desde.
prose: Oh most lame and impotent conclusion. Do not learne of him Aemillia, though he be thy husband. How say you (Cassio) is he not a most prophane, and liberall Counsailor?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: He speakes home (Madam) you may rellish him more in the Souldier, then in the Scholler.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: He takes her by the palme: I, well said, whisper. With as little a web as this, will I ensnare as great a Fly as Cassio. I smile vpon her, do: I will giue thee in thine owne Courtship. You say true, 'tis so indeed. If such tricks as these strip you out of your Lieutenantrie, it had beene better you had not kiss'd your three fingers so oft, which now againe you are most apt to play the Sir, in. Very good: well kiss'd, and excellent Curtsie: 'tis so indeed. Yet againe, your fingers to your lippes? Would they were Cluster-pipes for your sake.
The Moore I know his Trumpet.

speeches.speaker: Cassio,
prose: 'Tis truely so.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Let's meete him, and recieue him.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Loe, where he comes.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: O, my faire Warriour.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: My deere Othello.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: It giues me wonder great, as my content
To see you heere before me.
Oh my Soules Ioy:
If after euery Tempest, come such Calmes,
May the windes blow, till they haue waken'd death:
And let the labouring Barke climbe hills of Seas
Olympus high: and duck againe as low.
As hell's from Heauen. If it were now to dye,
'Twere now to be most happy. For I feare,
My Soule hath her content so absolute,
That not another comfort like to this,
Succeedes in vnknowne Fate.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: The Heauen's forbid
But that our Loues
And Comforts should encrease
Euen as our dayes do grow.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Amen to rhat (sweet Powers)
I cannot speake enough of this content,
It stoppes me heere: it is too much of ioy.
And this, and this the greatest discords be
That ere our hearts shall make.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Oh you are well tun'd now: But Ile set downe the peggs that make this Musicke, as honest as I am.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Come: let vs to the Castle.
Newes (Friends) our Warres are done:
The Turkes are drown'd.
How do's my old Acquaintance of this Isle?
(Hony) you shall be well desir'd in Cyprus,
I haue round great loue among'st them. Oh my Sweet,
I prattle out of fashion, and I do ate
In mine owne comforts. I prythee, good Iago,
Go to the Bay, and disimbarke my Coffers:
Bring thou the Master to the Cittadell,
He is a good one, and his worthynesse
Do's challenge much respect. Come Desdemona,
Once more well met at Cyprus.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Do thou meet me presently at the Harbour. Come thither, if thou be'st Valiant, (as they say base men being in Loue, haue then a Nobilitie in their Natures, more then is natiue to them) lift-me; the Lieutenant to night watches on the Court of Guard. First, I must tell thee this: Desdemona, is directly in loue with him.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: With him? Why, 'tis not possible.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Lay thy finger thus: and let thy soule be instructed. Marke me with what violence she first lou'd the Moore, but for bragging, and telling her fantasticall lies. To loue him still for prating, let not thy discreet heart thinke it. Her eye must be fed. And what delight shall she haue to looke on the diuell? When the Blood is made dull with the Act of Sport, there should be a game to enflame it, and to giue Satiety a fresh appetite. Louelinesse in fauour, simpathy in yeares, Manners, and Beauties: all which the Moore is defectiue in. Now for want of these requir'd Conueniences, her delicate tendernesse wil finde it selfe abus'd, begin to heaue the, gorge, disrellish and abhorre the Moore, very Nature wil instruct her in it, and compell her to some second choice. Now Sir, this granted (as it is a most pregnant and vnforc'd position) who stands so eminent in the degree of this Forune, as Cassio do's: a knaue very voluble: no further conscionable, then in putting on the meere forme of Ciuill, and Humaine seeming, for the better compasse of his salt, and most hidden loose Affection? Why none, why none: A slipper, and subtle knaue, a finder of occasion: that he's an eye can stampe, and counterfeit Aduantages, though true Aduantage neuer present it selfe. A diuelish knaue: besides, the knaue is handsome, young: and hath all those requisites in him, that folly and greene mindes looke after. A pestilent compleat knaue, and the woman hath found him already.

speeches.speaker: Rodo.
prose: I cannot beleeue that in her, she's full of most bless'd condition.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Bless'd figges-end. The Wine she drinkes is made of grapes. If shee had beene bless'd, shee would neuer haue lou'd the Moore: Bless'd pudding. Didst thou not see her paddle with the palme of his hand? Didst not marke that?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Yes, that I did: but that was but curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Leacherie by this hand: an Index, and obscure prologue to the History of Lust and foule Thoughts. They met so neere with their lippes, that their breathes embrac'd together. Villanous thoughts Rodorigo, when these mutabilities so marshall the way, hard at hand comes the Master, and maine exercise, th' incorporate conclusion: Pish. But Sir, be you rul'd by me. I haue brought you from Venice. Watch you to night: for the Command, Ile lay't vpon you. Cassio knowes you not: Ile not be farre from you. Do you finde some occasion to anger Cassio, either by speaking too loud, or tainting his discipline, or from what other course you please, which the time shall more fauorably minister.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Well.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Sir, he's rash, and very sodaine in Choller: and happely may strike at you, prouoke him that he may: for euen out of that will I cause these of Cyprus to Mutiny. Whose qualification shall come into no true taste againe, but by the displan^ng of Cassio. So shall you haue a shorter iourney to your desires, by the meanes I shall then haue to preferre them. And the impediment most profitably remoued, without the which there were no expectation of our prosperitie.

speeches.speaker: Rodo.
prose: I will do this, if you can bring it to any opportunity.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I warrant thee. Meete me by and by at the Cittadell. I must fetch his Necessaries a Shore. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Rodo.
prose: Adieu.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: That Cassio loues her, I do well beleeu't:
That she loues him, 'tis apt, and of great Credite.
The Moore (how beit that I endure him not)
Is of a constant, louing Noble Nature,
And I dare thinke, he'le proue to Desdemona
A most deere husband. Now I do loue her too,
Not out of absolute Lust, (though peraduenture
I stand accomptant for as great a sin)
But partely led to dyet my Reuenge,
For that I do suspect the lustie Moore
Hath leap'd into my Seate. The thought whereof,
Doth (like a poysonous Minerall) gnaw my Inwardes:
And nothing can, or shall content my Soule
Till I am eeuen'd with him, wife, for wift.
Or fayling so, yet that I put the Moore,
At least into a Ielouzie so strong
That iudgement cannot cure. Which thing to do,
If this poore Trash of Venice, whom I trace
For his quicke hunting, stand the putting on,
Ile haue our Michael Cassio on the hip,
Abuse him to the Moore, in the right garbe
(For I feare Cassio with my Night-Cape too)
Make the Moore thanke me, loue me, and reward me,
Fo^ making him egregiously an Asse,
And practising vpon his peace, and quiet,
Euen to madnesse. 'Tis heere: but yet confus'd,
Knaueries plaine face, is neuer seene, till vs'd.

speeches.speaker: Herald.
prose:
It is Othello's pleasure, our Noble and Valiant Generall. That vpon certaine tydings now arriu'd, importing the meere perdition of the Turkish Fleete: euery man put himselfe into Triumph. Some to daunce, some to make Bonfires, each man, to what Sport and Reuels his addition leads him. For besides these beneficiall Newes, it is the Celebration of his Nuptiall. So much was his pleasure should be proclaimed. All offices are open, & there is full libertie of Feasting from this

present houre of fiue, till the Bell haue told eleuen. Blesse the Isle of Cyprus, and our Noble Generall Othello.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Good Michael, looke you to the guard to night.
Let's teach our selues that Honourable stop,
Not to out-sport discretion.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Iago, hath direction what to do.
But notwithstanding with my personall eye
Will I looke to't.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Iago, is most honest:
Michael, goodnight. To morrow with your earliest,
Let me haue speech with you. Come my deere Loue,
The purchase made, the fruites are to ensue,
That profit's yet to come 'tweene me, and you.
Goodnight.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Welcome Iago: we must to the Watch.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Not this houre Lieutenant: 'tis not yet ten o' th' clocke. Our Generall cast vs thus earely for the loue of his Desdemona: Who, let vs not therefore blame; he hath not yet made wanton the night with her: and she is sport for Ioue.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: She's a most exquisite Lady.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: And Ile warrant her, full of Game.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Indeed shes a most fresh and delicate creature.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: What an eye she ha's?
Methinkes it sounds a parley to prouocation.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: An inuiting eye:
And yet me thinkes right modest.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: And when she speakes,
Is it not an Alarum to Loue?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: She is indeed perfection.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Well: happinesse to their Sheetes. Come Lieutenant, I haue a stope of Wine, and heere without are a brace of Cyprus Gallants, that would faine haue a measure to the health of blacke Othello.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Not to night, good Iago, I haue very poore, and vnhappie Braines for drinking. I could well wish Curtesie would inuent some other Custome of entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Oh, they are our Friends: but one Cup, Ile drinke for you.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: I haue drunke but one Cup to night, and that was craftily qualified too: and behold what inouation it makes heere. I am infortunate in the infirmity, and dare not taske my weakenesse with any more.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What man? 'Tis a night of Reuels, the Gallants desire it.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Where are they?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Heere, at the doore: I pray you call them in.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Ile do't, but it dislikes me.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: If I can fasten but one Cup vpon him
With that which he hath drunke to night alreadie,
He'l be as full of Quarrell, and offence
As my yong Mistris dogge.
Now my sicke Foole Rodorigo,
Whom Loue hath turn'd almost the wrong side out,
To Desdemona hath to night Carrows'd.
Potations, pottle-deepe; and he's to watch.
Three else of Cyprus, Noble swelling Spirites,
(That hold their Honours in a wary distance,
The very Elements of this Warrelike Isle)
Haue I to night fluster'd with flowing Cups,
And they Watch too.
Now 'mongst this Flocke of drunkards
Am I put to our Cassio in some Action
That may offend the Isle. But here they come.
If Consequence do but approue my dreame,
My Boate sailes freely, both with winde and Streame.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: 'Fore heauen, they haue giuen me a rowse already.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: Good-faith a litle one: not past a pint, as I am a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Some Wine hoa.
And let me the Cannakin clinke, clinke:
And let me the Cannakin clinke.
A Souldiers a man: Oh, mans life's but a span,
Why then let a Souldier drinke.
Some Wine Boyes.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: 'Fore Heauen: an excellent Song.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I learn'd it in England: where indeed they are most potent in Potting. Your Dane, your Germaine, and your swag-belly'd Hollander, (drinke hoa) are nothing to your English.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Is your Englishmen so exquisite in his drinking?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why, he drinkes you with facillitie, your Dane dead drunke. He sweates not to ouerthrow your Almaine. He giues your Hollander a vomit, ere the next Pottle can be fill'd.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: To the health of our Generall.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: I am for it Lieutenant: and Ile do you Iustice.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Oh sweet England.
King Stephen was and-a worthy Peere,
His Breeches cost him but a Crowne,
He held them Six pence all to deere,
With that he cal'd the Tailor Lowne:
He was a wight of high Renowne,
And thou art but of low degree:
'Tis Pride that pulls the Country downe,
And take thy awl'd Cloake about thee.
Some Wine hoa.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Why this is a more exquisite Song then the other.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Will you heare't againe?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: No: for I hold him to be vnworthy of his Place, that do's those things. Well: heau'ns aboue all: and there be soules must be saued, and there be soules must not be saued.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: It's true, good Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: For mine owne part, no offence to the Generall, nor any man of qualitie: I hope to be saued.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: And so do I too Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: I: (but by your leaue) not before me. The Lieutenant is to be saued before the Ancient. Let's haue no more of this: let's to our Affaires. Forgiue vs our sinnes: Gentlemen let's looke to our businesse. Do not thinke Gentlemen, I am drunke: this is my Ancient, this is my right hand, and this is my left. I am not drunke now: I can stand well enough, and I speake well enough.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: Excellent well.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Why very well then: you must not thinke then, that I am drunke.

speeches.speaker: Monta.
prose: To th' Platforme (Masters) come, let's set the Watch.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: You see this Fellow, that is gone before,
He's a Souldier, fit to stand by Caesar,
And giue direction. And do but see his vice,
'Tis to his vertue, a iust Equinox,
The one as long as th' other. 'Tis pittie of him:
I feare the trust Othello puts him in,
On some odde time of his infirmitie
Will shake this Island.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: But is he often thus?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: 'Tis euermore his prologue to his sleepe,
He'le watch the Horologe a double Set,
If Drinke rocke not his Cradle.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: It were well
The Generall were put in mind of it:
Perhaps he sees it not, or his good nature
Prizes the vertue that appeares in Cassio,
And lookes not on his euills: is not this true?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: How now Rodorigo?
I pray you after the Lieutenant, go.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: And 'tis great pitty, that the Noble Moore
Should hazard such a Place, as his owne Second
With one of an ingraft Infirmitie,
It were an honest Action, to say so
To the Moore.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Not I, for this faire Island,
I do loue Cassio well: and would do much
To cure him of this euill, But hearke, what noise?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: You Rogue: you Rascall.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: What's the matter Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: A Knaue teach me my dutie? Ile beate the
Knaue into a Twiggen-Bottle.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Beate me?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Dost thou prate, Rogue?

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Nay, good Lieutenant:
I pray you Sir, hold your hand.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Let me go (Sir)
Or Ile knocke you o're the Mazard.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: Come, come: you're drunke.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Drunke?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Away I say: go out and cry a Mutinie.
Nay good Lieutenant. Alas Gentlemen:
Helpe hoa. Lieutenant. Sir Montano:
Helpe Masters. Heere's a goodly Watch indeed.
Who's that which rings the Bell: Diablo, hoa:
The Towne will rise. Fie, fie Lieutenant,
You'le be asham'd for euer.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: What is the matter heere?

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: I bleed still, I am hurt to th' death. He dies.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Hold for your liues.

speeches.speaker: Iag.
verse: Hold hoa: Lieutenant, Sir Montano, Gentlemen:
Haue you forgot all place of sense and dutie?
Hold. The Generall speaks to you: hold for shame.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Why how now hoa? From whence ariseth this?
Are we turn'd Turkes? and to our selues do that
Which Heauen hath forbid the Ottamittes.
For Christian shame, put by this barbarous Brawle:
He that stirs next, to carue for his owne rage,
Holds his soule light: He dies vpon his Motion.
Silence that dreadfull Bell, it frights the Isle,
From her propriety. What is the matter, Masters?
Honest Iago that lookes dead with greeuing,
Speake: who began this? On thy loue I charge thee?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I do not know: Friends all, but now, euen now.
In Quarter, and in termes like Bride, and Groome
Deuesting them for Bed: and then, but now:
(As if some Planet had vnwitted men)
Swords out, and tilting one at others breastes,
In opposition bloody. I cannot speake
Any begining to this peeuish oddes.
And would, in Action glorious, I had lost
Those legges, that brought me to a part of it.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: How comes it (Michaell) you are thus forgot?

speeches.speaker: C^
prose: I pray you pardon me, I cannot speake.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Worthy Montano, you were wont to be ciuill:
The grauitie, and stillnesse of your youth
The world hath noted. And your name is great
In mouthes of wisest Censure. What's the matter
That you vnlace your reputation thus,
And spend your rich opinion, for the name
Of a night-brawler? Giue me answer to it.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Worthy Othello, I am hurt to danger,
Your Officer Iago, can informe you,
While I spare speech which something now offends me.
Of all that I do know, nor know I ought
By me, that's said, or done amisse this night,
Vnlesse selfe-charitie be sometimes a vice,
And to defend our selues, it be a sinne
When violence assailes vs.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Now by Heauen,
My blood begins my safer Guides to rule,
And passion (hauing my best iudgement collied)
Assaies to leade the way. If I once stir,
Or do but lift this Arme, the best of you
Shall sinke in my rebuke. Giue me to know
How this foule Rout began: Who set it on,
And he that is approu'd in this offence,
Though he had twinn'd with me, both at a birth,
Shall loose me. What in a Towne of warre,
Yet wilde, the peoples hearts brim-full of feare,
To Manage priuate, and domesticke Quarrell?
In night, and on the Court and Guard of safetie?
'Tis monstrous: Iago, who began't?

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: If partially Affin'd, or league in office,
Thou dost deliuer more, or lesse then Truth.
Thou art no Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Touch me not so neere,
I had rather haue this tongue cut from my mouth,
Then it should do offence to Michaell Cassio.
Yet I perswade my selfe, to speake the truth
Shall nothing wrong him. This it is Generall:
Montano and my selfe being in speech,
There comes a Fellow crying out for helpe,
And Cassio following him with determin'd Sword
To execute vpon him. Sir, this Gentleman,
Steppes in to Cassio, and entreats his pause:
My selfe, the crying Fellow did pursue,
Least by his clamour (as it so fell out)
The Towne might fall in fright. He, (swift of foote)
Out-ran my purpose: and I return'd then rather
For that I heard the clinke. and fall of Swords,
And Cassio high in oath: Which till to night
I nere might say before. When I came backe
(For this was briefe) I found them close together
At blow, and thrust, euen as againe they were
When you your selfe did part them.
More of this matter cannot I report.
But Men are Men: The best sometimes forget,
Though Cassio did some little wrong to him,
As men in rage strike those that wish them best,
Yet surely Cassio. I beleeue receiu'd
From him that fled, some strange Indignitie,
Which patience could not passe.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: I know Iago
Thy honestie, and loue doth mince this matter,
Making it light to Cassio: Cassio, I loue thee,
But neuer more be Officer of mine.
Looke if my gentle Loue be not rais'd vp:
Ile make thee an example.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: What is the matter (Deere?)

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: All's well, Sweeting:
Come away to bed. Sir for your hurts,
My selfe will be your Surgeon. Lead him off:
Iago, looke with care about the Towne,
And silence those whom this vil'd brawle distracted.
Come Desdemona, 'tis the Soldiers life,
To haue their Balmy slumbers wak'd with strife.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What are you hurt Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: I, past all Surgery.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Marry Heauen forbid.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Reputation, Reputation, Reputation: Oh I haue lost my Reputation. I haue lost the immortall part of myselfe, and what remaines is bestiall. My Reputation, Iago, my Reputation.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: As I am an honest man I had thought you had receiued some bodily wound; there is more sence in that then in Reputation. Reputation is an idle, and most false imposition; oft got without merit, and lost without deseruing. You haue lost no Reputation at all, vnlesse you repute your selfe such a looser. What man, there are more wayes to recouer the Generall againe. You are but now cast in his moode, (a punishment more in policie, then in malice) euen so as one would beate his offencelesse dogge, ro affright an Imperious Lyon. Sue to him againe, and he's yours.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: I will rather sue to be despis'd, then to deceiue so good a Commander, with so slight, so drunken, and so indiscreet an Officer. Drunke? And speake Parrat? And squabble? Swagger? Sweare? And discourse Fustian with ones owne shadow? Oh thou invisible spirit of Wine, if thou hast no name to be knowne by, let vs call thee Diuell.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What was he that you follow'd with your Sword? What had he done to you?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: I know not.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Is't possible?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: I remember a masse of things, but nothing distinctly: a Quarrell, but nothing wherefore. Oh, that men should put an Enemie in their mouthes, to steale away their Braines? that we should with ioy, pleasance, reuell and applause, transforme our selues into Beasts.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why? But you are now well enough: how came you thus recouered?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: It hath pleas'd the diuell drunkennesse, to giue place to the diuell wrath, one vnpe^fectnesse, shewes me another to make me frankly despise my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Come, you are too seuere^ a Moraller. As the Time, the Place, & the Condition of this Country stands I could hartily wish this had not befalne: but since it is, as it is, mend it for your owne good.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: I will aske him for my Place againe, he shall tell me, I am a drunkard: had I as many mouthes as Hydra, such an answer would stop them all. To be now a sensible man, by and by a Foole, an^ presently a Beast. Oh strange! Euery inordinate cup is vnbless'd, and the Ingredient is a diuell.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Come, come: good wine, is a good famillar Creature, if it be well vs'd: exclaime no more against it. And good Lieutenant, I thinke, you thinke I loue you.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: I haue well approued it, Sir. I drunke?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: You, or any man liuing, may be drunke at a time man. I tell you what you shall do: Our General's Wife, is now the Generall. I may say so, in this respect, for that he hath deuoted, and giuen vp himselfe to the Contemplation, marke: and deuotement of her parts and Graces. Confesse your selfe freely to her: Importune her helpe to put you in your place againe. She is of so free, so kinde, so apt, so blessed a disposition, she holds it a vice in her goodnesse, not to do more then she is requested. This broken ioynt betweene you, and her husband, entreat her to splinter. And my Fortunes against any lay worth naming, this cracke of your Loue, shall grow stronger, then it was before.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: You aduise me well.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I protest in the sinceritie of Loue, and honest kindnesse.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: I thinke it freely: and betimes in the morning, I will beseech the vertuous Desdemona to vndertake for me: I am desperate of my Fortunes if they check me.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: You are in the right: good night Lieutenant, I must to the Watch.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Good night, honest Iago.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: And what's he then,
That saies I play the Villaine?
When this aduise is free I giue, and honest,
Proball to thinking, and indeed the course
To win the Moore againe.
For 'tis most easie
Th' inclyning Desdemona to subdue
In any honest Suite. She's fram'd as fruitefull
As the free Elements. And then for her
To win the Moore, were to renownce his Baptisme,
All Seales, and Simbols of redeemed sin:
His Soule is so enfetter'd to her Loue,
That she may make, vnmake, do what she list,
Euen as her Appetite shall play the God,
With his weake Function. How am I then a Villaine,
To Counsell Cassio to this paralell course,
Directly to his good? Diuinitie of hell,
When diuels will the blackest sinnes put on,
They do suggest at first with heauenly shewes,
As I do now. For whiles this honest Foole
Plies Desdemona, to repaire his Fortune,
And she for him, pleades strongly to the Moore,
Ile powre this pestilence into his eare:
That she repeales him, for her bodies Lust.
And by how much she striues to do him good,
She shall vndo her Credite with the Moore.
So will I turne her vertue into pitch,
And out of her owne goodnesse make the Net,
That shall en-mash them all.
How now Rodorigo?

speeches.speaker: Rodorigo.
prose:
I do follow heere in the Chace, not like a Hound that hunts, but one that filles vp the Crie. My Money is almost spent; I haue bin to night exceedingly well Cudgell'd: And I thinke the issue

will bee, I shall haue so much experience for my paines; And so, with no money at all, and a little more Wit, returne againe to Venice.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: How poore are they that haue not Patience?
What wound did euer heale but by degrees?
Thou know'st we worke by Wit, and not by Witchcraft
And Wit depends on dilatory time:
Dos't not go well? Cassio hath beaten thee,
And thou by that small hurt hath casheer'd Cassio:
Though other things grow faire against the Sun,
Yet Fruites that blossome first, will first be ripe:
Content thy selfe, a-while. Introth 'tis Morning;
Pleasure, and Action, make the houres seeme short.
Retire thee, go where thou art Billited:
A way, I say, thou shalt know more heereafter:
Nay get thee gone.
Two things are to be done:
My Wife must moue for Cassio to her Mistris:
Ile set her on my selfe, a while, to draw the Moor apart,
And bring him iumpe, when he may Cassio finde
Soliciting his wife: I, that's the way:
Dull not Deuice, by coldnesse, and delay.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Masters, play heere, I wil content your paines,
Something that's briefe: and bid, goodmorrow General.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Why Masters, haue your Instruments bin in Naples, that they speake i' th' Nose thus?

speeches.speaker: Mus.
prose: How Sir? how?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Are these I pray you, winde Instruments?

speeches.speaker: Mus.
prose: I marry are they sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Oh, thereby hangs a tale.

speeches.speaker: Mus.
prose: Whereby hangs a tale, sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Marry sir, by many a winde Instrument that I know. But Masters, heere's money for you: and the Generall so likes your Musick, that he desires you for loues sake to make no more noise with it.

speeches.speaker: Mus.
prose: Well Sir, we will not.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: If you haue any Musicke that may not be heard, too't againe. But (as they say) to heare Musicke, the Generall do's not greatly care.

speeches.speaker: Mus.
prose: We haue none such, sir.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Then put vp your Pipes in your bagge, for Ile away. Go, vanish into ayre, away.

speeches.speaker: Cassio
prose: Dost thou heare me, mine honest Friend?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: No, I heare not your honest Friend:
I heare you.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Prythee keepe vp thy Quillets, ther's a poore peece of Gold for thee: if the Gentlewoman that attends the Generall be stirring, tell her, there's one Cassio entreats her a little fauour of Speech. Wilt thou do this?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: She is stirring sir: if she will stirre hither, I shall seeme to notifie vnto her.
In happy time, Iago.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: You haue not bin a-bed then?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Why no: the day had broke before we parted.
I haue made bold (Iago) to send in to your wife:
My suite to her is, that she will to vertuous Desdemona
Procure me some accesse.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Ile send her to you presently:
And Ile deuise a meane to draw the Moore
Out of the way, that your conuerse and businesse
May be more free.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: I humbly thanke you for't. I neuer knew
A Flo^ntine more kinde, and honest.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Goodmorrow (good Lieutenant) I am sorrie
For your displeasure: but all will sure be well.
The Generall and his wife are talking of it,
And she speakes for you stoutly. The Moore replies,
That he you hurt is of great Fame in Cyprus,
And great Affinitie: and that in wholsome Wisedome
He might not but refuse you. But he protests he loues you
And needs no other Suitor, but his likings
To bring you in againe.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Yet I beseech you,
If you thinke fit, or that it may be done,
Giue me aduantage of some breefe Discourse
With Desdemon alone.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Pray you come in:
I will bestow you where you shall haue time
To speake your bosome freely.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: I am much bound to you.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: These Letters giue (Iago) to the Pylot,
And by him do my duties to the Senate:
That done, I will be walking on the Workes,
Repaire there to mee.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Well, my good Lord, Ile doo't.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: This Fortification (Gentlemen) shall we see't?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: Well waite vpon your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Be thou assur'd (good Cassio) I will do
All my abilities in thy behalfe.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Good Madam do:
I warrant it greeues my Husband,
As if the cause were his.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Oh that's an honest Fellow, Do not doubt Cassio
But I will haue my Lord, and you againe
As friendly as you were.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Bounteous Madam,
What euer shall become of Michael Cassio,
He's neuer any thing but your true Seruant.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I know't: I thanke you: you do loue my Lord:
You haue knowne him long, and be you well assur'd
He shall in strangenesse stand no farther off,
Then in a politique distance.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: I, but Lady,
That policie may either last so long,
Or feede vpon such nice and waterish diet,
Or breede it selfe so out of Circumstances,
That I being absent, and my place supply'd,
My Generall will forget my Loue, and Seruice.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Do not doubt ^hat: before Aemilia here,
I giue thee warrant of thy place. Assure thee,
If I do vow a friendship, Ile performe it
To the last Article. My Lord shall neuer rest,
Ile watch him tame, and talke him out of patience;
His Bed shall seeme a Schoole, his Boord a Shrift,
Ile intermingle euery thing he do's
With Cassio's suite: Therefore be merry Cassio,
For thy Solicitor shall rather dye,
Then giue thy cause away.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Madam, heere comes my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Madam, Ile take my leaue.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Why stay, and heare me speake.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Madam, not now: I am very ill at ease,
Vnfit for mine owne purposes.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Well, do your discretion.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Hah? I like not that,

speeches.speaker: Othel.
prose: What dost thou say?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Nothing my Lord; or if—I know not what.

speeches.speaker: Othel.
prose: Was not that Cassio parted from my wife?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Cassio my Lord? No sure, I cannot thinke it
That he would steale away so guilty-like,
Seeing your comming.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I do beleeue 'twas he.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: How now my Lord?
I haue bin talking with a Suitor heere,
A man that languishes in your displeasure.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Who is't you meane?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Why your Lieutenant Cassio: Good my Lord,
If I haue any grace, or power to moue you,
His present reconciliation take.
For if he be not one, that truly loues you,
That erres in Ignorance, and not in Cunning,
I haue no iudgement in an honest face.
I prythee call him backe.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Went he hence now?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I sooth; so humbled,
That he hath left part of his greefe with mee
To suffer with him. Good Loue, call him backe.

speeches.speaker: Othel.
prose: Not now (sweet Desdemon) some other time.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: But shall't be shortly?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: The sooner (Sweet) for you.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Shall't be to night, at Supper?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: No, not to night.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: To morrow Dinner then?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I shall not dine at home:
I meete the Captaines at the Cittadell.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Why then to morrow night, on Tuesday morne,
On Tuesday noone, or night; on Wensday Morne.
I prythee name the time, but let it not
Exceed three dayes. Infaith hee's penitent:
And yet his Trespasse, in our common reason
(Saue that they say the warres must make example)
Out of her best, is not almost a fault
T' encurre a priuate checke. When shall he come?
Tell me Othello. I wonder in my Soule
What you would aske me, that I should deny.
Or stand so mam'ring on? What? Michael Cassio,
That came a woing wirh you? and so many a time
(When I haue spoke of you dispraisingly)
Hath tane your part, to haue so much to do
To bring him in? Trust me, I could do much.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Prythee no more: Let him come when he will:
I will deny thee nothing.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Why, this is not a Boone:
'Tis as I should entreate you weare your Gloues,
Or feede on nourishing dishes, or keepe you warme,
Or sue to you, to do a peculiar profit
To your owne person. Nay, when I haue a suite
Wherein I meane to touch your Loue indeed,
It shall be full of poize, and difficult waight,
And fearefull to be granted.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I will deny thee nothing.
Whereon, I do beseech thee, grant me this,
To leaue me but a little to my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Shall I deny you? No: farewell my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Farewell my Desdemona, Ile come to thee strait.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Aemilia come; be as your Fancies teach you:
What ere you be, I am obedient.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Excellent wretch: Perdition catch my Soule
But I do loue thee: and when I loue thee not,
Chaos is come againe.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: My Noble Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: What dost thou say, Iago?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Did Michael Cassio
When he woo'd my Lady, know of your loue?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: He did, from first to last:
Why dost thou aske?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: But for a satisfaction of my Thought,
No further harme.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Why of thy thought, Iago?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I did not thinke he had bin acquainted with hir.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: O yes, and went betweene vs very oft.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Indeed? I indeed. Discern'st thou ought in that?
Is he not honest?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Honest, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Honest? I, Honest.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: My Lord, for ought I know.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: What do'st thou thinke?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Thinke, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Thinke, my Lord? Alas, thou ecchos't me;
As if there were some Monster in thy thought
Too hideous to be shewne. Thou dost mean somthing:
I heard thee say euen now, thou lik'st not that,
When Cassio left my wife. What didd'st not like?
And when I told thee, he was of my Counsaile,
Of my whole course of wooing; thou cried'st, Indeede?
And didd'st contract, and purse thy brow together,
As if thou then hadd'st shut vp in thy Braine
Some horrible Conceite. If thou do'st loue me,
Shew me thy thought.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: My Lord, you know I loue you.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I thinke thou do'st:
And for I know thou'rt full of Loue, and Honestie,
And weigh'st thy words before thou giu'st them breath,
Therefore these stops of thine, fright me the more:
For such things in a false disloyall Knaue
Are trickes of Custome: but in a man that's iust,
They're close dilations, working from the heart,
That Passion cannot rule.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: For Michael Cassio,
I dare be sworne, I thinke that he is honest.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I thinke so too.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Men should be what they seeme,
Or those that be not, would they might seeme none.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Certaine, men should be what they seeme.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why then I thinke Cassio's an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Nay, yet there's more in this?
I prythee speake to me, as to thy thinkings,
As thou dost ruminate, and giue thy worst of thoughts
The worst of words.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Good my Lord pardon me,
Though I am bound to euery Acte of dutie,
I am not bound to that: All Slaues are free:
Vtter my Thoughts? Why say, they are vild, and falce?
As where's that Palace, whereinto foule things
Sometimes intrude not? Who ha's that breast so pure,
Wherein vncleanly Apprehensions
Keepe Leetes, and Law-dayes, and in Sessions sit
With meditations lawfull?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Thou do'st conspire against thy Friend (Iago)
If thou but think'st him wrong'd, and mak'st his eare
A stranger to thy Thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I do beseech you,
Though I perchance am vicious in my guesse
(As I confesse it is my Natures plague
To spy into Abuses, and of my iealousie
Shapes faults that are not) that your wisedome
From one, that so imperfectly conceits,
Would take no notice, nor build your selfe a trouble
Out of his scattering, and vnsure obseruance:
It were not for your quiet, nor your good,
Nor for my Manhood, Honesty, and Wisedome,
To let you know my thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: What dost thou meane?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Good name in Man, & woman (deere my Lord)
Is the immediate Iewell of their Soules;
Who steales my purse, steales trash:
'Tis something, nothing;
'Twas mine, 'tis his, and has bin slaue to thousands:
But he that filches from me my good Name,
Robs me of that, which not enriches him,
And makes me poore indeed.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Ile know thy Thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: You cannot, if my heart were in your hand,
Nor shall not, whil'st 'tis in my custodie.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Oh, beware my Lord, of iealousie,
It is the greene-ey'd Monster, which doth mocke
The meate it feeds on. That Cuckold liues in blisse,
Who certaine of his Fate, loues not his wronger:
But oh, what damned minutes ^els he ore,
Who dotes, yet doubts: Suspects, yet soundly loues?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: O miserie.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Poore, and Content, is rich, and rich enough,
But Riches finelesse, is as poore as Winter,
To him that euer feares he shall be poore:
Good Heauen, the Soules of all my Tribe defend
From Iealousie.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Why? why is this?
Think'st thou, I'ld make a Life of Iealousie;
To follow still the changes of the Moone
With fresh suspitions? No: to be once in doubt,
Is to be resolu'd: Exchange me for a Goat,
When I shall turne the businesse of my Soule
To such exufflicate, and blow'd Surmises,
Matching thy inference. Tis not to make me Iealious,
To say my wife is faire, feeds well, loues company,
Is free of Speech, Sings, Playes, and Dances:
Where Vertue is, these are more vertuous.
Nor from mine owne weake merites, will I draw
The smallest feare, or doubt of her reuolt,
For she had eyes, and chose me. No Iago,
Ile see before I doubt; when I doubt, proue;
And on the proofe, there is no more but this,
Away at once with Loue, or Iealousie.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: I am glad of this: For now I shall haue reason
To shew the Loue and Duty that I beare you
With franker spirit. Therefore (as I am bound)
Receiue it from me. I speake not yet of proofe:
Looke to your wife, obserue her well with Cassio,
Weare your eyes, thus: not Iealious, nor Secure:
I would not haue your free, and Noble Nature,
Out of selfe-Bounty, be abus'd: Looke too't:
I know our Country disposition well:
In Venice, they do let Heauen see the prankes
They dare not shew their Husbands.
Their best Conscience,
Is not to leaue't vndone, but kept vnknowne.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Dost thou say so?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: She did deceiue her Father, marrying you,
And when she seem'd to shake, and feare your lookes,
She lou'd them most.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: And so she did.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Why go too then:
Shee that so young could giue out such a Seeming
To seele her Fathers eyes vp, close as Oake,
He thought 'twas Witchcraft.
But I am much too blame:
I humbly do beseech you of your pardon
For too much louing you.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I am bound to thee for euer.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I see this hath a little dash'd your Spirits:

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Not a iot, not a iot.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Trust me, I feare it has:
I hope you will consider what is spoke
Comes from your Loue.
But I do see y'are moou'd:
I am to pray you, not to straine my speech
To grosser issues, nor to larger reach,
Then to Suspition.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I will not.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Should you do so (my Lord)
My speech should fall into such vilde successe,
Which my Thoughts aym'd not.
Cassio's my worthy Friend:
My Lord, I see y'are mou'd.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: No, not much mou'd:
I do not thinke but Desdemona's honest.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Long liue she so;
And long liue you to thinke so.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: And yet how Nature erring from it selfe.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I, there's the point:
As (to be bold with you)
Not to affect many proposed Matches
Of her owne Clime, Complexion, and Degree,
Whereto we see in all things, Nature tends:
Foh, one may smel in such, a will most ranke,
Foule disproportions, Thoughts vnnaturall.
But (pardon me) I do not in position
Distinctly speake of her, though I may feare
Her will, recoyling to her better iudgement,
May fal to match you with her Country formes,
And happily repent.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Farewell, farewell:
If more thou dost perceiue, let me know more:
Set on thy wife to obserue.
Leaue me Iago.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: My Lord, I take my leaue.

speeches.speaker: Othel.
verse: Why did I marry?
This honest Creature (doubtlesse)
Sees, and knowes more, much more then he vnfolds.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: My Lord, I would I might intreat your Honor
To scan this thing no farther: Leaue it to time,
Although 'tis fit that Cassio haue his Place;
For sure he filles it vp with great Ability;
Yet if you please, to him off a-while:
You shall by that perceiue him, and his meanes:
Note if your Lady straine his Entertainment
With any strong, or vehement importunitie,
Much will be seene in that: In the meane time,
Let me be thought too busie in my feares,
(As worthy cause I haue to feare I am)
And hold her free, I do beseech your Honor.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Feare not my gouernment.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I once more take my leaue.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: This Fellow's of exceeding honesty,
And knowes all Quantities with a learn'd Spirit
Of humane dealings. If I do proue her Haggard,
Though that her lesses were my deere heart-strings,
I'ld whistle her off, and let her downe the winde
To prey at Fortune. Haply, for I am blacke,
And haue not those soft parts of Conuersation
That Chamberers haue: Or for I am declin'd
Into the vale of yeares (yet that's not much)
Shee's gone. I am abus'd, and my releefe
Must be to loath her. Oh Curse of Marriage!
That we can call these delicate Creatures ours,
And not their Appetites? I had rather be a Toad,
And liue vpon the vapour of a Dungeon,
Then keepe a corner in the thing I loue
For others vses. Yet 'tis the plague to Great-ones,
Prerogatiu'd are they lesse then the Base,
'Tis destiny vnshunnable, like death:
Euen then, this forked plague is Fated to vs,
When we do quicken. Looke where she comes:
If she be false, Heauen mock'd it selfe:
Ile not beleeue't.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: How now, my deere Othello?
Your dinner, and the generous Islanders
By you inuited, do attend your presence.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I am too blame.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Why do you speake so faintly?
Are you not well?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I haue a paine vpon my Forehead, heere.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Why that's with watching, 'twill away againe.
Let me but binde it hard, within this houre
It will be well.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Your Napkin is too little:
Let it alone: Come, Ile go in with you.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I am very sorry that you are not well.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: I am glad I haue found this Napkin:
This was her first remembrance from the Moore,
My wayward Husband hath a hundred times
Woo'd me to steale it. But she so loues the Token,
(For he coniur'd her, she should euer keepe it)
That she reserues it euermore about her,
To kisse, and talke too. Ile haue the worke tane out,
And giu't Iago: what he will do with it
Heauen knowes, not I:
I nothing, but to please his Fantasie.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: How now? What do you heere alone?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Do not you chide: I haue a thing for you.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: You haue a thing for me?
It is a common thing —

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Hah?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: To haue a foolish wife.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Oh, is that all? What will you giue me now
For that same Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What Handkerchiefe?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: What Handkerchiefe?
Why that the Moore first gaue to Desdemona,
That which so often you did bid me steale.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Hast stolne it from her?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: No: but she let it drop by negligence,
And to th' aduantage, I being heere, took't vp:
Looke, heere 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: A good wench, giue it me.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: What will you do with't, that you haue bene so earnest to haue me filch it?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why, what is that to you?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: If it be not for some purpose of import,
Giu't me againe. Poore Lady, shee'l run mad
When she shall lacke it.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Be not acknowne on't:
I haue vse for it. Go, leaue me.
I will in Cassio's Lodging loose this Napkin,
And let him finde it. Trifles light as ayre,
Are to the iealious, confirmations strong,
As proofes of holy Writ. This may do something.
The Moore already changes with my poyson:
Dangerous conceites, are in their Natures poysons,
Which at the first are scarse found to distaste:
But with a little acte vpon the blood,
Burne like the Mines of Sulphure. I did say so.
Looke where he comes: Not Poppy, nor Mandragora,
Nor all the drowsie Syrrups of the world
Shall euer medicine thee to that sweete sleepe
Which thou owd'st yesterday.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Ha, Ha, false to mee?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why how now Generall? No more of that.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Auant, be gone: Thou hast set me on the Racke:
I sweare 'tis better to be much abus'd,
Then but to know't a little.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: How now, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: What sense had I, in her stolne houres of Lust?
I saw't not, thought it not: it harm'd not me:
I slept the next night well, fed well, was free, and merrie.
I found not Cassio's kisses on her Lippes:
He that is robb'd, not wanting what is stolne,
Let him not know't, and he's not robb'd at all.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I am sorry to heare this?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I had beene happy, if the generall Campe,
Pyoners and all, had tasted her sweet Body,
So I had nothing knowne. Oh now, for euer
Farewell the Tranquill minde; farewell Content;
Farewell the plumed Troopes, and the bigge Warres,
That makes Ambition, Vertue! Oh farewell;
Farewell the neighing Steed, and the shrill Trumpe,
The Spirit-stirring Drum, th' Eare-piercing Fife,
The Royall Banner, and all Qualitie,
Pride, Pompe, and Circumstance of glorious Warre:
And O you mortall Engines, whose rude throates
Th' immortall Ioues dread Clamours, counterfet,
Farewell: Othello's Occupation's gone.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Is't possible my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Villaine, be sure thou proue my Loue a Whore;
Be sure of it: Giue me the Occular proofe,
Or by the worth of mine eternall Soule,
Thou had'st bin better haue bin borne a Dog
Then answer my wak'd wrath.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Is't come to this?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Make me to see't: or (at the least) so proue it,
That the probation beare no Hindge, nor Loope,
To hang a doubt on: Or woe vpon thy life.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: My Noble Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: If thou dost slander her, and torture me,
Neuer pray more: Abandon all remorse
On Horrors head, Horrors accumulate:
Do deeds to make Heauen weepe, all Earth amaz'd;
For nothing canst thou to damnation adde,
Greater then that.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: O Grace! O Heauen forgiue me!
Are you a Man? Haue you a Soule? or Sense?
God buy you: take mine Office. Oh wretched Foole,
That lou'st to make thine Honesty, a Vice!
Oh monstrous world! Take note, take note (O World)
To be direct and honest, is not safe.
I thanke you for this profit, and from hence
Ile loue no Friend, sith Loue breeds such offence.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Nay stay: thou should'st be honest.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I should be wise; for Honestie's a Foole,
And looses that it workes for.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: By the World,
I thinke my Wife be honest, and thinke she is not:
I thinke that thou art iust, and thinke thou art not:
Ile haue some proofe. My name that was as fresh
As Dians Visage, is now begrim'd and blacke
As mine owne face. If there be Cords, or Kniues,
Poyson, or Fire, or suffocating streames,
Ile not indure it. Would I were satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I see you are eaten vp with Passion:
I do repent me, that I put it to you.
You would be satisfied?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Would? Nay, and I will.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: And may: but how? How satisfied, my Lord?
Would you the super-vision grossely gape on?
Behold her top'd?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Death, and damnation. Oh!

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: It were a tedious difficulty, I thinke,
To bring them to that Prospect: Damne them then,
If euer mortall eyes do see them boulster
More then their owne. What then? How then?
What shall I say? Where's Satisfaction?
It is impossible you should see this,
Were they as prime as Goates, as hot as Monkeyes,
As salt as Wolues in pride, and Fooles as grosse
As Ignorance, made drunke. But yet, I say,
If imputation, and strong circumstances,
Which leade directly to the doore of Truth,
Will giue you satisfaction, you might haue't.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Giue me a liuing reason she's disloyall.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I do not like the Office.
But sith I am entred in this cause so farre
(Prick'd too't by foolish Honesty, and Loue)
I will go on. I lay with Cassio lately,
And being troubled with a raging tooth,
I could not sleepe. There are a kinde of men,
So loose of Soule, that in their sleepes will mutter
Their Affayres: one of this kinde is Cassio:
In sleepe I heard him say, sweet Desdemona,
Let vs be wary, let vs hide our Loues,
And then (Sir) would he gripe, and wring my hand:
Cry, oh sweet Creature: then kisse me hard,
As if he pluckt vp kisses by the rootes,
That grew vpon my lippes, laid his Leg ore my Thigh,
And sigh, and kisse, and then cry cursed Fate,
That gaue thee to the Moore.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: O monstrous! monstrous!

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Nay, this was but his Dreame.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: But this denoted a fore-gone conclusion,
'Tis a shrew'd doubt, though it be but a Dreame.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: And this may helpe to thicken other proofes,
That do demonstrate thinly.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Ile teare her all to peeces.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Nay yet be wise; yet we see nothing done,
She may be honest yet: Tell me but this,
Haue you not sometimes seene a Handkerchiefe
Spotted with Strawberries, in your wiues hand?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I gaue her such a one: 'twas my first gift.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I know not that: but such a Handkerchiefe
(I am sure it was your wiues) did I to day
See Cassio wipe his Beard with.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: If it be that.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: If it be that, or any, it was hers.
It speakes against her with the other proofes.

speeches.speaker: Othel.
verse: O that the Slaue had forty thousand liues:
One is too poore, too weake for my reuenge.
Now do I see 'tis true. Looke heere Iago,
All my fond loue thus do I blow to Heauen. 'Tis gone,
Arise blacke vengeance, from the hollow hell,
Yeeld vp (O Loue) thy Crowne, and hearted Throne
To tyrannous Hate. Swell bosome with thy fraught,
For 'tis of Aspickes tongues.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Yet be content.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Oh blood, blood, blood.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Patience I say: your minde may change.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Neuer Iago. Like to the Ponticke Sea,
Whose Icie Current, and compulsiue course,
Neu'r keepes retyring ebbe, but keepes due on
To the Proponticke, and the Hellespont:
Euen so my bloody thoughts, with violent pace
Shall neu'r looke backe, neu'r ebbe to humble Loue,
Till that a capeable, and wide Reuenge
Swallow them vp. Now by yond Marble Heauen,
In the due reuerence of a Sacred vow,
I heere engage my words.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Do not rise yet:
Witnesse you euer-burning Lights aboue,
You Elements, that clip vs round about,
Witnesse that heere Iago doth giue vp
The execution of his wit, hands, heart,
To wrong'd Othello's Seruice. Let him command,
And to obey shall be in me remorse,
What bloody businesse euer.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I greet thy loue,
Not with vaine thanks, but with acceptance bounteous,
And will vpon the instant put thee too't.
Within these three dayes let me heare thee say,
That Cassio's not aliue.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: My Friend is dead:
'Tis done at your Request.
But let her liue.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Damne her lewde Minx:
O damne her, damne her.
Come go with me a-part, I will withdraw
To furnish me with some swift meanes of death
For the faire Diuell.
Now art thou my Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I am your owne for euer.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Do you know Sirrah, where Lieutenant Cassio lyes?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I dare not say he lies any where.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Why man?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: He's a Soldier, and for me to say a Souldier lyes, 'tis stabbing.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Go too: where lodges he?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: To tell you where he lodges, is to tel you where I lye.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Can any thing be made of this?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I know not where he lodges, and for mee to deuise a lodging, and say he lies heere, or he lies there, were to lye in mine owne throat.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Can you enquire him out? and be edified by report?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I will Catechize the world for him, that is, make Questions, and by them answer.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Seeke him, bidde him come hither: tell him, I haue moou'd my Lord on his behalfe, and hope all will be well.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: To do this, is within the compasse of mans Wit, and therefore I will attempt the doing it.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Where should I loose the Handkerchiefe, Aemilia?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: I know not Madam.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Beleeue me, I had rather haue lost my purse
Full of Cruzadoes. And but my Noble Moore
Is true of minde, and made of no such basenesse,
As iealious Creatures are, it were enough
To put him to ill-thinking.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Is he not iealious?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Who, he? I thinke the Sun where he was borne,
Drew all such humors from him.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Looke where he comes.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I will not leaue him now, till Cassio be
Call'd to him. How is't with you, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Well my good Lady. Oh hardnes to dissemble!
How do you, Desdemona?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Well, my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Giue me your hand.
This hand is moist my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: It hath felt no age, nor knowne no sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: This argues fruitfulnesse, and liberall heart:
Hot, hot, and moyst. This hand of yours requires
A sequester from Liberty: Fasting, and Prayer,
Much Castigation, Exercise deuout,
For heere's a yong, and sweating Diuell heere
That commonly rebels: 'Tis a good hand,
A franke one.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: You may (indeed) say so:
For 'twas that hand that gaue away my heart.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: A liberall hand. The hearts of old, gaue hands:
But our new Heraldry is hands, not hearts.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I cannot speake of this:
Come, now your promise.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: What promise, Chucke?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I haue sent to bid Cassio come speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I haue a salt and sorry Rhewme offends me:
Lend me thy Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Heere my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: That which I gaue you.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I haue it not about me.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Not?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: No indeed, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: That's a fault: That Handkerchiefe
Did an Aegyptian to my Mother giue:
She was a Charmer, and could almost read
The thoughts of people. She told her, while she kept it,
'T would make her Amiable, and subdue my Father
Intirely to her loue: But if she lost it,
Or made a Guift of it, my Fathers eye
Should hold her loathed, and his Spirits should hunt
After new Fancies. She dying, gaue it me,
And bid me (when my Fate would haue me W^u'd)
To giue it her. I did to; and take heede on't,
Make it a Darling, like your precious eye:
To loose't, or giue't away, were such perdition,
As nothing else could match.

speeches.speaker: Des,
prose: Is't possible?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: 'Tis true: There's Magicke in the web of it:
A Sybill that had numbred in the world
The Sun to course, two hundred compasses,
In her Prophetticke furie sow'd the Worke:
The Wormes were hallowed, that did breede the Silke,
And it was dyde in Mummey, which the Skilfull
Conseru'd of Maidens hearts.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Indeed? Is't true?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Most veritable, therefore looke too't well.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Then would to Heauen, that I had neuer seene't?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Ha? wherefore?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Why do you speake so startingly and rash?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Is't lost? Is't gon? Speak, is't out o' th' way?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Blesse vs.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Say you?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: It is not lost: but what and if it were?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I say it is not lost.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Fetcht, let me see't.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Why so I can: but I will not now:
This is a tricke to put me from my suite,
Pray you let Cassio be receiu'd againe.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Fetch me the Handkerchiefe,
My minde mis-giues.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Come, come: you'l neuer meete a more sufficient man.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: The Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: A man that all his time
Hath founded his good Fortunes on your loue;
Shar'd dangers with you.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: The Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Insooth, you are too blame.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Away.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Is not this man iealious?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I neu'r saw this before.
Sure, there's some wonder in this Handkerchikfe,
I am most vnhappy in the losse of it.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: 'Tis not a yeare or two shewes vs a man:
They are all but Stomackes, and we all but Food,
They eate vs hungerly, and when they are full
They belch vs.
Looke you, Cassio and my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: There is no other way: 'tis she must doo't:
And loe the happinesse: go, and importune her.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: How now (good Cassio) what's the newes with you?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Madam, my former suite. I do beseech you,
That by your vertuous meanes, I may againe
Exist, and be a member of his loue,
Whom I, with all the Office of my heart
Intirely honour, I would not be delayd.
If my offence, be of such mortall kinde,
That nor my Seruice past, nor present Sorrowes,
Nor purpos'd merit in futurity,
Can ransome me into his loue againe,
But to know so, must be my benefit:
So shall I cloath me in a forc'd content,
And shut my selfe vp in some other course
To Fortunes Almes.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Alas (thrice-gentle Cassio)
My Aduocation is not now in Tune;
My Lord, is not my Lord; nor should I know him,
Were he in Fauour, as in Humour alter'd.
So helpe me euery spirit sanctified,
As I haue spoken for you all my best,
And stood within the blanke of his displeasure
For my free speech. You must awhile be patient:
What I can do, I will: and more I will
Then for my selfe, I dare. Let that suffice you.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Is my Lord angry?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: He went hence but now:
And certainly in strange vnquietnesse.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Can he be angry? I haue seene the Cannon
When it hath blowne his Rankes into the Ayre,
And like the Diuell from his very Arme
Puff't his owne Brother: And is he angry?
Something of moment then: I will go meet him,
There's matter in't indeed, if he be angry.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I prythee do so. Something sure of State,
Either from Venice, or some vnhatch'd practise
Made demonstrable heere in Cyprus, to him,
Hath pudled his cleare Spirit: and in such cases,
Mens Natures wrangle with inferiour things,
Though great ones are their obiect. 'Tis euen so.
For let our finger ake, and it endues
Our other healthfull members, euen to a sense
Of paine. Nay, we must thinke men are not Gods,
Nor of them looke for such obseruancie
As fits the Bridall. Beshrew me much, Aemilia,
I was (vnhandsome Warrior, as I am)
Arraigning his vnkindnesse with my soule:
But now I finde, I had suborn'd the Witnesse,
And he's Indited falsely.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Pray heauen it bee
State matters, as you thinke, and no Conception,
Nor no Iealious Toy, concerning you.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Alas the day, I neuer gaue him cause.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: But Iealious soules will not be answer'd so;
They are not euer iealious for the cause,
But iealious, for they're iealious. It is a Monster
Begot vpon it selfe, borne on it selfe.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Heauen keepe the Monster from Othello's mind.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Lady, Amen.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I will go seeke him. Cassio, walke heere about:
If I doe finde him fit, Ile moue your suite,
And seeke to effect it to my vttermost.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: I humbly thanke your Ladyship.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: 'Saue you (Friend Cassio.)

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: What make you from home?
How is't with you, my most faire Bianca?
Indeed (sweet Loue) I was comming to your house.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: And I was going to your Lodging, Cassio.
What? keepe a weeke away? Seuen dayes, and Nights?
Eight score eight houres? And Louers absent howres
More tedious then the Diall, eight score times?
Oh weary reck'ning.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Pardon me, Bianca:
I haue this while with leaden thoughts beene prest,
But I shall in a more continuate time
Strike off this score of absence. Sweet Bianca
Take me this worke out.

speeches.speaker: Bianca.
verse: Oh Cassio, whence came this?
This is some Token from a newer Friend,
To the felt-Absence: now I feele a Cause:
Is't come to this? Well, well.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: Go too, woman:
Throw your vilde gesses in the Diuels teeth,
From whence you haue them. You are iealious now,
That this is from some Mistris, some remembrance;
No, in good troth Bianca.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Why, who's is it?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: I know not neither:
I found it in my Chamber,
I like the worke well; Ere it be demanded
(As like enough it will) I would haue it coppied:
Take it, and doo't, and leaue me for this time.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Leaue you? Wherefore?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: I do attend heere on the Generall,
And thinke it no addition nor my wish
To haue him see me woman'd.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Why, I ptay you?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Not that I loue you not.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: But that you do not loue me.
I pray you bring me on the way a little,
And say, if I shall see you soone at night?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: 'Tis but a little way that I can bring you,
For I attend heere: But Ile see you soone.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: 'Tis very good: I must be circumstanc'd.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Will you thinke so?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Thinke so, Iago?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What, to kisse in priuate?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: An vnauthoriz'd kisse?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Or to be naked with her Friend in bed,
An houre, or more, not meaning any harme?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Naked in bed (Iago) and not meane harme?
It is hypocrisie against the Diuell:
They that meane vertuously, and yet do so,
The Diuell their vertue tempts, and they tempt Heauen.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: If they do nothing, 'tis a Veniall slip:
But if I giue my wife a Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: What then?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Why then 'tis hers (my Lord) and being hers,
She may (I thinke) bestow't on any man.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: She is Protectresse of her honor too:
May she giue that?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Her honor is an Essence that's not seene,
They haue it very oft, that haue it not.
But for the Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: By heauen, I would most gladly haue forgot it:
Thou saidst (oh, it comes ore my memorie,
As doth the Rauen o're the infectious house:
Boading to all) he had my Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I: what of that?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: That's not so good now.

speeches.speaker: Iag.
verse: What if I had said, I had seene him do you wrong?
Or heard him say (as Knaues be such abroad,
Who hauing by their owne importunate suit,
Or voluntary dotage of some Mistris,
Conuinced or supply'd them cannot chuse
But they must blab.)

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Hath he said any thing?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: He hath (my Lord) but be you well assur'd,
No more then he'le vn-sweare.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: What hath he said?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why, that he did: I know not what he did.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: What? What?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Lye.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: With her?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: With her? On her: what you will.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Lye with her? lye on her? We say lye on her, when they be-lye-her. Lye with her: that's fullsome: Handkerchiefe: Confessions: Handkerchiefe. To confesse, and be hang'd for his labour. First, to be hang'd, and then to confesse: I tremble at it. Nature would not inuest her selfe in such shadowing passion, without some Instruction. It is not words that shakes me thus, (pish) Noses, Eares, and Lippes: is't possible. Confesse? Handkerchiefe? O diuell.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Worke on,
My Medicine workes. Thus credulous Fooles are caught,
