And many worthy, and chast Dames euen thus,
(All guiltlesse) meete reproach: what hoa? My Lord?
My Lord, I say: Othello.
How now Cassio?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: My Lord is falne into an Epilepsie,
This is his second Fit: he had one yesterday.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Rub him about the Temples.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: The Lethargie must haue his quyet course:
If not, he foames at mouth: and by and by
Breakes out to sauage madnesse. Looke, he stirres:
Do you withdraw your selfe a little while,
He will recouer straight: when he is gone,
I would on great occasion, speake with you.
How is it Generall? Haue you not hurt your head?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Dost thou mocke me?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I mocke you not, by Heauen:
Would you would beare your Fortune like a Man.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: A Horned man's a Monster, and a Beast.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Ther's many a Beast then in a populous Citty,
And many a ciuill Monster.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Did he confesse it?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Good Sir, be a man:
Thinke euery bearded fellow that's but yoak'd
May draw with you. There's Millions now aliue,
That nightly lye in those vnproper beds,
Which they dare sweare peculiar. Your case is better.
Oh, 'tis the spight of hell, the Fiends Arch-mock,
To lip a wanton in a secure Cowch;
And to suppose her chast. No, let me know,
And knowing what I am, I know what she shall be.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Oh, thou art wise: 'tis certaine.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Stand you a while apart,
Confine your selfe but in a patient Lis^,
Whil'st you were heere, o're-whelmed with your griefe
(A passion most resulting such a man)
Cassio came hither. I shifted him away,
And layd good scuses vpon your Extasie,
Bad him anon returne: and heere speake with me,
The which he promis'd. Do but encaue your selfe,
And marke the Fleeres, the Gybes, and notable Scornes
That dwell in euery Region of his face.
For I will make him tell the Tale anew;
Where, how, how oft, how long ago, and when
He hath, and is againe to cope your wife.
I say, but marke his gesture: marry Patience,
Or I shall say y' are all in all in Spleene,
And nothing of a man.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Do'st thou heare, Iago,
I will be found most cunning in my Patience:
But (do'st thou heare) most bloody.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: That's not amisse,
But yet keepe time in all: will you withdraw?
Now will I question Cassio of Bianca,
A Huswife, that by selling her desires
Buyes her selfe Bread, and Cloath. It is a Creature
That dotes on Cassio, (as 'tis the Strumpets plague
To be-guile many, and be be-guil'd by one)
He, when he heares of her, cannot restraine
From the excesse of Laughter. Heere he comes.
As he shall smile, Othells shall go mad:
And his vnbookish Ielousie must conserue
Poore Cassio's smiles, gestures, and light behauiours
Quite in the wrong. How do you Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: The worser, that you giue me the addition,
Whose want euen killes me.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Ply Desdemona well, and you are sure on't:
Now, if this Suit lay in Bianca's dowre,
How quickely should you speed?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Alas poore Caitiffe.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Looke how he laughes already.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I neuer knew woman loue man so.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Alas poore Rogue, I thinke indeed she loues me.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Now he denies it faintly: and laughes it out.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Do you heare Cassio?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Now he importunes him
To tell it o're: go too, well said, well said.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: She giues it out, that you shall marry her.
Do you intend it?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Do ye triumph, Romaine? do you triumph?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I marry. What? A customer; prythee beare
Some Charitie to my wit, do not thinke it
So vnwholesome. Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: So, so, so, so: they laugh, that winnes.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why the cry goes, that you marry her.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Prythee say true.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I am a very Villaine else.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Haue you scoar'd me? Well.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: This is the Monkeys owne giuing out:
She is perswaded I will marry her
Out of her owne loue & flattery, not out of my promise.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Iago becomes me: now he begins the story.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: She was heere euen now: she haunts me in euery place. I was the other day talking on the Sea-banke with certaine Venetians, and thither comes the Bauble, and falls me thus about my neck.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Crying oh deere Cassio, as it were: his iesture imports it.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: So hangs, and lolls, and weepes vpon me:
So shakes, and pulls me. Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Now he tells how she pluckt him to my Chamber: oh, I see that nose of yours, but not that dogge, I shall throw it to.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Well, I must leaue her companie.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Before me: looke where she comes.

speeches.speaker: Cas
verse: 'Tis such another Fitchew: marry a perfum'd one?
What do you meane by this haunting of me?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Let the diuell, and his dam haunt you: what did you meane by that same Handkerchiefe, you gaue me euen now? I was a fine Foole to take it: I must take out the worke? A likely piece of worke, that you should finde it in your Chamber, and know not who left it there. This is some Minxes token, & I must take out the work^? There, giue it your Hobbey-horse, wheresoeuer you had it, Ile take out no worke on't.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: How now, my sweete Bianca?
How now? How now?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: By Heauen, that should be my Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: If you'le come to supper to night you may, if you will not, come when you are next prepar'd for.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: After her: after her.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: I must, shee'l rayle in the streets else.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Will you sup there?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Yes, I intend so.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Well, I may chance to see you: for I would very fame speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Prythee come: will you?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Go too: say no more.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: How shall I murther him, Iago.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Did you perceiue how he laugh'd at his vice?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Oh, Iago.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: And did you see the Handkerchiefe?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Was that mine?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Yours by this hand: and to see how he prizes the foolish woman your wife: she gaue it him, and he hath giu'n it his whore.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I would haue him nine yeeres a killing:
A fine woman, a faire woman, a sweete woman?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Nay, you must forget that.

speeches.speaker: Othello.
prose: I, let her ^ot and perish, and be damn'd to night, for she shall not liue. No, my heart is turn'd to stone: I strike it, and it hurts my hand. Oh, the world hath not a sweeter Creature: she might lye by an Emperours side, and command him Taskes.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Nay, that's not your way.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Hang her, I do but say what she is: so delicate with her Needle: an admirable Musitian. Oh she will sing the Sauagenesse out of a Beare: of so high and plenteous wit, and inuention?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: She's the worse for all this.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Oh, a thousand, a thousand times:
And the^ of so gentle a condition?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I too gentle.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Nay that's certaine:
But yet the pitty of it, Iago: oh Iago, the pitty of it Iago.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: If you are so fond ouer her iniquitie: giue her pattent to offend, for if it touch not you, it comes neere no body.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I will chop her into Messes: Cuckold me?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Oh, 'tis foule in her.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: With mine Officer?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: That's fouler.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Get me some poyson, Iago, this night. Ile not expostulate with her: least her body and beautie vnprouide my mind againe: this night Iago.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Do it not with poyson, strangle her in her bed,
Euen the bed she hath contaminated.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Good, good:
The Iustice of it pleases: very good.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: And for Cassio, let me be his vndertaker:
You shall heare more by midnight.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Excellent good: What Trumpet is that same?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I warrant something from Venice,
'Tis Lodouico, this, comes from the Duke.
See, your wife's with him.

speeches.speaker: Lodo.
prose: Saue you worthy Generall.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: With all my heart Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: The Duke, and the Senators of Venice greet you.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: I kisse the Instrument of their pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: And what's the newes, good cozen Lodouico?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I am very glad to see you Signior:
Welcome to Cyprus.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: I thanke you: how do's Lieutenant Cassio?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Liues Sir,

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Cozen, there's falne betweene him, & my Lord,
An vnkind breach: but you shall make all well.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Are you sure of that?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: My Lord?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: This faile you not to do, as you will —

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: He did not call: he's busie in the paper,
Is there deuision 'twixt my Lord, and Cassio?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: A most vnhappy one: I would do much
T' attone them, for the loue I beare to Cassio.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Fire, and brimestone.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Are you wise?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: What is he angrie?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: May be th Letter mou'd him.
For as I thinke, they do command him home,
Deputing Cassio in his Gouernment.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Trust me, I am glad on't.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: My Lord?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: I am glad to see you mad.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Why, sweete Othello?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Diuell.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I haue not deseru'd this.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: My Lord, this would not be beleeu'd in Venice,
Though I should sweare I saw't. 'Tis very much,
Make her amends: she weepes.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Oh diuell, diuell:
If that the Earth could teeme with womans teares,
Each drop she falls, would proue a Crocodile:
Out of my sight.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I will not stay to offend you.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Truely obedient Lady:
I do beseech your Lordship call her backe.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: What would you with her, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: Who I, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: I, you did wish, that I would make her turne:
Sir, she can turne, and turne: and yet go on
And turne againe. And she can weepe, Sir, weepe.
And she's obedient: as you say obedient.
Very obedient: proceed you in your teares.
Concerning this Sir, (oh well-painted passion)
I am commanded home: get you away:
Ile send for you anon. Sir I obey the Mandate,
And will returne to Venice. Hence, auaunt:
Cassio shall haue my Place. And Sir, to night
I do entreat, that we may sup together.
You are welcome Sir to Cyprus.
Goates, and Monkeys.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Is this the Noble Moore, whom our full Senate
Call all in all sufficient? Is this the Nature
Whom Passion could not shake? Whose solid vertue
The shot of Accident, nor dart of Chance
Could neither graze, nor pierce?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: He is much chang'd.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: Are his wits safe? Is he not light of Braine?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: He's that he is: I may not breath my censure.
What he might be: if what he might, he is not,
I would to heauen he were.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: What? Strike his wife?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: 'Faith that was not so well: yet would I knew
That stroke would proue the worst.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Is it his vse?
Or did the Letters, worke vpon his blood,
And new create his fault?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Alas, alas:
It is not honestie in me to speake
What I haue seene, and knowne. You shall obserue him,
And his owne courses will deonte him so,
That I may saue my speech: do but go after
And marke how he continues.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: I am sorry that I am deceiu'd in him.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: You haue seene nothing then?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Nor euer heard: nor euer did suspect.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Yes; you haue seene Cassio, and she together.

speeches.speaker: Aemi.
verse: But then I saw no harme: and then I heard,
Each syllable that breath made vp betweene them.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: What? Did they neuer whisper?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Neuer my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Nor send you out o' th' way?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Neuer.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: To fetch her Fan, her Gloues, her Mask, nor nothing?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Neuer my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: That's strange.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: I durst (my Lord) to wager, she is honest:
Lay downe my Soule at stake: If you thinke other,
Remoue your thought. It doth abuse your bosome:
If any wretch haue put this in your head,
Let Heauen requit it with the Serpents curse,
For if she be not honest, chaste, and true,
There's no man happy. The purest of their Wiues
Is foule as Slander.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Bid her come hither: go.
She saies enough: yet she's a simple Baud
That cannot say as much. This is a subtile Whore:
A Closset Locke and Key of Villanous Secrets,
And yet she'le kneele, and pray: I haue seene her do't.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: My Lord, what is your will?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Pray you Chucke come hither.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: What is your pleasure?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Let me see your eyes: looke in my face.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: What horrible Fancie's this?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Some of your Function Mistris:
Leaue Procreants alone, and shut the doore:
Cough, or cry hem; if any body come:
Your Mystery, your Mystery: May dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Vpon my knee, what doth your speech import.
I vnderstand a Fury in your words.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Why? What art thou?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Your wife my Lord: your true and loyall wife.

speeches.speaker: Othello.
prose: Come sweare it: damne thy selfe, least being like one of Heauen, the diuells themselues should feare to ceaze thee. Therefore be double damn'd: sweare thou art honest.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Heauen doth truely know it.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Heauen truely knowes, that thou art false as hell.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: To whom my Lord?
With whom? How am I false?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Ah Desdemon, away, away, away.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Alas the heauy day: why do you weepe?
Am I the motiue of these teares my Lord?
If happely you my Father do suspect,
An Instrument of this your calling backe,
Lay not your blame on me: if you haue lost him,
I haue lost him too.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Had^t pleas'd Heauen,
To try me with Affliction, had they rain'd
All kind of Sores, and Shames on my bare-head:
Steep'd me in pouertie to the very lippes,
Giuen to Captiuitie, me, and my vtmost hopes,
I should haue found in some place of my Soule
A drop of patience. But alas, to make me
The fixed Figure for the time of Scorne,
To point his slow, and mouing finger at.
Yet could I beare that too, well, very well:
But there where I haue garnerd vp my heart,
Where either I must liue, or beare no life,
The Fountaine from the which my currant runnes,
Or else dries vp: to be discarded thence,
Or keepe it as a Cesterne, for foule Toades
To knot and gender in. Turne thy complexion there:
Patience, thou young and Rose-lip'd Cherubin,
I heere looke grim as hell.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I hope my Noble Lord esteemes me honest.

speeches.speaker: Oth^.
verse: Oh I, as Sommer Flyes are in the Shambles,
That quicken euen with blowing. Oh thou weed:
Who art so louely faire, and smell'st so sweete,
That the Sense akes at thee,
Would thou had'st neuer bin borne.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Alas, what ignorant sin haue I committed?

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: Was this faire Paper? This most goodly Booke
Made to write Whore vpon? What commited,
Committed? Oh, thou publicke Commoner,
I should make very Forges of my cheekes,
That would to Cynders burne vp Modestie,
Did I but speake thy deedes. What commited?
Heauen stoppes the Nose at it, and the Moone winks:
The baudy winde that kisses all it meetes,
Is hush'd within the hollow Myne of Earth
And will not hear't. What commited?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: By Heauen you do me wrong.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Are not you a Strumpet?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: No, as I am a Christian.
If to preserue this vessell for my Lord,
From any other foule vnlawfull touch
Be not to be a Strumpet, I am none.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: What, not a Whore?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: No, as I shall be sau'd.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
prose: Is't possible?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Oh Heauen forgiue vs.

speeches.speaker: Othe.
verse: I cry you mercy then.
I tooke you for that cunning Whore of Venice,
That married with Othello. You Mistris,
That haue the office opposite to Saint Peter,
And keepes the gate of hell. You, you: I you.
We haue done our course: there's money for your paines:
I pray you turne the key, and keepe our counsaile.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Alas, what do'^ this Gentleman conceiue?
How do you Madam? how do you my good Lady?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Faith, halfe a sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Aemi.
verse: Good Madam,
What's the matter with my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: With who?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Why, with my Lord, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Who is thy Lord?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: He that is yours, sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I haue none: do not talke to me, Aemilia,
I cannot weepe: nor answeres haue I none,
But what should go by water. Prythee to night,
Lay on my bed my wedding sheetes, remember,
And call thy husband hither.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Heere's a change indeed.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: 'Tis meete I should be vs'd so: very meete.
How haue I bin behau'd, that he might sticke
The small'st opinion on my least misvse?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: What is your pleasure Madam?
How is't with you?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I cannot tell: those that do teach yong Babes
Do it with gentle meanes, and easie taskes.
He might haue chid me so: for in good faith
I am a Child to chiding.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What is the matter Lady?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Alas (Iago) my Lord hath so bewhor'd her,
Throwne such dispight, and heauy termes vpon her
That true hear^s cannot beare it.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Am I that name, Iago?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What name (faire Lady?)

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Such as she said my Lord did say I was.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: He call'd her whore: a Begger in his drinke:
Could not haue laid such termes vpon his Callet.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why did he so?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I do not know: I am sure I am none such.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Do not weepe, do not weepe: alas the day.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Hath she forsooke so many Noble Matches?
Her Father? And her Country? And her Friends?
To be call'd Whore? Would it not make one weepe?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: It is my wretched Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Beshrew him for't:
How comes this Tricke vpon him?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Nay, Heauen doth know.

speeches.speaker: Aemi.
verse: I will be hang'd, if some eternall Villaine,
Some busie and insinuating Rogue,
Some cogging, cozening Slaue, to get some Office,
Haue not deuis'd this Slander: I will be hang'd else.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Fie, there is no such man: it is impossible.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: If any such there be, Heauen pardon him.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: A halter pardon him:
And hell gnaw his bones.
Why should he call her Whore?
Who keepes her companie?
What Place? What Time?
What Forme? What liklyhood?
The Moore's abus'd by some most villanous Knaue,
Some base notorious Knaue, some scuruy Fellow.
Oh Heauens, that such companions thou'd'st vnfold,
And put in euery honest hand a whip
To lash the Rascalls naked through the world,
Euen from the East to th' West.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Speake within doore.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Oh fie vpon them: some such Squire he was
That turn'd your wit, the seamy-side without,
And made you to suspect me with the Moore.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: You are a Foole: go too.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Alas Iago,
What shall I do to win my Lord againe?
Good Friend, go to him: for by this light of Heauen,
I know not how I lost him. Heere I kneele:
If ere my will did trespasse 'gainst his Loue,
Either in discourse of thought, or actuall deed,
Or that mine Eyes, mine Eares, or any Sence
Delighted them: or any other Forme.
Or that I do not yet, and euer did,
And euer will, (though he do shake me off
To beggerly diuorcement) Loue him deerely,
Comfort forsweare me. Vnkindnesse may do much,
And his vnkindnesse may defeat my life,
But neuer taynt my Loue. I cannot say Whore,
It do's abhorre me now I speake the word,
To do the Act, that might the addition earne,
Not the worlds Masse of vanitie could make me.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I pray you be content: 'tis but his humour:
The businesse of the State do's him offence.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: If 'twere no other.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: It is but so, I warrant,
Hearke how these Instruments summon to supper:
The Messengers of Venice staies the meate,
Go in, and weepe not: all things shall be well.
How now Rodorigo?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I do not finde
That thou deal'st iustly with me.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What in the contrarie?

speeches.speaker: Rodori.
prose: Euery day thou dafts me with some deuise Iago, and rather, as it seemes to me now, keep'st from me all conueniencie, then suppliest me with the least aduantage of hope: I will indeed no longer endure it. Nor am I yet perswaded to put vp in peace, what already I haue foolishly suffred.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Will you heare me Rodorigo?

speeches.speaker: Rodori.
prose: I haue heard too much: and your words and Performances are no kin together.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: You charge me most vniustly.

speeches.speaker: Rodo.
prose: With naught but truth: I haue wasted my selfe out of my meanes. The Iewels you haue had from me to deliuer Desdemona, would halfe haue corrupted a Votarist. You haue told me she hath receiu'd them, and return'd me expectations and comforts of sodaine respect, and acquaintance, but I finde none.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Well, go too: very well.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Very well. go too: I cannot go too, (man) nor tis not very well. Nay I think it is scuruy: and begin to finde my selfe fopt in it.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Very well.

speeches.speaker: Rodor.
prose: I tell you, 'tis not very well: I will make my selfe knowne to Desdemona. If she will returne me my Iewels, I will giue ouer my Suit, and repent my vnlawfull solicitation. If not, assure your selfe, I will seeke satisfaction of you.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: You haue said now.

speeches.speaker: Rodo.
prose: I: and said nothing but what I protest intendment of doing.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why, now I see there's mettle in thee: and euen from this instant do build on thee a better opinion then euer before: giue me thy ^and Rodorigo. Thou hast taken against me a most iust exception: but yet I protest I haue dealt most directly in thy Affaire.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: It hath not appeer'd.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I grant indeed it hath not appeer'd: and your suspition is not without wit and iudgement. But Rodorigo, if thou hast that in thee indeed, which I haue greater reason to. beleeue now then euer (I meane purpose, Courage, and Valour) this night shew it. If thou the next night following enioy not Desdemona, take me from this world with Treacherie, and deuise Engines for my life.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Well: what is it? Is it within, reason and compasse?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Sir, there is especiall Commission come from Venice to depute Cassio in Othello's place.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Is that true? Why then Othello and Desdemona returne againe to Venice.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Oh no: he goes into Mauritania and taketh away with him the faire Desdemona, vnlesse his abode be lingred heere by some accident. Wherein none can be so determinate, as the remouing of Cassio.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: How do you meane remouing him?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Why, by making him vncapable of Othello's place: knocking out his braines.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: And that you would haue me to do.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I: if you dare do your selfe a profit, and a right. He sups to night with a Harlotry: and thither will I go to him. He knowes not yet of his Honourable Fortune, if you will watch his going thence (which I will fashion to fall out betweene twelue and one) you may take him at your pleasure. I will be neere to second your Attempt, and he shall fall betweene vs. Come, stand not amaz'd at it, but go along with me: I will shew you such a necessitie in his death, that you shall thinke your selfe bound to put it on him. It is now high supper time: and the night growes to wast. About it.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: I will heare further reason for this.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: And you shalbe satisfi'd.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: I do beseech you Sir, trouble your selfe no further.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Oh pardon me: 'twill do me good to walke.

speeches.speaker: Lodoui.
prose: Madam, good night: I humbly thanke your Ladyship.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Your Honour is most welcome.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Will you walke Sir? Oh Desdemona.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Othello.
prose: Get you to bed on th' instant, I will be return'd forth with: dismisse your Attendant there: look't be done.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I will my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Aem.
prose: How goes it now? He lookes gentler then he did.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: He saies he will returne incontinent,
And hath commanded me to go to bed,
And bid me to dismisse you.

speeches.speaker: Aemi.
prose: Dismisse me?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: It was his bidding: therefore good Aemilia,
Giue me my nightly wearing. and adieu.
We must not now displease him.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: I, would you had neuer seene him.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: So would not I: my loue doth so approue him,
That euen his stubbornesse, his checks, his frownes,
(Prythee vn-pin me) haue grace and fauour.

speeches.speaker: Aemi.
prose: I haue laid those Sheetes you bad me on the bed.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: All's one: good Father, how foolish are our minds?
If I do die before, prythee shrow'd me
In one of these same Sheetes.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Come, come: you talke.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: My Mother had a Maid call'd Barbarie,
She was in loue: and he she lou'd prou'd mad,
And did forsake her. She had a Song of Willough,
An old thing 'twas: but it express'd her Fortune,
And she dy'd singing it. That Song to night,
Will not go from my mind: I haue much to do,
But to go hang my head all at one side
And sing it like poore Brabarie: prythee dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Aemi.
prose: Shall I go fetch your Night-gowne?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: No. va-pin me here,
This Lodouico is a proper man.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: A very handsome man.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: He speakes well.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: I know a Lady in Venice would haue walk'd barefoot to Palestine for a touch of his nether lip.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: The poore Soule sat singing, by a Sicamour tree.
Sing all a greene Willough:
Her hand on her bosome her head on her knee,
Sing Willough, Willough, Willough.
The fresh Streames ran by her, and murmur'd her moanes
Sing Willough, &c.
Her salt teares fell from her, and softned the stones,
Sing Willough, &c. (Lay by these)
Willough, Willough. (Prythee high thee: he'le come anon)
Sing all a greene Willough must be my Garland.
Let no body blame him, his scorne I approue.
(Nay that's not next. Harke, who is't that knocks?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: It's the wind.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I call'd my Loue false Loue: but what said he then?
Sing Willough, &c.
If I court mo women, you'le couch with mo men.
So get thee gone, good night: mine eyes do itch:
Doth that boade weeping?

speeches.speaker: Aemil,
prose: 'Tis neyther heere, nor there.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: I haue heard it said so. O these Men, these men!
Do'st thou in conscience thinke (tell me Aemilia)
That there be women do abuse their husbands
In such grosse kinde?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: There be some such, no question.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Would'st thou do such a deed for all the world?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Why, would not you?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: No, by this Heauenly light.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Nor I neither, by this Heauenly light:
I might doo't as well i' th' darke.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Would'st thou do such a deed for al the world?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: The world's a huge thing:
It is a great price, for a small vice.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Introth, I thinke thou would'st not.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Introth I thinke I should, and vndoo't when I had done. Marry, I would not doe such a thing for a ioynt Ring, nor for measures of Lawne, nor for Gownes, Petticoats, nor Caps, nor any petty exhibition. But for all the whole world: why, who would not make her husband a Cuckold, to make him a Monarch? I should venture Purgatory for't.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Beshrew me, if I would do such a wrong
For the whole world.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Why, the wrong is but a wrong i' th' world; and hauing the world for your labour, 'tis a wrong in your owne world, and you might quickly make it right.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I do not thinke there is any such woman.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Yes, a dozen: and as many to' th' vantage, as would store the world they plaid for.
But I do thinke it is their Husbands faults
If Wiues do fall: (Say, that they slacke their duties,
And powre our Treasures into forraigne laps;
Or else breake out in peeuish Iealousies,
Throwing restraint vpon vs: Or say they strike vs,
Or scant our former hauing in despight)
Why we haue galles: and though we haue some Grace,
Yet haue we some Reuenge. Let Husbands know,
Their wiues haue sense like them: They see, and smell,
And haue their Palats both for sweet, and sowre,
As Husbands haue. What is it that they do,
When they change vs for others? Is it Sport?
I thinke it is: and doth Affection breed it?
I thinke it doth. Is't Frailty that thus erres?
It is so too. And haue not we Affections?
Desires for Sport? and Frailty, as men haue?
Then let them vse vs well: else let them know,
The illes we do, their illes instruct vs so.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Good night, good night:
Heauen me such vses send,
Not to picke bad, from bad; but by bad, mend.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Heere, stand behinde this Barke,
Straight will he come:
Weare thy good Rapier bare, and put it home:
Quicke, quicke, feare nothing; Ile be at thy Elbow,
It makes vs, or it marres vs, thinke on that,
And fixe most firme thy Resolution.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Be neere at hand, I may miscarry in't.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Heere, at thy hand: Be bold, & take thy stand.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I haue no great deuotion to the deed,
And yet he hath giuen me satisfying Reasons:
'Tis but a man gone. Forth my Sword: he dies.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I haue rub'd this yong Q^at almost to the sense,
And he growes angry. Now, whether he kill Cassio,
Or Cassio him, or each do kill the other,
Euery way makes my gaine. Liue Rodorigo,
He calles me to a restitution large
Of Gold, and Iewels, that I bob'd from him,
As Guifts to Desdemona.
It must not be: If Cassio do remaine,
He hath a dayly beauty in his life,
That makes me vgly: and besides, the Moore
May vnfold me to him: there stand I in much perill:
No, he must dye. But so, I heard him comming.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: I know his gate, 'tis he: Villaine thou dyest.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: That thrust had beene mine enemy indeed,
But that my Coate is better then thou know'st:
I will make proofe of thine.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Oh, I am slaine.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: I am maym'd for euer:
Helpe hoa: Murther, murther.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: The voyce of Cassio. Iago keepes his word.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: O Villaine that I am.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: It is euen so.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Oh helpe hoa: Light, a Surgeon.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: 'Tis he: O braue Iago, honest, and iust,
That hast such Noble sense of thy Friends wrong,
Thou teachest me. Minion, your deere lyes dead,
And your vnblest Fate highes: Strumpet I come:
For of my heart, those Charmes thine Eyes, are blotted.
Thy Bed lust-stain'd, shall with Lusts blood bee spotted.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: What hoa? no Watch? No passage?
Murther, Murther.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: 'Tis some mischance, the voyce is very direfull.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Oh helpe.

speeches.speaker: Lodo.
prose: Hearke.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Oh wretched Villaine.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Two or three groane. 'Tis heauy night;
These may be counterfeits: Let's think't vnsafe
To come into the cry, without more helpe.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: Nobody come: then shall I bleed to death.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: Hearke.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Here's one comes in his shirt, with Light, and Weapons.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Who's there?
Who's noyse is this that cries on murther?

speeches.speaker: Lodo.
prose: We do not know.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Do not you heare a cry?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Heere, heere: for heauen sake helpe me.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: This is Othello's Ancient, as I take it.

speeches.speaker: Lodo.
prose: The same indeede, a very valiant Fellow.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: What are you heere, that cry so greeuously?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Iago? Oh I am spoyl'd, vndone by Villaines:
Giue me some helpe.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: O mee, Lieutenant!
What Villaines haue done this?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I thinke that one of them is heereabout.
And cannot make away.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Oh treacherous Villaines:
What are you there? Come in, and giue some helpe.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: O helpe me there.

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: That's one of them.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Oh murd'rous Slaue! O Villaine!

speeches.speaker: Rod.
prose: O damn'd Iago! O inhumane Dogge.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Kill men i' th' darke?
Where be these bloody Theeues?
How silent is this Towne? Hoa, murther, murther.
What may you be? Are you of good, or euill?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: As you shall proue vs, praise vs.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Signior Lodouico?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: He Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I cry you mercy: here's Cassio hurt by Villaines.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Cassio?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: How is't Brother?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: My Legge is cut in two.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Marry heauen forbid:
Light Gentlemen, Ile binde it with my shirt.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: What is the matter hoa? Who is't that cry'd?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Who is't that cry'd?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Oh my deere Cassio,
My sweet Cassio: Oh Cassio, Cassio, Cassio.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: O notable Strumpet. Cassio, may you suspect
Who they should be, that haue thus mangled you?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
verse: I am sorry to finde you thus;
I haue beene to seeke you.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Lend me a Garter. So:—Oh for a Chaire
To beare him easily hence.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Alas he faints. Oh Cassio, Cassio, Cassio.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Gentlemen all, I do suspect this Trash
To be a party in this Iniurie.
Patience a while, good Cassio. Come, come;
Lend me a Light: know we this face, or no?
Alas my Friend, and my deere Countryman
Rodorigo? No: Yes sure: Yes, 'tis Rodorigo.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: What, of Venice?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Euen he Sir: Did you know him?

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Know him? I.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Signior Gratiano? I cry your gentle pardon:
These bloody accidents must excuse my Manners,
That so neglected you.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: I am glad to see you.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: How do you Cassio? Oh. a Chaire, a Chaire.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Rodorigo?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: He, he, 'tis he:
Oh that's well said, the Chaire.
Some good man beare him carefully from hence,
Ile fetch the Generall's Surgeon. For you Mistris,
Saue you your labour. He that lies slaine heere (Cassio)
Was my deere friend. What malice was between you?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: None in the world: nor do I know the man?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: What? looke you pale? Oh beare him o' th' Ayre.
Stay you good Gentlemen. Looke you pale, Mistris?
Do you perceiue the gastnesse of her eye?
Nay, if you stare, we shall heare more anon.
Behold her well: I pray you looke vpon her:
Do you see Gentlemen? Nay, guiltinesse will speake
Though tongues were out of vse.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Alas, what is the matter?
What is the matter, Husband?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Cassio hath heere bin set on in the darke
By Rodorigo, and Fellowes that are scap'd:
He's almost slaine, and Rodorigo quite dead.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Alas good Gentleman: alas good Cassio.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: This is the fruits of whoring. Prythe Aemilia,
Go know of Cassio where he supt to night.
What, do you shake at that?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: He supt at my house, but I therefore shake not.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: O did he so? I charge you go with me.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Oh fie vpon thee Strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: I am no Strumpet, but of life as honest,
As you that thus abuse me.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: As I? Fie vpon thee.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: Kinde Gentlemen:
Let's go see poore Cassio drest.
Come Mistris, you must tel's another Tale.
Aemilia, run you to the Cittadell,
And tell my Lord and Lady, what hath happ'd:
Will you go on afore? This is the night
That either makes me, or foredoes me quight.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: It is the Cause, it is the Cause (my Soule)
Let me not name it to you, you chaste Starres,
It is the Cause. Yet Ile not shed her blood,
Nor scarre that whiter skin of hers, then Snow.
And smooth as Monumentall Alablaster:
Yet she must dye, else shee'l betray more men:
Put out the Light, and then put out the Light:
If I quench thee, thou flaming Minister,
I can againe thy former light restore,
Should I repent me. But once put out thy Light,
Thou cunning'st Patterne of excelling Nature,

I know not where is that Promethae^
heate
That can thy Light re-Lume.
When I haue pluck'd thy Rose,
I cannot giue it vitall growth againe,
It needs must wither. Ile smell thee on the Tree.
Oh Balmy breath, that dost almost perswade
Iustice to breake her Sword. One more, one more:
Be thus when thou art dead, and I will kill thee,
And loue thee after. One more, and that's the last.
So sweet, was ne're so fatall. I must weepe,
But they are cruell Teares: This sorrow's heauenly,
It strikes, where it doth loue. She wakes.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Who's there? Othello?

speeches.speaker: Othel.
prose: I Desdemona.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Will you come to bed, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Haue you pray'd to night, Desdemon?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: If you bethinke your selfe of any Crime
Vnreconcil'd as yet to Heauen, and Grace,
Solicite for it straight.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: Alacke, my Lord,
What may you meane by that?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Well, do it, and be breefe, I will walke by:
I would not kill thy vnprepared Spirit,
No, Heauens fore-fend) I would not kill thy Soule.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Talke you of killing?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I, I do.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Then Heauen haue mercy on mee.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Amen, with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: If you say, I hope you will not kill me.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Humh.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: And yet I feare you: for you're fatall then
When your eyes rowle so.
Why I should feare, I know not,
Since guiltinesse I know not: But yet I feele I feare.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Thinke on thy sinnes.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: They are Loue^ I beare to you.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I, and for that thou dy'st.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: That death's vnnaturall, that kils for louing.
Alas, why gnaw you so your nether-lip?
Some bloody passion shakes your very Frame:
These are portent^: but yet I hope, I hope,
They do not point on me.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Peace, and be still.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I will so: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: That Handkerchiefe
Which I so lou'd, and gaue thee, thou gau'st to Cassio.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: No by my Life, and Soule: send for the man,
And aske him.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Sweet Soule, take heed, take heed of Periury,
Thou art on thy death-bed.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: I, but not yet to dye.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Presently.
Therefore confesse thee freely of thy sinne:
For to deny each Article with Oath,
Cannot remoue, nor choake the strong Conception
That I do grone withall. Thou art to dye.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: O Heauen haue mercy on me.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I say, Amen.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: And haue you mercy too. I neuer did
Offend you in my life: neuer lou'd Cassio,
But with such generall warrantie of Heauen,
As I might loue. I neuer gaue him Token.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: By Heauen I saw my Handkerchiefe in's hand.
O periur'd woman, thou do'st stone my heart,
And makes me call, what I intend to do,
A Murther, which I thought a Sacrifice.
I saw the Handkerchiefe.

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: He found it then:
I neuer gaue it him: Send, for him hither:
Let him confesse a truth.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: He hath confest.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: What, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: That he hath vs'd thee.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: How? vnlawfully?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: He will not say so.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: No: his mouth is stopp'd:
Honest Iago hath 'tane order for't.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Oh, my feare interprets. What is he dead?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Had all his haires bin liues, my great Reuenge
Had stomacke for them all.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Alas, he is betray'd, and I vndone.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Out Strumpet: weep'st thou for him to my face?

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: O banish me, my Lord, but kill me not.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Downe Strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: Kill me to morrow, let me liue to night.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Nay, if you striue.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: But halfe an houre.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Being done, there is no pawse.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: But while I say one prayer.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: It is too late.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: My Lord, my Lord? What hoa?
My Lord, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: What noise is this? Not dead? not yet quite dead?
I that am cruell, am yet mercifull,
I would not haue thee linger in thy paine?
So, so.

speeches.speaker: Aemil. within.
prose: What hoa? my Lord, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Oh good my Lord, I would speake a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Yes: 'Tis Aemilia: by and by. Shee's dead.
'Tis like she comes to speake of Cassio's death:
The noise was high. Hah, no more moouing?
Still as the Graue. Shall ^he come in? Wer't good?
I thinke she stirres againe. No, what's best to do?
If she come in, shee'l sure speake to my wife:
My wife, my wife: what wife? I haue no wife.
Oh insupportable! Oh heauy houre!
Me thinkes, it should be now a huge Eclipse
Of Sunne, and Moone; and that th' affrighted Globe
Did yawne at Alteration.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: I do beseech you
That I may speake with you. Oh good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I had forgot thee: oh come in Aemilia.
Soft, by and by, let me the Curtaines draw.
Where art thou? What's the matter with thee now?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Oh my good Lord, yonders foule Murthers done.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: What? now?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: But now, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: It is the very error of the Moone,
She comes more neerer Earth then she was wont,
And makes men mad.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Cassio, my Lord, hath kill'd
A young Venetian, call'd Rodorigo.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Rodorigo kill'd? and Cassio kill'd?

speeches.speaker: Aemil
prose:
No.
Cassio is not kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Not Cassio kill'd? Then Murther's out of tune,
And sweet Reuenge growes harsh.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: O falsely, falsely murder'd.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Alas! what cry is that?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: That? What?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Out, and alas, that was my Ladies voice.
Helpe, helpe hoa, helpe. Oh Ladie speake againe,
Sweet Desdemona, oh sweet Mistris, speake.

speeches.speaker: Des.
prose: A guiltlesse death, I dye.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Oh who hath done this deed?

speeches.speaker: Des.
verse: No body: I my selfe, farewell:
Commend me to my kinde Lord: oh farewell.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Why, how should she be murdred?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Alas: who knowes?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: You heare her say her selfe, it was not I.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: She said so: I must needs report the truth.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: She's like a Liar gone to burning hell,
'Twas I that kill'd her.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Oh the more Angell she, and you the blacker Diuell.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: She turn'd to folly: and she was a whore.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: Thou do'st bely her, and thou art a diuell.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: She wa^ false as water.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Thou a^t rash as fire, to say
That she was false. Oh she was heauenly true.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Cassio did top her: Ask thy husband else.
O, I were damn'd beneath all depth in hell:
But that I did proceed vpon iust grounds
To this extremity. Thy Husband knew it all.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: My Husband?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Thy Husband.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: That she was false to Wedlocke?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I, with Cassio: had she bin true,
If Heauen would make me such another world,
Of one entyre and perfect Chrysolite,
I'ld not haue sold her for it.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: My Husband?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I, 'twas he that told me on her first,
An honest man he is, and hates the slime
That stickes on filthy deeds.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
prose: My Husband?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: What needs this itterance, Woman?
I say, thy Husband.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Oh Mistris,
Villany hath made mockes with loue:
My Husband say she was false?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: He, Woman;
I say thy Husband: Do'st vnderstand the word?
My Friend, thy Husband; honest, honest Iago.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: If he say so, may his pernicious Soule
Rot halfe a graine a day: he lyes to' th' heart,
She was too fond of her most filthy Bargaine.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Hah?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Do thy worst:
This deede of thine is no more worthy Heauen,
Then thou was't worthy her.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Peace, you were best.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Thou hast not halfe that powre to do me harm,
As I haue to be hurt. Oh Gull, oh dolt,
As ignorant as durt: thou hast done a deed
(I care not for thy Sword) Ile make thee known,
Though I lost twenty liues. Helpe, helpe, hoa, helpe:
The Moore hath kill'd my Mistris. Murther, murther.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: What is the matter? How now Generall?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Oh, are you come, Iago: you haue done well,
That men must lay their Murthers on your necke.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: What is the matter?

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: Disproue this Villaine, if thou bee'st a man:
He sayes, thou told'st him that his wife was false:
I know thou did'st not: thou'rt not such a Villain.
Speake, for my heart is full.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: I told him what I thought,
And told no more
Then what he found himselfe was apt, and true.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: But did you euer tell him,
She was false?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I did.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: You ^old a Lye an odious damned Lye:
Vpon my Soule, a Lye; a wicked Lye.
Shee false with Cassio?
Did you say with Cassio?

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: With Cassio, Mistris?
Go too, charme your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: I will not charme my Tongue;
I am bound to speake,
My Mistris heere lyes murthered in her bed.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Oh Heauens, foresend.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
prose: And your reports haue set the Murder on.

speeches.speaker: Othello.
verse: Nay stare not Masters,
It is true indeede.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: 'Tis a strange Truth.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: O monstrous Acte.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Villany, villany, villany:
I thinke vpon't, I thinke: I smel't: O Villany:
I thought so then: Ile kill my selfe for greefe.
O villany! villany!

speeches.speaker: Iago.
verse: What, are you mad?
I charge you get you home.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Good Gentlemen, let me haue leaue to speake:
'Tis proper I obey him; but not now:
Perchance Iago, I will ne're go home.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Oh, oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Nay, lay thee downe, and roare:
For thou hast kill'd the sweetest innocent,
That ere did lift vp eye.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Oh she was fowle!
I scarse did know you Vnkle, there lies your Neece,
Whose breath (indeed) these hands haue newly stopp'd:
I know this acte shewes horrible and grim.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
verse: Poore Desdemon:
I am glad thy Father's dead,
Thy Match was mortall to him: and pure greefe
Shore his old thred in twaine. Did he liue now,
This sight would make him do a desperate turne:
Yea, curse his better Angell from his side,
And fall to Reprobance.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: 'Tis pittifull: but yet Iago knowes
That she with Cassio, hath the Act of shame.
A thousand times committed. Cassio confest it,
And she did gratifie his amorous workes
With that Recognizance and pledge of Loue
Which I first gaue her: I saw it in his hand:
It was a Handkerchiefe, an Antique Token
My Father gaue my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
prose: Oh Heauen! oh heauenly Powres!

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Come, hold your peace.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: 'Twill out, 'twill out. I peace?
No, I will speake as liberall as the North;
Let Heauen, and Men, and Diuels, let them all,
All, all, crie shame against me, yet Ile speake.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Be wise, and get you home.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
prose: I will not.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Fye, your Sword vpon a Woman.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Oh thou dull Moore,
That Handkerchiefe thou speak'st of
I found by Fortune, and did giue my Husband:
For often, with a solemne earnestnesse,
(More then indeed belong'd to such a Trifle)
He begg'd of me, to steale't.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Villanous Whore.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: She giue it Cassio? No, alas I found it,
And I did giu't my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: Filth, thou lyest.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: By Heauen I do not, I do not Gentlemen:
Oh murd'rous Coxcombe, what should such a Foole
Do with so good a wife?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Are there no stones in Heauen,
But what serues for the Thunder?
Precious Villaine.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
verse: The woman falles:
Sure he hath kill'd his Wife.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
prose: I, I: oh lay me by my Mistris side.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Hee's gone, but his wife's kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: 'Tis a notorious Villain: take you this weapon
Which I haue recouer'd from the Moore:
Come guard the doore without, let him not passe,
But kill him rather. Ile after that same villaine,
For 'tis a damned Slaue.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I am not valiant neither:
But euery Punie whipster gets my Sword.
But why should Honor out-liue Honesty?
Let it go all.

speeches.speaker: Aemil.
verse: What did thy Song boad Lady?
Hearke, canst thou heare me? I will play the Swan,
And dye in Musicke: Willough, Willough, Willough.
Moore, she was chaste: She lou'd thee, cruell Moore,
So come my Soule to blisse, as I speake true:
So speaking as I thinke, alas, I dye.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I haue another weapon in this Chamber,
It was a Sword of Spaine, the Ice brookes temper:
Oh heere it is: Vnkle I must come forth.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
verse: If thou attempt it, it will cost thee deere;
Thou hast no weapon, and perforce must suffer.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Looke in vpon me then, and speake with me,
Or naked as I am I will assault thee.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: What is the matter?

speeches.speaker: Othel.
verse: Behold, I haue a weapon:
A better neuer did it selfe sustaine
Vpon a Soldiers Thigh. I haue seene the day,
That with this little Arme, and this good Sword,
I haue made my way through more impediments
Then twenty times your stop. But (oh vaine boast)
Who can controll his Fate? 'Tis not so now.
Be not affraid, though you do see me weapon'd:
Heere is my iournies end, heere is my butt
And verie Sea-marke of my vtmost Saile.
Do you go backe dismaid? 'Tis a lost feare:
Man but a Rush against Othello's brest,
And he retires. Where should Othello go?
Now: how dost thou looke now? Oh ill-Starr'd wench,
Pale as thy Smocke: when we shall meete at compt,
This looke of thine will hurle my Soule from Heauen,
And Fiends will snatch at it. Cold, cold, my Girle?
Euen like thy Chastity. O cursed, cursed Slaue!
Whip me ye Diuels,
From the possession of this Heauenly sight:
Blow me about in windes, roast me in Sulphure,
Wash me in steepe-downe gulfes of Liquid fire.
Oh Desdemon! dead Desdemon: dead. Oh, oh!

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: Where is this rash, and most vnfortunate man?

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: That's he that was Othello: heere I am.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Where is that Viper?
Bring the Villaine forth.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I look down towards his feet; but that's a Fable,
If that thou bee'st a Diuell, I cannot kill thee.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: Wrench his Sword from him.

speeches.speaker: Iago.
prose: I bleed Sir, but not kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Othel.
verse: I am not sorry neither, Il'd haue thee liue:
For in my sense, 'tis happinesse to die.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Oh thou Othello, that was once so good,
Falne in the practise of a cursed Slaue,
What shall be saide to thee.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Why any thing:
An honourable Murderer, if you will:
For nought I did in hate, but all in Honour.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: This wretch hath part confest his Villany:
Did you and he consent in Cassio's death.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
prose: Deere Generall, I neuer gaue you cause.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I do beleeue it, and I aske your pardon:
Will you, I pray, demand that demy-Diuell,
Why he hath thus ensnar'd my Soule and Body.

speeches.speaker: Iag.
verse: Demand me nothing: what you know, you know:
From this time forth, I neuer will speake word.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: What? not to pray?

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: Torments will ope your lips.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: Well, thou dost best.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Sir,
You shall vnderstand what hath befalne,
(Which, as I thinke, you know not) heere is a Letter
Found in the pocket of the slaine Rodorigo,
And heere another, the one of them imports
The death of Cassio, to be vndertooke
By Rodorigo.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
prose: O Villaine!

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
prose: Most Heathenish, and most grosse.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Now, heere's another discontented paper
Found in his pocket too: and this it seemes
Rodorigo meant t' haue sent this damned villaine:
But that (belike) Iago in the interim
Came in, and satisfi'd him.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Oh thou pernitious Caitiffe;
How came you (Cassio) by that Handkerchiefe
That was my wiues?

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: I found it in my Chamber:
And he himselfe confest it but euen now,
That there he dropt it for a speciall purpose,
Which wrought to his desire.

speeches.speaker: Othel.
prose: O Foole, foole, foole!

speeches.speaker: Cassio.
verse: There is besides, in Rodorigo's Letter,
How he vpbraides Iago, that he made him
Braue me vpon the Watch: whereon it came
That I was cast: and euen but now he spake
(After long seeming dead) Iago hurt him,
Iago set him on.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: You must forsake this roome, and go with vs:
Your Power, and your Command is taken off,
And Cassio rules in Cyprus. For this Slaue,
If there be any cunning Crueltie,
That can torment him much, and hold him long,
It shall be his. You shall close Prisoner rest,
Till that the Nature of your fault be knowne
To the Venetian State. Come, bring away.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: Soft you; a word or two before you goe:
I haue done the State some seruice, and they know't:
No more of that. I pray you in your Letters,
When you shall these vnluckie deeds relate,
Speake of me, as I am. Nothing extenuate,
Nor set downe ought in malice.
Then must you speake,
Of one that lou'd not wisely, but too well:
Of one, not easily Iealious, but being wrought,
Perplexed in the extreame: Of one, whose hand
(Like the base Iudean) threw a Pearle away
Richer then all his Tribe: Of one, whose subdu'd Eyes,
Albeit vn-vsed to the melting moode,
Drops teares as fast as the Arabian Trees
Their Medicinable gumme. Set you downe this:
And say besides, that in Aleppo once,
Where a malignant, and a Turbond-Turke
Beate a Venetian, and traduc'd the State,
I tooke by th' throat the circumcised Dogge,
And smoate him, thus.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: Oh bloody period.

speeches.speaker: Gra.
prose: All that is spoke, is marr'd.

speeches.speaker: Oth.
verse: I kist thee, ere I kill'd thee: No way but this,
Killing my selfe, to dye vpon a kisse.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: This did I feare, but thought he had no weapon:
For he was great of heart.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Oh Sparton Dogge:
More fell then Anguish, Hunger, or the Sea:
Looke on the Tragicke Loading of this bed:
This is thy worke:
The Obiect poysons Sight,
Let it be hid. Gratiano, keepe the house,
And seize vpon the Fortunes of the Moore,
For they succeede on you. To you, Lord Gouernor,
Remaines the Censure of this hellish villaine:
The Time, the Place, the Torture, oh inforce it:
My selfe will straight aboord, and to the State,
This heauie Act, with heauie heart relate.

plays.play_title: THE TRAGEDIE OF Anthonie, and Cleopatra.

speeches.speaker: Philo.
verse: NAy, but this dotage of our Generals
Ore-flowes the measure: those his goodly eyes
That o're the Files and Musters of the Warre,
Haue glow'd like plated Mars:
Now bend, now turne
The Office and Deuotion of their view
Vpon a Tawny Front. His Captaines heart,
Which in the scuffles of great Fights hath burst
The Buckles on his brest, reneages all temper,
And is become the Bellowes and the Fan
To coole a Gypsies Lust.
Looke where they come:
Take but good note, and you shall see in him
(The triple Pillar of the world) transform'd
Into a Strumpets Foole. Behold and see.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: If it be Loue indeed, tell me how much.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: There's beggery in the loue that can be reckon'd

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Ile set a bourne how farre to be belou'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Then must thou needes finde our new Heauen, new Earth.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
prose: Newes (my good Lord) from Rome.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Grates me, the summe.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Nay heare them Anthony.
Fuluia perchance is angry: Or who knowes,
If the scarse-bearded Caesar haue not sent
His powrefull Mandate to you. Do this, or this;
Take in that Kingdome, and Infranchise that:
Perform't, or else we damne thee.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: How, my Loue?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Perchance? Nay, and most like:
You must not stay heere longer, your dismission
Is come from Caesar, therefore heare it Anthony.
Where's Fuluias Processe? (Caesars I would say) both?
Call in the Messengers: As I am Egypts Queene,
Thou blushest Anthony, and that blood of thine
Is Caesars homager: else so thy cheeke payes shame,
When shrill-tongu'd Fuluia scolds. The Messengers.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let Rome in Tyber melt, and the wide Arch
Of the raing'd Empire fall: Heere is my space,
Kingdomes are clay: Our dungie earth alike
Feeds Beast as Man; the Noblenesse of life
Is to do thus: when such a mutuall paire,
And such a twaine can doo't in which I binde
One paine of punishment, the world to weete
We stand vp Peerelesse.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Excellent falshood:
Why did he marry Fuluia, and not loue her?
Ile seeme the Foole I am not. Anthony will be himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: But stirr'd by Cleopatra.
Now for the loue of Loue, and her soft houres,
Let's not confound the time with Conference harsh;
There's not a minute of our liues should stretch
Without some pleasure now. What sport to night?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Heare the Ambassadors.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Fye wrangling Queene:
Whom euery thing becomes, to chide, to laugh,
To weepe: who euery passion fully striues
To make it selfe (in Thee) faire, and admir'd.
No Messenger but thine, and all alone, to night
Wee'l wander through the streets, and note
The qualities of people. Come my Queene,
Last night you did desire it. Speake not to vs.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
prose: Is Caesar with Anthonius priz'd so slight?

speeches.speaker: Philo.
verse: Sir sometimes when he is not Anthony,
He comes too short of that great Property
Which still should go with Anthony.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
prose: I am full sorry, that hee approues the common Lyar, who thus speakes of him at Rome; but I will hope of better deeds to morrow. Rest you happy.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: L. Alexas, sweet Alexas, most any thing Alexas, almost most absolute Alexas, where's the Soothsayer that you prais'd so to' th' Queene? Oh that I knewe this Husband, which you say, must change his Hornes with Garlands.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Soothsayer.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: Your will?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Is this the Man? Is't you sir that know things?

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: In Natures infinite booke of Secrecie, a little I can read.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Shew him your hand.

speeches.speaker: Enob.
verse: Bring in the Banket quickly: Wine enough,
Cleopatra's health to drinke.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Good sir, giue me good Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: I make not, but foresee.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Pray then, foresee me one.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: You shall be yet farre fairer then you are.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: He meanes in flesh.

speeches.speaker: Iras.
prose: No, you shall paint when you are old.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Wrinkles forbid.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Vex not his prescience, be attentiue.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Hush.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: You shall be more belouing, then beloued.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I had rather heate my Liuer with drinking.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Nay, heare him.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Good now some excellent Fortune: Let mee be married to three Kings in a forenoone, and Widdow them all: Let me haue a Childe at fifty, to whom Herode of Iewry may do Homage. Finde me to marrie me with Octauius Caesar, and companion me with my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: You shall out-liue the Lady whom you serue.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Oh excellent, I loue long life better then Figs.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: You haue seene and proued a fairer former fortune, then that which is to approach.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Then belike my Children shall haue no names:
Prythee how many Boyes and Wenches must I haue.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: If euery of your wishes had a wombe, & foretell euery wish, a Million.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Out Foole, I forgiue thee for a Witch.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: You thinke none but your sheets are priuie to your wishes.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Nay come, tell Iras hers.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Wee'l know all our Fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Enob.
prose: Mine, and most of our Fortunes to night, shall be drunke to bed.

speeches.speaker: Iras.
prose: There's a Palme presages Chastity, if nothing els.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: E'ne as the o're-flowing Nylus presageth Famine.

speeches.speaker: Iras.
prose: Go you wilde Bedfellow, you cannot Soothsay.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Nay, if an oyly Palme bee not a fruitfull Prognostication, I cannot scratch mine eare. Prythee tel her but a worky day Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: Your Fortunes are alike.

speeches.speaker: Iras.
prose: But how, but how, giue me particulars.

speeches.speaker: Sooth.
prose: I haue said.

speeches.speaker: Iras.
prose: Am I not an inch of Fortune better then she?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Well, if you were but an inch of fortune better then I: where would you choose it.

speeches.speaker: Iras.
prose: Not in my Husbands nose.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Our worser thoughts Heauens mend.

speeches.speaker: Alexas.
prose: Come, his Fortune, his Fortune. Oh let him mary a woman that cannot go, sweet Isis, I beseech thee, and let her dye too, and giue him a worse, and let worse follow worse, till the worst of all follow him laughing to his graue, fifty-fold a Cuckold. Good Isis heare me this Prayer, though thou denie me a matter of more waight: good Isis I beseech thee.

speeches.speaker: Iras.
prose: Amen, deere Goddesse, heare that prayer of the people. For, as it is a heart-breaking to see a handsome man loose-Wiu'd, so it is a deadly sorrow, to beholde a foule Knaue vncuckolded: Therefore deere Isis keep decorum, and Fortune him accordingly.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Lo now, if it lay in their hands to make mee a Cuckold, they would make themselues Whores, but they'ld doo't.

speeches.speaker: Enob.
prose: Hush, heere comes Anthony.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Not he, the Queene.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Saue you, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Enob.
prose: No Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Was he not heere?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: No Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: He was dispos'd to mirth, but on the sodaine
A Romane thought hath strooke him.
Enobarbus?

speeches.speaker: Enob.
prose: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Seeke him, and bring him hither: wher's Alexias?

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: Heere at your seruice.
My Lord approaches.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: We will not looke vpon him:
Go with vs.

speeches.speaker: Messen.
verse: Fuluia thy Wife,
First came into the Field.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Against my Brother Lucius?

speeches.speaker: Messen.
verse: I: but soone that Warre had end,
And the times state
Made friends of them, ioynting their force 'gainst Caesar,
Whose better issue in the warre from Italy,
Vpon the first encounter draue them.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Well, what worst.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
prose: The Nature of bad newes infects the Teller.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: When it concernes the Foole or Coward: On.
Things that are past, are done, with me. 'Tis thus,
Who tels me true, though in his Tale lye death,
I heare him as he flatter'd.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: Labienus (this is stiffe-newes)
Hath with his Parthian Force
Extended Asia: from Euphrates his conquering
Banner shooke, from Syria to Lydia,
And to Ionia, whil'st —

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Anthony thou would'st say.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
prose: Oh my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Speake to me home,
Mince not the generall tongue, name
Cleopatra as she is call'd in Rome:
Raile thou in Fuluia's phrase, and taunt my faults
With such full License, as both Truth and Malice
Haue power to vtter. Oh then we forth weeds,
When our quicke windes lye still, and our illes told vs
Is as our earing: fare thee well awhlle.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
prose: At your Noble pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: From Scicion how the newes? Speake there.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mes.
verse: The man from Scicion,
Is there such an one?

speeches.speaker: 2. Mes.
prose: He stayes vpon your will.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let him appeare:
These strong Egyptian Fetters I must breake,
Or loose my selfe in dotage.
What are you?

speeches.speaker: 3. Mes.
prose: Fuluia thy wife is dead.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Where dyed she.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: In Scicion, her length of sicknesse,
With what else more serious,
Importeth thee to know, this beares.

speeches.speaker: Antho.
verse: Forbeare me
There's a great Spirit gone, thus did I desire it:
What our contempts doth of ten hurle from vs,
We with it ours againe. The present pleasure,
By reuolution lowring, does become
The opposite of it selfe: she's good being gon,
The hand could plucke her backe, that shou'd her on.
I must from this enchanting Queene breake off,
Ten thousand harmes, more then the illes I know
My idlenesse doth hatch.
How now Enobarbus.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: What's your pleasure, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Anth.
prose: I must with haste from hence.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: Why then we kill all our Women. We see how mortall an vnkindnesse is to them, if they suffer our departure death's the word.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I must be gone.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose:
Vnder a compelling an occasion, let women die. It were pitty to cast them away for nothing, though betweene them and a great cause, they should be esteemed nothing. Cleopatra catching but the least noyse of this, ^ instantly: I haue seene her dye twenty times vppon fa^
^orer moment: I do think there is mettle in death, which ^mits some louing acte vpon her, she hath such a celerity in dying.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: She is cunning past mans thought.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: Alacke Sir no, her passions are made of nothing but the finest part of pure Loue. We cannot cal her winds and waters, sighes and teares: They are greater stormes and Tempests then Almanackes can report. This cannot be cunning in her; if it be, she makes a showre of Raine as well as Ioue.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Would I had neuer seene her.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: Oh sir, you had then left vnseene a wonderfull peece of worke, which not to haue beene blest withall, would haue discredited your Trauaile.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Fuluia is dead.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Fuluia is dead.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: Fuluia?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Dead.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: Why sir, giue the Gods a thankefull Sacrifice: when it pleaseth their Deities to take the wife of a man from him, it shewes to man the Tailors of the earth: comforting therein, that when olde Robes are worne out, there are members to make new. If there were no more Women but Fuluia, then had you indeede a cut, and the case to be lamented: This greefe is crown'd with Consolation, your old Smocke brings foorth a new Petticoate, and indeed the teares liue in an Onion, that should water this sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: The businesse she hath broached in the State,
Cannot endure my absence.

speeches.speaker: Eno.
prose: And the businesse you haue broach'd heere cannot be without you, especially that of Cleopatra's, which wholly depends on your abode.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No more light Answeres:
Let our Officers
Haue notice what we purpose. I shall breake
The cause of our Expedience to the Queene,
And get her loue to part. For not alone
The death of Fuluia, with more vrgent touches
Do strongly speake to vs: but the Letters too
Of many our contriuing Friends in Rome,
Petition vs at home. Sextus Pompeius
Haue giuen the dare to Caesar, and commands
The Empire of the Sea. Our slippery people,
Whose Loue is neuer link'd to the deseruer,
Till his deserts are past, begin to throw
Pompey the great, and all his Dignities
Vpon his Sonne, who high in Name and Power,
Higher then both in Blood and Life, stands vp
For the maine Souldier. Whose quality going on,
The sides o' th' world may danger. Much is breeding,
Which like the Coursers heire, hath yet but life,
And not a Serpents poyson. Say our pleasure,
To such whose places vnder vs, require
Our quicke remoue from hence.

speeches.speaker: Enob.
prose: I shall doo't.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I did not see him since.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: See where he is,
Whose with him, what he does:
I did not send you. If you finde him sad,
Say I am dauncing: if in Myrth, report
That I am sodaine sicke. Quicke, and returne.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Madam, me thinkes if you did loue him deerly,
You do not hold the method, to enforce
The like from him.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: What should I do, I do not?

speeches.speaker: Ch.
prose: In each thing giue him way, crosse him in nothing.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Thou teachest like a foole: the way to lose him.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Tempt him not so too farre. I wish forbeare,
In time we hate that which we often feare.
But heere comes Anthony.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: I am sicke, and sullen.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: I am sorry to giue breathing to my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Helpe me away deere Charmian, I shall fall,
It cannot be thus long, the sides of Nature
Will not sustaine it.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Now my deerest Queene.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
prose: Pray you stand farther from mee.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: I know by that same eye ther's some good news.
What sayes the married woman you may goe?
Would she had neuer giuen you leaue to come.
Let her not say 'tis I that keepe you heere,
I haue no power vpon you: Hers you are.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The Gods best know.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Oh neuer was there Queene
So mightily betrayed: yet at the first
I saw the Treasons planted.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Cleopatra.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Why should I thinke you can be mine, & true,
(Though you in swearing shake the Throaned Gods)
Who haue beene false to Fuluia?
Riotous madnesse,
To be entangled with those mouth-made vowes,
Which breake themselues in swearing.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Most sweet Queene.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Nay pray you seeke no colour for your going,
But bid farewell, and goe:
When you sued staying,
Then was the time for words: No going then,
Eternity was in our Lippes, and Eyes,
Blisse in our browes bent: none our parts so poore,
But was a race of Heauen. They are so still,
Or thou the greatest Souldier of the world,
Art turn'd the greatest Lyar.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: How now Lady?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: I would I had thy inches, thou should'st know
There were a heart in Egypt.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Heare me Queene:
The strong necessity of Time, commands
Our Seruicles a-while: but my full heart
Remaines in vse with you. Our Italy,
Shines o're with ciuill Swords; Sextus Pompeius
Makes his approaches to the Port of Rome,
Equality of two Domesticke powers,
Breed scrupulous faction: The hated growne to strength
Are newly growne to Loue: The condemn'd Pompey,
Rich in his Fathers Honor, creepes apace
Into the hearts of such, as haue not thriued
Vpon the present state, whose Numbers threaten,
And quietnesse growne sicke of rest, would purge
By any desperate change: My more particular,
And that which most with you should safe my going,
Is Fuluias death.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Though age from folly could not giue me freedom
It does from childishnesse. Can Fuluia dye?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: She's dead my Queene.
Looke heere, and at thy Soueraigne leysure read
The Garboyles she awak'd: at the last, best,
See when, and where shee died.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: O most false Loue!
Where be the Sacred Violles thou should'st fill
With sorrowfull water? Now I see, I see,
In Fuluias death, how mine receiu'd shall be.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Quarrell no more, but bee prepar'd to know
The purposes I beare: which are, or cease,
As you shall giue th' aduice. By the fire
That quickens Nylus slime, I go from hence
Thy Souldier, Seruant, making Peace or Warre,
As thou affects.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Cut my Lace, Charmian come,
But let it be, I am quickly ill, and well,
